--- Makefile ---
PROJECT_HOME := .
VULTRON_DIR := $(PROJECT_HOME)/vultron
TEST_DIR := $(PROJECT_HOME)/test

# Load environment variables from .env file if it exists
ifneq (,$(wildcard .env))
  include .env
  export
endif

PROJECT_NAME ?= vultron

# Display help information about available targets
.PHONY: help
help:  ## Show this help message
	@grep -E '^[a-zA-Z_-]+:.*?## .*$$' $(filter-out .env,$(MAKEFILE_LIST)) | sort | awk 'BEGIN {FS = ":.*?## "}; {printf "  %-20s %s\n", $$1, $$2}'

# set up dev environment
.PHONY: setup_dev
setup_dev:  ## Set up development environment
	uv sync --dev

# upgrade dev dependencies
.PHONY: upgrade_dev
upgrade_dev:  ## Upgrade dev dependencies
	uv sync --upgrade --dev

# upgrade dependencies
.PHONY: upgrade_deps
upgrade_deps:  ## Upgrade all dependencies
	uv sync --upgrade

# run tests locally
.PHONY: test
test:  ## Run tests locally
	uv run pytest test

# black code formatting
.PHONY: black
black:  ## Format code with black
	uv run black .

# markdownlint-cli2 code formatting
.PHONY: mdlint
mdlint:  ## Lint markdown files
	./mdlint.sh

# flake8
.PHONY: flake8
flake8:  ## Check code with flake8
	# edit $(PROJECT_HOME)/.flake8 to configure flake8 options
	uv run flake8 ${VULTRON_DIR} ${TEST_DIR}

# flake8 code linting
.PHONY: flake8-lint
flake8-lint:  ## Lint code with flake8
	# edit $(PROJECT_HOME)/.flake8 to configure flake8 options
	uv run flake8 --exit-zero ${VULTRON_DIR} ${TEST_DIR}

# mypy type checking
.PHONY: mypy
mypy:  ## Run mypy for type checking
	# edit $(PROJECT_HOME)/.mypy.ini to configure mypy options
	uv run mypy

# pyright static type checking
.PHONY: pyright
pyright:  ## Run pyright for static type checking
	uv run pyright

# run all linters
.PHONY: lint
lint: black mdlint flake8-lint mypy ## Run all linters (black, markdownlint)

# serve docs locally
.PHONY: docs
docs:  ## Serve documentation locally
	uv run mkdocs serve

# build docker images

project.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#what-is-an-adr","title":"What is an ADR?","text":"<p>An architectural decision record (ADR) is a document that captures an important architectural decision made along with its context and consequences. We're using the expanded concept of an Any Decision Record (ADR) to capture any decision that is important to the project, not just architectural decisions. We use Markdown Any Decision Records (MADR) to document our architectural decisions.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#when-to-write-an-adr","title":"When to write an ADR","text":"<p>The primary signal for an ADR is evaluated alternatives: if you considered more than one option and rejected at least one, document the decision. The record preserves context for future maintainers who might otherwise re-open a settled question.</p> <p>Concretely, write an ADR when:</p> <ul> <li>You adopted a structural or architectural approach over one or more   alternatives (e.g., hexagonal architecture over layered, SQLModel over   TinyDB).</li> <li>You made a one-time process or tooling decision with lasting project-wide   impact (e.g., CalVer over SemVer, pinning CI action SHAs).</li> <li>A decision will be hard or costly to reverse, so the rationale should be   preserved explicitly.</li> </ul> <p>ADR vs. spec: an ADR records why a choice was made; a spec entry records what the system must do going forward. When a significant decision also generates recurring testable requirements, create both \u2014 see <code>notes/specs-vs-adrs.md</code> for the full delineation guidelines and worked examples.</p> <p>You do not need an ADR for:</p> <ul> <li>Uncontested conventions with no real alternatives (write a spec entry   instead).</li> <li>Small tactical choices where the rationale is obvious from the code.</li> </ul> <p>If you're unsure, err on the side of writing one \u2014 a brief ADR is better than losing context.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#revising-vs-amending-an-adr","title":"Revising vs. amending an ADR","text":"<p>An ADR records the decision that was made and why. Its value to a future reader is that they can understand the current expectation in one pass.</p> <p>When to revise in-place: If a recently-accepted ADR contains a statement that its own implementation contradicted \u2014 e.g., an option label that says \"rejected\" for something the chosen option actually requires, or a \"what is removed\" list that conflicts with MUST-level spec entries \u2014 revise the ADR body directly to make the current expectation accurate.</p> <p>When to write a new ADR: If the decision itself changed (you adopted a different option than originally chosen), write a new ADR that supersedes the old one.</p> <p>Do not append <code>### Amendment</code> sections: An append-only trail of amendments forces future readers to reconcile the body against its own addenda to determine which statement is currently authoritative. This defeats the primary purpose of the record. The only exception is an ADR with <code>status: provisional</code> where the amendment explicitly finalises that status.</p> <p>Source: ISSUE-1777 / learning 2026-07-31</p>"},{"location":"adr/#how-to-write-an-adr","title":"How to write an ADR","text":"<p>For new ADRs, please use adr-template.md as basis. ActivityStreams 2.0 (AS2) structural types leaked into domain logic; semantic extraction was scattered across multiple files; handler functions instantiated the persistence layer directly; and the root <code>vultron/</code> package mixed domain enums with wire-format enums. An architectural review (<code>archived_notes/architecture-review.md</code>) catalogued twelve violations of the intended separation of concerns, ranging in severity from minor to critical. A clear architecture decision was needed to guide remediation and prevent the same violations from re-accumulating.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0009-hexagonal-architecture/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Wire format replaceability: AS2 is the current wire format because its   vocabulary matches Vultron's domain vocabulary. That match must not collapse   the boundary between wire concerns and domain concerns.  If AS2 is replaced   or extended, the change must be absorbable in the wire layer alone.</li> <li>Testability: Core domain logic should be testable with plain domain   objects, without constructing AS2 activities or making HTTP requests.</li> <li>Single extraction seam: The mapping from AS2 vocabulary to domain   semantics must live in exactly one place so that future wire format changes   have a single point of entry.</li> <li>Dependency injection over direct instantiation: Driven adapters   (persistence, delivery) must be injectable to support testing and alternate   backends.</li> <li>Alignment with existing clean points: Several existing patterns are   already architecturally sound (the <code>DataLayer</code> Protocol, <code>DispatchEvent</code>   wrapper, <code>MessageSemantics</code> enum vocabulary, FastAPI 202 + BackgroundTasks)   and should be preserved.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0009-hexagonal-architecture/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Continue organic layering \u2014 Impose light conventions without a formal   architecture pattern. requires every object to have an <code>id</code> field. The <code>generate_new_id()</code> utility in <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/base/utils.py</code> currently returns a bare UUID-4 string (e.g., <code>2196cbb2-fb6f-407c-b473-1ed8ae806578</code>) as the default <code>as_id</code> for new objects. The AS2 specification and the Vultron object-IDs spec (<code>specs/object-ids.yaml</code> OID-01-001) require that <code>id</code> values be full URI identifiers. Bare UUIDs are not valid AS2 identifiers and will cause interoperability problems once federation is implemented.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0010-standardize-object-ids/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>AS2 compliance: ActivityStreams 2.0 requires <code>id</code> to be an absolute   IRI. Bare UUIDs cannot be resolved across systems.</li> <li>Blackboard key safety: py_trees blackboard keys derived from full-URI   IDs must not use the raw URI (which contains slashes). Using the last path   segment or UUID suffix as the key avoids hierarchical key-parsing issues   (OID-03-001).</li> <li>DataLayer compatibility: The DataLayer uses <code>as_id</code> as the primary   lookup key. ADR originally chose Option B \u2014 namespace prefix per actor in one file. That choice did not deliver CM-01-001: a namespace prefix (and its SQLite successor, an <code>actor_id</code> filter column over a globally unique primary key) partitions reads only, so one actor's writes could still affect what another actor read (issue #2238). ADR-0073 adopts Option A \u2014 one store per actor instead, making isolation a property of the storage layout rather than of each individual query. The rejection of Option A below \u2014 that it \"creates many files and complicates the DataLayer reset endpoint\" \u2014 was a prototype-convenience argument that does not outweigh the isolation requirement.</p> <p>The remaining three decisions in this ADR (DI-1, IO-A, OX-B) are unaffected and still stand. That is why <code>status:</code> stays <code>accepted</code> and the frontmatter carries <code>partially_superseded_by:</code> instead: marking the whole ADR superseded would retire three live decisions along with the one that was replaced.</p> <p>Option A creates many files and complicates the DataLayer reset endpoint used by demo scripts. Option C has no persistence and cannot be used for Docker demos. A pure MongoDB-first approach (Option D alone) is the right production target, but implementing it as the sole P100 step adds Docker infrastructure risk on the critical path.</p> <p><code>get_datalayer</code> DI strategy: DI-1 \u2014 closure lambda.</p> <p><code>Depends(lambda actor_id=Path(...): get_datalayer(actor_id))</code> is the simplest pattern, requires no new classes, and is consistent with FastAPI conventions. It supports future dynamic actor instantiation without architectural change. DI-2 adds unnecessary ceremony; DI-3 is too invasive across 20+ route files.</p> <p><code>actor_io.py</code> inbox/outbox ownership: IO-A \u2014 migrate into per-actor DataLayer.</p> <p>Inbox and outbox activities are persistent state. Storing them as TinyDB collections (<code>{actor_id}_inbox</code>, <code>{actor_id}_outbox</code>) alongside other per-actor records is architecturally consistent and avoids a parallel, in-memory-only state management path. DataLayer.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0012-per-actor-datalayer-isolation/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because per-actor TinyDB tables enforce data isolation with minimal PR #577 added an <code>_STUB_OBJECT_MODEL_MAP</code> workaround in <code>outbox_handler.py</code> that covers only <code>VulnerabilityCase</code> and requires per-type manual registration.</p> <p>Wire-format concerns also leak into the domain: AS2 freely models a nested object as an inline object, a bare ID string, or a <code>Link</code> reference, which forces core fields into <code>Object | str | Link | None</code> unions. problem it addresses. The historical name \"case ledger\" was ambiguous: it sat too close to Python <code>logging</code> and invited use as a generic event sink. Going forward, the project uses ledger vocabulary for the canonical, append-only, hash-chained, replicated record of protocol-significant case events:</p> Canonical term Meaning Case Ledger The canonical, append-only, replicated shared history. <code>CaseLedgerEntry</code> The wire-serialisable canonical ledger entry model. <code>CaseLedger</code> The in-memory append-only ledger aggregate for one case. <code>HashChainLedgerRecord</code> The in-memory hash-chain record used by <code>CaseLedger</code>. <code>case_ledger_entry</code> module Core and wire module name for ledger entry types. <code>case_ledger</code> module Core module name for the in-memory ledger model. <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> The sync wire envelope used for canonical replication. case audit ledger Preferred phrase for the replicated audit surface. <code>commit_ledger_entry()</code> Canonical append API on the CaseActor side. <p><code>record_event()</code> is not renamed \u2014 it is the legacy <code>CaseEvent</code> path, which is scheduled for removal in #792. The new canonical append API on the CaseActor side is named <code>commit_ledger_entry()</code> to align with the commit-discipline vocabulary in <code>notes/sync-ledger-replication.md</code> and to make it self-evident that the method appends to the authoritative ledger, not to a generic log sink.</p> <p>The \"process log\" remains the standard term for per-actor Python <code>logging</code> output, governed by <code>specs/structured-logging.yaml</code>. It is ephemeral, per-actor, never replicated, and never part of any hash chain.</p> <p>Rationale. \"Ledger\" carries the exact semantic properties the canonical record must have: append-only, authoritative, immutable, audit-grade, and amenable to hash-chained / Merkle-tree representation. It maps cleanly onto distributed-systems precedent (blockchain ledgers, event-sourcing ledgers, Raft log entries reframed as ledger appends) and removes the naming collision with Python <code>logging</code>.</p> <p>Migration. <code>CommitCaseLedgerEntryNode</code>. The guarded commit BT emits <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> activities as if authored by the CaseActor while running in the wrong actor's outbox context, which is either silently dropped or produces hash-chain divergence.</p> <p>The project has stated this rule in scattered form across <code>AGENTS.md</code>, <code>notes/case-communication-model.md</code>, and <code>specs/case-ledger-processing.yaml</code>, but the explicit, ADR-level statement of the only correct end-to-end path has been missing. As a result, agents and contributors keep re-discovering the shortcut (resolve CaseActor ID, run BT) and believing it is a valid \"delegation\" pattern.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0021-caseactor-inbox-routing-canonical-ledger/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li><code>notes/case-communication-model.md</code> establishes that all post-creation   participant messages route through the Case Actor exclusively.</li> <li>ADR-0018 established a single-writer canonical ledger authored by the   CaseActor. The CaseActor is a participant with extra duties; it is not exempt from CLP-10-001.</p> <p>When the CaseActor originates an activity (e.g., <code>invite_actor_to_case</code>), the activity is addressed to the external recipient(s) via <code>to:</code>. To ensure the CaseActor's own inbox receives the activity for archival, the CaseActor MUST add its own actor ID to the <code>cc:</code> field of the outbound activity. ASGI self-delivery then routes the <code>cc:</code> copy to the CaseActor's received-side use case, where the <code>GuardedCommitCaseLedgerEntryBT</code> fires under the correct <code>actor_id = case_actor_id</code> identity.</p> <p>Why <code>cc:</code> instead of adding <code>case_actor_id</code> to <code>to:</code>: The primary recipient of an <code>Invite(VulnerabilityCase)</code> is the invitee. The CaseActor's copy is an archival side-channel, not a primary delivery. Using <code>to:</code> for both would misrepresent the CaseActor as a co-primary recipient of its own outbound message. <code>cc:</code> preserves the correct semantic: the invitee is in <code>to:</code>, the self-archival copy is in <code>cc:</code>. Delivery for Received-Side CaseActor Routing","text":""},{"location":"adr/0022-single-bt-execution-for-received-side-case-actor-routing/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p>ADR-0021 established that the CaseActor's own inbox delivery is the sole path to a canonical ledger commit, and introduced a pre-flight guard (CLP-10-002, CLP-10-003): a received-side use case compares <code>receiving_actor_id</code> to the resolved <code>case_actor_id</code> in Python before deciding whether to execute the guarded-commit BT (<code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>).</p> <p>Issue #1036 found that implementing that guard produced a second anti-pattern: every adopting use case now runs two separate <code>BTBridge.execute_with_setup()</code> calls per inbox delivery \u2014 one for the use case's main operation (often under the message's own actor identity, e.g. the invitee or accepting actor), and a second, conditionally dispatched call for the guarded commit (under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>). The condition that decides whether the second call happens at all is plain Python control flow (<code>if receiving_actor_id != case_actor_id: return</code>), not a node inside either tree.</p> <p>An audit (issue #1036, broadened during planning to also resolve a follow-on Concern, issue #1047, which independently named the same anti-pattern in <code>status.py</code> and asked for it to be codified as a spec-level invariant) found the underlying violation in 9 use cases across 6 modules, but not all in the same precise shape. There are three distinct ways the \"execute() does nothing but build one tree, run it once, handle the result\" intent was violated:</p> <p>(1) Genuine actor-identity switching \u2014 a real second <code>execute_with_setup()</code> call under a different actor than the main operation's. This is the literal anti-pattern #1036 and #1047 describe:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/embargo.py</code>:   <code>RemoveEmbargoEventFromCaseReceivedUseCase</code>,   <code>InviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase</code>,   <code>AcceptInviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 main tree runs under   <code>request.actor_id</code> / <code>invitee_id</code> / <code>accepting_actor_id</code>; a second,   separately constructed <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>   runs under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>. Notably, the main tree (built by   <code>vultron/core/behaviors/embargo/announce_teardown_tree.py</code>'s factory   functions) already composes the identical guarded-commit branch as its   own last child \u2014 but because the main tree executes under the   invitee's/accepting actor's identity, <code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code> inside it   is a guaranteed no-op (that actor is essentially never the CaseActor).   The second, separately-dispatched call is the one that actually fires,   on the rare second attempt under the correct identity. The fix is not   \"add a guarded-commit branch\" (it already exists) \u2014 it is \"stop calling   the tree under the wrong actor a second time, and run the one tree that   already has the branch under <code>receiving_actor_id</code> instead.\"</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/report.py</code>:   <code>ValidateReportReceivedUseCase</code> (main operation is a separate   <code>ValidateCaseUseCase</code> call under <code>actor_id</code>, not even a tree of its own),   <code>AckReportReceivedUseCase</code> (main tree under <code>request.actor_id</code>) \u2014 both   followed by a second, separately-gated guarded-commit call under   <code>receiving_actor_id</code>/<code>case_actor_id</code>.</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/status.py</code>:   <code>AddParticipantStatusToParticipantReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 main tree   (<code>add_participant_status_tree</code>) under <code>request.actor_id</code>, then a second   guarded-commit call under <code>case_actor_id</code> via <code>_commit_log_cascade_bt()</code>.   This is the exact site #1047 cited as its primary evidence.</li> </ul> <p>(2) Single BT call, but non-BT procedural code precedes it \u2014 only one <code>execute_with_setup()</code> call exists (the commit), but <code>execute()</code> still does domain-significant work outside any tree before reaching it, so it is not \"build one tree, run it, handle the result\" either:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/note.py</code>: <code>AddNoteToCaseReceivedUseCase</code>   \u2014 appends to <code>case.notes</code>, calls <code>dl.save()</code>, and broadcasts to peers, all   in plain Python, before the single guarded-commit <code>execute_with_setup()</code>   call.</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/actor/case_manager_role.py</code>:   <code>OfferCaseManagerRoleReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 idempotent-creates the activity   and calls a trigger-activity port directly in Python, before the single   guarded-commit call. This is a pre-existing BT-06-001 gap (the main   operation was never expressed as a BT at all), not actor-switching.</li> </ul> <p>(3) Single BT call under the correct actor, but assembled ad hoc \u2014 no actor-switching and no procedural code outside the tree, but the tree itself is built inline in <code>execute()</code> rather than via a <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> factory function:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/case/lifecycle.py</code>:   <code>CloseCaseReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 constructs a one-off   <code>py_trees.composites.Sequence</code> directly inside <code>execute()</code>, combining   <code>StoreActivityNode</code> and the guarded-commit subtree, and runs it once   under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>. This is the same class of problem the \"Post-BT Procedural Cascade Anti-Pattern\" (<code>notes/bt-integration.md</code>) already names for the validate\u2192prioritize cascade: a cascade that is a child of the triggering operation in the canonical model must be expressed as a BT subtree, not as a procedural call (or a second, conditionally-dispatched tree execution, or any other domain-significant code) sitting outside the tree in <code>execute()</code>. The fact that the in-tree guard (<code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code>) is itself correctly role-gated does not fix category (1): the decision of whether to even ask the question is still made in Python, once per inbox delivery, instead of being one branch of one BT run.</p> <p>A related architectural question raised during planning \u2014 whether the inbox dispatch pipeline itself needs to be restructured so a use case never has to ask \"which actor am I running as\" \u2014 turned out not to apply. Investigation found <code>receiving_actor_id</code> is already resolved before dispatch (<code>FastAPIDispatchAdapter.dispatch()</code>, which sets it from the canonical actor ID resolved off the inbox URL path) and is already present on every received-side event by the time <code>execute()</code> runs. The dispatcher (<code>vultron/core/dispatcher.py</code>) has no CaseActor awareness and needs none \u2014 it is a pure routing-table lookup keyed on <code>semantic_type</code>. The gap is entirely at the use-case/BT boundary, not the dispatch layer; no change to ADR-0020's proposed <code>process_payload</code> seam is required by this decision.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0022-single-bt-execution-for-received-side-case-actor-routing/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The BT is the domain documentation (<code>specs/behavior-tree-integration.yaml</code> BT-06-001); a cascade that is invisible outside the tree structure is   invisible to analysis and audit, regardless of whether the gating logic   is \"correct\" in isolation.</li> <li>CLP-09-001 already requires the commit to be reached only through a   role-gated composition \u2014 a Selector/Sequence/Success idiom evaluated   inside the tree. The term implied a specific kind of implementor (an autonomous AI entity) when the shapes are actually abstract interface contracts. A capability implementation may be anything that honours the blackboard contract. The implementation choice is made at deployment time, not at design time.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0024-coordination-agent-taxonomy/#amendment-2026-07-07-fifth-canonical-shape-actuator","title":"Amendment (2026-07-07): Fifth canonical shape \u2014 Actuator","text":"<p>During the FUZZ-08a-ter audit (PR #1195, issue #1239), 11 nodes classified as <code>Composer</code> were found not to generate content artifacts in the ADR-0024 sense. A Sentinel monitors a condition over time and fires a trigger endpoint when that condition is met.</p> <p>A capability that queries an external system synchronously and returns only a binary (yes/no) result is still a Retriever capability: a boolean is the simplest possible structured fact. The defining characteristic is the synchronous on-demand query pattern, not the richness of the returned data.</p> <p>Nodes such as <code>MitigationDeployed</code>, <code>MitigationAvailable</code>, and <code>HaveExploit</code> fit the Retriever shape: they receive a query (implicitly, \"is X the case?\"), call an external system to retrieve the current status, and return SUCCESS/FAILURE based on that status. They do not monitor continuously or fire a trigger \u2014 they answer a point-in-time question when the BT reaches them.</p> <p>A Sentinel, by contrast, runs continuously (or is invoked by an external event) and calls a trigger endpoint when a condition becomes true. The flow direction is reversed: Sentinel \u2192 trigger endpoint \u2192 protocol, not protocol \u2192 query \u2192 external system.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0024-coordination-agent-taxonomy/#retriever-over-data-retriever","title":"\"Retriever\" over \"Data Retriever\"","text":"<p>The qualifier \"Data\" was dropped to achieve parallel naming with the other single-word shape nouns (Sentinel, Evaluator, Composer). The definition in <code>CONTEXT.md</code> makes clear that a Retriever returns structured external facts, not generated content \u2014 the qualifier is redundant.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0025-call-out-point-abstraction-layer/","title":"Call-Out Point Abstraction Layer: Factory-Based Injection with Typed Backends","text":""},{"location":"adr/0025-call-out-point-abstraction-layer/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p>Vultron's Behavior Trees contain call-out points \u2014 nodes where the protocol cannot proceed autonomously and must request input from an external party (see ADR-0024 for the taxonomy of capability shapes). After FUZZ-01 through FUZZ-07 (#860\u2013#866), each call-out point has a probabilistic fuzzer node as its stand-in. The fuzzer is not a permanent implementation: it is an adapter that will be replaced over time by real data lookups, policy evaluations, or capability implementations.</p> <p>Before those replacements can happen, the call-out points must be expressed as proper injection seams: the BT tree must be built so that the fuzzer is the default backend, not the only option. Without an abstraction layer, swapping any call-out point requires finding and editing the concrete node class instead of injecting a different factory \u2014 and with roughly 93 call-out point nodes across all domains, the maintenance burden is unacceptable.</p> <p>The design question is: What mechanism makes each call-out point backend swappable while remaining consistent with the existing py_trees Behaviour pattern, factory-function conventions, and blackboard contract model?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0025-call-out-point-abstraction-layer/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Must be consistent with the existing BT factory-function pattern   (tree composition functions, not ad-hoc node instantiation)</li> <li>Must allow individual call-out points to be swapped without changing the   calling tree structure (incremental replacement)</li> <li>Must maintain the same blackboard contract whether the backend is a fuzzer   or a real implementation \u2014 downstream nodes must be unaffected by the swap</li> <li>Must keep simulation artifacts (<code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/</code>) out of   <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> (BT-16-001)</li> <li>Must be compatible with the five capability shapes from ADR-0024 (Sentinel,   Evaluator, Retriever, Composer, Actuator), each of which has different   input/output semantics</li> <li>Must support partial replacement: a scenario can use real implementations   for some call-out points and fuzzer backends for others in the same run</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0025-call-out-point-abstraction-layer/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>No abstraction \u2014 leave fuzzer nodes as concrete hardcoded classes; This rule is not specific to participant roles. ASK-01-004 states it for every ask: the ask is authoritative and the reply is only a yes. Whatever action a reply authorizes MUST be read from the stored ask, never from the reply's content \u2014 otherwise the answerer can alter what it grants itself, in any exchange, not just this one. ADR-0080 also adds the time dimension: an ask carries a deadline, and for ask kinds whose expiry is void, a reply arriving after it does not authorize the action (ASK-03-006). Trusting when a reply arrives is the same class of mistake as trusting what it claims.</p> <p>The routing tree and stored-ask record described below are the reference implementations the ADR-0080 primitive generalizes; see <code>notes/protocol-asks.md</code>.</p> <p>When the CaseActor processes <code>Accept(Offer(CaseParticipant))</code> from the Case Owner, the roles assigned to the new participant MUST be taken from the stored outgoing <code>Offer(CaseParticipant)</code> that the CaseActor sent, not from the embedded <code>CaseParticipant</code> object inside the received <code>Accept</code>.</p> <p>Why this is a security boundary, not just an implementation detail:</p> <ul> <li>The accepting actor (Case Owner) may modify the embedded <code>CaseParticipant</code>   in the <code>Accept</code> payload, or may send only a bare ID reference.</li> <li>Reading roles from the received <code>Accept</code> allows the accepting actor to   unilaterally escalate or modify the roles the invitee would receive.</li> <li>The stored <code>Offer</code> is the CaseActor's own record of what was proposed;   it is the authoritative source of truth for the intended participant roles.</li> </ul> <p>Failure pattern that violates this rule:</p> <ul> <li>Reading the <code>CaseParticipant</code> role list from <code>event.object_.roles</code>   (the object embedded in the received <code>Accept</code>) instead of from the   stored <code>Offer</code> activity.</li> <li>Reading roles from the BT blackboard across ticks: the blackboard is   cleared between BT executions, so a role written in the offer-received   tick is gone by the accept-received tick.</li> </ul> <p>Implementation: the CaseActor stores the outgoing <code>Offer(CaseParticipant)</code> in its DataLayer at offer-emit time. At accept-received time, it reads the stored offer to recover the intended roles, then creates the participant record. See <code>vultron/core/behaviors/case/nodes/suggest_actor/</code> for the canonical implementation pattern (PR #1745).</p> <p>Source: ISSUE-1745, <code>plan/incoming/learnings/20260728-offer-trust-boundary-implicit.md</code>.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0026-caseactor-routed-actor-suggestion/#more-information","title":"More Information","text":"<ul> <li>ADR-0021: CaseActor Inbox Routing as the Sole Path to Canonical Ledger Entries</li> <li>ADR-0022: Single BT Execution Per Inbox Delivery for Received-Side CaseActor Routing</li> <li><code>notes/case-communication-model.md</code> \u2014 canonical PCR-08 routing rules</li> <li><code>notes/case-bootstrap-trust.md</code> \u2014 late-joiner trust establishment</li> <li><code>specs/participant-case-replica.yaml</code> PCR-08 \u2014 invite/accept/bootstrap chain</li> <li>Issue #1292 \u2014 invite/embargo consent completeness epic</li> <li>Issue #1295 \u2014 tracking issue for this ADR + spec additions PR</li> </ul> <p>Generated spec requirements: <code>case-management.yaml</code> CM-16, CM-17.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0027-exploit-strategy-bt-collapse/","title":"Exploit-Strategy Subtree Collapse: Five Simulator Nodes \u2192 EvaluateExploitStrategy","text":"<p>Implemented by issue #1309 (<code>task/1309-evaluate-exploit-strategy</code>).</p>"},{"location":"adr/0027-exploit-strategy-bt-collapse/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p>The simulator BT for exploit acquisition (<code>AcquireExploit</code>) encodes a single policy-driven question \u2014 \"should we acquire an exploit for this vulnerability?\" \u2014 as a sequence of five granular nodes: <code>HaveExploit</code> (Retriever), <code>ExploitPrioritySet</code> (ProtocolInternal flag check), <code>EvaluateExploitPriority</code> (Evaluator), <code>ExploitDeferred</code> (ProtocolInternal), <code>ExploitDesired</code> (ProtocolInternal). Types","text":""},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p>Core domain helpers throughout <code>vultron/core/</code> are peppered with <code>if x is None: return None</code> chains. These silent failures propagate far from their source \u2014 the error surfaces at the point of use rather than the point of origin, making debugging difficult and creating a class of bug where program state is quietly corrupted or silently skipped.</p> <p>The root cause is structural: loose wire-layer types (where <code>Optional</code> fields are correct \u2014 AS2 permits many fields to be absent) leak directly into core logic without being promoted to tighter representations. Core functions then defensively guard every field they actually require.</p> <p>A secondary symptom is collection-typed fields and parameters that default to <code>None</code> instead of an empty collection, forcing every call-site to write <code>x or []</code> / <code>x or {}</code> boilerplate before iteration.</p> <p>The DataLayer already established the right precedent: <code>dl.read()</code> raises <code>VultronNotFoundError</code> rather than returning <code>None</code>. This ADR generalises that precedent to all core domain helpers and domain model fields.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Silent <code>None</code> propagation causes failures far from the error source.</li> <li>Core functions should express their contracts in their type signatures.</li> <li>The type system should make illegal states unrepresentable within core logic.</li> <li>Idiomatic Python prefers <code>raise</code> over sentinel return values (EAFP culture).</li> <li><code>dl.read()</code> raising <code>VultronNotFoundError</code> is an existing, working precedent   to generalise from.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>Return <code>None</code> and guard at every call-site \u2014 current pattern.</li> <li><code>Result</code>/<code>Option</code> monadic types (e.g. the <code>returns</code> library).</li> <li>One rich domain class with Optional fields and <code>None</code> guards in core.</li> <li>Validate at the edge, promote to strict core types (chosen).</li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: Validate at the edge, promote to strict core types, because it is idiomatic Python, fail-fast, provides a stack trace pointing to the origin of the error, and allows the type checker to verify guarantees.</p> <p>The pattern in three steps:</p> <ol> <li>Edge objects may be loose. Wire-layer and adapter Pydantic models may    have <code>Optional</code> fields where the protocol or external source permits absence.</li> <li>Promote at the boundary. At the boundary (extractor, rehydration layer,    use-case entry point), required fields are validated. If absent, a    descriptive exception is raised immediately \u2014 not propagated as <code>None</code>.</li> <li>Core receives strict types. What crosses into core logic is a type that    makes the required fields non-optional. Core functions declare these tighter    types in their signatures; the type system enforces the contract.</li> </ol> <p>The Vultron analogy for the blog post's drone pattern: <code>VultronActivity</code> (wire, loose) \u2192 validated at extractor/rehydration \u2192 <code>FooReceivedEvent</code> or use-case request type (core, tight). Use <code>field(default_factory=list)</code> etc. in Pydantic models and dataclasses. <code>None</code> is reserved for fields where absence is semantically distinct from empty (e.g. AS2 fields where <code>None</code> omits the key from the wire payload).</p>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#corollary-bt-node-helpers-raise-update-catches","title":"Corollary \u2014 BT node helpers raise; <code>update()</code> catches","text":"<p>BT node helper methods must either complete successfully or raise a domain exception (e.g. <code>BtNodePreconditionError</code>). They must not return <code>None</code> as a failure signal. The <code>update()</code> method is the single <code>try/except</code> handler that converts the exception to <code>Status.FAILURE</code> and sets <code>self.feedback_message</code>.</p> <pre><code># BtNodePreconditionError(f\"case {case_id!r} not in blackboard\")\n    if not is_case_model(obj):\n        raise BtNodePreconditionError(\n            f\"blackboard entry {case_id!r} is not a VulnerabilityCase\"\n        )\n    return obj\n\ndef update(self, ...) -&gt; Status:\n    try:\n        case_obj = self._read_case_obj(case_id)\n        ...\n    except BtNodePreconditionError as e:\n        self.feedback_message = str(e)\n        return Status.FAILURE\n</code></pre> <p>This eliminates the class of bug where a helper returns <code>None</code> silently with no Changes","text":""},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p><code>VulnerabilityCase</code> is the canonical \"fat class\" named in ADR-0032: one type represents a case at every lifecycle stage. Core functions that require a case to have reached a particular stage (e.g. \"there is an active embargo\") cannot express that requirement in their type signatures, so they fall back on runtime guards (<code>if case.active_embargo is None: ...</code>, <code>if case.current_status.em_state == EM.ACTIVE: ...</code>).</p> <p>The Idea (#1362) proposed distinct types per lifecycle stage \u2014 illustratively <code>IncomingReport</code>, <code>TriagedCase</code>, <code>ActiveCase</code> \u2014 so a core function accepting a stage-specific type would reject earlier-stage data at the type level, with no <code>if x is None</code> needed. The Idea explicitly deferred deriving the actual stages from the protocol until a design was reviewed.</p> <p>Two protocol facts, verified against the code, shape the answer and make the naive \"one type per RM state\" framing unworkable:</p> <ol> <li>RM state is per-participant, not case-universal. Each <code>CaseParticipant</code>    runs its own RM state machine (<code>ParticipantStatus.rm_state</code>). There is no    such thing as \"the case is in RM.VALID\" \u2014 valid according to whom? A case    type named <code>ValidCase</code>/<code>TriagedCase</code> would be ill-defined.</li> <li>Only a few facts are genuinely case-universal. Case existence,    structural minimums (\u22651 report, reporter + receiver participants), the    embargo state (<code>EM</code>, one per case), and public state (<code>pxa</code>) are the only    monotonic facts that hold case-wide.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Make illegal shapes unrepresentable in core logic (ADR-0032 continuation).</li> <li>Do not introduce a type whose fields are identical to its parent's \u2014 that is   ceremony without a type-checker payoff and invites combinatorial proliferation   (2\u00b3 for the independent P/X/A dimensions alone).</li> <li>The design must survive DataLayer round-trip: rehydration always yields a   valid object, so the design must specify how a rehydrated record acquires its   staged type.</li> <li>Reuse the existing precedents: the role-specific <code>CaseParticipant</code> subclasses,   the <code>RM_ACTIVE</code> / <code>EM_NEGOTIATING</code> state-group tuples, and the   <code>is_rm_at_least()</code> predicate family.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>One type per RM/EM/CS state \u2014 rejected: RM is per-participant, so most    such types are ill-defined at the case level.</li> <li>Staged types on every state-bearing class, keyed on any monotonic    milestone \u2014 rejected: proliferates types that add no fields.</li> <li>Field-set-anchored staged types (chosen): a milestone earns a type only    when it changes the guaranteed (non-None) field set; As a result, <code>dl.read()</code> and <code>dl.list_objects()</code> return wire-layer types (e.g. <code>as_VulnerabilityCase</code> from <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/objects/</code>) rather than core domain types (e.g. <code>VulnerabilityCase</code> from <code>vultron/core/models/</code>).</p> <p>Core BT nodes and use cases call <code>dl.read()</code> and operate on the result. To avoid a compile-time <code>core \u2192 wire</code> import (forbidden by ARCH-01-001), core depends on structural duck-typing Protocols and <code>TypeGuard</code> helpers in <code>vultron/core/models/protocols.py</code> (<code>CaseModel</code>, <code>is_case_model()</code>, etc.). These let core call methods on wire objects at runtime without importing the wire classes. The boundary \"works\" only because wire and core types share field names and the same <code>type_</code> string value.</p> <p>This produces three problems:</p> <ol> <li>Core validators never run on stored data. A wire object satisfies core    call sites by structural coincidence; core's domain invariants are never    enforced on DataLayer-sourced data.</li> <li>The Protocols evade rather than honour ARCH-01-001. They hide a runtime    <code>core \u2192 wire</code> dependency from static analysis; mypy/pyright pass while core    operates on wire objects.</li> <li>The seam is fragile. After ADR-0017 / issue #1387 renamed wire classes    to the <code>as_</code> prefix (<code>as_VulnerabilityCase</code>), the classes are now genuinely    distinct \u2014 but the runtime boundary violation remains, held together only by    the shared <code>type_</code> string and field names.</li> </ol> <p>It was also unclear where wire\u2194core translation belongs. Each Actor is an isolated process: it owns a DataLayer of core domain objects, and (per the Actor Knowledge Model) its knowledge of the world is bounded strictly by what it has received. No actor can reach into another actor's DataLayer. Wire (AS2) exists solely as the transport by which one actor's core state informs another's \u2014 an AS2 Activity is an envelope carrying a core domain fact across the process boundary, not a domain object in its own right.</p> <p>ADR-0017 established that wire is a projection of core, and ARCH-09-001 requires core models to be as rich as or richer than their wire counterparts. The 29 AS2 protocol Activities (<code>Offer</code>, <code>Invite</code>, <code>Accept</code>, <code>Reject</code>, \u2026) break this: they were built wire-first and were never given a core counterpart. For these types the projection is inverted \u2014 wire is the only representation, and is therefore richer than core.</p> <p>The concrete consequence: when an actor must remember what a message told it (the case id an <code>Invite</code> carried, the recommender an <code>Offer</code> named, the report embedded in a submit <code>Offer</code>, the pending embargo proposal for a case), there is no core object to hold that fact, so core reaches back through the DataLayer and re-reads the stored wire envelope \u2014 <code>dl.read(activity_id)</code> inside <code>vultron/core/</code>. Concern #1506 audited these sites. ADR-0034 recognised activity read-back as a boundary violation but explicitly scoped it out and deferred it to a separate concern; this ADR is that concern's decision.</p> <p>The <code>dl.read(activity_id)</code> call in core is a symptom. The root cause is a missing layer of core domain representation for protocol facts. A second, subtler question surfaced during analysis: emitting a reply (e.g. an <code>Accept</code>) requires the full inline verbatim original activity in the reply's <code>object_</code> (the Actor Knowledge Model forbids bare URIs), and activity ids are non-regenerable random <code>urn:uuid:</code> values \u2014 so the original envelope cannot be losslessly reconstructed from core state. That stream travels over a transport with no ordering guarantee, and Vultron may not be the only protocol implementation on the wire, so a replica can receive an entry before its hash-chain predecessor arrives.</p> <p>The original receive path (<code>CheckHashOrRejectOnMismatchNode</code>) treated any entry whose <code>prev_log_hash</code> did not match the local tail as a divergence: it dropped the entry and sent a <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> so the CaseActor would replay the missing prefix. At case closure this stalled a late-joining replica (Vendor2 in the FVV/FVCV demos) indefinitely and <code>wait_for_contiguous_ledger_coverage</code> timed out (issue #1556). How should a replica handle an entry that is valid but arrives before its predecessor?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Convergence must not depend on <code>Announce</code> delivery order (SYNC-10-004 requires   a contiguous prefix; the transport does not provide ordering).</li> <li>The fix must interoperate with unknown implementations \u2014 we cannot assume the   sender retries, or that any recovery message is delivered in order either.</li> <li>Must preserve the effects-before-persist invariant (SYNC-12-001) and the   DataLayer-presence-means-committed invariant (SYNC-13-001).</li> <li>Bounded memory under a broken or hostile peer that streams far-future entries.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>A. Repair the <code>Reject \u2192 replay</code> loop only \u2014 keep dropping out-of-order   entries; make the CaseActor reliably process the participant's Reject and   replay the missing prefix promptly.</li> <li>B. Receiver-side buffering \u2014 hold out-of-order entries locally and apply   them in hash-chain order once their predecessor arrives.</li> <li>C. Both \u2014 buffering plus a hardened replay loop.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: B, receiver-side buffering (which subsumes most of C).</p> <p>Option A alone is insufficient: the replay path re-announces each missing entry as a separate <code>Announce</code>, which travels the same unordered transport and can reorder again \u2014 hitting the very same drop. Repairing replay narrows the race but cannot close it under adversarial reordering. Buffering, by contrast, makes convergence order-independent: any valid entry is retained until the entry that closes its gap arrives, then drained in order.</p> <p>Buffering also makes the existing <code>Reject \u2192 replay</code> recovery order-robust for free, because replayed entries flow through the same (now buffering) receive path. We therefore did not redesign the replay loop; we keep sending the <code>Reject</code> at buffer time purely as the backstop for entries that are genuinely lost (never delivered) rather than merely reordered. A companion correctness fix makes <code>SyncActivityAdapter.send_reject_log_entry</code> enqueue against the explicit receiving <code>actor_id</code> (like the announce path) instead of the DataLayer's own scope, so the Reject is delivered correctly even from a shared or differently-scoped DataLayer.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good: a late-joining replica converges to a contiguous prefix within a few   seconds of the tail arriving, regardless of <code>Announce</code> order (SYNC-10-004).</li> <li>Good: no new dependence on sender retry behavior \u2014 robust against other   implementations and lossy/reordering transports.</li> <li>Good: the buffer is a non-ledger holding area (SYNC-13-003), so the   \"DataLayer presence \u21d2 committed + effects applied\" invariant is preserved.</li> <li>Neutral: buffered state is in-memory and lost on restart; no durability is   required because the committed prefix survives the restart intact, and any   dropped forward-gap entries re-enter via the ordinary diverge/reject/replay   path (SYNC-14-002, SYNC-08-005) when the next <code>Announce</code> does not match the   committed tail.</li> <li>Bad: adds a per-actor in-memory structure and a drain step on the receive   path; Repair the <code>Reject \u2192 replay</code> loop only","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because it reuses the existing recovery mechanism with no new state.</li> <li>Bad, because replay re-announces entries individually over the same unordered   transport, so the reorder-and-drop race reappears \u2014 it cannot guarantee   convergence under adversarial ordering.</li> <li>Bad, because correctness depends on the CaseActor reliably processing every   Reject during a rapid closure fan-out, which is exactly what failed.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#b-receiver-side-buffering","title":"B. Only recipients on a different host/port fall through to HTTP POST (<code>DemoHttpDeliveryAdapter</code>).</p> <p>This in-process shortcut makes the co-located case behave differently from the remote case. Vultron's protocol model treats every actor as an independent, autonomous federated peer whose only knowledge of the world comes from Activities it has received over its inbox (the Actor Knowledge Model, AKM-01). The ASGI shortcut violates the spirit of that model in practice: demos and tests that run actors co-located in one process exercise a delivery path that would not exist if those actors were deployed as separate containers. The result is false confidence \u2014 inter-actor delivery bugs (addressing, serialization, inbox routing) can be masked in-process and only surface once actors are genuinely separated.</p> <p>The shortcut also carries accidental complexity that exists solely to support in-process delivery: a <code>contextvars</code> reentrancy guard, scheme+netloc locality classification, and mount-prefix stripping (root cause of several delivery bugs: #531, #534, #557, and #558).</p> <p>Should Vultron keep the co-located ASGI fast path, or deliver everything uniformly over HTTP as if every recipient were remote?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0042-http-only-inter-actor-delivery/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Fidelity to the autonomous-actor model. \"Something that works for   remote must work for local too.\" Actors are independent peers; delivery   should not depend on co-location.</li> <li>Bug visibility. But not every ADR is equally settled. Some are ratified and validated; some are explicitly \"formed in sand\" pending validation (ADR-0025); some were never given a status at all (ADR-0024 had a blank status field); and <code>docs/adr/index.md</code> has drifted from the per-file <code>status:</code> frontmatter (ADR-0027 is listed as (provisional) in the index while its file says <code>accepted</code>).</p> <p>The consequence is a recurring, expensive failure mode: an implementer builds on an ADR's premise as though it were validated, the premise turns out to be provisional or wrong, and a maintainer has to interject and unwind the work. Its transition table, however, treats <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> as a pre-consent state: the only way out is <code>INVITE</code>, so consent can only ever be reached via <code>NO_EMBARGO \u2192 INVITED \u2192 SIGNATORY</code>.</p> <p>These two readings contradict each other, and the transition table's reading is wrong. Consent does not always arrive through an invitation:</p> <ol> <li> <p>Self-determined embargo. A Finder who creates a case for their own    finding and sets its default embargo is not invited by anyone. There is no    counterparty to issue an <code>Invite</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Embargo created with the case. Under ADR-0041, the CaseActor initializes    the default embargo during case initialization, in the same BT sequence that    adds the vendor (CASE_OWNER) and reporter participants. The reporter's consent is expressed by    submitting the report. The spec requires they be seeded <code>SIGNATORY</code>; no    invitation is ever sent.</p> </li> </ol> <p>Forcing these paths through <code>INVITED</code> requires fabricating an invitation event that never occurred, and writing it into the canonical case ledger as though it had.</p> <p>The contradiction is already causing a silent MUST-level failure in production code. <code>_SignEmbargoConsentLeafNode</code> (<code>vultron/core/behaviors/case/accept_invite_tree.py:493</code>) calls:</p> <pre><code>participant.embargo_consent_state = apply_pec_trigger(\n    PEC.NO_EMBARGO, PEC_Trigger.ACCEPT\n)\n</code></pre> <p><code>apply_pec_trigger</code> rejects this transition, logs a warning, and returns <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> unchanged \u2014 and the node then logs \"signed embargo consent for invitee\" and returns <code>SUCCESS</code>. A participant who accepts an invitation to an embargoed case is recorded as having never consented, violating CM-10-001. The author of that node clearly expected <code>NO_EMBARGO \u2192 SIGNATORY</code> to be legal; the FSM silently disagreed.</p> <p>A second, related defect motivates the same fix. A sweep of <code>embargo_consent_state =</code> finds ten consent-write sites, none of which persists the resulting <code>ParticipantStatus</code>. Routing through <code>apply_pec_trigger</code> is necessary but not sufficient. Five of the seven are in <code>EmbargoLifecycle</code>, the intended long-term owner of all PEC transitions (#538), which makes them the highest-value conversions rather than the safest to skip.</p> <p>The correct machinery to prevent this already exists and is simply unused: <code>ParticipantStatus.consent</code> is a <code>PecDimension</code> (ADR-0036, SDO-01-001), and <code>PecDimension.transition()</code> performs fail-closed FSM validation, raising <code>VultronInvalidStateTransitionError</code> on an illegal trigger.</p> <p>The question is: is <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> an absence-of-embargo state or a not-yet-consented state, and what follows for the transition table and for case-initialization ledger entries?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0048-pec-no-embargo-is-absence-not-pre-consent/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The PEC docstring's own definition of <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> should be authoritative</li> <li>The ledger MUST NOT record protocol events that did not occur (ADR-0019)</li> <li>Single-actor and self-determined-embargo cases must be representable without   fiction</li> <li>Consent writes should be fail-closed, validated by the dimension object</li> <li>Avoid <code>log_index</code> churn: PR #1746 was reverted for shifting ledger indices and   breaking <code>fvcv-extension</code> VFD replication timing</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0048-pec-no-embargo-is-absence-not-pre-consent/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li> <p><code>NO_EMBARGO</code> is absence of embargo (chosen): add    <code>ACCEPT: NO_EMBARGO \u2192 SIGNATORY</code> and <code>DECLINE: NO_EMBARGO \u2192 DECLINED</code>. But the system underneath is asynchronous \u2014 a trigger endpoint returns HTTP 202 and the protocol effect is committed later by a <code>BackgroundTasks</code> job on a different container. Writing \"A and then B\" when the truth is \"B is only possible because A completed\" makes every step boundary a race.</p> <p>This is not a theoretical concern. Of the nineteen sub-issues of Epic #2136 (\"Demo CI: restore green main\"), seven were the same defect in a different scenario: a step proceeded before the event that would enable it had propagated. Two more were partially this. Each was fixed locally \u2014 a wait inserted here, a different observable polled there \u2014 and the shared cause was never addressed, so the next scenario rediscovered it. Bug #2178's own triage comment states the diagnosis plainly: \"the demo treated async causal steps as sequential (x then y) rather than causally linked (x therefore y).\"</p> <p>Three symptoms show the problem is structural rather than a run of bad luck:</p> <ol> <li> <p>The specs duplicated the workaround instead of stating the rule. Seven    scenario-specific requirements (DEMOMA-06-006, -11-009, -12-004, -19-005,    -19-009, -21-003, -21-004) each say \"poll here before proceeding\" for one    scenario. DEMOMA-11-009 states the general rule correctly but is scoped to    FVCV-handoff alone.</p> </li> <li> <p>The gates did not gate. Both <code>demo_step</code> and <code>demo_check</code> record the    failure and continue \u2014 \"no re-raise\", by their own docstrings and by    DEMOCI-01-003. So a precondition written with <code>demo_check</code> is advisory: it    reads like a gate in review and does nothing at runtime, and the dependent step    proceeds on state that was never established. The concrete instance is the    <code>RM.VALID</code>-before-<code>engage-case</code> gate added by the #2134 fix on the    <code>fix/demo-ci</code> branch, whose regression test passes only because it patches    <code>demo_check</code> out with <code>contextlib.nullcontext</code>. That test idiom is not    isolated: seven demo test modules on <code>main</code> patch these context managers out    the same way, so no test in the suite exercises their real control flow.</p> </li> <li> <p>Which observable proves the cause landed was guesswork. The gate before    <code>validate-report</code> in <code>run_invite_path_rm_triage</code> was re-picked three times in    one week: a ledger <code>submit_report</code> entry, then a <code>VultronOfferRecord</code> object,    then a ledger <code>add_report_to_case</code> entry.</p> </li> </ol> <p>The question this ADR answers: what should the demo harness be required to observe before advancing, and where should that requirement live?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0058-causal-gating-in-demo-scenarios/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The same defect class must not be able to recur in the next scenario written.</li> <li>The prototype's observability is limited: an actor having processed a   delivery leaves no completion record, so not every precondition is directly   observable.</li> <li>Demo CI must keep reporting every failure in a run (DEMOCI-01-003), so a fix   cannot simply convert gates into hard aborts.</li> <li>Nine scenario modules totalling roughly 9,700 lines already exist; a solution   requiring all of them to be rewritten in a new form is unlikely to be finished.</li> <li>ADR-0037 and ADR-0059 (buffer pre-genesis ledger entries) already moved one   class of ordering problem into actor-side buffering. A harness rule must not   contradict that.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0058-causal-gating-in-demo-scenarios/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Causal gates in shared helpers, plus domain narratives as a conformance   oracle \u2014 state the rule once, express preconditions with a gating primitive   that actually stops dependent work, and check the intended causal chain against   the observed one.</li> <li>Keep per-scenario polling with tuned timeouts \u2014 the status quo: continue   adding scenario-specific wait requirements and raising timeouts as CI reveals   races.</li> <li>Push all ordering into the actors \u2014 extend the ADR-0037/0055 buffering   approach until the harness never needs to sequence around delivery at all.</li> <li>Declarative scenario dependency graph with static validation \u2014 replace   imperative phase functions with declared causal edges validated before a run.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0058-causal-gating-in-demo-scenarios/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: causal gates in shared helpers, plus domain narratives as a conformance oracle.</p> <p>The rule is stated once, at the conceptual layer that already governs demo scripts (<code>EDF-06</code>), and generalized across scenarios in <code>DEMOMA-22</code>. Concretely:</p> <ul> <li>A step that depends on an asynchronous effect is gated on positive evidence   that the effect was committed by the actor that produces it, read from   that actor's own container. Elapsed time, step position, and an HTTP 202   return are not evidence.</li> <li>Gating on an observable that resolves synchronously during the triggering   request is prohibited \u2014 that observable proves the cause started, not that it   finished. This is the #2134 defect.</li> <li>A causally derived object (one created by a received-side use case forwarding a   new activity) is discovered by scanning the recipient's state for semantic   properties \u2014 type, target, object \u2014 never by polling for the sender's original   identifier. This is the #2178 defect.</li> <li>Preconditions are expressed with a new <code>demo_gate</code> context manager that   accumulates the failure exactly as <code>demo_check</code> does but additionally stops the   steps that depend on it. <code>demo_check</code> stays advisory. This resolves the tension   with DEMOCI-01-003 by separating reporting from control flow rather than   choosing between them.</li> <li>Waits that are irreducibly temporal \u2014 liveness probes, embargo deadlines,   transport backoff \u2014 are identified as temporal and are not counted as causal   gates.</li> </ul> <p>Each scenario additionally gets a narrative page under <code>docs/topics/scenarios/</code> describing the case's progress in CVD domain terms with each step's antecedent named, carrying a machine-readable list of causal edges. The invariant harness asserts every declared edge appears in the observed case ledger with the antecedent's <code>log_index</code> preceding the consequent's. Because <code>log_index</code> order is causal order (ADR-0079, CLP-14-001) and the harness already reads per-scenario ledger dumps, this needs no new instrumentation.</p> <p>The narrative is the part of this decision that does work the gates cannot. A gate enforces that the harness waited for the right thing. The narrative states, independently of the implementation, what the protocol is supposed to cause \u2014 so it can disagree with the code. That is what makes it an oracle rather than a restatement.</p> <p>Resolved: nested-block scoping model (PR #2348). The <code>demo_gate</code> context manager is implemented in <code>vultron/demo/utils.py</code> and validated by 14 unit tests in <code>TestDemoGate</code>. The scoping question the ADR left open \u2014 \"whether by phase function, by nested block, or by an explicit sentinel\" \u2014 is answered: nested block. Python's native exception unwinding exits the <code>with</code> body on failure; dependent steps follow the precondition assertion inside the same block. No sentinel variable, no return value, no modified calling convention.</p> <p>The causal-edge schema for scenario narratives (<code>docs/topics/scenarios/</code>) was finalised in PR #2204. The schema and its update-together rule are documented in <code>docs/topics/scenarios/index.md</code>, which is the authoritative source.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0058-causal-gating-in-demo-scenarios/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because the rule lives in one place, so a new scenario inherits it   instead of rediscovering it.</li> <li>Good, because <code>demo_gate</code> makes a failed precondition stop the work that   depends on it, which removes the cascade of secondary failures that buried the   real cause in #2180 and #2195.</li> <li>Good, because the narrative check fails when the demo and the intended   protocol disagree, which no existing invariant detects.</li> <li>Good, because it composes with ADR-0037/0055 rather than competing: where the   actor buffers, the harness needs no gate, and some of the 26   <code>wait_for_case_on_container</code> sites may now be removable.</li> <li>Bad, because migrating nine scenarios and roughly 20 gate call sites is   substantial mechanical work, and the timeout constants are hand-tuned per site.</li> <li>Bad, because some preconditions are not observable today. \"The receiver   processed activity X\" has no completion record, so those gates remain   inferential \u2014 they observe a downstream effect and assume the antecedent   caused it.</li> <li>Bad, because narratives are a new artifact class that can rot; Writing that statement down in domain terms gives both the demo and the reader the same causal spine, and makes the places where the demo has no reason for its ordering visible.</p> <p>One claim in CONCERN-2181 is contradicted by the evidence and is recorded here so it is not inherited. Both travel over a transport with no ordering guarantee (HTTP <code>BackgroundTasks</code> fan-out), so a replica can receive a ledger entry before the case that anchors it. In that pre-genesis window <code>_reconstruct_tail_hash</code> cannot derive the per-case genesis hash (CLP-08-005): there is no local tail and no case object to seed one from.</p> <p>ADR-0037 buffers forward-gap entries \u2014 those for a case whose genesis anchor is already known \u2014 but its forward-gap test (<code>log_index &gt; tail_index + 1</code>) never fires when there is no chain at all, so a pre-genesis entry falls straight through to the reject-on-missing-case path (<code>ReconstructOrRejectOnMissingCase</code>, SYNC-15-001) and is dropped, leaving convergence to the reject \u2192 replay round-trip.</p> <p>That round-trip is exactly the mechanism ADR-0037 showed does not converge under adversarial reordering, and it has two observed costs: transient CLP-08-005 churn logged during fvcv-handoff (issue #2169), and \u2014 fatally for the fcvcv V1 demo \u2014 the <code>add_report_to_case</code> entry being dropped so no <code>VultronOfferRecord</code> is ever created and the report offer 404s (issue #2180). That makes option C strictly weaker (it re-introduces a dependence on redelivery order) and lets B reuse the ADR-0037 drain unchanged: a buffered genesis entry's <code>prev_log_hash</code> equals the per-case genesis hash, so once the case is seeded <code>_reconstruct_tail_hash</code> returns <code>(genesis_hash, -1)</code>, <code>take_next(genesis_hash)</code> finds it, and the rest cascade in hash-chain order.</p> <p>A new <code>BufferPreGenesisEntryNode</code> is wired as the first child of the <code>ReconstructOrRejectOnMissingCase</code> fallback (wrapped in <code>FailureIsSuccess</code> so the <code>Reject</code> still fires), mirroring the buffer-and-reject structure of <code>CheckHashOrRejectOnMismatchNode</code>. It encodes the case-state (CS) rules as six-character strings and regular expressions \u2014 <code>\"vfdpxa\"</code>, <code>\"v..P..\"</code> \u2014 validated by <code>validations.py</code> and analysed by <code>hypercube.py</code> (a networkx / numpy / pandas model that enumerates states, transitions, histories, and scores them). That filtered object is what gets persisted, appended to the participant, and snapshotted in the canonical ledger entry. It runs as a read-only precondition guard of <code>add_participant_status_tree</code>, replacing <code>CheckParticipantRMNotClosedNode</code>.</p> <p>Per-dimension rules:</p> <ul> <li><code>rm</code> \u2014 accepted when it confirms the current value, is a valid adjacent   transition, or is a monotone forward jump. <code>RM.CLOSED</code> is terminal: once a   participant has closed, no further <code>rm</code> value is accepted, including <code>CLOSED</code> again.</li> <li><code>vfd</code> and <code>pxa</code> \u2014 each is a triple of independent one-way latches   (<code>v\u2192V</code>, <code>f\u2192F</code>, <code>d\u2192D</code>; <code>p\u2192P</code>, <code>x\u2192X</code>, <code>a\u2192A</code>). Adjudicating each dimension on its own cannot see a claim that is impossible only in combination. A snapshot can pass every rule above and still describe a state no sequence of events could produce \u2014 a fix reported ready or deployed by a participant whose <code>rm</code> has not reached acceptance, or a fix deployed without being ready.</p> <p>A final pass therefore evaluates the cross-machine entailments \u2014 RM\u2194VF and RM\u2194D (CSB-18-001) and VF\u2194D (CSB-17-001) \u2014 and refuses the dimension whose asserted value moved, carrying the current value forward like any other refusal (RSH-05-020). Which side gets refused is load-bearing: VF\u2194D constrains a pair, and refusing the incumbent side carries its value straight back, which would leave the impossible combination recorded while reporting a refusal that changed nothing. A dimension the sender omitted is never reported as refused.</p> <p>The pass runs on the effective post-adjudication state so a refused or carried-forward <code>vf</code> cannot license the <code>d</code> the sender paired it with. For <code>rm</code> this is not a tightening \u2014 <code>rm</code> is refused only when the asserted value is not a forward move, so the carried value always ranks at or above the asserted one on the RM progress scale.</p> <p>Emit and receive share one evaluator, <code>composite_state_violations()</code> in <code>vultron/core/states/composite_state_invariants.py</code>. Before this amendment the receive path composed only VF\u2194D by hand while the emit path composed all three, so an assertion the actor would have refused to emit was accepted, hash-chained and replicated when it arrived from a peer instead.</p> <p>The guarantee is conditional: if the participant's current state satisfies the entailments, so does the recorded state. An already-impossible incumbent state cannot be repaired by refusing a dimension, because every carry-forward writes the offending value back; that case is logged instead. It is reachable via the replica-apply path, which detects the violation, emits <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code>, and refuses the entry (RSH-05-021).</p> <p>This does not narrow the monotone-forward rule above: multi-step <code>vf</code>, <code>d</code> and <code>pxa</code> advances remain accepted (CSB-16-001), because a peer may have advanced several steps between status messages. Nor does it treat an absent dimension as an initial state \u2014 a non-VENDOR participant has no vendor path (ADR-0075), so no entailment applies through it, and a first observation of a dimension is accepted when nothing contradicts it.</p> <p>Under the ADR-0075 VFD split the <code>vfd</code> rule above now reads as two independent dimensions, <code>vf</code> (<code>v\u2192V</code>, <code>f\u2192F</code>) and <code>d</code> (<code>d\u2192D</code>).</p> <p>The refusal is made visible through the canonical ledger rather than a new wire message: the committed entry snapshots the accepted portion, so it differs from what the sender asserted and every participant sees the receiver's actual view. ARCH-12-003 forbids exactly this \u2014 <code>alias_generator=to_camel</code> is a wire-specific concern and core-branch types MUST NOT carry it. The violation has been tracked as a known deviation (#1991) behind an <code>xfail(strict=False)</code> ratchet in <code>test/architecture/test_hierarchy_invariants.py</code> for long enough that downstream code came to depend on it.</p> <p><code>ParticipantStatus</code> compounds the problem with a <code>_migrate_flat_fields</code> <code>model_validator(mode=\"before\")</code> that accepts flat wire spellings (<code>rm_state</code>/<code>rmState</code>, <code>vfd_state</code>/<code>vfdState</code>, <code>em_consent_state</code>/<code>emConsentState</code>) and rewrites them into the ADR-0036 dimension objects. SDO-03-003 says the old flat enum fields MUST NOT be retained as aliases or shim properties after the dimension migration \u2014 so this shim violates a MUST-level requirement independently of ARCH-12-003.</p> <p>The reason the alias generator is load-bearing rather than merely wrong is that core code needs camelCase JSON for one specific purpose: building <code>CaseLedgerEntry.payloadSnapshot</code> values. The case ledger's purpose is to wrap \"things that were received or sent to/from the case manager in the course of managing the case\", and those are by definition wire-shaped. CLP-07-001 requires the snapshot to be the verbatim AS2 activity or a deterministic canonical normalization of it, and CLP-01-003/CLP-01-004 make the ledger the replication substrate that receivers project into their own replica. A payload snapshot must therefore be valid wire JSON that a receiver can reconstitute \u2014 camelCase is correct there.</p> <p>So core reached for the nearest thing that produced camelCase: it set <code>alias_generator</code> on the core class and called <code>model_dump(by_alias=True)</code>. That is a wire concern implemented by mutating the domain model, and it does not even work correctly: <code>build_add_participant_status_snapshot</code> in <code>vultron/core/behaviors/case/ledger_snapshots.py</code> has to hand-patch <code>consent</code> \u2192 <code>emConsentState</code> after the dump, because a core <code>model_dump</code> cannot produce the wire's flat <code>emConsentState</code> field from the nested <code>PecDimension</code>. That hand-patch is a partial, drifting reimplementation of <code>as_ParticipantStatus.from_core()</code>.</p> <p>Three additional consumers depend on the same core-side aliasing: <code>_inline_snapshot_reference_value</code> in <code>vultron/core/use_cases/_helpers.py</code> (CLP-07-006 inline nesting of <code>dl.read()</code> results, which are core objects per DL-05-001); <code>GET /actors/{id}</code> in <code>vultron/adapters/driving/fastapi/routers/actors/_routes.py</code>, which dumps a core actor class with <code>by_alias=True</code> straight into an <code>AS2JSONResponse</code>; and <code>vultron/demo/utils.py</code>, which dumps core objects the same way for demo output.</p> <p>A fifth consumer depends on the shim rather than the alias generator: <code>FilterParticipantStatusDimensionsNode._to_core_status</code> (added by ADR-0061) normalises a wire status by dumping it <code>by_alias=True</code> and revalidating through core <code>ParticipantStatus</code>, and its docstring names the dependency outright \u2014 \"the core model's <code>_migrate_flat_fields</code> validator accepts that shape, so a dump-and-revalidate normalises both\". The shim and that idiom have to retire together.</p> <p>The hand-patching is likewise not confined to one site: <code>_build_patch</code> in the same module writes <code>patch[\"caseStatus\"] = {\"emState\": ..., \"pxaState\": ...}</code>, and <code>accept_invite.py</code>'s <code>_build_snapshot</code> hand-builds a wire-spelled fallback dict. CM-18-002 defines the pocket veto: <code>INVITED \u2192 DECLINED</code> MAY be driven by timer expiry on \"a configurable policy window (default: 7 days).\" That window is receiver-local and implicit \u2014 nothing about it appears on the wire, so the two parties have no shared instant at which the invite lapses. The CaseActor (<code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code>) enforces expiry, by    lazy evaluation: lapse is derived from <code>(end_time, now)</code> whenever PEC state    is read or an <code>Accept</code>/<code>Reject</code> is processed. If it is incompatible, the CaseActor issues a fresh    invite carrying the current embargo rather than rejecting: the late    accepter has signalled willingness to engage, so the protocol keeps them and    re-syncs their terms. accept silently.</li> <li>Non-adjacent forward jump \u2014 the sender skipped intermediate states    (e.g. <code>RECEIVED \u2192 ACCEPTED</code> without passing through <code>VALID</code>). The existing    <code>FilterParticipantStatusDimensionsNode._rm_is_acceptable()</code> already accepts    these and documents the rationale (\"sender is authoritative about own RM    progress\"), but acceptance is silent.</li> <li>Backward regression \u2014 the sender reports a state earlier on the RM    progress scale than what the receiver has already observed (e.g.    <code>ACCEPTED \u2192 VALID</code>). <code>ValidateRMTransitionNode</code> refuses these, which is    correct, but the refusal is also silent.</li> </ol> <p>Two independent bugs arise from the silent treatment:</p> <ul> <li>Forward jumps are accepted without any log entry at WARNING level or any   protocol-level notification. An anomaly that should trigger a clarification   request passes through as if nothing unusual happened (ISSUE-2258).</li> <li>Backward regressions are refused without emitting a protocol-level note.   A remote actor's replica is now permanently diverged from the receiver's, with   no signal to either party.</li> </ul> <p>The broader principle: CVD is inherently asynchronous. Events happen at time t\u2080 but are only recognised as anomalous at time t\u2081 &gt; t\u2080. When a protocol-level anomaly is detected on receipt, the receiver must both act correctly and act non-silently. Silence on anomalies breaks the protocol's observability and makes diagnosis impossible.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0067-rm-nonadj-accept-and-notify/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Liberal accept / Postel's law (ISSUE-2229): accept everything acceptable;   refuse only what must be refused.</li> <li>Sender is authoritative about its own RM progress: refusing a   non-adjacent forward jump would leave the receiver's replica permanently wrong,   because the sender will not resend the intermediate transitions it never   reported.</li> <li>RM is monotonic: backward regressions indicate either a protocol error or   a divergent replica state.
