The SQLite DataLayer does not provide that. It treats one database file as a multi-tenant store, using <code>actor_id</code> as a filter column over a globally unique primary key. Reads are partitioned; writes are not.</p> <p>Issue #2238 is the visible consequence. <code>VultronObjectRecord.id_</code> is the sole primary key, so two actors sharing a store cannot both hold a replica of the same object ID:</p> <ul> <li><code>crud.create()</code> checked existence with a bare primary-key <code>get</code>, so the   second actor's <code>create()</code> raised <code>ValueError</code>. Both case-bootstrap sites   swallowed that as a benign concurrent insert, leaving that actor with no   replica row it could read.</li> <li><code>crud.save()</code> had the same unscoped lookup and no error. One actor's   <code>save()</code> silently overwrote another actor's row contents while leaving the   row owned by the original actor \u2014 so the writer could not read its own   write back, and the original owner read the writer's data.</li> </ul> <p>Neither case is hypothetical. A single container hosts an actor plus the CaseActors it self-hosts (CP-08-003, pending #1700), and single-server demo mode runs every actor against one configured store.</p> <p>The deeper problem is that isolation was a property of every individual query rather than of the storage layout. <code>SqliteDataLayer._scoped()</code> had to be applied by hand, and any path that forgot it \u2014 every write path did \u2014 reopened the leak. The <code>ARCH-13</code> requirement group and the <code>ActorScopedDataLayer</code> protocol refinement exist only to police that hazard, and <code>notes/datalayer-design.md</code> carries two further pitfalls (<code>outbox_list()</code> requires <code>clone_for_actor</code>; the dual-DataLayer isolation guard) that are symptoms of the same root cause.</p> <p>The unscoped mode is also load-bearing in ways that contradict the invariant. <code>deps.py</code> states it plainly: \"Operational data (actors, offers, reports, cases) is stored in the shared DataLayer.\"</p> <p>There is a second leak, in execution identity rather than storage layout. <code>BTBridge.setup_tree</code> puts <code>datalayer</code> and <code>actor_id</code> on the blackboard as two independent facts, so they can disagree. Under per-actor storage they are one fact: a store is always some actor's own, so the executing actor's identity determines which store the tree operates on.</p> <p>The delegated-emit pattern is where this bites. A trigger emitting on the CaseActor's behalf runs with <code>actor_id</code> set to the CaseActor (CM-24-001) while the injected DataLayer belongs to the requesting actor. So the activity is created in the requester's store and queued in the CaseActor's outbox: the CaseActor never delivers it, and its outbox names an activity its own store does not hold (PCR-08-007, CM-24-004).</p> <p>There is a third leak, and it is the one this decision originally failed to name. Per-actor storage makes cross-actor access impossible; it does nothing about cross-actor expectation. Code can still be written as though a co-located actor's knowledge were its own, and nothing in the layout says otherwise \u2014 the read simply comes back empty.</p> <p>Issue #2548 is that leak in the field. A single container hosts the report receiver and the CaseActor it self-hosts. Under ADR-0041 the receiver does not create the case: it submits a <code>CaseProposal</code>, and the CaseActor creates the case in its own store and replicates it back as <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code>. The receiver's <code>validate-report</code> tree ran before that replica arrived, found no case \u2014 correctly \u2014 and advanced anyway, writing the report-phase <code>RM.VALID</code> latch while the case-scoped <code>CaseParticipant</code> stayed at <code>RECEIVED</code>. Because the guard that decides whether to run the transition reads that same latch, the two halves could never reconverge. The case state had split across two stores and the split was permanent.</p> <p>Nothing in this ADR licensed that, but nothing forbade it either. The invariant as originally stated is about writes (\"one actor's writes must never affect what another actor could read\"); the missing half is about reads, and it has to be stated as a property of the protocol rather than of the storage layout, because the temptation it removes is a deployment-shaped one.</p> <p>An outbox call-site survey missed this, and it is worth recording why. The four <code>record_outbox_item</code> sites traced below name the actor in an argument, and all four are genuinely self-directed. This seam is different: the mismatch arrives through the blackboard, so no call site reads as cross-actor. \"Every outbox call site passes the executing actor's own id\" is true of the traced sites and false at the trigger seam.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0073-per-actor-storage-isolation/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>CM-01-001: each actor MUST have an isolated protocol state domain.</li> <li>The invariant to enforce is absolute: one actor's writes must never affect   what another actor could read. \"Ever\" rules out guarantees that depend on   every query being written correctly.</li> <li>Co-location is an implementation choice the protocol must remain   indifferent to. One host or a hundred, actors exchange information only by   protocol message. No back-end cheats: no direct writes into another actor's   store, no out-of-band signalling between actors that happen to share a   process. A guarantee that holds only when the topology cooperates is not a   protocol guarantee.</li> <li>Core must stay agnostic to the storage layout \u2014 a robust database, a folder   of JSON files per actor, or anything between (the DataLayer port is the   contract; see <code>notes/datalayer-design.md</code> \u00a7 \"Key principle\").</li> <li>The Actor Knowledge Model: an actor's knowledge of the world is bounded by   what it has received. An actor's view of its peers is that actor's own   data, not node-global data.</li> <li>Isolation guarantees that rely on discipline have already failed here once   (#2232 produced two ratchets for one problem).</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0073-per-actor-storage-isolation/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Option A \u2014 One store per actor; <code>actor_id</code> mandatory; no unscoped mode.</li> <li>Option B \u2014 One store, composite primary key <code>(id_, actor_id)</code>, scoping   enforced in every query.</li> <li>Option C \u2014 Per-actor schema or <code>ATTACH</code>-ed database inside one file.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0073-per-actor-storage-isolation/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: Option A \u2014 one store per actor, <code>actor_id</code> mandatory.</p> <p>Only Option A makes the invariant structural. With a separate engine per actor there is no <code>WHERE</code> clause to omit, no <code>actor_id</code> column to mis-populate, and no query that could return another actor's row. Options B and C both leave cross-actor access expressible in SQL, so they convert the invariant into a code-review obligation \u2014 which is the failure mode being removed.</p> <p>Concretely:</p> <ul> <li>The configured <code>db_url</code> becomes a template.   <code>sqlite:////app/data/mydb.sqlite</code> yields <code>mydb-&lt;slug&gt;.sqlite</code> per actor;   <code>sqlite:///:memory:</code> yields one private in-memory engine per actor.</li> <li><code>SqliteDataLayer</code> requires an <code>actor_id</code>.   <code>_scoped()</code>, the <code>actor_id</code> column, <code>get_shared_dl()</code>, and   <code>get_datalayer()</code>-with-no-actor are deleted.</li> <li>The URL path segment is   resolved to a canonical actor URI by computation,   not lookup: <code>VULTRON_SERVER__BASE_URL + \"actors/\" + segment</code>. This removes   the last genuine need for a cross-actor scan. It holds for CaseActors too,   whose id is the container-level <code>{base_url}/actors/case-actor</code> under   ADR-0041 \u2014 one per container, not one per case. The per-case   <code>case-actor-{slug}</code> form this ADR was first drafted against is deleted by   the same change, so the co-location discussion below \u2014 which speaks of   CaseActors per container \u2014 is the one this bullet must be read against.</li> <li><code>record_outbox_item(actor_id, \u2026)</code> and   <code>outbox_list_for_actor(actor_id)</code> collapse into <code>outbox_append()</code> /   <code>outbox_list()</code> at all call sites. The   explicit-actor form existed because the injected DataLayer might be unscoped,   not because any site wrote to a genuinely foreign queue.</li> </ul> <p>Four sites make that non-obvious, because they name the actor via a variable   (<code>case_actor_id</code>, <code>sender_actor_id</code>, <code>enqueue_actor_id</code>) rather than   <code>self.actor_id</code>. Traced through, all four are self-directed: two author as the   executing actor or merely re-queue an activity authored earlier   (<code>case/nodes/participant/common.py</code>, <code>fastapi/pending_retry.py</code>), and two \u2014   <code>case/update_support.py</code> and <code>sync/nodes/replay.py</code> \u2014 emit activities whose   <code>actor</code> is the CaseActor while running as the CaseActor.</p> <p>Those last two conflate three separate ideas that CM-24 keeps apart on the   wire and then muddles in storage: the activity's <code>actor</code> (CM-24-001), its   <code>attributed_to</code> (CM-24-002), and whose store this is. The first two are   wire authorship; the third is infrastructure. Spelling the first and third   with one variable made a local write look like a foreign one.</p> <p>Resolution: gate on the role, not on an identity comparison. A CaseActor-   authored emit MUST sit inside a role-gated composite that verifies the   executing actor holds <code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code> for the case   (<code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code>), exactly as CLP-09 already requires for canonical   ledger commits \u2014 appending to the log and announcing the append are one   privilege. Code MUST NOT instead compare <code>actor_id</code> against a computed   <code>case_actor_id</code>; the authority is a role held in the case, and the holder may   be any Actor type. Once gated, the executing actor is the case manager, so   <code>outbox_append()</code> is correct by construction.</p> <p>This also fixes a latent defect the isolation exposes. Those sites <code>create()</code>   the activity in the executing actor's store and enqueue its id under the   named actor. A shared pool made that work by accident; with per-actor stores   the reader would find no activity for the id. Gating makes both halves land in   one store.</p> <p>Ungated, this is identity spoofing \u2014 any actor reaching the helper could emit   an <code>Announce</code> authored as the CaseActor to every participant \u2014 which   <code>AGENTS.md</code> already forbids for received-side use cases. - <code>ActorScopedDataLayer</code> merges back into   <code>DataLayer</code>: with no unscoped mode, the distinction has no referent. - Peer actor records live in the   address book of each hosted actor that needs them. This is safe because   delivery derives a recipient's inbox URL from its URI alone   (<code>http_delivery.py</code>: <code>recipient_id.rstrip(\"/\") + \"/inbox/\"</code>) and never reads   the peer's stored record. - <code>GET /actors/</code> returns only the actors   this node hosts. A peer is not something the node hosts; it is an address   some hosted actor happens to know.</p> <ul> <li>A BT's store follows its   executing actor, reconciled once in <code>BTBridge</code>   rather than at each BT invocation (<code>_store_for_actor</code>). Chosen over fixing only   the trigger seam for the same reason isolation must not depend on every query   remembering a filter: correctness must not depend on every BT invocation   remembering to re-scope. Normative as BT-05-005.</li> </ul> <p>The stronger choice is not free, and the cost was measured rather than   estimated. Fixing only the trigger seam left 139 failing tests across 10 extra   files; forcing the store to follow the executing actor everywhere took the   suite to 622 failures across 123 files. The maintainer took the structural fix   with that number in hand.</p> <p>A related invariant falls out and is normative as BT-05-006: where a tree is   gated on a role, the role holder, the receiving actor and the store owner must   be one actor. Letting any two drift makes the gate evaluate against an actor   holding no role, which returns SUCCESS-by-skip and writes nothing. Nothing   raises, which is what makes it worth a MUST.</p> <p>The store is not the only thing that holds a store, and reconciling it   alone leaves the other half looking correct. Normative as DL-07-009: every   store reference reachable from an actor-scoped execution follows that actor,   not just the one on the blackboard. The driven adapters injected into a BT \u2014   <code>TriggerActivityPort</code>, <code>SyncActivityPort</code> \u2014 keep the DataLayer they were   constructed with, and the adapter is what persists the outbound activity. So   BT-05-005 alone fixed the queue and left the activity behind: a delegated emit   created the <code>Invite</code> in the requesting actor's store while the node appended   its id to the executing actor's outbox. Delivery then found the queue entry,   could not read the activity, logged \"not found in DataLayer\", and skipped \u2014 the   invitee was never told it had been invited, and no error surfaced anywhere.</p> <p>Rebinding is opt-in: a component declares a named way to be rebound   (<code>for_store</code>) or holds no store at all. Opt-in rather than automatic because a   stateless collaborator must not be replaced behind its caller's back, and the   declaration is read off the type rather than the instance because a test   double answers any attribute \u2014 an instance-level probe would silently rebind   every mock in the suite. - Cross-actor access must be   named. <code>clone_for_actor</code> is the only route to   another actor's store, and <code>CasePersistence</code> declares it, so a fan-out is   explicit in the type as well as in the code rather than something a forgotten   filter grants.</p> <ul> <li>The protocol is indifferent   to co-location, and code must be too.   Normative as PCR-01-003. Actors exchange information only through protocol   messages \u2014 never a direct read or write into another actor's store, never   out-of-band communication between actors that happen to share a host. The   operative consequence for the case lifecycle: an actor that has asked a   CaseActor to create a case MUST treat that case as absent from its own   knowledge until the CaseActor's <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code> has been delivered   to it. Co-location does not make the case visible sooner. Absence of the   replica is a legitimate, transient state \u2014 the correct response is to fail the   case-scoped work and retry, never to proceed as though the case were there   (ARCH-15-001).</li> </ul> <p>This is not merely about where bytes live, so it is worth being exact about   who holds what. The CaseActor creates the case and holds   <code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code>: what it owns is write privilege on the case ledger.   The actor whose <code>CaseProposal</code> caused the case to exist \u2014 the report receiver,   whatever other roles it also holds \u2014 holds <code>CVDRole.CASE_OWNER</code>. That role is   never delegated to the CaseActor. \"The case-actor's store holds the   canonical case\" and \"the case-actor owns the case\" are different claims, and   only the first is true. CBT-01-003 is amended accordingly: it previously said   \"case creator/owner\", which under ADR-0041 names two different actors.</p> <p>Stated flatly, because #2548 showed the question had no written answer: when a   container hosts both a primary actor and a co-located CaseActor, the case lives   in the CaseActor's store, and the primary actor holds a replica it receives by   protocol message. There is no write-through from the CaseActor into the   primary actor's store, and no shared per-container store. The two rejected   alternatives fail for the same reason:</p> <ul> <li>The primary actor owns the case and the CaseActor writes through to it via     <code>clone_for_actor</code> \u2014 this is a back-end cheat. It works only while the two     actors are co-located, so it is not a protocol guarantee, and it makes the     CaseActor's authority over the ledger depend on the deployment topology.</li> <li>A container has one store shared by the roles it wears; isolation applies     only across containers \u2014 this contradicts CM-01-001 directly and reinstates     the multi-tenant store this decision exists to remove. It would also make a     self-hosted CaseActor structurally different from a remotely-hosted one,     which is exactly the indifference PCR-01-003 requires.</li> </ul> <p>The consequence a reader must carry away is a timing one, not a location one:   the replica arrives later than the case exists, so any case-scoped work in the   primary actor is gated on the replica having actually landed in its own store.   That gate is the fix; it is not an optimisation to be skipped when the actors   happen to share a host.</p> <ul> <li> <p>What the sibling knows must be   asked for on the wire. Normative as   CP-01-007. The same rule that makes the timing gate necessary also decides   where a fact comes from: an actor that needs something only a sibling   observed has to be told, in a protocol message, at the moment it is told   anything at all. CP-01-004 already established this for the report itself \u2014   the <code>CaseProposal</code> carries the <code>VulnerabilityReport</code> inline because the   CaseActor cannot read the proposer's store. Under #2548 the report's offer   provenance turned out to need the same treatment: only the actor that   received <code>Offer(VulnerabilityReport)</code> holds the <code>VultronOfferRecord</code> for it, so   the CaseActor's scan of its own store came back empty, the canonical   <code>add_report_to_case</code> entry went out without an <code>offerId</code>, and every replica's   <code>ApplyOfferReportFromLedgerNode</code> read that absence as \"not about an offer\" and   skipped. The first visible symptom was an invited actor's <code>validate-report</code>   answering <code>404 Offer not found</code>, four steps and one container away. A   cross-store read is the shape to distrust here, whether what it wants is an   object or a single id.</p> </li> <li> <p>The latch is written last. Normative as   ID-04-005. When a transition has   more than one half and one half doubles as the evidence a later guard reads,   that half MUST be written only after the others have succeeded. Writing it   first turns a recoverable \"not yet\" into a permanent \"already done\": the guard   suppresses every retry, and nothing raises. This is the mechanism by which the   #2548 store split became irreversible rather than merely late, and it belongs   here because per-actor isolation is what makes \"not yet\" a routine state   instead of a rare one.</p> </li> <li> <p>Only the ledger's own store mints   its indices. Normative as CLP-10-014.   Per-actor isolation turns a log index into a claim one store makes, so two   stores claiming the same index fork the chain instead of colliding in it. The   delegated-emit path is where the second claimant comes from: a trigger the case   owner runs emits as the case's CaseActor, and BT-05-005's foreign-authority   exception deliberately leaves that tree running in the requester's store so the   activity can actually be delivered. The ledger commit must not ride along on   that exception. Before this decision the two commits could not be told apart,   because a container's single store was both the owner's and the co-located   CaseActor's \u2014 which is precisely the conflation the previous bullet rejects as a   back-end cheat. <code>CommitLogEntryBT</code> therefore declines when the actor it executes   as is not one this container hosts, and the entry arrives by replication from   the canonical log instead (#2626). Nothing is lost: the activity still carries   the CaseActor as <code>cc:</code>, which is the only way a remote store ever learns   anything (CLP-10-001).</p> </li> </ul> <p>This supersedes the \"DataLayer isolation strategy\" half of ADR-0012, which chose Option B \u2014 namespace prefix per actor in one file. ADR-0012's other three decisions (DI-1 closure lambda, IO-A queues in the DataLayer, OX-B deferral) are unaffected. ADR-0012's own reasoning for rejecting one-file-per-actor was that it \"creates many files and complicates the DataLayer reset endpoint\" and \"diverges from the MongoDB collection model\" \u2014 a prototype-convenience argument that does not survive being weighed against CM-01-001.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0073-per-actor-storage-isolation/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because cross-actor access becomes impossible rather than incorrect.   A future contributor cannot reintroduce the leak by forgetting a filter.</li> <li>Good, because it deletes guard rails instead of adding them: ARCH-13-001,   ARCH-13-002, ARCH-13-004 and ARCH-13-005 become vacuous,   <code>ActorScopedDataLayer</code> disappears, and two long-standing DataLayer test   pitfalls stop existing. (ARCH-13-003 survives, amended \u2014 see Compliance.)</li> <li>Good, because per-container behaviour now matches the deployed topology,   where each container already has its own volume.</li> <li>Good, because it makes the demo's per-container seeding protocol-correct   rather than a shared pool that merely looks partitioned. Peer seeding is   not yet correct: a peer is registered through <code>POST /actors/</code>, which mints a   local store for a foreign-authority id, so a node still claims to host   processes it does not serve. It is stored as <code>CaseLedgerEntry.payloadSnapshot</code> and    replicated to other participants via <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code>. Mutating    it before ledger storage breaks replication fidelity: other actors reconstruct    their local state from the replicated form, so they would see a different    representation than what was originally received.</p> </li> <li> <p>Outbound: a factory-constructed Activity is an artifact \u2014 it captures    exactly what was sent. The same object must serve as both the delivery payload    and the <code>payloadSnapshot</code> in the ledger entry. Adapter enrichment after the    factory seals the blob creates a gap: the ledger records one form while the    recipient receives another, breaking the accountability invariant.</p> </li> </ol> <p>Currently nothing in the type system prevents mutation. <code>as_Object</code> uses <code>ConfigDict(validate_assignment=False)</code> (ADR-0064) to stay lenient for inbound AS2 data, but has no <code>frozen=True</code>. Post-factory mutation creates a permanent divergence.</li> <li>Replication fidelity: other actors reconstruct state from the replicated   <code>payloadSnapshot</code>. If the frozen artifact is mutated before ledger storage,   replications propagate the mutated form.</li> <li>Type-level enforcement: \"do not mutate\" as a convention enforced only by   documentation is insufficient; the runtime should raise on accidental mutation   during development and testing.</li> <li>Orthogonality: <code>validate_assignment=False</code> (wire branch leniency,   ARCH-12-002) and <code>frozen=True</code> (post-construction immutability) are   independent properties that can coexist. Under Pydantic v2 the rejection is a <code>ValidationError</code> carrying   <code>type=frozen_instance</code>, not a <code>TypeError</code> \u2014 code that means to clear a field   must build a new object with <code>model_copy(update=...)</code> instead (issue #2904).</li> <li>Good, because the ledger entry and delivery payload are guaranteed identical   \u2014 the accountability invariant becomes structurally enforced.</li> <li>Good, because <code>frozen=True</code> and <code>validate_assignment=False</code> are orthogonal;   no change to the wire branch's lenient field-type policy is required.</li> <li>Bad, because any code that currently mutates wire Activity objects in place   must be refactored \u2014 three known mutation sites in <code>outbox_delivery.py</code> and   one in <code>EmitInviteActorToCaseNode._call_factory()</code> (renamed from <code>_emit()</code> by #2881).</li> <li>Bad, because <code>TriggerActivityPort</code> methods must change their return type   from <code>dict[str, Any]</code> to a frozen wire object, requiring callers to be   updated.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0074-wire-activity-artifact-immutability/#validation","title":"Validation","text":"<ul> <li><code>test/architecture/test_wire_artifact_immutability.py</code>: xfail tests for   VM-08-002 and VM-08-003; promote to passing once implementation is complete.</li> <li><code>specs/vocabulary-model.yaml</code> VM-08-002 and VM-08-003 (MUST-level requirements).</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0074-wire-activity-artifact-immutability/#more-information","title":"More Information","text":"<p>Implementation tracked in:</p> <p>Source: CONCERN-2545. Both gates defaulted to <code>AlwaysSucceed</code>, inheriting the ADR-0025 ceiling/floor rule that maps a stochastic node with <code>p \u2265 0.5</code> to <code>AlwaysSucceed</code> in DETERMINISTIC mode.</p> <p>CONCERN-2092 identified that this default creates a protocol-exploitable channel: any admitted participant \u2014 including a hostile or malfunctioning Observer admitted as a sentinel \u2014 can post <code>Add(ParticipantStatus)</code> carrying PXA state changes (<code>CS.P</code>, <code>CS.X</code>, <code>CS.A</code>) and, without any Case Owner confirmation, force PXA adoption as canonical case state and trigger embargo teardown. The current answer to \"what prevents this?\" is \"don't deploy with the default\" \u2014 a configuration posture, not a protocol guarantee.</p> <p>The design question is: what should the default backend be for security-significant Evaluator call-out gates, and should that default be implemented as a reusable pattern?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0076-security-significant-gates-default-require-case-owner-approval/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>A permissive default for gates that control unilateral state change or   embargo consequences is a protocol-level security risk, not just an   inconvenience</li> <li>The same approval pattern recurs: status adoption, invitation suggestions,   embargo proposals, and other protocol actions all benefit from a   Case Owner approval gate</li> <li>Existing AS2 <code>Offer</code>/<code>Accept</code>/<code>Reject</code> vocabulary is sufficient for the   round-trip \u2014 no new message types are needed</li> <li>The ADR-0025 ceiling/floor rule was designed for simulation-domain fuzzer   nodes where permissive defaults are a prototype-stage convenience; it does   not apply where permissiveness creates an exploitable channel</li> <li>Reusable tree factory reduces per-gate implementation cost and ensures   consistent semantics across all approval flows</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0076-security-significant-gates-default-require-case-owner-approval/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>Keep <code>AlwaysSucceed</code> as default \u2014 permissive; production hardening is    opt-in configuration. The internal Offer/Accept/Reject mechanics are an implementation detail of the default backend, not a property of the seam.</p> <p>Amended by ADR-0080 (2026-08-31). The capability-shape assignment above is incorrect, and the deny-always stub that satisfied this ADR is the symptom. At the moment authorization is first needed no answer exists, so an Evaluator asked \"is this approved?\" can only ever answer no \u2014 which is exactly what <code>RequireCaseOwnerApprovalNode</code> does. The round-trip is therefore not an implementation detail hidden behind an Evaluator seam; it determines the shape of the seam. Each gate is a conversation-state routing subtree (ASK-02-001, RSH-07-004): it routes on whether authorization has been recorded, refused, requested-and-outstanding, or never requested, and in the last case emits the request and terminates successfully \u2014 <code>SUCCESS</code> meaning I asked.</p> <p>The conservative-default requirement this ADR establishes is unchanged, and so is the project-wide floor rule for security-significant call-out points. The property is real and intended; what is missing is the decision record. Three related pieces need to be unified as normative requirements:</p> <ol> <li>The CaseActor's obligation: <code>log_index</code> order is causal order from the    CaseActor's own perspective.</li> <li>Testable temporal invariants: constraints on <code>CaseLedgerEntry.published</code>    and <code>log_index</code> that conformance tests can verify.</li> <li>Participant emission obligations: what a well-behaved participant must do    to preserve causal fidelity in the assertions it submits to the CaseActor.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0079-case-ledger-causal-ordering/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>DEMOMA-22-005 requires that invariant tests check declared causal edges   against observed ledger order, but \"observed ledger order is causal order\"   is not itself a normative spec entry.</li> <li>The ledger is the replicated source of truth for all participants; the   ordering model must be unambiguous.</li> <li>The CaseActor is a single writer (ADR-0041, CLP-01-003), which uniquely   positions it to enforce a deterministic ordering model without distributed   consensus overhead.</li> <li>Residual uncertainty about external actor clocks must be explicitly   acknowledged rather than papered over.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0079-case-ledger-causal-ordering/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<p>A. CaseActor observation order \u2014 the <code>log_index</code> sequence assigned by the CaseActor's single authoritative write path defines causal order. For internally-generated events, order is known by construction. For inbound participant assertions, the CaseActor's receipt and commit order is authoritative. The CaseActor's own <code>published</code> timestamp stamps the ledger envelope; the participant's claimed timestamp is preserved inside the <code>payloadSnapshot</code> but does not determine ledger order.</p> <p>B. Vector clock causal tracking \u2014 each activity carries a logical clock vector across all known participants. The ledger records vector values; receivers can reconstruct a partial causal order across participants without routing everything through the CaseActor.</p> <p>C. Pure wall-clock ordering \u2014 entries are ordered by their <code>published</code> timestamp alone. Log index is a convenience counter; the authoritative order is timestamp sort order.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0079-case-ledger-causal-ordering/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: A, CaseActor observation order, because:</p> <ul> <li>The CaseActor is already the single writer (ADR-0041). There is no   concurrent-write hazard to model.</li> <li>Option B requires propagating vector clocks through every wire activity.   The federated protocol has no guarantee that all participants maintain   compatible clock vectors, and the complexity cost is not justified when a   single-writer regime already resolves the ordering problem.</li> <li>Option C is unreliable: clock skew between the CaseActor's clock and   participants' clocks means physically simultaneous events can receive   arbitrary timestamp order. Timestamps are useful supporting evidence but   must not be the sole determinant.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0079-case-ledger-causal-ordering/#the-ordering-model","title":"The Ordering Model","text":"<p>The <code>CaseLedger</code> is authoritative from the CaseActor's perspective only \u2014 a postal cancellation stamp, not a forensic record. The CaseActor records the sequence in which it observed and processed events. It makes no claim about when events occurred at other actors.</p> <ul> <li>For internal events generated by the CaseActor itself (e.g., the   native case-initialization entries in ADR-0041), causal order is known by   construction: each entry is committed sequentially in a single execution   path, so the resulting <code>log_index</code> sequence is the causal sequence.</li> <li>For external events (inbound participant assertions), the CaseActor's   receipt and commit order is the authoritative ordering. The CaseActor   cannot verify causal claims about events it did not observe.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0079-case-ledger-causal-ordering/#caseactor-timestamp-obligation","title":"CaseActor Timestamp Obligation","text":"<p>The CaseActor MUST ensure:</p> <ul> <li>If event A causally precedes event B (from the CaseActor's perspective),   then <code>log_index(B) &gt; log_index(A)</code>. Gaps in the <code>log_index</code> sequence are   permitted (entries may be sparse); reversal is not.</li> <li>The <code>published</code> timestamps on consecutive ledger entries MUST be   monotonically non-decreasing in <code>log_index</code> order. An entry stamped later   in the sequence MUST NOT carry an earlier timestamp than its predecessor.</li> <li>Every ledger entry's <code>published</code> timestamp MUST be on or after the case's   own <code>published</code> timestamp. A ledger entry cannot predate the case it   belongs to.</li> </ul> <p>This is not a claim that B immediately follows A (gaps are permitted); only that B cannot appear before A.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0079-case-ledger-causal-ordering/#participant-emission-obligation","title":"Participant Emission Obligation","text":"<p>Participants MUST emit protocol messages in causal order, with timestamps that reflect the actual sequence of events. A participant MUST NOT batch events and emit them in arbitrary order. If A caused B caused C, the participant MUST send them in that sequence with monotonically non-decreasing <code>published</code> timestamps. A participant that violates this produces a malformed assertion \u2014 that is a protocol violation on the participant's part, not a CaseActor failure.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0079-case-ledger-causal-ordering/#residual-uncertainty","title":"Residual Uncertainty","text":"<p>Even with the participant obligation above, the CaseActor cannot verify causal claims from external actors. The ledger is authoritative for what the CaseActor observed; it is not a guarantee of real-world causal fidelity when external actors self-report events. The CaseActor SHOULD reject payload assertions with timestamps that are implausibly far in the future or past relative to its own clock, but it cannot eliminate all timestamp spoofing from a malicious or malfunctioning participant.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0079-case-ledger-causal-ordering/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good: the <code>log_index</code> sequence is the unambiguous causal order. The CaseActor can flag implausible   timestamps (SHOULD-level) but cannot always determine the ground truth.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0079-case-ledger-causal-ordering/#validation","title":"Validation","text":"<p>Enforcement splits along the two timestamps an entry carries, and the split is load-bearing \u2014 conflating them produces either a vacuous check or a false rejection (Issue #2824).</p> <p>Commit timestamp (<code>CaseLedgerEntry.published</code>, stamped by the CaseActor). <code>check_clp14_timestamp_invariants</code> in <code>test/ci/invariants/common.py</code>, run by every scenario through <code>universal_harness.py</code>, verifies:</p> <ul> <li><code>entry.published</code> is non-null for all entries.</li> <li><code>entry[N].published &gt;= entry[N-1].published</code> for all consecutive recorded   entries within a case.</li> <li><code>log_index</code> values are unique within a case and form a gapless sequence.</li> <li>All entries in a case share the same <code>case_id</code>.</li> <li>No entry's <code>published</code> precedes the case-creation entry's timestamp.</li> </ul> <p>A single writer stamping from one clock satisfies these by construction; the harness is what catches a replica that does not.</p> <p>Claimed timestamp (<code>payloadSnapshot.published</code>, chosen by the asserting actor). Its presence is guaranteed upstream: <code>parse_activity</code> refuses an inbound activity that carries no <code>published</code> (CLP-15-006), because ActivityStreams makes the field optional and the wire base class defaults it to <code>now_utc</code> \u2014 so a receiver that let it through could no longer tell a claimed time from its own clock, which is exactly how CLP-14-007 and CLP-14-008 were left vacuous (Issue #3149).</p> <p><code>_validate_entry_timestamps</code>, reached from every commit through <code>CreateLogEntryNode</code>, then refuses an assertion that:</p> <ul> <li>predates the case by more than the configured clock-skew tolerance   (CLP-14-006);</li> <li>sits beyond the future tolerance or staleness window (CLP-14-007,   CLP-14-008).</li> </ul> <p>and reports without refusing an assertion whose claimed timestamp regresses behind that same actor's previous assertion (CLP-15-003) \u2014 at <code>INFO</code> within the clock-skew tolerance, at <code>WARNING</code> beyond it.</p> <p>That asymmetry is the load-bearing part. CLP-15-003 binds the participant, and the CaseActor observes arrival order, not causal order: the transport gives no ordering guarantee (ADR-0037), so two assertions from one actor can legitimately be committed in the reverse of the order they were emitted, and CLP-15-003 constrains only assertions that are actually causally related. Refusing on that signal would be the reconstruction CLP-15-005 forbids \u2014 and it would discard the assertion outright, because the guarded commit precedes the effect nodes (CLP-10-006), leaving no ledger record and no retry. Recording it and reporting it keeps the signal without losing the assertion.</p> <p>Monotonicity of the claimed timestamp is scoped to one actor's stream. Applying it across actors would reintroduce option C: two participants' clocks are not comparable, so a later-committed assertion from one legitimately carries an earlier claimed time than an earlier-committed one from another. For the same reason a snapshot the CaseActor builds on a participant's behalf must carry that participant's claimed time, not the CaseActor's clock \u2014 mixing the two inside one actor's stream manufactures a regression. Thresholds are tunable via <code>AppConfig.ledger</code> (CLP-14-009).</p> <p>The participant emission obligations CLP-15-001 and CLP-15-002 are not enforceable per-assertion \u2014 that is the point of the residual uncertainty above, and CLP-15-005 forbids the attempt. They are validated at the conformance layer by <code>check_causal_edges</code>, which compares declared causal edges against observed ledger order across a whole scenario (DEMOMA-22-005).</p>"},{"location":"adr/0079-case-ledger-causal-ordering/#more-information","title":"More Information","text":"<ul> <li>Source concern: #2334</li> <li><code>DEMOMA-22-005</code> now cites this ADR instead of ADR-0041.</li> <li><code>notes/case-ledger-authority.md</code> informally anticipated this decision;   that note now cross-references this ADR.</li> <li>Issue #2207 (ADR-0041 mis-citation) can be fixed once this ADR and the   generated spec entries (CLP-14, CLP-15) are in place.</li> </ul> <p>Generated spec requirements: <code>specs/case-ledger-processing.yaml</code> CLP-14-001 through CLP-14-009, CLP-15-001 through CLP-15-005.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0080-protocol-asks-not-suspended-behaviors/","title":"Asking Permission Is a Protocol Message, Not a Suspended Behavior","text":""},{"location":"adr/0080-protocol-asks-not-suspended-behaviors/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p>Several independently filed Concerns bottom out on the same missing mechanism: core has no established way for an actor to request something it lacks the authority to do on its own, wait for an answer that arrives later, and act on that answer when it comes.</p> <p>The most visible symptom is <code>RequireCaseOwnerApprovalNode</code> (<code>vultron/core/behaviors/call_out/nodes.py</code>), the DETERMINISTIC default for both authorization gates of ADR-0046. It returns <code>Status.FAILURE</code> unconditionally. ADR-0076 specifies its intended behavior as an <code>Offer</code>/<code>Accept</code>/<code>Reject</code> round-trip with the Case Owner, but records no mechanism for hosting that exchange, and CONCERN-2812 filed the resulting gap: \"the Offer/Accept/Reject round-trip requires a BT-hosted async request/response pattern that does not exist in the framework.\"</p> <p>Three findings reframed the problem during planning:</p> <ol> <li> <p>The framework cannot host in-tree suspension, and never has. <code>BTBridge.execute_tree()</code> ticks in a <code>while iteration &lt; max_iterations</code> loop    (default 100), treats root <code>RUNNING</code> as \"keep ticking\", logs <code>ERROR</code> and    returns <code>FAILURE</code> when the loop is exhausted, and discards the tree in a    <code>finally: bt.shutdown()</code>. Meanwhile no node anywhere in <code>vultron/</code> returns    <code>Status.RUNNING</code>. EDF-04-002 requires an external decision node to return    <code>RUNNING</code> while awaiting input; that requirement has zero implementations,    and any node that complied would busy-loop and then fail.</p> </li> <li> <p>The mechanism already exists in production, built by hand, once. <code>create_recommend_actor_to_case_received_tree</code>    (<code>vultron/core/behaviors/case/suggest_actor_tree.py</code>, ADR-0026 / CM-16)    records receipt, then routes through a Selector whose branches are disjoint:    already a participant, invite in flight, Case Owner already asked and not yet    answered, or fresh. The fresh branch forwards <code>Offer(CaseParticipant)</code> to the    Case Owner and stops. Two further trees handle the <code>Accept</code> and the <code>Reject</code>.    <code>InviteInFlightNode</code> and <code>PendingOfferCaseParticipantNode</code> read open/closed    state from the case ledger via <code>find_protocol_pair</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>The durable per-ask record also exists, built by hand, once. <code>VultronOfferRecord</code> (<code>vultron/core/models/offer_record.py</code>) is a    DataLayer-backed core record keyed deterministically off an Offer's ID, written    by the adapter that calls the factory, registered as wire vocabulary, and    usable before a case exists. Its justification (ADR-0035, DL-06-002) is that a    domain fact an actor must remember MUST be recorded as core state rather than    recovered by re-reading a stored activity.</p> </li> </ol> <p>So the question was never how to host an asynchronous exchange. It was: why does each instance cost a bespoke implementation, and what is the shape that makes the next one cheap?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0080-protocol-asks-not-suspended-behaviors/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Nothing can suspend, so any design premised on suspension is unimplementable   in this framework and would require replacing the execution model</li> <li>The pattern recurs (status adoption, embargo teardown, participant admission,   ownership transfer, case proposal) and each instance has so far been rebuilt   from scratch</li> <li>The current conservative default is not merely unfinished \u2014 it is   unsatisfiable, so the authorization model of ADR-0046 and ADR-0076 cannot be   reached by any pathway</li> <li>An asker that never learns its request failed stalls silently and   indefinitely; route on conversation state.</p> <p>An actor that cannot act on its own authority emits <code>Offer(Proposal)</code> and terminates successfully. <code>SUCCESS</code> means I asked, not I was told yes. Nothing suspends, because the work is divided at the question rather than paused there: asking is one complete behavior, and acting on the answer is another, begun by the answer's arrival.</p> <p>Each gated interaction is one tree that routes on conversation state before doing anything:</p> <pre><code>GatedAction  (first fitting branch wins)\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 reply in hand      \u2192 Accept: perform the action.  Reject: refuse, record, stop.\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 asked, waiting     \u2192 stop.  Do not ask again.\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 asked, expired     \u2192 re-ask with a fresh deadline, stop.\n\u2514\u2500\u2500 never asked        \u2192 record the not-yet state, emit Offer(Proposal), stop.\n</code></pre> <p>Because the branches are disjoint, re-entry never retries completed work. This is why option 2 fails: a replayed tree re-executes its pre-gate effects and dies at the first idempotency guard, which CLP-13-001 requires to return <code>FAILURE</code> and write nothing \u2014 aborting before the gate is ever reached. Option 3 was rejected because two halves can drift; a single routing tree cannot.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0080-protocol-asks-not-suspended-behaviors/#the-rules-that-follow","title":"The rules that follow","text":"<p>Authority comes from the stored ask, never from the reply. ADR-0026's trust rule \u2014 roles come from the stored <code>Offer</code>, not the received <code>Accept</code> \u2014 is generalized: the Proposal is authoritative and the reply is only a yes. An asker reads what to do from the ask it stored, never from what the answer claims.</p> <p>Every ask carries its own deadline in <code>end_time</code>, which is already present on every AS2 object and is therefore visible to the answerer.</p> <p>Expiry consequence is fixed per ask kind; duration is configurable. Some asks remain useful when answered late (admitting a participant); others must not (adopting a case status). Whether a late reply counts is a protocol rule fixed in the spec, not a deployment setting \u2014 two actors disagreeing about whether a late answer authorized something is divergence, not preference. The duration is safe to configure per actor precisely because it travels on the wire, so both parties read the same number from the same object.</p> <p>Outstanding asks are recorded, in both directions, durably. A register holds asks an actor is waiting on and asks it owes: appended when an ask is emitted and when one is received, removed when the reply lands. It is actor-scoped rather than case-scoped, so it works before a case exists. It generalizes <code>VultronOfferRecord</code>.</p> <p>The register never authorizes. Two questions, two sources: what am I waiting on, and what do I owe? is answered by the register; was this authorized? is answered by the case ledger, always. A gate reads the ledger and never the register, so a corrupted or forged register entry cannot permit an action. This is the same division as <code>actor_participant_index</code> (fast index) versus the canonical record (authority).</p> <p>One register class, two instances. The create / close-on-named-event / time-out lifecycle, its reaping, and its enumeration are implemented once. The durable ask register and the existing in-memory <code>PendingAssertionStore</code> are two instances of it with different durability and different authority: the ask register is durable and may block; the suppressor is ephemeral, is forgotten on restart by design, and may never block (CLP-06-002, CLP-06-005). CLP-11-002 is clarified rather than reversed \u2014 do not unify the registers; do share the lifecycle.</p> <p>Expiry is noticed opportunistically, plus a Sentinel seam. The next entry into a tree observes an expired ask, and a peer's own retry is frequently the clock. For prompt reaping, core exposes a general-purpose <code>reap-expired-asks</code> trigger. Per <code>notes/coordination-agents.md</code>, a Sentinel operates exclusively on the call-in surface and has no BT call-out point, so reaping belongs to an external watcher rather than a loop inside core. The same endpoint makes expiry testable causally instead of by elapsed time, which EDF-06-001 requires.</p> <p>Asks are visible to the case. An ask is an ordinary canonical entry and replicates normally, so an outstanding decision \u2014 and a stalled one \u2014 is visible to participants. Consequently an ask MUST NOT carry content that cannot be disclosed to every case participant; private rationale belongs in a directly-addressed <code>Note</code>. Delivering the fact of an ask while directing its detail would require redaction with proofs, which the project does not have \u2014 <code>notes/stub-objects.md</code> describes redaction as future work \u2014 and committing a stub instead would violate CLP-02-003 and CLP-07-012.</p> <p>Failure to process is answered, not left to time out. An authenticated sender whose message fails after authentication receives <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code>. This closes the asker's register entry immediately rather than costing it a full deadline of silence for a failure that took milliseconds. It is a dedicated object type rather than a reason field on an existing reply, because SE-08-003 prefers a dedicated type over field-level discrimination, and <code>Create(&lt;minted object&gt;)</code> is the established idiom (<code>Create(CaseProposal)</code>) \u2014 <code>Reject</code> presupposes something rejectable, which unreadable traffic does not provide. Unauthenticated or unparseable traffic is dropped silently; explaining a parser failure to a stranger is an oracle.</p> <p>The fault carries a failure class and a pointer, never an echo: in the protocol-invalid case a typed copy of the failed activity cannot be constructed, because constructing it is what failed. It is structured as RFC 9457 Problem Details, with fault types as URIs minted in the Vultron namespace (VM-10-001, ADR-0069) \u2014 so the canonical list is dereferenceable and extensible without a schema change.</p> <p>The unreadable message never enters the ledger; there is no legible assertion to record. The fault statement does \u2014 it is a true, legible statement about a message that arrived, replicated like any other recorded entry. It is not per-actor observability content, so CLP-07-004 is unaffected: the fact of a fault is protocol history, while the diagnosis of why belongs in the actor's own log.</p> <p>A duplicate request after a reply re-sends the stored reply. Where a request is repeated because the reply was lost, the answerer re-sends the frozen original unchanged (VM-08-003), same identity. It reads as the original arriving late rather than a second decision, which is what CP-05-005's irrevocability rule requires.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0080-protocol-asks-not-suspended-behaviors/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good: no framework change is needed; the execution model that appeared to be   the blocker turns out never to have been on the path</li> <li>Good: <code>RequireCaseOwnerApprovalNode</code> becomes reachable, so the ADR-0046 /   ADR-0076 authorization model is implementable for the first time</li> <li>Good: the same mechanism serves permission asks, participant admission,   ownership transfer, and pre-case proposal handshakes \u2014 the register is   actor-scoped, so it does not require a case to exist</li> <li>Good: a Case Owner gains an enumerable list of decisions they owe, which is   the surface a human, a UI, or an agent acts through</li> <li>Good: silent indefinite stalls become bounded \u2014 by a deadline, by a fault, or   by a peer's retry</li> <li>Neutral: <code>RequireCaseOwnerApprovalNode</code> is deleted rather than completed. Because <code>actor_slug()</code> strips scheme and authority, two ids with the same final path segment but different authorities (e.g. <code>http://finder:7999/.../alice</code> and <code>http://vendor:7999/.../alice</code>) mapped to the same SQLite file. The wire branch (<code>as_*</code> classes under <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/</code>) is the ActivityStreams 2.0 projection: camelCase keys, AS2 <code>@context</code>, lenient field types. The core branch (<code>CoreObject</code> subclasses under <code>vultron/core/models/</code>) is the domain model: snake_case, narrowed types, and \u2014 since ADR-0036 \u2014 nested dimension objects where the wire keeps flat fields. ADR-0017 established the two-branch hierarchy and ADR-0062 established where wire\u2192core normalisation happens.</p> <p>The boundary between them exists in the type system but almost nothing enforces it, and the knowledge needed to cross it is duplicated four ways.</p> <p>1. \"Which fields are AS2 references\" is known in three places. The type annotations (<code>as_ObjectRef</code>-typed fields) are the truth. <code>_AS_OBJECT_REF_FIELDS</code> in <code>vultron/adapters/driven/db_record.py</code> is a hand-maintained frozenset whose own comment describes it as \"ActivityStreams fields typed as <code>as_ObjectRef</code>\" \u2014 a copy of the annotations that can drift. And individual <code>to_core()</code> methods call <code>_scalar_ref_id_or_value(...)</code> on those fields by hand, a third restatement.</p> <p>2. The core\u2194wire pairing is known in four places, none of them declarative. <code>As2WireRenderAdapter.render()</code> resolves a core class to its wire counterpart with <code>VOCABULARY.get(type(obj).__name__)</code> \u2014 that is, it relies on the bare-name collision between <code>VOCABULARY</code> and <code>CORE_VOCABULARY</code> as an implicit pairing index. The collision is between registry keys, not class names: the wire class is <code>as_CaseParticipant</code>, but it registers under the bare key <code>CaseParticipant</code>, which is also the core class's <code>__name__</code>, so looking the core name up in <code>VOCABULARY</code> happens to land on the wire counterpart. <code>_WIRE_ACTOR_TO_CORE</code> in <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/objects/vultron_actor.py</code> is a hand-rolled pairing table for actor types only, built because someone needed exactly this mapping and no general one existed. <code>_NORMALIZE_WIRE_TO_CORE</code> in <code>db_record.py</code> is a third hand-maintained list of paired types. And three registries (<code>VOCABULARY</code>, <code>CORE_VOCABULARY</code>, <code>CORE_TYPE_MAP</code>) are chained by <code>find_in_vocabulary()</code>.</p> <p>This is why issue #2403 \u2014 \"make the two <code>type_</code> namespaces disjoint\" \u2014 has looked risky rather than obvious: the collision it proposes to remove is currently load-bearing. Fifteen wire registry keys shadow a core type's key, and the render adapter depends on that shadowing to find its counterpart.</p> <p>3. Projection is declarative in one direction and hand-written in the other. <code>VultronAS2Object.from_core()</code> is generic: dump, apply the declarative <code>_field_map</code> renames, validate. <code>to_core()</code> raises <code>NotImplementedError</code> at the base and is overridden in twelve wire classes \u2014 195 lines across the twelve overrides plus the base raiser, against 152 lines of <code>from_core()</code>, so 354 lines is the both-directions total. Six of those overrides are pure boilerplate around one per-type fact:</p> <pre><code>data = self._to_core_data()\ndata.pop(\"context_\", None)                             # repeated 4x\ndata[\"attributed_to\"] = _scalar_ref_id_or_value(...)   # repeated 3x\ndata[\"context\"]       = _scalar_ref_id_or_value(...)   # repeated 3x\nreturn CoreX.model_validate(data)                      # &lt;- only per-type part\n</code></pre> <p>The single per-type element is which core class to validate against \u2014 the pairing from (2). A generic <code>to_core()</code> mirroring the generic <code>from_core()</code> is blocked only by the absence of a declarative pairing table.</p> <p>4. Boundary enforcement lives in three places. ADR-0062 named this as its own negative consequence: \"the same projection is expressed in two places, and a reader can reasonably wonder which one is authoritative.\" Since then a third appeared \u2014 the per-class reject-guard in <code>CaseParticipant</code>.</p> <p>Meanwhile the boundary is not actually closed. Pydantic v2 defaults to <code>extra=\"ignore\"</code>, so handing a wire-shaped payload to a core type silently discards every key whose only spelling is snake_case. Every mechanism that needs the pairing either re-derives it from a name collision or hand-maintains a private copy. Introducing one authoritative pairing registry makes the other three duplications collapse rather than requiring separate fixes, and it converts issue #2403 from a risky rename into a consequence.</p> <p>Concretely:</p> <ol> <li> <p>A declarative pairing registry becomes the single source of truth for    core\u2194wire correspondence. It subsumes the bare-name collision that    <code>As2WireRenderAdapter</code> relies on, <code>_WIRE_ACTOR_TO_CORE</code>, and    <code>_NORMALIZE_WIRE_TO_CORE</code>. Once the pairing is explicit, <code>VOCABULARY</code> and    <code>CORE_VOCABULARY</code> are free to use disjoint keys \u2014 which is what #2403 asked    for, obtained as a by-product rather than as a rename with an unmeasured blast    radius.</p> </li> <li> <p>AS2 ref-field sets are derived from the type annotations, once.    <code>_AS_OBJECT_REF_FIELDS</code> is deleted and the scattered    <code>_scalar_ref_id_or_value(...)</code> calls in individual <code>to_core()</code> methods are    replaced by the derived set. The annotations were always the truth; nothing    else needs to restate them.</p> </li> <li> <p>A generic <code>to_core()</code> mirrors the generic <code>from_core()</code>, driven by    <code>_field_map</code>, the derived ref-field set, and the pairing registry. Six of the    twelve hand-written overrides are deleted outright; <code>as_EmbargoEvent</code>'s    reduces to a declarative drop-list. Only the genuinely structural    projections \u2014 <code>as_VulnerabilityCase</code>, <code>as_CaseStatus</code>,    <code>as_CaseParticipant</code>, which project nested children \u2014 keep bespoke code.</p> </li> <li> <p>Projection logic moves off the wire classes into translator modules on the    adapter side. This is what makes ARCH-22 achievable rather than    redefined: wire classes become pure AS2 shape with no domain knowledge, and    the translator modules \u2014 which are allowed to see both branches \u2014 own the    pairing registry and the projection. ARCH-12-005 is amended accordingly.    ADR-0063's decision stands; its mechanism is revised, because the render    adapter no longer calls <code>wire_cls.from_core()</code> but delegates to the    translator.</p> </li> <li> <p>A <code>WireParsePort</code> completes the ADR-0063 symmetry. It is    strictly stronger than a camelCase-specific guard: a typo, a renamed field,    and a stale key are all caught, not only wire spellings. Two central    cleanups are prerequisites, each defensible independently:</p> </li> <li> <p>computed fields (<code>embargo_adherence</code>, a <code>@computed_field</code> per ADR-0056) must      be stripped before re-validation, because they appear in <code>model_dump()</code>      output but are not settable;</p> </li> <li>a <code>model_validator(mode=\"before\")</code> must not inject an alias key beside a      field-name key that the incoming payload already carries. <code>VultronBase</code>      resolves <code>validate_by_name=True</code>, so both <code>id</code> and <code>id_</code> are sanctioned      inputs \u2014 but only one of them may be present when validation proper begins,      or the other is left over as <code>extra</code>. Each injecting validator must      therefore normalise the payload to one spelling before writing its computed      value.</li> </ol> <p>With <code>extra=\"forbid\"</code> in place, <code>_NORMALIZE_WIRE_TO_CORE</code>, its grow-only    ratchet test, and the per-class camelCase reject-guards are all dead code and    are deleted. The formal protocol (Message Types) defines 28 shorthand symbols partitioned by which state machine a message belongs to: RM, EM, CS, and General. The implementation has a <code>SEMANTIC_REGISTRY</code> of AS2 wire activities, each pairing an <code>ActivityPattern</code> with a <code>MessageSemantics</code> value, an event class, a use case, and a rendering phrase.</p> <p>These two sets do not correspond one-to-one, and until now nothing said so plainly. The prevailing implicit assumption \u2014 that a shorthand and a wire activity are two names for one thing \u2014 is wrong in three distinct ways, and it has already produced a normative defect and a documented-but-never-built wire format.</p> <p>Concretely, at the time of this decision:</p> <ul> <li>Several shorthands collapse onto one wire activity. <code>CV</code> and <code>CF</code> both ride   <code>as_ParticipantStatus.vf_state</code>; <code>CP</code>, <code>CX</code>, and <code>CA</code> all ride   <code>as_CaseStatus.pxa_state</code>; <code>EV</code>, <code>EJ</code>, and <code>EC</code> are sent as <code>EP</code>, <code>ER</code>, and   <code>EA</code>. The discriminator is a payload field, not the activity type.</li> <li>Several shorthands expand into many wire activities. <code>EP</code> is realized by   four; <code>GI</code> covers the whole note lifecycle and the actor-suggestion   handshake. The <code>Create(X)</code> + <code>Add(X \u2192 Y)</code> split is itself an expansion with no   formal counterpart at all.</li> <li>Roughly half the registry has no formal counterpart: case lifecycle,   participant roster, invitations, role delegation, ownership transfer, case   proposal, and ledger replication.</li> </ul> <p>Two consequences of the unstated assumption were already live defects. MSM-03-001 through MSM-03-003 asserted at <code>MUST</code> that <code>CV</code>, <code>CF</code>, and <code>CD</code> dispatch as <code>ADD_CASE_STATUS_TO_CASE</code> and that <code>as_CaseStatus</code> carries <code>vendor_aware</code> / <code>fix_ready</code> / <code>fix_deployed</code> payload flags. No such fields exist; the V/F/D dimensions are participant-scoped and live on <code>as_ParticipantStatus</code> per ADR-0075. And <code>howto/activitypub/activities/error.md</code> documents a four-way wire fault taxonomy (<code>RmError</code>, <code>EmError</code>, <code>CsError</code>, <code>GmError</code>, discriminated by <code>as:inReplyTo</code>) that exists in no ontology file and no code, while <code>ActivityPattern.in_reply_to_</code> is used by no registered pattern.</p> <p>The question this ADR settles: is the divergence a defect to be driven to zero, or a deliberate property to be documented?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0083-formal-message-set-and-as2-vocabulary-are-different-shapes/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The formal message set is normative and versioned with the protocol   specification; it must remain stable for interoperability and conformance   claims.</li> <li>The AS2 wire vocabulary must remain idiomatic ActivityStreams, reusing existing   verbs rather than minting Vultron-specific ones.</li> <li>Implementers need one place that answers \"what is this message, when is it   sent, what does it look like on the wire, and where do I handle it.\"</li> <li>Silent divergence between the two sets has already produced a wrong <code>MUST</code>   requirement and a phantom wire format. Whatever is chosen must make divergence   visible rather than merely absent.</li> <li>Hand-maintained correspondence tables in this project have a demonstrated   failure record.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0083-formal-message-set-and-as2-vocabulary-are-different-shapes/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Treat the divergence as deliberate and make the mapping a first-class,   rendered artifact</li> <li>Force the wire vocabulary to mirror the formal message set one-to-one</li> <li>Retire the formal message set and treat the wire vocabulary as the only   message definition</li> <li>Leave both sets as they are and document neither the mapping nor the divergence</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0083-formal-message-set-and-as2-vocabulary-are-different-shapes/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: treat the divergence as deliberate and make the mapping a first-class, rendered artifact, because the two sets are answering different questions and flattening either one onto the other destroys information that the protocol needs.</p> <p>The formal set partitions by which state machine a message concerns, which is the right axis for reasoning about protocol conformance and for the transition tables. The wire vocabulary partitions by what ActivityStreams verb and object faithfully express the act, which is the right axis for interoperability with ActivityPub tooling. Neither axis is derivable from the other, so the mapping is irreducible and belongs in the specification rather than in a reader's head.</p> <p>Three commitments follow.</p> <p>1. The mapping is normative and bidirectional. <code>specs/message-semantics-mapping.yaml</code> (MSM) is the authoritative bridge. It records collapses and expansions explicitly, and every row carries a status saying which kind of relationship it is. MSM-04 adds the General shorthands that were previously absent from the corpus.</p> <p>2. Fault and acknowledgement mechanisms are partitioned on their own axes, and that is recorded rather than treated as a gap. MSM-05 specifies both:</p> <ul> <li>Faults are partitioned by failure mode, not by state machine:   <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code> for received-but-not-understood, <code>as:Reject</code> for   understood-but-declined, and <code>Create(Note)</code> / <code>Add(Note \u2192 Case)</code> for a   condition needing narrative explanation. Failure mode is actionable to a   receiver in a way that originating state machine is not, which is why the   formal <code>RE</code>/<code>EE</code>/<code>CE</code>/<code>GE</code> partition was not reproduced.</li> <li>Acknowledgement of ledger-replicated state is cumulative and implicit via   hash-chain continuity: a matching <code>prev_log_hash</code> is the acknowledgement, and a   mismatch triggers <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> and gap-fill replay. Per-message   <code>EK</code>/<code>CK</code>/<code>GK</code> would be redundant. <code>RK</code> survives as a real wire activity   because report submission is not ledger-replicated.</li> </ul> <p>Both were previously recorded in MSM only as absences (\"no AS2 wire representation\"), which invited the reading that the behaviour was unimplemented. It is implemented; it is shaped differently.</p> <p>3. Reference material is rendered from the registries, never hand-written. MSM-06 requires the consolidated per-message-type pages under <code>docs/reference/messages/</code> to render their mapping tables at build time from the MSM spec registry joined against <code>SEMANTIC_REGISTRY</code>, following the existing <code>docs/reference/specs/*.md</code> pattern, and requires a ratchet asserting every registry entry reaches its designated primary page. None of that machinery exists yet \u2014 this ADR decides the approach; the pages and the ratchet are built by the issues listed under \"More Information\".</p>"},{"location":"adr/0083-formal-message-set-and-as2-vocabulary-are-different-shapes/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because the collapses become documented facts rather than traps. An   implementer reading the <code>CS</code> page learns that six shorthands share two wire   activities and which payload field discriminates them.</li> <li>Good, because the wire vocabulary can evolve toward better ActivityStreams   idiom without being pinned to the formal set's partitioning, and the formal set   can stay stable for conformance without being dragged by prototype churn.</li> <li>Good, because divergence becomes detectable once MSM-06-002's ratchet is built:   a new registry entry with no MSM row, or an MSM row with no registry entry, will   fail a check instead of quietly becoming a stale table.</li> <li>Good, because it caught the MSM-03 defect: the mapping could not be rendered   correctly from an incorrect spec, which forced the error into the open.</li> <li>Bad, because there are now two vocabularies a contributor must learn, and the   mapping is a third artifact to keep correct.</li> <li>Bad, because the mapping is genuinely many-to-many, so no simple lookup table   suffices and the reference pages must carry per-row status annotations to be   honest.</li> <li>Neutral, because the divergences MSM-05 records are now visible enough to   reopen deliberately. Owner-close advances exactly two participants to <code>RM.CLOSED</code>: the Case Owner (the leaver) and the Case Actor (CM-23-002). It advances no others. A <code>Leave</code> advances only the leaving actor's own RM state, regardless of the rung it was on, because a <code>Leave</code> is that actor's own self-declaratory closure act (ADR-0084). Every remaining (\"bystander\") participant retains its last RM state when the case closes around it; closure never force-advances a participant that did not itself leave. Atomicity is a statement about what gets written; it says nothing about what gets reported.</p> <p>A third question surfaced while investigating and is settled here because leaving it implicit is what invited the confusion: the receive path deliberately does the opposite of the emit path, and nothing recorded why the two differ.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0086-report-every-violation-reject-the-batch/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Atomicity and diagnostic completeness are independent properties. A census of the <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> tree (#3101) found that lookup open-coded at ~78 call sites, each having independently re-invented the \"case evaporated underneath me\" branch. The dispositions had drifted apart along two axes that no design ever reconciled:</p> <ul> <li>Verdict on absence. Some sites returned <code>FAILURE</code>, some <code>SUCCESS</code>, some   fell through with an empty result \u2014 with no principle distinguishing them.</li> <li>Loudness. The authority commits a <code>CaseLedgerEntry</code> and broadcasts; the participant asserts and waits for the broadcast.</p> <p>The distinction is correct and load-bearing. The problem is twofold.</p> <p>First, the question is answered in many places, in different ways. There is no single shared way to determine authority, so the check is re-derived per site and the discipline is held together only by convention. Specs CLP-09-002 and CLP-09-003 mandate commit-authorization ratchets \u2014 an enumeration that fails when a site commits unguarded, and a coverage test that every use case reaches a commit \u2014 but those enforcement tests are not yet implemented; only CLP-09-001's per-node role check has unit tests today. A ratchet, specified or in place, only fires when a site forgets to check \u2014 the signature of a convention, not a structural guarantee (<code>notes/case-ledger-authority.md</code>, \"Authorization Was a Convention, Not a Gate\").</p> <p>Second \u2014 and this is the deeper error \u2014 some of those ways determine authority from the wrong thing. They key off where a thing is hosted or the shape of a URL rather than off the role. \"Case Actor\" is a placeholder name \u2014 the readable label a demo gives to whichever actor is enacting <code>CASE_MANAGER</code>, exactly like \"vendor\" or \"finder\". Nobody adopts a \"Case Actor\" identity. The identity is defined entirely by \"the entity enacting <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> must do these things.\" Treating the name or URL as a protocol signal elevates a demo convention to protocol truth.</p> <p>This ADR settles one decision: authority, recognition, and routing key off the <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> role, and nothing else. The Vultron Protocol defines four levels, each building on the previous:</p> L1 \u2014 Syntax Well-formed messages that conform to the wire format.   This level is covered by the wire format specifications. L2 \u2014 Semantic Correct state transitions in response to received messages and local events.   This level is covered by the Vultron Protocol spec (VP) and the   Transition Functions. L3 \u2014 Behavioral <p>Correct observable outputs \u2014 the right messages emitted and the right states reached   in response to a given (input state + received message/event) combination.   This level is covered by the protocol behavioral specifications:</p> <ul> <li>RMB \u2014 Report Management Behavioral Requirements</li> <li>EMB \u2014 Embargo Management Behavioral Requirements</li> <li>CSB \u2014 CVD Case State Behavioral Requirements</li> </ul> L4 \u2014 Process Correct internal decision structure \u2014 for example, precondition checks before state writes   before protocol effects, audit-log ordering, and idempotency guarantees.   This level is enforceable only through a reference implementation.   The <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> behavior tree layer in this repository provides the   reference implementation for L4. <p>Start with L2</p> <p>Most implementations will naturally achieve L1 by using a compliant message serializer. L2 conformance is the practical minimum for interoperability: a Participant that transitions states correctly can exchange messages with any other L2-conformant Participant. During development and simulation, each call-out point is filled by a fuzzer node: a stub that returns a random SUCCESS or FAILURE based on a probability. In production, you replace a fuzzer node with a real capability backend that applies actual business logic.</p> <p>The three-step process is:</p> <ol> <li>Identify the call-out point you want to implement (find the fuzzer node, read its blackboard contract).</li> <li>Implement a backend factory that satisfies the <code>CallOutBackendFactory</code> Protocol.</li> <li>Wire the backend by passing it through the domain bundle to the tree builder.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#step-1-identify-the-call-out-point","title":"Step 1 \u2014 Identify the call-out point","text":""},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#find-the-fuzzer-node","title":"Find the fuzzer node","text":"<p>Every call-out point in the reference implementation has a corresponding fuzzer node in <code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/</code>. Any callable that matches this signature is valid \u2014 a plain function, a lambda, or a class with <code>__call__</code>. No registration, inheritance, or decorator is required.</p>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#implementing-as-a-py_treesbehaviourbehaviour-subclass","title":"Implementing as a <code>py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour</code> subclass","text":"<p>Subclass <code>py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour</code> and implement both <code>setup()</code> and <code>update()</code>. The <code>setup()</code> method runs once when the tree is first started \u2014 it registers the blackboard keys your node will write. The <code>update()</code> method runs on every BT tick.</p> <p>Blackboard access requires <code>setup()</code></p> <p>py_trees does not create <code>self.blackboard</code> automatically. These include:</p> <ul> <li><code>as:Read</code></li> <li><code>as:View</code></li> <li><code>as:Listen</code></li> </ul> <p>Since most CVD cases are text-centric, <code>as:Read</code> is the most commonly used activity. <code>as:View</code> and <code>as:Listen</code> activities may be used in some cases, such as when a case participant views a video or listens to an audio recording.</p> <p><code>RmReadReport</code> is defined as a subclass of <code>as:Read</code> to indicate that a report has been read. This allows the receiver of a report to acknowledge receipt without indicating anything more than that the report has been read. That leaves <code>RmValidateReport</code> and <code>RmInvalidateReport</code> to indicate a more specific action (accept, reject) on the part of the receiver.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\n    subgraph RM:Received\n        a{Accept?}\n        subgraph as:Read\n            RmReadReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Start\n        subgraph as:Offer\n            RmSubmitReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Accepted\n        subgraph as:Accept\n            RmValidateReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Invalid\n        subgraph as:Reject\n            RmInvalidateReport\n        end\n    end\n    a --&gt;|y| RmValidateReport\n    a --&gt;|undecided| RmReadReport\n    a --&gt;|n| RmInvalidateReport\n    RmSubmitReport --&gt; a</code></pre> <p>More Acknowledgements in the Ontology</p> <p>The Vultron AS ontology defines a number of ActivityStreams activities that can serve as the various acknowledgements that are used in the Vultron protocol. These include messages that are specifically <code>as:inReplyTo</code> a message defined as one of the core protocol message types.</p> <p>For example, it is not necessary to send a separate <code>RmReadReport</code> message if the <code>RmValidateReport</code> message is sent as a reply to the <code>RmSubmitReport</code> message. The <code>RmValidateReport</code> message logically indicates that the report has been read in order to have been validated.</p> <p>Like, Dislike and Flag</p> <p>The ActivityStreams vocabulary also includes actions that indicate an opinion  about a message or object, such as <code>as:Like</code>, <code>as:Dislike</code>, and <code>as:Flag</code>. While these may be relevant to implementations of the Vultron protocol, no specific use cases for them are defined at this time.</p>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/acknowledge/#acknowledgement-for-ledger-replicated-state","title":"Acknowledgement for ledger-replicated state","text":"<p>The <code>RK</code> pattern above applies to report submission, which is not ledger-replicated.
