part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Inviting an actor to a case is a way to add them as a participant in the case. The invitation is sent to the actor as an <code>as:Invite</code> activity. Depending on the actor's response, they may become a participant in the case.</p> <p> </p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Invite Actor to Case\n---\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor O as Case Owner\n    participant CA as CASE_MANAGER\n    actor A as Actor\n    activate O\n    O -&gt;&gt; CA: [trigger invite]\n    activate CA\n    CA -&gt;&gt;+ A: Invite(actor=CASE_MANAGER, object=Actor, target=Case, attributedTo=CaseOwner)\n    note over A: Consider invitation\n    alt Accept Invitation\n        A --&gt;&gt; CA: Accept(object=Invite)\n        CA -&gt;&gt; CA: Create(object=CaseParticipant(actor=Actor), target=Case)\n        note over CA: Actor becomes participant in case\n    else Reject Invitation\n        A --&gt;&gt; CA: Reject(object=Invite)\n        note over CA: Actor is not participant in case\n    end\n    deactivate A\n    deactivate CA\n    deactivate O</code></pre> <p>CASE_MANAGER routing (PCR-08-007, PCR-08-008)</p> <p>The <code>Invite</code> activity is sent by the CASE_MANAGER, not the Case Owner. The Case Owner triggers the invite, but the CASE_MANAGER MUST be the ActivityStreams <code>actor</code> on the outbound <code>Invite</code>. The <code>attributedTo</code> field on the activity MAY carry the Case Owner's ID to record who initiated it.</p> <p>The invitee MUST address their <code>Accept</code> or <code>Reject</code> reply to the CASE_MANAGER, not directly back to the Case Owner. The CASE_MANAGER is the authoritative recipient of all case-management handshake messages after case creation.</p> <p>Invite vs Add?</p> <p>When a case is first created, the Case Owner and any known participants (e.g., the Reporter) should be automatically added to the case. It's not even necessary for these to be emitted as separate <code>as:Add</code> activities. The <code>as:Create</code> activity for the case can include the Case Owner and any known participants as <code>CaseParticipant</code> objects. See Initializing a Case for more.</p> <p>However, over the lifespan of a case, there may be other actors that were not already involved at the time the case was created, but who should be invited to participate in the case. This is where the <code>as:Invite</code> activity comes in.</p> <p>Avoid bogging down in details</p> <p>Adding a participant to a case involves creating the participant object and a participant status object. As discussed elsewhere, emitting separate <code>as:Create</code> and <code>as:Add</code> events for each of these events is likely overkill.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\n\na[create participant] --&gt; b[create participant status]\nb --&gt; c[add participant status to participant]\nc --&gt; d[add participant to case]</code></pre> <p>Instead, a single <code>as:Create</code> event for the participant, already containing a status object, could be emitted, with the <code>target</code> of the <code>as:Create</code> event as the case object.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\na[create particpant with status] --&gt;|target| b[case]</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/invite_actor/#invite-to-case","title":"Invite to Case","text":"<p>A vendor invites a coordinator to a case.</p> The Case Owner triggers the invite action, but the CASE_MANAGER MUST be the ActivityStreams <code>actor</code> on the outbound <code>Invite</code> activity. The invited actor MUST send their <code>Accept</code> or <code>Reject</code> reply to the CASE_MANAGER, not directly to the Case Owner. See Inviting an Actor to a Case for the full sequence diagram.</p> <p>Create or Add?</p> <p>There appears to be some logical interchangeability of <code>as:Create</code>  with <code>as:Add</code> since both include a <code>target</code> property that can be used to specify the object to which the new object is being added. We chose to  represent them separately here to acknowledge the difference between creating a new object and adding an existing object to another object, but in an actual implementation it may be acceptable to use either activity for both cases. It seems likely that the general idea should be to use <code>as:Create</code> when creating a new object to  add to another object (as the <code>target</code> of the activity), and <code>as:Add</code> when adding an existing object to another object. </p> <p>Vultron intends to be consistent with however ActivityPub handles this. An <code>Offer</code> can include a <code>Report</code> object that the sender created immediately before sending. While a <code>Create(Report)</code> technically precedes an <code>Offer(Report)</code>, in practice the receiver usually only observes the <code>Offer</code> because the report was created entirely on the sender's side.</p> <p>In other cases the <code>Report</code> may have been created earlier or by a different actor (for example, a platform or intermediary). When that happens the <code>Create(Report)</code> and <code>Offer(Report)</code> are distinct activities. We show both patterns here to cover both workflows.</p> <p>When would <code>Create(Report)</code> be separate from <code>Offer(Report)</code>?</p> <p>A Reporter files a report with a bug-bounty platform that implements Vultron. not considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Role delegation is the protocol flow by which the Case Owner (or another authorized participant) offers a specific <code>CVDRole</code> to another actor in the case. The recipient may accept or reject the offer.</p> <p>The canonical wire format uses a dedicated <code>as_CaseParticipantRole</code> object (introduced in ADR-0039) to unambiguously distinguish a role offer from a case ownership-transfer offer. Both previously serialized as <code>Offer(VulnerabilityCase)</code>, creating an ambiguity resolved only by registry ordering. Case","text":"<p>This page is not normative</p> <p>This page is not considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>During the course of coordinating a case, an existing case participant might recognize that another actor should be invited to participate in the case. The following mechanisms provide a way for a case participant to suggest that another actor be invited to participate in the case.</p> <p> </p> <p>Why Suggest instead of just Invite?</p> <p>The process described here makes an assumption that there is a case owner who is responsible for coordinating the  case. Participants having the case owner role can in principle just directly invite other actors to participate in  the case, and they might not need the suggestion mechanism described here. However, this mechanism is included to account for the possibilities that:</p> <ul> <li>there could be multiple case owners, and they might not all agree on who should be invited to participate in the    case.</li> <li>a non-case-owner participant might want to suggest that another actor be invited to participate in the case</li> </ul> <p>Of these, the latter is the more likely scenario, but the mechanism described here can be used in either case.    </p> <p>Reasons to Invite other Actors</p> <p>There are many reasons why a case participant might want to suggest another actor to participate in a case. The following are some examples:</p> <ul> <li>A finder, having reported to one vendor, might further discover that the vulnerability is actually in a    third-party library, and suggest inviting the library vendor to participate in the case.</li> <li>A vendor might be a participant in (but not the owner of) a case, and wants to suggest that the case owner   invite a sector-specific coordinator to participate in the case to address critical infrastructure concerns.</li> <li>A reporter participant might suggest a technical expert (for example, a member of a protocol working group) to    include in the case.</li> <li>A coordinator might suggest to the case owner that a large deployer be invited to participat in a case to    address concerns about the impact of deploying a fix for a vulnerability on infrastructure and operations.</li> </ul> <p>Below is a sequence diagram showing the process of suggesting an actor for a case. We used a sequence diagram instead of a flow chart since the process is relatively simple and the sequence diagram is easier to read.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Suggesting an Actor for a Case (ADR-0026 CaseActor-routed)\n---\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor A as Recommender\n    participant CA as CaseActor\n    actor B as Case Owner\n    actor D as Invitee\n    Note over A: Recognize that Actor should be invited\n    A -&gt;&gt; CA: Offer(object=Actor, target=Case)\n    activate CA\n    Note over CA: Record in ledger, assign default roles\n    CA -&gt;&gt; B: Offer(object=CaseParticipant{actor,roles}, target=Case, origin=Offer.id)\n    activate B\n    alt Accept Suggestion\n        B -&gt;&gt; CA: Accept(object=Offer(CaseParticipant))\n        CA -&gt;&gt; A: AcceptActorRecommendation\n        CA -&gt;&gt;+ D: Invite(CaseStub + embargo + roles)\n        note over D: Respond to invitation (not shown)\n        deactivate D\n    else Reject Suggestion\n        B -&gt;&gt; CA: Reject(object=Offer(CaseParticipant))\n        CA -&gt;&gt; A: RejectActorRecommendation\n    end\n    deactivate B\n    deactivate CA</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/suggest_actor/#recommend-actor","title":"Recommend Actor","text":"<p>A participant recommends another actor to the CaseActor by sending an <code>Offer</code> activity with the <code>object</code> property set to the actor being recommended and the <code>target</code> set to the case. A broad port is generic and untyped (e.g., <code>DataLayer</code> with <code>get(table, id)</code>, <code>by_type(type)</code>). It is the only protocol-salient signal of authority: an actor is the authority for a case iff it holds this role in the case roster.</li> <li>A Case Actor is the concrete actor the prototype/demo implements to hold <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> \u2014 a specific identity labelled <code>case-actor</code>. It is not a synonym for the authority and not an identity to match on: its name and URL are cosmetic and carry no protocol meaning (ADR-0088).</li> <li>A case actor service is the provisioning endpoint (<code>case_actor_service_url</code>) that spawns <code>case-actor</code> identities \u2014 a hosting concern, not the authority.</li> <li>Recommendation: In protocol-normative prose, name the authority \"the CASE_MANAGER\" (the role holder), never \"the CaseActor\". Reserve \"CaseActor\" for the prototype/demo actor that enacts the role, and \"case actor service\" for the provisioning endpoint. Never determine authority, recognition, or routing from the <code>case-actor</code> name or URL shape, and never compare <code>actor_id</code> against a computed <code>case_actor_id</code> to decide authority \u2014 gate on the role (CM-24-004, CM-02-011).</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"Participant Case Replica\" vs. \"Case State\":</p> <ul> <li>A Participant Case Replica is a local copy of case state on a participant's node; must be seeded via Trust Bootstrap and maintain Eventual Consistency with the CASE_MANAGER's authoritative state.</li> <li>Case State (CS) is the formal six-dimensional state model (VfDpxa lattice) tracking vulnerability awareness and readiness.</li> <li>Recommendation: Use \"Participant Case Replica\" for participant-local state copies; \"Case State\" for the formal model.</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"CVDRole\" vs. \"CVDRolesFlag\":</p> <ul> <li>CVDRole is a StrEnum (string enum) representing individual, atomic roles; participants hold zero or more roles as <code>list[CVDRole]</code>; this is the preferred representation for all new code.</li> <li>CVDRolesFlag is a legacy Flag enum (bitmask) used only by the <code>vultron.bt</code> simulator layer; it existed before the migration to list-based roles and is retained for backward compatibility only.</li> <li>Recommendation: Always use <code>list[CVDRole]</code> in new code; never use CVDRolesFlag outside the <code>vultron.bt</code> simulator. When discussing roles, say \"CVDRole\" or \"role list,\" never \"CVDRoles\" (plural, deprecated name).</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"Call-Out Point\" vs. \"Fuzzer Node\":</p> <ul> <li>A Call-Out Point is the abstract concept \u2014 a BT location requiring external input.</li> <li>A Fuzzer Node is the concrete simulator-layer stub that occupies that location until a real capability is wired in.</li> <li>Recommendation: Use \"Call-Out Point\" when discussing design or integration seams; use \"Fuzzer Node\" only when discussing the simulator implementation.</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"Composer\" vs. \"Actuator\" (capability shape classification):</p> <ul> <li>A Composer reads context, runs a generation process, and writes a content artifact to the blackboard (e.g., advisory draft text).</li> <li>An Actuator receives a trigger, calls an external system, and confirms the side effect; no artifact is placed on the blackboard.</li> <li>Misclassification risk: nodes that \"do something\" to an external system look like Composers if you only notice they dispatch outbound calls. The discriminator is whether a content artifact lands on the blackboard. If not, it is an Actuator capability shape.</li> <li>Recommendation: Before classifying a node as Composer, verify it writes a content artifact to the blackboard. If the only output is a SUCCESS/FAILURE confirming an external side effect, it is an Actuator capability shape.</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"Coordination Agent\" vs. \"Capability shape\":</p> <ul> <li>A Capability shape is the current term for the abstract interface contract at a call-out point (Sentinel, Evaluator, Retriever, Composer, Actuator).</li> <li>Coordination Agent was the previous term. It is deprecated because \"agent\" has acquired connotations of LLM-based autonomous systems, which was not the original intent.</li> <li>Recommendation: Use \"capability shape\" in all new text. When reading older code or docs, treat \"Coordination Agent\" as a synonym for \"capability shape.\"</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"Dimension Object\" vs. \"status field\":</p> <ul> <li>A Dimension Object (per ADR-0036) is an immutable <code>BaseModel</code> containing the state of one machine; it is a first-class structured type, not a flat field.</li> <li>\"Status field\" is informal language that may mean a flat scalar (<code>rmState: \"ACCEPTED\"</code>) or a Dimension Object (<code>rm: {\"state\": \"ACCEPTED\"}</code>); both appear in real ledger snapshots.</li> <li>Recommendation: Say \"Dimension Object\" when referring to the structured sub-model; say \"flat legacy field\" when referring to the pre-ADR-0036 serialization. When extracting state from JSONL, probe both shapes (see 2026-07-22 learning on three nesting shapes).</li> </ul> </li> </ol>"},{"location":"reference/glossary/#example-dialogues","title":"Example Dialogues","text":""},{"location":"reference/glossary/#formal-protocol-structure-example","title":"Formal Protocol Structure Example","text":"<p>Protocol Designer: \"OK, so in the formal model, we have N processes. Several of the modules it names no longer exist, and the semantics-to-pattern mapping shown below as a <code>dict</code> is now the ordered <code>SEMANTIC_REGISTRY</code> list in <code>vultron/semantic_registry/</code>. Read it for the design reasoning, not for current file locations or symbol names.</p> <p>Vultron is designed with the ActivityPub protocol in mind. Most activity in Vultron involves actors exchanging activity messages containing objects.</p> <p>Submitting a Vulnerability Report</p> <p>For example, an actor might create a <code>VulnerabilityReport</code> object and then offer it to another actor, who can then accept, tentatively reject, or  reject the offer.</p> <p>Actors in ActivityPub can be of various types, such as <code>Person</code>, <code>Organization</code>, <code>Group</code>, <code>Application</code>, <code>Service</code>, etc. Each actor has an inbox and an outbox. The inbox is where the actor receives activities, and the outbox is where the actor sends activities.</p> <p>Actor Inboxes and Outboxes</p> <p>For example, if Alice is a <code>Person</code> actor, she has an inbox at <code>https://example.com/users/alice/inbox</code> and an outbox at <code>https://example.com/users/alice/outbox</code>. If Bob is another <code>Person</code> actor, he has his own inbox and outbox.</p> <p>When Alice wants to send an activity to Bob, she creates the activity with the <code>to</code> field set to Bob's actor ID (e.g., <code>https://example.com/users/bob</code>) and places it in her outbox. The ActivityPub server then delivers the activity to Bob's inbox. Bob can then process the activity and respond by sending an activity to his outbox, with the <code>to</code> field set to Alice's actor ID. He can also set the <code>inReplyTo</code> field to reference the original activity from Alice to indicate that it is a response. The ActivityPub server handles the delivery of the activity to Alice's inbox,  and the cycle continues.</p> <p>Scope of Vultron's ActivityPub Implementation</p> <p>However, the Vultron prototype does not implement a full ActivityPub server. Instead, it initially focuses on the core functionality of actors sending activities directly to each other's inboxes. This simplifies the implementation while still demonstrating the core concepts of ActivityPub interactions.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#inbox-handler-architecture","title":"Inbox Handler Architecture","text":"<p>The initial architecture is as follows: An actor has an inbox implemented as a FastAPI endpoint that accepts POST requests containing activity messages. When a message is received, the inbox handler processes the activity and routes it to an appropriate handler based on the activity's semantics.</p> <p>Activity Handling</p> <p>For example, if the activity is an <code>Offer</code> of a <code>VulnerabilityReport</code>, it would be routed to a <code>submit_report</code> handler function, which contains the logic for processing a vulnerability report submission.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#out-of-scope","title":"Out of scope","text":"<p>Authentication, authorization, and server-to-server federation are deferred to future implementation.</p> <p>This design also does not describe what happens inside each handler function; that is left to the specific handler implementations to come later. If the validation failed, it can respond with an appropriate error status (e.g., 400 Bad Request) and log the error.</li> <li>Extract Routing Information: The inbox handler extracts key fields from the activity message (e.g., <code>type</code>, <code>object</code>, <code>to</code>, <code>inReplyTo</code>) to determine routing.    It creates a <code>DispatchEvent</code> header object containing the routing information and attaches the original activity message as the payload.</li> <li>Dispatch Activity: The inbox handler invokes a dispatch function that routes the <code>DispatchEvent</code> object to the appropriate handler function based on the activity's semantic type.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#activity-patterns-and-semantics","title":"Activity Patterns and Semantics","text":"<p>Routing semantics are identified by <code>ActivityPattern</code> objects, which define patterns for matching activity messages to specific enumerated semantic meanings. This decouples the raw activity message structure from the higher-level semantics of the Vultron protocol, allowing raw messages to be translated into meaningful semantics that drive application logic.</p> <p>Defining Activity Patterns</p> <p>An activity pattern for submitting a vulnerability report might be defined as an <code>Offer</code> activity with an object of type <code>VulnerabilityReport</code>.  Responses to that offer follow their own patterns:</p> <pre><code>ReportSubmission = ActivityPattern(\n    activity_=TAtype.OFFER,\n    object_=VOtype.VULNERABILITY_REPORT,\n)\nAckReport = ActivityPattern(activity_=TAtype.READ, object_=ReportSubmission)\nValidateReport = ActivityPattern(\n    activity_=TAtype.ACCEPT, object_=ReportSubmission\n)\nInvalidateReport = ActivityPattern(\n    activity_=TAtype.TENTATIVE_REJECT, object_=ReportSubmission\n)\nCloseReport = ActivityPattern(\n    activity_=TAtype.REJECT, object_=ReportSubmission\n)\n</code></pre> <p>The various <code>*type</code>s are string enumerations defined elsewhere.</p> <p>Mapping Activity Patterns to Semantics</p> <p>The mapping from raw activity message patterns to higher-level semantics is defined as follows:</p> <pre><code>SEMANTICS_ACTIVITY_PATTERNS: dict[MessageSemantics, ActivityPattern] = {\n    MessageSemantics.SUBMIT_REPORT: ap.ReportSubmission,\n    MessageSemantics.ACK_REPORT: ap.AckReport,\n    MessageSemantics.VALIDATE_REPORT: ap.ValidateReport,\n    MessageSemantics.INVALIDATE_REPORT: ap.InvalidateReport,\n    MessageSemantics.CLOSE_REPORT: ap.CloseReport,\n    # ...etc.\n}\n</code></pre> <p>Activity semantics are determined by the <code>type</code> field of the activity message, along with fields such as <code>object</code>, <code>to</code>, and <code>inReplyTo</code>. The dispatch function uses this information to determine which handler function should process the activity.</p> <p>DispatchEvent Object</p> <p>A <code>DispatchEvent</code> object encapsulates the routing information needed by the dispatch function. The handler function is then invoked with the <code>DispatchEvent</code> object as an argument.</p> <p>Example</p> <p>The following is an example of the <code>ActivityDispatcher</code> Protocol that defines   the interface for dispatching activities:</p> <pre><code>class ActivityDispatcher(Protocol):\n    \"\"\"\n    Protocol for dispatching activities to their corresponding handlers based on message semantics.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def dispatch(self, dispatchable: DispatchEvent) -&gt; None:\n        \"\"\"Dispatches an activity to the appropriate handler based on its semantic type.\"\"\"\n        ...\n</code></pre> <p>On the Modularity of Dispatchers</p> <p>The dispatch function is designed as a Python <code>Protocol</code> to allow for different dispatcher implementations. This provides flexibility in connecting the inbox  handler to specific handler functions for each semantic type. A simple  implementation might use a dictionary mapping from semantic types to handler  functions, while a more complex implementation could involve message queues  or other routing mechanisms.</p> <p>This modularity allows dispatching logic to be extended easily by defining new  <code>ActivityPattern</code>s with corresponding <code>MessageSemantics</code>, then adding new  handler functions to the dispatch mapping. Decoupling routing logic from  handling logic maintains clean separation of concerns and facilitates  future protocol extensions.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#direct-dispatch-implementation","title":"Direct Dispatch Implementation","text":"<p>The first dispatch function implementation uses a simple direct dispatch approach with a dictionary mapping from <code>MessageSemantics</code> to handler functions. This distinction is most prominent in the connections from the Received and Deferred RM states in the two figures above. These differences are the result of the relative timing of the two different decisions they support within a CVD case.</p> <p>The decision to Coordinate (i.e., whether the Coordinator should move from RM Valid to RM Accept  (\\(q^{rm} \\in V \\xrightarrow{a} A\\)) occurs early in the Coordinator's RM process. The SSVC Supplier Engagement decision point is an attempt to capture this information. This early in the process, allowances must be made for Vendors who may not have completed their own validation or  prioritization processes.  Hence, the mapping allows Vendors in any valid yet unclosed state (\\(q^{rm} \\in \\{R,V,A,D\\}\\)) to be categorized as  Active for this decision point.</p> <p>On the other hand, the decision to Publish\u2014a choice that falls entirely within the Coordinator's RM Accepted  state\u2014occurs later, at which time, more is known about each Vendor's level of involvement in the case to that point.  By the time the publication decision is made, the Vendor(s) have had ample opportunity to engage in the CVD process. They might already have a Fix-Ready (\\(q^{cs} \\in VF \\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\)), or they might be working toward it (i.e., SSVC Cooperative). However, if the Coordinator has reached the point where they are making a publication decision, and the Vendor has  yet to actively engage in the case for whatever reason\u2014as indicated by their failure to reach the RM Accepted state or demonstrate progress toward it by at least getting to RM Valid  (\\(q^{rm} \\in \\{A,V\\}\\))\u2014then they can be categorized as Uncooperative/Unresponsive.</p> <p>SSVC Decision Points and Anticipated Transitions</p> <p>Other SSVC decision points may be informative about which transitions to expect in a case. Implementations of the Vultron Protocol are expected to have their own versioning schemes.</p> <p>Current Version</p> <p>The current version of the Vultron Protocol is</p> <p>2024.4.4.dev6496+gb9388ca98.d20260915</p> <p>Vultron Protocol versions follow Calendar Versioning (CalVer) using the format <code>YYYY.M.Patch</code>, where:</p> <ul> <li> <p><code>YYYY</code> is the four-digit year of the most recent non-patch release.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>M</code> is the month of the most recent non-patch release,     with no zero padding (e.g., <code>1</code>, <code>2</code>, <code>3</code>, ..., <code>12</code>).</p> </li> <li> <p><code>Patch</code> is the patch number for that release.     For the first (or only) release in a given month, the patch number     starts at <code>0</code> and is normally omitted, so <code>2024.4.0</code> and <code>2024.4</code>     denote the same version.</p> </li> </ul> <p>Version increments work as follows:</p> <ul> <li> <p>Significant releases use the current year and month, with the patch     number starting at <code>0</code> (normally omitted).     Example: the first significant release in April 2024 is <code>2024.4</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Patch releases increment the patch number from the most recent     non-patch release, even if the patch is published in a later month or year.     Example: the third small update to <code>2024.4</code> is <code>2024.4.3</code>, even if it     is released in May 2024 or later.</p> </li> </ul> <p>No backward compatibility commitments are made or implied at this stage. The abstract Vultron protocol: the state machines (RM, EM, PEC, VFD, PXA), the valid transitions between states, the process logic that drives those transitions, and the behavioral conformance rules that define correct observable behavior.</p> <p>What is in scope.</p> <ul> <li>The five state machines and their transition tables</li> <li>The behavioral conformance specifications (RMB, EMB, CSB) that state correct outputs for given inputs</li> <li>The ordering and cascade rules between dimensions (for example, when an EM transition must trigger a PEC bulk update)</li> <li>The process model: how N independent participants coordinate through message passing</li> </ul> <p>What is out of scope.</p> <ul> <li>The Python module <code>vultron/core/</code> \u2014 that is the reference implementation of this concept, not the concept itself</li> <li>The behavior trees \u2014 those are one valid mechanism for executing vultron-core, not a required part of it</li> <li>The message format \u2014 that is vultron-wire</li> <li>The delivery mechanism \u2014 that is vultron-transport</li> </ul> <p>Relationship to other concepts.</p> <ul> <li>vultron-wire carries the semantic meaning that vultron-core defines.</li> <li>vultron-transport moves vultron-wire messages between participants.</li> <li>The behavioral conformance specifications (RMB, EMB, CSB) are part of the vultron-core capability set. Instead, it defines a minimal set of properties necessary to support the protocol.</p> <p>The example below shows a <code>VulnerabilityReport</code> object containing a simple text description of a vulnerability in the <code>content</code> property. In a real implementation, the <code>content</code> property may contain any vulnerability report format that can be embedded as part of the JSON object.</p> <p>Examples of what might go into the <code>content</code> property of a <code>VulnerabilityReport</code> object include:</p> <ul> <li>Community-developed Structured formats like CSAF or   CVE JSON</li> <li>Quasi-structured text formats based on templates like the   OWASP Vulnerability Template</li> <li>Proprietary formats used by vendors, coordinators, or finders, such as might be found behind a web form like   CERT/CC's Vulnerability Reporting Form</li> <li>A plain text description of the vulnerability, for example a markdown-formatted text description with section   headings and links to external resources</li> </ul> <p>The format of the <code>content</code> property is deliberately open-ended to allow for flexibility in the types of vulnerability reports that can be represented. The <code>content</code> property SHOULD represent a widely-used structured format whenever possible, since this allows for more automation in the processing of vulnerability reports.</p> <p>Binary attachments (PDF documents, images, audio files, video files) are supported; in those cases, the <code>content</code> property MAY contain a link to the binary file or an embedded encoding. This design allows us to separate the core domain logic from the infrastructure and external interfaces, making the system more modular, testable, and adaptable to different use cases and environments.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Hexagonal Architecture Overview\n---\nflowchart LR\n\nadapters1[Driving Adapters]\nadapters2[Driven Adapters]\nports1[Driving Ports]\nports2[Driven Ports]\ncore{{Core Domain Logic}}\nadapters1 --o ports1\nports1 --o core\ncore --o ports2\nports2 --o adapters2</code></pre> <p>In this architecture:</p> <ul> <li>The Driving Adapters implement the driving ports using specific   technologies (e.g., FastAPI endpoints, CLI commands, etc.) and translate   external inputs into calls to the core domain logic.</li> <li>The Driving Ports define the interfaces through which external actors   (e.g., finders, vendors, coordinators) can interact with the core domain logic. These are the entry points for commands and queries that drive the system's behavior.</li> <li>The Core Domain Logic contains the business rules, policies, and behavior trees that govern how the system operates. It is completely agnostic to how it is accessed or what technologies are used to implement the interfaces.</li> <li>The Driven Ports define the interfaces through which the core domain   logic can interact with external systems (e.g., databases, message queues,   external APIs). These are the exit points for the core to perform actions   that have side effects or require external resources.</li> <li>The Driven Adapters implement the driven ports using specific technologies   (e.g., MongoDB for database access, Celery for task queues, etc.)   and   translate calls from the core domain logic into interactions with external   systems.</li> </ul> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Hexagonal Architecture Details\n---\nflowchart LR\n\nsubgraph driving_adapters [Driving Adapters]\n    direction LR\n    api[API Endpoints]\n    cli[CLI Commands]\n    mcp[MCP Tools]\nend\nsubgraph driving_ports [Driving Ports]\n    direction LR\n    use_cases[Use Cases]\n    commands[Commands]\nend\nsubgraph core [Core Domain Logic]\n    direction LR\n    domain_models[Domain Models]\n    services[Domain Services]\n    behavior_trees[Behavior Trees]\nend\nsubgraph driven_ports [Driven Ports]\n    direction LR\n    database[Database Access]\n    message_queue[Message Queue]\n    external_apis[External APIs]\nend\nsubgraph driven_adapters [Driven Adapters]\n    direction LR\n    mongo[MongoDB Adapter]\n    celery[Celery Adapter]\n    vince[VINCE Adapter]\nend\n\ndriving_adapters --&gt; driving_ports\ndriving_ports --&gt; core\ncore --&gt; driven_ports\ndriven_ports --&gt; driven_adapters</code></pre>"},{"location":"reference/code/api/actor_inbox_handler/","title":"Actor Inbox Handler","text":"<p>The Actor Inbox Handler is the hub that processes incoming activities. It</p> <ul> <li>receives activities sent to an actor's inbox</li> <li>looks up the appropriate handler based on the activity type and object type</li> <li>invokes the handler to process the activity</li> <li>if necessary, delegates to sub-handlers for more specific processing</li> </ul> <p>Some <code>Activity</code>/<code>Object</code> handlers have more than one job</p> <p>For some <code>Activity</code>/<code>Object</code> pairs, there may be multiple jobs to select from. The blank test comes from <code>vocab.base.utils.is_blank</code>, the wire layer's single definition of blank, shared with <code>parser.parse_activity</code>'s required-field guards (CS-22-001).</p> <p>A blank string is absence, not a malformed value: it carries no time, and the alternative \u2014 raising \u2014 is not available to a nested object. <code>parser._expand_inline_value</code> refuses an inline object that fails its own class's validation, so treating a cosmetic blank as a fault would reject the whole message over a field the nested object is allowed to omit outright.</p> <p>Absence here means <code>None</code>, not the field default.  <code>published</code> and <code>updated</code> carry <code>default_factory=now_utc</code>, so omitting the key yields the receiver's clock while a blank yields <code>None</code> \u2014 blank is therefore equivalent to an explicit <code>null</code>, not to omission.  That is the more honest of the two: <code>None</code> records that the sender supplied no time, where the default would fabricate one and present it as the sender's claim.  <code>start_time</code> and <code>end_time</code> default to <code>None</code> already, so for them the two spellings do coincide.</p> <p>A non-blank string that is not a timestamp stays an error: blank means \"not provided\", and reporting corrupt data as missing data would tell the sender to supply a field they already sent (ISSUE-3217).</p>"},{"location":"reference/code/as_vocab/as_objects/#vultron.wire.as2.vocab.base.objects.actors","title":"<code>vultron.wire.as2.vocab.base.objects.actors</code>","text":"<p>This module provides actor classes</p>"},{"location":"reference/code/as_vocab/as_objects/#vultron.wire.as2.vocab.base.objects.actors.as_Actor","title":"<code>as_Actor</code>","text":"<p>               Bases: <code>as_Object</code></p> <p>Base class for all ActivityPub actors. You can still do that with the default Blackboard class, but you'll need to create a new Blackboard object instance for each tree.</p> <p>If you want to run multiple trees in multiple processes with shared state, you'll need to use a Blackboard object that can communicate with some external data store, such as a key-value store on a server. The default Blackboard class is not designed for that use case, but you can subclass it to use any object that implements the <code>__getitem__</code> and <code>__setitem__</code> methods to provide a python dict-like interface. and runs it until either it closes or 1000 ticks have passed. This demo is basically simulating a CVD agent coordinating a CVD case with itself. The agent's role is set to <code>FINDER_REPORTER_VENDOR_DEPLOYER_COORDINATOR</code>, which means it will perform all the roles in the CVD case. Messages emitted in one tick might be received later in the same tick, or in a future tick.</p> <p>Tip</p> <p>This demo leverages the ability to use leaf nodes as stochastic process fuzzers.  Using this feature, we can simulate the behavior of a CVD agent without having to  implement any actual communication mechanisms or simulate any complex real-world processes.</p> <p>One interesting effect of this design is that the places where the demo uses a fuzzer node are often  indicative of places where an actual bot would either need to call out to either a data source or  a human to decide what to do next. This is a good example of how the Vultron behavior tree  can be used to model complex reactive processes in a way that is still easy to understand and reason about.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>There is no underlying communication mechanism in this demo, so messages are not actually  sent anywhere. Instead, they are just added to the blackboard's incoming message queue.  They also have no content, and are only represented as message types.</p> <p>Warning</p> <p>This demo is not intended to be a fully realistic simulation of a CVD case. It is only intended  to demonstrate the behavior of the Vultron behavior tree.</p>"},{"location":"reference/code/demo/","title":"Demo Package","text":"<p>The <code>vultron.demo</code> package contains This is a normative section of the documentation.</p> <p>The MPCVD process can be described as a Communicating Hierarchical State Machine. This section begins by laying out the requirements for a formal protocol definition, followed by a step-by-step walkthrough of each of those requirements as they relate to the RM, EM, and CS models described elsewhere.</p> <p>Do Not Start Here</p> <p>If this is your first time reading about the Vultron Protocol, we recommend that you start with Explanation. This section is heavy on formalism and is intended for readers who are already familiar with the Vultron Protocol concepts and design principles.</p>"},{"location":"reference/formal_protocol/#communication-protocol-definitions","title":"Communication Protocol Definitions","text":"<p>A communication protocol allows independent processes, represented as finite state machines, to coordinate their state transitions through the passing of messages. Brand and Zafiropulo defined a protocol as follows.</p> <p>Protocol Formally Defined</p> <p>A protocol with \\(N\\) processes is a quadruple:</p> \\[ protocol =      \\Big \\langle          { \\langle S_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1},          { \\langle o_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1},         { \\langle M_{i,j} \\rangle}^N_{i,j=1},         { succ }     \\Big \\rangle\\] <p>Where</p> <ul> <li> <p>\\(N\\) is a positive integer representing the number of processes.</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(\\langle S_i \\rangle_{i=1}^N\\) are \\(N\\) disjoint finite sets (\\(S_i\\) represents the set of states of process \\(i\\)).</p> </li> <li> <p>Each \\(o_i\\) is an element of \\(S_i\\) representing the initial state of process \\(i\\).</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(\\langle M_{ij} \\rangle_{i,j=1}^N\\) are \\(N^2\\) disjoint finite sets with \\(M_{ii}\\) empty for all \\(i\\). \\(M_{ij}\\) represents the messages that can be sent from process \\(i\\) to process \\(j\\),</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(succ\\) is a partial function mapping for each \\(i\\) and \\(j\\), $\\(S_i \\times M_{ij} \\rightarrow S_i \\textrm{ and } S_i \\times M_{ji} \\rightarrow S_i\\)$ \\(succ(s,x)\\) is the state entered after a process transmits or receives message \\(x\\) in state \\(s\\). It is a transmission if \\(x\\) is from \\(M_{ij}\\) and a reception if \\(x\\) is from \\(M_{ji}\\).</p> </li> </ul> <p>Global State Formally Defined</p> <p>The global state of a protocol given by the above is a pair \\(\\langle S, C \\rangle\\), where</p> <ul> <li> <p>\\(S\\) is an \\(N\\)-tuple of states \\(\\langle s_1,\\dots,s_N \\rangle\\) with each \\(s_i\\) representing the current state of process \\(i\\).</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(C\\) is an \\(N^2\\)-tuple \\(\\langle c_{1,1},\\dots, c_{1,N}, c_{2,1}, \\dots \\dots, c_{N,N} \\rangle\\), where each \\(c_{i,j}\\) is a sequence of messages from \\(M_{i,j}\\). The importance of clearly communicating expectations across all parties involved in a CVD process cannot be overemphasized. If we expect cooperation between all parties and stakeholders, we should do our best to match their expectations of being \"in the loop\" and minimize their surprise. The Status column states the kind of relationship:</p> Status Meaning <code>direct</code> One shorthand maps to exactly one wire activity. <code>collapse</code> Several shorthands share one wire activity. Multiple shorthands appear in a single row; the Discriminator column names the payload field (or context) that distinguishes them. <code>expansion</code> One shorthand is realized by several wire activities. The same shorthand appears in more than one row. <code>evolved</code> The shorthand's purpose is served by a mechanism partitioned on a different axis (fault reporting or cumulative acknowledgement), not by a dedicated wire activity. <code>\u2014</code> The wire activity has no formal shorthand counterpart. <p>Reading the many-to-many relationship from a table:</p> <ul> <li>Multiple shorthands in one row is a collapse \u2014 for example <code>CP CX CA</code>   ride a single <code>Add(CaseStatus)</code>, discriminated by <code>pxa_state</code>.</li> <li>One shorthand across multiple rows is an expansion \u2014 for example <code>EP</code>   spans four embargo wire activities.</li> </ul> <p>The <code>evolved</code> shorthands (<code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code>, <code>CE</code>, <code>GE</code>, <code>EK</code>, <code>CK</code>, <code>GK</code>) have no dedicated wire activity. Faults are conveyed by <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code>, <code>as:Reject</code>, or <code>Create(Note)</code>, partitioned by failure mode. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>The Vultron Protocol does not make its appearance in uncharted territory, where no existing CVD systems or processes exist. Rather, it is offered as an improvement to interactions among humans, systems, and business processes that already perform MPCVD around the world every day. Thus, for adoption to occur, it will be necessary to map existing systems and processes into the semantics (and eventually, the syntax) of whatever protocol emerges as a descendant of this proposal.</p> <p>Combined with the abstract case class model, an ontology (e.g., using OWL) can accelerate the semantic interoperability between independent Participant processes and tools that this effort set out to improve.</p> <p>A few OWL ontology files describe the Vultron protocol. Refines: ARCH-19-001 <code>ARCH-19-002</code> MUST Emission (stage 1) MUST be idempotent with respect to the outbox: writing the same activity ID twice MUST NOT create a duplicate outbox entry. Refines: ARCH-19-001 <code>ARCH-19-003</code> MUST Transport delivery (stage 2) MUST be retried on transient network failures. The retry mechanism MUST be implemented in the outbox worker, not in the use-case or handler. Refines: ARCH-19-001 <code>ARCH-19-004</code> MUST NOT A transport delivery failure (stage 2 error) MUST NOT be interpreted as recipient rejection (stage 3 semantics). Automation potential describes whether the call-out point logic can be executed without human involvement; shape describes the structural pattern of the seam (what flows in, what flows out, and in what direction). A Retriever backed by a REST API is still a Retriever; the automation just means the Retriever implementation does not require human action. The defining criterion for Retriever shape is the synchronous on-demand query pattern, not the richness of the returned data; a boolean is the simplest possible structured fact a Retriever may return. A Sentinel, by contrast, monitors a condition continuously or is triggered by an external event and calls a trigger endpoint when the condition becomes true \u2014 the flow direction is Sentinel \u2192 trigger endpoint \u2192 protocol, not protocol \u2192 query \u2192 external system.The Sentinel vs. Retriever ambiguity surfaced with nodes such as MitigationDeployed, MitigationAvailable, and HaveExploit (issue #1240). That is the Retriever pattern. A true Sentinel is not invoked by the BT; it runs independently and calls a trigger endpoint when a condition fires. Clarifying this distinction prevents future misclassification of on-demand binary-query nodes as Sentinels. The two are independent, and conflating them produced a fix-one-resubmit loop on the add-participant-status trigger path (ISSUE-2112). <code>EH-07-002</code> MUST When a validation boundary reports multiple violations, each violation MUST be classified as root or derived. A rule reading a single dimension is always root. A rule reading more than one dimension is derived when any dimension it reads already carries a single-dimension violation, and root otherwise. Dimension overlap is a proxy for the real test, which is remediation: a violation is derived when the remediation the caller is expected to apply to the overlapping single-dimension violation also clears it. The proxy holds only while that premise does. For a transition fault the expected remediation is asserting a legal value, which clears the entailment that read the illegal one. For a role gate the expected remediation is withdrawing the assertion, not acquiring the role \u2014 a participant does not hold a dimension it has no role for at all (a non-DEPLOYER's <code>d</code> is absent, not initial; ADR-0075) and an actor cannot grant itself a role. The classification test is dimension overlap rather than a rule-to-rule dependency graph, so a newly added rule is classified correctly by construction and the labelling cannot go stale. The root multi-dimension case is the informative one: every dimension moved legally on its own and the combination is impossible. The remediation premise is stated normatively above because it is load-bearing and was previously left implicit: three separate reviewers read the overlap rule as a pure graph property, concluded a role gate mislabels its entailments, and built a repro that put a participant on a dimension it had no role for \u2014 a state ADR-0075 makes unreachable. Puppeteering an actor means calling a trigger endpoint that invokes the actor's own use case, which in turn emits the correct protocol message and awaits any required round-trip confirmation (e.g., a CaseActor ledger entry).Direct DataLayer writes bypass the protocol entirely: no ActivityStreams message is emitted, no CaseActor ledger round-trip occurs, and the actor's local state is never established through the protocol. This produces demos that appear to work but do not exercise the real protocol path. For example, a demo that stamps RM.CLOSED directly via <code>add_participant_status</code> gives the appearance that the participant left the case, but no <code>Leave(VulnerabilityCase)</code> message was ever sent or confirmed by the CaseActor. An actor participates in many cases; the CASE_MANAGER is whichever participant the case owner delegated <code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code> to. That is the role, not an entity, which is why the role is the marker and a <code>Service</code> record is redundant with it. Resending <code>Accept</code> on retry would cause the vendor to see a duplicate acceptance and potentially re-enter the initialization flow. Re-sending the frozen original (VM-08-003) reads as the first acceptance arriving late; a new <code>Accept</code> is indistinguishable from a second, independent decision, which CP-05-005's irrevocability rule precludes. Refines: ASK-08-001 <code>CP-05-007</code> MUST A vendor that has sent <code>Create(as_CaseProposal)</code> and received neither <code>Accept(as_CaseProposal)</code> nor <code>Reject(as_CaseProposal)</code> by the proposal's deadline MUST treat the proposal as expired and MUST NOT continue waiting indefinitely.CONCERN-2367 found that a silently lost <code>Accept</code> stalls the handshake permanently, because no party holds a timeout. The proposal is an ask (ASK-01-001), so it carries a deadline (ASK-03-004) and sits in the vendor's outstanding-ask register (ASK-04-001), which is actor-scoped and therefore works before a case exists. Re-proposal is a later decision, not an automatic retry (ASK-05-004) \u2014 and it is also what lets the case-actor recover (CP-05-006). The formal set partitions both concerns by which state machine the message belonged to; the implementation partitions faults by failure mode and acknowledges replicated state cumulatively. These are orthogonal axes, so the shorthands have no one-to-one wire counterparts even though the behaviours they describe are implemented.</p> ID Priority Requirement Related <code>MSM-05-001</code> MUST Fault reporting MUST be partitioned by failure mode rather than by state machine, using exactly three mechanisms: <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code> when a message was received but not understood; <code>as:Reject</code> when a message was received and understood but declined; and <code>Create(Note)</code> or <code>Add(Note)[target=VulnerabilityCase]</code> when the condition requires narrative explanation.Failure mode is actionable to a receiver in a way that originating state machine is not. Not-understood calls for a format or version fix, declined calls for a protocol-level decision, and needs-explanation calls for a human. The formal RE, EE, CE and GE partition carries no such signal, which is why it was not reproduced. <code>MSM-05-002</code> MUST Acknowledgement of replicated case-ledger state MUST be cumulative and implicit via hash-chain continuity. A receiver whose <code>prev_log_hash</code> matches its local tail MUST NOT emit an acknowledgement, and MUST emit <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> on a mismatch, whereupon the CASE_MANAGER replays all entries after the last accepted hash.A matching <code>prev_log_hash</code> already proves receipt of every prior entry, so per-message positive acknowledgement would be redundant. PEC is a participant-local state machine tracking each actor's relationship to the shared case embargo; its transitions are not independent protocol messages and have no formal shorthands in the 28-shorthand set. PEC state answers the question: \"has this participant explicitly accepted or rejected the current active embargo?\" Unlike RM state (self-reported by the participant) and VF/D state (self-reported by vendor/deployer), PEC state is set by the CASE_MANAGER (CM-28-003) based on observed participant behavior \u2014 incoming Accept/Reject wire activities, timer-enforced lapses, and cascades from shared EM state changes. The five states are NO_EMBARGO (no embargo in scope), INVITED (awaiting response), SIGNATORY (accepted current terms), LAPSED (terms changed since last acceptance), and DECLINED (explicitly refused or timed out without responding). Normative authority: specs/case-management.yaml CM-18. Decision: ADR-0048.</p> ID Priority Requirement Related <code>MSM-07-001</code> MUST The Participant Embargo Consent (PEC) state machine MUST NOT be assigned any formal shorthand in the 28-shorthand protocol message set; all PEC transitions are either side-effects of EM wire activities (MSM-07-002 through MSM-07-005) or timer-based internal events (MSM-07-006) with no dedicated wire message or dispatch value of their own.PEC is participant-local state tracking each actor's relationship to the shared EM state, not a parallel message-driven machine. Extending the formal set with PEC-specific shorthands would imply dedicated wire messages where none exist and none are needed \u2014 the EM messages already carry the PEC signal as a side-effect. Documenting PEC as a side-effect is the faithful description of the design. Derives from: CM-18-003 <code>MSM-07-002</code> MUST The wire activity INVITE_TO_EMBARGO_ON_CASE (EP wire form: Invite(Event)[context=VulnerabilityCase]) MUST apply the PEC INVITE trigger to the invited participant, advancing their consent state from NO_EMBARGO, DECLINED, or LAPSED to INVITED.An embargo proposal is an invitation to consent; the EP wire activity conveys the invitation and the PEC machine records each participant's position. Participants already in SIGNATORY are unaffected by EP; INVITE is a no-op from SIGNATORY (CM-18-004). The PEC trigger is applied via EmbargoLifecycle.record_participant_consent() inside the InviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase received-side handler. An unacceptable value in one dimension MUST NOT cause the values reported in the other dimensions to be discarded. *RM, VFD, EM, PXA and PEC are independent state machines. A value that is unacceptable in one dimension carries no information about the others, so discarding the whole snapshot destroys state the receiver has no grounds to refuse. Liberal accept (ISSUE-2229): accept everything acceptable. * <code>RSH-05-002</code> MUST When a dimension is refused, the receiver MUST record the participant's current value for that dimension alongside the accepted values from the other dimensions, as a single <code>ParticipantStatus</code>. *The recorded status must remain a coherent snapshot of the receiver's view of the participant. Omitting the refused dimension would leave it undefined; recording the asserted value would adopt a claim the receiver just refused. * <code>RSH-05-003</code> MUST A refused dimension MUST NOT prevent the StatusAdoptionGate emit (RSH-01-003) from running. Appending it would grow the participant's status history and the hash chain without recording any state change. * <code>RSH-05-006</code> MUST <code>RM.CLOSED</code> MUST be treated as terminal for the <code>rm</code> dimension only. The local value MUST be carried forward for that dimension; all other dimensions are applied as the entry describes them. *Monotonic visibility (see notes/sync-ledger-replication.md). The Case Actor is authoritative for which transition happened, but a replayed, reordered, or divergent entry would otherwise un-see progress the replica has already observed. Lateral moves at the same rank (<code>VALID</code> &lt;-&gt; <code>INVALID</code>) are re-adjudication, not regression, and are applied unchanged. * <code>RSH-05-008</code> SHOULD The <code>em</code> dimension SHOULD NOT be adjudicated at StatusAdoptionGate; embargo state belongs to EmbargoTeardownAuthorizationGate (<code>add_case_status_tree</code>). *EM is per-case rather than per-participant and its authorization gate is the EmbargoTeardownAuthorizationGate (RSH-02-001). Publishing a field patch instead makes shape preservation structural rather than a property the guard has to remember to maintain. * <code>RSH-05-010</code> MUST A producer of <code>ledger_payload_object_override</code> MUST write <code>None</code> to the key unconditionally at the start of every tick \u2014 before any early return \u2014 so that a stale value from a previous execution cannot bleed into the current one. *The py_trees blackboard is process-global. <code>BTBridge.execute_with_setup</code> does not reset application-level keys between runs, so a producer that only writes on its active path leaves the key at its previous value on every no-op tick. <code>CommitCaseLedgerEntryNode</code> would then apply that stale patch to a different payload snapshot. The required shape is <code>{\"object_id\": &lt;id&gt;, \"producer_type\": &lt;str&gt;, \"fields\": {&lt;wire alias&gt;: &lt;value&gt;}}</code>. *Multiple producers are anticipated (ISSUE-2256 adds EM adjudication in <code>EmbargoTeardownAuthorizationGate</code> as a second producer). Any other asserted PXA value MUST be refused and the current PXA value carried forward (RSH-05-016). *PXA state is monotone: bits only advance from unaware to aware (p\u2192P, x\u2192X, a\u2192A) and never reverse. The received-side filter uses the weaker <code>is_monotonic_pxa_forward()</code> check \u2014 not the strict single-step adjacency <code>is_valid_pxa_transition()</code> that applies to local write nodes (CSB-16-002) \u2014 because a remote peer may have observed multiple PXA events between messages and report a combined advance that skips intermediate steps. Applying the strict check would refuse a valid multi-step advance from a peer that simply missed delivering earlier messages. * <code>RSH-05-020</code> MUST After adjudicating each dimension of a received <code>Add(ParticipantStatus, CaseParticipant)</code> independently, the receiver MUST evaluate the cross-machine entailments (RM\u2194VF and RM\u2194D per CSB-18-001, VF\u2194D per CSB-17-001) against the effective \u2014 post-adjudication \u2014 state. For each violated entailment the receiver MUST refuse the dimension whose asserted value the sender moved, carrying the participant's current value for it forward (RSH-05-002), and MUST NOT report as refused a dimension the sender omitted or restated unchanged. The receiver MUST evaluate the same entailment set the emit path evaluates. Per-dimension adjudication cannot see a claim that is impossible only in combination: a fix that is ready or deployed entails a report the participant has already accepted, and a deployed fix entails a ready one. Before this requirement the receive path composed only VF\u2194D, so an assertion the actor would have refused to emit was accepted, recorded, hash-chained and replicated to every participant when it arrived from a peer instead (ISSUE-2906). Refusing the dimension that moved* is what makes the refusal effective rather than cosmetic. VF\u2194D constrains a pair, so either side can be the offending claim; refusing the incumbent side carries its value straight back, which leaves the impossible combination recorded while reporting a refusal that changed nothing. Requiring one shared evaluator rather than two equivalent ones is what keeps the emit and receive paths from silently diverging again. Silence is the specific problem: the contradiction is only discoverable by reading devlogs. Using <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code> rather than <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> avoids triggering a CASE_MANAGER replay loop \u2014 the committed entry cannot be uncommitted, so replaying it would produce the same refusal indefinitely. <code>ProcessingFault</code> is the right signal for semantic invalidity (ASK-07-001). persistence layer. The CS participant-specific axes (RM, VFD) are owned by each participant's <code>CaseParticipant</code> record and are intentionally excluded from this restriction. This path is distinct from VP-17-001 and is not a bypass of the CASE_MANAGER write constraint. Participants exchange asynchronous messages and track the case across four dimensions of shared state, realized as five state machines. Any number of organizations may take part in a single case.</p> <p>Coordination is scoped to the case rather than to a system: the case-management role is held per case, and different cases may be managed by different actors. No single service holds every case. Within a case, one participant holds write authority over the case's shared state, so that concurrent claims resolve to one answer.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#1-introduction-i","title":"1. Introduction [I]","text":""},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#11-background-and-motivation","title":"1.1 Background and Motivation","text":"<p>A vulnerability divides the world into two sets: those who know about it, and those who do not. From the moment of discovery, every party in the knowing set repeatedly answers two questions. What should it do next, and who else needs to know what, and when? Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) continues until the answers are \"nothing\" and \"nobody\".</p> <p>Multi-Party CVD (MPCVD) is CVD involving three or more independent organizations with different interests and roles. The shapes vary. A reporter may go to one vendor, which discovers that other vendors ship the same component. A reporter may go to a coordinator, which finds and notifies the affected vendors. A reporter may go to a vendor and a coordinator at once. What the cases have in common is that the set of participants grows after coordination has begun, each vendor works to its own timeline, and the parties must agree when disclosure happens.</p> <p>Each of those organizations usually already runs its own vulnerability tracking system. The coordination problem is therefore not only one of people talking to each other; it is one of separate systems needing to stay consistent about a shared case. That is the problem Vultron addresses.</p> <p>Email carries the content of a CVD case but records none of its state. No participant can see which vendors have read the report, which have agreed to an embargo, or in what order events occurred. Adding a party mid-case means re-sending the history by hand, and nothing detects the gap if that fails. Vultron gives each of these an explicit, machine-checkable representation: report status per participant (\u00a76), embargo agreement per participant (\u00a79), and an ordered case ledger that every participant replicates (\u00a75.4).</p> <p>Embargo timing is worth noting early. In practice the first two parties to a case establish the initial embargo, and it carries forward as further participants join and agree to it. Establishing terms early is generally easier than negotiating them once many parties are already involved.</p> <p>The protocol tracks coordination state across four dimensions: the report lifecycle (RM), the embargo (EM), what is known about the vulnerability (CS), and each participant's agreement to the embargo (PEC). Because CS is a compound of two independent axes, an implementation runs five state machines (\u00a73.3). Messages are ActivityStreams 2.0 Activities delivered over HTTP. Delivery is asynchronous: no exchange requires both parties to be available at the same moment.</p> <p>Who this specification is for</p> <p>This specification is written for implementers building software that takes part in Vultron cases, and for reviewers assessing whether an implementation conforms.</p> <p>It assumes familiarity with coordinated vulnerability disclosure as a practice \u2014 reporters, vendors, coordinators, embargoes, CVE IDs. It does not assume prior knowledge of Vultron. Where it relies on an external specification, it says so and cites it (\u00a71.3).</p> <p>See also</p> <ul> <li>CVD as a Coordination Problem</li> <li>What Does Success Mean in CVD?</li> <li>The Need for Interoperability</li> <li>CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#12-design-goals","title":"1.2 Design Goals","text":"<p>Actor-local state. Each participant keeps its own replica of the case, assembled from the messages it has received. A participant is the authority on its own report and fix status. What the case as a whole asserts \u2014 its embargo state and what is publicly known \u2014 has a single writer, the participant holding the Case Manager role, so that concurrent claims resolve to one answer (\u00a75.4.1).</p> <p>Coordination is scoped to a case, not to a system. The Case Manager role is held per case, and different cases may be managed by different actors. The protocol does not require every case to pass through one shared service. It does require, within a case, that shared state have one writer.</p> <p>Informative: how centralized is this?</p> <p>Two readings should both be avoided.</p> <p>Vultron does not require a single central authority holding all cases. Any actor able to satisfy the Case Manager role can manage a case, and the role is transferable (\u00a711.3).</p> <p>Equally, Vultron as it stands is not a fully decentralized design. Within a case there is one writer, and its availability bounds how fast the case can progress. The current reference implementation goes further and runs a dedicated service actor per case.</p> <p>The protocol leaves more distributed realizations open \u2014 a shared ledger among peers, for instance \u2014 and this version does not specify one (\u00a75.4.2).</p> <p>Asynchronous, message-driven coordination. Participants announce their own transitions rather than being polled, and no exchange requires two parties to be online at once. A participant that is temporarily unreachable does not block the others from making progress.</p> <p>Extensible role model. Roles are not exclusive: a participant may hold Reporter, Vendor and Coordinator at the same time (\u00a73.5). Roles that confer protocol authority are kept separate from roles that describe what an actor does in the world, so the two can vary independently.</p> <p>Interoperable wire format. ActivityStreams 2.0 is the normative wire vocabulary. Reusing an established open standard means the message format is already specified and already understood, and it leaves ActivityPub-based delivery available as a path to potentially compatible tooling. Vultron has not yet been integrated with the wider ActivityPub ecosystem.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#13-relationship-to-existing-standards","title":"1.3 Relationship to Existing Standards","text":"<p>ActivityStreams 2.0 and ActivityPub. Vultron uses the ActivityStreams 2.0 vocabulary as its wire format, and ActivityPub HTTP delivery is the anticipated transport.</p> <p>This version requires the vocabulary but not full ActivityPub server behavior: inbox and outbox HTTP delivery, WebFinger discovery and HTTP Signatures are not conformance requirements here. This specification writes state names in full, in prose form: Received, Active, Signatory, Fix Ready. Where the name of a specific enumerated value matters \u2014 for example when citing an implementation's enumeration \u2014 the value is written in code font with its machine as a prefix, as in <code>RM.RECEIVED</code> or <code>PEC.SIGNATORY</code>. Vulnerabilities are the subject of every Vultron case. Report A document describing a specific vulnerability, submitted to initiate coordination. It determines what a participant is obliged to do and which transitions it is authorized to cause. Roles are granted through the case's authority chain (\u00a711.1), not claimed. A participant may hold several at once.</p> <p>Roles fall into two categories, which \u00a712.3 develops further.</p> <p>Process roles describe what an actor does in a case:</p> Role Definition Reporter A participant that submitted the report. The protocol is concerned with who reported the vulnerability, not who discovered it; a discoverer who reports holds the Reporter role. Vendor A participant that produces a product containing the vulnerability and is responsible for developing a fix. Coordinator A participant that facilitates multi-party coordination without being responsible for developing a fix itself. Deployer A participant that deploys a vendor's fix to systems it operates. Distinct from Vendor: producing a fix and applying it are separate acts. CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) A participant authorized to assign CVE IDs directly, rather than delegating assignment to an external service. Orthogonal to the other process roles and commonly held alongside Coordinator or Vendor. Observer A participant with no obligation to drive vendor/fix/deploy transitions. An Observer still tracks case state, is subject to embargo consent, and may report observations about the world. <p>Protocol authority roles describe what an actor controls in the protocol itself:</p> Role Definition Case Owner The party whose disclosure decision the case exists to serve. It decides who is admitted, which roles they hold, and whether embargo terms are accepted or torn down. Case ownership is never delegated, though it may be transferred (\u00a711.3). Case Manager The participant that writes the canonical case ledger and relays case-scoped messages, acting on the Case Owner's behalf. It is the case's single-writer authority (\u00a75.4.1). The Case Owner may delegate this role. <p>Observer names two different things</p> <p>Observer is used in this specification for the process role defined above, and also as the name of the minimum conformance capability set that every participant must provide (\u00a712.2). The reuse is deliberate \u2014 the capability set is named after the least-privileged role \u2014 but the two are not the same kind of thing. A role is a position in a case; a capability set is a property of software (\u00a712.3.3).</p> <p>Informative: the CASE_MANAGER role and the actor that holds it</p> <p>Authority over a case follows the Case Manager role. It does not follow any actor's name, URI, or hosting location. The reporter's first message goes to a vendor directly, because no case exists and so no CASE_MANAGER exists to route through. Every later message routes through the CASE_MANAGER (\u00a75.4.2). The transition between those two regimes is the bootstrap, and it is where a case's trust is established.</p> <p>The case-creation message is the trust root. When the receiving party creates the case, it sends the reporter a case-creation message signed by the creating actor. That message introduces the actor holding the <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> role. Every participant's trust in the ledger derives from it: a participant accepts entries from the CASE_MANAGER because it accepts the message that established which actor holds the role.</p> <p>A late joiner inherits that trust transitively. An actor invited after the case is under way never sees the original creation message. It receives the case snapshot and the prior ledger entries from the CASE_MANAGER (\u00a710.1), and it trusts them because it trusts the invitation that named the CASE_MANAGER. The hash-chaining of the ledger lets the joiner verify it received an unbroken history \u2014 a check against tampering and omission, not a second source of trust.</p> <p>Messages that arrive before their case. A case-scoped message may reach a participant before the case it refers to has. A participant MUST NOT apply such a message to a case it has not yet received. It holds the message until the case arrives, and discards it if the case never does. Applying it early would create case state from a message whose context was never established.</p> <p>The threat model, identity verification, and the limits of this trust chain are covered at \u00a714.1.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#46-error-and-acknowledgement-messages","title":"4.6 Error and Acknowledgement Messages","text":"<p>The formal protocol defines an acknowledgement and an error message for each of the three state machines: <code>RK</code>, <code>EK</code>, <code>CK</code> and <code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code>, <code>CE</code>. Their status here is not uniform, and an implementation MUST NOT assume symmetry across the three.</p> <p>Of the six, only <code>RK</code> exists on the wire. <code>EK</code>, <code>CK</code>, <code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code> and <code>CE</code> have no wire representation. An implementation MUST NOT expect to receive any of the five, and MUST NOT wait on one.</p> <p>The two absences have different reasons.</p> <p><code>EK</code> and <code>CK</code> are redundant. Embargo and case state changes are replicated through the case ledger, and a participant establishes that it received them by holding an unbroken hash chain. A per-message acknowledgement would restate what the chain already shows. <code>RK</code> survives because report submission happens before the case exists, so there is no ledger to carry it.</p> <p><code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code> and <code>CE</code> are deliberately unmodeled, not merely unimplemented. The protocol does not model inbound error messages typed by the state machine that produced them, because that grouping tells a receiver nothing it can act on: knowing which machine was confused does not indicate what to do about it. Errors are grouped by failure mode instead, which is actionable:</p> Failure mode When it applies What the sender can do Not understood The message could not be parsed, or its meaning is unrecognized Re-send, or send a simpler equivalent Understood but declined The message was well-formed and meaningful, but the receiver will not act on it given the case's state Reconsider; the state, not the message, is the obstacle Needs explanation The condition cannot be expressed as a structured message and requires prose Read the explanation; there is no automatic recovery <p>\u00a75.3 gives the wire form of each failure mode.</p> <p>What is still missing. A message that cannot be processed is currently set aside for administrative attention, and its sender is not told. The three failure modes give a receiver a way to report a problem where it is implemented, but this version does not require it to.</p> <p>Open question: negative-acknowledgement semantics are unspecified</p> <p>Error message types (<code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code>, <code>CE</code>) are deliberately unmodeled (ADR-0049). Unprocessable inbound messages are dead-lettered with no sender notification. The three-way fault partition (\u00a74.6, ADR-0083) provides structured error signaling where it is implemented, but whether the protocol needs a normative negative-acknowledgement facet \u2014 and if so, what the expected sender behavior (retry, suppress, escalate) should be \u2014 remains open.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#47-knowledge-model-and-actor-isolation","title":"4.7 Knowledge Model and Actor Isolation","text":"<p>Each participant knows only what it has been told. Three are defined: Observer, which every participant must provide, and Authority and Hosting, which add the obligations of deciding for a case and of running one.</p> <p>Most of what a capability set requires is expressed as maintaining a state machine, so that phrase needs pinning down first.</p> <p>What 'implement a state machine' means</p> <p>Implementing a state machine has two components:</p> <ol> <li>Track: maintain a local value for the machine, and update it as    incoming messages report transitions.</li> <li>Drive: cause a transition that the participant's roles authorize, and    announce it so the other participants learn of it.</li> </ol> <p>The two are separate obligations. A test supplies a sequence of messages and an input state, and checks the messages the implementation emits and the state it reaches. It does not inspect internal structure.</p> <p>Each test case is therefore a message-sequence scenario paired with the state outcome it expects.</p> <p>Some capabilities that define a role are not protocol-observable at all. Developing a fix, deploying a fix and publishing an advisory happen outside the protocol. Conformance verifies the protocol messages that this work produces, not the work itself.</p> <p>Conformance testing is organized in four layers, which describe what a test verifies. Layers are orthogonal to the capability sets of \u00a712.2, which describe what an implementation provides (see the warning in \u00a712.1):</p> Layer Verifies L1 \u2014 Syntax Messages are well-formed against the wire format (\u00a75) L2 \u2014 Semantics Each message drives the correct state transition (\u00a74, \u00a76\u2013\u00a711) L3 \u2014 Behavior Correct observable outputs: right messages emitted and states reached, given input state plus received message L4 \u2014 Process Correct internal decision structure (e.g. precondition before state write before side-effect) <p>L4 is only enforceable against a reference implementation and is therefore outside the scope of independent conformance claims. The protocol uses actor URIs as process identifiers. An actor URI is the identity anchor for all messages sent by that actor, and for the canonical case ledger if the actor holds the CASE_MANAGER role. Implementations MUST treat actor URI equality as identity equality: two messages with the same <code>actor</code> URI are from the same actor.</p> <p>Verification. The protocol does not currently mandate a specific identity verification mechanism. The reference implementation anticipates HTTP Signatures (as used in ActivityPub) as the authentication layer for inbound messages. A future version of this specification is expected to normatively require HTTP Signatures at the transport layer.</p> <p>Case bootstrap as the trust establishment mechanism. The <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code> message signed by the originating actor is the trust root for a case. Late joiners receive a case snapshot and prior ledger entries from the CASE_MANAGER. A late joiner trusts the CASE_MANAGER's delivery because it trusts the <code>Create</code> message that introduced the CASE_MANAGER. This chain is the minimal trust model; cryptographic ledger integrity (hash-chaining) provides tamper detection.</p> <p>See also</p> <ul> <li>\u00a74.5 (trust and bootstrap semantics)</li> <li>\u00a75.4 (addressing and channels)</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#142-embargo-integrity","title":"14.2 Embargo Integrity","text":"<p>Protocol adherence. An active embargo is an agreement, not a technical enforcement. The protocol provides the signaling infrastructure \u2014 PEC state tracks which participants have consented, \u00a79.5 ensures all participants receive meta-protocol messages \u2014 but it cannot prevent a participant from disclosing outside the protocol.</p> <p>Defection. If a participant discloses publicly while an embargo is <code>ACTIVE</code>, the <code>CP</code> (public awareness) message will trigger the embargo teardown cascade (\u00a710.3). The teardown is a state machine consequence, not a penalty mechanism. The protocol has no built-in penalty for defection; enforcement is an out-of-band organizational matter.</p> <p>Confidentiality gate. Sensitive case content is gated on embargo consent (\u00a79.7). A participant that has not achieved <code>PEC.SIGNATORY</code> does not receive full case details.
