Every one also appears inline at the point in the specification where it first matters, so a reader meeting the gap in context sees it there rather than only here.</p> <p>Open question: CS ordering constraints are unspecified</p> <p>CS ordering constraints \u2014 including the <code>pX\u2192PX</code> invariant (exploit-public implies public-aware) and the rule that <code>CP</code> must precede <code>ET</code> where public disclosure triggers embargo teardown \u2014 exist in three non-normative places: a code docstring, a measurement-oriented reference document (Possible Histories), and a design note. No spec group covers them normatively.</p> <p>A conformance claim cannot meaningfully cover CS ordering until this gap is closed. Treat the material cited here as informative until a normative spec is issued.</p> <p>Open question: who may assert that a vendor became aware</p> <p>The first VFD transition \u2014 <code>v\u2192V</code>, vendor becomes aware \u2014 has no trigger-side specification and no implementation. Design intent is a third-party assertion (\"I notified this Vendor\"), not a self-report.</p> <p>Open questions: who may assert it, whether the subject Vendor may dispute it, and whether transport-level delivery success (HTTP 200) suffices to constitute the assertion.</p> <p>Do not infer a rule from this document's silence.</p> <p>Open question: negative-acknowledgement semantics are unspecified</p> <p>Error message types (<code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code>, <code>CE</code>) are deliberately unmodeled (ADR-0049). Unprocessable inbound messages are dead-lettered with no sender notification. The three-way fault partition (\u00a74.6, ADR-0083) provides structured error signaling where it is implemented, but whether the protocol needs a normative negative-acknowledgement facet \u2014 and if so, what the expected sender behavior (retry, suppress, escalate) should be \u2014 remains open.</p> <p>Open question: two machines have a state called \\\"no embargo\\\"</p> <p>Embargo Management has a None state meaning no embargo is in effect for the case. Embargo consent has a No Embargo state meaning no embargo is in scope for one participant. The reference implementation spells both <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> \u2014 in the embargo enumeration as an alias for <code>NONE</code>, and in the consent enumeration as a state in its own right.</p> <p>The two are genuinely different states in different machines, and they can legitimately disagree. But sharing a name invites the reading that the consent state is a projection of the case's embargo state, which is exactly the conflation these two machines exist to prevent.</p> <p>Open: whether the consent state should be renamed to something that states its meaning more plainly, whether the embargo alias should be dropped, and whether either can be changed without altering the values that appear in the case ledger. Until that is settled, this specification names the machine wherever the distinction matters.</p> <p>Open question: acquiring a role after joining a case</p> <p>This specification says how the Case Owner assigns a role and how a role is offered and accepted. It does not say how a participant already in a case asks for an additional one.</p> <p>A participant admitted as a Vendor that later also needs the Coordinator role has no protocol path to request it. In practice the request is made out of band, or as a <code>Add(Note)</code> on the case, and the Case Owner then issues a role offer. Neither is a specified mechanism.</p> <p>Open: whether the protocol should define a role-request activity, whether a participant may decline a role it was assigned, and how a role that is removed rather than added is represented in the case history.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_abstract/","title":"abstract","text":""},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_abstract/#abstract","title":"Abstract","text":"<p>The Vultron Protocol coordinates vulnerability disclosure among multiple organizations. Participants exchange asynchronous messages and track the case across four dimensions of shared state, realized as five state machines. Any number of organizations may take part in a single case.</p> <p>Coordination is scoped to the case rather than to a system: the case-management role is held per case, and different cases may be managed by different actors. No single service holds every case. Case State (CS) Dimensions [N]","text":"<p>Case State records what is known about the vulnerability. It answers two different questions, and it is a compound of two machines because those questions have different owners.</p> <p>The first is what each vendor has done about the vulnerability: is it aware, does it have a fix, has the fix been deployed? The participants are refusing the proposed change, not the embargo. The previously agreed terms remain in force. An implementation that returns to None here silently drops an embargo that everyone still expects to hold.</p> <p>Reaching Exited. Exited means the embargo has been torn down at the case level. A participant does not put the case into Exited by deciding to stop observing the embargo. What a participant may do is report that it intends to exit, propose a shorter embargo, or propose an earlier end date; the CASE_MANAGER then terminates the embargo and records the termination (\u00a710.2). Terminating an embargo requires Case Owner authorization by default, on the same terms as any other change to canonical case state (\u00a710.3).</p> <p>Embargo duration selection. Other policies are also admissible: an implementation MAY defer the choice to the Case Owner, or apply its own organizational policy. This specification does not mandate shortest-wins.</p> <p>Tacit acceptance. A receiver MAY publish a default embargo policy. Introduction [I]","text":""},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_introduction/#11-background-and-motivation","title":"1.1 Background and Motivation","text":"<p>A vulnerability divides the world into two sets: those who know about it, and those who do not. From the moment of discovery, every party in the knowing set repeatedly answers two questions. What should it do next, and who else needs to know what, and when? Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) continues until the answers are \"nothing\" and \"nobody\".</p> <p>Multi-Party CVD (MPCVD) is CVD involving three or more independent organizations with different interests and roles. The shapes vary. A reporter may go to one vendor, which discovers that other vendors ship the same component. A reporter may go to a coordinator, which finds and notifies the affected vendors. A reporter may go to a vendor and a coordinator at once. What the cases have in common is that the set of participants grows after coordination has begun, each vendor works to its own timeline, and the parties must agree when disclosure happens.</p> <p>Each of those organizations usually already runs its own vulnerability tracking system. The coordination problem is therefore not only one of people talking to each other; it is one of separate systems needing to stay consistent about a shared case. That is the problem Vultron addresses.</p> <p>Email carries the content of a CVD case but records none of its state. No participant can see which vendors have read the report, which have agreed to an embargo, or in what order events occurred. Adding a party mid-case means re-sending the history by hand, and nothing detects the gap if that fails. Vultron gives each of these an explicit, machine-checkable representation: report status per participant (\u00a76), embargo agreement per participant (\u00a79), and an ordered case ledger that every participant replicates (\u00a75.4).</p> <p>Embargo timing is worth noting early. In practice the first two parties to a case establish the initial embargo, and it carries forward as further participants join and agree to it. Establishing terms early is generally easier than negotiating them once many parties are already involved.</p> <p>The protocol tracks coordination state across four dimensions: the report lifecycle (RM), the embargo (EM), what is known about the vulnerability (CS), and each participant's agreement to the embargo (PEC). Because CS is a compound of two independent axes, an implementation runs five state machines (\u00a73.3). Messages are ActivityStreams 2.0 Activities delivered over HTTP. Delivery is asynchronous: no exchange requires both parties to be available at the same moment.</p> <p>Who this specification is for</p> <p>This specification is written for implementers building software that takes part in Vultron cases, and for reviewers assessing whether an implementation conforms.</p> <p>It assumes familiarity with coordinated vulnerability disclosure as a practice \u2014 reporters, vendors, coordinators, embargoes, CVE IDs. It does not assume prior knowledge of Vultron. Where it relies on an external specification, it says so and cites it (\u00a71.3).</p> <p>See also</p> <ul> <li>CVD as a Coordination Problem</li> <li>What Does Success Mean in CVD?</li> <li>The Need for Interoperability</li> <li>CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_introduction/#12-design-goals","title":"1.2 Design Goals","text":"<p>Actor-local state. Each participant keeps its own replica of the case, assembled from the messages it has received. A participant is the authority on its own report and fix status. What the case as a whole asserts \u2014 its embargo state and what is publicly known \u2014 has a single writer, the participant holding the Case Manager role, so that concurrent claims resolve to one answer (\u00a75.4.1).</p> <p>Coordination is scoped to a case, not to a system. The Case Manager role is held per case, and different cases may be managed by different actors. The protocol does not require every case to pass through one shared service. It does require, within a case, that shared state have one writer.</p> <p>Informative: how centralized is this?</p> <p>Two readings should both be avoided.</p> <p>Vultron does not require a single central authority holding all cases. Any actor able to satisfy the Case Manager role can manage a case, and the role is transferable (\u00a711.3).</p> <p>Equally, Vultron as it stands is not a fully decentralized design. Within a case there is one writer, and its availability bounds how fast the case can progress. The current reference implementation goes further and runs a dedicated service actor per case.</p> <p>The protocol leaves more distributed realizations open \u2014 a shared ledger among peers, for instance \u2014 and this version does not specify one (\u00a75.4.2).</p> <p>Asynchronous, message-driven coordination. Participants announce their own transitions rather than being polled, and no exchange requires two parties to be online at once. A participant that is temporarily unreachable does not block the others from making progress.</p> <p>Extensible role model. Roles are not exclusive: a participant may hold Reporter, Vendor and Coordinator at the same time (\u00a73.5). Roles that confer protocol authority are kept separate from roles that describe what an actor does in the world, so the two can vary independently.</p> <p>Interoperable wire format. ActivityStreams 2.0 is the normative wire vocabulary. Reusing an established open standard means the message format is already specified and already understood, and it leaves ActivityPub-based delivery available as a path to potentially compatible tooling. Vultron has not yet been integrated with the wider ActivityPub ecosystem.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_introduction/#13-relationship-to-existing-standards","title":"1.3 Relationship to Existing Standards","text":"<p>ActivityStreams 2.0 and ActivityPub. Both timer paths end in Declined.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_pec-state-machine/#93-what-no-embargo-means","title":"9.3 What No Embargo Means","text":"<p>No Embargo means there is no embargo in scope for this participant. It does not mean \"has not yet agreed\".</p> <p>That reading matters because consent does not always arrive through an invitation. A finder who opens a case for its own finding and sets its default embargo was invited by nobody. A reporter's consent is expressed by submitting the report. In both cases the participant is a signatory without any invitation having been sent, and the case history MUST NOT record an invitation that did not happen.</p> <p>Two consequences follow:</p> <ul> <li>Accept and decline are valid directly from No Embargo. No invitation is   required.</li> <li>The transition from Signatory to Invited MUST be rejected. Consent already   given cannot be withdrawn by re-inviting the participant; if the terms change,   the revise trigger lapses the consent instead.</li> </ul> <p>No Embargo is also the state every participant returns to when an embargo ends, which is independent evidence for the absence reading: reset fires when the embargo goes away, not when an answer is pending.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_pec-state-machine/#94-deadlines-and-the-pocket-veto","title":"9.4 Deadlines and the Pocket Veto","text":"<p>An embargo invitation does not stay open indefinitely. A participant that neither accepts nor declines before the deadline is recorded as having declined \u2014 the pocket veto. Silence is treated as refusal rather than assent, because proceeding on an unanswered invitation would mean asserting agreement the participant never gave.</p> <p>The deadline may be explicit or defaulted:</p> <ul> <li>An embargo invitation MAY carry its own <code>endTime</code>, giving an explicit   respond-by instant. Where present, it is authoritative.</li> <li>Where absent, a configurable policy window applies. The default window is   7 days.</li> </ul> <p>The pocket veto is the implicit form of this one mechanism, not a second mechanism alongside it.</p> <p>One invitation carries two different end times</p> <p>The invitation's <code>endTime</code> is the respond-by deadline for the invitee. The embargo event nested inside the invitation has its own <code>endTime</code>, which is when the embargo would expire. They sit one nesting level apart and mean different things.</p> <p>An implementation that reads the embargo's expiry as the RSVP deadline will hold invitations open for the entire embargo period. One that reads the RSVP deadline as the embargo expiry will tear down embargoes days after they were agreed.</p> <p>Enforcing the deadline. The CASE_MANAGER enforces it. It does so lazily: when it next handles the case, it compares the deadline against the current time. No scheduler or timer service is required.</p> <p>A minimum window applies. The CASE_MANAGER MUST enforce a minimum respond-by window, by default 72 hours. Where an invitation carries a shorter deadline, the CASE_MANAGER MUST extend the deadline to the minimum. It MUST NOT reject the invitation for this reason: a too-short deadline is the proposer's error, and refusing the invitation would penalize the invitee for it.</p> <p>A late acceptance is not refused. The CASE_MANAGER MUST NOT refuse a late accept on deadline grounds. Three cases apply. If the terms it accepts are still current, the CASE_MANAGER records the consent. If the terms are stale, the CASE_MANAGER sends a fresh invitation carrying the current terms. If no embargo remains, the CASE_MANAGER records the accept as a no-op; the participant keeps its place in the case either way.</p> <p>A lapse and a refusal reach the same state. Both record Declined. The case history distinguishes them \u2014 it holds the decline that was sent, or the absence of any answer \u2014 but the consent machine does not, because nothing in the protocol treats the two differently. Both can be invited again.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_pec-state-machine/#95-embargo-traffic-reaches-non-signatories","title":"9.5 Embargo Traffic Reaches Non-Signatories","text":"<p>Embargo consent gates case content. No participant reads another's state directly. Each learns about the others from the messages it receives.</p> <p>A participant's own view is therefore always a replica: its local copy of what it believes the case state to be, assembled from the messages that have reached it. The protocol uses actor URIs as process identifiers. An actor URI is the identity anchor for all messages sent by that actor, and for the canonical case ledger if the actor holds the CASE_MANAGER role. Implementations MUST treat actor URI equality as identity equality: two messages with the same <code>actor</code> URI are from the same actor.</p> <p>Verification. The protocol does not currently mandate a specific identity verification mechanism. The reference implementation anticipates HTTP Signatures (as used in ActivityPub) as the authentication layer for inbound messages. A future version of this specification is expected to normatively require HTTP Signatures at the transport layer.</p> <p>Case bootstrap as the trust establishment mechanism. The <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code> message signed by the originating actor is the trust root for a case. Late joiners receive a case snapshot and prior ledger entries from the CASE_MANAGER. A late joiner trusts the CASE_MANAGER's delivery because it trusts the <code>Create</code> message that introduced the CASE_MANAGER. This chain is the minimal trust model; cryptographic ledger integrity (hash-chaining) provides tamper detection.</p> <p>See also</p> <ul> <li>\u00a74.5 (trust and bootstrap semantics)</li> <li>\u00a75.4 (addressing and channels)</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_security/#142-embargo-integrity","title":"14.2 Embargo Integrity","text":"<p>Protocol adherence. An active embargo is an agreement, not a technical enforcement. The protocol provides the signaling infrastructure \u2014 PEC state tracks which participants have consented, \u00a79.5 ensures all participants receive meta-protocol messages \u2014 but it cannot prevent a participant from disclosing outside the protocol.</p> <p>Defection. If a participant discloses publicly while an embargo is <code>ACTIVE</code>, the <code>CP</code> (public awareness) message will trigger the embargo teardown cascade (\u00a710.3). The teardown is a state machine consequence, not a penalty mechanism. The protocol has no built-in penalty for defection; enforcement is an out-of-band organizational matter.</p> <p>Confidentiality gate. Sensitive case content is gated on embargo consent (\u00a79.7). A participant that has not achieved <code>PEC.SIGNATORY</code> does not receive full case details. Duplicate delivery does not change state.</p> <p>Ledger idempotency. The canonical case ledger is append-only and hash-chained. Content-level encryption \u2014 protecting case details from the CASE_MANAGER itself, or supporting future multi-party computation \u2014 is not specified by this version. Implementations SHOULD treat any unencrypted case content as accessible to whoever operates the CASE_MANAGER.</p> <p>Scope. This section covers security requirements for the protocol as specified. The transition between those two regimes is the bootstrap, and it is where a case's trust is established.</p> <p>The case-creation message is the trust root. When the receiving party creates the case, it sends the reporter a case-creation message signed by the creating actor. That message introduces the actor holding the <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> role. Every participant's trust in the ledger derives from it: a participant accepts entries from the CASE_MANAGER because it accepts the message that established which actor holds the role.</p> <p>A late joiner inherits that trust transitively. An actor invited after the case is under way never sees the original creation message. It receives the case snapshot and the prior ledger entries from the CASE_MANAGER (\u00a710.1), and it trusts them because it trusts the invitation that named the CASE_MANAGER. The hash-chaining of the ledger lets the joiner verify it received an unbroken history \u2014 a check against tampering and omission, not a second source of trust.</p> <p>Messages that arrive before their case. A case-scoped message may reach a participant before the case it refers to has. A participant MUST NOT apply such a message to a case it has not yet received. It holds the message until the case arrives, and discards it if the case never does. A per-message acknowledgement would restate what the chain already shows. <code>RK</code> survives because report submission happens before the case exists, so there is no ledger to carry it.</p> <p><code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code> and <code>CE</code> are deliberately unmodeled, not merely unimplemented. Vulnerabilities are the subject of every Vultron case. Report A document describing a specific vulnerability, submitted to initiate coordination. Case The coordination context around a specific vulnerability: the participants, the shared state, the messages exchanged, and any embargo agreement. The case is the unit of Vultron protocol activity. Actor An identity in the protocol, named by a URI. An actor may be an organization, a person, or a service. Actors exist independently of any case. Participant An actor that has joined a specific case. The case holds a <code>CaseParticipant</code> record for each participant, associating that actor with the roles it holds and the state it owns. An actor is a participant in a case; the same actor may participate in many. <p>Source of the vulnerability definition</p> <p>The definition of vulnerability above is taken unchanged from the CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure. It is also consistent with ISO/IEC 29147:2018 \u00a75.4, which defines the term in the same policy-violation terms (ISO crosswalks).</p> <p>Note what the definition does not require: it says nothing about whether the vulnerability is known, reported, fixed or public. It determines what a participant is obliged to do and which transitions it is authorized to cause. Roles are granted through the case's authority chain (\u00a711.1), not claimed. A participant may hold several at once.</p> <p>Roles fall into two categories, which \u00a712.3 develops further.</p> <p>Process roles describe what an actor does in a case:</p> Role Definition Reporter A participant that submitted the report. The protocol is concerned with who reported the vulnerability, not who discovered it; a discoverer who reports holds the Reporter role. Vendor A participant that produces a product containing the vulnerability and is responsible for developing a fix. Coordinator A participant that facilitates multi-party coordination without being responsible for developing a fix itself. Deployer A participant that deploys a vendor's fix to systems it operates. Distinct from Vendor: producing a fix and applying it are separate acts. CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) A participant authorized to assign CVE IDs directly, rather than delegating assignment to an external service. Orthogonal to the other process roles and commonly held alongside Coordinator or Vendor. Observer A participant with no obligation to drive vendor/fix/deploy transitions. An Observer still tracks case state, is subject to embargo consent, and may report observations about the world. <p>Protocol authority roles describe what an actor controls in the protocol itself:</p> Role Definition Case Owner The party whose disclosure decision the case exists to serve. It decides who is admitted, which roles they hold, and whether embargo terms are accepted or torn down. Case ownership is never delegated, though it may be transferred (\u00a711.3). Case Manager The participant that writes the canonical case ledger and relays case-scoped messages, acting on the Case Owner's behalf. It is the case's single-writer authority (\u00a75.4.1). The Case Owner may delegate this role. <p>Observer names two different things</p> <p>Observer is used in this specification for the process role defined above, and also as the name of the minimum conformance capability set that every participant must provide (\u00a712.2). The reuse is deliberate \u2014 the capability set is named after the least-privileged role \u2014 but the two are not the same kind of thing. A role is a position in a case; a capability set is a property of software (\u00a712.3.3).</p> <p>Informative: the CASE_MANAGER role and the actor that holds it</p> <p>Authority over a case follows the Case Manager role. It does not follow any actor's name, URI, or hosting location. Normative text in this specification therefore names the authority the CASE_MANAGER, meaning whichever participant currently holds the role.</p> <p>The reference implementation happens to satisfy the role with an automated software actor it labels a case actor, provisioned by a case actor service. Those are implementation labels with no protocol meaning. An implementation MUST NOT infer authority from them.</p> <p>Informative: Finder is not a protocol role</p> <p>Earlier CVD models distinguish the finder of a vulnerability from its reporter. Vultron does not: nothing in the protocol depends on who discovered the vulnerability, so an actor that discovers and reports holds the Reporter role. The discoverer's identity may be recorded in the report content or in a case note.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_terminology/#23-protocol-objects-and-messages","title":"2.3 Protocol Objects and Messages","text":"<p>These terms name the things a case is made of and the messages that move between participants.</p> Term Definition Activity The wire form of a Vultron message: an ActivityStreams 2.0 Activity. The last two are the pair most often conflated.</p> Term Definition State The current value of one state machine. Always qualified in this specification \u2014 RM state, embargo state, case state \u2014 because the unqualified word is ambiguous. Transition A change from one state to another. Track To maintain a local value for a state machine and update it as incoming messages report transitions. Every participant tracks all five machines (\u00a712.2). Drive To cause a transition that the participant's roles authorize, and announce it so the other participants learn of it. Which transitions a participant may drive depends on its roles (\u00a712.4). Embargo A time-bounded agreement among the participants of a case not to disclose the vulnerability publicly before an agreed point. Tracked for the case by the embargo state machine (\u00a77) and per participant by embargo consent (\u00a79). Teardown Ending an active embargo. The CASE_MANAGER performs the teardown and records it; a participant may report that it intends to exit, or propose an earlier end, but does not end the case's embargo itself (\u00a710.2). Publication is something a participant does, and the embargo constrains when a participant may do it. Public awareness may arise with no participant publishing anything: an attacker may discover the vulnerability independently, a commit may reveal it, or a non-participant may write about it. <p>Publication and public awareness are not the same thing</p> <p>Vultron governs publication \u2014 what a participant may deliberately disclose, and when. A test supplies a sequence of messages and an input state, and checks the messages the implementation emits and the state it reaches. It does not inspect internal structure.</p> <p>Each test case is therefore a message-sequence scenario paired with the state outcome it expects.</p> <p>Some capabilities that define a role are not protocol-observable at all. Developing a fix, deploying a fix and publishing an advisory happen outside the protocol. Conformance verifies the protocol messages that this work produces, not the work itself.</p> <p>Conformance testing is organized in four layers, which describe what a test verifies. Layers are orthogonal to the capability sets of \u00a712.2, which describe what an implementation provides (see the warning in \u00a712.1):</p> Layer Verifies L1 \u2014 Syntax Messages are well-formed against the wire format (\u00a75) L2 \u2014 Semantics Each message drives the correct state transition (\u00a74, \u00a76\u2013\u00a711) L3 \u2014 Behavior Correct observable outputs: right messages emitted and states reached, given input state plus received message L4 \u2014 Process Correct internal decision structure (e.g. precondition before state write before side-effect) <p>L4 is only enforceable against a reference implementation and is therefore outside the scope of independent conformance claims. Conformance [N]","text":""},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_conformance/_intro/#121-conformance-model-overview","title":"12.1 Conformance Model Overview","text":"<p>Conformance is two-dimensional: capability sets (what protocol machinery an implementation provides) and a role profile (which roles it claims). A conformance claim names capability sets and roles directly:</p> <p><code>CapabilitySet [+ CapabilitySet ...] / Role [+ Role ...]</code></p> <p>Examples: <code>Observer / Reporter</code>, <code>Observer / Vendor</code>, <code>Observer / Vendor + Deployer</code>, <code>Observer + Authority + Hosting / Coordinator + Case Owner</code>.</p> <p>The Observer capability set is required for all participation. Role obligations are additive and orthogonal: no role subsumes another.</p> <p>Capability set names and role names come from \u00a712.2 and \u00a712.3 respectively.</p> <p>Roles and capability expectations. The relationship between roles and capabilities is bidirectional. An implementation must have the capability prerequisites for a role before it can be assigned that role (\u00a712.3.1). Conversely, holding a role in a case creates an expectation that the implementation has those capabilities \u2014 other participants act on that assumption. It is for implementers who want to understand why the protocol behaves as it does, in any programming language.</p> <p>Read this page to learn three things:</p> <ul> <li>Each actor works like a worker that reads messages from a queue.</li> <li>One message can cause a chain of further messages. This is a cascade.</li> <li>Some steps stop because the actor must ask another actor for permission. The actor asks, and then it stops. It does not wait.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#an-actor-is-a-worker-with-two-queues","title":"An actor is a worker with two queues","text":"<p>Each actor in Vultron has an inbox and an outbox.</p> <ul> <li>The inbox holds messages that other actors sent to this actor.</li> <li>The outbox holds messages that this actor sends to other actors.</li> </ul> <p>The actor takes one message from its inbox. It processes that message. If the result is that other actors must be told something, the actor puts new messages in its outbox. Delivery then moves each outbox message to the inbox of the actor it is addressed to.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Two actors exchanging messages\n---\nflowchart LR\n    subgraph A[\"Actor A\"]\n        a_in([inbox]) --&gt; a_proc[process] --&gt; a_out([outbox])\n    end\n    subgraph B[\"Actor B\"]\n        b_in([inbox]) --&gt; b_proc[process] --&gt; b_out([outbox])\n    end\n    a_out --&gt;|delivery| b_in</code></pre> <p>This model has one important consequence. An actor never reaches into another actor's state. It can only send a message. The other actor decides what that message means and what to do about it. Every rule in the protocol follows from this limit.</p> <p>The queue model is a way to think, not a required design</p> <p>Vultron does not require message-broker software. The reference implementation is a single process and uses ordinary HTTP requests for delivery. The queue model is useful because it shows the intended flow of information, and because it keeps a distributed implementation possible later.</p>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#primary-events-and-cascades","title":"Primary events and cascades","text":"<p>Two kinds of things happen in Vultron, and the difference matters.</p> <p>A primary event comes from outside the protocol. Something in the world changed, and a person, a service, or another organisation must tell Vultron. Examples:</p> <ul> <li>A finder submits a vulnerability report.</li> <li>A vendor decides the report is valid.</li> <li>A participant proposes an embargo period.</li> </ul> <p>A cascade is everything that follows automatically from a primary event. The actor that received the primary event updates its own state and sends the messages the protocol requires. Each actor that receives one of those messages runs its own cascade. Together these form a chain.</p> <p>For example, one primary event \u2014 a finder submits a report \u2014 causes this chain:</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Cascade from a single primary event\n---\nflowchart TD\n    A[finder submits report] --&gt; B[vendor records the report]\n    B --&gt; C[vendor opens a case]\n    C --&gt; D[vendor adds the finder as a participant]\n    D --&gt; E[vendor tells the finder the case exists]</code></pre> <p>Nobody instructs the vendor to open a case. The vendor does it because it received a report. This is the central design rule: supply the primary event only, and let the protocol produce the consequences.</p>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#why-this-rule-is-useful","title":"Why this rule is useful","text":"<p>The rule gives you a test for correctness. If you must send a second message by hand to make the process continue, then one of two things is true:</p> <ul> <li>That step is genuinely a new primary event, because new information from outside was needed.</li> <li>Or the implementation has a gap, because the step should have happened automatically.</li> </ul> <p>The test tells you which kind of problem you have. It is the reason Vultron test scenarios inject only primary events and then check the resulting state.</p>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#causal-order-not-time-order","title":"Causal order, not time order","text":"<p>It is natural to describe a process as a list of steps in time: A, then B, then C. The protocol is not built on time. It is built on cause: A, and therefore B, and therefore C.</p> <p>The difference is not a matter of style. Delivery and processing take time, and they can fail. So \"B happened five seconds after A\" tells you almost nothing, while \"B happened because A happened\" tells you the process is correct.</p> <p>A single step between two actors is really a chain of smaller events:</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Steps in a single message delivery\n---\nflowchart LR\n    addr[\"A addresses\"] --&gt; send[\"A sends\"] --&gt; arr[\"arrives at B\"] --&gt; proc[\"B processes\"] --&gt; rec[\"B records\"] --&gt; rep[\"B replies\"]</code></pre> <p>Only the last links prove anything. That a message was sent proves only that the sender tried. That it arrived proves only that the network worked. That the receiver recorded it proves the receiver accepted it and acted.</p> <p>If you write tests or monitoring for a Vultron implementation, check the recorded state of the actor that owns the effect, and read it from that actor. Do not accept elapsed time as evidence, and do not accept an acknowledgement of receipt as evidence that processing succeeded.</p>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#when-an-actor-must-ask-permission","title":"When an actor must ask permission","text":"<p>Some steps in a cascade cannot be automatic, because the actor is not allowed to decide alone. A participant may report that a vulnerability is now public. Whether that report becomes the shared, agreed state of the case is not the reporting participant's decision. The case owner decides.</p> <p>Here Vultron does something that surprises people. The actor asks, and then it stops.</p> <ol> <li>The actor needs permission.</li> <li>The actor sends the case owner a request that carries a deadline.</li> <li>The actor finishes. Its work succeeded, because asking was the work.</li> <li>Later, the case owner replies: agreed, or refused.</li> <li>That reply is a new message. It arrives in an inbox, and it starts new work.</li> </ol> <p>Step 3 is the part worth understanding. Success means \"I asked\", not \"I was told yes.\" Nothing is left waiting or held open. The work is divided at the question rather than paused there. Asking is one complete piece of work; acting on the answer is another piece of work, and the answer's arrival is what starts it.</p> <p>This is why the request carries a deadline. The deadline is part of the message, so the case owner can see how long they have, and the asking actor knows when the question has gone stale.</p>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#what-happens-while-the-actor-waits","title":"What happens while the actor waits","text":"<p>Nothing is held open, so the case must be in a sensible state during the wait. It usually already is. In the example above, the participant's report is recorded as what that participant claims. Only its promotion to what the case agrees waits for permission. Those are two different facts, and recording the first while the second is undecided is honest and useful.</p> <p>This gives a rule for implementers: you may only ask about an action whose not-yet-done state can be described. If \"not yet decided\" cannot be represented, the actor must refuse instead of asking, because there is nowhere for the case to rest.</p>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#asking-twice-and-not-asking-twice","title":"Asking twice, and not asking twice","text":"<p>Because an actor stops after asking, it may reach the same point again later \u2014 for instance, when the same participant reports the same thing again. So an actor that reaches a step needing permission first works out where the conversation stands:</p> What the actor finds What it does A reply agreeing Do the action. A reply refusing Do not do the action. Record the refusal. A request already sent, deadline not passed Nothing. Do not ask twice. A request already sent, deadline passed Ask again, with a new deadline. No request yet Record the not-yet state, ask, and stop. <p>These situations do not overlap, so returning to this step is always safe. Whether to admit a new participant to a case is one \u2014 the answer is as useful next week as it is today.</p> <p>Other questions are not. Permission to change the agreed state of a case is granted against the case as it was when the question was asked. If the reply arrives after the deadline, the case may have moved on: an embargo may have been agreed, or another participant may have published. Acting on that permission would apply an old decision to a new situation.</p> <p>So each kind of request declares which it is. For requests of the second kind, a late reply does not grant permission, and the asking actor must ask again if it still wants to act. It is the list a person, an interface, or an automated service works from. Without it, a case owner has no way to discover that a decision is waiting for them, so permission could only ever be granted by accident. This list is what makes the case owner's role something they can actually perform.</p> <p>Both lists are working notes. They say what is outstanding. They never say what was permitted \u2014 for that, an actor reads the recorded history of the case, which is the shared, verifiable record. No message arrives when time runs out. So something must look.</p> <p>Vultron uses two mechanisms, and neither is a timer inside the protocol.</p> <p>Looking when you pass by. The next time an actor reaches the step that asked the question, it notices the deadline has passed. This is often enough. When a message is lost, the sender usually sends it again, and that repeat is what causes both actors to look. In that case the other party's retry is the clock.</p> <p>An external watcher. For prompt handling, an implementation can run a service that watches for passed deadlines and notifies the actor. This is deliberately outside the protocol: watching the clock is not a protocol behaviour, and keeping it outside means an implementation can choose how attentive to be. It also means deadline behaviour can be tested by asking for a check directly, rather than by waiting.</p> <p>Noticing an expired request never sends it again by itself. Expiry is information. The message may be malformed, or it may refer to something the actor does not know about, or the sender may not be permitted to send it.</p> <p>Silence is a poor answer. A sender waiting for a reply would wait for its whole deadline over a failure that took a fraction of a second.</p> <p>So an actor that cannot process a message from a known, authenticated sender tells that sender so. Two reasons: those details are useless to the sender, and explaining exactly why a message was refused helps an attacker probe the receiver.</p> <p>An actor does not answer a message it cannot authenticate. It answers three questions: what the hexagonal boundary means, how an incoming message flows from Hyper Text Transfer Protocol (HTTP) delivery to behavior-tree execution, and what the reference implementation supplies versus what an adopter must build.</p> <p>Reference implementation, not the protocol</p> <p>Vultron is a reference implementation of the CVD coordination protocol. The structure described here \u2014 hexagonal layering, an ActivityStreams Vocabulary 2.0 (AS2) inbox pipeline, behavior-tree orchestration \u2014 is one valid way to realize the protocol. The domain logic sits in an inner circle that knows nothing about how messages arrive, how they are formatted, or where state is stored. Everything external reaches the domain only through ports \u2014 typed interface contracts \u2014 and each port is fulfilled by an adapter at the edge.</p> <p>The codebase splits into three concentric responsibilities.</p> Layer Python package Owns Must not import Core <code>vultron/core/</code> Domain models, state machines, use cases, ports, behavior trees <code>vultron/wire/</code>, <code>vultron/adapters/</code>, web frameworks Wire <code>vultron/wire/as2/</code> AS2 vocabulary, structural parser, semantic extractor, activity factories Core domain logic, web frameworks Adapters <code>vultron/adapters/</code> HTTP inbox, CLI, persistence, outbound delivery, connectors Core domain rules <p>The wire format is a separate concern from the domain, not a subset of it. AS2 was chosen because it maps cleanly to Vultron semantics (ADR-0005), but that alignment does not make it a domain dependency. Domain objects and their wire counterparts share a common base but form two structurally distinct branches: a strict core branch and a lenient wire branch (ADR-0017). The core branch is authoritative and represents every field the wire can carry; the wire branch tolerates the loose, optional shapes that arrive over the network.</p> <p>We keep this boundary for two reasons. Wire formats change, and the domain logic should not have to change with them. Parsing and shape validation are edge concerns, so pushing them out of the core keeps the state-machine logic small and testable. The rule that core carries no wire or framework imports (ARCH-01-001) is enforced by ratchet tests under <code>test/architecture/</code>, so a violation fails continuous integration rather than merely drawing a review comment.</p> <p>vultron-core the concept versus <code>vultron/core/</code> the package</p> <p>vultron-core names the abstract protocol. <code>vultron/core/</code> names the Python package that implements it here. The package is the reference realization of the concept, not the concept itself.</p>"},{"location":"topics/reference_architecture/#from-http-delivery-to-behavior-tree-the-inbox-pipeline","title":"From HTTP delivery to behavior tree: the inbox pipeline","text":"<p>An incoming message crosses every layer of the hexagon in one pass. It arrives as AS2 JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) at an HTTP endpoint and leaves as a committed state change with any resulting messages queued for delivery. The stages below each do one job and hand off to the next.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Inbound message pipeline\n---\nflowchart TD\n    http[\"HTTP POST /inbox&lt;br/&gt;(AS2 JSON)\"]\n    parse[\"AS2 parser&lt;br/&gt;structural validity\"]\n    rehydrate[\"rehydrate&lt;br/&gt;resolve referenced objects\"]\n    extract[\"semantic extractor&lt;br/&gt;AS2 pattern \u2192 MessageSemantics\"]\n    dispatch[\"behavior dispatcher&lt;br/&gt;semantics \u2192 use case\"]\n    bt[\"use case runs a behavior tree&lt;br/&gt;guards \u2192 commit \u2192 effects\"]\n    persist[\"persist via DataLayer&lt;br/&gt;and queue outbound messages\"]\n\n    http --&gt; parse\n    parse --&gt; rehydrate\n    rehydrate --&gt; extract\n    extract --&gt; dispatch\n    dispatch --&gt; bt\n    bt --&gt; persist</code></pre> <p>A driving adapter receives the request. The AS2 parser checks structural validity, <code>rehydrate()</code> resolves referenced objects into full inline objects, and the semantic extractor (<code>vultron/wire/as2/extractor/</code>) matches the activity against an ordered pattern registry to produce a domain-level <code>MessageSemantics</code> value. The semantic extractor is the single place where AS2 structure becomes domain intent (ARCH-03-001), so the rest of the core never inspects wire shapes.</p> <p>The core layer decides what to do. The behavior dispatcher (<code>vultron/core/dispatcher.py</code>) maps the extracted semantics to a use case through a table lookup, and the use case runs the appropriate behavior tree. Routing all inbound case activity through the Case Actor is what lets a single behavior-tree execution produce a canonically ordered ledger entry (ADR-0021, ADR-0022). The reference implementation retired an earlier in-process shortcut so that co-located actors talk to each other exactly as remote actors would (ADR-0042). This keeps the transport uniform: the same JSON payload is deliverable whether the recipient is in the same process or across the internet.</p> <p>Delivery is treated as unreliable and bounded. The outbox retries with backoff, classifies <code>4xx</code> responses as terminal, and moves an activity to a dead-letter store once its per-activity attempt budget is exhausted rather than retrying forever (ADR-0066). A behavior tree is a hierarchy of nodes ticked from the root; each node returns Success, Failure, or Running, and the control-flow nodes above them compose those results into higher-level behavior. Vultron uses this structure because CVD activities compose the same way: validate a report, propose an embargo, publish an advisory \u2014 each is a small tree that slots into a larger one (ADR-0002).</p> <p>On the received side, a tree runs guards first, commits the ledger entry, then fires effects, in that order (CLP-10-006). A read or write of Report Management (RM), Embargo Management (EM), or Case State (CS) goes through a dedicated state node rather than touching state inline, which keeps every transition auditable.</p> <p>This page stays at the summary level by design. These are call-out points \u2014 locations where automated execution pauses and waits for an answer from an external service.</p> <p>During development and simulation, a call-out point is filled by a Fuzzer Node that returns a probabilistic success or failure. In production, an adopter replaces that stub with a real service that satisfies one of five capability shapes \u2014 Sentinel, Evaluator, Retriever, Composer, or Actuator (ADR-0024). In the hexagonal layout, a capability shape is a port and a concrete capability is the adapter that fulfills it.</p> <p>Not every external question is a call-out point. The reference implementation provides the protocol machinery: the five state machines, the wire vocabulary and its semantic mapping, the inbox and outbox pipelines, the behavior trees that orchestrate transitions, and the persistence and delivery adapters that make a local actor run. What an adopter supplies are the capabilities behind the call-out points \u2014 the judgment and the connections to outside systems that the protocol deliberately leaves open.</p> <p>This division tracks the protocol's conformance levels. Correct message syntax and correct state transitions (levels L1 and L2) come from using a conformant serializer and implementing the state machines. Correct observable behavior (L3) is stated by the behavioral conformance specifications. Correct internal decision structure \u2014 precondition checks before state writes before effects, audit-log ordering, idempotency \u2014 is level L4, which is only demonstrable through a reference implementation, and the <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> behavior-tree layer is that demonstration. As we wrote in The CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure:</p> <p>Excerpt from The CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure</p> <p>Perhaps the simplest description of the CVD process is that it starts with at least one individual becoming aware of a vulnerability in a product. In the Voltron animated series, a team of protectors joins forces to defend the universe from their adversaries. Their defensive mission requires a combination of independent defenders coordinating their efforts to achieve their goals. Like Voltron, our Vultron Protocol comprises a combination of humans and the technical processes and mechanisms that empower them. The goal of this documentation is to lay the foundation for the semantic interoperability of CVD processes across Participants. Syntactic interoperability, in the form of message formats and the like, is the focus of our ongoing effort.</p> <p>Addressing semantic interoperability first is a deliberate choice. If we were to go in the reverse order, we might wind up with systems that exchange data quickly and accurately yet still fail to accomplish the mutually beneficial outcomes that MPCVD sets out to achieve. Carney et al. illustrate the importance of semantic interoperability in their 2005 report Some Current Approaches to Interoperability:</p> <p>Carney et al. on semantic interoperability</p> <p>There is a limited number of ways that agreements on meaning can be achieved. In the context of design-time interoperability, semantic agreements are reached in the same manner as interface agreements between the constituent systems... However, in the context of run-time interoperability, the situation is more complex, since there is need for some manner of universal agreement, so that a new system can join, ad-hoc, some other group of systems. The new system must be able to usefully share data and meaning with those other systems, and those other systems must be able to share data and meaning from an unfamiliar newcomer.</p> <p>In this excerpt, replace the word \"system\" with the concept of a \"CVD Case Participant,\" and the need for semantic interoperability as a means of achieving coordination in MPCVD becomes clear:</p> <p>Paraphrasing Carney et al. in the context of CVD</p> <p>[...] However, in the context of run-time interoperability, the situation is more complex, since there is need for some manner of universal agreement, so that a new CVD Participant can join, ad-hoc, some other group of CVD Participants [in a CVD Case]. The new CVD Case Participant must be able to usefully share data and meaning with those other CVD Case Participants, and those other Participants must be able to share data and meaning from an unfamiliar newcomer.</p> <p>Elsewhere in the same report, Carney et al. write,</p> <p>Carney et al. on the necessity of trust in interoperability</p> <p>In the hoped-for context of unbounded systems of systems, trust in the actions and capabilities provided by interoperating parties is essential. Each party to an interaction must have, develop, or perceive a sense of whether the actions of interoperating parties can be trusted. This sense of trust is not Boolean (e.g., parties can be trusted to varying degrees), is context dependent (Party A can be trusted in a particular context but not in another), and is time sensitive (Party A can be trusted for a certain period). Further, the absence of trust-----distrust-----is less dangerous than misplaced trust: it is better to know that you cannot trust a particular party than to misplace trust in a party</p> <p>The protocol we propose is intended to promote trust between MPCVD Participants both within an individual case as well as over time and across cases.</p>"},{"location":"topics/background/interoperability/#objectives","title":"Objectives","text":"<p>The objectives of this documentation are as follows:</p> <ol> <li> <p>Provide a set of common primitives to serve as an ontological     foundation for CVD process definitions across     organizations.</p> </li> <li> <p>Construct abstract workflows that support the inter-organizational     coordination and synchronization required for the     CVD process to     be successful.</p> </li> <li> <p>From those primitives and workflows, identify a set of message types     needed for the CVD process to function.</p> </li> <li> <p>Provide high-level requirements for the semantic content of those     message types.</p> </li> <li> <p>Explore options for the syntactic representation of those message     types.</p> </li> </ol>"},{"location":"topics/background/what-is-vultron/","title":"What Is Vultron?","text":"<p>Is this page for me?</p> <p>This page is written for two readers:</p> <ul> <li>A CVD practitioner (security researcher, coordinator, CERT/CSIRT   analyst) who wants to know whether Vultron solves a problem they   actually have.</li> <li>A systems architect who wants to understand what \"Vultron   conformance\" would mean for their organization's tools and processes.</li> </ul> <p>If you are already sold and want to implement, jump to How-to Guides.</p> <p>CVD is a multi-party coordination problem. See the Behaviors Reference for auto-generated documentation from the current implementation.</p> <p>With the formal definition of the Vultron Protocol behind us, we now turn our attention to reflect on one of many possible paths toward implementation. We find that Behavior Trees have a number of desirable properties when it comes to automating the kinds of complex behaviors our protocol demands.</p> <p>For more about Behavior Trees</p> <p>For more about Behavior Trees, see </p> <ul> <li>Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction</li> <li>A behavior language for story-based believable agents</li> <li>GDC 2005 Proceeding: Handling Complexity in the Halo 2 AI</li> <li>Increasing Modularity of UAV Control Systems using Computer Game Behavior Trees</li> <li>An integrated system for autonomous robotics manipulation</li> </ul> <p>Behavior Trees are a way of designing and programming hierarchical behaviors. They originated in the computer gaming industry to develop realistic AIs to control NPCs in games. More recently, Behavior Trees have been used in robotics to create adaptive behaviors using autonomous AI agents. Behavior Trees offer a high potential for automating complex tasks. Agent processes can be modeled as sets of behaviors (pre-conditions, actions, and post-conditions) and the logic that joins them. Behavior Trees offer a way to organize and describe agent behaviors in a straightforward, understandable way.</p> <p>In this section, we use Behavior Trees as a method for describing MPCVD Participant activities and their interactions with the formal protocol. These behaviors map approximately to the activities described in the CVD Guide (e.g., validate report, prioritize report, create fix, publish report, publish fix, deploy fix).</p> <p>If Behavior Trees were merely a notational convention, they would already have been useful enough to include here to structure the high-level business logic of the Vultron Protocol. But they also offer a way to prototype software agents that reflect the activities of CVD Participants. Because Behavior Trees are inherently hierarchical, they are composable. Both conditions and actions can be composed into small task-oriented behaviors, which can, in turn, be composed to represent more complex agent behaviors. As a result, independent agents using Behavior Trees can be composed into multi-agent behaviors that achieve goals.</p>"},{"location":"topics/behavior_logic/#a-brief-introduction-to-behavior-tree-notation","title":"A Brief Introduction to Behavior Tree Notation","text":"<p>Behavior Trees consist of a hierarchy of nodes represented as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). A Behavior Tree execution always begins at the root node, and execution is passed along the tree by ticking each child node according to the logic built into the tree. When ticked, each node does its job and returns one of three statuses: Success, Failure, or Running. A full introduction to Behavior Trees can be found in Colledanchise and \u00d6gren's book Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction.</p> <p>Behavior Tree Node Types</p> Node Type Shape or Symbol Description Root any control flow type has no parent nodes, has one or more child nodes, and can be of any of the control-flow types. Condition rounded oval does not change the state of the world, has no child nodes, and returns only Success or Failure. Task rectangle has no child nodes; performs a task, which might change the state of the world; and returns Success, Failure, or Running. Sequence \u2192 ticks each child node, returning the last Success or the first Failure, or Running if a child returns Running. Fallback ? ticks each child node, returning the first Success or the last Failure, or Running if a child returns Running. Loop \u21ba repeatedly ticks child nodes until an exit condition is met. Parallel \u21c9 ticks all child nodes simultaneously, and returns Success when \\(m\\) of \\(n\\) children have returned Success. <p>A basic Behavior Tree is shown below. When a tree is presented in the vertical orientation, each node's children should be read left to right. In the example below, we see two motifs that come up through the remainder of this section. On the left side is a Fallback node (\\(\\boxed{?}\\)), which short-circuits to Success when the \\(postcondition\\) is already met. Otherwise, some activity will occur in \\(task_a\\) and, assuming that it succeeds, the \\(postcondition\\) is set. As a result, the fallback node ensures that Success means that the \\(postcondition\\) is met.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: A Basic Behavior Tree\n---\nflowchart TD\n    root[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    l[?]\n    root --&gt; l\n    r[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    root --&gt; r\n    l0([postcondition])\n    l --&gt; l0\n    l1[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    l --&gt; l1\n    l10[task_a]\n    l1 --&gt; l10\n    l11[set postcondition]\n    l1 --&gt; l11\n    r0([precondition])\n    r --&gt; r0\n    r1[task_b]\n    r --&gt; r1\n    r2[?]\n    r --&gt; r2\n    r20[task_c]\n    r2 --&gt; r20\n    r21[task_d]\n    r2 --&gt; r21</code></pre> <p>On the right side is a sequence (\\(\\boxed{\\rightarrow}\\)) that hinges on a \\(precondition\\) being met prior to some set of actions being taken. Assuming the \\(precondition\\) is met, \\(task_b\\) fires and, assuming it succeeds execution, proceeds to another fallback node. This fallback node represents a set of tasks in which one only needs to succeed for the fallback to return Success. If \\(task_c\\) succeeds, then \\(task_d\\) does not run.</p> <p>Behavior Trees can sometimes be wider than they are tall, so we sometimes display them in a horizontal orientation to save space. The semantics remain the same, but each node's children should be read top-to-bottom rather than left-to-right. The same tree as above is shown below in horizontal form.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: A Basic Behavior Tree (horizontal)\n---\nflowchart LR\n    root[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    l[?]\n    root --&gt; l\n    r[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    root --&gt; r\n    l0([postcondition])\n    l --&gt; l0\n    l1[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    l --&gt; l1\n    l10[task_a]\n    l1 --&gt; l10\n    l11[set postcondition]\n    l1 --&gt; l11\n    r0([precondition])\n    r --&gt; r0\n    r1[task_b]\n    r --&gt; r1\n    r2[?]\n    r --&gt; r2\n    r20[task_c]\n    r2 --&gt; r20\n    r21[task_d]\n    r2 --&gt; r21</code></pre> <p>Behavior Trees are composable\u2014that is, a task node in one tree can be replaced with a more refined Behavior Tree in another. We leverage this feature throughout the remainder of this chapter to describe an agent model for an MPCVD Participant as a set of nested Behavior Trees that reflect the protocol described in the previous chapters.</p>"},{"location":"topics/behavior_logic/acquire_exploit_bt/","title":"Acquire Exploit Behavior","text":"<p>Some Vendors or other CVD Participants might require a proof-of-concept exploit to accompany an incoming report for it to pass their validation checks. It bears some structural similarity to the Report Validation Behavior Tree just described: An initial post-condition check (A) falls back to the main process (B) leading toward \\(accept\\), which, in turn, falls back to the deferral process (C).</p> <p>In more detail, (A) if the report is already in either the Accepted or Deferred states and no new information is available to prompt a change, the behavior ends.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Report Prioritization Behavior Tree\n---\nflowchart LR\n    fb[\"?\"]\n    seq1[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    fb --&gt;|A| seq1\n    rm_d_or_a([\"RM in D or A?\"])\n    seq1 --&gt; rm_d_or_a\n    seq1fb[\"?\"]\n    seq1 --&gt; seq1fb\n    enough_info([\"enough info?\"])\n    seq1fb --&gt; enough_info\n    gather_seq[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    seq1fb --&gt; gather_seq\n    gather_info[\"gather info\"]\n    gather_seq --&gt; gather_info\n    no_info[\"no new info\"]\n    gather_seq --&gt; no_info\n    seq2[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    fb --&gt;|B| seq2\n    rm_v_d_a([\"RM in V, D, or A?\"])\n    seq2 --&gt; rm_v_d_a\n    eval_priority[\"evaluate priority\"]\n    seq2 --&gt; eval_priority\n    priority_not_defer([\"priority is not defer?\"])\n    seq2 --&gt; priority_not_defer\n    accept_fb[\"?\"]\n    seq2 --&gt; accept_fb\n    rm_a([\"RM in A?\"])\n    accept_fb --&gt; rm_a\n    accept_seq[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    accept_fb --&gt; accept_seq\n    accept[\"accept\"]\n    accept_seq --&gt; accept\n    accept_to_a[\"RM &amp;rarr; A&lt;br/&gt;(emit RA)\"]\n    accept_seq --&gt; accept_to_a\n    defer_fb[\"?\"]\n    fb --&gt;|C| defer_fb\n    rm_d([\"RM in D?\"])\n    defer_fb --&gt; rm_d\n    defer_seq[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    defer_fb --&gt; defer_seq\n    defer[\"defer\"]\n    defer_seq --&gt; defer\n    defer_to_d[\"RM &amp;rarr; D&lt;br/&gt;(emit RD)\"]\n    defer_seq --&gt; defer_to_d</code></pre> <p>Failing that, we enter the main prioritization sequence (B). The preconditions of the main sequence are that either the report has not yet been prioritized out of the Valid state (\\(q^{rm} \\in V\\)) or new information has been made available to a report in either \\(q^{rm} \\in \\{ D, A \\}\\) to trigger a reevaluation.</p> <p>Assuming the preconditions are met, the report priority is evaluated. For example, a Participant using SSVC could insert that process here. The evaluation task is expected to always set the report priority. The subsequent check returns Failure on a defer priority or Success on any non-deferral priority. On Success, an accept task is included as a placeholder for any intake process that a Participant might have for Accepted reports. Assuming that it succeeds, the report is explicitly moved to the Accepted (\\(q^{rm} \\xrightarrow{a} A\\)) state, and an \\(RA\\) message is emitted.</p> <p>(C) Should any item in the main sequence fail, the case is deferred, its state set to \\(q^{rm} \\xrightarrow{d} D\\), and an \\(RD\\) message is emitted accordingly. If the current information available in the report is sufficient, no further action is necessary and the entire behavior returns Success. However, a previous validation pass might have left some indicator that more information was needed. In that case, execution proceeds to the sequence in which the gather info task runs. If nothing new is found, the entire branch returns Success, and the report remains Invalid. If new information is found, though, the branch fails, driving execution over to the main validation sequence.</p> <p>(C) The main validation sequence follows when none of the above conditions have been met. In other words, the validation sequence is triggered when the report is in Received and its validity has never been evaluated or when the report was originally determined to be Invalid but new information is available to prompt reconsideration. The validation process shown here is comprised of two main steps: a credibility check followed by a validity check as outlined in our introduction of the Received (R) state.</p> <p>As a reminder, a report might be in one of three categories: (a) neither credible nor valid, (b) credible but invalid, or (c) both credible and valid. Vultron handles all of that automatically using behavior trees (BTs) \u2014 a kind of state machine that runs as protocol activities arrive.</p> <p>But some steps require judgment that Vultron cannot make by itself:</p> <ul> <li>Is this vulnerability report credible?</li> <li>Should we accept this embargo proposal?</li> <li>Has a CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) ID already been assigned?</li> <li>Is it time to publish the advisory?</li> </ul> <p>These are call-out points \u2014 places where the BT pauses and waits for an answer from an external service before it can continue.</p> <p>A call-out point is answerable now; asking another actor is not</p> <p>A call-out point waits for a service you run, so it can be answered while the BT is still running. That is what makes pausing viable.</p> <p>Some questions cannot be answered that way, because they need a decision from another actor in the case \u2014 for example, whether the case owner permits a change to the case's agreed state. No service can answer that on the owner's behalf, and the answer may take days. There the actor does not pause: it sends a request and finishes, and the reply starts new work when it arrives. See Protocol Event Flow.</p> <p>During development and simulation, call-out points are filled by fuzzer nodes \u2014 stubs that return a random success or failure based on a probability. In production, you replace a fuzzer node with a real service: a capability implementation.</p>"},{"location":"topics/capability_model/#the-two-integration-surfaces","title":"The two integration surfaces","text":"<p>There are two ways an external service interacts with Vultron:</p> <p>Call-out \u2014 Vultron calls you. The BT reaches a call-out point, packages up a question as a structured payload, sends it to your service, and waits for a structured answer. Your service decides and responds.</p> <p>Call-in \u2014 You call Vultron. Your service monitors something externally \u2014 a timer, a threat feed, a deployment system \u2014 and, when a condition is met, sends a trigger to Vultron. Vultron acts on it.</p> <p>Most services use the call-out surface. One shape \u2014 the Sentinel \u2014 works exclusively on the call-in side (see The five shapes below).</p>"},{"location":"topics/capability_model/#three-level-taxonomy","title":"Three-level taxonomy","text":"<p>Every integration point in Vultron fits into a three-level hierarchy:</p> <p>Shape \u2192 Capability \u2192 Capability implementation</p> Level What it is Example Shape The abstract type of interaction \u2014 what the service receives, what it returns, and how the BT uses the result Evaluator Capability A specific named integration point with its own input/output contract <code>EvaluateCveEligibility</code> Capability implementation The concrete service you build that fulfills a capability at runtime A microservice that applies CNA Operational Rules and returns pass/fail <p>Think of the shape as a job description, the capability as the open role, and your implementation as the service hired into that role.</p> <p>Some capabilities are sub-steps of a larger workflow capability.
