Each one keeps its own copy of the case. This page explains how those copies stay in agreement, and it answers two questions:</p> <ul> <li>Who decides the order in which things happened?</li> <li>What happens when messages arrive in the wrong order?</li> </ul> <p>Vultron answers the first question with a single writer. It answers the second by holding an early message until the message it depends on arrives.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#one-writer-many-copies","title":"One writer, many copies","text":"<p>Every participant in a case keeps a local copy of the case, called a replica. No participant can read or write another participant's replica. Knowledge travels only in messages \u2014 see the Actor Knowledge Model.</p> <p>One peer is different. Whichever participant holds the <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> role is the case's single-writer authority \u2014 the CASE_MANAGER. It keeps the case ledger: the append-only history that is authoritative for the case, and it is the only peer that appends to that history (CLP-01-003). In the prototype this authority is enacted by a dedicated service actor (the Case Actor), but the authority derives from the role, never from that actor's name or URL (ADR-0088).</p> <p>The flow of a change is always the same:</p> <ol> <li>A participant sends the CASE_MANAGER an assertion \u2014 I accept the embargo,    my report is now validated, here is a note.</li> <li>The CASE_MANAGER judges the assertion and appends one entry recording the    outcome. An entry's <code>disposition</code> says whether the assertion was    <code>recorded</code> (accepted) or <code>rejected</code>, so a refusal leaves a trace rather    than a silence.</li> <li>The CASE_MANAGER sends the new entry to every participant as    <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code>.</li> <li>Each participant records the entry, and applies its effects to its own    replica if the entry was <code>recorded</code>.</li> </ol> <p>Because there is exactly one writer, no participant ever has to reconcile two competing versions of the case history. There is only one version. A participant's replica is a projection of that history, not an independent record.</p> <p>The same rule applies in reverse: a participant accepts a case update only from the CASE_MANAGER for that case, and rejects an update from any other sender (PCR-03-001). Nobody else can write to a replica, and the replica's owner does not edit it directly either \u2014 even when that owner is the organization that opened the case.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#two-views-of-the-ledger","title":"Two views of the ledger","text":"<p>The ledger can be read two ways, and most of this page is about the second one.</p> <ul> <li>The audit log is every entry the CASE_MANAGER appended, in the order it   appended them \u2014 rejections included.</li> <li>The recorded projection is the subset whose <code>disposition</code> is <code>recorded</code>.   That projection is the authoritative history of the case   (CLP-04-001).</li> </ul> <p>Case state is reconstructed from the recorded projection alone; a replica ignores rejected entries when working out what is true of the case (CLP-04-002). The hash chain is computed over that projection too (CLP-04-003), so a rejection does not advance the chain: the next recorded entry names the previous recorded entry as its predecessor, not a rejection appended in between.</p> <p>A rejection is therefore evidence \u2014 the CASE_MANAGER saw this assertion and refused it \u2014 rather than a fact about the case. Where the rest of this page says \"the chain\" or \"the history\", it means the recorded projection.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-a-ledger-entry-carries","title":"What a ledger entry carries","text":"<p>Each entry is a small, immutable record. These are the fields that carry the ordering and integrity guarantees this page is about.</p> Field Meaning <code>case_id</code> The case this entry belongs to <code>log_index</code> Position in the case history; starts at 0 and counts up <code>published</code> When the CASE_MANAGER stamped the entry, by its own clock <code>prevLogHash</code> Hash of the previous <code>recorded</code> entry <code>entryHash</code> Hash of this entry's own content <code>payloadSnapshot</code> A copy of the assertion the entry records <p><code>prevLogHash</code> and <code>entryHash</code> link the entries into a chain, like the teeth of a zipper. Each entry names its predecessor in the recorded projection, so a receiver can tell whether an entry belongs at the end of the history it already holds. The first entry in a case names the genesis hash, a value derived from the case object itself, so the chain is anchored to the case it describes.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#log-index-is-the-causal-order","title":"Log index is the causal order","text":"<p>The <code>log_index</code> sequence is the causal order of the case. If the CASE_MANAGER observed event A before event B, then A has the lower <code>log_index</code> (CLP-14-001, ADR-0079). Anything that needs to know what happened first compares log indexes. It does not compare clocks.</p> <p>This matters because clocks disagree. Two organizations on different continents, running different software, will not agree on the millisecond at which an event occurred. Sorting a shared history by wall-clock time would make the order depend on whose clock was fast. Sorting by <code>log_index</code> does not.</p> <p>Timestamps are still recorded, and they are still useful \u2014 as corroborating evidence, and for spotting a participant whose clock is wrong. They are not the order.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-the-ledger-claims-and-what-it-does-not","title":"What the ledger claims, and what it does not","text":"<p>The ledger is authoritative from the CASE_MANAGER's point of view. It is a postmark, not a forensic reconstruction. It records the sequence in which the CASE_MANAGER observed and processed events, and it makes no claim about when those events happened inside another organization (CLP-15-005).</p> <ul> <li>For events the CASE_MANAGER generates itself, causal order is known by   construction: the entries are written one after another on a single path.</li> <li>For events reported by participants, the CASE_MANAGER's own receive-and-commit   order is the order. The CASE_MANAGER cannot verify a causal claim about   something it did not see.</li> </ul> <p>The CASE_MANAGER never reorders entries to match timestamps supplied by someone else. Doing so would let external data override the one thing the CASE_MANAGER knows first-hand.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#rules-the-case_manager-follows","title":"Rules the CASE_MANAGER follows","text":"Rule Requirement Order is never reversed: an event observed earlier never gets a higher <code>log_index</code> CLP-14-001 Every entry carries a timestamp; none may be empty CLP-14-002 Timestamps on consecutive recorded entries never move backwards as <code>log_index</code> increases CLP-14-003 Every entry in a ledger belongs to the same case CLP-14-004 No two entries in a case share a <code>log_index</code> CLP-14-005 No entry predates the case it belongs to CLP-14-006 <p>Whether the index run may contain holes is not settled. A replica must hold a contiguous run from the genesis entry through the position it has acknowledged before it may take new protocol-significant actions on the case (SYNC-10-004), and in practice a receiver treats a hole as a missing entry. But <code>log_index</code> is consumed by every appended entry, rejections included, and rejections are not part of the recorded projection \u2014 so a hole in that projection is not by itself proof of loss. ADR-0079 states the rule both ways in different sections; the contradiction is tracked in #2752 and is not resolved here.</p> <p>The CASE_MANAGER should also refuse an assertion whose own timestamp is far in the future or far in the past compared to its clock \u2014 by default, more than five minutes ahead or more than seven days old (CLP-14-007, CLP-14-008). A deployment that knows its own clock conditions may tune both thresholds (CLP-14-009). These are sanity checks, not proof of honesty; a participant with a badly wrong clock can still produce a well-formed but misleading assertion.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#two-timestamps-two-different-rules","title":"Two timestamps, two different rules","text":"<p>An entry carries two timestamps, and the rules above do not all apply to the same one:</p> Timestamp Written by Rules it answers to <code>published</code> on the entry the CASE_MANAGER, at commit time CLP-14-002, CLP-14-003, CLP-14-006 read across the whole ledger <code>published</code> inside <code>payloadSnapshot</code> the asserting participant CLP-14-006 at the commit boundary, CLP-14-007, CLP-14-008, CLP-15-003, CLP-15-006 <p>The distinction matters most for the \"never move backwards\" rule. Across the CASE_MANAGER's own commit timestamps it holds because one writer stamps every entry from one clock. Applied to participants' timestamps it would be wrong: two participants' clocks are not synchronized, so an assertion recorded later by one of them can legitimately claim an earlier time than an assertion recorded earlier by the other. The CASE_MANAGER therefore compares a participant's claimed timestamp only against that same participant's previous assertion, and allows a small tolerance when comparing it against the case's creation time.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-participants-must-do","title":"What participants must do","text":"<p>The CASE_MANAGER can only record the order it sees. That places an obligation on each participant: send events in the order they happened.</p> <ul> <li>If A caused B, send A first   (CLP-15-001).</li> <li>Do not collect several related events and send them in an arbitrary order   (CLP-15-002).</li> <li>Give B a timestamp no earlier than A's   (CLP-15-003).</li> <li>Timestamp an event with when it happened, not when the batch went out or a   retry was attempted   (CLP-15-004).</li> </ul> <p>A participant that breaks these rules produces a malformed assertion. That is a fault on the sending side, not a CASE_MANAGER failure.</p> <p>The CASE_MANAGER cannot police these at the moment an assertion arrives, and it must not try: it may not reconstruct an order it did not observe (CLP-15-005). It sees the order messages arrived in, which is not the order they were sent in \u2014 the transport makes no such promise.</p> <p>So when an assertion's claimed time falls behind the same participant's previous assertion, the CASE_MANAGER records it and says so, rather than refusing it. A small regression is reported quietly; one beyond the configured tolerance is reported as a warning. Refusing would throw the message away \u2014 the ledger commit happens before any of the receiving work, so a refusal loses the whole thing \u2014 and the CASE_MANAGER cannot tell a participant that really did misorder its events from two messages that simply arrived out of order.</p> <p>The two ordering rules are visible only across a whole case, by comparing the causal links a scenario declares against the order the ledger recorded; the conformance suite checks them there.</p> <p>One thing the CASE_MANAGER does refuse outright: an activity that arrives with no <code>published</code> time at all. Because the field is optional in ActivityStreams, a receiver that filled in the blank with its own clock could no longer tell what the sender claimed from what it invented \u2014 and every check above would then be comparing the CASE_MANAGER's clock against itself. A message without a claimed time is therefore rejected at the door (CLP-15-006).</p> <p>A field that is present but empty carries no claimed time either. A blank <code>published</code> \u2014 an empty string, or one holding only whitespace \u2014 is refused the same way as an omitted one, and reports the same reason (MV-03-002).</p> <p>A value that is present and not blank but unreadable as a timestamp is a different fault. The CASE_MANAGER reports it as malformed data, not as a missing field, so a sender is never told to supply something it already sent.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#when-entries-arrive-out-of-order","title":"When entries arrive out of order","text":"<p>Ledger entries travel over ordinary message transport, which gives no ordering guarantee. Vultron may also not be the only implementation on the wire. So a replica can receive entry 7 before entry 6.</p> <p>The naive response is to reject entry 7, on the grounds that it does not extend the chain, and wait for the CASE_MANAGER to send it again. That does not work. The replay travels the same unordered transport and can arrive out of order again, so under repeated reordering an entry can be lost indefinitely. In an earlier version of this implementation, that is what stalled a late-joining vendor at case closure.</p> <p>Instead, a replica keeps an early entry (ADR-0037, SYNC-14-001). It puts the entry in a holding area and waits for the predecessor. Convergence then no longer depends on delivery order at all.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-gets-held-and-what-does-not","title":"What gets held, and what does not","text":"<p>A replica holds an entry when the entry does not extend its chain but belongs later in the history \u2014 its <code>log_index</code> is more than one past the end of what the replica holds. That is a forward gap: the predecessor has not arrived yet.</p> <p>Two kinds of entry are not held:</p> <ul> <li>An entry at or behind the end of the chain. That is a duplicate or a stale   replay, not a gap.</li> <li>An entry exactly one past the end of the chain whose <code>prevLogHash</code> does not   match the hash of the replica's last recorded entry. Nothing is missing in   front of it, so it is not a gap \u2014 it is a fork, a claim about a history the   replica does not share.</li> </ul> <p>Both go to the ordinary duplicate and divergence handling instead.</p> <p>Even when it does hold an entry, the replica still sends <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> naming the last entry it accepted (SYNC-14-002). Holding solves reordering; it cannot solve loss. If the missing entry was never delivered at all, the reject is what prompts the CASE_MANAGER to send it again.</p> <p>The CASE_MANAGER does not replay on demand without limit. If a peer keeps rejecting from the same position, the CASE_MANAGER waits out a short cooldown before replaying to it again (SYNC-15-003). Without that bound, a peer that cannot anchor its chain rejects every entry it is sent, each reject triggers another full replay, and the two feed each other into a storm. A reject from a position that has advanced always triggers a replay, so a peer making progress is never held back.</p> <p>The holding area should also be bounded, so that a hostile or broken peer streaming far-future entries cannot exhaust memory. When it is full, the replica discards the entry farthest ahead of the gap and logs a warning (SYNC-14-006). Discarding is safe because the reject for that gap has already been sent \u2014 but the eviction itself sends nothing, so recovery waits on the replay that reject triggers, or on the next entry that fails to match the tail. The cooldown above may delay either.</p> <p>The holding area is deliberately not the ledger (SYNC-14-005). Across Vultron, the presence of an entry in an actor's own store means this entry is committed and its effects are applied (SYNC-13-001). A held entry is neither, so storing it would break that meaning.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#entries-that-arrive-before-the-case","title":"Entries that arrive before the case","text":"<p>The same holding area covers a related race: an entry can arrive before the participant has the case object at all. Without the case, the replica cannot compute the genesis hash and so cannot anchor the chain.</p> <p>A replica holds these entries too (SYNC-15-004), with no gap comparison \u2014 there is no chain yet to compare against, so every entry for the unknown case is held, including entry 0. When the case is later delivered, the replica drains the holding area for that case (SYNC-15-005). Seeding the case is enough, because the genesis hash is derived from the case object; the genesis ledger entry does not have to be re-sent (ADR-0059).</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#draining-the-held-entries","title":"Draining the held entries","text":"<p>Each held entry is filed under the hash of the predecessor it is waiting for. So after the replica commits a new last entry, finding the successor is a single lookup: the held entry whose <code>prevLogHash</code> equals the hash of the entry just committed.</p> <p>The drain then repeats. Commit the successor, look up its successor, and continue until no held entry extends the chain (SYNC-14-003). A run of ten entries that arrived in reverse order clicks into place in one cascade, in <code>log_index</code> order.</p> <p>Three properties make the drain safe:</p> <ul> <li>Same path. A drained entry goes through the same processing as an entry   that arrived in order \u2014 no separate code path with its own behavior   (SYNC-14-008). In this   implementation that means the drain re-runs the announce receive behavior   tree on each held entry, in <code>log_index</code> order.</li> <li>Effects before storage. The entry's consequences \u2014 an embargo ending, a   participant joining, a status changing \u2014 are applied first, and the entry is   stored only if they all succeed   (SYNC-12-001,   SYNC-14-004).</li> <li>Applied once. An entry already in the local ledger is skipped entirely,   so a replay or a duplicate cannot apply the same effects twice   (SYNC-12-003,   SYNC-14-007).</li> </ul> <p>Because held entries are replayed through the ordinary path, the reject-and-replay recovery becomes order-tolerant as well, at no extra cost.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#why-state-checks-wait-for-the-drain","title":"Why state checks wait for the drain","text":"<p>Holding an entry has a consequence that is easy to get wrong. Case State (CS) has ordering rules of its own: an ephemeral state cannot be a resting place, so it has exactly one permitted successor and must be followed by it; the recorded history must remain a valid sequence throughout; and a move to public awareness must be recorded before the embargo termination that it triggers.</p> <p>If a replica checked those rules at the moment an entry arrived, an out-of-order entry would look like a violation. An entry naming a state that is only reachable from its predecessor would appear to arrive from nowhere.</p> <p>That is why the checks run at drain time instead (CSB-19-001). A held entry is parked before any case-state effect is applied, so the state machine is never touched at arrival time. When the gap closes, the entries replay in <code>log_index</code> order \u2014 which is causal order \u2014 and the guards see them in the sequence they were meant to be seen in.</p> <p>An entry waiting in the holding area therefore raises no state violation at all (CSB-19-002). An entry naming an ephemeral state is perfectly well-formed on its own; it would only be a real violation if the entry that resolves it never arrived. Flagging it on arrival would be a false alarm, and rejecting it would prevent the replica from ever converging.</p> <p>The public-awareness-before-embargo-termination ordering survives reordering for free (CSB-19-003). The CASE_MANAGER commits the public-awareness entry first, so it holds the lower <code>log_index</code>. The drain works in <code>log_index</code> order, so it can never present the termination entry first. No receiver-side re-check of the timing is needed; the order in the ledger is sufficient.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-a-replica-guarantees","title":"What a replica guarantees","text":"<p>Taken together, the ledger rules and the holding area give each participant these properties:</p> Property Meaning Append-only A committed entry is immutable and identified by its content hash Deterministic projection The same run of entries produces the same state in every conforming implementation Idempotent replay Re-processing entries already seen changes nothing Monotonic progress A replica never regresses the position it has acknowledged Reject on divergence An entry that does not extend the chain is not silently accepted Order-independent convergence Delivery order does not affect the final state <p>The result is eventual consistency with a strong bound: given the same entries, every replica reaches the same state as the CASE_MANAGER, no matter what order those entries arrived in.</p> <p>The holding area itself is in memory only, and is lost on restart. considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Our Observational analysis supports the conclusion that vulnerability disclosure as currently practiced demonstrates skill. In both data sets examined, our estimated \\(\\alpha_d\\) is positive for most \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\). However, there is uncertainty in our estimates due to the application of the principle of indifference to unobserved data. This principle assumes a uniform distribution across event transitions in the absence of CVD, which is an assumption we cannot readily test. The spread of the estimates in Observing Skill represents the variance in our samples, not this assumption-based uncertainty. Our interpretation of \\(\\alpha_d\\) values near zero is therefore that they reflect an absence of evidence rather than evidence that skill is absent. While we cannot rule definitively on luck or low skill, values of \\(\\alpha_d &gt; 0.9\\) should reliably indicate skillful defenders.</p> <p>If, as seems plausible from the evidence, it turns out that further observations of \\(h\\) are significantly skewed toward the higher end of the poset \\((\\mathcal{H},\\leq_{\\mathbb{D}})\\), then it may be useful to empirically calibrate our metrics rather than using the a priori frequencies in Reasoning over Histories as our baseline. We can at least state that we would prefer that most cases reach fix ready before attacks (\\(\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{A}\\)).</p> <p>Per the Event Frequency table in Reasoning Over Possible Histories, (reproduced below for convenience), even in a world without skill we would expect \\(\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{A}\\) to hold in 37.5% of cases.</p> <p>Expected Frequency of \\({row} \\prec {col}\\) when events are chosen uniformly from possible transitions in each state</p> \\(\\mathbf{V}\\) \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) \\(\\mathbf{P}\\) \\(\\mathbf{X}\\) \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) \\(\\mathbf{V}\\) 0 1 1 0.333 0.667 0.750 \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) 0 0 1 0.111 0.333 0.375 \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) 0 0 0 0.037 0.167 0.187 \\(\\mathbf{P}\\) 0.667 0.889 0.963 0 0.500 0.667 \\(\\mathbf{X}\\) 0.333 0.667 0.833 0.500 0 0.500 \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) 0.250 0.625 0.812 0.333 0.500 0 <p>This means that \\(\\alpha_{\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{A}} &lt; 0\\) for anything less than a 0.375 success rate.</p> <p>Benchmarking CVD</p> <p>In fact, we propose to generalize this for any \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\), such that \\(\\alpha_d\\) should be greater than some benchmark constant \\(c_d\\):</p> \\[\\alpha_d \\geq c_d \\geq 0\\] <p>where \\(c_d\\) is a based on observations of \\(\\alpha_d\\) collected across some collection of CVD cases.</p> <p>We propose as a starting point a na\u00efve benchmark of \\(c_d = 0\\). This is a low bar, as it only requires that CVD actually do better than possible events which are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) within each case. For example, given a history in which \\((\\mathbf{V}, \\mathbf{F}, \\mathbf{P})\\) have already happened (i.e., state \\(q \\in VFdPxa\\)), \\(\\mathbf{D}\\), \\(\\mathbf{X}\\), or \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) are equally likely to occur next.</p> <p>The i.i.d. assumption may not be warranted.</p> <p>We anticipate that event ordering probabilities might be conditional on history: for example, exploit publication may be more likely when the vulnerability is public (\\(p(\\mathbf{X}|q \\in \\mathcal{Q}_P) &gt; p(\\mathbf{X}|q \\in \\mathcal{Q}_p)\\)) or attacks may be more likely when an exploit is public (\\(p(\\mathbf{A}|q \\in \\mathcal{Q}_{X}) &gt; p(\\mathbf{A}|q \\in \\mathcal{Q}_{x})\\)). If the i.i.d. assumption fails to hold for transition events \\(\\sigma \\in \\Sigma\\), observed frequencies of \\(h \\in \\mathcal{H}\\) could differ significantly from the rates predicted by the uniform probability assumption behind the Event Frequency table above.</p> <p>Supporting Observations</p> <p>Some example suggestive observations are:</p> <ul> <li> <p>There is reason to suspect that only a fraction of vulnerabilities ever reach the exploit public event \\(\\mathbf{X}\\), and fewer still reach the attack event \\(\\mathbf{A}\\). Recent work by the Cyentia Institute found that \"5% of all CVEs are both observed within organizations AND known to be exploited\", which suggests that \\(f_{\\mathbf{D} \\prec \\mathbf{A}} \\approx 0.95\\).</p> </li> <li> <p>Likewise, \\(\\mathbf{D} \\prec \\mathbf{X}\\) holds in 28 of 70 (0.4) \\(h\\). However, we could choose a slightly different goal than differentiating skill and \"blind luck\" as represented by the i.i.d. assumption. One could aim to measure \"more skillful than the average for some set of teams\" rather than more skillful than blind luck.</p> <p>If this were the \"reasonable\" baseline expectation, the primary limitation is available observations. The need for MPCVD arises due to the inherent nature of the software supply chain CERT Guide to CVD. A vulnerability that affects a low-level component (such as a library or operating system API) can require fixes from both the originating vendor and any vendor whose products incorporate the affected component. Known only to its finder, the vulnerability can be described by that singular state.</p> <p>As it becomes clear that the vulnerability affects multiple vendors' products, both finder/reporters and coordinators might begin to track the state of each individual vendor as a separate instance of the model. For example, if 3 vendors are known to be affected, but only 1 has been notified, the case might be considered to be in a superposition of states \\(\\{Vfdpxa,vfdpxa,vfdpxa\\}\\).</p> <p>Each vendor, in turn, might then ascertain whether they are able to produce fixes for all their available products at once, or if those fixes will be staggered over time. In either case, the vendor might track the case as a superposition of states for each affected product dependent on its fix readiness status. For example, a vendor might have four products affected, with two in the fix-ready state and two fixes still in progress. Should they opt for transparency into their internal process, they might communicate their status as the superposition of \\(\\{VFdpxa,VFdpxa,Vfdpxa,Vfdpxa\\}\\). Alternatively, they might choose to only share the lowest state across their products, which in this example would be \\(\\{Vfdpxa\\}\\).</p> <p>The above example implies a need to expand our notation.</p> <p>MPCVD Cases have Participant-Specific States</p> <p>In the MPCVD case, we need to think of each state \\(q \\in \\mathcal{Q}\\) as a set of states \\(q_M\\):</p> \\[ q_M \\stackrel{\\mathsf{def}}{=}\\{ q_1,q_2,\\dots,q_n \\} \\] <p>where \\(q_i\\) represents the state \\(q\\) for the \\(i\\)th affected vendor and/or product. For example, \\(\\{ {Vfdpxa}_1, {vfdpxa}_2 \\}\\) would represent the state in which vendor 1 has been notified but vendor 2 has not. Very often, vendor notification occurs as new products and vendors are identified as affected in the course of analyzing a vulnerability report. So the individual events \\(\\mathbf{V}_i\\) in \\(\\mathbf{V}_M\\) (representing the status of all the vendor notifications) might be spread out over a period of time.</p> <p>Some transitions are more readily synchronized than others. For example, if an MPCVD case is already underway, and information about the vulnerability appears in a public media report, we can say that \\(\\mathbf{P}_M\\) occurred simultaneously for all coordinating vendors.</p> <p>Regardless, in the maximal case, each vendor-product pair is effectively behaving independently of all the others. Therefore:</p> <p>Dimensionality of an MPCVD Case</p> <p>The maximum dimensionality of the MPCVD model for a case is</p> \\[ D_{max} = 5 * N_{vprod} \\] <p>where \\(N_{vprod}\\) represents the number of vendor-product pairs.</p> <p>This is undesirable, as it would result in a wide distribution of realized histories that more closely resemble the randomness assumptions outlined above than a skillful, coordinated effort. Further discussion of measuring MPCVD skill can be found below.</p> <p>Reducing Dimensionality of MPCVD Cases is a good thing</p> <p>For now, we posit that the goal of a good MPCVD process is to reduce the dimensionality of a given MPCVD case as much as is possible (i.e., to the 5 dimensions of a single vendor CVD case we have presented above). Experience shows that a full dimension reduction is unlikely in most cases, but that does not detract from the value of having the goal.</p> <p>Reducing Complexity within a Vendor Organization</p> <p>Vendors may be able to reduce their internal tracking dimensionality---which may be driven by things like component reuse across products or product lines---through in-house coordination of fix development processes. Within an individual vendor organization, PSIRTs are a common organizational structure to address this internal coordination process.</p> <ul> <li>The FIRST PSIRT Services Framework provides guidance regarding vendors' internal processes for coordinating vulnerability response.</li> <li>Additional guidance can be found in ISO/IEC 30111:2019.</li> </ul> <p>Regardless, the cross-vendor dimension is largely the result of component reuse across vendors, for example through the inclusion of third party libraries or OEM SDKs. Visibility of cross-vendor component reuse remains an unsolved problem, although efforts such as the Software Bill of Materials are promising in this regard. Thus, dimensionality reduction can be achieved through both improved transparency of the software supply chain and the process of coordination toward synchronized state transitions, especially for \\(\\mathbf{P}\\), if not for \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) and \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) as well.</p> <p>As a result of the dimensionality problem, coordinators and other parties to an MPCVD case need to decide how to apply disclosure policy rules in cases where different products or vendors occupy different case states with potentially contradictory recommended actions. For example, when four out of five vendors involved in a case have reached \\(VFdpxa\\) and are ready to publish, but the fifth is still in \\(Vfdpxa\\). Essentially this can be expected to take the form of a weighting function that acts on a vector of case states, and outputs a set of recommended actions derived from those states.</p> <p>One possible function would be to apply a simple voting heuristic such as waiting for a simple majority of vendors to reach a state before taking action as that state recommends. In our 4/5 \\(VFdpxa\\) example, the coordinating parties would behave as if the case were in that state for all.</p> <p>Another function could be to weight vendors and products by some other factor, such as size of the installed user base, or even based on a risk analysis of societal costs associated with potential actions. Here we acknowledge that our example is under-specified: does the fifth vendor (the one in \\(Vfdpxa\\)) represent a sizable fraction of the total user base? Or does it concentrate the highest risk use cases for the software? Challenges in efficiently assessing consistent answers to these questions are easy to imagine. The status quo for MPCVD appears consistent with defaulting to simple majority in the absence of additional information, with consideration given to the distribution of both users and risk on a case-by-case basis. At present, there is no clear consensus on such policies, although we hope that future work can use the model presented here to formalize the necessary analysis.</p> <p>Integrating FIRST MPCVD Guidance</p> <p>FIRST has published Guidelines and Practices for Multi-Party Vulnerability Coordination and Disclosure. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Does CVD as observed in the wild demonstrate skillful behavior?</p> <p>In order to answer this question, we need a way to measure skillful behavior in CVD. This section defines a method for measuring skill in CVD.</p> <p>The measurement method makes use of all the modeling tools and baselines established thus far: a comprehensive set of possible histories \\(\\mathcal{H}\\), a partial order over them in terms of the presence of desired event precedence \\((\\mathcal{H},\\leq_{\\mathbb{D}})\\), and the a priori expected frequency of each desiderata \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\).</p> <p>If we expected to be able to observe all events in all CVD cases, we could be assured of having complete histories and could be done here. But the real world is messy. Not all events \\(\\mathbf{e} \\in \\mathcal{E}\\) are always observable. We need to develop a way to make sense of what we can observe, regardless of whether we are ever able to capture complete histories. Continuing towards our goal of measuring efficacy, we return to considering the balance between skill and luck in determining our observed outcomes.</p>"},{"location":"topics/measuring_cvd/discriminating_skill_and_luck/#a-measure-of-skill-in-cvd","title":"A Measure of Skill in CVD","text":"<p>We have established a set of desiderata \\(\\mathbb{D}\\) that we would like to see in a CVD case. Now, we want to measure the degree to which a CVD practice is skillful in achieving those desiderata. In a world of pure skill, one would expect that a player could achieve all 12 desiderata \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\) consistently. That is, a maximally skillful player could consistently achieve the specific ordering \\(h=(\\mathbf{V},\\mathbf{F},\\mathbf{D},\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{X},\\mathbf{A})\\) with probability \\(p_{skill} = 1\\).</p> <p>Factors that could affect the observed frequency of a desideratum</p> <p>There are many reasons why we might expect our observations to differ from the expected frequencies we established  in Reasoning Over Possible Histories. Adversaries might be rare, or conversely very well equipped. Vendors might be very good at releasing fixes faster  than adversaries can discover vulnerabilities and develop exploits for them. System owners might be diligent at applying patches. (We did say might, didn't we?) Regardless, for now we will lump all of those possible explanations into a single attribute called \"skill.\"</p> <p>Thus, we construct the following model: for each of our preferred orderings \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\), we model their occurrence due to luck using the binomial distribution with parameter \\(p_{luck} = f_d\\) taken from the event frequency table in Reasoning Over Possible Histories, reproduced below for convenience:</p> <p>Expected Frequency of \\({row} \\prec {col}\\) when events are chosen uniformly from possible transitions in each state</p> \\(\\mathbf{V}\\) \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) \\(\\mathbf{P}\\) \\(\\mathbf{X}\\) \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) \\(\\mathbf{V}\\) 0 1 1 0.333 0.667 0.750 \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) 0 0 1 0.111 0.333 0.375 \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) 0 0 0 0.037 0.167 0.187 \\(\\mathbf{P}\\) 0.667 0.889 0.963 0 0.500 0.667 \\(\\mathbf{X}\\) 0.333 0.667 0.833 0.500 0 0.500 \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) 0.250 0.625 0.812 0.333 0.500 0 <p>Recall that the mean of a binomial distribution is the probability of success \\(p\\), and that the mean of a weighted mixture of two binomial distributions is the weighted mixture of the individual means. Therefore our model adds a parameter \\(\\alpha_d\\) to represent the weighting between our success rates arising from skill \\(p_{skill}\\) and luck \\(p_{luck}\\). Because there are 12 desiderata \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\), each \\(d\\) will have its own observations and corresponding value for \\(\\alpha_d\\) for each history \\(h_a\\).</p> <p>Modeling Skill and Luck in Observations</p> <p>We model the observed frequency of desiderata \\(d\\) as a weighted mixture of the success rates due to skill and luck:</p> \\[ f_d^{obs} = \\alpha_d \\cdot p_{skill} + (1 - \\alpha_d) \\cdot p_{luck} \\] <p>Where \\(f_d^{obs}\\) is the observed frequency of successes for desiderata \\(d\\). Because \\(p_{skill} = 1\\), one of those binomial distributions is degenerate. Substituting \\(p_{skill} = 1\\), \\(p_{luck} = f_d\\) and solving the previous equation for \\(\\alpha\\), we get</p> <p>Skill Coefficient</p> <p>The value of \\(\\alpha_d\\) therefore gives us a measure of the observed skill normalized against the background success rate provided by luck \\(f_d\\).</p> \\[ \\alpha_d \\stackrel{\\mathsf{def}}{=}\\frac{f_d^{obs} - f_d} {1 - f_d} \\] <p>Skill Coefficient Set</p> <p>We denote the set of \\(\\alpha_d\\) values for a given history as \\(\\alpha_\\mathbb{D}\\). When we refer to the \\(\\alpha_d\\) coefficient for a specific \\(d\\) we will use the specific ordering as the subscript, for example: \\(\\alpha_{\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{P}}\\).</p> \\[ \\alpha_\\mathbb{D} \\stackrel{\\mathsf{def}}{=}\\{ \\alpha_d : d \\in \\mathbb{D} \\} \\] <p>The concept embodied by \\(f_d\\) is founded on the idea that if attackers and defenders are in a state of equilibrium, the frequency of observed outcomes (i.e., how often each desiderata \\(d\\) and history \\(h\\) actually occurs) will appear consistent with those predicted by chance. So another way of interpreting \\(\\alpha_d\\) is as a measure of the degree to which a set of observed histories is out of equilibrium.</p> <p>Interpreting \\(\\alpha_d\\) Behavior</p> <p>The following are a few comments on how \\(\\alpha_d\\) behaves. Note that \\(\\alpha_d &lt; 0\\) when \\(0 \\leq f_d^{obs} &lt; f_d\\) and \\(0 \\leq \\alpha_d \\leq 1\\) when \\(f_d \\leq f_d^{obs} \\leq 1\\). The implication is that a negative value for \\(\\alpha_d\\) indicates that our observed outcomes are actually worse than those predicted by pure luck. In other words, we can only infer positive skill when the observations are higher (\\(f_d^{obs} &gt; f_d\\)). That makes intuitive sense: if you are likely to win purely by chance, then you have to attribute most of your wins to luck rather than skill. From the event frequency table above, the largest value for any \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\) is \\(f_{\\mathbf{V} \\prec \\mathbf{A}}=0.75\\), implying that even if a vendor knows about 7 out of 10 vulnerabilities before attacks occur (\\(f_{\\mathbf{V} \\prec \\mathbf{A}}^{obs} = 0.7\\)), they are still not doing better than random.</p> <p>On the other hand, when \\(f_d\\) is small it is easier to infer skill should we observe anything better than \\(f_d\\). We cannot derive this model by observation. Even when CVD was first practiced in the 1980s, some people may have had social, technical, or organizational skills that transferred to better CVD. We follow the principle of indifference as stated below.</p> <p></p> <p>Benjamin Eva in Principles of Indifference</p> <p>Let \\(X = \\{x_1,x_2,...,x_n\\}\\) be a partition of the set \\(W\\) of possible worlds into \\(n\\) mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive possibilities. In the absence of any relevant evidence pertaining to which cell of the partition is the true one, a rational agent should assign an equal initial credence of \\(n\\) to each cell.</p> <p>While the principle of indifference is rather strong, it is inherently difficult to reason about absolutely skill-less CVD when the work of CVD is, by its nature, a skilled job. The PageRank algorithm provides a probability estimate for each state based on a Markov random walk of the directed graph of states. PageRank assumes each available transition is equally probable, consistent with our model. To avoid becoming stuck in dead ends, PageRank adds a teleport feature by which walks can, with a small probability, randomly jump to another node in the graph.</p> <p>Before proceeding, we need to make a small modification of our state digraph. Without modification, the PageRank algorithm will tend to be biased toward later states because the only way to reach the earlier states is for the algorithm to teleport there. Teleportation chooses states uniformly, so for example there is only a \\(1/32\\) chance of our actual start state (\\(q_0={vfdpxa}\\)) ever being chosen. Therefore, to ensure that the early states in our process are fairly represented we add a single link from VFDPXA to vfdpxa, representing a model reset whenever the end state is reached. This modification allows PageRank traversals to wrap around naturally and reach the early states in the random walk process without needing to rely on teleportation. With our modification in place, we are ready to compute the PageRank of each node in the graph. Related tracking:</p> <ul> <li>#1189 \u2014 ActivityPub/WebFinger-compatible   directory service</li> <li>#2068 \u2014 Design and build a full   ActivityPub service for Vultron</li> <li>#2469 \u2014 Actor discovery Retriever   call-out seam (added to the BT; backend implementation remains future work)</li> </ul> <p>The idea of CVD embargoes implies a means of dividing the world into</p> <ol> <li>those who belong in the embargo</li> <li>those who do not</li> </ol> <p>Because authentication is not the same as authorization, knowing who a Participant is does not suffice; we also have to be able to identify why they are relevant to a particular case.</p> <p>Thus, we must ask:</p> <p>Question</p> <p>How do Participants find other relevant potential Participants to invite to a case?</p> <p>security.txt</p> <p>Vendors can improve their discoverability by using a <code>security.txt</code> file on their websites. See securitytxt.org and RFC 9116 for more information.</p> <p>In small CVD cases, the answer might be straightforward: The affected product comes from a known Vendor, so the only question to answer is how best to contact them. As a first approximation, Internet search engines offer a de facto baseline CVD directory service because they allow any potential Reporter to search for <code>&lt;vendor name&gt; vulnerability report</code> or similar terms to find an individual Vendor contact.</p> <p>But in larger MPCVD cases, there are a few entangled problems:</p> <ol> <li> <p>It can be difficult and inefficient to collect contact information     for all possibly relevant parties.</p> </li> <li> <p>Even if contact information is widely available using searchable     resources, many Vendors' preferred contact methods might preclude     automation of mass notification (or require customized integration     to ensure interoperability between report senders and receivers).     Some Vendors only want email. Others require Reporters to create an     account on their bespoke bug-tracking system before reporting.     Others ask for submissions via a customized web form. These and other examples     hinder the interoperability of MPCVD processes.</p> </li> <li> <p>It is not always clear which other Vendors' products contain the     affected product, which limits the ability for an MPCVD cases to follow the software     supply chain.</p> </li> <li> <p>Sometimes vulnerabilities arise in protocols or specifications where     multiple implementations are affected. It can be difficult to     identify Vendors whose products implement specific technologies.     Software reverse engineering methods can be used to identify     affected products in some cases.</p> </li> <li> <p>At the same time, some Vendors treat their product's subcomponents     as proprietary close-hold information for competitive advantage;     this might happen, for example, with OEM or white label licensing agreements.     While it is certainly their prerogative to do so, this desire to     avoid disclosing internal components of a product can inhibit     discovery---and therefore disclosure to the Vendor---that a     vulnerability affects a product.</p> </li> </ol> <p>For more information</p> <ul> <li>FIRST Teams</li> <li>Disclose.io website and on GitHub</li> </ul> <p>When it comes to larger scale MPCVD, the inefficiency of ad hoc contact collection via search engines is evident. Disclosure policies specify commitments by coordinating parties to ensure the occurrence of certain state transitions within a specific period of time. While the model presented here does not directly address timing choices, we can point out some ways to relate the model to those choices. Specifically, we intend to demonstrate how disclosure policy SLEs can be stated as rules triggered within subsets of states or by particular transitions between subsets of states in \\(\\mathcal{Q}\\).</p> <p>SLEs and Publication Timing</p> <p>For example, a finder, reporter, or coordinator might commit to publishing information about a vulnerability 30 days after vendor notification. This translates to starting a timer at \\({v} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{V}} {V}\\) and ensuring \\({Vp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {VP}\\) when the timer expires. Notice that the prospect of \\({Vfp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {VfP}\\) is often used to motivate vendors to ensure a reasonable SLE to produce fixes (\\({Vf} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{F}} {VF}\\))  (See for example Optimal Policy for Software Vulnerability Disclosure by Arora, Telang, and Xu).</p> <p>SLEs and Fix Readiness Timing</p> <p>Similarly, a vendor might commit to providing public fixes within 5 business days of report receipt. It may be possible to resolve some apparent policy conflicts by delaying notifications to some vendors to ensure that all embargo end timers expire simultaneously. We informally refer to this as the Thanksgiving Dinner problem, due to its similarity to the familiar annual holiday meal in which a number of dishes with varying preparation times are expected to be delivered to the table simultaneously, each at its appropriate temperature and doneness. For example, when one party has a \"minimum 90 days to publish\" policy and another has a \"maximum 5 days to publish\" policy, the resolution could be to notify the first vendor 85 days before notifying the second. Such a model of graduated disclosure could work well for cases where notifications are automated and vendor dependencies are small or where coordinating parties' policies can be resolved as compatible. Technology such as Theorem Provers and Solvers seem likely to be suited to this sort of problem.</p> <p>However, when formal policies are incompatible, the failure to resolve them automatically becomes an opportunity for human intervention as the exception handler of last resort. Of potential concern here are MPCVD cases in which a vendor with a long policy timer is dependent on one with a short policy timer to provide fixes. The serial nature of the dependency creates the potential for a compatibility conflict. For example, this can happen when an OS kernel provider's disclosure policy specifies a shorter embargo timer than the policies of device manufacturers whose products depend on that OS kernel. One such caveat worth noting here is that valid states must follow what we call the Vendor fix path.</p> <p>The reason is causal: For a fix to be deployed (D), it must have been ready (F) for deployment. Use of a public exploit in an attack meets both exploit public and     attacks observed.</p> </li> </ul> <p>Therefore, while we appreciate the existence of a hidden exploit exists event as causal predecessor of both exploit public and attacks observed, we assert no causal relationship between exploit public and attacks observed in our model. This is a normative section of the documentation.</p> <p>Here we describe the basic primitives necessary for the CVD Embargo Management (EM) process.</p> <p>For our purposes, an embargo is an informal agreement among peer CVD case Participants to refrain from publishing information about a vulnerability until some future point in time relative to the report at hand. Once an embargo has expired, there is no further restriction on publishing information about the vulnerability.</p> <p>Reminder</p> <p>Exploits are information about vulnerabilities too.</p> <p>CVD case Participants must be able to propose, accept, and reject embargo timing proposals according to their individual needs. Additionally, Participants may want to attempt to gain agreement that enables specific details about a vulnerability to be shared with other Participants or made public. Such content considerations are outside the scope of this proposal. We focus our discussion on the when of an embargo, not the what.</p> <p>Embargo Definition</p> <p>An embargo is an informal agreement among peer CVD case Participants to refrain from publishing information about a vulnerability until some future point in time.</p> <p>Unlike the RM model, in which each Participant has their own instance of the RM DFA, EM states are a global property of a CVD case.</p> <p>A CVD case SHALL NOT have more than one active embargo at a time.</p> <p>(We define the term active below.)</p> <p>Even in an MPCVD case having a vertical supply chain\u2014in which Vendors must wait on their upstream suppliers to produce fixes before they can take action on their own, as in the figure below\u2014our intent is that the embargo period terminates when as many Vendors as possible have been given an adequate opportunity to produce a fix.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: A Vertical Supply Chain\n---\nstateDiagram-v2\n    direction LR\n    v1: Originating&lt;br/&gt;Vendor\n    v2: Vendor 2\n    v3: Vendor 3\n    v4: Vendor 4\n    v5: Vendor 5\n    v6: Vendor 6\n\n    v1 --&gt; v2\n    v1 --&gt; v3\n    v2 --&gt; v4\n    v3 --&gt; v5\n    v2 --&gt; v5\n    v5 --&gt; v6</code></pre> <p></p> <p>CVD Embargoes Are Not NDAs</p> <p>CVD embargoes are not Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs). An NDA (also known as a Confidentiality agreement) is a legally binding contract between parties, often accompanied by a reward for compliance and/or some penalty in the event of unauthorized disclosure. This is intentional, and it results directly from the asymmetry mentioned in Negotiating Embargoes The Receiver is faced with a choice to either accept the Reporter's proposal and attempt to extend it or to reject the proposal and end up with no embargo at all. Therefore, if we take the stance that for a vulnerability with no fix available, any embargo is better than no embargo, it should be obvious that it is in the Receiver's interest to accept even a short proposed embargo before immediately working to revise it.</p> <p>The alternative is impractical because the Reporter is not obligated to provide the report to the Receiver at all. In the scenario where a Reporter proposes a short embargo and the Receiver rejects it because it is not long enough, the Reporter might choose to exit the negotiation entirely and publish whenever they choose without ever providing the report to the Receiver. That is not to say that we recommend this sort of behavior from Reporters. In fact, we specifically recommend the opposite in Negotiating Embargoes. Rather, it once more acknowledges the time-dependent informational asymmetry inherent to the CVD process.</p> <p>A Logical Argument for Accepting the Shortest Proposed Embargo</p> <p>Perhaps the above reasoning comes across as too Machiavellian for some readers. Here is a different perspective: Say a Reporter proposes an embargo of n days, while the Vendor would prefer m days. If n and m are given in units of days, we can look at them as a series of individual agreements, each of 1 day in length. We will represent each Participant as a vector representing that Participant's willingness to perpetuate the embargo on each day. Embargo willingness will be represented as a 1 if the Participant is willing to commit to keeping the embargo on that day, and a 0 if they are not. For simplicity's sake, we assume that each Participant is willing to maintain the embargo up to a certain point, and then their willingness goes away. In other words, each vector will be a series of zero or more _1_s followed by zero or more _0_s. For example, \\([1,1,1,1,0,0,0]\\) represents a Participant's willingness to engage in a 4-day embargo.</p> <p>For our two Participants, let \\(\\mathbf{x}_ and _\\mathbf{y}\\) be zero-indexed vectors of length \\(max(n,m)\\).</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     |\\mathbf{x}| &amp;= max(n,m) \\\\     |\\mathbf{y}| &amp;= max(n,m) \\end{aligned}\\] <p>The elements of each vector represent each respective Participant's willingness for the embargo to persist on each consecutive day.</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     \\mathbf{x} =          \\begin{bmatrix} x_i :         x_i =          \\begin{cases}             1 &amp;\\text{if }i &lt; n \\\\             0 &amp;\\text{otherwise} \\\\         \\end{cases}         &amp; \\text{for } 0 \\leq i &lt; max(n,m)         \\end{bmatrix} \\\\     \\mathbf{y} =         \\begin{bmatrix} y_i :          y_i =          \\begin{cases}             1 &amp;\\text{if }i &lt; m \\\\             0 &amp;\\text{otherwise}         \\end{cases}         &amp; \\text{ for } 0 \\leq i &lt; max(n,m)     \\end{bmatrix} \\end{aligned}\\] <p>Note that we have constructed these vectors so that each vector's scalar sum is just the length of embargo they prefer.</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     \\Sigma(\\mathbf{x}) &amp;= n \\\\     \\Sigma(\\mathbf{y}) &amp;= m  \\end{aligned}\\] <p>Now we can define an agreement vector \\(\\mathbf{z}\\) as the pairwise logical AND (\\(\\wedge\\)) of elements from \\(\\mathbf{x}_ and _\\mathbf{y}\\):</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     \\mathbf{z} =      \\begin{bmatrix} z_i :          z_i = x_i \\land y_i         &amp; \\text{for }0 \\leq i &lt; max(n,m)     \\end{bmatrix} \\end{aligned}\\] <p>For example, if one party prefers an embargo of length \\(n=4\\) days while another prefers one of length \\(m=7\\) days, we can apply \\(\\mathbf{x}\\), \\(\\mathbf{y}\\), and \\(\\mathbf{z}\\) as follows:</p> \\[\\begin{split}     \\mathbf{x} &amp;= [1,1,1,1,0,0,0] \\\\     \\wedge~\\mathbf{y} &amp;= [1,1,1,1,1,1,1] \\\\     \\hline     \\mathbf{z} &amp;= [1,1,1,1,0,0,0]     \\end{split}\\] <p>From this, we can see that the scalar sum of the agreement vector---and therefore the longest embargo acceptable to both parties---is the lesser of n and m:</p> \\[\\Sigma ( \\mathbf{z} ) = min(n,m)\\] <p>As an example:</p> <p>The Shortest Proposed Embargo Wins</p> <p>If a Reporter proposes a 90-day embargo, but the Vendor prefers a 30-day embargo, we can think of this as a series of 1-day agreements in which both parties agree to the first 30 days of the embargo and disagree beyond that. By accepting the shorter 30-day embargo, the Reporter now has 30 days to continue negotiations with the Vendor to extend the embargo. Even if those continued negotiations fail, both parties get at least the 30-day embargo period they agreed on in the first place. This should be preferable to both parties versus the alternative of no embargo at all were they to reject the shorter proposal.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Embargo Agreement in a Nutshell\n---\nstateDiagram-v2\n    direction LR\n    dots: ...\n    state Agreement {\n        direction LR\n        [*] --&gt; 1\n        1 --&gt; 2\n        2 --&gt; dots\n        dots --&gt; 30\n        negotiate: negotiate extension\n        [*] --&gt; negotiate\n        negotiate --&gt; 30\n    }\n    30 --&gt; 31\n    state Disagreement {\n        dots2: ...\n        31 --&gt; dots2\n        dots2 --&gt; 90\n    }</code></pre> <p>Typically it is the Reporter who desires a shorter embargo than the Vendor. We chose our example to demonstrate that this analysis works between any two parties, regardless of which party wants the shorter embargo.</p> <p>Resolving Multiple Proposals at Once</p> <p>On our way to making this principle explicit, we immediately came across a second scenario worth a brief diversion: What to do when multiple revisions are up for negotiation simultaneously? Based on the idea of extending the above to an efficient pairwise evaluation of multiple proposals, we suggest the following heuristic:</p> <ol> <li>Sort the proposals in order from earliest to latest according to their expiration date.</li> <li>Set the current candidate to the earliest proposal.</li> <li>Loop over each remaining (later) proposal, evaluating it against the current candidate.</li> <li>If the newly evaluated proposal is accepted, it becomes the current candidate and the loop repeats.</li> <li>Otherwise, the loop exits at the first rejected proposal.</li> <li>The current candidate (i.e., the latest accepted proposal) becomes the new Active embargo.</li> <li>If the earliest proposed revision is rejected---implying that none of the later ones would be acceptable either---then the existing Active embargo remains intact.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"topics/process_models/em/defaults/#resolving-proposals-and-revisions","title":"Resolving Proposals and Revisions","text":"<p>Summarizing the principles just laid out as rules</p> <p>When two or more embargo proposals are open (i.e., none have yet been accepted) and \\(q^{em} \\in P\\), Participants SHOULD accept the shortest one and propose the remainder as revisions.</p> <p>When two or more embargo revisions are open (i.e., an embargo is active yet none of the proposals have been decided) and \\(q^{em} \\in R\\), Participants SHOULD accept or reject them individually, in earliest to latest expiration order.</p>"},{"location":"topics/process_models/em/early_termination/","title":"Early Termination","text":"<p>This page is normative</p> <p>This page is considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol. This is a normative section of the documentation.</p> <p>Embargoes are a means of inhibiting public disclosure of a vulnerability while defenses are prepared (e.g., until fix development has completed for a reasonable quorum of Vendors).</p> <p>The goal of the EM process is not to establish an exact publication schedule for every Participant to adhere to. Rather,</p> <p>Embargo Management Process Goal</p> <p>The goal of the Embargo Management process is to establish a window spanning from the present to some future time, during which Participants are expected to not publish or otherwise disclose information about the vulnerability to non-Participants outside of the CVD case.</p> <p>Hence our definition of an embargo:</p> <p>Embargo Definition</p> <p>An embargo is an informal agreement among peer CVD case Participants to refrain from publishing information about a vulnerability until some future point in time.</p>"},{"location":"topics/process_models/em/principles/#embargoes-are-a-social-agreement","title":"Embargoes Are a Social Agreement","text":"<p>An embargo is a social agreement between independent parties acting in the interest of providing vulnerability fixes to users in a timely manner while minimizing attacker advantage in the interim. The more people involved in an embargo, the more likely the embargo is to fail.</p> <p>Embargo participation SHOULD be limited to the smallest possible set of individuals and organizations needed to adequately address the vulnerability report.</p> <p>Similarly, the longer an embargo lasts, the more likely it is to fail.</p> <p>Embargo duration SHOULD be limited to the shortest duration possible to adequately address the vulnerability report.</p> <p>Furthermore, we need to establish a few norms related to embargo timing.</p> <p>An embargo SHALL specify an unambiguous date and time as its endpoint.</p> <p>An embargo SHALL NOT be used to indefinitely delay publication of vulnerability information, whether through repeated extension or by setting a long-range endpoint.</p> <p>An embargo SHALL begin at the moment it is accepted.</p> <p>Embargoes SHOULD be of short duration, from a few days to a few months.</p> <p></p> <p>CVD Embargoes Are Not NDAs</p> <p>CVD embargoes are not Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs). An NDA (also known as a Confidentiality agreement) is a legally binding contract between parties, often accompanied by a reward for compliance and/or some penalty in the event of unauthorized disclosure. NDAs do, on occasion, have a place in CVD processes, but the relatively rapid pace and scale of most MPCVD embargoes makes per-case NDAs prohibitively difficult. As a result, we are intentionally setting aside NDA negotiation as beyond the scope of this proposal.</p> <p>On the surface, many bug bounty programs may appear to fall outside our scope because they are often structured as  NDAs in which compliance is rewarded. For some bounty programs, the penalty for non-compliance or early disclosure is limited to the loss of the reward. Built on CERT/CC's decades of experience coordinating global software vulnerability response, Vultron aims to serve as a lingua franca for sharing CVD case coordination data across independent organizations, tools, and policies. It targets security researchers, vulnerability coordinators, tool builders, and anyone seeking interoperability in the CVD ecosystem.</p> <p>Work in progress</p> <p>Vultron is a collection of ideas, models, code, and work in progress, and is not yet ready for production use. Our focus so far is on</p> <ul> <li>Explanation, which describes the   protocol in detail</li> <li>How-to Guides, which provides guidance for   potential implementations of Vultron</li> <li>Reference, which provides the formal   protocol specification</li> </ul> <p>Current Version</p> <p>The current version of the Vultron Protocol is</p> <p>2024.4.4.dev6496+gb9388ca98.d20260915</p>"},{"location":"#so-what-is-vultron","title":"So what is Vultron?","text":"<p>Looking for the full answer?</p> <p>See What Is Vultron? for an in-depth explanation aimed at CVD practitioners and systems architects evaluating whether to adopt the protocol.</p> <p>Vultron is:</p> <ul> <li>A set of high-level processes representing the steps involved in coordinated   vulnerability disclosure</li> <li>A formal protocol describing the interactions of those processes</li> <li>A set of behavior logic that can be implemented as either procedures for humans   to follow or (in many cases) code that can perform actions in response to state   changes in a case with minimal human input</li> <li>A minimal data model for what information is necessary to track participant   status and the overall case status through the course of handling a CVD case</li> </ul> <p>The above were all initially described in the Designing Vultron: A Protocol for Multi-Party Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (MPCVD) report. Therefore, our position is that end-to-end encryption would be better implemented as a layer on top of the ActivityPub protocol, rather than as a specific feature of the Vultron Protocol. From what we can tell, the topic has come up before in the ActivityPub community, but there is no standardized solution yet. We're currently focused on developing the Vultron Protocol, but we realize that encryption may be a requirement for widespread adoption, so we're keeping an eye on the topic.</p> <p>Some relevant links include:</p> <ul> <li>A November 2022 blog   post Towards End-to-End Encryption for Direct Messages in the Fediverse</li> <li>Issue #225 on the W3C ActivityPub Github repo talks about the   need for encrypted content, but it seems to have been closed without a solution in 2017.</li> <li>However, a much more       recent April 2023 comment       mentions:       &gt; If we restrict to direct message (with a single recipient) one may just encrypt the message (Note) payload using       the       public key of the recipient. project.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#what-is-an-adr","title":"What is an ADR?","text":"<p>An architectural decision record (ADR) is a document that captures an important architectural decision made along with its context and consequences. We're using the expanded concept of an Any Decision Record (ADR) to capture any decision that is important to the project, not just architectural decisions. We use Markdown Any Decision Records (MADR) to document our architectural decisions.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#when-to-write-an-adr","title":"When to write an ADR","text":"<p>The primary signal for an ADR is evaluated alternatives: if you considered more than one option and rejected at least one, document the decision. The record preserves context for future maintainers who might otherwise re-open a settled question.</p> <p>Concretely, write an ADR when:</p> <ul> <li>You adopted a structural or architectural approach over one or more   alternatives (e.g., hexagonal architecture over layered, SQLModel over   TinyDB).</li> <li>You made a one-time process or tooling decision with lasting project-wide   impact (e.g., CalVer over SemVer, pinning CI action SHAs).</li> <li>A decision will be hard or costly to reverse, so the rationale should be   preserved explicitly.</li> </ul> <p>ADR vs. spec: an ADR records why a choice was made; a spec entry records what the system must do going forward. When a significant decision also generates recurring testable requirements, create both \u2014 see <code>notes/specs-vs-adrs.md</code> for the full delineation guidelines and worked examples.</p> <p>You do not need an ADR for:</p> <ul> <li>Uncontested conventions with no real alternatives (write a spec entry   instead).</li> <li>Small tactical choices where the rationale is obvious from the code.</li> </ul> <p>If you're unsure, err on the side of writing one \u2014 a brief ADR is better than losing context.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#revising-vs-amending-an-adr","title":"Revising vs. amending an ADR","text":"<p>An ADR records the decision that was made and why. Its value to a future reader is that they can understand the current expectation in one pass.</p> <p>When to revise in-place: If a recently-accepted ADR contains a statement that its own implementation contradicted \u2014 e.g., an option label that says \"rejected\" for something the chosen option actually requires, or a \"what is removed\" list that conflicts with MUST-level spec entries \u2014 revise the ADR body directly to make the current expectation accurate.</p> <p>When to write a new ADR: If the decision itself changed (you adopted a different option than originally chosen), write a new ADR that supersedes the old one.</p> <p>Do not append <code>### Amendment</code> sections: An append-only trail of amendments forces future readers to reconcile the body against its own addenda to determine which statement is currently authoritative. This defeats the primary purpose of the record. The only exception is an ADR with <code>status: provisional</code> where the amendment explicitly finalises that status.</p> <p>Source: ISSUE-1777 / learning 2026-07-31</p>"},{"location":"adr/#how-to-write-an-adr","title":"How to write an ADR","text":"<p>For new ADRs, please use adr-template.md as basis. requires every object to have an <code>id</code> field. The <code>generate_new_id()</code> utility in <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/base/utils.py</code> currently returns a bare UUID-4 string (e.g., <code>2196cbb2-fb6f-407c-b473-1ed8ae806578</code>) as the default <code>as_id</code> for new objects. Bare UUIDs are not valid AS2 identifiers and will cause interoperability problems once federation is implemented.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0010-standardize-object-ids/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>AS2 compliance: ActivityStreams 2.0 requires <code>id</code> to be an absolute   IRI. When these references use mutable identifiers \u2014 version tags (e.g., <code>@v4</code>) or branch names (e.g., <code>@main</code>) \u2014 a compromised or modified upstream action can silently inject malicious code into CI without any change to the repository. The I/O cost is therefore O(n) relative to total database size, not query size. The codebase, however, was built wire-first, so these classes currently live under <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/objects/</code> and inherit from the AS2 base class hierarchy (<code>as_Base</code> \u2192 <code>as_Object</code> \u2192 ...).</p> <p>This produces a layer-boundary inversion. The core layer (<code>vultron/core/</code>) is forbidden from importing the wire layer (<code>vultron/wire/as2/</code>); to satisfy that rule, <code>VultronActivity.object_</code> in <code>vultron/core/models/activity.py</code> is typed <code>Any | None</code>. Round-trips through <code>model_dump() \u2192 model_validate()</code> therefore lose typed object identity: nested domain objects deserialize as plain <code>dict</code>s, and <code>DataLayer.hydrate()</code> is silently skipped. PR #577 added an <code>_STUB_OBJECT_MODEL_MAP</code> workaround in <code>outbox_handler.py</code> that covers only <code>VulnerabilityCase</code> and requires per-type manual registration.</p> <p>Wire-format concerns also leak into the domain: AS2 freely models a nested object as an inline object, a bare ID string, or a <code>Link</code> reference, which forces core fields into <code>Object | str | Link | None</code> unions. Behavior-tree code, persistence code, and use-case handlers all pay the cost.</p> <p>Issue #699 tracks the per-type migration. Before any migration can land, core needs a parallel base class hierarchy that mirrors the wire layer's <code>as_Base</code> / <code>as_Object</code> shape \u2014 without inheriting from it. This ADR records the decision to introduce that hierarchy, the naming convention used by the migrated types, and the rule that core fields hold full objects rather than wire-style references. Issue #724 lands only the foundation; no per-type migrations occur in the same change.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0017-domain-wire-object-separation/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Restore the hexagonal boundary: domain logic lives in <code>core/</code>, wire   logic lives in <code>wire/</code>. Option B was the correct first step; its code artifacts (<code>CoreObject</code>, <code>CORE_VOCABULARY</code>, and the migrated domain types from the #699 chain) are fully preserved and become the core branch under Option D. Concern #796 and the post-merge analysis of PR #794 revealed that completely independent hierarchies block the <code>from_core()</code>/<code>to_core()</code> translation protocol defined by ARCH-12 and force workarounds (<code>CoreActor | as_Actor</code> unions in adapters; re-export instead of proper wire types). Option D resolves this by connecting both branches at a shared lenient root.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0017-domain-wire-object-separation/#decision-details","title":"Decision details","text":"<ol> <li> <p>Shared root. <code>VultronBase</code> and <code>VultronObject</code> (already in    <code>vultron/core/models/base.py</code>) are the shared root for both    hierarchies. They define all shared fields with the most lenient    types (<code>str | None</code>, <code>Any | None</code>, <code>datetime | None</code>). The core branch narrows    inherited fields via Pydantic <code>AfterValidator</code> annotations (e.g.,    <code>NonEmptyString | None</code>) and enforces domain invariants (required fields,    URI validation). Routing as the Sole Path to Canonical Ledger Entries","text":""},{"location":"adr/0021-caseactor-inbox-routing-canonical-ledger/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p>The two-actor demo CI invariant test (<code>test_invariant_5_expected_event_types_present</code>) failed after PR #1024 introduced the CASE_MANAGER role gate on <code>CommitCaseLedgerEntryNode</code>. Investigation (issue #1026) revealed that most vendor-side trigger and received-side use cases never send an activity to the CaseActor's inbox. Consequently the CaseActor's canonical ledger was missing entries for <code>validate_report</code>, <code>ack_report</code>, <code>add_note_to_case</code>, <code>invite_to_embargo_on_case</code>, <code>accept_invite_to_embargo_on_case</code>, and <code>close_case</code>.</p> <p>Deeper inspection found that some received-side use cases (<code>note.py</code>, <code>embargo.py</code>) worked around this by resolving the CaseActor's ID from the DataLayer and then executing <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code> with <code>actor_id=case_actor_id</code> \u2014 even when the use case was running inside the vendor actor's inbox, not the CaseActor's. This violates the identity contract documented in ADR-0018 and the identity-spoofing pitfall in <code>AGENTS.md</code>: a received-side use case MUST NOT execute a BT with an <code>actor_id</code> different from the actor whose DataLayer is active. The guarded commit BT emits <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> activities as if authored by the CaseActor while running in the wrong actor's outbox context, which is either silently dropped or produces hash-chain divergence.</p> <p>The project has stated this rule in scattered form across <code>AGENTS.md</code>, <code>notes/case-communication-model.md</code>, and <code>specs/case-ledger-processing.yaml</code>, but the explicit, ADR-level statement of the only correct end-to-end path has been missing. As a result, agents and contributors keep re-discovering the shortcut (resolve CaseActor ID, run BT) and believing it is a valid \"delegation\" pattern.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0021-caseactor-inbox-routing-canonical-ledger/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li><code>notes/case-communication-model.md</code> establishes that all post-creation   participant messages route through the Case Actor exclusively.</li> <li>ADR-0018 established a single-writer canonical ledger authored by the   CaseActor. The CaseActor is a participant with extra duties; it is not exempt from CLP-10-001.</p> <p>When the CaseActor originates an activity (e.g., <code>invite_actor_to_case</code>), the activity is addressed to the external recipient(s) via <code>to:</code>. To ensure the CaseActor's own inbox receives the activity for archival, the CaseActor MUST add its own actor ID to the <code>cc:</code> field of the outbound activity. ASGI self-delivery then routes the <code>cc:</code> copy to the CaseActor's received-side use case, where the <code>GuardedCommitCaseLedgerEntryBT</code> fires under the correct <code>actor_id = case_actor_id</code> identity.</p> <p>Why <code>cc:</code> instead of adding <code>case_actor_id</code> to <code>to:</code>: The primary recipient of an <code>Invite(VulnerabilityCase)</code> is the invitee. The CaseActor's copy is an archival side-channel, not a primary delivery. Using <code>to:</code> for both would misrepresent the CaseActor as a co-primary recipient of its own outbound message. <code>cc:</code> preserves the correct semantic: the invitee is in <code>to:</code>, the self-archival copy is in <code>cc:</code>. OX-08-004 narrows its WARNING scope to exclude this purposeful self-copy pattern (the only valid use of <code>cc:</code> in the protocol).</p> <p>The working precedent for this pattern is <code>offer_case_manager_role</code>: its <code>ResolveCaseManagerOfferContextNode</code> sets <code>blackboard.offer_case_manager_to = [case_actor_id]</code> and the Offer is addressed to the CaseActor's own ID in <code>to:</code> (a special case where the CaseActor is genuinely the primary recipient). The <code>invite_actor_to_case</code> fix follows the same principle but uses <code>cc:</code> because the invitee is the primary recipient.</p> <p>Distinguishing self-delivery from external delivery in received-side use cases: The CaseActor's received-side <code>InviteActorToCaseReceivedUseCase</code> does not need to special-case \"did I send this myself?\" \u2014 the <code>GuardedCommitCaseLedgerEntryBT</code>'s <code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code> role gate is the only pre-flight guard needed.
