Delivery for Received-Side CaseActor Routing","text":""},{"location":"adr/0022-single-bt-execution-for-received-side-case-actor-routing/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p>ADR-0021 established that the CaseActor's own inbox delivery is the sole path to a canonical ledger commit, and introduced a pre-flight guard (CLP-10-002, CLP-10-003): a received-side use case compares <code>receiving_actor_id</code> to the resolved <code>case_actor_id</code> in Python before deciding whether to execute the guarded-commit BT (<code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>).</p> <p>Issue #1036 found that implementing that guard produced a second anti-pattern: every adopting use case now runs two separate <code>BTBridge.execute_with_setup()</code> calls per inbox delivery \u2014 one for the use case's main operation (often under the message's own actor identity, e.g. the invitee or accepting actor), and a second, conditionally dispatched call for the guarded commit (under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>). The condition that decides whether the second call happens at all is plain Python control flow (<code>if receiving_actor_id != case_actor_id: return</code>), not a node inside either tree.</p> <p>An audit (issue #1036, broadened during planning to also resolve a follow-on Concern, issue #1047, which independently named the same anti-pattern in <code>status.py</code> and asked for it to be codified as a spec-level invariant) found the underlying violation in 9 use cases across 6 modules, but not all in the same precise shape. There are three distinct ways the \"execute() does nothing but build one tree, run it once, handle the result\" intent was violated:</p> <p>(1) Genuine actor-identity switching \u2014 a real second <code>execute_with_setup()</code> call under a different actor than the main operation's. This is the literal anti-pattern #1036 and #1047 describe:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/embargo.py</code>:   <code>RemoveEmbargoEventFromCaseReceivedUseCase</code>,   <code>InviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase</code>,   <code>AcceptInviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 main tree runs under   <code>request.actor_id</code> / <code>invitee_id</code> / <code>accepting_actor_id</code>; a second,   separately constructed <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>   runs under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>. Notably, the main tree (built by   <code>vultron/core/behaviors/embargo/announce_teardown_tree.py</code>'s factory   functions) already composes the identical guarded-commit branch as its   own last child \u2014 but because the main tree executes under the   invitee's/accepting actor's identity, <code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code> inside it   is a guaranteed no-op (that actor is essentially never the CaseActor).   The second, separately-dispatched call is the one that actually fires,   on the rare second attempt under the correct identity. The fix is not   \"add a guarded-commit branch\" (it already exists) \u2014 it is \"stop calling   the tree under the wrong actor a second time, and run the one tree that   already has the branch under <code>receiving_actor_id</code> instead.\"</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/report.py</code>:   <code>ValidateReportReceivedUseCase</code> (main operation is a separate   <code>ValidateCaseUseCase</code> call under <code>actor_id</code>, not even a tree of its own),   <code>AckReportReceivedUseCase</code> (main tree under <code>request.actor_id</code>) \u2014 both   followed by a second, separately-gated guarded-commit call under   <code>receiving_actor_id</code>/<code>case_actor_id</code>.</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/status.py</code>:   <code>AddParticipantStatusToParticipantReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 main tree   (<code>add_participant_status_tree</code>) under <code>request.actor_id</code>, then a second   guarded-commit call under <code>case_actor_id</code> via <code>_commit_log_cascade_bt()</code>.   This is the exact site #1047 cited as its primary evidence.</li> </ul> <p>(2) Single BT call, but non-BT procedural code precedes it \u2014 only one <code>execute_with_setup()</code> call exists (the commit), but <code>execute()</code> still does domain-significant work outside any tree before reaching it, so it is not \"build one tree, run it, handle the result\" either:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/note.py</code>: <code>AddNoteToCaseReceivedUseCase</code>   \u2014 appends to <code>case.notes</code>, calls <code>dl.save()</code>, and broadcasts to peers, all   in plain Python, before the single guarded-commit <code>execute_with_setup()</code>   call.</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/actor/case_manager_role.py</code>:   <code>OfferCaseManagerRoleReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 idempotent-creates the activity   and calls a trigger-activity port directly in Python, before the single   guarded-commit call. This is a pre-existing BT-06-001 gap (the main   operation was never expressed as a BT at all), not actor-switching.</li> </ul> <p>(3) Single BT call under the correct actor, but assembled ad hoc \u2014 no actor-switching and no procedural code outside the tree, but the tree itself is built inline in <code>execute()</code> rather than via a <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> factory function:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/case/lifecycle.py</code>:   <code>CloseCaseReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 constructs a one-off   <code>py_trees.composites.Sequence</code> directly inside <code>execute()</code>, combining   <code>StoreActivityNode</code> and the guarded-commit subtree, and runs it once   under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>. This already satisfies the actor-identity   requirement; the fix here is purely \"move this tree into a named factory   function in <code>behaviors/case/</code>,\" not an actor-switching repair.</li> </ul> <p>All nine sites import <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code> directly into <code>vultron/core/use_cases/</code>, which is what the structural test (below) detects \u2014 but the underlying defect, and the fix required, differs by category. This is the same class of problem the \"Post-BT Procedural Cascade Anti-Pattern\" (<code>notes/bt-integration.md</code>) already names for the validate\u2192prioritize cascade: a cascade that is a child of the triggering operation in the canonical model must be expressed as a BT subtree, not as a procedural call (or a second, conditionally-dispatched tree execution, or any other domain-significant code) sitting outside the tree in <code>execute()</code>. The fact that the in-tree guard (<code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code>) is itself correctly role-gated does not fix category (1): the decision of whether to even ask the question is still made in Python, once per inbox delivery, instead of being one branch of one BT run.</p> <p>A related architectural question raised during planning \u2014 whether the inbox dispatch pipeline itself needs to be restructured so a use case never has to ask \"which actor am I running as\" \u2014 turned out not to apply. Investigation found <code>receiving_actor_id</code> is already resolved before dispatch (<code>FastAPIDispatchAdapter.dispatch()</code>, which sets it from the canonical actor ID resolved off the inbox URL path) and is already present on every received-side event by the time <code>execute()</code> runs. The dispatcher (<code>vultron/core/dispatcher.py</code>) has no CaseActor awareness and needs none \u2014 it is a pure routing-table lookup keyed on <code>semantic_type</code>. The gap is entirely at the use-case/BT boundary, not the dispatch layer; no change to ADR-0020's proposed <code>process_payload</code> seam is required by this decision.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0022-single-bt-execution-for-received-side-case-actor-routing/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The BT is the domain documentation (<code>specs/behavior-tree-integration.yaml</code> BT-06-001); a cascade that is invisible outside the tree structure is   invisible to analysis and audit, regardless of whether the gating logic   is \"correct\" in isolation.</li> <li>CLP-09-001 already requires the commit to be reached only through a   role-gated composition \u2014 a Selector/Sequence/Success idiom evaluated   inside the tree. Each received-side use case calls <code>BTBridge.execute_with_setup()</code> exactly once, with <code>actor_id=receiving_actor_id</code>. The use case's tree-factory function composes the main operation subtree and the guarded-commit subtree (<code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>, or an equivalent Selector/Sequence/Success branch) as siblings or a sequence within one tree. Any identity referenced by the message other than <code>receiving_actor_id</code> (invitee, accepting actor, sender) is threaded into the tree as leaf-node constructor arguments or blackboard keys \u2014 data, not a second <code>actor_id</code>.</p> <p>Option B \u2014 Keep the current two-call shape; tighten only the pre-flight guard's correctness (status quo, amended). The term implied a specific kind of implementor (an autonomous AI entity) when the shapes are actually abstract interface contracts. The fuzzer is not a permanent implementation: it is an adapter that will be replaced over time by real data lookups, policy evaluations, or capability implementations.</p> <p>Before those replacements can happen, the call-out points must be expressed as proper injection seams: the BT tree must be built so that the fuzzer is the default backend, not the only option. This rule is not specific to participant roles. ASK-01-004 states it for every ask: the ask is authoritative and the reply is only a yes. Whatever action a reply authorizes MUST be read from the stored ask, never from the reply's content \u2014 otherwise the answerer can alter what it grants itself, in any exchange, not just this one. ADR-0080 also adds the time dimension: an ask carries a deadline, and for ask kinds whose expiry is void, a reply arriving after it does not authorize the action (ASK-03-006). Trusting when a reply arrives is the same class of mistake as trusting what it claims.</p> <p>The routing tree and stored-ask record described below are the reference implementations the ADR-0080 primitive generalizes; see <code>notes/protocol-asks.md</code>.</p> <p>When the CaseActor processes <code>Accept(Offer(CaseParticipant))</code> from the Case Owner, the roles assigned to the new participant MUST be taken from the stored outgoing <code>Offer(CaseParticipant)</code> that the CaseActor sent, not from the embedded <code>CaseParticipant</code> object inside the received <code>Accept</code>.</p> <p>Why this is a security boundary, not just an implementation detail:</p> <ul> <li>The accepting actor (Case Owner) may modify the embedded <code>CaseParticipant</code>   in the <code>Accept</code> payload, or may send only a bare ID reference.</li> <li>Reading roles from the received <code>Accept</code> allows the accepting actor to   unilaterally escalate or modify the roles the invitee would receive.</li> <li>The stored <code>Offer</code> is the CaseActor's own record of what was proposed;   it is the authoritative source of truth for the intended participant roles.</li> </ul> <p>Failure pattern that violates this rule:</p> <ul> <li>Reading the <code>CaseParticipant</code> role list from <code>event.object_.roles</code>   (the object embedded in the received <code>Accept</code>) instead of from the   stored <code>Offer</code> activity.</li> <li>Reading roles from the BT blackboard across ticks: the blackboard is   cleared between BT executions, so a role written in the offer-received   tick is gone by the accept-received tick.</li> </ul> <p>Implementation: the CaseActor stores the outgoing <code>Offer(CaseParticipant)</code> in its DataLayer at offer-emit time. Types","text":""},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p>Core domain helpers throughout <code>vultron/core/</code> are peppered with <code>if x is None: return None</code> chains. These silent failures propagate far from their source \u2014 the error surfaces at the point of use rather than the point of origin, making debugging difficult and creating a class of bug where program state is quietly corrupted or silently skipped.</p> <p>The root cause is structural: loose wire-layer types (where <code>Optional</code> fields are correct \u2014 AS2 permits many fields to be absent) leak directly into core logic without being promoted to tighter representations. Core functions then defensively guard every field they actually require.</p> <p>A secondary symptom is collection-typed fields and parameters that default to <code>None</code> instead of an empty collection, forcing every call-site to write <code>x or []</code> / <code>x or {}</code> boilerplate before iteration.</p> <p>The DataLayer already established the right precedent: <code>dl.read()</code> raises <code>VultronNotFoundError</code> rather than returning <code>None</code>. This ADR generalises that precedent to all core domain helpers and domain model fields.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Silent <code>None</code> propagation causes failures far from the error source.</li> <li>Core functions should express their contracts in their type signatures.</li> <li>The type system should make illegal states unrepresentable within core logic.</li> <li>Idiomatic Python prefers <code>raise</code> over sentinel return values (EAFP culture).</li> <li><code>dl.read()</code> raising <code>VultronNotFoundError</code> is an existing, working precedent   to generalise from.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>Return <code>None</code> and guard at every call-site \u2014 current pattern.</li> <li><code>Result</code>/<code>Option</code> monadic types (e.g. the <code>returns</code> library).</li> <li>One rich domain class with Optional fields and <code>None</code> guards in core.</li> <li>Validate at the edge, promote to strict core types (chosen).</li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: Validate at the edge, promote to strict core types, because it is idiomatic Python, fail-fast, provides a stack trace pointing to the origin of the error, and allows the type checker to verify guarantees.</p> <p>The pattern in three steps:</p> <ol> <li>Edge objects may be loose. Wire-layer and adapter Pydantic models may    have <code>Optional</code> fields where the protocol or external source permits absence.</li> <li>Promote at the boundary. At the boundary (extractor, rehydration layer,    use-case entry point), required fields are validated. If absent, a    descriptive exception is raised immediately \u2014 not propagated as <code>None</code>.</li> <li>Core receives strict types. What crosses into core logic is a type that    makes the required fields non-optional. Core functions declare these tighter    types in their signatures; the type system enforces the contract.</li> </ol> <p>The Vultron analogy for the blog post's drone pattern: <code>VultronActivity</code> (wire, loose) \u2192 validated at extractor/rehydration \u2192 <code>FooReceivedEvent</code> or use-case request type (core, tight). They must not return <code>None</code> as a failure signal. The <code>update()</code> method is the single <code>try/except</code> handler that converts the exception to <code>Status.FAILURE</code> and sets <code>self.feedback_message</code>.</p> <pre><code># GOOD \u2014 helper raises; update() catches\ndef _read_case_obj(self, case_id: str) -&gt; VulnerabilityCase:\n    try:\n        obj = self.blackboard[case_id]\n    except KeyError:\n        raise BtNodePreconditionError(f\"case {case_id!r} not in blackboard\")\n    if not is_case_model(obj):\n        raise BtNodePreconditionError(\n            f\"blackboard entry {case_id!r} is not a VulnerabilityCase\"\n        )\n    return obj\n\ndef update(self, ...) -&gt; Status:\n    try:\n        case_obj = self._read_case_obj(case_id)\n        ...\n    except BtNodePreconditionError as e:\n        self.feedback_message = str(e)\n        return Status.FAILURE\n</code></pre> <p>This eliminates the class of bug where a helper returns <code>None</code> silently with no <code>self.feedback_message</code> set.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good: stack traces point to the origin of Each Actor is an isolated process: it owns a DataLayer of core domain objects, and (per the Actor Knowledge Model) its knowledge of the world is bounded strictly by what it has received. No actor can reach into another actor's DataLayer. Wire (AS2) exists solely as the transport by which one actor's core state informs another's \u2014 an AS2 Activity is an envelope carrying a core domain fact across the process boundary, not a domain object in its own right.</p> <p>ADR-0017 established that wire is a projection of core, and ARCH-09-001 requires core models to be as rich as or richer than their wire counterparts. The 29 AS2 protocol Activities (<code>Offer</code>, <code>Invite</code>, <code>Accept</code>, <code>Reject</code>, \u2026) break this: they were built wire-first and were never given a core counterpart. For these types the projection is inverted \u2014 wire is the only representation, and is therefore richer than core.</p> <p>The concrete consequence: when an actor must remember what a message told it (the case id an <code>Invite</code> carried, the recommender an <code>Offer</code> named, the report embedded in a submit <code>Offer</code>, the pending embargo proposal for a case), there is no core object to hold that fact, so core reaches back through the DataLayer and re-reads the stored wire envelope \u2014 <code>dl.read(activity_id)</code> inside <code>vultron/core/</code>. Concern #1506 audited these sites. ADR-0034 recognised activity read-back as a boundary violation but explicitly scoped it out and deferred it to a separate concern; this ADR is that concern's decision.</p> <p>The <code>dl.read(activity_id)</code> call in core is a symptom. The root cause is a missing layer of core domain representation for protocol facts. A second, subtler question surfaced during analysis: emitting a reply (e.g. an <code>Accept</code>) requires the full inline verbatim original activity in the reply's <code>object_</code> (the Actor Knowledge Model forbids bare URIs), and activity ids are non-regenerable random <code>urn:uuid:</code> values \u2014 so the original envelope cannot be losslessly reconstructed from core state. That stream travels over a transport with no ordering guarantee, and Vultron may not be the only protocol implementation on the wire, so a replica can receive an entry before its hash-chain predecessor arrives.</p> <p>The original receive path (<code>CheckHashOrRejectOnMismatchNode</code>) treated any entry whose <code>prev_log_hash</code> did not match the local tail as a divergence: it dropped the entry and sent a <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> so the CaseActor would replay the missing prefix. Repairing replay narrows the race but cannot close it under adversarial reordering. Buffering, by contrast, makes convergence order-independent: any valid entry is retained until the entry that closes its gap arrives, then drained in order.</p> <p>Buffering also makes the existing <code>Reject \u2192 replay</code> recovery order-robust for free, because replayed entries flow through the same (now buffering) receive path. We therefore did not redesign the replay loop; we keep sending the <code>Reject</code> at buffer time purely as the backstop for entries that are genuinely lost (never delivered) rather than merely reordered. A companion correctness fix makes <code>SyncActivityAdapter.send_reject_log_entry</code> enqueue against the explicit receiving <code>actor_id</code> (like the announce path) instead of the DataLayer's own scope, so the Reject is delivered correctly even from a shared or differently-scoped DataLayer.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good: a late-joining replica converges to a contiguous prefix within a few   seconds of the tail arriving, regardless of <code>Announce</code> order (SYNC-10-004).</li> <li>Good: no new dependence on sender retry behavior \u2014 robust against other   implementations and lossy/reordering transports.</li> <li>Good: the buffer is a non-ledger holding area (SYNC-13-003), so the   \"DataLayer presence \u21d2 committed + effects applied\" invariant is preserved.</li> <li>Neutral: buffered state is in-memory and lost on restart; In a single-actor    deployment (the <code>fvv</code> scenario, where the vendor is the CaseActor) the    snapshot actor equals <code>case_actor_id</code>, the guard does fire, and the    <code>(\"Add\", \"CaseStatus\")</code> signature must additionally be authorized.</p> <ol> <li>Latent scenario-dependent breakage: the prologue <code>add_case_status_to_case</code>    entry is silently skipped in passing runs (the genesis <code>CaseStatus</code> is    already inlined in the <code>create_case</code> entry), so the ledger \"works\" while    quietly dropping an entry. Only recipients on a different host/port fall through to HTTP POST (<code>DemoHttpDeliveryAdapter</code>).</p> <p>This in-process shortcut makes the co-located case behave differently from the remote case. Vultron's protocol model treats every actor as an independent, autonomous federated peer whose only knowledge of the world comes from Activities it has received over its inbox (the Actor Knowledge Model, AKM-01). The ASGI shortcut violates the spirit of that model in practice: demos and tests that run actors co-located in one process exercise a delivery path that would not exist if those actors were deployed as separate containers. The result is false confidence \u2014 inter-actor delivery bugs (addressing, serialization, inbox routing) can be masked in-process and only surface once actors are genuinely separated.</p> <p>The shortcut also carries accidental complexity that exists solely to support in-process delivery: a <code>contextvars</code> reentrancy guard, scheme+netloc locality classification, and mount-prefix stripping (root cause of several delivery bugs: #531, #534, #557, and #558).</p> <p>Should Vultron keep the co-located ASGI fast path, or deliver everything uniformly over HTTP as if every recipient were remote?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0042-http-only-inter-actor-delivery/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Fidelity to the autonomous-actor model. \"Something that works for   remote must work for local too.\" Actors are independent peers; delivery   should not depend on co-location.</li> <li>Bug visibility. In-process delivery hides inter-actor delivery defects   that would appear in a real multi-container deployment.</li> <li>Simplicity. The reentrancy guard, locality check, and mount-prefix   stripping exist only because of the in-process shortcut.</li> <li>Agent/developer confusion. Two delivery mechanisms behind one port read   as two rival \"paths\"; contributors are unsure which to follow when   diagnosing delivery failures (the originating concern, #1723).</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0042-http-only-inter-actor-delivery/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Option A \u2014 Keep <code>ASGIEmitter</code> as the production default (status quo).</li> <li>Option B \u2014 Deliver all inter-actor communication over HTTP; retire the   in-process ASGI shortcut. The <code>ActivityEmitter</code> production default is a single HTTP delivery adapter (<code>HttpDeliveryAdapter</code>, renamed from <code>DemoHttpDeliveryAdapter</code>). There is no co-located special case: a recipient hosted on the same server receives its activity via HTTP POST to <code>{actor}/inbox/</code> just like any remote recipient. The CaseActor's canonical-ledger self-delivery (adding its own URI to <code>cc:</code> so a copy loops back to its own inbox) is delivered over HTTP loopback to its own inbox \u2014 the same code path as every other recipient.</p> <p>Application code MUST NOT construct <code>httpx.ASGITransport</code> directly. But not every ADR is equally settled. Some are ratified and validated; some are explicitly \"formed in sand\" pending validation (ADR-0025); some were never given a status at all (ADR-0024 had a blank status field); and <code>docs/adr/index.md</code> has drifted from the per-file <code>status:</code> frontmatter (ADR-0027 is listed as (provisional) in the index while its file says <code>accepted</code>).</p> <p>The consequence is a recurring, expensive failure mode: an implementer builds on an ADR's premise as though it were validated, the premise turns out to be provisional or wrong, and a maintainer has to interject and unwind the work. Its transition table, however, treats <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> as a pre-consent state: the only way out is <code>INVITE</code>, so consent can only ever be reached via <code>NO_EMBARGO \u2192 INVITED \u2192 SIGNATORY</code>.</p> <p>These two readings contradict each other, and the transition table's reading is wrong. Consent does not always arrive through an invitation:</p> <ol> <li> <p>Self-determined embargo. A Finder who creates a case for their own    finding and sets its default embargo is not invited by anyone. There is no    counterparty to issue an <code>Invite</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Embargo created with the case. Under ADR-0041, the CaseActor initializes    the default embargo during case initialization, in the same BT sequence that    adds the vendor (CASE_OWNER) and reporter participants. From the moment those    participants exist, an embargo is already in scope for them \u2014 so there is no    instant at which <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> is a truthful description of their position.</p> </li> <li> <p>Implicit consent (CM-14-005). The reporter's consent is expressed by    submitting the report. The spec requires they be seeded <code>SIGNATORY</code>; no    invitation is ever sent.</p> </li> </ol> <p>Forcing these paths through <code>INVITED</code> requires fabricating an invitation event that never occurred, and writing it into the canonical case ledger as though it had.</p> <p>The contradiction is already causing a silent MUST-level failure in production code. <code>_SignEmbargoConsentLeafNode</code> (<code>vultron/core/behaviors/case/accept_invite_tree.py:493</code>) calls:</p> <pre><code>participant.embargo_consent_state = apply_pec_trigger(\n    PEC.NO_EMBARGO, PEC_Trigger.ACCEPT\n)\n</code></pre> <p><code>apply_pec_trigger</code> rejects this transition, logs a warning, and returns <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> unchanged \u2014 and the node then logs \"signed embargo consent for invitee\" and returns <code>SUCCESS</code>. A participant who accepts an invitation to an embargoed case is recorded as having never consented, violating CM-10-001. The author of that node clearly expected <code>NO_EMBARGO \u2192 SIGNATORY</code> to be legal; the FSM silently disagreed.</p> <p>A second, related defect motivates the same fix. A sweep of <code>embargo_consent_state =</code> finds ten consent-write sites, none of which persists the resulting <code>ParticipantStatus</code>. Three assign the scalar field with no FSM involvement at all (<code>case_proposal_received_tree.py:873</code>, <code>nodes/embargo.py:433</code>, <code>nodes/participant/participant_add.py:389</code>):</p> <pre><code>participant.embargo_consent_state = PEC.SIGNATORY\n</code></pre> <p>This is a plain Pydantic field write. It does not call <code>_sync_latest_status_metadata()</code>, so the participant's existing <code>ParticipantStatus</code> retains <code>consent.state = NO_EMBARGO</code>. The resulting ledger snapshot is internally contradictory \u2014 verified directly:</p> <pre><code>participant.embargo_consent_state = SIGNATORY\nsnapshot: {\"embargoAdherence\": true, \"emConsentState\": \"NO_EMBARGO\"}\n</code></pre> <p>The remaining seven fail more subtly: they route the trigger through <code>apply_pec_trigger()</code> \u2014 so the machine is used correctly \u2014 but the write it feeds is still a scalar assignment, so the snapshot is stale in exactly the same way (<code>accept_invite_tree.py:494</code>, <code>embargo/nodes/proposal.py:84</code>, <code>use_cases/_helpers.py:488</code>, and <code>services/embargo_lifecycle.py:690, 841, 894, 935, 968</code>). Routing through <code>apply_pec_trigger</code> is necessary but not sufficient. Five of the seven are in <code>EmbargoLifecycle</code>, the intended long-term owner of all PEC transitions (#538), which makes them the highest-value conversions rather than the safest to skip.</p> <p>The correct machinery to prevent this already exists and is simply unused: <code>ParticipantStatus.consent</code> is a <code>PecDimension</code> (ADR-0036, SDO-01-001), and <code>PecDimension.transition()</code> performs fail-closed FSM validation, raising <code>VultronInvalidStateTransitionError</code> on an illegal trigger.</p> <p>The question is: is <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> an absence-of-embargo state or a not-yet-consented state, and what follows for the transition table and for case-initialization ledger entries?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0048-pec-no-embargo-is-absence-not-pre-consent/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The PEC docstring's own definition of <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> should be authoritative</li> <li>The ledger MUST NOT record protocol events that did not occur (ADR-0019)</li> <li>Single-actor and self-determined-embargo cases must be representable without   fiction</li> <li>Consent writes should be fail-closed, validated by the dimension object</li> <li>Avoid <code>log_index</code> churn: PR #1746 was reverted for shifting ledger indices and   breaking <code>fvcv-extension</code> VFD replication timing</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0048-pec-no-embargo-is-absence-not-pre-consent/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li> <p><code>NO_EMBARGO</code> is absence of embargo (chosen): add    <code>ACCEPT: NO_EMBARGO \u2192 SIGNATORY</code> and <code>DECLINE: NO_EMBARGO \u2192 DECLINED</code>. The invariant-harness job declares <code>needs: demo</code>, which \u2014 per GitHub Actions semantics \u2014 creates a full fan-in barrier: every invariant job must wait for the slowest of all 7 demo jobs before any invariant job can start. The actual logical dependency is pairwise (fv-invariant depends only on fv-demo, not on fvcv-handoff-demo), so the barrier introduces systematic lag proportional to the variance in demo scenario runtimes.</p> <p>Three structural options were evaluated for eliminating or reducing this lag.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0052-demo-ci-job-structure-barrier-accepted/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>DEMOCI-04-001: invariant failures MUST produce a separate, independent   pass/fail status on the PR, visible even when the demo job fails.</li> <li>DEMOCI-02-011: the workflow MUST define a <code>concurrency</code> group to cancel   superseded PR runs \u2014 this is an unimplemented MUST already in spec.</li> <li>Workflow maintainability: the YAML must remain easy to add new scenarios to.</li> <li>GitHub Actions platform constraints: <code>needs:</code> on a matrix job name waits for   all entries of that matrix, with no native pairwise-dependency syntax.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0052-demo-ci-job-structure-barrier-accepted/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Option A \u2014 Merge demo + invariant into one job per matrix entry (single   13-step matrix job that runs both the demo and pytest inline)</li> <li>Option B \u2014 Expand to 14 named jobs (replace both matrix blocks with 14   individually-named jobs so each invariant job can <code>needs:</code> its specific demo   job by name)</li> <li>Option C \u2014 Accept barrier, add concurrency group (keep the current   two-matrix structure; A reviewer can no longer   distinguish \"demo passed, invariant failed\" from \"demo failed\" \u2014 exactly the   failure mode that motivated the separate-job design.</li> <li>Option B achieves pairwise ordering but multiplies YAML maintenance cost   14\u00d7. Additionally,   even with named pairwise <code>needs:</code>, GitHub Actions does not guarantee that   artifact uploads from a named job are visible to its dependent before the   dependent starts; the download-artifact step already handles this correctly.</li> <li>Option C recovers the most impactful practical improvement: on active PR   branches, every push cancels the prior queued run, so the accumulated   \"all 7 demo jobs must finish before any invariant job starts\" wall-clock cost   only occurs once per PR commit, not for every intermediate push. Renaming makes the intent explicit.</li> <li>Option 2 (keep OTHER, add OBSERVER) creates two roles whose distinction is   unclear at admission time; agents and implementers would need to decide which   to use, recreating the ambiguity.</li> <li>Option 3 (docs-only) leaves the enum name misleading for all future   implementers.</li> </ul> <p>Observer semantics (normative requirements in CM-25):</p> <ul> <li>An Observer is a full Tier-1 case participant: it holds a <code>CaseParticipant</code>   record, runs the RM lifecycle, and must satisfy the same embargo-consent gate   as any other participant.</li> <li>Observer is the base role \u2014 the lowest non-null privilege set in the   protocol. But the system underneath is asynchronous \u2014 a trigger endpoint returns HTTP 202 and the protocol effect is committed later by a <code>BackgroundTasks</code> job on a different container. Writing \"A and then B\" when the truth is \"B is only possible because A completed\" makes every step boundary a race.</p> <p>This is not a theoretical concern. Of the nineteen sub-issues of Epic #2136 (\"Demo CI: restore green main\"), seven were the same defect in a different scenario: a step proceeded before the event that would enable it had propagated. Two more were partially this. Each was fixed locally \u2014 a wait inserted here, a different observable polled there \u2014 and the shared cause was never addressed, so the next scenario rediscovered it. Bug #2178's own triage comment states the diagnosis plainly: \"the demo treated async causal steps as sequential (x then y) rather than causally linked (x therefore y).\"</p> <p>Three symptoms show the problem is structural rather than a run of bad luck:</p> <ol> <li> <p>The specs duplicated the workaround instead of stating the rule. Seven    scenario-specific requirements (DEMOMA-06-006, -11-009, -12-004, -19-005,    -19-009, -21-003, -21-004) each say \"poll here before proceeding\" for one    scenario. DEMOMA-11-009 states the general rule correctly but is scoped to    FVCV-handoff alone.</p> </li> <li> <p>The gates did not gate. Both <code>demo_step</code> and <code>demo_check</code> record the    failure and continue \u2014 \"no re-raise\", by their own docstrings and by    DEMOCI-01-003. So a precondition written with <code>demo_check</code> is advisory: it    reads like a gate in review and does nothing at runtime, and the dependent step    proceeds on state that was never established. The concrete instance is the    <code>RM.VALID</code>-before-<code>engage-case</code> gate added by the #2134 fix on the    <code>fix/demo-ci</code> branch, whose regression test passes only because it patches    <code>demo_check</code> out with <code>contextlib.nullcontext</code>. That test idiom is not    isolated: seven demo test modules on <code>main</code> patch these context managers out    the same way, so no test in the suite exercises their real control flow.</p> </li> <li> <p>Which observable proves the cause landed was guesswork. Concretely:</p> <ul> <li>A step that depends on an asynchronous effect is gated on positive evidence   that the effect was committed by the actor that produces it, read from   that actor's own container. Elapsed time, step position, and an HTTP 202   return are not evidence.</li> <li>Gating on an observable that resolves synchronously during the triggering   request is prohibited \u2014 that observable proves the cause started, not that it   finished. Because <code>log_index</code> order is causal order (ADR-0079, CLP-14-001) and the harness already reads per-scenario ledger dumps, this needs no new instrumentation.</p> <p>The narrative is the part of this decision that does work the gates cannot. A gate enforces that the harness waited for the right thing. The narrative states, independently of the implementation, what the protocol is supposed to cause \u2014 so it can disagree with the code. That is what makes it an oracle rather than a restatement.</p> <p>Resolved: nested-block scoping model (PR #2348). The <code>demo_gate</code> context manager is implemented in <code>vultron/demo/utils.py</code> and validated by 14 unit tests in <code>TestDemoGate</code>. The scoping question the ADR left open \u2014 \"whether by phase function, by nested block, or by an explicit sentinel\" \u2014 is answered: nested block. Python's native exception unwinding exits the <code>with</code> body on failure; dependent steps follow the precondition assertion inside the same block. No sentinel variable, no return value, no modified calling convention.</p> <p>The causal-edge schema for scenario narratives (<code>docs/topics/scenarios/</code>) was finalised in PR #2204. It is a snapshot of several independent state machines: <code>rm</code> (Report Management), <code>vfd</code> (vendor fix path), <code>em</code> (Embargo Management), <code>pxa</code> (public state) and <code>consent</code> (Participant Embargo Consent). When one arrives over the wire in <code>Add(ParticipantStatus, CaseParticipant)</code>, the receiving CaseActor must decide what to believe.</p> <p>Before this decision it decided all-or-nothing. <code>ValidateRMTransitionNode</code> refused any backwards <code>rm</code> step and any status for a participant already at terminal <code>RM.CLOSED</code>, and its FAILURE inside the <code>AppendParticipantStatusBT</code> Sequence discarded the entire snapshot \u2014 including dimensions the receiver had no grounds to refuse. That filtered object is what gets persisted, appended to the participant, and snapshotted in the canonical ledger entry. It runs as a read-only precondition guard of <code>add_participant_status_tree</code>, replacing <code>CheckParticipantRMNotClosedNode</code>.</p> <p>Per-dimension rules:</p> <ul> <li><code>rm</code> \u2014 accepted when it confirms the current value, is a valid adjacent   transition, or is a monotone forward jump. <code>RM.CLOSED</code> is terminal: once a   participant has closed, no further <code>rm</code> value is accepted, including <code>CLOSED</code> again.</li> <li><code>vfd</code> and <code>pxa</code> \u2014 each is a triple of independent one-way latches   (<code>v\u2192V</code>, <code>f\u2192F</code>, <code>d\u2192D</code>; <code>p\u2192P</code>, <code>x\u2192X</code>, <code>a\u2192A</code>). Tracked in ISSUE-2256.</li> </ul> <p>Amended by ISSUE-2906 (2026-09-01). Per-dimension rules are necessary but not sufficient. Adjudicating each dimension on its own cannot see a claim that is impossible only in combination. A snapshot can pass every rule above and still describe a state no sequence of events could produce \u2014 a fix reported ready or deployed by a participant whose <code>rm</code> has not reached acceptance, or a fix deployed without being ready.</p> <p>A final pass therefore evaluates the cross-machine entailments \u2014 RM\u2194VF and RM\u2194D (CSB-18-001) and VF\u2194D (CSB-17-001) \u2014 and refuses the dimension whose asserted value moved, carrying the current value forward like any other refusal (RSH-05-020). Which side gets refused is load-bearing: VF\u2194D constrains a pair, and refusing the incumbent side carries its value straight back, which would leave the impossible combination recorded while reporting a refusal that changed nothing. A dimension the sender omitted is never reported as refused.</p> <p>The pass runs on the effective post-adjudication state so a refused or carried-forward <code>vf</code> cannot license the <code>d</code> the sender paired it with. For <code>rm</code> this is not a tightening \u2014 <code>rm</code> is refused only when the asserted value is not a forward move, so the carried value always ranks at or above the asserted one on the RM progress scale.</p> <p>Emit and receive share one evaluator, <code>composite_state_violations()</code> in <code>vultron/core/states/composite_state_invariants.py</code>. Before this amendment the receive path composed only VF\u2194D by hand while the emit path composed all three, so an assertion the actor would have refused to emit was accepted, hash-chained and replicated when it arrived from a peer instead.</p> <p>The guarantee is conditional: if the participant's current state satisfies the entailments, so does the recorded state. An already-impossible incumbent state cannot be repaired by refusing a dimension, because every carry-forward writes the offending value back; that case is logged instead. It is reachable via the replica-apply path, which detects the violation, emits <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code>, and refuses the entry (RSH-05-021).</p> <p>This does not narrow the monotone-forward rule above: multi-step <code>vf</code>, <code>d</code> and <code>pxa</code> advances remain accepted (CSB-16-001), because a peer may have advanced several steps between status messages. Nor does it treat an absent dimension as an initial state \u2014 a non-VENDOR participant has no vendor path (ADR-0075), so no entailment applies through it, and a first observation of a dimension is accepted when nothing contradicts it.</p> <p>Under the ADR-0075 VFD split the <code>vfd</code> rule above now reads as two independent dimensions, <code>vf</code> (<code>v\u2192V</code>, <code>f\u2192F</code>) and <code>d</code> (<code>d\u2192D</code>).</p> <p>The refusal is made visible through the canonical ledger rather than a new wire message: the committed entry snapshots the accepted portion, so it differs from what the sender asserted and every participant sees the receiver's actual view. No new message type is introduced (an outbound refusal is deferred; see ISSUE-2255 for the separate problem that the HTTP response is <code>202 Accepted</code> regardless of outcome).</p> <p>A status update whose accepted portion is indistinguishable from the participant's current state is refused in full \u2014 nothing appended, no ledger entry committed. Such an assertion carries no acceptable information, and recording it would grow both the status history and the hash chain with no state change.</p> <p>On the replica side, <code>ApplyParticipantStatusFromLedgerNode</code> enforces two invariants. First, the RM ratchet (RSH-05-007): an <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> that would move the local <code>rm</code> backwards has that dimension carried forward at the local value, while every other dimension is applied as the entry describes it. Lateral moves at the same rank (<code>VALID</code> \u2194 <code>INVALID</code>, <code>DEFERRED</code> \u2194 <code>ACCEPTED</code>) are the Case Actor re-adjudicating, not a regression, and are applied unchanged. Second, the composite-state fault (RSH-05-021): if the entry's effective state violates <code>composite_state_violations()</code>, the tree MUST NOT apply the status and MUST emit <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code> with failure class <code>StatusAssertionRefused/ImpossibleState</code> to the CaseActor.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0061-per-dimension-partial-accept/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because a refused dimension no longer destroys accepted state, and no   longer kills the StatusAdoptionGate \u2192 EmbargoTeardownAuthorizationGate emit or embargo teardown.</li> <li>Good, because the canonical ledger \u2014 the thing that actually replicates \u2014 now   records what the receiver believes rather than what the sender claimed.</li> <li>Good, because the guard is read-only with respect to the DataLayer, so it   fits CLP-10-006 ordering and can run before the commit.</li> <li>Good, because a <code>RM.CLOSED</code> participant can still report VFD/PXA progress.</li> <li>Bad, because the sender still gets no explicit signal that a dimension was   refused; it must observe the canonical ledger. The core types nest their dimensions (<code>rm: RmDimension</code>, <code>vfd: VfdDimension</code> \u2014 SDO-03-002, ADR-0036); the wire projections carry them flat (<code>rm_state</code>, <code>vfd_state</code>). Ingress projection is what makes the behaviour correct \u2014 inbound data is converted where it arrives, so no core reader ever sees a wire shape and no reader has to degrade. Persistence-boundary normalisation is what makes the invariant hold \u2014 it is the single choke point every write passes through, so it can guarantee the stored row is canonical no matter which ingress path missed.</p> <p>Concretely:</p> <ul> <li>Ingress (primary). <code>_project_to_core_participant()</code> in   <code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/case/_helpers.py</code> projects each embedded   participant of a received case snapshot via <code>to_core()</code> before anything reads   it. Absence (an empty status list) remains a legitimate <code>None</code>.</li> </ul> <p>Rejected for now: unifying the two shapes. It is the right end state \u2014 one class per concept, wire as a pure projection (ADR-0017) \u2014 but it is a breaking change across the AS2 vocabulary and the persisted-row format, and #2232 is a live data corruption bug. ARCH-12-003 forbids exactly this \u2014 <code>alias_generator=to_camel</code> is a wire-specific concern and core-branch types MUST NOT carry it. The violation has been tracked as a known deviation (#1991) behind an <code>xfail(strict=False)</code> ratchet in <code>test/architecture/test_hierarchy_invariants.py</code> for long enough that downstream code came to depend on it.</p> <p><code>ParticipantStatus</code> compounds the problem with a <code>_migrate_flat_fields</code> <code>model_validator(mode=\"before\")</code> that accepts flat wire spellings (<code>rm_state</code>/<code>rmState</code>, <code>vfd_state</code>/<code>vfdState</code>, <code>em_consent_state</code>/<code>emConsentState</code>) and rewrites them into the ADR-0036 dimension objects. SDO-03-003 says the old flat enum fields MUST NOT be retained as aliases or shim properties after the dimension migration \u2014 so this shim violates a MUST-level requirement independently of ARCH-12-003.</p> <p>The reason the alias generator is load-bearing rather than merely wrong is that core code needs camelCase JSON for one specific purpose: building <code>CaseLedgerEntry.payloadSnapshot</code> values. The case ledger's purpose is to wrap \"things that were received or sent to/from the case manager in the course of managing the case\", and those are by definition wire-shaped. CLP-07-001 requires the snapshot to be the verbatim AS2 activity or a deterministic canonical normalization of it, and CLP-01-003/CLP-01-004 make the ledger the replication substrate that receivers project into their own replica. A payload snapshot must therefore be valid wire JSON that a receiver can reconstitute \u2014 camelCase is correct there.</p> <p>So core reached for the nearest thing that produced camelCase: it set <code>alias_generator</code> on the core class and called <code>model_dump(by_alias=True)</code>. That is a wire concern implemented by mutating the domain model, and it does not even work correctly: <code>build_add_participant_status_snapshot</code> in <code>vultron/core/behaviors/case/ledger_snapshots.py</code> has to hand-patch <code>consent</code> \u2192 <code>emConsentState</code> after the dump, because a core <code>model_dump</code> cannot produce the wire's flat <code>emConsentState</code> field from the nested <code>PecDimension</code>. That hand-patch is a partial, drifting reimplementation of <code>as_ParticipantStatus.from_core()</code>.</p> <p>Three additional consumers depend on the same core-side aliasing: <code>_inline_snapshot_reference_value</code> in <code>vultron/core/use_cases/_helpers.py</code> (CLP-07-006 inline nesting of <code>dl.read()</code> results, which are core objects per DL-05-001); <code>GET /actors/{id}</code> in <code>vultron/adapters/driving/fastapi/routers/actors/_routes.py</code>, which dumps a core actor class with <code>by_alias=True</code> straight into an <code>AS2JSONResponse</code>; and <code>vultron/demo/utils.py</code>, which dumps core objects the same way for demo output.</p> <p>A fifth consumer depends on the shim rather than the alias generator: <code>FilterParticipantStatusDimensionsNode._to_core_status</code> (added by ADR-0061) normalises a wire status by dumping it <code>by_alias=True</code> and revalidating through core <code>ParticipantStatus</code>, and its docstring names the dependency outright \u2014 \"the core model's <code>_migrate_flat_fields</code> validator accepts that shape, so a dump-and-revalidate normalises both\". The shim and that idiom have to retire together.</p> <p>The hand-patching is likewise not confined to one site: <code>_build_patch</code> in the same module writes <code>patch[\"caseStatus\"] = {\"emState\": ..., \"pxaState\": ...}</code>, and <code>accept_invite.py</code>'s <code>_build_snapshot</code> hand-builds a wire-spelled fallback dict. The protocol has no bounded commitment window, so a coordinator waiting on one non-responsive invitee cannot tell whether the invite is still live, and coordination stalls without anyone having decided anything.</p> <p>A deadline mechanism is in fact already specified. CM-18-002 defines the pocket veto: <code>INVITED \u2192 DECLINED</code> MAY be driven by timer expiry on \"a configurable policy window (default: 7 days).\" That window is receiver-local and implicit \u2014 nothing about it appears on the wire, so the two parties have no shared instant at which the invite lapses. It is also entirely unimplemented: <code>PEC_Trigger.DECLINE</code> was fired from exactly two sites (<code>vultron/core/behaviors/embargo/announce_teardown_tree.py</code>, <code>vultron/core/services/embargo_lifecycle.py</code>), both explicit-<code>Reject</code> paths. No timer existed.</p> <p>The question is therefore not \"should invites expire\" \u2014 that is settled \u2014 but where the deadline lives and who is authoritative about it.</p> <p>Source: IDEA-2066, under epic #2088 (Protocol vocabulary extension).</p>"},{"location":"adr/0065-embargo-invite-rsvp-deadline/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Both parties MUST be able to compute the same lapse instant, ideally without   exchanging any additional message. An invitee who never responds is by   definition the party least likely to send a notification.</li> <li>No new AS2 noun or verb should be required. Epic #2088 is vocabulary   extension, not vocabulary invention.</li> <li>The existing pocket veto must be reconciled, not duplicated. Two parallel   notions of \"the invite timed out\" would drift.</li> <li>A deadline is coercive if unbounded downward: an artificially short window   weaponises the mechanism to exclude a participant who had no realistic   chance to answer.</li> <li>Being liberal in what is accepted serves CVD outcomes. An invitee who answers   late is still volunteering to coordinate; the protocol should not eject them.</li> <li>No scheduler or Sentinel runtime exists in production, so the design must not   depend on one.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0065-embargo-invite-rsvp-deadline/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Activity-level <code>Invite.end_time</code> \u2014 use the AS2 field the activity already   inherits, on the invitation itself.</li> <li>Object-level RSVP field on <code>EmbargoEvent</code> \u2014 add a new field (e.g.   <code>rsvp_by</code>) to the embargo object carried as the invite's <code>object_</code>.</li> <li>Receiver-local policy only \u2014 implement CM-18-002 as written and put   nothing on the wire.</li> <li>A dedicated RSVP/expiry activity type \u2014 a new message announcing the   deadline separately from the invitation.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0065-embargo-invite-rsvp-deadline/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: activity-level <code>Invite.end_time</code>.</p> <p><code>as_Object.end_time</code> (<code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/base/objects/base.py</code>) is inherited by <code>as_Activity</code> and therefore by every Vultron activity, so the field already exists and needs no extension. On an Activity, AS2 <code>end_time</code> already means \"this activity is valid until\" \u2014 an RSVP-by deadline is the idiomatic reading, not a repurposing.</p> <p>Note that the embargo invitation is an <code>as_Invite</code>, not an <code>as_Offer</code>: <code>em_propose_embargo_activity()</code> (<code>vultron/wire/as2/factories/embargo.py</code>) returns <code>as_Invite</code>, and <code>InviteToEmbargoOnCasePattern</code> (<code>vultron/wire/as2/extractor/_instances.py</code>) matches <code>activity_=TAtype.INVITE, object_=AOtype.EVENT, context_=VULNERABILITY_CASE</code>. IDEA-2066 was framed as <code>Offer.end_time</code>; the mechanism is unchanged but the field is on the Invite. The generic semantic \u2014 activity-level <code>end_time</code> on a response-soliciting activity means \"respond by\" \u2014 applies to both <code>Invite</code> and <code>Offer</code>; only <code>Invite(EmbargoEvent)</code> is normatively enforced for now, because it is the only place the domain currently has a timeout concept.</p> <p>The decision has five parts:</p> <ol> <li> <p>Field and meaning. <code>Invite.end_time</code> is the RSVP-by deadline for the    invitation. It is distinct from <code>Invite.object_.end_time</code>, which is the    embargo's own expiry. When <code>Invite.end_time</code> is absent, the CM-18-002    policy window applies, preserving current behaviour.</p> </li> <li> <p>Authority. The wire value is authoritative when present; the local    policy window is the fallback. The pocket veto is not a second mechanism \u2014    it is this mechanism with the deadline left implicit.</p> </li> <li> <p>Enforcement. The CaseActor (<code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code>) enforces expiry, by    lazy evaluation: lapse is derived from <code>(end_time, now)</code> whenever PEC state    is read or an <code>Accept</code>/<code>Reject</code> is processed. This requires no scheduler.    The <code>EmbargoTimerExpired</code> Sentinel (#1893) is an optional proactive    accelerator, never a prerequisite.</p> </li> <li> <p>Late <code>Accept</code> is not refused. If the accepted embargo is still    compatible with the case's current embargo, the CaseActor honours it even    after <code>end_time</code>. If it is incompatible, the CaseActor issues a fresh    invite carrying the current embargo rather than rejecting: the late    accepter has signalled willingness to engage, so the protocol keeps them and    re-syncs their terms. If no current embargo exists (EM <code>EXITED</code> or <code>NONE</code>),    the <code>Accept</code> is acknowledged as a no-op on embargo state and the actor's case    participation MUST NOT be dropped \u2014 following the EMB-07-003 precedent for    post-terminal messages.</p> </li> <li> <p>No new PEC state. A lapsed invite records <code>DECLINED</code>, the same as an    explicit refusal. Nothing branches on the difference: re-invite    (<code>DECLINED \u2192 INVITED</code>), content gating, and meta-protocol delivery treat the    two identically. The distinction is provenance, and the canonical ledger    already carries it \u2014 a <code>Reject(Invite)</code> entry versus a CaseActor-authored    lapse entry. Encoding it as state would put path history in the machine and    re-expand the table ADR-0048 simplified.</p> </li> </ol> <p>Abuse mitigation: a minimum RSVP window is specified, and a receiver that gets a sub-floor deadline clamps it up to the floor rather than rejecting the invite. Clamping keeps both parties deterministic and makes a coercively short deadline ineffective rather than fatal \u2014 rejecting outright would hand the sender a way to get their own invite discarded.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0065-embargo-invite-rsvp-deadline/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because lapse becomes computable by both parties from a shared field,   with no message exchange and no scheduler.</li> <li>Good, because no new AS2 noun or verb is introduced.</li> <li>Good, because CM-18-002's unimplemented timer gains a concrete, testable   definition instead of remaining aspirational.</li> <li>Good, because the liberal late-<code>Accept</code> rule means a deadline never silently   ejects a willing participant.</li> <li>Bad, because <code>end_time</code> now carries two distinct meanings one nesting level   apart in the same JSON document (<code>Invite.end_time</code> = RSVP-by,   <code>Invite.object_.end_time</code> = embargo expiry). Ledger entry ordering can therefore trail   the deadline. Acceptable while the derived state is correct on read; the #1893   Sentinel narrows the window if it is ever a problem.</li> <li>Neutral, because the minimum-window floor is a policy number chosen without   operational data. A remote actor's replica is now permanently diverged from the receiver's, with   no signal to either party.</li> </ul> <p>The broader principle: CVD is inherently asynchronous. Without a stable namespace URI, the draft Vultron protocol specification cannot cite a normative <code>@context</code> value, blocking external review and independent implementation.</p> <p>The blocker is deciding the namespace URI and making it dereferenceable. The SQLite DataLayer does not provide that. It treats one database file as a multi-tenant store, using <code>actor_id</code> as a filter column over a globally unique primary key. Reads are partitioned; writes are not.</p> <p>Issue #2238 is the visible consequence. <code>VultronObjectRecord.id_</code> is the sole primary key, so two actors sharing a store cannot both hold a replica of the same object ID:</p> <ul> <li><code>crud.create()</code> checked existence with a bare primary-key <code>get</code>, so the   second actor's <code>create()</code> raised <code>ValueError</code>. Both case-bootstrap sites   swallowed that as a benign concurrent insert, leaving that actor with no   replica row it could read.</li> <li><code>crud.save()</code> had the same unscoped lookup and no error. One actor's   <code>save()</code> silently overwrote another actor's row contents while leaving the   row owned by the original actor \u2014 so the writer could not read its own   write back, and the original owner read the writer's data.</li> </ul> <p>Neither case is hypothetical. A single container hosts an actor plus the CaseActors it self-hosts (CP-08-003, pending #1700), and single-server demo mode runs every actor against one configured store.</p> <p>The deeper problem is that isolation was a property of every individual query rather than of the storage layout. <code>SqliteDataLayer._scoped()</code> had to be applied by hand, and any path that forgot it \u2014 every write path did \u2014 reopened the leak. The <code>ARCH-13</code> requirement group and the <code>ActorScopedDataLayer</code> protocol refinement exist only to police that hazard, and <code>notes/datalayer-design.md</code> carries two further pitfalls (<code>outbox_list()</code> requires <code>clone_for_actor</code>; the dual-DataLayer isolation guard) that are symptoms of the same root cause.</p> <p>The unscoped mode is also load-bearing in ways that contradict the invariant. <code>deps.py</code> states it plainly: \"Operational data (actors, offers, reports, cases) is stored in the shared DataLayer.\"</p> <p>There is a second leak, in execution identity rather than storage layout. <code>BTBridge.setup_tree</code> puts <code>datalayer</code> and <code>actor_id</code> on the blackboard as two independent facts, so they can disagree. Under per-actor storage they are one fact: a store is always some actor's own, so the executing actor's identity determines which store the tree operates on.</p> <p>The delegated-emit pattern is where this bites. A trigger emitting on the CaseActor's behalf runs with <code>actor_id</code> set to the CaseActor (CM-24-001) while the injected DataLayer belongs to the requesting actor. So the activity is created in the requester's store and queued in the CaseActor's outbox: the CaseActor never delivers it, and its outbox names an activity its own store does not hold (PCR-08-007, CM-24-004).</p> <p>There is a third leak, and it is the one this decision originally failed to name. Per-actor storage makes cross-actor access impossible; it does nothing about cross-actor expectation. Code can still be written as though a co-located actor's knowledge were its own, and nothing in the layout says otherwise \u2014 the read simply comes back empty.</p> <p>Issue #2548 is that leak in the field. A single container hosts the report receiver and the CaseActor it self-hosts. Under ADR-0041 the receiver does not create the case: it submits a <code>CaseProposal</code>, and the CaseActor creates the case in its own store and replicates it back as <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code>. The receiver's <code>validate-report</code> tree ran before that replica arrived, found no case \u2014 correctly \u2014 and advanced anyway, writing the report-phase <code>RM.VALID</code> latch while the case-scoped <code>CaseParticipant</code> stayed at <code>RECEIVED</code>. Because the guard that decides whether to run the transition reads that same latch, the two halves could never reconverge. The case state had split across two stores and the split was permanent.</p> <p>Nothing in this ADR licensed that, but nothing forbade it either. The invariant as originally stated is about writes (\"one actor's writes must never affect what another actor could read\"); the missing half is about reads, and it has to be stated as a property of the protocol rather than of the storage layout, because the temptation it removes is a deployment-shaped one.</p> <p>An outbox call-site survey missed this, and it is worth recording why. The four <code>record_outbox_item</code> sites traced below name the actor in an argument, and all four are genuinely self-directed. This seam is different: the mismatch arrives through the blackboard, so no call site reads as cross-actor. \"Every outbox call site passes the executing actor's own id\" is true of the traced sites and false at the trigger seam.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0073-per-actor-storage-isolation/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>CM-01-001: each actor MUST have an isolated protocol state domain.</li> <li>The invariant to enforce is absolute: one actor's writes must never affect   what another actor could read. \"Ever\" rules out guarantees that depend on   every query being written correctly.</li> <li>Co-location is an implementation choice the protocol must remain   indifferent to. One host or a hundred, actors exchange information only by   protocol message. No back-end cheats: no direct writes into another actor's   store, no out-of-band signalling between actors that happen to share a   process. A guarantee that holds only when the topology cooperates is not a   protocol guarantee.</li> <li>Core must stay agnostic to the storage layout \u2014 a robust database, a folder   of JSON files per actor, or anything between (the DataLayer port is the   contract; see <code>notes/datalayer-design.md</code> \u00a7 \"Key principle\").</li> <li>The Actor Knowledge Model: an actor's knowledge of the world is bounded by   what it has received. An actor's view of its peers is that actor's own   data, not node-global data.</li> <li>Isolation guarantees that rely on discipline have already failed here once   (#2232 produced two ratchets for one problem).</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0073-per-actor-storage-isolation/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Option A \u2014 One store per actor; <code>actor_id</code> mandatory; no unscoped mode.</li> <li>Option B \u2014 One store, composite primary key <code>(id_, actor_id)</code>, scoping   enforced in every query.</li> <li>Option C \u2014 Per-actor schema or <code>ATTACH</code>-ed database inside one file.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0073-per-actor-storage-isolation/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: Option A \u2014 one store per actor, <code>actor_id</code> mandatory.</p> <p>Only Option A makes the invariant structural. With a separate engine per actor there is no <code>WHERE</code> clause to omit, no <code>actor_id</code> column to mis-populate, and no query that could return another actor's row. Options B and C both leave cross-actor access expressible in SQL, so they convert the invariant into a code-review obligation \u2014 which is the failure mode being removed.</p> <p>Concretely:</p> <ul> <li>The configured <code>db_url</code> becomes a template.   <code>sqlite:////app/data/mydb.sqlite</code> yields <code>mydb-&lt;slug&gt;.sqlite</code> per actor;   <code>sqlite:///:memory:</code> yields one private in-memory engine per actor.</li> <li><code>SqliteDataLayer</code> requires an <code>actor_id</code>.   <code>_scoped()</code>, the <code>actor_id</code> column, <code>get_shared_dl()</code>, and   <code>get_datalayer()</code>-with-no-actor are deleted.</li> <li>The URL path segment is   resolved to a canonical actor URI by computation,   not lookup: <code>VULTRON_SERVER__BASE_URL + \"actors/\" + segment</code>. This removes   the last genuine need for a cross-actor scan. It holds for CaseActors too,   whose id is the container-level <code>{base_url}/actors/case-actor</code> under   ADR-0041 \u2014 one per container, not one per case. The per-case   <code>case-actor-{slug}</code> form this ADR was first drafted against is deleted by   the same change, so the co-location discussion below \u2014 which speaks of   CaseActors per container \u2014 is the one this bullet must be read against.</li> <li><code>record_outbox_item(actor_id, \u2026)</code> and   <code>outbox_list_for_actor(actor_id)</code> collapse into <code>outbox_append()</code> /   <code>outbox_list()</code> at all call sites. The   explicit-actor form existed because the injected DataLayer might be unscoped,   not because any site wrote to a genuinely foreign queue.</li> </ul> <p>Four sites make that non-obvious, because they name the actor via a variable   (<code>case_actor_id</code>, <code>sender_actor_id</code>, <code>enqueue_actor_id</code>) rather than   <code>self.actor_id</code>. Traced through, all four are self-directed: two author as the   executing actor or merely re-queue an activity authored earlier   (<code>case/nodes/participant/common.py</code>, <code>fastapi/pending_retry.py</code>), and two \u2014   <code>case/update_support.py</code> and <code>sync/nodes/replay.py</code> \u2014 emit activities whose   <code>actor</code> is the CaseActor while running as the CaseActor.</p> <p>Those last two conflate three separate ideas that CM-24 keeps apart on the   wire and then muddles in storage: the activity's <code>actor</code> (CM-24-001), its   <code>attributed_to</code> (CM-24-002), and whose store this is. The first two are   wire authorship; the third is infrastructure. Spelling the first and third   with one variable made a local write look like a foreign one.</p> <p>Resolution: gate on the role, not on an identity comparison. A CaseActor-   authored emit MUST sit inside a role-gated composite that verifies the   executing actor holds <code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code> for the case   (<code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code>), exactly as CLP-09 already requires for canonical   ledger commits \u2014 appending to the log and announcing the append are one   privilege. Code MUST NOT instead compare <code>actor_id</code> against a computed   <code>case_actor_id</code>; the authority is a role held in the case, and the holder may   be any Actor type. Once gated, the executing actor is the case manager, so   <code>outbox_append()</code> is correct by construction.</p> <p>This also fixes a latent defect the isolation exposes. Those sites <code>create()</code>   the activity in the executing actor's store and enqueue its id under the   named actor. A shared pool made that work by accident; with per-actor stores   the reader would find no activity for the id. Gating makes both halves land in   one store.</p> <p>Ungated, this is identity spoofing \u2014 any actor reaching the helper could emit   an <code>Announce</code> authored as the CaseActor to every participant \u2014 which   <code>AGENTS.md</code> already forbids for received-side use cases. - <code>ActorScopedDataLayer</code> merges back into   <code>DataLayer</code>: with no unscoped mode, the distinction has no referent. - Peer actor records live in the   address book of each hosted actor that needs them. This is safe because   delivery derives a recipient's inbox URL from its URI alone   (<code>http_delivery.py</code>: <code>recipient_id.rstrip(\"/\") + \"/inbox/\"</code>) and never reads   the peer's stored record. - <code>GET /actors/</code> returns only the actors   this node hosts. A peer is not something the node hosts; it is an address   some hosted actor happens to know.</p> <ul> <li>A BT's store follows its   executing actor, reconciled once in <code>BTBridge</code>   rather than at each BT invocation (<code>_store_for_actor</code>). Chosen over fixing only   the trigger seam for the same reason isolation must not depend on every query   remembering a filter: correctness must not depend on every BT invocation   remembering to re-scope. Normative as BT-05-005.</li> </ul> <p>The stronger choice is not free, and the cost was measured rather than   estimated. Fixing only the trigger seam left 139 failing tests across 10 extra   files; forcing the store to follow the executing actor everywhere took the   suite to 622 failures across 123 files. The maintainer took the structural fix   with that number in hand.</p> <p>A related invariant falls out and is normative as BT-05-006: where a tree is   gated on a role, the role holder, the receiving actor and the store owner must   be one actor. Letting any two drift makes the gate evaluate against an actor   holding no role, which returns SUCCESS-by-skip and writes nothing. Nothing   raises, which is what makes it worth a MUST.</p> <p>The store is not the only thing that holds a store, and reconciling it   alone leaves the other half looking correct. Normative as DL-07-009: every   store reference reachable from an actor-scoped execution follows that actor,   not just the one on the blackboard. The driven adapters injected into a BT \u2014   <code>TriggerActivityPort</code>, <code>SyncActivityPort</code> \u2014 keep the DataLayer they were   constructed with, and the adapter is what persists the outbound activity. So   BT-05-005 alone fixed the queue and left the activity behind: a delegated emit   created the <code>Invite</code> in the requesting actor's store while the node appended   its id to the executing actor's outbox. Delivery then found the queue entry,   could not read the activity, logged \"not found in DataLayer\", and skipped \u2014 the   invitee was never told it had been invited, and no error surfaced anywhere.</p> <p>Rebinding is opt-in: a component declares a named way to be rebound   (<code>for_store</code>) or holds no store at all. Opt-in rather than automatic because a   stateless collaborator must not be replaced behind its caller's back, and the   declaration is read off the type rather than the instance because a test   double answers any attribute \u2014 an instance-level probe would silently rebind   every mock in the suite. - Cross-actor access must be   named. <code>clone_for_actor</code> is the only route to   another actor's store, and <code>CasePersistence</code> declares it, so a fan-out is   explicit in the type as well as in the code rather than something a forgotten   filter grants.</p> <ul> <li>The protocol is indifferent   to co-location, and code must be too.   Normative as PCR-01-003. Actors exchange information only through protocol   messages \u2014 never a direct read or write into another actor's store, never   out-of-band communication between actors that happen to share a host. The   operative consequence for the case lifecycle: an actor that has asked a   CaseActor to create a case MUST treat that case as absent from its own   knowledge until the CaseActor's <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code> has been delivered   to it. Co-location does not make the case visible sooner. Absence of the   replica is a legitimate, transient state \u2014 the correct response is to fail the   case-scoped work and retry, never to proceed as though the case were there   (ARCH-15-001).</li> </ul> <p>This is not merely about where bytes live, so it is worth being exact about   who holds what. The CaseActor creates the case and holds   <code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code>: what it owns is write privilege on the case ledger.   The actor whose <code>CaseProposal</code> caused the case to exist \u2014 the report receiver,   whatever other roles it also holds \u2014 holds <code>CVDRole.CASE_OWNER</code>. That role is   never delegated to the CaseActor. \"The case-actor's store holds the   canonical case\" and \"the case-actor owns the case\" are different claims, and   only the first is true. CBT-01-003 is amended accordingly: it previously said   \"case creator/owner\", which under ADR-0041 names two different actors.</p> <p>Stated flatly, because #2548 showed the question had no written answer: when a   container hosts both a primary actor and a co-located CaseActor, the case lives   in the CaseActor's store, and the primary actor holds a replica it receives by   protocol message. There is no write-through from the CaseActor into the   primary actor's store, and no shared per-container store. The two rejected   alternatives fail for the same reason:</p> <ul> <li>The primary actor owns the case and the CaseActor writes through to it via     <code>clone_for_actor</code> \u2014 this is a back-end cheat. It works only while the two     actors are co-located, so it is not a protocol guarantee, and it makes the     CaseActor's authority over the ledger depend on the deployment topology.</li> <li>A container has one store shared by the roles it wears; isolation applies     only across containers \u2014 this contradicts CM-01-001 directly and reinstates     the multi-tenant store this decision exists to remove. It would also make a     self-hosted CaseActor structurally different from a remotely-hosted one,     which is exactly the indifference PCR-01-003 requires.</li> </ul> <p>The consequence a reader must carry away is a timing one, not a location one:   the replica arrives later than the case exists, so any case-scoped work in the   primary actor is gated on the replica having actually landed in its own store.   That gate is the fix; it is not an optimisation to be skipped when the actors   happen to share a host.</p> <ul> <li> <p>What the sibling knows must be   asked for on the wire. Normative as   CP-01-007. The same rule that makes the timing gate necessary also decides   where a fact comes from: an actor that needs something only a sibling   observed has to be told, in a protocol message, at the moment it is told   anything at all. CP-01-004 already established this for the report itself \u2014   the <code>CaseProposal</code> carries the <code>VulnerabilityReport</code> inline because the   CaseActor cannot read the proposer's store. Under #2548 the report's offer   provenance turned out to need the same treatment: only the actor that   received <code>Offer(VulnerabilityReport)</code> holds the <code>VultronOfferRecord</code> for it, so   the CaseActor's scan of its own store came back empty, the canonical   <code>add_report_to_case</code> entry went out without an <code>offerId</code>, and every replica's   <code>ApplyOfferReportFromLedgerNode</code> read that absence as \"not about an offer\" and   skipped. The first visible symptom was an invited actor's <code>validate-report</code>   answering <code>404 Offer not found</code>, four steps and one container away. A   cross-store read is the shape to distrust here, whether what it wants is an   object or a single id.</p> </li> <li> <p>The latch is written last. Normative as   ID-04-005. When a transition has   more than one half and one half doubles as the evidence a later guard reads,   that half MUST be written only after the others have succeeded. Writing it   first turns a recoverable \"not yet\" into a permanent \"already done\": the guard   suppresses every retry, and nothing raises. This is the mechanism by which the   #2548 store split became irreversible rather than merely late, and it belongs   here because per-actor isolation is what makes \"not yet\" a routine state   instead of a rare one.</p> </li> <li> <p>Only the ledger's own store mints   its indices. Normative as CLP-10-014.   Per-actor isolation turns a log index into a claim one store makes, so two   stores claiming the same index fork the chain instead of colliding in it. The   delegated-emit path is where the second claimant comes from: a trigger the case   owner runs emits as the case's CaseActor, and BT-05-005's foreign-authority   exception deliberately leaves that tree running in the requester's store so the   activity can actually be delivered. The ledger commit must not ride along on   that exception. Before this decision the two commits could not be told apart,   because a container's single store was both the owner's and the co-located   CaseActor's \u2014 which is precisely the conflation the previous bullet rejects as a   back-end cheat. <code>CommitLogEntryBT</code> therefore declines when the actor it executes   as is not one this container hosts, and the entry arrives by replication from   the canonical log instead (#2626). Nothing is lost: the activity still carries   the CaseActor as <code>cc:</code>, which is the only way a remote store ever learns   anything (CLP-10-001).</p> </li> </ul> <p>This supersedes the \"DataLayer isolation strategy\" half of ADR-0012, which chose Option B \u2014 namespace prefix per actor in one file. ADR-0012's other three decisions (DI-1 closure lambda, IO-A queues in the DataLayer, OX-B deferral) are unaffected. ADR-0012's own reasoning for rejecting one-file-per-actor was that it \"creates many files and complicates the DataLayer reset endpoint\" and \"diverges from the MongoDB collection model\" \u2014 a prototype-convenience argument that does not survive being weighed against CM-01-001.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0073-per-actor-storage-isolation/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because cross-actor access becomes impossible rather than incorrect.
