It is stored as <code>CaseLedgerEntry.payloadSnapshot</code> and    replicated to other participants via <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code>. Mutating    it before ledger storage breaks replication fidelity: other actors reconstruct    their local state from the replicated form, so they would see a different    representation than what was originally received.</p> </li> <li> <p>Outbound: a factory-constructed Activity is an artifact \u2014 it captures    exactly what was sent. The same object must serve as both the delivery payload    and the <code>payloadSnapshot</code> in the ledger entry. Adapter enrichment after the    factory seals the blob creates a gap: the ledger records one form while the    recipient receives another, breaking the accountability invariant.</p> </li> </ol> <p>Currently nothing in the type system prevents mutation. <code>as_Object</code> uses <code>ConfigDict(validate_assignment=False)</code> (ADR-0064) to stay lenient for inbound AS2 data, but has no <code>frozen=True</code>. Downstream code can and does mutate Activity objects in place \u2014 three mutation sites in <code>outbox_delivery.py</code> overwrite <code>outbound_activity.object_</code> after the ledger entry has already been written.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0074-wire-activity-artifact-immutability/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Ledger integrity: <code>CaseLedgerEntry.payloadSnapshot</code> must be identical to   the delivered payload. Post-factory mutation creates a permanent divergence.</li> <li>Replication fidelity: other actors reconstruct state from the replicated   <code>payloadSnapshot</code>. If the frozen artifact is mutated before ledger storage,   replications propagate the mutated form.</li> <li>Type-level enforcement: \"do not mutate\" as a convention enforced only by   documentation is insufficient; the runtime should raise on accidental mutation   during development and testing.</li> <li>Orthogonality: <code>validate_assignment=False</code> (wire branch leniency,   ARCH-12-002) and <code>frozen=True</code> (post-construction immutability) are   independent properties that can coexist. ADR-0064 established the former;   this ADR establishes the latter.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0074-wire-activity-artifact-immutability/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>Full <code>frozen=True</code> on <code>as_Object</code> + A/B split for inbound routing</li> <li>Per-field freeze \u2014 mark only <code>payloadSnapshot</code>-bound fields as frozen</li> <li>Mutable Activities with a documentation-only immutability convention</li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0074-wire-activity-artifact-immutability/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: \"Full <code>frozen=True</code> + A/B split\", because it is the only option that enforces the invariant at the type level for both the inbound and outbound pipelines.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0074-wire-activity-artifact-immutability/#inbound-ab-split","title":"Inbound: A/B split","text":"<p>Two distinct objects serve the two needs of the inbound pipeline:</p> <ul> <li>A \u2014 the frozen artifact: the wire Activity exactly as received. The capability-shape assignment above is incorrect, and the deny-always stub that satisfied this ADR is the symptom. Each gate is a conversation-state routing subtree (ASK-02-001, RSH-07-004): it routes on whether authorization has been recorded, refused, requested-and-outstanding, or never requested, and in the last case emits the request and terminates successfully \u2014 <code>SUCCESS</code> meaning I asked.</p> <p>The conservative-default requirement this ADR establishes is unchanged, and so is the project-wide floor rule for security-significant call-out points. The formal protocol definition (Brand &amp; Zafiropulo, <code>docs/reference/formal_protocol/index.md</code>) characterised the participant pool as \"Finders, Vendors, Coordinators, Deployers, and Others.\"</p> <p>The draft Vultron Protocol Spec (PR #2078, \u00a77.3.1) provisionally listed <code>Finder</code> as a protocol role while deferring its finalisation pending this ADR. For internally-generated events, order is known by construction. For inbound participant assertions, the CaseActor's receipt and commit order is authoritative. The CaseActor's own <code>published</code> timestamp stamps the ledger envelope; the participant's claimed timestamp is preserved inside the <code>payloadSnapshot</code> but does not determine ledger order.</p> <p>B. Vector clock causal tracking \u2014 each activity carries a logical clock vector across all known participants. The ledger records vector values; receivers can reconstruct a partial causal order across participants without routing everything through the CaseActor.</p> <p>C. Pure wall-clock ordering \u2014 entries are ordered by their <code>published</code> timestamp alone. There is no   concurrent-write hazard to model.</li> <li>Option B requires propagating vector clocks through every wire activity. The CaseActor records the sequence in which it observed and processed events. It makes no claim about when events occurred at other actors.</p> <ul> <li>For internal events generated by the CaseActor itself (e.g., the   native case-initialization entries in ADR-0041), causal order is known by   construction: each entry is committed sequentially in a single execution   path, so the resulting <code>log_index</code> sequence is the causal sequence.</li> <li>For external events (inbound participant assertions), the CaseActor's   receipt and commit order is the authoritative ordering. An entry stamped later   in the sequence MUST NOT carry an earlier timestamp than its predecessor.</li> <li>Every ledger entry's <code>published</code> timestamp MUST be on or after the case's   own <code>published</code> timestamp. A participant MUST NOT batch events and emit them in arbitrary order. If A caused B caused C, the participant MUST send them in that sequence with monotonically non-decreasing <code>published</code> timestamps. A participant that violates this produces a malformed assertion \u2014 that is a protocol violation on the participant's part, not a CaseActor failure.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0079-case-ledger-causal-ordering/#residual-uncertainty","title":"Residual Uncertainty","text":"<p>Even with the participant obligation above, the CaseActor cannot verify causal claims from external actors. Its presence is guaranteed upstream: <code>parse_activity</code> refuses an inbound activity that carries no <code>published</code> (CLP-15-006), because ActivityStreams makes the field optional and the wire base class defaults it to <code>now_utc</code> \u2014 so a receiver that let it through could no longer tell a claimed time from its own clock, which is exactly how CLP-14-007 and CLP-14-008 were left vacuous (Issue #3149).</p> <p><code>_validate_entry_timestamps</code>, reached from every commit through <code>CreateLogEntryNode</code>, then refuses an assertion that:</p> <ul> <li>predates the case by more than the configured clock-skew tolerance   (CLP-14-006);</li> <li>sits beyond the future tolerance or staleness window (CLP-14-007,   CLP-14-008).</li> </ul> <p>and reports without refusing an assertion whose claimed timestamp regresses behind that same actor's previous assertion (CLP-15-003) \u2014 at <code>INFO</code> within the clock-skew tolerance, at <code>WARNING</code> beyond it.</p> <p>That asymmetry is the load-bearing part. CLP-15-003 binds the participant, and the CaseActor observes arrival order, not causal order: the transport gives no ordering guarantee (ADR-0037), so two assertions from one actor can legitimately be committed in the reverse of the order they were emitted, and CLP-15-003 constrains only assertions that are actually causally related. Refusing on that signal would be the reconstruction CLP-15-005 forbids \u2014 and it would discard the assertion outright, because the guarded commit precedes the effect nodes (CLP-10-006), leaving no ledger record and no retry. Recording it and reporting it keeps the signal without losing the assertion.</p> <p>Monotonicity of the claimed timestamp is scoped to one actor's stream. Applying it across actors would reintroduce option C: two participants' clocks are not comparable, so a later-committed assertion from one legitimately carries an earlier claimed time than an earlier-committed one from another. For the same reason a snapshot the CaseActor builds on a participant's behalf must carry that participant's claimed time, not the CaseActor's clock \u2014 mixing the two inside one actor's stream manufactures a regression. Thresholds are tunable via <code>AppConfig.ledger</code> (CLP-14-009).</p> <p>The participant emission obligations CLP-15-001 and CLP-15-002 are not enforceable per-assertion \u2014 that is the point of the residual uncertainty above, and CLP-15-005 forbids the attempt. It returns <code>Status.FAILURE</code> unconditionally. ADR-0076 specifies its intended behavior as an <code>Offer</code>/<code>Accept</code>/<code>Reject</code> round-trip with the Case Owner, but records no mechanism for hosting that exchange, and CONCERN-2812 filed the resulting gap: \"the Offer/Accept/Reject round-trip requires a BT-hosted async request/response pattern that does not exist in the framework.\"</p> <p>Three findings reframed the problem during planning:</p> <ol> <li> <p>The framework cannot host in-tree suspension, and never has. <code>BTBridge.execute_tree()</code> ticks in a <code>while iteration &lt; max_iterations</code> loop    (default 100), treats root <code>RUNNING</code> as \"keep ticking\", logs <code>ERROR</code> and    returns <code>FAILURE</code> when the loop is exhausted, and discards the tree in a    <code>finally: bt.shutdown()</code>. Meanwhile no node anywhere in <code>vultron/</code> returns    <code>Status.RUNNING</code>. EDF-04-002 requires an external decision node to return    <code>RUNNING</code> while awaiting input; that requirement has zero implementations,    and any node that complied would busy-loop and then fail.</p> </li> <li> <p>The mechanism already exists in production, built by hand, once. <code>create_recommend_actor_to_case_received_tree</code>    (<code>vultron/core/behaviors/case/suggest_actor_tree.py</code>, ADR-0026 / CM-16)    records receipt, then routes through a Selector whose branches are disjoint:    already a participant, invite in flight, Case Owner already asked and not yet    answered, or fresh. The fresh branch forwards <code>Offer(CaseParticipant)</code> to the    Case Owner and stops. Two further trees handle the <code>Accept</code> and the <code>Reject</code>.    <code>InviteInFlightNode</code> and <code>PendingOfferCaseParticipantNode</code> read open/closed    state from the case ledger via <code>find_protocol_pair</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>The durable per-ask record also exists, built by hand, once. <code>VultronOfferRecord</code> (<code>vultron/core/models/offer_record.py</code>) is a    DataLayer-backed core record keyed deterministically off an Offer's ID, written    by the adapter that calls the factory, registered as wire vocabulary, and    usable before a case exists. Its justification (ADR-0035, DL-06-002) is that a    domain fact an actor must remember MUST be recorded as core state rather than    recovered by re-reading a stored activity.</p> </li> </ol> <p>So the question was never how to host an asynchronous exchange. It was: why does each instance cost a bespoke implementation, and what is the shape that makes the next one cheap?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0080-protocol-asks-not-suspended-behaviors/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Nothing can suspend, so any design premised on suspension is unimplementable   in this framework and would require replacing the execution model</li> <li>The pattern recurs (status adoption, embargo teardown, participant admission,   ownership transfer, case proposal) and each instance has so far been rebuilt   from scratch</li> <li>The current conservative default is not merely unfinished \u2014 it is   unsatisfiable, so the authorization model of ADR-0046 and ADR-0076 cannot be   reached by any pathway</li> <li>An asker that never learns its request failed stalls silently and   indefinitely; silence is the failure mode common to every member Concern</li> <li>A Case Owner has no surface on which to discover that a decision is waiting   for them, so approval can only happen by accident</li> <li>CLP-11-001 and DL-06-002 already contradict each other on whether outstanding   protocol state is derived from the ledger or recorded as core state</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0080-protocol-asks-not-suspended-behaviors/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>Suspend the behavior tree \u2014 implement <code>RUNNING</code> propagation, hold the    tree across invocations, and resume it when the reply arrives.</li> <li>Replay the original message \u2014 on reply, feed the triggering activity back    through the inbox so the same tree runs again and passes the gate.</li> <li>Split each gated tree in two \u2014 an ask half and an act half, with the    reply handler invoking the act half as a shared subtree.</li> <li>Ask and stop; route on conversation state (chosen) \u2014 the ask is an    ordinary protocol message that terminates the behavior successfully; each    interaction is one tree whose first act is to determine where the    conversation stands, with disjoint branches per state.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0080-protocol-asks-not-suspended-behaviors/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: ask and stop; route on conversation state.</p> <p>An actor that cannot act on its own authority emits <code>Offer(Proposal)</code> and terminates successfully. <code>SUCCESS</code> means I asked, not I was told yes. Nothing suspends, because the work is divided at the question rather than paused there: asking is one complete behavior, and acting on the answer is another, begun by the answer's arrival.</p> <p>Each gated interaction is one tree that routes on conversation state before doing anything:</p> <pre><code>GatedAction  (first fitting branch wins)\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 reply in hand      \u2192 Accept: perform the action.  Reject: refuse, record, stop.\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 asked, waiting     \u2192 stop.  Do not ask again.\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 asked, expired     \u2192 re-ask with a fresh deadline, stop.\n\u2514\u2500\u2500 never asked        \u2192 record the not-yet state, emit Offer(Proposal), stop.\n</code></pre> <p>Because the branches are disjoint, re-entry never retries completed work. This is why option 2 fails: a replayed tree re-executes its pre-gate effects and dies at the first idempotency guard, which CLP-13-001 requires to return <code>FAILURE</code> and write nothing \u2014 aborting before the gate is ever reached. Option 3 was rejected because two halves can drift; a single routing tree cannot.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0080-protocol-asks-not-suspended-behaviors/#the-rules-that-follow","title":"The rules that follow","text":"<p>Authority comes from the stored ask, never from the reply. ADR-0026's trust rule \u2014 roles come from the stored <code>Offer</code>, not the received <code>Accept</code> \u2014 is generalized: the Proposal is authoritative and the reply is only a yes. An asker reads what to do from the ask it stored, never from what the answer claims.</p> <p>Every ask carries its own deadline in <code>end_time</code>, which is already present on every AS2 object and is therefore visible to the answerer.</p> <p>Expiry consequence is fixed per ask kind; duration is configurable. Some asks remain useful when answered late (admitting a participant); others must not (adopting a case status). Whether a late reply counts is a protocol rule fixed in the spec, not a deployment setting \u2014 two actors disagreeing about whether a late answer authorized something is divergence, not preference. The duration is safe to configure per actor precisely because it travels on the wire, so both parties read the same number from the same object.</p> <p>Outstanding asks are recorded, in both directions, durably. A register holds asks an actor is waiting on and asks it owes: appended when an ask is emitted and when one is received, removed when the reply lands. It is actor-scoped rather than case-scoped, so it works before a case exists. It generalizes <code>VultronOfferRecord</code>.</p> <p>The register never authorizes. Two questions, two sources: what am I waiting on, and what do I owe? is answered by the register; was this authorized? is answered by the case ledger, always. A gate reads the ledger and never the register, so a corrupted or forged register entry cannot permit an action. This is the same division as <code>actor_participant_index</code> (fast index) versus the canonical record (authority).</p> <p>One register class, two instances. The create / close-on-named-event / time-out lifecycle, its reaping, and its enumeration are implemented once. The durable ask register and the existing in-memory <code>PendingAssertionStore</code> are two instances of it with different durability and different authority: the ask register is durable and may block; the suppressor is ephemeral, is forgotten on restart by design, and may never block (CLP-06-002, CLP-06-005). CLP-11-002 is clarified rather than reversed \u2014 do not unify the registers; do share the lifecycle.</p> <p>Expiry is noticed opportunistically, plus a Sentinel seam. The next entry into a tree observes an expired ask, and a peer's own retry is frequently the clock. For prompt reaping, core exposes a general-purpose <code>reap-expired-asks</code> trigger. Per <code>notes/coordination-agents.md</code>, a Sentinel operates exclusively on the call-in surface and has no BT call-out point, so reaping belongs to an external watcher rather than a loop inside core. The same endpoint makes expiry testable causally instead of by elapsed time, which EDF-06-001 requires.</p> <p>Asks are visible to the case. An ask is an ordinary canonical entry and replicates normally, so an outstanding decision \u2014 and a stalled one \u2014 is visible to participants. Consequently an ask MUST NOT carry content that cannot be disclosed to every case participant; private rationale belongs in a directly-addressed <code>Note</code>. Delivering the fact of an ask while directing its detail would require redaction with proofs, which the project does not have \u2014 <code>notes/stub-objects.md</code> describes redaction as future work \u2014 and committing a stub instead would violate CLP-02-003 and CLP-07-012.</p> <p>Failure to process is answered, not left to time out. An authenticated sender whose message fails after authentication receives <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code>. This closes the asker's register entry immediately rather than costing it a full deadline of silence for a failure that took milliseconds. It is a dedicated object type rather than a reason field on an existing reply, because SE-08-003 prefers a dedicated type over field-level discrimination, and <code>Create(&lt;minted object&gt;)</code> is the established idiom (<code>Create(CaseProposal)</code>) \u2014 <code>Reject</code> presupposes something rejectable, which unreadable traffic does not provide. Unauthenticated or unparseable traffic is dropped silently; explaining a parser failure to a stranger is an oracle.</p> <p>The fault carries a failure class and a pointer, never an echo: in the protocol-invalid case a typed copy of the failed activity cannot be constructed, because constructing it is what failed. It is structured as RFC 9457 Problem Details, with fault types as URIs minted in the Vultron namespace (VM-10-001, ADR-0069) \u2014 so the canonical list is dereferenceable and extensible without a schema change.</p> <p>The unreadable message never enters the ledger; there is no legible assertion to record. The fault statement does \u2014 it is a true, legible statement about a message that arrived, replicated like any other recorded entry. It is not per-actor observability content, so CLP-07-004 is unaffected: the fact of a fault is protocol history, while the diagnosis of why belongs in the actor's own log.</p> <p>A duplicate request after a reply re-sends the stored reply. Where a request is repeated because the reply was lost, the answerer re-sends the frozen original unchanged (VM-08-003), same identity. Because <code>actor_slug()</code> strips scheme and authority, two ids with the same final path segment but different authorities (e.g. <code>http://finder:7999/.../alice</code> and <code>http://vendor:7999/.../alice</code>) mapped to the same SQLite file.  The collision was logged as a warning and the second write silently returned the first actor's record, so <code>hosted_actor_ids()</code> reported remote actors as locally hosted and subsequent delivery attempts failed in surprising ways.</p> <p>Issue #2549 identified the root cause as two separate confusions:</p> <ol> <li> <p>Route confusion \u2014 <code>POST /actors/</code> should only create actors whose    authority matches the serving node's <code>base_url</code>. The check is at the route layer; <code>canonical_actor_uri()</code> and <code>actor_slug()</code> are not changed.</p> <p>Peer knowledge is stored as a <code>CoreActor</code> record in the host actor's own store via a new <code>POST /actors/{actor_id}/peers/</code> endpoint.</p> <p>The new endpoint:</p> <ul> <li>Validates that <code>actor_id</code> (the path parameter) names an actor hosted on this   node (returns 404 otherwise).</li> <li>Accepts <code>{ \"id\": \"&lt;peer_uri&gt;\", \"name\": \"...\", \"actor_type\": \"...\" }</code>.</li> <li>Writes a <code>CoreActor</code> record into the host actor's DataLayer (not as a   separately hosted actor).</li> <li>Is idempotent: a second call with the same peer id returns 200 with the   existing record.</li> </ul> <p>The peer record lives in the host actor's store. The wire branch (<code>as_*</code> classes under <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/</code>) is the ActivityStreams 2.0 projection: camelCase keys, AS2 <code>@context</code>, lenient field types. The core branch (<code>CoreObject</code> subclasses under <code>vultron/core/models/</code>) is the domain model: snake_case, narrowed types, and \u2014 since ADR-0036 \u2014 nested dimension objects where the wire keeps flat fields. ADR-0017 established the two-branch hierarchy and ADR-0062 established where wire\u2192core normalisation happens.</p> <p>The boundary between them exists in the type system but almost nothing enforces it, and the knowledge needed to cross it is duplicated four ways.</p> <p>1. \"Which fields are AS2 references\" is known in three places. The type annotations (<code>as_ObjectRef</code>-typed fields) are the truth. <code>_AS_OBJECT_REF_FIELDS</code> in <code>vultron/adapters/driven/db_record.py</code> is a hand-maintained frozenset whose own comment describes it as \"ActivityStreams fields typed as <code>as_ObjectRef</code>\" \u2014 a copy of the annotations that can drift. And individual <code>to_core()</code> methods call <code>_scalar_ref_id_or_value(...)</code> on those fields by hand, a third restatement.</p> <p>2. The core\u2194wire pairing is known in four places, none of them declarative. <code>As2WireRenderAdapter.render()</code> resolves a core class to its wire counterpart with <code>VOCABULARY.get(type(obj).__name__)</code> \u2014 that is, it relies on the bare-name collision between <code>VOCABULARY</code> and <code>CORE_VOCABULARY</code> as an implicit pairing index. The collision is between registry keys, not class names: the wire class is <code>as_CaseParticipant</code>, but it registers under the bare key <code>CaseParticipant</code>, which is also the core class's <code>__name__</code>, so looking the core name up in <code>VOCABULARY</code> happens to land on the wire counterpart. <code>_WIRE_ACTOR_TO_CORE</code> in <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/objects/vultron_actor.py</code> is a hand-rolled pairing table for actor types only, built because someone needed exactly this mapping and no general one existed. <code>_NORMALIZE_WIRE_TO_CORE</code> in <code>db_record.py</code> is a third hand-maintained list of paired types. And three registries (<code>VOCABULARY</code>, <code>CORE_VOCABULARY</code>, <code>CORE_TYPE_MAP</code>) are chained by <code>find_in_vocabulary()</code>.</p> <p>This is why issue #2403 \u2014 \"make the two <code>type_</code> namespaces disjoint\" \u2014 has looked risky rather than obvious: the collision it proposes to remove is currently load-bearing. Fifteen wire registry keys shadow a core type's key, and the render adapter depends on that shadowing to find its counterpart.</p> <p>3. Projection is declarative in one direction and hand-written in the other. <code>VultronAS2Object.from_core()</code> is generic: dump, apply the declarative <code>_field_map</code> renames, validate. <code>to_core()</code> raises <code>NotImplementedError</code> at the base and is overridden in twelve wire classes \u2014 195 lines across the twelve overrides plus the base raiser, against 152 lines of <code>from_core()</code>, so 354 lines is the both-directions total. Six of those overrides are pure boilerplate around one per-type fact:</p> <pre><code>data = self._to_core_data()\ndata.pop(\"context_\", None)                             # repeated 4x\ndata[\"attributed_to\"] = _scalar_ref_id_or_value(...)   # repeated 3x\ndata[\"context\"]       = _scalar_ref_id_or_value(...)   # repeated 3x\nreturn CoreX.model_validate(data)                      # &lt;- only per-type part\n</code></pre> <p>The single per-type element is which core class to validate against \u2014 the pairing from (2). A generic <code>to_core()</code> mirroring the generic <code>from_core()</code> is blocked only by the absence of a declarative pairing table.</p> <p>4. Boundary enforcement lives in three places. ADR-0062 named this as its own negative consequence: \"the same projection is expressed in two places, and a reader can reasonably wonder which one is authoritative.\" Since then a third appeared \u2014 the per-class reject-guard in <code>CaseParticipant</code>.</p> <p>Meanwhile the boundary is not actually closed. Pydantic v2 defaults to <code>extra=\"ignore\"</code>, so handing a wire-shaped payload to a core type silently discards every key whose only spelling is snake_case. That is the #2232 defect: <code>participantStatuses</code> dropped, the field left empty, <code>_init_participant_status_if_empty</code> re-seeding one status at <code>RM.START</code>, and a participant's RM ladder <code>['START','RECEIVED']</code> silently becoming <code>['START']</code>. Issue #2232 fixed this for <code>CaseParticipant</code> alone; issue #2262 asks for the general case. <code>CaseParticipant</code> is the only one of the eighteen <code>CORE_VOCABULARY</code> entries carrying the guard, so the other seventeen registered core types \u2014 and 29 of the 30 <code>CoreObject</code> subclasses overall \u2014 still drop silently.</p> <p>Separately, <code>test_wire_no_core_model_imports.py</code> carries an <code>xfail(strict=True)</code> goal test asserting that <code>vultron/wire/</code> will eventually have zero <code>vultron.core.models</code> imports. Issue #2670's acceptance criterion is quoted as \"all 29 entries removed\"; that count is wrong at the source \u2014 the issue's own enumeration lists 31 files, and <code>KNOWN_VIOLATIONS</code> in the ratchet test holds 31 entries matching the 31 measured imports exactly. The target is in any case unreachable while three MUST-level requirements stand: ARCH-12-001 mandates that <code>as_Base</code> inherit <code>VultronBase</code> (which lives in <code>vultron/core/models/base.py</code>), ARCH-20-002 in its pre-ADR-0082 form mandates that the rendering port's adapter locate the core object's wire counterpart and invoke that class's <code>from_core()</code> projection \u2014 so a wire class must keep a <code>from_core()</code> whose parameter is a core type \u2014 and ARCH-12-010 mandates that <code>find_in_vocabulary()</code> consult the core <code>CORE_TYPE_MAP</code>. An agent working #2670 would clear the easy files, reach the base classes, and have to choose which MUST to violate. (ARCH-12-005 is easily read as a fourth blocker and is not one: in its pre-ADR-0082 form it permitted <code>to_core()</code>/<code>from_core()</code> on wire types and stated that they were not required for structurally-compatible types.)</p>"},{"location":"adr/0082-wire-core-boundary-pairing-registry/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Silent data loss is the highest-severity item in scope. #2262 is a   silent-drop default across the whole core vocabulary, and ARCH-15-001 /   ARCH-15-002 already forbid exactly this failure mode.</li> <li>Serialized AS2 output must not change shape. Every mechanism that needs the pairing either re-derives it from a name collision or hand-maintains a private copy. Introducing one authoritative pairing registry makes the other three duplications collapse rather than requiring separate fixes, and it converts issue #2403 from a risky rename into a consequence.</p> <p>Concretely:</p> <ol> <li> <p>A declarative pairing registry becomes the single source of truth for    core\u2194wire correspondence. It subsumes the bare-name collision that    <code>As2WireRenderAdapter</code> relies on, <code>_WIRE_ACTOR_TO_CORE</code>, and    <code>_NORMALIZE_WIRE_TO_CORE</code>. Once the pairing is explicit, <code>VOCABULARY</code> and    <code>CORE_VOCABULARY</code> are free to use disjoint keys \u2014 which is what #2403 asked    for, obtained as a by-product rather than as a rename with an unmeasured blast    radius.</p> </li> <li> <p>AS2 ref-field sets are derived from the type annotations, once.    <code>_AS_OBJECT_REF_FIELDS</code> is deleted and the scattered    <code>_scalar_ref_id_or_value(...)</code> calls in individual <code>to_core()</code> methods are    replaced by the derived set. The annotations were always the truth; nothing    else needs to restate them.</p> </li> <li> <p>A generic <code>to_core()</code> mirrors the generic <code>from_core()</code>, driven by    <code>_field_map</code>, the derived ref-field set, and the pairing registry. Six of the    twelve hand-written overrides are deleted outright; <code>as_EmbargoEvent</code>'s    reduces to a declarative drop-list. Only the genuinely structural    projections \u2014 <code>as_VulnerabilityCase</code>, <code>as_CaseStatus</code>,    <code>as_CaseParticipant</code>, which project nested children \u2014 keep bespoke code.</p> </li> <li> <p>Projection logic moves off the wire classes into translator modules on the    adapter side. This is what makes ARCH-22 achievable rather than    redefined: wire classes become pure AS2 shape with no domain knowledge, and    the translator modules \u2014 which are allowed to see both branches \u2014 own the    pairing registry and the projection. ARCH-12-005 is amended accordingly.    ADR-0063's decision stands; its mechanism is revised, because the render    adapter no longer calls <code>wire_cls.from_core()</code> but delegates to the    translator.</p> </li> <li> <p>A <code>WireParsePort</code> completes the ADR-0063 symmetry. Core currently reaches    for a wire capability by duck-typing \u2014 <code>getattr(obj, \"to_core\", None)</code> \u2014 at    three sites, one of which is ADR-0062's primary ingress projection    (<code>_project_to_core_participant</code> in    <code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/case/_helpers.py</code>). These become port calls,    which is the remedy ARCH-01-004 already prescribes and the one ADR-0063    applied to the rendering direction.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>extra=\"forbid\"</code> on <code>CoreObject</code> is the boundary contract. It is    strictly stronger than a camelCase-specific guard: a typo, a renamed field,    and a stale key are all caught, not only wire spellings. Two central    cleanups are prerequisites, each defensible independently:</p> </li> <li> <p>computed fields (<code>embargo_adherence</code>, a <code>@computed_field</code> per ADR-0056) must      be stripped before re-validation, because they appear in <code>model_dump()</code>      output but are not settable;</p> </li> <li>a <code>model_validator(mode=\"before\")</code> must not inject an alias key beside a      field-name key that the incoming payload already carries. <code>VultronBase</code>      resolves <code>validate_by_name=True</code>, so both <code>id</code> and <code>id_</code> are sanctioned      inputs \u2014 but only one of them may be present when validation proper begins,      or the other is left over as <code>extra</code>. Each injecting validator must      therefore normalise the payload to one spelling before writing its computed      value.</li> </ol> <p>With <code>extra=\"forbid\"</code> in place, <code>_NORMALIZE_WIRE_TO_CORE</code>, its grow-only    ratchet test, and the per-class camelCase reject-guards are all dead code and    are deleted. The invariant becomes a property of the type system rather than a    list somebody must remember to update.</p> <ol> <li> <p>ARCH-22-003 gains an explicit exemption clause. Its \"shrink toward empty\"    aspiration is retained, but the target becomes \"empty except the declared    structural exemptions\", the exemption set is enumerated \u2014 one entry, the    <code>find_in_core_type_map</code> import in <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/base/registry.py</code>,    mandated by ARCH-12-010 \u2014 rather than stated as a count, and the    <code>xfail(strict=True)</code> goal test is retargeted to equality with that    enumeration. Everything else in the 31-entry ratchet set is a relocation    target, not an exemption, and clears only when the relocation that owns it    lands:</p> </li> <li> <p>the shared-base and shared-primitive imports \u2014 the bulk of the set \u2014 clear      when item 8 lands the branch-neutral module;</p> </li> <li>the projection imports in the <code>as_*</code> classes clear when item 4 moves      <code>to_core()</code>/<code>from_core()</code> onto the adapter side;</li> <li><code>factories/actor.py</code> and <code>factories/case.py</code> clear only because AF-01-005 is      amended here: in its pre-ADR-0082 form it mandated that the factory accept      the core object and project internally, which pinned those two imports in      place permanently. It is inverted to require a complete translator-produced      wire object as the argument;</li> <li><code>vultron/wire/as2/enums.py</code> (<code>VultronActorType</code>) and the semantic extractor      (<code>extractor/_instances.py</code>, <code>_builders.py</code>, <code>_pattern.py</code>, <code>_extract.py</code>,      taking <code>VultronObjectType</code>, <code>MessageSemantics</code>, <code>VultronEvent</code>, <code>CoreActor</code>,      <code>VultronCaseLedgerEntry</code> and the dimension types) are cross-cutting      vocabulary rather than domain models, so the ADR-0031 neutral-layer      treatment in item 8 is the likely answer \u2014 but each is its own relocation      with its own task, and this ADR does not pre-judge them.</li> </ol> <p>Until all of those have landed, <code>KNOWN_VIOLATIONS</code> stays a superset of the    exemption set and the two-sided ratchet (ARCH-22-002) stays in force. Stating    the exemption set as an enumeration rather than a total is deliberate: a count    in a requirement drifts the moment a relocation lands, and the residue is only    reachable after all of them.</p> <ol> <li> <p>The shared base moves to a neutral bottom layer. <code>VultronBase</code> and    <code>VultronObject</code> are shared by both branches, so hosting them in    <code>vultron/core/models/base.py</code> makes every wire class a definitional ARCH-22    violation. They move to a neutral layer, following the ADR-0031 precedent that    introduced <code>vultron/enums/</code> for cross-cutting enumerations. The shared    primitives (<code>NonEmptyString</code>, <code>UriString</code>, <code>VO_type</code>, <code>_now_utc</code>,    <code>parse_duration</code>, <code>coerce_cvd_roles</code>, <code>coerce_em_consent_state</code>,    <code>compute_genesis_hash</code>) move with them. ARCH-12-001 is amended to name the    new home.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>| CoreObject</code> is removed from <code>as_ObjectRef</code>. The AS2-faithful part of    that union \u2014 <code>as_Object | as_Link | str</code> \u2014 stays: the standard explicitly    permits a property to hold an embedded object or an IRI reference, and    <code>rehydrate()</code> (VM-06-001) resolves it at a defined point. The <code>| CoreObject</code>    member is not AS2; it was added in PR #730 as a migration convenience and    places a core type inside a wire annotation. Removing it is also what lets the    boundary guard fail loudly: <code>VultronValidationError</code> is not a <code>ValueError</code>    subclass, so a guard firing inside union resolution escapes the whole    operation instead of being absorbed as a failed union branch.</p> </li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0082-wire-core-boundary-pairing-registry/#measured-evidence","title":"Measured evidence","text":"<p>The choice between options 1 and 2 was measured, not argued. Not one of those failures is a camelCase key. The rejected keys are <code>embargo_adherence</code> (1096 occurrences) and <code>id_</code> (110) \u2014 our own code failing to round-trip its own objects. Diagnosing that is what turned <code>extra=\"forbid\"</code> from \"not viable\" into \"viable and stronger\".</p> <p>Two further findings came out of the same measurement:</p> <ul> <li>The #2260 sequencing hazard does not exist. Issue #2262 states that a   <code>CoreObject</code> guard must be sequenced against #2260 because   <code>ParticipantStatus</code> carries <code>alias_generator=to_camel</code> and legitimately   accepts camelCase. Measured: any class carrying an alias generator yields an   empty forbidden-key set. The guard is structurally inert on such classes and   arms itself when #2288/#2289 remove the alias. No ordering constraint.</li> <li>Persisted rows are keyed by Python field name, and one class cannot read its   own back. <code>Record.from_obj()</code> calls   <code>obj.model_dump(mode=\"json\", serialize_as_any=True)</code> with no <code>by_alias</code>, so   rows are stored with <code>id_</code>/<code>type_</code> rather than <code>id</code>/<code>type</code>. That alone is   harmless: <code>VultronBase</code> resolves <code>validate_by_name=True</code>, so <code>id_</code> is a   sanctioned input and <code>Record.from_obj(p).to_obj().id_ == p.id_</code> round-trips.   The 110 rejected <code>id_</code> keys are all one class. <code>CaseLedgerEntry</code>'s   <code>_set_id_from_case</code> is a <code>model_validator(mode=\"before\")</code> that writes   <code>data[\"id\"] = f\"{case_id}/log/{log_index}\"</code> into a payload that already   carries <code>id_</code> from the dump; the alias satisfies the field, and the   field-name key it was meant to replace survives as <code>extra</code>. Under   <code>extra=\"ignore\"</code> it is discarded silently; under <code>extra=\"forbid\"</code> it raises.   The same inject-an-alias-beside-the-field-name pattern occurs in   <code>pending_case_inbox.py:73</code>, <code>pending_create_case_activity.py:97</code>,   <code>case.py:130,166</code>, <code>case_participant.py:161,416,465</code>, <code>offer_record.py:82</code>,   and \u2014 for <code>type</code> rather than <code>id</code> \u2014 <code>base.py:260</code>. The constraint that follows   is not \"emit wire-facing names everywhere\"; it is \"normalise to one spelling   before injecting\".</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0082-wire-core-boundary-pairing-registry/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because the boundary invariant becomes a property of the type system. The formal protocol (Message Types) defines 28 shorthand symbols partitioned by which state machine a message belongs to: RM, EM, CS, and General. The implementation has a <code>SEMANTIC_REGISTRY</code> of AS2 wire activities, each pairing an <code>ActivityPattern</code> with a <code>MessageSemantics</code> value, an event class, a use case, and a rendering phrase.</p> <p>These two sets do not correspond one-to-one, and until now nothing said so plainly. The prevailing implicit assumption \u2014 that a shorthand and a wire activity are two names for one thing \u2014 is wrong in three distinct ways, and it has already produced a normative defect and a documented-but-never-built wire format.</p> <p>Concretely, at the time of this decision:</p> <ul> <li>Several shorthands collapse onto one wire activity. <code>CV</code> and <code>CF</code> both ride   <code>as_ParticipantStatus.vf_state</code>; <code>CP</code>, <code>CX</code>, and <code>CA</code> all ride   <code>as_CaseStatus.pxa_state</code>; <code>EV</code>, <code>EJ</code>, and <code>EC</code> are sent as <code>EP</code>, <code>ER</code>, and   <code>EA</code>. The discriminator is a payload field, not the activity type.</li> <li>Several shorthands expand into many wire activities. <code>EP</code> is realized by   four; <code>GI</code> covers the whole note lifecycle and the actor-suggestion   handshake. The <code>Create(X)</code> + <code>Add(X \u2192 Y)</code> split is itself an expansion with no   formal counterpart at all.</li> <li>Roughly half the registry has no formal counterpart: case lifecycle,   participant roster, invitations, role delegation, ownership transfer, case   proposal, and ledger replication.</li> </ul> <p>Two consequences of the unstated assumption were already live defects. MSM-03-001 through MSM-03-003 asserted at <code>MUST</code> that <code>CV</code>, <code>CF</code>, and <code>CD</code> dispatch as <code>ADD_CASE_STATUS_TO_CASE</code> and that <code>as_CaseStatus</code> carries <code>vendor_aware</code> / <code>fix_ready</code> / <code>fix_deployed</code> payload flags. No such fields exist; the V/F/D dimensions are participant-scoped and live on <code>as_ParticipantStatus</code> per ADR-0075. And <code>howto/activitypub/activities/error.md</code> documents a four-way wire fault taxonomy (<code>RmError</code>, <code>EmError</code>, <code>CsError</code>, <code>GmError</code>, discriminated by <code>as:inReplyTo</code>) that exists in no ontology file and no code, while <code>ActivityPattern.in_reply_to_</code> is used by no registered pattern.</p> <p>The question this ADR settles: is the divergence a defect to be driven to zero, or a deliberate property to be documented?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0083-formal-message-set-and-as2-vocabulary-are-different-shapes/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The formal message set is normative and versioned with the protocol   specification; it must remain stable for interoperability and conformance   claims.</li> <li>The AS2 wire vocabulary must remain idiomatic ActivityStreams, reusing existing   verbs rather than minting Vultron-specific ones.</li> <li>Implementers need one place that answers \"what is this message, when is it   sent, what does it look like on the wire, and where do I handle it.\"</li> <li>Silent divergence between the two sets has already produced a wrong <code>MUST</code>   requirement and a phantom wire format. Whatever is chosen must make divergence   visible rather than merely absent.</li> <li>Hand-maintained correspondence tables in this project have a demonstrated   failure record.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0083-formal-message-set-and-as2-vocabulary-are-different-shapes/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Treat the divergence as deliberate and make the mapping a first-class,   rendered artifact</li> <li>Force the wire vocabulary to mirror the formal message set one-to-one</li> <li>Retire the formal message set and treat the wire vocabulary as the only   message definition</li> <li>Leave both sets as they are and document neither the mapping nor the divergence</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0083-formal-message-set-and-as2-vocabulary-are-different-shapes/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: treat the divergence as deliberate and make the mapping a first-class, rendered artifact, because the two sets are answering different questions and flattening either one onto the other destroys information that the protocol needs.</p> <p>The formal set partitions by which state machine a message concerns, which is the right axis for reasoning about protocol conformance and for the transition tables. The wire vocabulary partitions by what ActivityStreams verb and object faithfully express the act, which is the right axis for interoperability with ActivityPub tooling. Neither axis is derivable from the other, so the mapping is irreducible and belongs in the specification rather than in a reader's head.</p> <p>Three commitments follow.</p> <p>1. The mapping is normative and bidirectional. <code>specs/message-semantics-mapping.yaml</code> (MSM) is the authoritative bridge. It records collapses and expansions explicitly, and every row carries a status saying which kind of relationship it is. MSM-04 adds the General shorthands that were previously absent from the corpus.</p> <p>2. Fault and acknowledgement mechanisms are partitioned on their own axes, and that is recorded rather than treated as a gap. MSM-05 specifies both:</p> <ul> <li>Faults are partitioned by failure mode, not by state machine:   <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code> for received-but-not-understood, <code>as:Reject</code> for   understood-but-declined, and <code>Create(Note)</code> / <code>Add(Note \u2192 Case)</code> for a   condition needing narrative explanation. Failure mode is actionable to a   receiver in a way that originating state machine is not, which is why the   formal <code>RE</code>/<code>EE</code>/<code>CE</code>/<code>GE</code> partition was not reproduced.</li> <li>Acknowledgement of ledger-replicated state is cumulative and implicit via   hash-chain continuity: a matching <code>prev_log_hash</code> is the acknowledgement, and a   mismatch triggers <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> and gap-fill replay. Per-message   <code>EK</code>/<code>CK</code>/<code>GK</code> would be redundant. <code>RK</code> survives as a real wire activity   because report submission is not ledger-replicated.</li> </ul> <p>Both were previously recorded in MSM only as absences (\"no AS2 wire representation\"), which invited the reading that the behaviour was unimplemented. It is implemented; it is shaped differently.</p> <p>3. Reference material is rendered from the registries, never hand-written. MSM-06 requires the consolidated per-message-type pages under <code>docs/reference/messages/</code> to render their mapping tables at build time from the MSM spec registry joined against <code>SEMANTIC_REGISTRY</code>, following the existing <code>docs/reference/specs/*.md</code> pattern, and requires a ratchet asserting every registry entry reaches its designated primary page. None of that machinery exists yet \u2014 this ADR decides the approach; the pages and the ratchet are built by the issues listed under \"More Information\".</p>"},{"location":"adr/0083-formal-message-set-and-as2-vocabulary-are-different-shapes/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because the collapses become documented facts rather than traps. The authority commits a <code>CaseLedgerEntry</code> and broadcasts; the participant asserts and waits for the broadcast.</p> <p>The distinction is correct and load-bearing. The problem is twofold.</p> <p>First, the question is answered in many places, in different ways. There is no single shared way to determine authority, so the check is re-derived per site and the discipline is held together only by convention. Specs CLP-09-002 and CLP-09-003 mandate commit-authorization ratchets \u2014 an enumeration that fails when a site commits unguarded, and a coverage test that every use case reaches a commit \u2014 but those enforcement tests are not yet implemented; only CLP-09-001's per-node role check has unit tests today. A ratchet, specified or in place, only fires when a site forgets to check \u2014 the signature of a convention, not a structural guarantee (<code>notes/case-ledger-authority.md</code>, \"Authorization Was a Convention, Not a Gate\").</p> <p>Second \u2014 and this is the deeper error \u2014 some of those ways determine authority from the wrong thing. They key off where a thing is hosted or the shape of a URL rather than off the role. \"Case Actor\" is a placeholder name \u2014 the readable label a demo gives to whichever actor is enacting <code>CASE_MANAGER</code>, exactly like \"vendor\" or \"finder\". Nobody adopts a \"Case Actor\" identity. The identity is defined entirely by \"the entity enacting <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> must do these things.\" Treating the name or URL as a protocol signal elevates a demo convention to protocol truth.</p> <p>This ADR settles one decision: authority, recognition, and routing key off the <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> role, and nothing else. The scope is authority determination. Both required-field guards were spelled <code>if body.get(field) is None</code>, which answers \"was the key absent?\" The requirements they enforce are about the value: CLP-15-006 refuses an inbound activity that \"carries no <code>published</code>\", and MV-01-001 requires a recognisable <code>type</code>. A sender who transmits <code>\"\"</code> has supplied the key and nothing else, so the guard passed and the value went on to <code>model_validate</code>, which reported it as a schema fault. The consequences differed by field:</p> <ul> <li><code>published: \"\"</code> still produced a 422, but with a Pydantic isoformat dump in   place of the CLP-15-006 explanation the sender needed.</li> <li><code>type: \"\"</code> produced <code>UnknownTypeError</code> and therefore a 422, while an   omitted <code>type</code> produces <code>MissingTypeError</code> and a 400 \u2014 two spellings of   the same omission drawing two different status codes.</li> </ul> <p>A nested object that failed validation was silently downgraded. <code>_expand_inline_value</code> types nested dicts so pattern matching can see structures like <code>Accept(Invite(...))</code>. It wrapped that validation in <code>except Exception: return expanded</code>, handing the parent the raw dict instead. The parent then accepted the dict as a bare <code>as_Link</code>, so the activity parsed successfully, extracted as <code>UNKNOWN</code>, lost the case id, and drew a 202 for a message the receiver never understood. No log line, no error.</p> <p>Instrumenting that fallback and running the whole suite showed it fired 52 times, and every single occurrence was one cause: <code>find_in_vocabulary</code> falls back to <code>CORE_TYPE_MAP</code> (ARCH-12-003), and <code>OrderedCollection</code> is registered only there. An inline actor's <code>inbox</code> therefore expanded to a core <code>CoreActorCollection</code>, which <code>as_VultronOrganization.inbox</code> rejects \u2014 degrading the entire actor to an <code>as_Link</code>. Absent, <code>null</code>, and blank (including whitespace-only) all raise the same \"missing field\" error. Blankness is decided by <code>not value.strip()</code>, matching the project's canonical predicate in <code>core.models.base._non_empty</code>. A non-blank value that will not parse stays a schema fault \u2014 blank means \"not provided\", and reporting corrupt data as missing data tells the sender to supply a field they already sent.</p> <p>A recognised inline object that fails its own class's validation is refused. The Vultron Protocol defines four levels, each building on the previous:</p> L1 \u2014 Syntax Well-formed messages that conform to the wire format.   This level is covered by the wire format specifications. L2 \u2014 Semantic Correct state transitions in response to received messages and local events.   This level is covered by the Vultron Protocol spec (VP) and the   Transition Functions. L3 \u2014 Behavioral <p>Correct observable outputs \u2014 the right messages emitted and the right states reached   in response to a given (input state + received message/event) combination.   This level is covered by the protocol behavioral specifications:</p> <ul> <li>RMB \u2014 Report Management Behavioral Requirements</li> <li>EMB \u2014 Embargo Management Behavioral Requirements</li> <li>CSB \u2014 CVD Case State Behavioral Requirements</li> </ul> L4 \u2014 Process Correct internal decision structure \u2014 for example, precondition checks before state writes   before protocol effects, audit-log ordering, and idempotency guarantees.   This level is enforceable only through a reference implementation.   The <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> behavior tree layer in this repository provides the   reference implementation for L4. <p>Start with L2</p> <p>Most implementations will naturally achieve L1 by using a compliant message serializer. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Scope of this page</p> <p>This guide is for developers who want to replace a call-out stub in the Vultron reference implementation with real logic \u2014 a data lookup, a decision engine, an LLM (large language model) call, or any service that can answer the protocol's question at that point.</p> <p>For the conceptual model \u2014 what call-out points are, what the five capability shapes mean, and why the reference implementation uses fuzzer stubs during development \u2014 see Capability Model. For the overall reference implementation architecture, see Reference Implementation Architecture.</p>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#background","title":"Background","text":"<p>The reference implementation's behavior trees (BTs) contain call-out points \u2014 nodes where the protocol cannot determine the correct next action autonomously and must request a decision, fact, or side-effect from an external service. During development and simulation, each call-out point is filled by a fuzzer node: a stub that returns a random SUCCESS or FAILURE based on a probability. In production, you replace a fuzzer node with a real capability backend that applies actual business logic.</p> <p>The three-step process is:</p> <ol> <li>Identify the call-out point you want to implement (find the fuzzer node, read its blackboard contract).</li> <li>Implement a backend factory that satisfies the <code>CallOutBackendFactory</code> Protocol.</li> <li>Wire the backend by passing it through the domain bundle to the tree builder.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#step-1-identify-the-call-out-point","title":"Step 1 \u2014 Identify the call-out point","text":""},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#find-the-fuzzer-node","title":"Find the fuzzer node","text":"<p>Every call-out point in the reference implementation has a corresponding fuzzer node in <code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/</code>. Browse by domain:</p> Domain Fuzzer module Report validation <code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/report_management/validate.py</code> Report prioritization <code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/report_management/prioritize.py</code> Embargo management <code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/embargo.py</code> CVE / Vulnerability ID assignment <code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/report_management/assign_vul_id.py</code> Fix development <code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/report_management/develop_fix.py</code> Fix deployment <code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/report_management/deploy_fix.py</code> Exploit acquisition <code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/report_management/acquire_exploit.py</code> Publication <code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/report_management/publication.py</code> <p>The Capability Model page lists every known integration point by domain and shape.</p> <p>Each fuzzer node's docstring tells you:</p> <ul> <li>What decision or fact it represents (\"Assess whether the report's   source and content are credible\").</li> <li>Input category \u2014 <code>Human decision</code>, <code>Environmental check</code>, or   <code>System integration</code>.</li> <li>Automation potential \u2014 <code>High</code>, <code>Medium</code>, or <code>Low</code>.</li> <li>Success probability \u2014 which probability class the stub uses, and   therefore what the production default (the deterministic ceiling or floor)   will be.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#read-the-blackboard-contract","title":"Read the blackboard contract","text":"<p>The fuzzer node's docstring contains a blackboard contract section (BT-18-001). This contract lists the keys the node reads from and writes to the shared BT blackboard:</p> <pre><code>class EvaluateReportCredibility(EvaluatorCallOutPoint, AlmostAlwaysSucceed):\n    \"\"\"Assess whether the report's source and content are credible.\n\n    ...\n\n    Blackboard contract (BT-18-001):\n      Input keys:  (none \u2014 evaluates report context from caller's DataLayer)\n      Output keys: report_credibility_verdict: str  (SUCCESS only)\n    ...\n    \"\"\"\n\n    output_keys = {\"report_credibility_verdict\": str}\n</code></pre> <p>Your backend must honor this contract: read any declared input keys from the blackboard and write any declared output keys on SUCCESS. The tree will fail unexpectedly if you skip a required write.</p>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#step-2-implement-a-backend-factory","title":"Step 2 \u2014 Implement a backend factory","text":""},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#the-calloutbackendfactory-protocol","title":"The <code>CallOutBackendFactory</code> Protocol","text":"<p>A backend factory is any callable that satisfies the <code>CallOutBackendFactory</code> Protocol:</p> <pre><code>from vultron.core.behaviors.call_out import CallOutBackendFactory\n\nclass CallOutBackendFactory(Protocol):\n    def __call__(self, name: str) -&gt; py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour: ...\n</code></pre> <p>The factory accepts a single <code>name: str</code> argument (the BT node's display name) and returns a <code>py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour</code>. Any callable that matches this signature is valid \u2014 a plain function, a lambda, or a class with <code>__call__</code>. No registration, inheritance, or decorator is required.</p>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#implementing-as-a-py_treesbehaviourbehaviour-subclass","title":"Implementing as a <code>py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour</code> subclass","text":"<p>Subclass <code>py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour</code> and implement both <code>setup()</code> and <code>update()</code>. The <code>setup()</code> method runs once when the tree is first started \u2014 it registers the blackboard keys your node will write. The <code>update()</code> method runs on every BT tick.</p> <p>Blackboard access requires <code>setup()</code></p> <p>py_trees does not create <code>self.blackboard</code> automatically. You must call <code>self.attach_blackboard_client()</code> in <code>setup()</code> and register each key before <code>update()</code> can use them. Skipping this raises <code>AttributeError</code> on the first tick.</p> <pre><code>import py_trees\nfrom py_trees.common import Access, Status\n\n\nclass MyCredibilityEvaluator(py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour):\n    \"\"\"Real credibility evaluator backed by a reputation scoring service.\n\n    Blackboard contract (BT-18-001):\n      Input keys:  (none \u2014 queries reputation service using DataLayer context)\n      Output keys: report_credibility_verdict: str  (SUCCESS only)\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self, name: str) -&gt; None:\n        super().__init__(name=name)\n\n    def setup(self, **kwargs) -&gt; None:\n        # Register every blackboard key this node writes before update() runs.\n        self.blackboard = self.attach_blackboard_client(name=self.name)\n        self.blackboard.register_key(\n            \"report_credibility_verdict\", access=Access.WRITE\n        )\n\n    def update(self) -&gt; Status:\n        verdict = my_reputation_service.evaluate(...)\n        if verdict.credible:\n            self.blackboard.report_credibility_verdict = verdict.summary\n            return Status.SUCCESS\n        return Status.FAILURE\n\n\n# This function is the CallOutBackendFactory.\ndef my_credibility_factory(name: str) -&gt; py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour:\n    return MyCredibilityEvaluator(name)\n</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#implementing-as-a-factory-function-no-blackboard-writes","title":"Implementing as a factory function (no blackboard writes)","text":"<p>When your backend has no blackboard output keys \u2014 for example, a binary yes/no condition check that only needs to return SUCCESS or FAILURE \u2014 a plain module-level function and a minimal class are sufficient:</p> <pre><code>import py_trees\nfrom py_trees.common import Status\n\n\nclass _CredibilityCheck(py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour):\n    \"\"\"Backend that consults a reputation service. No blackboard writes.\"\"\"\n\n    def update(self) -&gt; Status:\n        score = my_reputation_service.score_reporter(reporter_id=...)\n        return Status.SUCCESS if score &gt;= 0.5 else Status.FAILURE\n\n\ndef my_credibility_factory(name: str) -&gt; py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour:\n    return _CredibilityCheck(name=name)\n</code></pre> <p>Use this pattern only when the call-out point's blackboard contract declares no output keys. If you need to write output keys, use the full <code>setup()</code> + <code>attach_blackboard_client()</code> pattern above.</p>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#what-to-return","title":"What to return","text":"Condition Return Blackboard writes Decision approved, fact retrieved, artifact created <code>SUCCESS</code> Write all declared output keys Decision denied, fact unavailable, error <code>FAILURE</code> None required <p>A call-out backend MUST answer synchronously: return <code>SUCCESS</code> or <code>FAILURE</code>, never <code>RUNNING</code> (BT-18-011). The reference implementation has nowhere to suspend a tick (ADR-0080), so this is enforced, not advisory. The domain bundle wraps every backend it hands out in a <code>SynchronousCallOut</code> guard: a <code>RUNNING</code> return raises <code>CallOutContractError</code> immediately, naming the offending node, instead of silently stalling the tree.</p>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#step-3-wire-the-backend-via-the-domain-bundle","title":"Step 3 \u2014 Wire the backend via the domain bundle","text":""},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#domain-bundles","title":"Domain bundles","text":"<p>Call-out factories are grouped into domain bundles \u2014 one frozen <code>@dataclass</code> per domain area. Each bundle holds exactly the set of <code>CallOutBackendFactory</code> fields consumed by the tree builders in that domain. The bundle lives in <code>vultron/core/behaviors/call_out/bundles/</code>.</p> <p>To wire in your backend, instantiate the appropriate bundle with your factory in the relevant field. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Activities are the core of the ActivityPub protocol. They are used to represent actions that are performed by actors. The ActivityStreams vocabulary defines a number of activities, extended with specific activities used in the Vultron AS vocabulary. The ActivityStreams vocabulary is sufficient for Vultron's needs, so extensions are limited to specifying the types of activities, actors, and objects that are used in the Vultron protocol.</p> <p>A full mapping of Vultron to ActivityStreams is available in the Vultron ActivityStreams Ontology.</p> <p>Design Goals</p> <p>The goal of each activity definition is to</p> <ul> <li>Avoid creating new activity types when an existing activity type can be used.</li> <li>Avoid creating defined activity types with the same objects and targets to avoid confusion. These include:</p> <ul> <li><code>as:Read</code></li> <li><code>as:View</code></li> <li><code>as:Listen</code></li> </ul> <p>Since most CVD cases are text-centric, <code>as:Read</code> is the most commonly used activity. <code>as:View</code> and <code>as:Listen</code> activities may be used in some cases, such as when a case participant views a video or listens to an audio recording.</p> <p><code>RmReadReport</code> is defined as a subclass of <code>as:Read</code> to indicate that a report has been read. This allows the receiver of a report to acknowledge receipt without indicating anything more than that the report has been read. That leaves <code>RmValidateReport</code> and <code>RmInvalidateReport</code> to indicate a more specific action (accept, reject) on the part of the receiver.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\n    subgraph RM:Received\n        a{Accept?}\n        subgraph as:Read\n            RmReadReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Start\n        subgraph as:Offer\n            RmSubmitReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Accepted\n        subgraph as:Accept\n            RmValidateReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Invalid\n        subgraph as:Reject\n            RmInvalidateReport\n        end\n    end\n    a --&gt;|y| RmValidateReport\n    a --&gt;|undecided| RmReadReport\n    a --&gt;|n| RmInvalidateReport\n    RmSubmitReport --&gt; a</code></pre> <p>More Acknowledgements in the Ontology</p> <p>The Vultron AS ontology defines a number of ActivityStreams activities that can serve as the various acknowledgements that are used in the Vultron protocol. These include messages that are specifically <code>as:inReplyTo</code> a message defined as one of the core protocol message types.</p> <p>For example, it is not necessary to send a separate <code>RmReadReport</code> message if the <code>RmValidateReport</code> message is sent as a reply to the <code>RmSubmitReport</code> message. The <code>RmValidateReport</code> message logically indicates that the report has been read in order to have been validated.</p> <p>Like, Dislike and Flag</p> <p>The ActivityStreams vocabulary also includes actions that indicate an opinion  about a message or object, such as <code>as:Like</code>, <code>as:Dislike</code>, and <code>as:Flag</code>. It is possible to create a new <code>VulnerabilityCase</code> object and add a new <code>CaseParticipant</code> object to it in a single <code>Create</code> activity.</p> <p>However, there times when all the case participants are not known at the time the case is created. In this scenario, the coordinator would create the case with just the coordinator and the finder/reporter to start, and then add the vendors as participants in separate steps as they are identified.</p> <p>What's the difference between a Case Participant and an Actor?</p> <p>ActivityStreams actor objects are used to represent long-lived identities of people, organizations, groups, or  software agents. The <code>CaseParticipant</code> object is a wrapper around an <code>as:Actor</code> object that associates the actor with a specific <code>VulnerabilityCase</code> object. part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Inviting an actor to a case is a way to add them as a participant in the case. The invitation is sent to the actor as an <code>as:Invite</code> activity. Depending on the actor's response, they may become a participant in the case.</p> <p> </p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Invite Actor to Case\n---\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor O as Case Owner\n    participant CA as CASE_MANAGER\n    actor A as Actor\n    activate O\n    O -&gt;&gt; CA: [trigger invite]\n    activate CA\n    CA -&gt;&gt;+ A: Invite(actor=CASE_MANAGER, object=Actor, target=Case, attributedTo=CaseOwner)\n    note over A: Consider invitation\n    alt Accept Invitation\n        A --&gt;&gt; CA: Accept(object=Invite)\n        CA -&gt;&gt; CA: Create(object=CaseParticipant(actor=Actor), target=Case)\n        note over CA: Actor becomes participant in case\n    else Reject Invitation\n        A --&gt;&gt; CA: Reject(object=Invite)\n        note over CA: Actor is not participant in case\n    end\n    deactivate A\n    deactivate CA\n    deactivate O</code></pre> <p>CASE_MANAGER routing (PCR-08-007, PCR-08-008)</p> <p>The <code>Invite</code> activity is sent by the CASE_MANAGER, not the Case Owner. The Case Owner triggers the invite, but the CASE_MANAGER MUST be the ActivityStreams <code>actor</code> on the outbound <code>Invite</code>. The <code>attributedTo</code> field on the activity MAY carry the Case Owner's ID to record who initiated it.</p> <p>The invitee MUST address their <code>Accept</code> or <code>Reject</code> reply to the CASE_MANAGER, not directly back to the Case Owner. The CASE_MANAGER is the authoritative recipient of all case-management handshake messages after case creation.</p> <p>Invite vs Add?</p> <p>When a case is first created, the Case Owner and any known participants (e.g., the Reporter) should be automatically added to the case. It's not even necessary for these to be emitted as separate <code>as:Add</code> activities. The <code>as:Create</code> activity for the case can include the Case Owner and any known participants as <code>CaseParticipant</code> objects. See Initializing a Case for more.</p> <p>However, over the lifespan of a case, there may be other actors that were not already involved at the time the case was created, but who should be invited to participate in the case. This is where the <code>as:Invite</code> activity comes in.</p> <p>Avoid bogging down in details</p> <p>Adding a participant to a case involves creating the participant object and a participant status object. As discussed elsewhere, emitting separate <code>as:Create</code> and <code>as:Add</code> events for each of these events is likely overkill.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\n\na[create participant] --&gt; b[create participant status]\nb --&gt; c[add participant status to participant]\nc --&gt; d[add participant to case]</code></pre> <p>Instead, a single <code>as:Create</code> event for the participant, already containing a status object, could be emitted, with the <code>target</code> of the <code>as:Create</code> event as the case object.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\na[create particpant with status] --&gt;|target| b[case]</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/invite_actor/#invite-to-case","title":"Invite to Case","text":"<p>A vendor invites a coordinator to a case.</p> While the most common activities are inviting and adding participants, this section also covers activities for removing participants.</p> <pre><code>flowchart TB\n    subgraph as:Invite \n        RmInviteToCase\n    end\n    subgraph as:Accept\n        RmAcceptInviteToCase\n    end\n    subgraph as:Reject\n        RmRejectInviteToCase\n    end\n    subgraph as:Create\n        RmCreateParticipant\n        RmCreateParticipantStatus\n    end\n    subgraph as:Add\n        AddParticipantToCase\n        AddStatusToParticipant\n    end\n    subgraph as:Remove\n        RemoveParticipantFromCase\n    end\n    start([Start])\n    start --&gt; RmInviteToCase\n    RmInviteToCase --&gt; a{Accept?}\n    a --&gt;|y| RmAcceptInviteToCase\n    a --&gt;|n| RmRejectInviteToCase\n    RmAcceptInviteToCase --&gt; RmCreateParticipant\n\n    RmCreateParticipantStatus --&gt; AddStatusToParticipant\n    RmCreateParticipant --&gt; AddParticipantToCase\n    AddParticipantToCase --&gt; s{Status?}\n    s --&gt;|y| RmCreateParticipantStatus\n    s --&gt;|n| r{Remove?}\n    AddStatusToParticipant --&gt; r\n    r --&gt;|y| RemoveParticipantFromCase\n    r --&gt;|n| s</code></pre> <p>CASE_MANAGER routing (PCR-08-007, PCR-08-008)</p> <p>The <code>Invite</code> in this flow is sent by the CASE_MANAGER (not the Case Owner directly). The Case Owner triggers the invite action, but the CASE_MANAGER MUST be the ActivityStreams <code>actor</code> on the outbound <code>Invite</code> activity. The invited actor MUST send their <code>Accept</code> or <code>Reject</code> reply to the CASE_MANAGER, not directly to the Case Owner. See Inviting an Actor to a Case for the full sequence diagram.</p> <p>Create or Add?</p> <p>There appears to be some logical interchangeability of <code>as:Create</code>  with <code>as:Add</code> since both include a <code>target</code> property that can be used to specify the object to which the new object is being added. We chose to  represent them separately here to acknowledge the difference between creating a new object and adding an existing object to another object, but in an actual implementation it may be acceptable to use either activity for both cases. It seems likely that the general idea should be to use <code>as:Create</code> when creating a new object to  add to another object (as the <code>target</code> of the activity), and <code>as:Add</code> when adding an existing object to another object. </p> <p>Vultron intends to be consistent with however ActivityPub handles this. If the approach described here is inconsistent with ActivityPub, please report it as an issue or  pull While a <code>Create(Report)</code> technically precedes an <code>Offer(Report)</code>, in practice the receiver usually only observes the <code>Offer</code> because the report was created entirely on the sender's side.</p> <p>In other cases the <code>Report</code> may have been created earlier or by a different actor (for example, a platform or intermediary). This object represents comments on a case.</p> <p>Create then Add vs Create with a Target</p> <p>In this documentation, <code>as:Create</code> represents the  creation of a new object, such as a new note or a new status. <code>as:Add</code>  represents the addition of an existing object to another  object, such as adding a status to a case.</p> <p>However, it is likely acceptable within an ActivityPub implementation to use the <code>as:Create</code> activity for both cases, since the <code>as:Create</code> activity includes a <code>target</code> property that can be used to specify the object to which the new object is being added.</p> <p>Sinilarly, it may also be acceptable to use the <code>as:Add</code> activity to represent the creation of a new object, since the Case","text":"<p>This page is not normative</p> <p>This page is not considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>During the course of coordinating a case, an existing case participant might recognize that another actor should be invited to participate in the case. The following mechanisms provide a way for a case participant to suggest that another actor be invited to participate in the case.</p> <p> </p> <p>Why Suggest instead of just Invite?</p> <p>The process described here makes an assumption that there is a case owner who is responsible for coordinating the  case. Participants having the case owner role can in principle just directly invite other actors to participate in  the case, and they might not need the suggestion mechanism described here. However, this mechanism is included to account for the possibilities that:</p> <ul> <li>there could be multiple case owners, and they might not all agree on who should be invited to participate in the    case.</li> <li>a non-case-owner participant might want to suggest that another actor be invited to participate in the case</li> </ul> <p>Of these, the latter is the more likely scenario, but the mechanism described here can be used in either case.    </p> <p>Reasons to Invite other Actors</p> <p>There are many reasons why a case participant might want to suggest another actor to participate in a case. The following are some examples:</p> <ul> <li>A finder, having reported to one vendor, might further discover that the vulnerability is actually in a    third-party library, and suggest inviting the library vendor to participate in the case.</li> <li>A vendor might be a participant in (but not the owner of) a case, and wants to suggest that the case owner   invite a sector-specific coordinator to participate in the case to address critical infrastructure concerns.</li> <li>A reporter participant might suggest a technical expert (for example, a member of a protocol working group) to    include in the case.</li> <li>A coordinator might suggest to the case owner that a large deployer be invited to participat in a case to    address concerns about the impact of deploying a fix for a vulnerability on infrastructure and operations.</li> </ul> <p>Below is a sequence diagram showing the process of suggesting an actor for a case. We used a sequence diagram instead of a flow chart since the process is relatively simple and the sequence diagram is easier to read.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Suggesting an Actor for a Case (ADR-0026 CaseActor-routed)\n---\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor A as Recommender\n    participant CA as CaseActor\n    actor B as Case Owner\n    actor D as Invitee\n    Note over A: Recognize that Actor should be invited\n    A -&gt;&gt; CA: Offer(object=Actor, target=Case)\n    activate CA\n    Note over CA: Record in ledger, assign default roles\n    CA -&gt;&gt; B: Offer(object=CaseParticipant{actor,roles}, target=Case, origin=Offer.id)\n    activate B\n    alt Accept Suggestion\n        B -&gt;&gt; CA: Accept(object=Offer(CaseParticipant))\n        CA -&gt;&gt; A: AcceptActorRecommendation\n        CA -&gt;&gt;+ D: Invite(CaseStub + embargo + roles)\n        note over D: Respond to invitation (not shown)\n        deactivate D\n    else Reject Suggestion\n        B -&gt;&gt; CA: Reject(object=Offer(CaseParticipant))\n        CA -&gt;&gt; A: RejectActorRecommendation\n    end\n    deactivate B\n    deactivate CA</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/suggest_actor/#recommend-actor","title":"Recommend Actor","text":"<p>A participant recommends another actor to the CaseActor by sending an <code>Offer</code> activity with the <code>object</code> property set to the actor being recommended and the <code>target</code> set to the case.
