Definition taken from the CERT Guide to CVD; Vultron uses it unchanged Bug, issue, flaw, weakness Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) A collaborative process where affected parties work together to manage vulnerability remediation and public disclosure Responsible disclosure, coordinated release Multi-Party CVD (MPCVD) CVD process involving three or more independent organizations with different interests and roles Multiparty coordination Report A formal notification of a discovered vulnerability, including technical details and potential impact Submission, notice Case A federated container tracking all parties, state, communications, and embargo agreements related to a specific vulnerability across multiple organizations Issue, coordination event"},{"location":"reference/glossary/#cvd-roles-and-participants","title":"CVD Roles and Participants","text":"Term Definition Aliases to avoid Finder The person or organization that discovers a vulnerability. Not a distinct protocol role per ADR-0078; an actor who discovers and reports holds the Reporter role. Discoverer identity is recorded in Report content or case Note entries. Researcher, discoverer Reporter The person or organization that submits a vulnerability report to affected parties (often the same as Finder) Submitter, notifier Vendor The organization that maintains or supplies the affected product or service Developer, supplier, maintainer Deployer An organization that deploys the Vendor's product and is responsible for applying patches in their own environment (distinct from Vendor) Operator, customer Coordinator A neutral third party (often a national CERT) that facilitates communication and negotiates embargo terms between other parties Mediator, facilitator Participant Any Actor engaged in a Case, holding one or more CVD Roles Stakeholder, party Actor Any URI-identified federated peer (person or organization) in the protocol Agent, endpoint Case Owner The Actor who creates and administers a Case (typically the party seeking vulnerability coordination) Case creator Case Actor The concrete actor the prototype/demo implements to hold <code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code> \u2014 an automated software actor spawned to enact the role and automate its duties (emitting activities, maintaining the canonical ledger). It is a specific identity/label (<code>case-actor</code>, <code>.../actors/case-actor</code>) with no protocol meaning. It is not a synonym for the authority and not an identity to match on: authority, recognition, and routing derive from the <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> role, never from this actor's name or URL, and code MUST NOT compare <code>actor_id</code> against a computed <code>case_actor_id</code> to decide authority (ADR-0088, refining ADR-0041). Name the authority Case Manager (the role holder); use Case Actor only for the prototype actor that happens to hold it. Case service actor, case coordinator, \"the CaseActor authority\" Case Manager The <code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code> role \u2014 the single-writer authority for a case. Whichever Participant holds it is authoritative for the canonical case ledger and case-scoped routing; authority is determined by the role and nothing else (ADR-0088). Often assigned via Offer \u2192 Accept handoff during case creation, and may co-manage embargo negotiations. Protocol-normative prose names the authority the CASE_MANAGER (the role holder), never the CaseActor (the prototype identity). Admin role, management role Case Actor Service The provisioning endpoint (configured as <code>case_actor_service_url</code>) that receives <code>CaseProposal</code>s and spawns the <code>case-actor</code> identities that enact <code>CASE_MANAGER</code>. A hosting/provisioning concern \u2014 distinct from the authority (the role) and from any one Case Actor identity it spawns. Hosting location and URL shape carry no authority signal (ADR-0088). Case actor URL, provisioning service CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) An organization authorized to directly assign CVE IDs; modeled as <code>CVDRole.CVE_NUMBERING_AUTHORITY</code>. A Participant holding this role may assign IDs directly rather than delegating to an external CNA service. CVE authority"},{"location":"reference/glossary/#case-state-model-six-dimensions","title":"Case State Model (Six Dimensions)","text":"<p>The Case State (CS) tracks awareness and readiness across six binary dimensions:</p> Abbreviation Uppercase Lowercase Meaning V/v V v Vendor is aware / unaware F/f F f Fix is ready / not ready D/d D d Fix is deployed / not deployed P/p P p Public is aware / unaware X/x X x Exploit code is public / not public A/a A a Active attacks have been observed / not observed <p>Each transition from lowercase to uppercase represents an event; once uppercase, it cannot revert. A broad port is generic and untyped (e.g., <code>DataLayer</code> with <code>get(table, id)</code>, <code>by_type(type)</code>). What exactly is a process?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Each Participant in a Case runs one Process. A Process maintains a Composite State \u2014 that's a 3-tuple: (Case State, RM State, EM State).\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"So if a Vendor is in the case, they're one Process?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Exactly. Meanwhile, a Coordinator in the same Case is another Process with their own RM state and the same EM state.\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"And they coordinate through Message Types?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Yes. When a Vendor transitions their RM from Valid to Accepted, they send an RA (Report Accepted) Message Type. That Activity carries the RA and is transmitted via the wire protocol. The Coordinator receives it and updates their model of the Vendor's RM State.\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"But that doesn't change the Coordinator's own RM state?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Correct. The RA message is an announcement \u2014 'I accepted the report.' It doesn't command the receiver to do anything. An unresponded Offer is a protocol event we record, but it doesn't create a Participant.\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"What happens to the RM state if a Vendor joins the Case late\u2014after we've already transitioned to PUBLISHED?\"</p> <p>Domain Expert: \"Their Participant Status records RM states from the point they joined onward. The Case Status is separate\u2014it shows the collective state across all parties.\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"And when we send an Activity about a State Transition to all participants, we're not telling them to do the transition\u2014we're informing them that we did it?\"</p> <p>Domain Expert: \"Exactly. An Activity is a state-change notification, not a command. If I send you an Activity saying 'Fix Deployed' (the D event), I'm informing you that my organization deployed the fix. You update your model of the Case State and potentially make your own decisions based on that new information.\"</p>"},{"location":"reference/glossary/#call-out-points-and-capability-shapes-example","title":"Call-Out Points and Capability Shapes Example","text":"<p>Developer: \"The BT has a <code>ReviewAdvisoryDraft</code> node \u2014 what actually runs there?\"</p> <p>Domain Expert: \"That's a Call-Out Point. In the simulator it's a Fuzzer Node that returns SUCCESS or FAILURE probabilistically. In production you wire in a capability \u2014 an Evaluator capability shape \u2014 that reviews the draft and records an Advisory Review Decision.\"</p> <p>Developer: \"What does the BT read from that decision? Several of the modules it names no longer exist, and the semantics-to-pattern mapping shown below as a <code>dict</code> is now the ordered <code>SEMANTIC_REGISTRY</code> list in <code>vultron/semantic_registry/</code>. Read it for the design reasoning, not for current file locations or symbol names.</p> <p>Vultron is designed with the ActivityPub protocol in mind. Most activity in Vultron involves actors exchanging activity messages containing objects.</p> <p>Submitting a Vulnerability Report</p> <p>For example, an actor might create a <code>VulnerabilityReport</code> object and then offer it to another actor, who can then accept, tentatively reject, or  reject the offer.</p> <p>Actors in ActivityPub can be of various types, such as <code>Person</code>, <code>Organization</code>, <code>Group</code>, <code>Application</code>, <code>Service</code>, etc. Each actor has an inbox and an outbox. The inbox is where the actor receives activities, and the outbox is where the actor sends activities.</p> <p>Actor Inboxes and Outboxes</p> <p>For example, if Alice is a <code>Person</code> actor, she has an inbox at <code>https://example.com/users/alice/inbox</code> and an outbox at <code>https://example.com/users/alice/outbox</code>. If Bob is another <code>Person</code> actor, he has his own inbox and outbox.</p> <p>When Alice wants to send an activity to Bob, she creates the activity with the <code>to</code> field set to Bob's actor ID (e.g., <code>https://example.com/users/bob</code>) and places it in her outbox. The ActivityPub server then delivers the activity to Bob's inbox. Bob can then process the activity and respond by sending an activity to his outbox, with the <code>to</code> field set to Alice's actor ID. He can also set the <code>inReplyTo</code> field to reference the original activity from Alice to indicate that it is a response. The ActivityPub server handles the delivery of the activity to Alice's inbox,  and the cycle continues.</p> <p>Scope of Vultron's ActivityPub Implementation</p> <p>However, the Vultron prototype does not implement a full ActivityPub server. Instead, it initially focuses on the core functionality of actors sending activities directly to each other's inboxes. This simplifies the implementation while still demonstrating the core concepts of ActivityPub interactions.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#inbox-handler-architecture","title":"Inbox Handler Architecture","text":"<p>The initial architecture is as follows: An actor has an inbox implemented as a FastAPI endpoint that accepts POST requests containing activity messages. When a message is received, the inbox handler processes the activity and routes it to an appropriate handler based on the activity's semantics.</p> <p>Activity Handling</p> <p>For example, if the activity is an <code>Offer</code> of a <code>VulnerabilityReport</code>, it would be routed to a <code>submit_report</code> handler function, which contains the logic for processing a vulnerability report submission.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#out-of-scope","title":"Out of scope","text":"<p>Authentication, authorization, and server-to-server federation are deferred to future implementation.</p> <p>This design also does not describe what happens inside each handler function; that is left to the specific handler implementations to come later. The focus of this design is on the inbox handler and dispatching logic that routes activities to the appropriate handler functions.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#inbox-handler-process","title":"Inbox Handler Process","text":"<p>The inbox handler process consists of the following steps:</p> <ol> <li>Receive Activity: The inbox endpoint receives a POST request containing an activity message in JSON format.</li> <li>Validate Activity: The inbox endpoint validates the activity message structure to ensure it conforms to the ActivityPub specification.</li> <li>Log Activity: The inbox endpoint logs the received activity message for debugging and auditing purposes.</li> <li>Queue Activity: (only if Validate Activity succeeds) The inbox endpoint places the activity message into an asynchronous processing call to the inbox handler function, allowing the endpoint to respond immediately while the activity is processed in the background.</li> <li>Acknowledge Receipt: The inbox endpoint responds to the POST request with a 200 OK status to acknowledge receipt of the activity message. If the validation failed, it can respond with an appropriate error status (e.g., 400 Bad Request) and log the error.</li> <li>Extract Routing Information: The inbox handler extracts key fields from the activity message (e.g., <code>type</code>, <code>object</code>, <code>to</code>, <code>inReplyTo</code>) to determine routing.    It creates a <code>DispatchEvent</code> header object containing the routing information and attaches the original activity message as the payload.</li> <li>Dispatch Activity: The inbox handler invokes a dispatch function that routes the <code>DispatchEvent</code> object to the appropriate handler function based on the activity's semantic type.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#activity-patterns-and-semantics","title":"Activity Patterns and Semantics","text":"<p>Routing semantics are identified by <code>ActivityPattern</code> objects, which define patterns for matching activity messages to specific enumerated semantic meanings. This decouples the raw activity message structure from the higher-level semantics of the Vultron protocol, allowing raw messages to be translated into meaningful semantics that drive application logic.</p> <p>Defining Activity Patterns</p> <p>An activity pattern for submitting a vulnerability report might be defined as an <code>Offer</code> activity with an object of type <code>VulnerabilityReport</code>.  Responses to that offer follow their own patterns:</p> <pre><code>ReportSubmission = ActivityPattern(\n    activity_=TAtype.OFFER,\n    object_=VOtype.VULNERABILITY_REPORT,\n)\nAckReport = ActivityPattern(activity_=TAtype.READ, object_=ReportSubmission)\nValidateReport = ActivityPattern(\n    activity_=TAtype.ACCEPT, object_=ReportSubmission\n)\nInvalidateReport = ActivityPattern(\n    activity_=TAtype.TENTATIVE_REJECT, object_=ReportSubmission\n)\nCloseReport = ActivityPattern(\n    activity_=TAtype.REJECT, object_=ReportSubmission\n)\n</code></pre> <p>The various <code>*type</code>s are string enumerations defined elsewhere.</p> <p>Mapping Activity Patterns to Semantics</p> <p>The mapping from raw activity message patterns to higher-level semantics is defined as follows:</p> <pre><code>SEMANTICS_ACTIVITY_PATTERNS: dict[MessageSemantics, ActivityPattern] = {\n    MessageSemantics.SUBMIT_REPORT: ap.ReportSubmission,\n    MessageSemantics.ACK_REPORT: ap.AckReport,\n    MessageSemantics.VALIDATE_REPORT: ap.ValidateReport,\n    MessageSemantics.INVALIDATE_REPORT: ap.InvalidateReport,\n    MessageSemantics.CLOSE_REPORT: ap.CloseReport,\n    # ...etc.\n}\n</code></pre> <p>Activity semantics are determined by the <code>type</code> field of the activity message, along with fields such as <code>object</code>, <code>to</code>, and <code>inReplyTo</code>. The dispatch function uses this information to determine which handler function should process the activity.</p> <p>DispatchEvent Object</p> <p>A <code>DispatchEvent</code> object encapsulates the routing information needed by the dispatch function. At the time of writing, the <code>DispatchEvent</code> object is defined as:</p> <pre><code>@dataclass\nclass DispatchEvent:\n    semantic_type: MessageSemantics\n    activity_id: str\n    payload: InboundPayload\n</code></pre>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#dispatch-function","title":"Dispatch Function","text":"<p>The dispatch function uses the <code>semantic_type</code> field of the <code>DispatchEvent</code> to look up the appropriate handler function from a mapping of <code>MessageSemantics</code> to handler functions. The handler function is then invoked with the <code>DispatchEvent</code> object as an argument.</p> <p>Example</p> <p>The following is an example of the <code>ActivityDispatcher</code> Protocol that defines   the interface for dispatching activities:</p> <pre><code>class ActivityDispatcher(Protocol):\n    \"\"\"\n    Protocol for dispatching activities to their corresponding handlers based on message semantics.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def dispatch(self, dispatchable: DispatchEvent) -&gt; None:\n        \"\"\"Dispatches an activity to the appropriate handler based on its semantic type.\"\"\"\n        ...\n</code></pre> <p>On the Modularity of Dispatchers</p> <p>The dispatch function is designed as a Python <code>Protocol</code> to allow for different dispatcher implementations. This provides flexibility in connecting the inbox  handler to specific handler functions for each semantic type. A simple  implementation might use a dictionary mapping from semantic types to handler  functions, while a more complex implementation could involve message queues  or other routing mechanisms.</p> <p>This modularity allows dispatching logic to be extended easily by defining new  <code>ActivityPattern</code>s with corresponding <code>MessageSemantics</code>, then adding new  handler functions to the dispatch mapping. Decoupling routing logic from  handling logic maintains clean separation of concerns and facilitates  future protocol extensions.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#direct-dispatch-implementation","title":"Direct Dispatch Implementation","text":"<p>The first dispatch function implementation uses a simple direct dispatch approach with a dictionary mapping from <code>MessageSemantics</code> to handler functions. The dispatch function looks up the <code>semantic_type</code> from the <code>DispatchEvent</code> object in the mapping and invokes the corresponding handler function with the <code>DispatchEvent</code> as an argument.</p> <p>This direct dispatch implementation is straightforward and allows activities to be handled quickly based on their semantics.</p> <p>Into the Unknown?</p> <p>What happens if an activity is received that does not match any known <code>ActivityPattern</code>?   In this case, the semantic match function can return a special   <code>MessageSemantics.UNKNOWN</code> value, which the dispatch function can handle by   logging an error or ignoring the activity. This gracefully handles   unexpected or malformed activities without crashing the system. This distinction is most prominent in the connections from the Received and Deferred RM states in the two figures above. These differences are the result of the relative timing of the two different decisions they support within a CVD case.</p> <p>The decision to Coordinate (i.e., whether the Coordinator should move from RM Valid to RM Accept  (\\(q^{rm} \\in V \\xrightarrow{a} A\\)) occurs early in the Coordinator's RM process. The SSVC Supplier Engagement decision point is an attempt to capture this information. This early in the process, allowances must be made for Vendors who may not have completed their own validation or  prioritization processes.  Hence, the mapping allows Vendors in any valid yet unclosed state (\\(q^{rm} \\in \\{R,V,A,D\\}\\)) to be categorized as  Active for this decision point.</p> <p>On the other hand, the decision to Publish\u2014a choice that falls entirely within the Coordinator's RM Accepted  state\u2014occurs later, at which time, more is known about each Vendor's level of involvement in the case to that point. They might already have a Fix-Ready (\\(q^{cs} \\in VF \\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\)), or they might be working toward it (i.e., SSVC Cooperative). However, if the Coordinator has reached the point where they are making a publication decision, and the Vendor has  yet to actively engage in the case for whatever reason\u2014as indicated by their failure to reach the RM Accepted state or demonstrate progress toward it by at least getting to RM Valid  (\\(q^{rm} \\in \\{A,V\\}\\))\u2014then they can be categorized as Uncooperative/Unresponsive.</p> <p>SSVC Decision Points and Anticipated Transitions</p> <p>Other SSVC decision points may be informative about which transitions to expect in a case. Implementations of the Vultron Protocol are expected to have their own versioning schemes.</p> <p>Current Version</p> <p>The current version of the Vultron Protocol is</p> <p>2024.4.4.dev6496+gb9388ca98.d20260915</p> <p>Vultron Protocol versions follow Calendar Versioning (CalVer) using the format <code>YYYY.M.Patch</code>, where:</p> <ul> <li> <p><code>YYYY</code> is the four-digit year of the most recent non-patch release.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>M</code> is the month of the most recent non-patch release,     with no zero padding (e.g., <code>1</code>, <code>2</code>, <code>3</code>, ..., <code>12</code>).</p> </li> <li> <p><code>Patch</code> is the patch number for that release.     For the first (or only) release in a given month, the patch number     starts at <code>0</code> and is normally omitted, so <code>2024.4.0</code> and <code>2024.4</code>     denote the same version.</p> </li> </ul> <p>Version increments work as follows:</p> <ul> <li> <p>Significant releases use the current year and month, with the patch     number starting at <code>0</code> (normally omitted).     Example: the first significant release in April 2024 is <code>2024.4</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Patch releases increment the patch number from the most recent     non-patch release, even if the patch is published in a later month or year.     Example: the third small update to <code>2024.4</code> is <code>2024.4.3</code>, even if it     is released in May 2024 or later.</p> </li> </ul> <p>No backward compatibility commitments are made or implied at this stage. The taxonomy of optional, pluggable capability patterns. Each capability shape defines a contract for a specific category of automation that can connect to the behavior engine at a call-out point.</p> <p>Previous name. This concept was previously named \"agent shapes\" or \"coordination agent taxonomy.\" That name was accurate when written. It is now replaced because \"agent\" has acquired strong connotations of LLM-based autonomous systems, which was not the original intent. \"Capability shape\" describes what the concept actually covers: the pattern that a capability takes.</p> <p>The five capability shapes.</p> Shape What it does Connection type Sentinel Independently monitors an external condition; when the condition fires, calls a Vultron trigger endpoint. Not called by the behavior engine. Call-in surface (no call-out point node) Evaluator Receives a situation and a set of options. Returns a structured recommendation. Gates downstream execution. Call-out point Retriever Receives a query. Returns structured facts from an external source. Call-out point Composer Receives context. Generates and records a new content artifact. Call-out point Actuator Receives a trigger. Invokes an external system for a side effect. Confirms success or failure. Produces no content artifact. Call-out point <p>A capability shape defines the contract. A concrete implementation that satisfies the contract is a Vultron-compatible capability of that shape.</p> <p>What is in scope.</p> <ul> <li>The five shapes and their contracts (what each shape accepts and returns)</li> <li>The classification rule for each shape</li> </ul> <p>What is out of scope.</p> <ul> <li>The specific technology used to fulfill a shape (a shape may be fulfilled by a human, an automated script, an LLM, or any other mechanism)</li> <li>The Fuzzer Node \u2014 that is a simulator-layer stub that occupies a call-out point until a real capability is wired in; it is not a capability shape itself</li> </ul> <p>Relationship to other concepts.</p> <ul> <li>Capability shapes are orthogonal to capability sets. They are assignments within a case.</p> <p>Two categories of roles.</p> <p>Process roles define what an actor does within a case and which protocol transitions it is authorized to drive.</p> Role Drive authority Reporter Initiates cases; drives RS (report submission) Vendor Drives its own VFD fix-ready transition (CF) Deployer Drives its own VFD fix-deployed transition (CD) Coordinator Drives case participant management; coordinates multi-party disclosure CNA May directly assign CVE IDs Observer No VFD drive obligations; may report PXA observations <p>Protocol authority roles define what an actor controls in the protocol machinery.</p> Role Protocol authority Case Owner Authoritative decision-maker for a case Case Manager AS actor performing case replica synchronization on behalf of the Case Owner <p>Role assignment.</p> <p>Roles are assigned, not self-declared.</p> <ol> <li>A case starts with a Case Owner (the actor who initiated the case).</li> <li>The Case Owner may delegate the Case Manager role to another actor.</li> <li>The Case Manager designates other actors into process roles.</li> </ol> <p>Self-assignment is not permitted. The <code>as:Actor</code> types represent persistent identities within a larger ActivityPub network, while a <code>CaseParticipant</code> is a contextual identity that associates an actor to a specific <code>VulnerabilityCase</code> object. This distinction allows the Vultron protocol to represent a single actor participating in multiple cases, with discrete roles and statuses within the context of each case.</p> <p>The standard ActivityStreams actor types can be used in Vultron. These include:</p> <ul> <li><code>as:Person</code></li> <li><code>as:Organization</code></li> <li><code>as:Group</code></li> <li><code>as:Service</code></li> <li><code>as:Application</code></li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/activitypub/objects/#other-non-activity-object-types","title":"Other (non-Activity) Object Types","text":"<p>ActivityStreams also includes a number of native object types, including:</p> <ul> <li><code>as:Article</code></li> <li><code>as:Collection</code></li> <li><code>as:CollectionPage</code>, including <code>as:OrderedCollection</code> and <code>as:OrderedCollectionPage</code></li> <li><code>as:Document</code>, including <code>as:Audio</code>, <code>as:Image</code>, and <code>as:Video</code></li> <li><code>as:Event</code></li> <li><code>as:Note</code></li> <li><code>as:Page</code></li> <li><code>as:Place</code></li> <li><code>as:Profile</code></li> <li><code>as:Relationship</code></li> <li><code>as:Tombstone</code></li> </ul> <p><code>as:Note</code> is used to represent comments on a <code>VulnerabilityCase</code>. Instead, it defines a minimal set of properties necessary to support the protocol.</p> <p>The example below shows a <code>VulnerabilityReport</code> object containing a simple text description of a vulnerability in the <code>content</code> property. In a real implementation, the <code>content</code> property may contain any vulnerability report format that can be embedded as part of the JSON object.</p> <p>Examples of what might go into the <code>content</code> property of a <code>VulnerabilityReport</code> object include:</p> <ul> <li>Community-developed Structured formats like CSAF or   CVE JSON</li> <li>Quasi-structured text formats based on templates like the   OWASP Vulnerability Template</li> <li>Proprietary formats used by vendors, coordinators, or finders, such as might be found behind a web form like   CERT/CC's Vulnerability Reporting Form</li> <li>A plain text description of the vulnerability, for example a markdown-formatted text description with section   headings and links to external resources</li> </ul> <p>The format of the <code>content</code> property is deliberately open-ended to allow for flexibility in the types of vulnerability reports that can be represented. The <code>content</code> property SHOULD represent a widely-used structured format whenever possible, since this allows for more automation in the processing of vulnerability reports.</p> <p>Binary attachments (PDF documents, images, audio files, video files) are supported; in those cases, the <code>content</code> property MAY contain a link to the binary file or an embedded encoding. This design allows us to separate the core domain logic from the infrastructure and external interfaces, making the system more modular, testable, and adaptable to different use cases and environments.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Hexagonal Architecture Overview\n---\nflowchart LR\n\nadapters1[Driving Adapters]\nadapters2[Driven Adapters]\nports1[Driving Ports]\nports2[Driven Ports]\ncore{{Core Domain Logic}}\nadapters1 --o ports1\nports1 --o core\ncore --o ports2\nports2 --o adapters2</code></pre> <p>In this architecture:</p> <ul> <li>The Driving Adapters implement the driving ports using specific   technologies (e.g., FastAPI endpoints, CLI commands, etc.) and translate   external inputs into calls to the core domain logic.</li> <li>The Driving Ports define the interfaces through which external actors   (e.g., finders, vendors, coordinators) can interact with the core domain logic. These are the entry points for commands and queries that drive the system's behavior.</li> <li>The Core Domain Logic contains the business rules, policies, and behavior trees that govern how the system operates. It is completely agnostic to how it is accessed or what technologies are used to implement the interfaces.</li> <li>The Driven Ports define the interfaces through which the core domain   logic can interact with external systems (e.g., databases, message queues,   external APIs). These are the exit points for the core to perform actions   that have side effects or require external resources.</li> <li>The Driven Adapters implement the driven ports using specific technologies   (e.g., MongoDB for database access, Celery for task queues, etc.)   and   translate calls from the core domain logic into interactions with external   systems.</li> </ul> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Hexagonal Architecture Details\n---\nflowchart LR\n\nsubgraph driving_adapters [Driving Adapters]\n    direction LR\n    api[API Endpoints]\n    cli[CLI Commands]\n    mcp[MCP Tools]\nend\nsubgraph driving_ports [Driving Ports]\n    direction LR\n    use_cases[Use Cases]\n    commands[Commands]\nend\nsubgraph core [Core Domain Logic]\n    direction LR\n    domain_models[Domain Models]\n    services[Domain Services]\n    behavior_trees[Behavior Trees]\nend\nsubgraph driven_ports [Driven Ports]\n    direction LR\n    database[Database Access]\n    message_queue[Message Queue]\n    external_apis[External APIs]\nend\nsubgraph driven_adapters [Driven Adapters]\n    direction LR\n    mongo[MongoDB Adapter]\n    celery[Celery Adapter]\n    vince[VINCE Adapter]\nend\n\ndriving_adapters --&gt; driving_ports\ndriving_ports --&gt; core\ncore --&gt; driven_ports\ndriven_ports --&gt; driven_adapters</code></pre>"},{"location":"reference/code/api/actor_inbox_handler/","title":"Actor Inbox Handler","text":"<p>The Actor Inbox Handler is the hub that processes incoming activities. It</p> <ul> <li>receives activities sent to an actor's inbox</li> <li>looks up the appropriate handler based on the activity type and object type</li> <li>invokes the handler to process the activity</li> <li>if necessary, delegates to sub-handlers for more specific processing</li> </ul> <p>Some <code>Activity</code>/<code>Object</code> handlers have more than one job</p> <p>For some <code>Activity</code>/<code>Object</code> pairs, there may be multiple jobs to select from. For example, handling an <code>Accept(Invite(VulnerabilityCase))</code> activity is different from handling an <code>Accept(Invite(Embargo))</code> activity. In such cases, the Actor Inbox Handler will invoke a handler for the Accept(Invite) activity, which will then delegate to the appropriate sub-handler based on the details of the offer being accepted.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Actor Inbox Handler\n---\nflowchart TB\n\nsource[client]\nsubgraph Actor\n  inbox\nend\nsubgraph handler\n  func[ActivityType,&lt;br/&gt;ObjectType]\nend\nsource --&gt;|1. Brand and Zafiropulo defined a protocol as follows.</p> <p>Protocol Formally Defined</p> <p>A protocol with \\(N\\) processes is a quadruple:</p> \\[ protocol =      \\Big \\langle          { \\langle S_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1},          { \\langle o_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1},         { \\langle M_{i,j} \\rangle}^N_{i,j=1},         { succ }     \\Big \\rangle\\] <p>Where</p> <ul> <li> <p>\\(N\\) is a positive integer representing the number of processes.</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(\\langle S_i \\rangle_{i=1}^N\\) are \\(N\\) disjoint finite sets (\\(S_i\\) represents the set of states of process \\(i\\)).</p> </li> <li> <p>Each \\(o_i\\) is an element of \\(S_i\\) representing the initial state of process \\(i\\).</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(\\langle M_{ij} \\rangle_{i,j=1}^N\\) are \\(N^2\\) disjoint finite sets with \\(M_{ii}\\) empty for all \\(i\\). \\(M_{ij}\\) represents the messages that can be sent from process \\(i\\) to process \\(j\\),</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(succ\\) is a partial function mapping for each \\(i\\) and \\(j\\), $\\(S_i \\times M_{ij} \\rightarrow S_i \\textrm{ and } S_i \\times M_{ji} \\rightarrow S_i\\)$ \\(succ(s,x)\\) is the state entered after a process transmits or receives message \\(x\\) in state \\(s\\). It is a transmission if \\(x\\) is from \\(M_{ij}\\) and a reception if \\(x\\) is from \\(M_{ji}\\).</p> </li> </ul> <p>Global State Formally Defined</p> <p>The global state of a protocol given by the above is a pair \\(\\langle S, C \\rangle\\), where</p> <ul> <li> <p>\\(S\\) is an \\(N\\)-tuple of states \\(\\langle s_1,\\dots,s_N \\rangle\\) with each \\(s_i\\) representing the current state of process \\(i\\).</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(C\\) is an \\(N^2\\)-tuple \\(\\langle c_{1,1},\\dots, c_{1,N}, c_{2,1}, \\dots \\dots, c_{N,N} \\rangle\\), where each \\(c_{i,j}\\) is a sequence of messages from \\(M_{i,j}\\). The message sequence \\(c_{i,j}\\) represents the contents of the channel from process \\(i\\) to \\(j\\). (Note that \\(c_{i,j}\\) is empty when \\(i = j\\) since processes are presumed to not communicate with themselves.)</p> </li> </ul> <p>Each of these is detailed below or in subsequent pages:</p> <ul> <li>\\(N\\) below</li> <li>\\({ \\langle S_i \\rangle}^N_{i=1}\\), and \\({ \\langle o_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1}\\) in States,</li> <li>\\({ \\langle M_{i,j} \\rangle }^N_{i,j=1}\\) in Message Types,</li> <li>\\({ succ }\\) in Transition Functions</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/formal_protocol/#number-of-processes","title":"Number of Processes","text":"<p>The processes in an MPCVD case represent the different Participants in their roles (Reporter, Vendor, Coordinator, Deployer, and Observer). This is a normative section of the documentation.</p> <p>The States page identified four main roles in the MPCVD process:</p> <ul> <li>Finder/Reporter</li> <li>Vendor</li> <li>Coordinator</li> <li>Deployer</li> </ul> <p>This page examines the messages passed between them. Revisiting the definitions from the Formal Protocol Introduction:</p> <p>Formalism</p> <p>\\(\\langle M_{ij} \\rangle_{i,j=1}^N\\) are \\(N^2\\) disjoint finite sets with \\(M_{ii}\\) empty for all \\(i\\): \\(M_{ij}\\) represents the messages that can be sent from process \\(i\\) to process \\(j\\).</p> <p>The message types in the Vultron Protocol arise primarily from the following principle taken directly from the CVD Guide:</p> <p>Avoid Surprise</p> <p>As with most situations in which multiple parties are engaged in a potentially stressful and contentious negotiation, surprise tends to increase the risk of a negative outcome. The importance of clearly communicating expectations across all parties involved in a CVD process cannot be overemphasized. If we expect cooperation between all parties and stakeholders, we should do our best to match their expectations of being \"in the loop\" and minimize their surprise. Publicly disclosing a vulnerability without coordinating first can result in panic and an aversion to future cooperation from Vendors and Finders alike. CVD promotes continued cooperation and increases the likelihood that future vulnerabilities will also be addressed and remedied.</p> <p>That principle condenses into the following protocol recommendation:</p> <p>Participants whose state changes in the RM, EM, or CVD State Models SHOULD send a message to other Participants for each transition.</p> <p>If you are looking for a one-sentence summary of the entire Vultron Protocol, that was it.</p> <p>State Transitions</p> <ul> <li>RM state transitions \\(\\Sigma^{rm} = \\{ r,v,a,i,d,c\\}\\)</li> <li>EM state transitions \\(\\Sigma^{em} = \\{ p,a,r,t\\}\\)</li> <li>CVD state transitions \\(\\Sigma^{cs} = \\{\\mathbf{V},\\mathbf{F},\\mathbf{D},\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{X},\\mathbf{A}\\}\\)</li> </ul> <p>As a reminder, those transitions are shown at right.</p> <p>The specific circumstances when each message should be emitted are addressed in Transitions; but first, the message types this recommendation implies are introduced here. However, because of the Role-specific limits just described, this overcounts the possible states significantly. A tighter bound is possible. Ignoring transient states while Participants converge on a consistent view of the global state of a case drastically reduces the state space for an MPCVD case. Why? There are two reasons:</p> <ol> <li> <p>Because they represent facts about the outside world, the eight     \\(\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot pxa \\rightarrow \\cdot\\cdot\\cdot PXA\\) CS substates are global to the case, not     to individual Participants. The Status column states the kind of relationship:</p> Status Meaning <code>direct</code> One shorthand maps to exactly one wire activity. <code>collapse</code> Several shorthands share one wire activity. Multiple shorthands appear in a single row; the Discriminator column names the payload field (or context) that distinguishes them. <code>expansion</code> One shorthand is realized by several wire activities. The same shorthand appears in more than one row. <code>evolved</code> The shorthand's purpose is served by a mechanism partitioned on a different axis (fault reporting or cumulative acknowledgement), not by a dedicated wire activity. <code>\u2014</code> The wire activity has no formal shorthand counterpart. <p>Reading the many-to-many relationship from a table:</p> <ul> <li>Multiple shorthands in one row is a collapse \u2014 for example <code>CP CX CA</code>   ride a single <code>Add(CaseStatus)</code>, discriminated by <code>pxa_state</code>.</li> <li>One shorthand across multiple rows is an expansion \u2014 for example <code>EP</code>   spans four embargo wire activities.</li> </ul> <p>The <code>evolved</code> shorthands (<code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code>, <code>CE</code>, <code>GE</code>, <code>EK</code>, <code>CK</code>, <code>GK</code>) have no dedicated wire activity. Faults are conveyed by <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code>, <code>as:Reject</code>, or <code>Create(Note)</code>, partitioned by failure mode. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>The Vultron Protocol does not make its appearance in uncharted territory, where no existing CVD systems or processes exist. Rather, it is offered as an improvement to interactions among humans, systems, and business processes that already perform MPCVD around the world every day. Thus, for adoption to occur, it will be necessary to map existing systems and processes into the semantics (and eventually, the syntax) of whatever protocol emerges as a descendant of this proposal.</p> <p>Combined with the abstract case class model, an ontology (e.g., using OWL) can accelerate the semantic interoperability between independent Participant processes and tools that this effort set out to improve.</p> <p>A few OWL ontology files describe the Vultron protocol. The combination of both labels MUST uniquely identify the open failure issue for a specific workflow, enabling the composite action to find and update rather than duplicate. <code>CISEC-05-004</code> SHOULD A CI verification test SHOULD confirm that every qualifying workflow (push to <code>main</code> or <code>schedule</code> trigger) includes the <code>.github/actions/notify-failure</code> composite action step. <code>CISEC-05-005</code> SHOULD A workflow triggered on the <code>issues: labeled</code> event SHOULD enforce that the <code>ci:main-failure</code> label is bot-managed: if <code>github.actor</code> is not <code>github-actions[bot]</code>, the label MUST be removed immediately. This prevents label spoofing that could suppress failure notification or create false alerts.The <code>ci:main-failure</code> label is the deduplication key used by the composite action to find and update an existing failure issue rather than creating a new one. If a human or external actor applies the label manually, the signal is corrupted \u2014 the action may comment on an unrelated issue or fail to file a new one. Bot-only enforcement keeps the alerting signal reliable. <code>CISEC-05-006</code> MUST The failure-conditioned notify step (CISEC-05-001) MUST NOT file a failure issue when the run was cancelled. A step keyed on the GitHub Actions <code>failure()</code> status function already satisfies this, because <code>failure()</code> is false on cancellation. A step keyed on the <code>needs.*.result</code> aggregate MUST pair the failure check with an explicit cancellation exclusion, i.e. <code>contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') &amp;&amp; !contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled')</code>, and MUST NOT file on cancellation directly (e.g. via <code>&amp;#124;&amp;#124; contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled')</code>).A push-to-<code>main</code> run cancelled by the concurrency group (superseded by a newer merge) is not an actual CI failure \u2014 a newer run is authoritative and will file or close as appropriate. Two ways a cancelled run otherwise registers as a failure: (1) a guard that files on cancellation directly (e.g. <code>&amp;#124;&amp;#124; contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled')</code>), and (2) a cancelled upstream job that leaves a downstream job to hard-fail on a missing artifact (#3249), laundering the cancellation into a <code>failure</code> result in the <code>needs.*.result</code> aggregate. The <code>failure()</code> status function is immune to both; the <code>needs.*.result</code> aggregate is not, so it needs the explicit <code>!contains(..., 'cancelled')</code> guard. This mirrors the close-step guard (CISEC-05-002), which already excludes cancellation. Rejecting atomically does not license reporting a single reason: no partial progress was accepted, so a caller told one reason at a time gains nothing from the round trip.Atomicity governs what is written; diagnostic completeness governs what is reported. The two are independent, and conflating them produced a fix-one-resubmit loop on the add-participant-status trigger path (ISSUE-2112). <code>EH-07-002</code> MUST When a validation boundary reports multiple violations, each violation MUST be classified as root or derived. A rule reading a single dimension is always root. A rule reading more than one dimension is derived when any dimension it reads already carries a single-dimension violation, and root otherwise. Dimension overlap is a proxy for the real test, which is remediation: a violation is derived when the remediation the caller is expected to apply to the overlapping single-dimension violation also clears it. The proxy holds only while that premise does. For a transition fault the expected remediation is asserting a legal value, which clears the entailment that read the illegal one. For a role gate the expected remediation is withdrawing the assertion, not acquiring the role \u2014 a participant does not hold a dimension it has no role for at all (a non-DEPLOYER's <code>d</code> is absent, not initial; ADR-0075) and an actor cannot grant itself a role. Any rule family added later whose expected remediation is neither of those MUST be checked against the remediation test before relying on the overlap proxy.One bad dimension frequently entails further violations, so unranked thoroughness degrades into a wall of errors that one fix clears most of. The classification test is dimension overlap rather than a rule-to-rule dependency graph, so a newly added rule is classified correctly by construction and the labelling cannot go stale. The root multi-dimension case is the informative one: every dimension moved legally on its own and the combination is impossible. The remediation premise is stated normatively above because it is load-bearing and was previously left implicit: three separate reviewers read the overlap rule as a pure graph property, concluded a role gate mislabels its entailments, and built a repro that put a participant on a dimension it had no role for \u2014 a state ADR-0075 makes unreachable. The finding dissolved each time, but only after re-deriving the domain premise the requirement never stated. Refines: CM-23-006 <code>CM-23-011</code> MUST When the CASE_MANAGER receives <code>Leave(VulnerabilityCase)</code> from the Case Owner while the case still holds an active embargo (<code>active_embargo</code> is non-None and the current EM state is <code>EM.ACTIVE</code> or <code>EM.REVISE</code>), it MUST decline the closure with an <code>as:Reject</code> response (\"received and understood but declined\", MSM-05-001) and MUST NOT execute the CM-23-002 closure sequence (no participant advances to <code>RM.CLOSED</code>; no <code>case_fully_closed</code> entry is emitted). Declining the close does NOT itself terminate the embargo \u2014 the embargo remains active until terminated through the normal EM path. This is the terminal, case-global counterpart to the participant-scoped VP-13-005 (participants SHOULD NOT close while embargoed) and VP-13-009 (a participant close while others remain engaged does not auto-terminate the embargo): owner-close ends the case for everyone, so the soft participant-level guidance is raised to a hard case-actor refusal.Owner-close is a hard, terminal write boundary (ADR-0085): the CASE_MANAGER then accepts no further external ledger writes. VP-13-009 keeps an embargo alive across a participant close only while others remain engaged; owner-close leaves none and no authority to lift it, so an embargo left active could never be discharged. Refusing the premature close forces an explicit terminate-then-close ordering. <code>Leave</code> is understood but declined \u2014 hence <code>as:Reject</code>, not <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code> (MSM-05-001). Refines: CM-23-002Refines: VP-13-005 <code>CM-23-012</code> MUST Leave(VulnerabilityCase) advances only the leaving actor's own RM state to RM.CLOSED, regardless of which RM rung that actor currently holds (START, RECEIVED, VALID, ACCEPTED, DEFERRED, or INVALID). Case closure MUST NOT advance any non-leaving (\"bystander\") participant's RM state: on owner Leave, only the Case Owner and the CASE_MANAGER advance to RM.CLOSED (CM-23-002); every other participant MUST retain its last RM state. The characterization of owner-close as ending \"the case for everyone\" (CM-23-011) refers to the case-level write boundary \u2014 the CASE_MANAGER accepts no further external ledger entries (ADR-0085) \u2014 and MUST NOT be read as a directive to force each remaining participant's RM dimension to RM.CLOSED.A participant's RM state is the self-declaratory record of how that participant handled the report (ADR-0084). A Leave is that participant's own authoritative closure act, so advancing the leaving actor to RM.CLOSED regardless of rung is legitimate self-declaration, not an externally imposed jump \u2014 which is why the RM source\u2192dest adjacency rule (RM.CLOSED reachable by adjacency only from ACCEPTED/INVALID/DEFERRED) is intentionally overridden at the leave/close write sites. A bystander that never sent Leave has made no closure declaration; forcing its RM to RM.CLOSED would fabricate a declaration it never made. Implements: CP-05-001 <code>CP-09-002</code> MUST When the CASE_MANAGER creates the <code>VulnerabilityCase</code> on proposal acceptance, it MUST add the report receiver as a <code>CASE_OWNER</code> participant at <code>RM.RECEIVED</code> and the reporter as a participant at <code>RM.ACCEPTED</code> in the CASE_MANAGER's DataLayer.The receiver's replica is seeded from the embedded participant objects in <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code>.  If participants are absent at emission time the replica starts with no participant records and downstream operations that require them (e.g. embargo consent, role guards) fail.  Hard-coding <code>CVDRole.VENDOR</code> for the receiver additionally mislabels coordinators, which makes VFD fix-lifecycle checks demand a fix they never produce. Refines: CP-09-001 <code>CP-09-006</code> MUST The report receiver and reporter participant records MUST be created in the CASE_MANAGER's DataLayer before the CASE_MANAGER emits <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code> to the receiver.The receiver's replica is seeded from participant objects embedded in <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code>; participants absent at emission time leave the replica without the records required for role guards and embargo consent. Refines: CP-09-002 <code>CP-09-007</code> MUST Any additional CVD roles the report receiver holds MUST come from <code>ActorConfig.default_case_roles</code> (CFG-07-002).Explicit role configuration is the only reliable source; a report receiver may be a coordinator rather than a vendor, so role inference is unsound. Refines: CP-09-002 <code>CP-09-008</code> MUST NOT Additional CVD roles for the report receiver MUST NOT be inferred.Inferring roles (e.g. hard-coding <code>CVDRole.VENDOR</code>) mislabels coordinators and causes VFD fix-lifecycle checks to demand a fix they never produce. Refines: CP-09-002 <code>CP-09-003</code> MUST The CASE_MANAGER MUST initialize the default embargo for the new case before emitting <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code>.Embargo state is protocol-significant.  Deferring initialization to the vendor or to a later message would produce a window in which embargo-gated operations are undefined (ADR-0041). Refines: CP-09-001 <code>CP-09-004</code> MUST The <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code> activity emitted by the CASE_MANAGER MUST embed participant objects inline (not as bare ID strings) so that the receiving vendor's <code>CreateCaseReceivedUseCase</code> can seed its local participant records without a DataLayer round-trip to the CASE_MANAGER.<code>_store_embedded_participants</code> and <code>EnsureReporterParticipantAtAcceptedNode</code> parse embedded participant objects.  Bare IDs produce empty participant records on the vendor's replica, causing role-guard failures for operations that require <code>CASE_OWNER</code> or <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> checks. Refines: CP-09-002 <code>CP-09-005</code> MUST NOT The receiving vendor MUST NOT create a <code>VulnerabilityCase</code> object in its own DataLayer before receiving <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code> from the CASE_MANAGER. This was the root cause of <code>WritePrologueLedgerEntriesNode</code> (Issue #1688) and of Issue #1767 (ADR-0041). PEC state answers the question: \"has this participant explicitly accepted or rejected the current active embargo?\" Unlike RM state (self-reported by the participant) and VF/D state (self-reported by vendor/deployer), PEC state is set by the CASE_MANAGER (CM-28-003) based on observed participant behavior \u2014 incoming Accept/Reject wire activities, timer-enforced lapses, and cascades from shared EM state changes. The local value MUST be carried forward for that dimension; all other dimensions are applied as the entry describes them. *Monotonic visibility (see notes/sync-ledger-replication.md). The Case Actor is authoritative for which transition happened, but a replayed, reordered, or divergent entry would otherwise un-see progress the replica has already observed. Lateral moves at the same rank (<code>VALID</code> &lt;-&gt; <code>INVALID</code>) are re-adjudication, not regression, and are applied unchanged. * <code>RSH-05-008</code> SHOULD The <code>em</code> dimension SHOULD NOT be adjudicated at StatusAdoptionGate; embargo state belongs to EmbargoTeardownAuthorizationGate (<code>add_case_status_tree</code>). *EM is per-case rather than per-participant and its authorization gate is the EmbargoTeardownAuthorizationGate (RSH-02-001). Adjudicating it in the StatusAdoptionGate guard would duplicate \u2014 and could contradict \u2014 EmbargoTeardownAuthorizationGate's decision. * <code>RSH-05-009</code> MUST Adjudicating a received status MUST NOT change the shape of the <code>payload_snapshot.object</code> it records: the entry MUST carry the same wire fields an unadjudicated entry for the same activity would carry, with only the adjudicated dimension values rewritten. *Every replica and the case-ledger invariant harness read the snapshot's flat wire aliases (<code>rmState</code>, <code>vfdState</code>, <code>emConsentState</code>, <code>cvdRole</code>) and its nested <code>caseStatus</code> (CLP-07-001, CM-18-006). A whole-object replacement built in <code>vultron.core</code> would emit core dimension objects (<code>rm: {state}</code>) and silently drop every field the guard never adjudicated, because core MUST NOT import <code>vultron.wire</code> to convert (ADR-0009, ADR-0017). Publishing a field patch instead makes shape preservation structural rather than a property the guard has to remember to maintain. * <code>RSH-05-010</code> MUST A producer of <code>ledger_payload_object_override</code> MUST write <code>None</code> to the key unconditionally at the start of every tick \u2014 before any early return \u2014 so that a stale value from a previous execution cannot bleed into the current one. *The py_trees blackboard is process-global. <code>BTBridge.execute_with_setup</code> does not reset application-level keys between runs, so a producer that only writes on its active path leaves the key at its previous value on every no-op tick. <code>CommitCaseLedgerEntryNode</code> would then apply that stale patch to a different payload snapshot. BT-17-003. * <code>RSH-05-011</code> MUST A producer of <code>ledger_payload_object_override</code> MUST include a <code>producer_type</code> field in the override dict. The required shape is <code>{\"object_id\": &lt;id&gt;, \"producer_type\": &lt;str&gt;, \"fields\": {&lt;wire alias&gt;: &lt;value&gt;}}</code>. *Multiple producers are anticipated (ISSUE-2256 adds EM adjudication in <code>EmbargoTeardownAuthorizationGate</code> as a second producer). Naming the source node in the dict enables targeted audit logging and per-producer diagnostics without out-of-band context. RSH-05-014 uses <code>producer_type</code> to emit a warning on unrecognized producers without failing the commit. * <code>RSH-05-012</code> MUST The <code>fields</code> value of <code>ledger_payload_object_override</code> MUST contain only wire alias keys recognized by <code>CommitCaseLedgerEntryNode</code>. Publishing an unrecognized key is a protocol error. *The consumer hard-fails on any unrecognized alias (RSH-05-013). An unknown alias applied to the canonical snapshot would abort the commit, blocking the receive-side BT. Declaring this as a producer obligation means callers can validate at construction time rather than catching a runtime failure. * <code>RSH-05-013</code> MUST <code>CommitCaseLedgerEntryNode</code> MUST raise a hard failure \u2014 not a warning \u2014 if the <code>fields</code> dict of <code>ledger_payload_object_override</code> contains a key that is not a recognized wire alias for the snapshot object type. *An unrecognized alias applied to the canonical snapshot would silently add unexpected content to the hash-chained ledger entry, which every replica and the invariant harness would then apply. Data integrity requires a hard stop; the correct response is to fix the producer (RSH-05-012), not to log and continue. * <code>RSH-05-014</code> SHOULD <code>CommitCaseLedgerEntryNode</code> SHOULD emit a WARNING when <code>ledger_payload_object_override</code> carries an unrecognized <code>producer_type</code> value, and MUST NOT fail the commit on that basis alone. *An unrecognized <code>producer_type</code> may indicate a newer node type operating against an older consumer. Logging preserves auditability without blocking a structurally valid override. Field-name validation (RSH-05-013) is the data-integrity guard; <code>producer_type</code> is an audit hint only. * <code>RSH-05-015</code> MUST A CASE_MANAGER receiving an <code>Add(CaseStatus, Case)</code> MUST adjudicate the EM and PXA dimensions of the reported case status independently. An unacceptable value in one dimension MUST NOT cause the value reported in the other dimension to be discarded. *EM and PXA are independent state machines within CaseStatus (parallel to RM, VFD, EM, PXA in ParticipantStatus). A value that is unacceptable in EM carries no information about PXA and vice versa. Discarding the whole snapshot destroys state the receiver has no grounds to refuse. Liberal accept (ISSUE-2229): accept everything acceptable. * <code>RSH-05-016</code> MUST When an EM or PXA dimension of a received <code>CaseStatus</code> is refused, the receiver MUST record the case's current value for that dimension alongside the accepted value from the other dimension, as a single <code>CaseStatus</code>. *The recorded status must remain a coherent snapshot of the receiver's view of the case. Omitting the refused dimension would leave it undefined; recording the asserted value would adopt a claim the receiver just refused. This is the CaseStatus parallel to RSH-05-002 for ParticipantStatus. * <code>RSH-05-017</code> MUST A received <code>CaseStatus</code> in which every refused dimension leaves the resulting snapshot indistinguishable from the case's current state MUST be refused in full: nothing is appended and no canonical ledger entry is committed. *Such an assertion carries no acceptable information. Appending it would grow the case's status history and the hash chain without recording any state change. This is the CaseStatus parallel to RSH-05-005 for ParticipantStatus. * <code>RSH-05-018</code> MUST When adjudicating the EM dimension of a received <code>Add(CaseStatus)</code>, the receiver MUST accept the asserted EM state if and only if it is identical to the current EM state or it is a valid EM state-machine transition from the current EM state, as determined by <code>is_valid_em_transition()</code>. Any other asserted EM value MUST be refused and the current EM value carried forward (RSH-05-016). *EM follows a directed state machine (NO_EMBARGO \u2192 PROPOSED \u2194 ACTIVE \u2194 REVISE \u2192 EXITED). Out-of-order or backward EM assertions do not correspond to legal protocol events; applying them would corrupt the canonical EM state shared by all participants. Using <code>is_valid_em_transition()</code> as the acceptance predicate ensures only structurally valid EM transitions are applied. * <code>RSH-05-019</code> MUST When adjudicating the PXA dimension of a received <code>Add(CaseStatus)</code>, the receiver MUST accept the asserted PXA state if and only if it is identical to the current PXA state or it is a monotone forward move from the current PXA state, as determined by <code>is_monotonic_pxa_forward()</code>. Any other asserted PXA value MUST be refused and the current PXA value carried forward (RSH-05-016). *PXA state is monotone: bits only advance from unaware to aware (p\u2192P, x\u2192X, a\u2192A) and never reverse. The received-side filter uses the weaker <code>is_monotonic_pxa_forward()</code> check \u2014 not the strict single-step adjacency <code>is_valid_pxa_transition()</code> that applies to local write nodes (CSB-16-002) \u2014 because a remote peer may have observed multiple PXA events between messages and report a combined advance that skips intermediate steps. Applying the strict check would refuse a valid multi-step advance from a peer that simply missed delivering earlier messages. * <code>RSH-05-020</code> MUST After adjudicating each dimension of a received <code>Add(ParticipantStatus, CaseParticipant)</code> independently, the receiver MUST evaluate the cross-machine entailments (RM\u2194VF and RM\u2194D per CSB-18-001, VF\u2194D per CSB-17-001) against the effective \u2014 post-adjudication \u2014 state. For each violated entailment the receiver MUST refuse the dimension whose asserted value the sender moved, carrying the participant's current value for it forward (RSH-05-002), and MUST NOT report as refused a dimension the sender omitted or restated unchanged. The receiver MUST evaluate the same entailment set the emit path evaluates. Per-dimension adjudication cannot see a claim that is impossible only in combination: a fix that is ready or deployed entails a report the participant has already accepted, and a deployed fix entails a ready one. Before this requirement the receive path composed only VF\u2194D, so an assertion the actor would have refused to emit was accepted, recorded, hash-chained and replicated to every participant when it arrived from a peer instead (ISSUE-2906). Refusing the dimension that moved* is what makes the refusal effective rather than cosmetic. VF\u2194D constrains a pair, so either side can be the offending claim; refusing the incumbent side carries its value straight back, which leaves the impossible combination recorded while reporting a refusal that changed nothing. Evaluating against the effective state matters for the <code>vf</code>\u2192<code>d</code> chain: a refused or carried-forward <code>vf</code> must not license the <code>d</code> the sender paired it with (ISSUE-2893). It is not a tightening for <code>rm</code> \u2014 <code>rm</code> is refused only when the asserted value is not a forward move, so the carried value always ranks at or above the asserted one on the RM progress scale, and <code>RM_STATES_CONSISTENT_WITH_FIX</code> is exactly the top of that scale. Requiring one shared evaluator rather than two equivalent ones is what keeps the emit and receive paths from silently diverging again. This is narrower than refusing a multi-step VF or D advance, which remains legal on the received path (CSB-16-001): the entailments refuse claims that no sequence of events could produce, not claims that skipped an intermediate report. * Refines: RSH-05-001 <code>RSH-05-021</code> MUST When applying an <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> for an <code>add_participant_status_to_participant</code> event, the behavior tree MUST evaluate the composite-state entailments (RM\u2194VF and RM\u2194D per CSB-18-001, VF\u2194D per CSB-17-001) against the effective participant state from the entry. If any entailment is violated the tree MUST NOT apply the status update, and MUST guarantee emission of <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code> with failure class <code>StatusAssertionRefused/ImpossibleState</code> to the CASE_MANAGER as a guaranteed side-effect of the failure path (tree-structural guarantee, not node-level side effect). A CASE_MANAGER that is buggy or hostile can commit an entry whose participant state violates <code>composite_state_violations()</code> \u2014 the same entailment set the emit and receive paths already enforce. Without this check, every replica silently adopts an impossible combination: the same actor would have refused to emit* the value, yet accepts it when the CASE_MANAGER broadcasts it. Silence is the specific problem: the contradiction is only discoverable by reading devlogs. Using <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code> rather than <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> avoids triggering a CASE_MANAGER replay loop \u2014 the committed entry cannot be uncommitted, so replaying it would produce the same refusal indefinitely. <code>ProcessingFault</code> is the right signal for semantic invalidity (ASK-07-001). The failure class <code>StatusAssertionRefused/ImpossibleState</code> is a URI sub-path of <code>StatusAssertionRefused</code>, so a consumer that understands the parent class recognises this as a narrower form of the same fault. The tree-structural guarantee (rather than node-level fault emission) keeps the apply node a pure domain check (returns FAILURE on violation) and the emission a composable side-effect, consistent with protocol-significant behavior living in the tree (BTND-01). * Refines: RSH-05-001Depends on: RSH-05-007 <code>RSH-05-022</code> MUST When <code>FilterParticipantStatusDimensionsNode</code> returns <code>FAILURE</code> for an <code>Add(ParticipantStatus, CaseParticipant)</code> (i.e. the assertion is wholly refused because the filtered status is indistinguishable from the participant's current state), the inbox processing pipeline MUST surface this as a <code>rejected</code> <code>InboxOutcome</code> rather than <code>202 Accepted / processed</code>. Participants exchange asynchronous messages and track the case across four dimensions of shared state, realized as five state machines. Any number of organizations may take part in a single case.</p> <p>Coordination is scoped to the case rather than to a system: the case-management role is held per case, and different cases may be managed by different actors. No single service holds every case. Within a case, one participant holds write authority over the case's shared state, so that concurrent claims resolve to one answer.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#1-introduction-i","title":"1. Introduction [I]","text":""},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#11-background-and-motivation","title":"1.1 Background and Motivation","text":"<p>A vulnerability divides the world into two sets: those who know about it, and those who do not. From the moment of discovery, every party in the knowing set repeatedly answers two questions. What should it do next, and who else needs to know what, and when? Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) continues until the answers are \"nothing\" and \"nobody\".</p> <p>Multi-Party CVD (MPCVD) is CVD involving three or more independent organizations with different interests and roles. The shapes vary. A reporter may go to one vendor, which discovers that other vendors ship the same component. A reporter may go to a coordinator, which finds and notifies the affected vendors. A reporter may go to a vendor and a coordinator at once. What the cases have in common is that the set of participants grows after coordination has begun, each vendor works to its own timeline, and the parties must agree when disclosure happens.</p> <p>Each of those organizations usually already runs its own vulnerability tracking system. The coordination problem is therefore not only one of people talking to each other; it is one of separate systems needing to stay consistent about a shared case. That is the problem Vultron addresses.</p> <p>Email carries the content of a CVD case but records none of its state. No participant can see which vendors have read the report, which have agreed to an embargo, or in what order events occurred. Adding a party mid-case means re-sending the history by hand, and nothing detects the gap if that fails. Vultron gives each of these an explicit, machine-checkable representation: report status per participant (\u00a76), embargo agreement per participant (\u00a79), and an ordered case ledger that every participant replicates (\u00a75.4).</p> <p>Embargo timing is worth noting early. In practice the first two parties to a case establish the initial embargo, and it carries forward as further participants join and agree to it. Establishing terms early is generally easier than negotiating them once many parties are already involved.</p> <p>The protocol tracks coordination state across four dimensions: the report lifecycle (RM), the embargo (EM), what is known about the vulnerability (CS), and each participant's agreement to the embargo (PEC). Because CS is a compound of two independent axes, an implementation runs five state machines (\u00a73.3). Messages are ActivityStreams 2.0 Activities delivered over HTTP. Delivery is asynchronous: no exchange requires both parties to be available at the same moment.</p> <p>Who this specification is for</p> <p>This specification is written for implementers building software that takes part in Vultron cases, and for reviewers assessing whether an implementation conforms.</p> <p>It assumes familiarity with coordinated vulnerability disclosure as a practice \u2014 reporters, vendors, coordinators, embargoes, CVE IDs. It does not assume prior knowledge of Vultron. Where it relies on an external specification, it says so and cites it (\u00a71.3).</p> <p>See also</p> <ul> <li>CVD as a Coordination Problem</li> <li>What Does Success Mean in CVD?</li> <li>The Need for Interoperability</li> <li>CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#12-design-goals","title":"1.2 Design Goals","text":"<p>Actor-local state. Each participant keeps its own replica of the case, assembled from the messages it has received. A participant is the authority on its own report and fix status. What the case as a whole asserts \u2014 its embargo state and what is publicly known \u2014 has a single writer, the participant holding the Case Manager role, so that concurrent claims resolve to one answer (\u00a75.4.1).</p> <p>Coordination is scoped to a case, not to a system. The Case Manager role is held per case, and different cases may be managed by different actors. The protocol does not require every case to pass through one shared service. It does require, within a case, that shared state have one writer.</p> <p>Informative: how centralized is this?</p> <p>Two readings should both be avoided.</p> <p>Vultron does not require a single central authority holding all cases. Any actor able to satisfy the Case Manager role can manage a case, and the role is transferable (\u00a711.3).</p> <p>Equally, Vultron as it stands is not a fully decentralized design. Within a case there is one writer, and its availability bounds how fast the case can progress. The current reference implementation goes further and runs a dedicated service actor per case.</p> <p>The protocol leaves more distributed realizations open \u2014 a shared ledger among peers, for instance \u2014 and this version does not specify one (\u00a75.4.2).</p> <p>Asynchronous, message-driven coordination. Participants announce their own transitions rather than being polled, and no exchange requires two parties to be online at once. A participant that is temporarily unreachable does not block the others from making progress.</p> <p>Extensible role model. Roles are not exclusive: a participant may hold Reporter, Vendor and Coordinator at the same time (\u00a73.5). Roles that confer protocol authority are kept separate from roles that describe what an actor does in the world, so the two can vary independently.</p> <p>Interoperable wire format. ActivityStreams 2.0 is the normative wire vocabulary. Reusing an established open standard means the message format is already specified and already understood, and it leaves ActivityPub-based delivery available as a path to potentially compatible tooling. Vultron has not yet been integrated with the wider ActivityPub ecosystem.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#13-relationship-to-existing-standards","title":"1.3 Relationship to Existing Standards","text":"<p>ActivityStreams 2.0 and ActivityPub. Vultron uses the ActivityStreams 2.0 vocabulary as its wire format, and ActivityPub HTTP delivery is the anticipated transport.</p> <p>This version requires the vocabulary but not full ActivityPub server behavior: inbox and outbox HTTP delivery, WebFinger discovery and HTTP Signatures are not conformance requirements here. A future version is expected to raise the floor to full ActivityPub for all participants, at which point the vocabulary-only profile may become a compatibility profile. An implementation built against this version should expect to be re-evaluated against that one. This paragraph is the specification's single statement of that roadmap; other sections cite it.</p> <p>ISO/IEC 29147 and 30111. ISO 29147 specifies vulnerability disclosure practices; ISO 30111 specifies vulnerability handling processes. Vultron implements the multi-party coordination layer those standards describe at a high level. The CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure provides the practitioner-level complement.</p> <p>See also</p> <ul> <li>ISO Crosswalks</li> <li>CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#14-document-conventions","title":"1.4 Document Conventions","text":"<p>This specification uses the key words defined in RFC 2119: MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY, and OPTIONAL.</p> <p>Sections marked <code>[N]</code> are normative. Sections marked <code>[I]</code> are informative. Sections marked <code>[N/I]</code> contain a mix; normative requirements are explicitly flagged.</p> <p>State names. This specification writes state names in full, in prose form: Received, Active, Signatory, Fix Ready. Where the name of a specific enumerated value matters \u2014 for example when citing an implementation's enumeration \u2014 the value is written in code font with its machine as a prefix, as in <code>RM.RECEIVED</code> or <code>PEC.SIGNATORY</code>. The two forms name the same state.</p> <p>Case-state notation. The Case State axes use one letter per condition. A lowercase letter means the condition is not met; an uppercase letter means it is. <code>Vfd</code> therefore means the vendor is aware, the fix is not ready, and the fix is not deployed. An arrow names the transition that flips one letter, so <code>f\u2192F</code> is the change from \"fix not ready\" to \"fix ready\". An asterisk is a wildcard: <code>pX*</code> matches any state in which <code>p</code> is lowercase and <code>X</code> is uppercase.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#2-terminology-ni","title":"2. Vulnerability is such a term.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#21-actors-participants-and-cases","title":"2.1 Actors, Participants and Cases","text":"<p>These four terms are ordered deliberately: each builds on the one before it.</p> Term Definition Vulnerability A set of conditions or behaviors that allows the violation of an explicit or implicit security policy. Vulnerabilities are the subject of every Vultron case. Report A document describing a specific vulnerability, submitted to initiate coordination. Case The coordination context around a specific vulnerability: the participants, the shared state, the messages exchanged, and any embargo agreement. The case is the unit of Vultron protocol activity. Actor An identity in the protocol, named by a URI. An actor may be an organization, a person, or a service. Actors exist independently of any case. Participant An actor that has joined a specific case. The case holds a <code>CaseParticipant</code> record for each participant, associating that actor with the roles it holds and the state it owns. An actor is a participant in a case; the same actor may participate in many. <p>Source of the vulnerability definition</p> <p>The definition of vulnerability above is taken unchanged from the CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure. It is also consistent with ISO/IEC 29147:2018 \u00a75.4, which defines the term in the same policy-violation terms (ISO crosswalks).</p> <p>Note what the definition does not require: it says nothing about whether the vulnerability is known, reported, fixed or public. Those are properties a Vultron case tracks about a vulnerability (\u00a78), not part of what makes something one.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#22-roles","title":"2.2 Roles","text":"<p>A role is a position held within a case. It determines what a participant is obliged to do and which transitions it is authorized to cause. Roles are granted through the case's authority chain (\u00a711.1), not claimed. A participant may hold several at once.</p> <p>Roles fall into two categories, which \u00a712.3 develops further.</p> <p>Process roles describe what an actor does in a case:</p> Role Definition Reporter A participant that submitted the report. The protocol is concerned with who reported the vulnerability, not who discovered it; a discoverer who reports holds the Reporter role. Vendor A participant that produces a product containing the vulnerability and is responsible for developing a fix. Coordinator A participant that facilitates multi-party coordination without being responsible for developing a fix itself. Deployer A participant that deploys a vendor's fix to systems it operates. Distinct from Vendor: producing a fix and applying it are separate acts. CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) A participant authorized to assign CVE IDs directly, rather than delegating assignment to an external service. Orthogonal to the other process roles and commonly held alongside Coordinator or Vendor. Observer A participant with no obligation to drive vendor/fix/deploy transitions. An Observer still tracks case state, is subject to embargo consent, and may report observations about the world. <p>Protocol authority roles describe what an actor controls in the protocol itself:</p> Role Definition Case Owner The party whose disclosure decision the case exists to serve. It decides who is admitted, which roles they hold, and whether embargo terms are accepted or torn down. Case ownership is never delegated, though it may be transferred (\u00a711.3). Case Manager The participant that writes the canonical case ledger and relays case-scoped messages, acting on the Case Owner's behalf. It is the case's single-writer authority (\u00a75.4.1). The Case Owner may delegate this role. <p>Observer names two different things</p> <p>Observer is used in this specification for the process role defined above, and also as the name of the minimum conformance capability set that every participant must provide (\u00a712.2). The reuse is deliberate \u2014 the capability set is named after the least-privileged role \u2014 but the two are not the same kind of thing. A role is a position in a case; a capability set is a property of software (\u00a712.3.3).</p> <p>Informative: the CASE_MANAGER role and the actor that holds it</p> <p>Authority over a case follows the Case Manager role. It does not follow any actor's name, URI, or hosting location. Normative text in this specification therefore names the authority the CASE_MANAGER, meaning whichever participant currently holds the role.</p> <p>The reference implementation happens to satisfy the role with an automated software actor it labels a case actor, provisioned by a case actor service. Those are implementation labels with no protocol meaning. An implementation MUST NOT infer authority from them.</p> <p>Informative: Finder is not a protocol role</p> <p>Earlier CVD models distinguish the finder of a vulnerability from its reporter. Vultron does not: nothing in the protocol depends on who discovered the vulnerability, so an actor that discovers and reports holds the Reporter role. The discoverer's identity may be recorded in the report content or in a case note.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#23-protocol-objects-and-messages","title":"2.3 Protocol Objects and Messages","text":"<p>These terms name the things a case is made of and the messages that move between participants.</p> Term Definition Activity The wire form of a Vultron message: an ActivityStreams 2.0 Activity.
