Each message is dispatched to one of four process-specific sub-trees:</p> </li> <li> <p>Process RM Messages \u2014 handles report-submission, error, and status messages       (<code>RS</code>, <code>RE</code>, <code>RV</code>, <code>RI</code>, <code>RA</code>, <code>RD</code>, <code>RC</code>, <code>RK</code>)</p> </li> <li>Process EM Messages \u2014 handles all embargo coordination messages       (<code>EP</code>, <code>EA</code>, <code>EV</code>, <code>EJ</code>, <code>EC</code>, <code>ET</code>, <code>ER</code>, <code>EE</code>, <code>EK</code>)</li> <li>Process CS Messages \u2014 handles case-state change notifications       (<code>CP</code>, <code>CX</code>, <code>CA</code>, <code>CV</code>, <code>CF</code>, <code>CD</code>, <code>CE</code>, <code>CK</code>)</li> <li> <p>Process Other Messages \u2014 handles general inquiry and acknowledgment messages       (<code>GI</code>, <code>GE</code>, <code>GK</code>)</p> </li> <li> <p>(C) Report Management. This task embodies the RM process     as integrated into the formal protocol. The \\({q^{cs}\\not\\in\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot pxa}\\) condition is true when attacks have been observed, an exploit has been made public, or information about the vulnerability has been made public. Vultron handles all of that automatically using behavior trees (BTs) \u2014 a kind of state machine that runs as protocol activities arrive.</p> <p>But some steps require judgment that Vultron cannot make by itself:</p> <ul> <li>Is this vulnerability report credible?</li> <li>Should we accept this embargo proposal?</li> <li>Has a CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) ID already been assigned?</li> <li>Is it time to publish the advisory?</li> </ul> <p>These are call-out points \u2014 places where the BT pauses and waits for an answer from an external service before it can continue.</p> <p>A call-out point is answerable now; asking another actor is not</p> <p>A call-out point waits for a service you run, so it can be answered while the BT is still running. That is what makes pausing viable.</p> <p>Some questions cannot be answered that way, because they need a decision from another actor in the case \u2014 for example, whether the case owner permits a change to the case's agreed state. No service can answer that on the owner's behalf, and the answer may take days. There the actor does not pause: it sends a request and finishes, and the reply starts new work when it arrives. See Protocol Event Flow.</p> <p>During development and simulation, call-out points are filled by fuzzer nodes \u2014 stubs that return a random success or failure based on a probability. In production, you replace a fuzzer node with a real service: a capability implementation.</p>"},{"location":"topics/capability_model/#the-two-integration-surfaces","title":"The two integration surfaces","text":"<p>There are two ways an external service interacts with Vultron:</p> <p>Call-out \u2014 Vultron calls you. The BT reaches a call-out point, packages up a question as a structured payload, sends it to your service, and waits for a structured answer. Your service decides and responds.</p> <p>Call-in \u2014 You call Vultron. Your service monitors something externally \u2014 a timer, a threat feed, a deployment system \u2014 and, when a condition is met, sends a trigger to Vultron. Vultron acts on it.</p> <p>Most services use the call-out surface. The current code uses factory injection (each call-out point has a factory function in a domain bundle). That approach is wrong.</p> <p>In ActivityStreams 2.0, <code>Create(X)</code> means \"I created X.\" A Vendor that sends <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code> is claiming to be the authoritative creator of the case. The Vendor is not. The Case Actor service is \u2014 it is the single-writer authority for the canonical ledger, the only peer that appends to the case history. Putting the Vendor as the <code>actor</code> on a <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code> violates that semantics. It assigns the wrong creator in every downstream replica.</p> <p>The <code>CaseProposal</code> object solves this. The Vendor proposes that the Case Actor create the case. The Case Actor does the creation and sends <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code> with itself as <code>actor</code>.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_initialization/#protocol-flow","title":"Protocol flow","text":"<pre><code>Vendor                              Case Actor Service\n  | This page explains how those copies stay in agreement, and it answers two questions:</p> <ul> <li>Who decides the order in which things happened?</li> <li>What happens when messages arrive in the wrong order?</li> </ul> <p>Vultron answers the first question with a single writer. No participant can read or write another participant's replica. Knowledge travels only in messages \u2014 see the Actor Knowledge Model.</p> <p>One peer is different. Whichever participant holds the <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> role is the case's single-writer authority \u2014 the CASE_MANAGER. It keeps the case ledger: the append-only history that is authoritative for the case, and it is the only peer that appends to that history (CLP-01-003). In the prototype this authority is enacted by a dedicated service actor (the Case Actor), but the authority derives from the role, never from that actor's name or URL (ADR-0088).</p> <p>The flow of a change is always the same:</p> <ol> <li>A participant sends the CASE_MANAGER an assertion \u2014 I accept the embargo,    my report is now validated, here is a note.</li> <li>The CASE_MANAGER judges the assertion and appends one entry recording the    outcome. An entry's <code>disposition</code> says whether the assertion was    <code>recorded</code> (accepted) or <code>rejected</code>, so a refusal leaves a trace rather    than a silence.</li> <li>The CASE_MANAGER sends the new entry to every participant as    <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code>.</li> <li>Each participant records the entry, and applies its effects to its own    replica if the entry was <code>recorded</code>.</li> </ol> <p>Because there is exactly one writer, no participant ever has to reconcile two competing versions of the case history. There is only one version. A participant's replica is a projection of that history, not an independent record.</p> <p>The same rule applies in reverse: a participant accepts a case update only from the CASE_MANAGER for that case, and rejects an update from any other sender (PCR-03-001). Nobody else can write to a replica, and the replica's owner does not edit it directly either \u2014 even when that owner is the organization that opened the case.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#two-views-of-the-ledger","title":"Two views of the ledger","text":"<p>The ledger can be read two ways, and most of this page is about the second one.</p> <ul> <li>The audit log is every entry the CASE_MANAGER appended, in the order it   appended them \u2014 rejections included.</li> <li>The recorded projection is the subset whose <code>disposition</code> is <code>recorded</code>.   That projection is the authoritative history of the case   (CLP-04-001).</li> </ul> <p>Case state is reconstructed from the recorded projection alone; a replica ignores rejected entries when working out what is true of the case (CLP-04-002). The hash chain is computed over that projection too (CLP-04-003), so a rejection does not advance the chain: the next recorded entry names the previous recorded entry as its predecessor, not a rejection appended in between.</p> <p>A rejection is therefore evidence \u2014 the CASE_MANAGER saw this assertion and refused it \u2014 rather than a fact about the case. Where the rest of this page says \"the chain\" or \"the history\", it means the recorded projection.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-a-ledger-entry-carries","title":"What a ledger entry carries","text":"<p>Each entry is a small, immutable record. If the CASE_MANAGER observed event A before event B, then A has the lower <code>log_index</code> (CLP-14-001, ADR-0079). Anything that needs to know what happened first compares log indexes. It does not compare clocks.</p> <p>This matters because clocks disagree. Two organizations on different continents, running different software, will not agree on the millisecond at which an event occurred. Sorting a shared history by wall-clock time would make the order depend on whose clock was fast. Sorting by <code>log_index</code> does not.</p> <p>Timestamps are still recorded, and they are still useful \u2014 as corroborating evidence, and for spotting a participant whose clock is wrong. They are not the order.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-the-ledger-claims-and-what-it-does-not","title":"What the ledger claims, and what it does not","text":"<p>The ledger is authoritative from the CASE_MANAGER's point of view. It is a postmark, not a forensic reconstruction. It records the sequence in which the CASE_MANAGER observed and processed events, and it makes no claim about when those events happened inside another organization (CLP-15-005).</p> <ul> <li>For events the CASE_MANAGER generates itself, causal order is known by   construction: the entries are written one after another on a single path.</li> <li>For events reported by participants, the CASE_MANAGER's own receive-and-commit   order is the order. The CASE_MANAGER cannot verify a causal claim about   something it did not see.</li> </ul> <p>The CASE_MANAGER never reorders entries to match timestamps supplied by someone else. Doing so would let external data override the one thing the CASE_MANAGER knows first-hand.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#rules-the-case_manager-follows","title":"Rules the CASE_MANAGER follows","text":"Rule Requirement Order is never reversed: an event observed earlier never gets a higher <code>log_index</code> CLP-14-001 Every entry carries a timestamp; none may be empty CLP-14-002 Timestamps on consecutive recorded entries never move backwards as <code>log_index</code> increases CLP-14-003 Every entry in a ledger belongs to the same case CLP-14-004 No two entries in a case share a <code>log_index</code> CLP-14-005 No entry predates the case it belongs to CLP-14-006 <p>Whether the index run may contain holes is not settled. A replica must hold a contiguous run from the genesis entry through the position it has acknowledged before it may take new protocol-significant actions on the case (SYNC-10-004), and in practice a receiver treats a hole as a missing entry. But <code>log_index</code> is consumed by every appended entry, rejections included, and rejections are not part of the recorded projection \u2014 so a hole in that projection is not by itself proof of loss. ADR-0079 states the rule both ways in different sections; the contradiction is tracked in #2752 and is not resolved here.</p> <p>The CASE_MANAGER should also refuse an assertion whose own timestamp is far in the future or far in the past compared to its clock \u2014 by default, more than five minutes ahead or more than seven days old (CLP-14-007, CLP-14-008). Across the CASE_MANAGER's own commit timestamps it holds because one writer stamps every entry from one clock. Applied to participants' timestamps it would be wrong: two participants' clocks are not synchronized, so an assertion recorded later by one of them can legitimately claim an earlier time than an assertion recorded earlier by the other. The CASE_MANAGER therefore compares a participant's claimed timestamp only against that same participant's previous assertion, and allows a small tolerance when comparing it against the case's creation time.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-participants-must-do","title":"What participants must do","text":"<p>The CASE_MANAGER can only record the order it sees. That places an obligation on each participant: send events in the order they happened.</p> <ul> <li>If A caused B, send A first   (CLP-15-001).</li> <li>Do not collect several related events and send them in an arbitrary order   (CLP-15-002).</li> <li>Give B a timestamp no earlier than A's   (CLP-15-003).</li> <li>Timestamp an event with when it happened, not when the batch went out or a   retry was attempted   (CLP-15-004).</li> </ul> <p>A participant that breaks these rules produces a malformed assertion. That is a fault on the sending side, not a CASE_MANAGER failure.</p> <p>The CASE_MANAGER cannot police these at the moment an assertion arrives, and it must not try: it may not reconstruct an order it did not observe (CLP-15-005). It sees the order messages arrived in, which is not the order they were sent in \u2014 the transport makes no such promise.</p> <p>So when an assertion's claimed time falls behind the same participant's previous assertion, the CASE_MANAGER records it and says so, rather than refusing it. A small regression is reported quietly; one beyond the configured tolerance is reported as a warning. Refusing would throw the message away \u2014 the ledger commit happens before any of the receiving work, so a refusal loses the whole thing \u2014 and the CASE_MANAGER cannot tell a participant that really did misorder its events from two messages that simply arrived out of order.</p> <p>The two ordering rules are visible only across a whole case, by comparing the causal links a scenario declares against the order the ledger recorded; the conformance suite checks them there.</p> <p>One thing the CASE_MANAGER does refuse outright: an activity that arrives with no <code>published</code> time at all. Because the field is optional in ActivityStreams, a receiver that filled in the blank with its own clock could no longer tell what the sender claimed from what it invented \u2014 and every check above would then be comparing the CASE_MANAGER's clock against itself. A message without a claimed time is therefore rejected at the door (CLP-15-006).</p> <p>A field that is present but empty carries no claimed time either. A blank <code>published</code> \u2014 an empty string, or one holding only whitespace \u2014 is refused the same way as an omitted one, and reports the same reason (MV-03-002).</p> <p>A value that is present and not blank but unreadable as a timestamp is a different fault. The CASE_MANAGER reports it as malformed data, not as a missing field, so a sender is never told to supply something it already sent.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#when-entries-arrive-out-of-order","title":"When entries arrive out of order","text":"<p>Ledger entries travel over ordinary message transport, which gives no ordering guarantee. Vultron may also not be the only implementation on the wire. So a replica can receive entry 7 before entry 6.</p> <p>The naive response is to reject entry 7, on the grounds that it does not extend the chain, and wait for the CASE_MANAGER to send it again. That does not work. The replay travels the same unordered transport and can arrive out of order again, so under repeated reordering an entry can be lost indefinitely. In an earlier version of this implementation, that is what stalled a late-joining vendor at case closure.</p> <p>Instead, a replica keeps an early entry (ADR-0037, SYNC-14-001). It puts the entry in a holding area and waits for the predecessor. Convergence then no longer depends on delivery order at all.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-gets-held-and-what-does-not","title":"What gets held, and what does not","text":"<p>A replica holds an entry when the entry does not extend its chain but belongs later in the history \u2014 its <code>log_index</code> is more than one past the end of what the replica holds. That is a forward gap: the predecessor has not arrived yet.</p> <p>Two kinds of entry are not held:</p> <ul> <li>An entry at or behind the end of the chain. That is a duplicate or a stale   replay, not a gap.</li> <li>An entry exactly one past the end of the chain whose <code>prevLogHash</code> does not   match the hash of the replica's last recorded entry. Nothing is missing in   front of it, so it is not a gap \u2014 it is a fork, a claim about a history the   replica does not share.</li> </ul> <p>Both go to the ordinary duplicate and divergence handling instead.</p> <p>Even when it does hold an entry, the replica still sends <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> naming the last entry it accepted (SYNC-14-002). Holding solves reordering; it cannot solve loss. If the missing entry was never delivered at all, the reject is what prompts the CASE_MANAGER to send it again.</p> <p>The CASE_MANAGER does not replay on demand without limit. If a peer keeps rejecting from the same position, the CASE_MANAGER waits out a short cooldown before replaying to it again (SYNC-15-003). Without that bound, a peer that cannot anchor its chain rejects every entry it is sent, each reject triggers another full replay, and the two feed each other into a storm. A reject from a position that has advanced always triggers a replay, so a peer making progress is never held back.</p> <p>The holding area should also be bounded, so that a hostile or broken peer streaming far-future entries cannot exhaust memory. When it is full, the replica discards the entry farthest ahead of the gap and logs a warning (SYNC-14-006). Discarding is safe because the reject for that gap has already been sent \u2014 but the eviction itself sends nothing, so recovery waits on the replay that reject triggers, or on the next entry that fails to match the tail. The cooldown above may delay either.</p> <p>The holding area is deliberately not the ledger (SYNC-14-005). Across Vultron, the presence of an entry in an actor's own store means this entry is committed and its effects are applied (SYNC-13-001). A held entry is neither, so storing it would break that meaning.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#entries-that-arrive-before-the-case","title":"Entries that arrive before the case","text":"<p>The same holding area covers a related race: an entry can arrive before the participant has the case object at all. Without the case, the replica cannot compute the genesis hash and so cannot anchor the chain.</p> <p>A replica holds these entries too (SYNC-15-004), with no gap comparison \u2014 there is no chain yet to compare against, so every entry for the unknown case is held, including entry 0. When the case is later delivered, the replica drains the holding area for that case (SYNC-15-005). Seeding the case is enough, because the genesis hash is derived from the case object; the genesis ledger entry does not have to be re-sent (ADR-0059).</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#draining-the-held-entries","title":"Draining the held entries","text":"<p>Each held entry is filed under the hash of the predecessor it is waiting for. So after the replica commits a new last entry, finding the successor is a single lookup: the held entry whose <code>prevLogHash</code> equals the hash of the entry just committed.</p> <p>The drain then repeats. Commit the successor, look up its successor, and continue until no held entry extends the chain (SYNC-14-003). A run of ten entries that arrived in reverse order clicks into place in one cascade, in <code>log_index</code> order.</p> <p>Three properties make the drain safe:</p> <ul> <li>Same path. A drained entry goes through the same processing as an entry   that arrived in order \u2014 no separate code path with its own behavior   (SYNC-14-008). In this   implementation that means the drain re-runs the announce receive behavior   tree on each held entry, in <code>log_index</code> order.</li> <li>Effects before storage. The entry's consequences \u2014 an embargo ending, a   participant joining, a status changing \u2014 are applied first, and the entry is   stored only if they all succeed   (SYNC-12-001,   SYNC-14-004).</li> <li>Applied once. An entry already in the local ledger is skipped entirely,   so a replay or a duplicate cannot apply the same effects twice   (SYNC-12-003,   SYNC-14-007).</li> </ul> <p>Because held entries are replayed through the ordinary path, the reject-and-replay recovery becomes order-tolerant as well, at no extra cost.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#why-state-checks-wait-for-the-drain","title":"Why state checks wait for the drain","text":"<p>Holding an entry has a consequence that is easy to get wrong. Case State (CS) has ordering rules of its own: an ephemeral state cannot be a resting place, so it has exactly one permitted successor and must be followed by it; the recorded history must remain a valid sequence throughout; and a move to public awareness must be recorded before the embargo termination that it triggers.</p> <p>If a replica checked those rules at the moment an entry arrived, an out-of-order entry would look like a violation. An entry naming a state that is only reachable from its predecessor would appear to arrive from nowhere.</p> <p>That is why the checks run at drain time instead (CSB-19-001). A held entry is parked before any case-state effect is applied, so the state machine is never touched at arrival time. When the gap closes, the entries replay in <code>log_index</code> order \u2014 which is causal order \u2014 and the guards see them in the sequence they were meant to be seen in.</p> <p>An entry waiting in the holding area therefore raises no state violation at all (CSB-19-002). An entry naming an ephemeral state is perfectly well-formed on its own; it would only be a real violation if the entry that resolves it never arrived. Flagging it on arrival would be a false alarm, and rejecting it would prevent the replica from ever converging.</p> <p>The public-awareness-before-embargo-termination ordering survives reordering for free (CSB-19-003). The CASE_MANAGER commits the public-awareness entry first, so it holds the lower <code>log_index</code>. The drain works in <code>log_index</code> order, so it can never present the termination entry first. No receiver-side re-check of the timing is needed; the order in the ledger is sufficient.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-a-replica-guarantees","title":"What a replica guarantees","text":"<p>Taken together, the ledger rules and the holding area give each participant these properties:</p> Property Meaning Append-only A committed entry is immutable and identified by its content hash Deterministic projection The same run of entries produces the same state in every conforming implementation Idempotent replay Re-processing entries already seen changes nothing Monotonic progress A replica never regresses the position it has acknowledged Reject on divergence An entry that does not extend the chain is not silently accepted Order-independent convergence Delivery order does not affect the final state <p>The result is eventual consistency with a strong bound: given the same entries, every replica reaches the same state as the CASE_MANAGER, no matter what order those entries arrived in.</p> <p>The holding area itself is in memory only, and is lost on restart. No <code>CaseLedgerEntry</code> was written after the role change. Participants who were not direct parties to the negotiation had no way to learn that the case's ownership had changed.</p> <p>The fix is simple: both activities MUST route through the Case Actor, for the same reason all case-scoped messages route there \u2014 so that the CASE_MANAGER can record the event in the canonical ledger and broadcast the result to every participant.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/ownership_transfer/#correct-routing-model","title":"Correct routing model","text":""},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/ownership_transfer/#offer-flow","title":"Offer flow","text":"<pre><code>Offering actor sends trigger: offer-case-ownership-transfer\n  \u2192 Case Actor sends Offer(VulnerabilityCase, target=transferee)\n      actor:        case_actor_id       (delegated-message contract)\n      attributed_to: offering_actor_id\n      to:           [case_actor_id]     \u2190 MUST route through Case Actor (CM-21-005)\n\nCase Actor inbox receives Offer:\n  1. establishes that a <code>Reject(Offer(VulnerabilityCase))</code> is addressed to the Case Actor's inbox \u2014 symmetric with the Accept path. What the Case Actor does on receiving that rejection is not yet specified:</p> <ul> <li>Is the rejection ledgered? The Accept path commits a <code>CaseLedgerEntry</code>   and broadcasts <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> (CM-21-007). Whether a declined   transfer earns a ledger entry of its own, or leaves no canonical trace, is   unresolved.</li> <li>Does the offerer learn of the rejection? With the Reject addressed to   the Case Actor rather than the offerer, the offerer is not a direct   recipient. A notification hop (or a ledger broadcast) would be needed for   the offerer to discover the decline.</li> <li>Is the case re-offerable? Whether a rejected Offer can be re-issued to   the same or a different transferee, and whether any state cleanup is   required first, is unspecified.</li> </ul> <p>Resolving these questions will In this section, we seek to fill that gap. In both data sets examined, our estimated \\(\\alpha_d\\) is positive for most \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\). This principle assumes a uniform distribution across event transitions in the absence of CVD, which is an assumption we cannot readily test. The spread of the estimates in Observing Skill represents the variance in our samples, not this assumption-based uncertainty. Our interpretation of \\(\\alpha_d\\) values near zero is therefore that they reflect an absence of evidence rather than evidence that skill is absent. The need for MPCVD arises due to the inherent nature of the software supply chain CERT Guide to CVD. A vulnerability that affects a low-level component (such as a library or operating system API) can require fixes from both the originating vendor and any vendor whose products incorporate the affected component. Alternatively, vulnerabilities are sometimes found in protocol specifications or other design-time issues where multiple vendors may have each implemented their own components based on a vulnerable design.</p>"},{"location":"topics/measuring_cvd/benchmarking_mpcvd/#state-tracking-in-mpcvd","title":"State Tracking in MPCVD","text":"<p>Applying our state-based model to MPCVD requires a forking approach to the state tracking.</p> <p>MPCVD Case State Tracking</p> <p>At the time of discovery, the vulnerability is in state \\(vfdpxa\\). Known only to its finder, the vulnerability can be described by that singular state.</p> <p>As it becomes clear that the vulnerability affects multiple vendors' products, both finder/reporters and coordinators might begin to track the state of each individual vendor as a separate instance of the model. For example, if 3 vendors are known to be affected, but only 1 has been notified, the case might be considered to be in a superposition of states \\(\\{Vfdpxa,vfdpxa,vfdpxa\\}\\).</p> <p>Each vendor, in turn, might then ascertain whether they are able to produce fixes for all their available products at once, or if those fixes will be staggered over time. In either case, the vendor might track the case as a superposition of states for each affected product dependent on its fix readiness status. For example, a vendor might have four products affected, with two in the fix-ready state and two fixes still in progress. Should they opt for transparency into their internal process, they might communicate their status as the superposition of \\(\\{VFdpxa,VFdpxa,Vfdpxa,Vfdpxa\\}\\). Alternatively, they might choose to only share the lowest state across their products, which in this example would be \\(\\{Vfdpxa\\}\\).</p> <p>The above example implies a need to expand our notation.</p> <p>MPCVD Cases have Participant-Specific States</p> <p>In the MPCVD case, we need to think of each state \\(q \\in \\mathcal{Q}\\) as a set of states \\(q_M\\):</p> \\[ q_M \\stackrel{\\mathsf{def}}{=}\\{ q_1,q_2,\\dots,q_n \\} \\] <p>where \\(q_i\\) represents the state \\(q\\) for the \\(i\\)th affected vendor and/or product. For example, \\(\\{ {Vfdpxa}_1, {vfdpxa}_2 \\}\\) would represent the state in which vendor 1 has been notified but vendor 2 has not. Very often, vendor notification occurs as new products and vendors are identified as affected in the course of analyzing a vulnerability report. For example, if an MPCVD case is already underway, and information about the vulnerability appears in a public media report, we can say that \\(\\mathbf{P}_M\\) occurred simultaneously for all coordinating vendors.</p> <p>Regardless, in the maximal case, each vendor-product pair is effectively behaving independently of all the others. Therefore:</p> <p>Dimensionality of an MPCVD Case</p> <p>The maximum dimensionality of the MPCVD model for a case is</p> \\[ D_{max} = 5 * N_{vprod} \\] <p>where \\(N_{vprod}\\) represents the number of vendor-product pairs.</p> <p>This is undesirable, as it would result in a wide distribution of realized histories that more closely resemble the randomness assumptions outlined above than a skillful, coordinated effort. Further discussion of measuring MPCVD skill can be found below.</p> <p>Reducing Dimensionality of MPCVD Cases is a good thing</p> <p>For now, we posit that the goal of a good MPCVD process is to reduce the dimensionality of a given MPCVD case as much as is possible (i.e., to the 5 dimensions of a single vendor CVD case we have presented above). Experience shows that a full dimension reduction is unlikely in most cases, but that does not detract from the value of having the goal.</p> <p>Reducing Complexity within a Vendor Organization</p> <p>Vendors may be able to reduce their internal tracking dimensionality---which may be driven by things like component reuse across products or product lines---through in-house coordination of fix development processes. Within an individual vendor organization, PSIRTs are a common organizational structure to address this internal coordination process.</p> <ul> <li>The FIRST PSIRT Services Framework provides guidance regarding vendors' internal processes for coordinating vulnerability response.</li> <li>Additional guidance can be found in ISO/IEC 30111:2019.</li> </ul> <p>Regardless, the cross-vendor dimension is largely the result of component reuse across vendors, for example through the inclusion of third party libraries or OEM SDKs. Visibility of cross-vendor component reuse remains an unsolved problem, although efforts such as the Software Bill of Materials are promising in this regard. Thus, dimensionality reduction can be achieved through both improved transparency of the software supply chain and the process of coordination toward synchronized state transitions, especially for \\(\\mathbf{P}\\), if not for \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) and \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) as well.</p> <p>As a result of the dimensionality problem, coordinators and other parties to an MPCVD case need to decide how to apply disclosure policy rules in cases where different products or vendors occupy different case states with potentially contradictory recommended actions. For example, when four out of five vendors involved in a case have reached \\(VFdpxa\\) and are ready to publish, but the fifth is still in \\(Vfdpxa\\). Essentially this can be expected to take the form of a weighting function that acts on a vector of case states, and outputs a set of recommended actions derived from those states.</p> <p>One possible function would be to apply a simple voting heuristic such as waiting for a simple majority of vendors to reach a state before taking action as that state recommends. In our 4/5 \\(VFdpxa\\) example, the coordinating parties would behave as if the case were in that state for all.</p> <p>Another function could be to weight vendors and products by some other factor, such as size of the installed user base, or even based on a risk analysis of societal costs associated with potential actions. Here we acknowledge that our example is under-specified: does the fifth vendor (the one in \\(Vfdpxa\\)) represent a sizable fraction of the total user base? Or does it concentrate the highest risk use cases for the software? Challenges in efficiently assessing consistent answers to these questions are easy to imagine. The status quo for MPCVD appears consistent with defaulting to simple majority in the absence of additional information, with consideration given to the distribution of both users and risk on a case-by-case basis. At present, there is no clear consensus on such policies, although we hope that future work can use the model presented here to formalize the necessary analysis.</p> <p>Integrating FIRST MPCVD Guidance</p> <p>FIRST has published Guidelines and Practices for Multi-Party Vulnerability Coordination and Disclosure. considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Does CVD as observed in the wild demonstrate skillful behavior?</p> <p>In order to answer this question, we need a way to measure skillful behavior in CVD. This section defines a method for measuring skill in CVD.</p> <p>The measurement method makes use of all the modeling tools and baselines established thus far: a comprehensive set of possible histories \\(\\mathcal{H}\\), a partial order over them in terms of the presence of desired event precedence \\((\\mathcal{H},\\leq_{\\mathbb{D}})\\), and the a priori expected frequency of each desiderata \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\).</p> <p>If we expected to be able to observe all events in all CVD cases, we could be assured of having complete histories and could be done here. But the real world is messy. Not all events \\(\\mathbf{e} \\in \\mathcal{E}\\) are always observable. We need to develop a way to make sense of what we can observe, regardless of whether we are ever able to capture complete histories. Continuing towards our goal of measuring efficacy, we return to considering the balance between skill and luck in determining our observed outcomes.</p>"},{"location":"topics/measuring_cvd/discriminating_skill_and_luck/#a-measure-of-skill-in-cvd","title":"A Measure of Skill in CVD","text":"<p>We have established a set of desiderata \\(\\mathbb{D}\\) that we would like to see in a CVD case. Now, we want to measure the degree to which a CVD practice is skillful in achieving those desiderata. In a world of pure skill, one would expect that a player could achieve all 12 desiderata \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\) consistently. That is, a maximally skillful player could consistently achieve the specific ordering \\(h=(\\mathbf{V},\\mathbf{F},\\mathbf{D},\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{X},\\mathbf{A})\\) with probability \\(p_{skill} = 1\\).</p> <p>Factors that could affect the observed frequency of a desideratum</p> <p>There are many reasons why we might expect our observations to differ from the expected frequencies we established  in Reasoning Over Possible Histories. Adversaries might be rare, or conversely very well equipped. Vendors might be very good at releasing fixes faster  than adversaries can discover vulnerabilities and develop exploits for them. System owners might be diligent at applying patches. (We did say might, didn't we?) Regardless, for now we will lump all of those possible explanations into a single attribute called \"skill.\"</p> <p>Thus, we construct the following model: for each of our preferred orderings \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\), we model their occurrence due to luck using the binomial distribution with parameter \\(p_{luck} = f_d\\) taken from the event frequency table in Reasoning Over Possible Histories, reproduced below for convenience:</p> <p>Expected Frequency of \\({row} \\prec {col}\\) when events are chosen uniformly from possible transitions in each state</p> \\(\\mathbf{V}\\) \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) \\(\\mathbf{P}\\) \\(\\mathbf{X}\\) \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) \\(\\mathbf{V}\\) 0 1 1 0.333 0.667 0.750 \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) 0 0 1 0.111 0.333 0.375 \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) 0 0 0 0.037 0.167 0.187 \\(\\mathbf{P}\\) 0.667 0.889 0.963 0 0.500 0.667 \\(\\mathbf{X}\\) 0.333 0.667 0.833 0.500 0 0.500 \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) 0.250 0.625 0.812 0.333 0.500 0 <p>Recall that the mean of a binomial distribution is the probability of success \\(p\\), and that the mean of a weighted mixture of two binomial distributions is the weighted mixture of the individual means. Therefore our model adds a parameter \\(\\alpha_d\\) to represent the weighting between our success rates arising from skill \\(p_{skill}\\) and luck \\(p_{luck}\\). Because there are 12 desiderata \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\), each \\(d\\) will have its own observations and corresponding value for \\(\\alpha_d\\) for each history \\(h_a\\).</p> <p>Modeling Skill and Luck in Observations</p> <p>We model the observed frequency of desiderata \\(d\\) as a weighted mixture of the success rates due to skill and luck:</p> \\[ f_d^{obs} = \\alpha_d \\cdot p_{skill} + (1 - \\alpha_d) \\cdot p_{luck} \\] <p>Where \\(f_d^{obs}\\) is the observed frequency of successes for desiderata \\(d\\). Because \\(p_{skill} = 1\\), one of those binomial distributions is degenerate. Substituting \\(p_{skill} = 1\\), \\(p_{luck} = f_d\\) and solving the previous equation for \\(\\alpha\\), we get</p> <p>Skill Coefficient</p> <p>The value of \\(\\alpha_d\\) therefore gives us a measure of the observed skill normalized against the background success rate provided by luck \\(f_d\\).</p> \\[ \\alpha_d \\stackrel{\\mathsf{def}}{=}\\frac{f_d^{obs} - f_d} {1 - f_d} \\] <p>Skill Coefficient Set</p> <p>We denote the set of \\(\\alpha_d\\) values for a given history as \\(\\alpha_\\mathbb{D}\\). When we refer to the \\(\\alpha_d\\) coefficient for a specific \\(d\\) we will use the specific ordering as the subscript, for example: \\(\\alpha_{\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{P}}\\).</p> \\[ \\alpha_\\mathbb{D} \\stackrel{\\mathsf{def}}{=}\\{ \\alpha_d : d \\in \\mathbb{D} \\} \\] <p>The concept embodied by \\(f_d\\) is founded on the idea that if attackers and defenders are in a state of equilibrium, the frequency of observed outcomes (i.e., how often each desiderata \\(d\\) and history \\(h\\) actually occurs) will appear consistent with those predicted by chance. So another way of interpreting \\(\\alpha_d\\) is as a measure of the degree to which a set of observed histories is out of equilibrium.</p> <p>Interpreting \\(\\alpha_d\\) Behavior</p> <p>The following are a few comments on how \\(\\alpha_d\\) behaves. Note that \\(\\alpha_d &lt; 0\\) when \\(0 \\leq f_d^{obs} &lt; f_d\\) and \\(0 \\leq \\alpha_d \\leq 1\\) when \\(f_d \\leq f_d^{obs} \\leq 1\\). The implication is that a negative value for \\(\\alpha_d\\) indicates that our observed outcomes are actually worse than those predicted by pure luck. In other words, we can only infer positive skill when the observations are higher (\\(f_d^{obs} &gt; f_d\\)). That makes intuitive sense: if you are likely to win purely by chance, then you have to attribute most of your wins to luck rather than skill. From the event frequency table above, the largest value for any \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\) is \\(f_{\\mathbf{V} \\prec \\mathbf{A}}=0.75\\), implying that even if a vendor knows about 7 out of 10 vulnerabilities before attacks occur (\\(f_{\\mathbf{V} \\prec \\mathbf{A}}^{obs} = 0.7\\)), they are still not doing better than random.</p> <p>On the other hand, when \\(f_d\\) is small it is easier to infer skill should we observe anything better than \\(f_d\\). However, it takes larger increments of observations \\(f_d^{obs}\\) to infer growth in skill when \\(f_d\\) is small than when it is large. The smallest \\(f_d\\) we see in the event frequency table is \\(f_{\\mathbf{D} \\prec \\mathbf{P}} = 0.037\\).</p> <p>Inherent to the binomial distribution is the expectation that the variance of results is lower for both extremes (as \\(p\\) approaches either 0 or 1) and highest at \\(p=0.5\\). Therefore we should generally be less certain of our observations when they fall in the middle of the distribution. An extensive discussion of uncertainty in the binomial distribution is given in Brown et al. (2001).</p> <p>However, for our purpose the Beta distribution lends itself to this problem nicely. It is common to interpret \\(a\\) as the number of successes and \\(b\\) as the number of failures in a set of observations of Bernoulli trials to estimate the mean of the binomial distribution from which the observations are drawn. We follow the principle of indifference as stated below.</p> <p></p> <p>Benjamin Eva in Principles of Indifference</p> <p>Let \\(X = \\{x_1,x_2,...,x_n\\}\\) be a partition of the set \\(W\\) of possible worlds into \\(n\\) mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive possibilities. In the absence of any relevant evidence pertaining to which cell of the partition is the true one, a rational agent should assign an equal initial credence of \\(n\\) to each cell.</p> <p>While the principle of indifference is rather strong, it is inherently difficult to reason about absolutely skill-less CVD when the work of CVD is, by its nature, a skilled job. The events \\(\\sigma \\in \\Sigma\\) trigger state transitions according to \\(\\delta\\) and the histories \\(h \\in \\mathcal{H}\\) are paths (traces) through the states. This meets the definition above because each \\(\\sigma \\in \\Sigma\\) is unique (mutually exclusive) and \\(\\delta\\) defines an exhaustive set of valid \\(\\sigma\\) at each state \\(q \\in \\mathcal{Q}\\).</p> <p>Initial State Probabilities</p> <p>For example, because causality requires \\(\\mathbf{V} \\prec \\mathbf{F}\\) and \\(\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{D}\\), only four of the six events in \\(\\Sigma\\) are possible at the beginning of each history at \\(q_0=vfdpxa\\): \\(\\{\\mathbf{V},\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{X},\\mathbf{A}\\}\\). Since the principle of indifference assigns each possible transition event as equally probable in this model of unskilled CVD, we assign an initial probability of 0.25 to each possible event. </p> \\[ \\begin{aligned}     p(\\mathbf{V}|q_0) = p(\\mathbf{P}|q_0) = p(\\mathbf{X}|q_0) = p(\\mathbf{A}|q_0) &amp;= 0.25\\\\     p(\\mathbf{F}|q_0) = p(\\mathbf{D}|q_0) &amp;= 0 \\end{aligned} \\] <p>From there, we see that the other rules dictate possible transitions from each subsequent state.</p> <p>More implications for initial state probabilities</p> <p>For example, in the CS Model Transitions, we  established that </p> <ul> <li>any \\(h\\) starting with \\((\\mathbf{P})\\) must start with \\((\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{V})\\)</li> <li>any \\(h\\) starting with \\((\\mathbf{X})\\) must proceed through \\((\\mathbf{X},\\mathbf{P})\\) which coupled with the previous rule yields \\((\\mathbf{X},\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{V})\\).</li> </ul> <p>Therefore, we expect histories starting with \\((\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{V})\\) or \\((\\mathbf{X},\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{V})\\) to occur  with frequency 0.25 as well.</p> <p>We can use these transition probabilities to estimate a neutral baseline expectation of which states would be common if we weren't doing anything special to coordinate vulnerability disclosures. Specifically, for each state we set the transition probability to any other state proportional to the inverse of the outdegree of the state, as shown in the \\(p(transition)\\) column of the table below. Real world data is unlikely to ever reflect such a sad state of affairs (because CVD is happening after all).</p> <p>State Transition Diagram</p> <p>For convenience, we've reproduced the CS model state transition diagram here. The PageRank algorithm provides a probability estimate for each state based on a Markov random walk of the directed graph of states. PageRank assumes each available transition is equally probable, consistent with our model. To avoid becoming stuck in dead ends, PageRank adds a teleport feature by which walks can, with a small probability, randomly jump to another node in the graph.</p> <p>Before proceeding, we need to make a small modification of our state digraph. Without modification, the PageRank algorithm will tend to be biased toward later states because the only way to reach the earlier states is for the algorithm to teleport there. Teleportation chooses states uniformly, so for example there is only a \\(1/32\\) chance of our actual start state (\\(q_0={vfdpxa}\\)) ever being chosen. Therefore, to ensure that the early states in our process are fairly represented we add a single link from VFDPXA to vfdpxa, representing a model reset whenever the end state is reached. This modification allows PageRank traversals to wrap around naturally and reach the early states in the random walk process without needing to rely on teleportation. With our modification in place, we are ready to compute the PageRank of each node in the graph. Disclosure policies specify commitments by coordinating parties to ensure the occurrence of certain state transitions within a specific period of time. While the model presented here does not directly address timing choices, we can point out some ways to relate the model to those choices. Specifically, we intend to demonstrate how disclosure policy SLEs can be stated as rules triggered within subsets of states or by particular transitions between subsets of states in \\(\\mathcal{Q}\\).</p> <p>SLEs and Publication Timing</p> <p>For example, a finder, reporter, or coordinator might commit to publishing information about a vulnerability 30 days after vendor notification. This translates to starting a timer at \\({v} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{V}} {V}\\) and ensuring \\({Vp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {VP}\\) when the timer expires. Notice that the prospect of \\({Vfp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {VfP}\\) is often used to motivate vendors to ensure a reasonable SLE to produce fixes (\\({Vf} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{F}} {VF}\\))  (See for example Optimal Policy for Software Vulnerability Disclosure by Arora, Telang, and Xu).</p> <p>SLEs and Fix Readiness Timing</p> <p>Similarly, a vendor might commit to providing public fixes within 5 business days of report receipt. In that case, the SLE timer would start at \\({vfp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{V}} {Vfp}\\) and and end at one of two transitions: First, the \"normal\" situation in which the vendor creates a fix and makes it public along with the vulnerability (\\(\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{P}\\), i.e., \\({VFp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {VFP}\\)). Second, a \"zero day\" situation in which events outside the vendor's control cause the \\({Vfp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {VfP}\\) transition to occur prior to the fix being ready (\\({VfP} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{F}} {VFP}\\)), i.e, \\(\\mathbf{P} \\prec \\mathbf{F}\\). Likewise, the \\({Vfp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {VfP} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{F}} {VFP}\\) path might also occur when a vendor has set their embargo timer too aggressively for their development process to keep up.</p> <p>It is therefore in the vendor's interest to tune their SLE to reduce the likelihood for unexpected public awareness (\\(\\mathbf{P}\\)) while providing sufficient time for \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) to occur, optimizing to achieve \\(\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{P}\\) in a substantial fraction of cases. As future work, measurement of both the incidence and timing of embargo failures through observation of \\(\\mathbf{P}\\), \\(\\mathbf{X}\\), and \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) originating from \\(\\mathcal{Q}_{E}\\) could give insight into appropriate vendor SLEs for fix readiness (\\(\\mathbf{F}\\)).</p> <p>SLEs and Fix Deployment Timing</p> <p>Service providers and VM practitioners might similarly describe their SLEs in terms of timing between states. Such policies will likely take the form of commitments to limit the time spent in \\({FdP}\\). When the vendor has already produced a patch, the clock starts at \\({Fdp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {FdP}\\), whereas if the vulnerability becomes public prior to patch the clock starts at \\({fdP} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{F}} {FdP}\\). In both cases, the timer ends at \\({FdP} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{D}} {FDP}\\).</p> <p>Formalizing Policy Statements</p> <p>Future formal definitions of policy statements might take the general form of specifications including</p> <ul> <li> <p>Starting state (\\(q \\in \\mathcal{Q}\\)) or subset of states (\\(S \\subset \\mathcal{Q}\\))</p> </li> <li> <p>Expected transitions (\\(\\sigma \\in \\Sigma\\)) and SLEs around their timing, including possible constraints such as \"not before\" and \"no later than\" specifications</p> </li> <li> <p>An indication of constraint rigidity (negotiable, fixed, MUST, SHOULD, MAY, etc.)</p> </li> <li> <p>Potential exceptions in the form of other transitions (\\(\\sigma \\in \\Sigma\\)) that might alter expected behavior, and a description of the anticipated response.</p> </li> </ul> <p>Policy Formalization and Embargo Conflict Resolution</p> <p>We cover this more extensively in our discussion of the EM model, but one reason to formalize policy definitions is the potential to automatically resolve embargo negotiations when those policies are compatible. It may be possible to resolve some apparent policy conflicts by delaying notifications to some vendors to ensure that all embargo end timers expire simultaneously. We informally refer to this as the Thanksgiving Dinner problem, due to its similarity to the familiar annual holiday meal in which a number of dishes with varying preparation times are expected to be delivered to the table simultaneously, each at its appropriate temperature and doneness. For example, when one party has a \"minimum 90 days to publish\" policy and another has a \"maximum 5 days to publish\" policy, the resolution could be to notify the first vendor 85 days before notifying the second. Such a model of graduated disclosure could work well for cases where notifications are automated and vendor dependencies are small or where coordinating parties' policies can be resolved as compatible. Technology such as Theorem Provers and Solvers seem likely to be suited to this sort of problem.</p> <p>However, when formal policies are incompatible, the failure to resolve them automatically becomes an opportunity for human intervention as the exception handler of last resort. Of potential concern here are MPCVD cases in which a vendor with a long policy timer is dependent on one with a short policy timer to provide fixes. The serial nature of the dependency creates the potential for a compatibility conflict. For example, this can happen when an OS kernel provider's disclosure policy specifies a shorter embargo timer than the policies of device manufacturers whose products depend on that OS kernel. Our model casts each event \\(\\sigma \\in \\Sigma\\) as a singular point event, even though some---such as fix deployed \\(\\mathbf{D}\\)---would be more accurately described as diffusion or multi-agent processes.</p> <p>That is, by the time a vulnerability case reaches the point of remediating individual instances of vulnerable deployments, every such instance has its own state to track in regards to whether \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) has occurred yet. To apply this model to real world observations, it may be pragmatic to adapt the event definition to include some defined threshold criteria.</p> <p>However, this problem is equivalent to an existing problem in VM practice: how best to address the question of whether the fix for a vulnerability has been deployed across the enterprise. Other organizations might track fix deployments by risk groups, for example by differentiating between end user systems, servers, and network infrastructure. The desired criteria (high median \\(\\alpha\\) score with low variance) would likely be unmet even though most users were protected.</p> <p>Similarly, a smaller set of vendor/product pairs might represent a disproportionate concentration of the total risk posed by a vulnerability. Again, aggregation across all vendor/product pairs could be misleading. In fact, risk concentration within a particular user population may lead to a need for strategies that appear inequitable at the vendor level while achieving greater outcome equity at a larger scale.</p> <p>Thinking about Risk</p> <p>User concentration is one way to think about risk, but it is not the only way.  Value density, as defined in SSVC is another.</p> <p>The core issue is that we lack a utility function to map from observed case histories to harm reduction.[^13] Potential features of such a function include aggregation across vendors and/or users. Alternatively, it may be possible to devise a method for weighting the achieved histories in an MPCVD case by some proxy for total user risk. Other approaches remain possible---for example, employing a heuristic to avoid catastrophic outcomes for all, then applying a weighted sum over the impact to the remaining users. Protocol. This is a normative section of the documentation.</p> <p>Here we describe the basic primitives necessary for the CVD Embargo Management (EM) process.</p> <p>For our purposes, an embargo is an informal agreement among peer CVD case Participants to refrain from publishing information about a vulnerability until some future point in time relative to the report at hand. Once an embargo has expired, there is no further restriction on publishing information about the vulnerability.</p> <p>Reminder</p> <p>Exploits are information about vulnerabilities too.</p> <p>CVD case Participants must be able to propose, accept, and reject embargo timing proposals according to their individual needs. Additionally, Participants may want to attempt to gain agreement that enables specific details about a vulnerability to be shared with other Participants or made public. Such content considerations are outside the scope of this proposal. We focus our discussion on the when of an embargo, not the what.</p> <p>Embargo Definition</p> <p>An embargo is an informal agreement among peer CVD case Participants to refrain from publishing information about a vulnerability until some future point in time.</p> <p>Unlike the RM model, in which each Participant has their own instance of the RM DFA, EM states are a global property of a CVD case.</p> <p>A CVD case SHALL NOT have more than one active embargo at a time.</p> <p>(We define the term active below.)</p> <p>Even in an MPCVD case having a vertical supply chain\u2014in which Vendors must wait on their upstream suppliers to produce fixes before they can take action on their own, as in the figure below\u2014our intent is that the embargo period terminates when as many Vendors as possible have been given an adequate opportunity to produce a fix.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: A Vertical Supply Chain\n---\nstateDiagram-v2\n    direction LR\n    v1: Originating&lt;br/&gt;Vendor\n    v2: Vendor 2\n    v3: Vendor 3\n    v4: Vendor 4\n    v5: Vendor 5\n    v6: Vendor 6\n\n    v1 --&gt; v2\n    v1 --&gt; v3\n    v2 --&gt; v4\n    v3 --&gt; v5\n    v2 --&gt; v5\n    v5 --&gt; v6</code></pre> <p></p> <p>CVD Embargoes Are Not NDAs</p> <p>CVD embargoes are not Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs). An NDA (also known as a Confidentiality agreement) is a legally binding contract between parties, often accompanied by a reward for compliance and/or some penalty in the event of unauthorized disclosure. NDAs do, on occasion, have a place in CVD processes, but the relatively rapid pace and scale of most MPCVD embargoes makes per-case NDAs prohibitively difficult. As a result, we are intentionally setting aside NDA negotiation as beyond the scope of this proposal.</p> <p>On the surface, many bug bounty programs may appear to fall outside our scope because they are often structured as  NDAs in which compliance is rewarded. For some bounty programs, the penalty for non-compliance or early disclosure is limited to the loss of the reward. For others, non-compliance can lead to the forfeiture of a promise of amnesty from the pursuit of civil or criminal charges that might otherwise apply because of security or acceptable-use policy violations. This is intentional, and it results directly from the asymmetry mentioned in Negotiating Embargoes The Receiver is faced with a choice to either accept the Reporter's proposal and attempt to extend it or to reject the proposal and end up with no embargo at all. Therefore, if we take the stance that for a vulnerability with no fix available, any embargo is better than no embargo, it should be obvious that it is in the Receiver's interest to accept even a short proposed embargo before immediately working to revise it.</p> <p>The alternative is impractical because the Reporter is not obligated to provide the report to the Receiver at all. In the scenario where a Reporter proposes a short embargo and the Receiver rejects it because it is not long enough, the Reporter might choose to exit the negotiation entirely and publish whenever they choose without ever providing the report to the Receiver. That is not to say that we recommend this sort of behavior from Reporters. In fact, we specifically recommend the opposite in Negotiating Embargoes. Rather, it once more acknowledges the time-dependent informational asymmetry inherent to the CVD process.</p> <p>A Logical Argument for Accepting the Shortest Proposed Embargo</p> <p>Perhaps the above reasoning comes across as too Machiavellian for some readers. Here is a different perspective: Say a Reporter proposes an embargo of n days, while the Vendor would prefer m days. If n and m are given in units of days, we can look at them as a series of individual agreements, each of 1 day in length. We will represent each Participant as a vector representing that Participant's willingness to perpetuate the embargo on each day. Embargo willingness will be represented as a 1 if the Participant is willing to commit to keeping the embargo on that day, and a 0 if they are not. For simplicity's sake, we assume that each Participant is willing to maintain the embargo up to a certain point, and then their willingness goes away. In other words, each vector will be a series of zero or more _1_s followed by zero or more _0_s. For example, \\([1,1,1,1,0,0,0]\\) represents a Participant's willingness to engage in a 4-day embargo.</p> <p>For our two Participants, let \\(\\mathbf{x}_ and _\\mathbf{y}\\) be zero-indexed vectors of length \\(max(n,m)\\).</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     |\\mathbf{x}| &amp;= max(n,m) \\\\     |\\mathbf{y}| &amp;= max(n,m) \\end{aligned}\\] <p>The elements of each vector represent each respective Participant's willingness for the embargo to persist on each consecutive day.</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     \\mathbf{x} =          \\begin{bmatrix} x_i :         x_i =          \\begin{cases}             1 &amp;\\text{if }i &lt; n \\\\             0 &amp;\\text{otherwise} \\\\         \\end{cases}         &amp; \\text{for } 0 \\leq i &lt; max(n,m)         \\end{bmatrix} \\\\     \\mathbf{y} =         \\begin{bmatrix} y_i :          y_i =          \\begin{cases}             1 &amp;\\text{if }i &lt; m \\\\             0 &amp;\\text{otherwise}         \\end{cases}         &amp; \\text{ for } 0 \\leq i &lt; max(n,m)     \\end{bmatrix} \\end{aligned}\\] <p>Note that we have constructed these vectors so that each vector's scalar sum is just the length of embargo they prefer.</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     \\Sigma(\\mathbf{x}) &amp;= n \\\\     \\Sigma(\\mathbf{y}) &amp;= m  \\end{aligned}\\] <p>Now we can define an agreement vector \\(\\mathbf{z}\\) as the pairwise logical AND (\\(\\wedge\\)) of elements from \\(\\mathbf{x}_ and _\\mathbf{y}\\):</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     \\mathbf{z} =      \\begin{bmatrix} z_i :          z_i = x_i \\land y_i         &amp; \\text{for }0 \\leq i &lt; max(n,m)     \\end{bmatrix} \\end{aligned}\\] <p>For example, if one party prefers an embargo of length \\(n=4\\) days while another prefers one of length \\(m=7\\) days, we can apply \\(\\mathbf{x}\\), \\(\\mathbf{y}\\), and \\(\\mathbf{z}\\) as follows:</p> \\[\\begin{split}     \\mathbf{x} &amp;= [1,1,1,1,0,0,0] \\\\     \\wedge~\\mathbf{y} &amp;= [1,1,1,1,1,1,1] \\\\     \\hline     \\mathbf{z} &amp;= [1,1,1,1,0,0,0]     \\end{split}\\] <p>From this, we can see that the scalar sum of the agreement vector---and therefore the longest embargo acceptable to both parties---is the lesser of n and m:</p> \\[\\Sigma ( \\mathbf{z} ) = min(n,m)\\] <p>As an example:</p> <p>The Shortest Proposed Embargo Wins</p> <p>If a Reporter proposes a 90-day embargo, but the Vendor prefers a 30-day embargo, we can think of this as a series of 1-day agreements in which both parties agree to the first 30 days of the embargo and disagree beyond that. By accepting the shorter 30-day embargo, the Reporter now has 30 days to continue negotiations with the Vendor to extend the embargo. Even if those continued negotiations fail, both parties get at least the 30-day embargo period they agreed on in the first place. This should be preferable to both parties versus the alternative of no embargo at all were they to reject the shorter proposal.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Embargo Agreement in a Nutshell\n---\nstateDiagram-v2\n    direction LR\n    dots: ...\n    state Agreement {\n        direction LR\n        [*] --&gt; 1\n        1 --&gt; 2\n        2 --&gt; dots\n        dots --&gt; 30\n        negotiate: negotiate extension\n        [*] --&gt; negotiate\n        negotiate --&gt; 30\n    }\n    30 --&gt; 31\n    state Disagreement {\n        dots2: ...\n        31 --&gt; dots2\n        dots2 --&gt; 90\n    }</code></pre> <p>Typically it is the Reporter who desires a shorter embargo than the Vendor. We chose our example to demonstrate that this analysis works between any two parties, regardless of which party wants the shorter embargo.</p> <p>Resolving Multiple Proposals at Once</p> <p>On our way to making this principle explicit, we immediately came across a second scenario worth a brief diversion: What to do when multiple revisions are up for negotiation simultaneously? Based on the idea of extending the above to an efficient pairwise evaluation of multiple proposals, we suggest the following heuristic:</p> <ol> <li>Sort the proposals in order from earliest to latest according to their expiration date.</li> <li>Set the current candidate to the earliest proposal.</li> <li>Loop over each remaining (later) proposal, evaluating it against the current candidate.</li> <li>If the newly evaluated proposal is accepted, it becomes the current candidate and the loop repeats.</li> <li>Otherwise, the loop exits at the first rejected proposal.</li> <li>The current candidate (i.e., the latest accepted proposal) becomes the new Active embargo.</li> <li>If the earliest proposed revision is rejected---implying that none of the later ones would be acceptable either---then the existing Active embargo remains intact.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"topics/process_models/em/defaults/#resolving-proposals-and-revisions","title":"Resolving Proposals and Revisions","text":"<p>Summarizing the principles just laid out as rules</p> <p>When two or more embargo proposals are open (i.e., none have yet been accepted) and \\(q^{em} \\in P\\), Participants SHOULD accept the shortest one and propose the remainder as revisions.</p> <p>When two or more embargo revisions are open (i.e., an embargo is active yet none of the proposals have been decided) and \\(q^{em} \\in R\\), Participants SHOULD accept or reject them individually, in earliest to latest expiration order.</p>"},{"location":"topics/process_models/em/early_termination/","title":"Early Termination","text":"<p>This page is normative</p> <p>This page is considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol. Protocol. This is a normative section of the documentation.</p> <p>Embargoes are a means of inhibiting public disclosure of a vulnerability while defenses are prepared (e.g., until fix development has completed for a reasonable quorum of Vendors).</p> <p>The goal of the EM process is not to establish an exact publication schedule for every Participant to adhere to. Rather,</p> <p>Embargo Management Process Goal</p> <p>The goal of the Embargo Management process is to establish a window spanning from the present to some future time, during which Participants are expected to not publish or otherwise disclose information about the vulnerability to non-Participants outside of the CVD case.</p> <p>Hence our definition of an embargo:</p> <p>Embargo Definition</p> <p>An embargo is an informal agreement among peer CVD case Participants to refrain from publishing information about a vulnerability until some future point in time.</p>"},{"location":"topics/process_models/em/principles/#embargoes-are-a-social-agreement","title":"Embargoes Are a Social Agreement","text":"<p>An embargo is a social agreement between independent parties acting in the interest of providing vulnerability fixes to users in a timely manner while minimizing attacker advantage in the interim. The more people involved in an embargo, the more likely the embargo is to fail.</p> <p>Embargo participation SHOULD be limited to the smallest possible set of individuals and organizations needed to adequately address the vulnerability report.</p> <p>Similarly, the longer an embargo lasts, the more likely it is to fail.</p> <p>Embargo duration SHOULD be limited to the shortest duration possible to adequately address the vulnerability report.</p> <p>Furthermore, we need to establish a few norms related to embargo timing.</p> <p>An embargo SHALL specify an unambiguous date and time as its endpoint.</p> <p>An embargo SHALL NOT be used to indefinitely delay publication of vulnerability information, whether through repeated extension or by setting a long-range endpoint.</p> <p>An embargo SHALL begin at the moment it is accepted.</p> <p>Embargoes SHOULD be of short duration, from a few days to a few months.</p> <p></p> <p>CVD Embargoes Are Not NDAs</p> <p>CVD embargoes are not Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs). An NDA (also known as a Confidentiality agreement) is a legally binding contract between parties, often accompanied by a reward for compliance and/or some penalty in the event of unauthorized disclosure. NDAs do, on occasion, have a place in CVD processes, but the relatively rapid pace and scale of most MPCVD embargoes makes per-case NDAs prohibitively difficult. As a result, we are intentionally setting aside NDA negotiation as beyond the scope of this proposal.</p> <p>On the surface, many bug bounty programs may appear to fall outside our scope because they are often structured as  NDAs in which compliance is rewarded. For some bounty programs, the penalty for non-compliance or early disclosure is limited to the loss of the reward. For others, non-compliance can lead to the forfeiture of a promise of amnesty from the pursuit of civil or criminal charges that might otherwise apply because of security or acceptable-use policy violations. Built on CERT/CC's decades of experience coordinating global software vulnerability response, Vultron aims to serve as a lingua franca for sharing CVD case coordination data across independent organizations, tools, and policies. It targets security researchers, vulnerability coordinators, tool builders, and anyone seeking interoperability in the CVD ecosystem.</p> <p>Work in progress</p> <p>Vultron is a collection of ideas, models, code, and work in progress, and is not yet ready for production use. We are currently working on the documentation of the Vultron CVD Protocol. Our focus so far is on</p> <ul> <li>Explanation, which describes the   protocol in detail</li> <li>How-to Guides, which provides guidance for   potential implementations of Vultron</li> <li>Reference, which provides the formal   protocol specification</li> </ul> <p>Current Version</p> <p>The current version of the Vultron Protocol is</p> <p>2024.4.4.dev6496+gb9388ca98.d20260915</p>"},{"location":"#so-what-is-vultron","title":"So what is Vultron?","text":"<p>Looking for the full answer?</p> <p>See What Is Vultron? for an in-depth explanation aimed at CVD practitioners and systems architects evaluating whether to adopt the protocol.</p> <p>Vultron is:</p> <ul> <li>A set of high-level processes representing the steps involved in coordinated   vulnerability disclosure</li> <li>A formal protocol describing the interactions of those processes</li> <li>A set of behavior logic that can be implemented as either procedures for humans   to follow or (in many cases) code that can perform actions in response to state   changes in a case with minimal human input</li> <li>A minimal data model for what information is necessary to track participant   status and the overall case status through the course of handling a CVD case</li> </ul> <p>The above were all initially described in the Designing Vultron: A Protocol for Multi-Party Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (MPCVD) report. Therefore, our position is that end-to-end encryption would be better implemented as a layer on top of the ActivityPub protocol, rather than as a specific feature of the Vultron Protocol. From what we can tell, the topic has come up before in the ActivityPub community, but there is no standardized solution yet. We're currently focused on developing the Vultron Protocol, but we realize that encryption may be a requirement for widespread adoption, so we're keeping an eye on the topic.</p> <p>Some relevant links include:</p> <ul> <li>A November 2022 blog   post Towards End-to-End Encryption for Direct Messages in the Fediverse</li> <li>Issue #225 on the W3C ActivityPub Github repo talks about the   need for encrypted content, but it seems to have been closed without a solution in 2017.</li> <li>However, a much more       recent April 2023 comment       mentions:       &gt; If we restrict to direct message (with a single recipient) one may just encrypt the message (Note) payload using       the       public key of the recipient. So, if the recipient holds her own private key, she can decrypt the message payload.       The       main obstacle I see is the common practice to use HTTP signature, so that private kays must resides on server and       not       on clients.</li> <li>There have been numerous Discussions on the   ActivityPub SocialHub that mention end-to-end encryption.</li> </ul> <p>We are interested in any developments in this space, please let us know if you are aware of more recent developments. project.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#what-is-an-adr","title":"What is an ADR?","text":"<p>An architectural decision record (ADR) is a document that captures an important architectural decision made along with its context and consequences. We're using the expanded concept of an Any Decision Record (ADR) to capture any decision that is important to the project, not just architectural decisions. We use Markdown Any Decision Records (MADR) to document our architectural decisions.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#when-to-write-an-adr","title":"When to write an ADR","text":"<p>The primary signal for an ADR is evaluated alternatives: if you considered more than one option and rejected at least one, document the decision. The record preserves context for future maintainers who might otherwise re-open a settled question.</p> <p>Concretely, write an ADR when:</p> <ul> <li>You adopted a structural or architectural approach over one or more   alternatives (e.g., hexagonal architecture over layered, SQLModel over   TinyDB).</li> <li>You made a one-time process or tooling decision with lasting project-wide   impact (e.g., CalVer over SemVer, pinning CI action SHAs).</li> <li>A decision will be hard or costly to reverse, so the rationale should be   preserved explicitly.</li> </ul> <p>ADR vs. spec: an ADR records why a choice was made; a spec entry records what the system must do going forward. When a significant decision also generates recurring testable requirements, create both \u2014 see <code>notes/specs-vs-adrs.md</code> for the full delineation guidelines and worked examples.</p> <p>You do not need an ADR for:</p> <ul> <li>Uncontested conventions with no real alternatives (write a spec entry   instead).</li> <li>Small tactical choices where the rationale is obvious from the code.</li> </ul> <p>If you're unsure, err on the side of writing one \u2014 a brief ADR is better than losing context.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#revising-vs-amending-an-adr","title":"Revising vs. amending an ADR","text":"<p>An ADR records the decision that was made and why. Its value to a future reader is that they can understand the current expectation in one pass.</p> <p>When to revise in-place: If a recently-accepted ADR contains a statement that its own implementation contradicted \u2014 e.g., an option label that says \"rejected\" for something the chosen option actually requires, or a \"what is removed\" list that conflicts with MUST-level spec entries \u2014 revise the ADR body directly to make the current expectation accurate.</p> <p>When to write a new ADR: If the decision itself changed (you adopted a different option than originally chosen), write a new ADR that supersedes the old one.</p> <p>Do not append <code>### Amendment</code> sections: An append-only trail of amendments forces future readers to reconcile the body against its own addenda to determine which statement is currently authoritative. This defeats the primary purpose of the record. The only exception is an ADR with <code>status: provisional</code> where the amendment explicitly finalises that status.</p> <p>Source: ISSUE-1777 / learning 2026-07-31</p>"},{"location":"adr/#how-to-write-an-adr","title":"How to write an ADR","text":"<p>For new ADRs, please use adr-template.md as basis. implemented as ActivityPub actors with inboxes and outboxes. Inbound messages are ActivityStreams objects, typically Activities that include domain-specific objects (e.g., Vulnerability Reports).</p> <p>Early prototypes implemented inbound message handling using a layered routing model:</p> <ul> <li>Inbox handler</li> <li>Activity-type handler</li> <li>Object-type handler</li> <li>Downstream \u201cwork\u201d execution</li> </ul> <p>This approach introduced several problems:</p> <ul> <li>Loss of semantic cohesion: separating activity handling from object handling discarded context required to determine correct behavior; downstream workers had to reconstruct state already known at receipt time.</li> <li>Poor alignment with existing behavior logic: Vultron already defines message types as (Activity Type, Object Type) tuples, with corresponding behavior trees defined in the protocol simulator. The routing model obscured this mapping.</li> <li>Tight coupling of protocol handling and execution: the inbox handler effectively controlled execution flow, making asynchronous or distributed execution difficult.</li> <li>Deployment inflexibility: the design did not cleanly support both local development (\u201cgit clone + docker-compose up\u201d) and integration into environments with job queues or workers.</li> </ul> <p>These issues indicated a missing architectural boundary between protocol handling and behavior execution.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0007-use-behavior-dispatcher/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Preserve semantic context when invoking behavior</li> <li>Align runtime </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0007-use-behavior-dispatcher/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Keep layered routing inside the inbox handler (current approach)</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0007-use-behavior-dispatcher/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: \"Introduce a Behavior Dispatcher abstraction between inbox handling and and implementation-agnostic with respect to invocation mechanics.</li> <li>Enables multiple implementations (in-process direct invocation or queued/asynchronous invocation), supporting both local development and distributed deployments.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0007-use-behavior-dispatcher/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good:</li> <li>Removes redundant ActivityStreams 2.0 (AS2) structural types leaked into domain logic; semantic extraction was scattered across multiple files; handler functions instantiated the persistence layer directly; and the root <code>vultron/</code> package mixed domain enums with wire-format enums. An architectural review (<code>archived_notes/architecture-review.md</code>) catalogued twelve violations of the intended separation of concerns, ranging in severity from minor to critical. A clear architecture decision was needed to guide remediation and prevent the same violations from re-accumulating.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0009-hexagonal-architecture/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Wire format replaceability: AS2 is the current wire format because its   vocabulary matches Vultron's domain vocabulary. That match must not collapse   the boundary between wire concerns and domain concerns.  If AS2 is replaced   or extended, the change must be absorbable in the wire layer alone.</li> <li>Testability: Core domain logic should be testable with plain domain   objects, without constructing AS2 activities or making HTTP requests.</li> <li>Single extraction seam: The mapping from AS2 vocabulary to domain   semantics must live in exactly one place so that future wire format changes   have a single point of entry.</li> <li>Dependency injection over direct instantiation: Driven adapters   (persistence, delivery) must be injectable to support testing and alternate   backends.</li> <li>Alignment with existing clean points: Several existing patterns are   already architecturally sound (the <code>DataLayer</code> Protocol, <code>DispatchEvent</code>   wrapper, <code>MessageSemantics</code> enum vocabulary, FastAPI 202 + BackgroundTasks)   and should be preserved.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0009-hexagonal-architecture/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Continue organic layering \u2014 Impose light conventions without a formal   architecture pattern. Use a separate wire layer for AS2   parsing and semantic extraction.</li> <li>Clean layered architecture (no hexagon) \u2014 Impose strict top-down   layering (controller \u2192 service \u2192 from the domain \u2014 a property that is especially important given that AS2 and the Vultron domain vocabulary are semantically isomorphic and will otherwise naturally collapse.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0009-hexagonal-architecture/#layer-model","title":"Layer Model","text":"<p>Four layers are defined:</p> <pre><code>wire (AS2 JSON)\n    \u2193\nAS2 Parser requires every object to have an <code>id</code> field. The <code>generate_new_id()</code> utility in <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/base/utils.py</code> currently returns a bare UUID-4 string (e.g., <code>2196cbb2-fb6f-407c-b473-1ed8ae806578</code>) as the default <code>as_id</code> for new objects. The AS2 specification and the Vultron object-IDs spec (<code>specs/object-ids.yaml</code> OID-01-001) require that <code>id</code> values be full URI identifiers. Bare UUIDs are not valid AS2 identifiers and will cause interoperability problems once federation is implemented.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0010-standardize-object-ids/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>AS2 compliance: ActivityStreams 2.0 requires <code>id</code> to be an absolute   IRI.
