Bare UUIDs cannot be resolved across systems.</li> <li>Blackboard key safety: py_trees blackboard keys derived from full-URI   IDs must not use the raw URI (which contains slashes). Using the last path   segment or UUID suffix as the key avoids hierarchical key-parsing issues   (OID-03-001).</li> <li>DataLayer compatibility: The DataLayer uses <code>as_id</code> as the primary   lookup key. The pivot point \u2014 when a report transitions to <code>RM.VALID</code> and a case is created \u2014 is implemented ad hoc with no formal transition from the report-phase record to the case-phase record. New participant status records are seeded with <code>rm_state=RM.START</code> rather than carrying forward the current <code>RM.VALID</code> state.</p> <p>This creates a situation where:</p> <ul> <li>RM history for the pre-case phase is not queryable or auditable.</li> <li>RM transition guards on case-engagement cannot verify that a report was truly   valid before <code>ACCEPTED</code>/<code>DEFERRED</code> was appended.</li> <li>The RM machine's <code>RECEIVE</code> trigger (START \u2192 RECEIVED) is never explicitly   executed anywhere in the <code>vultron.core</code> pipeline.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0013-unify-rm-state-tracking/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Protocol correctness: RM state should be a <li>Simplicity: a single mechanism for RM state is easier to guard and query than   two unconnected mechanisms.</li> <li>Minimal disruption: changes should be incremental and testable.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0013-unify-rm-state-tracking/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Option A \u2014 Persist the full RM lifecycle in When these references use mutable identifiers \u2014 version tags (e.g., <code>@v4</code>) or branch names (e.g., <code>@main</code>) \u2014 a compromised or modified upstream action can silently inject malicious code into CI without any change to the repository. This is a known software supply-chain attack vector.</p> <p>The Vultron project uses GitHub Actions for CI (tests, linting, deployment, link-checking) and needs a sustainable, low-maintenance policy that prevents this class of attack while keeping pins up-to-date.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0014-sha-pin-github-actions/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Prevent supply-chain compromise via tag or branch mutation in upstream   actions.</li> <li>Keep the maintenance burden low so that pins do not become stale.</li> <li>Maintain human-readable context for each pin so that reviewers can   understand which version is pinned without decoding a SHA.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0014-sha-pin-github-actions/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>SHA-pin every <code>uses:</code> line; use Dependabot for automatic pin updates</li> <li>SHA-pin only third-party (non-<code>actions/</code>) actions</li> <li>Rely on version tags only (no SHA pinning)</li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0014-sha-pin-github-actions/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: Option 1 \u2014 SHA-pin every <code>uses:</code> line with Dependabot, because it provides complete protection against tag/branch mutation for all actions (including first-party GitHub actions that are also susceptible), while Dependabot automates the routine maintenance of keeping SHAs current.</p> <p>All six workflow files under <code>.github/workflows/</code> have been updated to pin every <code>uses:</code> reference to a full 40-character commit SHA. Each pin carries an inline comment with the human-readable version tag (e.g., <code># v4.1.0</code>). Dependabot is configured (<code>.github/dependabot.yml</code>) to monitor <code>github-actions</code> on a weekly schedule, providing automatic pull requests whenever a new version is released.</p> <p>An automated pytest test (<code>test/ci/test_workflow_sha_pinning.py</code>) verifies at every CI run that no unpinned <code>uses:</code> line is accidentally introduced.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0014-sha-pin-github-actions/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good: Every <code>uses:</code> line is immutable at the referenced commit,   eliminating supply-chain risk from tag or branch mutation.</li> <li>Good: Dependabot opens PRs automatically when new versions are   released, so pins do not become stale without manual tracking.</li> <li>Good: Inline version comments preserve human-readable context for   code review.</li> <li>Good: The automated test (<code>CISEC-01-003</code>) catches any regression   before it reaches <code>main</code>.</li> <li>Neutral: SHA-only references are harder to read without the version   comment, mitigated by the mandatory comment requirement   (<code>CISEC-01-002</code>).</li> <li>Bad: Dependabot may open PRs for patch and minor releases that have   not been security-reviewed; PR #577 added an <code>_STUB_OBJECT_MODEL_MAP</code> workaround in <code>outbox_handler.py</code> that covers only <code>VulnerabilityCase</code> and requires per-type manual registration.</p> <p>Wire-format concerns also leak into the domain: AS2 freely models a nested object as an inline object, a bare ID string, or a <code>Link</code> reference, which forces core fields into <code>Object | str | Link | None</code> unions. Statement","text":"<p>The two-actor demo CI invariant test (<code>test_invariant_5_expected_event_types_present</code>) failed after PR #1024 introduced the CASE_MANAGER role gate on <code>CommitCaseLedgerEntryNode</code>. Investigation (issue #1026) revealed that most vendor-side trigger and received-side use cases never send an activity to the CaseActor's inbox. Consequently the CaseActor's canonical ledger was missing entries for <code>validate_report</code>, <code>ack_report</code>, <code>add_note_to_case</code>, <code>invite_to_embargo_on_case</code>, <code>accept_invite_to_embargo_on_case</code>, and <code>close_case</code>.</p> <p>Deeper inspection found that some received-side use cases (<code>note.py</code>, <code>embargo.py</code>) worked around this by resolving the CaseActor's ID from the DataLayer and then executing <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code> with <code>actor_id=case_actor_id</code> \u2014 even when the use case was running inside the vendor actor's inbox, not the CaseActor's. This violates the identity contract documented in ADR-0018 and the identity-spoofing pitfall in <code>AGENTS.md</code>: a received-side use case MUST NOT execute a BT with an <code>actor_id</code> different from the actor whose DataLayer is active. The guarded commit BT emits <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> activities as if authored by the CaseActor while running in the wrong actor's outbox context, which is either silently dropped or produces hash-chain divergence.</p> <p>The project has stated this rule in scattered form across <code>AGENTS.md</code>, <code>notes/case-communication-model.md</code>, and <code>specs/case-ledger-processing.yaml</code>, but the explicit, ADR-level statement of the only correct end-to-end path has been missing. As a result, agents and contributors keep re-discovering the shortcut (resolve CaseActor ID, run BT) and believing it is a valid \"delegation\" pattern.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0021-caseactor-inbox-routing-canonical-ledger/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li><code>notes/case-communication-model.md</code> establishes that all post-creation   participant messages route through the Case Actor exclusively.</li> <li>ADR-0018 established a single-writer canonical ledger authored by the   CaseActor. ADR-0019 sharpened the content boundary of that ledger.</li> <li>The guarded-commit BT (<code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>)   already enforces the CASE_MANAGER role gate. The problem is that the   activity must arrive at the CaseActor's inbox before that gate can   fire; there is no inbox delivery mechanism for events that skip it.</li> <li>A received-side use case that resolves a foreign actor ID and runs a BT   under that ID is the same class of identity-spoofing bug documented for   the <code>PrioritizeBT(actor_id=invitee_id)</code> anti-pattern (PCR-08-009,   PCR-08-010).</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0021-caseactor-inbox-routing-canonical-ledger/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<p>Option A \u2014 Explicit trigger-tree emit + received-UC pre-flight guard (this ADR's decision). Every protocol-significant trigger tree emits an outbound activity addressed to <code>case_manager_id</code>. ASGI delivers it to the CaseActor's inbox. The CaseActor's received use case checks <code>receiving_actor_id == case_actor_id</code> before executing the guarded commit \u2014 and only executes it when the check passes. Non-CaseActor received use cases do nothing at the commit step; they rely on the fact that the CaseActor's inbox will separately receive the same activity.</p> <p>Option B \u2014 \"Delegation\" via foreign actor_id resolution. Received-side use cases resolve <code>case_actor_id</code> from the DataLayer and execute the guarded-commit BT with <code>actor_id=case_actor_id</code>, regardless of which actor is actually running the use case. This is the pattern found in <code>note.py</code> and <code>embargo.py</code> before this fix.</p> <p>Option C \u2014 Shared commit helper called directly (no BT). Received-side use cases call <code>commit_ledger_entry()</code> directly after resolving the CaseActor ID, bypassing the BT and the role gate.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0021-caseactor-inbox-routing-canonical-ledger/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: Option A \u2014 Explicit trigger-tree emit + received-UC pre-flight guard.</p> <p>The canonical ledger entry path is:</p> <pre><code>Trigger tree\n  \u2192 emits outbound activity addressed to case_manager_id\n  \u2192 ASGI delivers to CaseActor inbox\n  \u2192 CaseActor's received use case runs with actor_id = case_actor_id\n  \u2192 pre-flight guard: receiving_actor_id == case_actor_id  [PASS]\n  \u2192 guarded commit BT executes with actor_id = case_actor_id\n  \u2192 CommitCaseLedgerEntryNode authors and broadcasts CaseLedgerEntry\n</code></pre> <p>When the activity is received by a non-CaseActor actor:</p> <pre><code>Non-CaseActor received use case runs with actor_id \u2260 case_actor_id\n  \u2192 pre-flight guard: receiving_actor_id == case_actor_id  [FAIL]\n  \u2192 commit step skipped entirely \u2014 no delegation, no BT, no spoofing\n</code></pre> <p>The pre-flight guard MUST use <code>receiving_actor_id</code> (the actor whose inbox is active), not a separately resolved CaseActor ID. This is the pattern already implemented correctly in <code>status.py</code>'s <code>_commit_log_cascade_bt()</code> and MUST be applied to every received-side use case that participates in ledger entry authorship.</p> <p>Why <code>announce_case_ledger_entry</code> is excluded from <code>EXPECTED_EVENT_TYPES</code>: <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> is the replication envelope: the mechanism by which the CaseActor broadcasts its canonical entries to participants. It cannot appear as the <code>payloadSnapshot</code> of a canonical entry because the snapshot is the protocol activity that triggered the entry, not the replication envelope that delivers it. Including it in <code>EXPECTED_EVENT_TYPES</code> for the case-actor log creates a circular requirement that can never be satisfied without corrupting the ledger.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0021-caseactor-inbox-routing-canonical-ledger/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because the delivery mechanism (ASGI self-delivery) is the same   trusted path already proven to work for case creation and status events.   No new infrastructure is needed.</li> <li>Good, because the pre-flight guard keeps received-side use cases honest:   a use case that runs in a non-CaseActor inbox simply skips the commit step   instead of spoofing the CaseActor's identity.</li> <li>Good, because the rule is symmetric with the existing \"actor MUST NOT   spoof another actor's identity\" pitfall and can be enforced structurally   (the BT's CASE_MANAGER role gate fires naturally once the activity arrives   at the right inbox).</li> <li>Bad, because every trigger tree that currently omits an emit node needs   one added \u2014 this is a mechanical but non-trivial change spread across   multiple trees.</li> <li>Bad, because received-side use cases that currently use the Option B   shortcut must have their shortcut removed and replaced with a strict   pre-flight guard, which is a semantics-changing fix that requires new   tests.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0021-caseactor-inbox-routing-canonical-ledger/#validation","title":"Validation","text":"<ul> <li><code>specs/case-ledger-processing.yaml</code> CLP-10 codifies the requirements   from this ADR as MUST-level rules.</li> <li>CI test <code>test_invariant_5_expected_event_types_present</code> (parameterized   per event type after issue #1026 implementation) is promoted from <code>xfail</code>   to a hard assertion for each event type as its routing gap is closed.</li> <li>A grep-based test (CLP-09-002) asserts that no bare, unguarded commit   invocation exists outside the guarded-commit factory.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0021-caseactor-inbox-routing-canonical-ledger/#clarification-caseactor-originated-activities-issue-1287","title":"Clarification: CaseActor-Originated Activities (Issue #1287)","text":"<p>The canonical path above applies symmetrically when the CaseActor is the originator, not just when it is a relay target. The CaseActor is a participant with extra duties; it is not exempt from CLP-10-001.</p> <p>When the CaseActor originates an activity (e.g., <code>invite_actor_to_case</code>), the activity is addressed to the external recipient(s) via <code>to:</code>. To ensure the CaseActor's own inbox receives the activity for archival, the CaseActor MUST add its own actor ID to the <code>cc:</code> field of the outbound activity. ASGI self-delivery then routes the <code>cc:</code> copy to the CaseActor's received-side use case, where the <code>GuardedCommitCaseLedgerEntryBT</code> fires under the correct <code>actor_id = case_actor_id</code> identity.</p> <p>Why <code>cc:</code> instead of adding <code>case_actor_id</code> to <code>to:</code>: The primary recipient of an <code>Invite(VulnerabilityCase)</code> is the invitee. The CaseActor's copy is an archival side-channel, not a primary delivery. Using <code>to:</code> for both would misrepresent the CaseActor as a co-primary recipient of its own outbound message. <code>cc:</code> preserves the correct semantic: the invitee is in <code>to:</code>, the self-archival copy is in <code>cc:</code>. OX-08-004 narrows its WARNING scope to exclude this purposeful self-copy pattern (the only valid use of <code>cc:</code> in the protocol).</p> <p>The working precedent for this pattern is <code>offer_case_manager_role</code>: its <code>ResolveCaseManagerOfferContextNode</code> sets <code>blackboard.offer_case_manager_to = [case_actor_id]</code> and the Offer is addressed to the CaseActor's own ID in <code>to:</code> (a special case where the CaseActor is genuinely the primary recipient). The <code>invite_actor_to_case</code> fix follows the same principle but uses <code>cc:</code> because the invitee is the primary recipient.</p> <p>Distinguishing self-delivery from external delivery in received-side use cases: The CaseActor's received-side <code>InviteActorToCaseReceivedUseCase</code> does not need to special-case \"did I send this myself?\" \u2014 the <code>GuardedCommitCaseLedgerEntryBT</code>'s <code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code> role gate is the only pre-flight guard needed. Statement","text":"<p>ADR-0021 established that the CaseActor's own inbox delivery is the sole path to a canonical ledger commit, and introduced a pre-flight guard (CLP-10-002, CLP-10-003): a received-side use case compares <code>receiving_actor_id</code> to the resolved <code>case_actor_id</code> in Python before deciding whether to execute the guarded-commit BT (<code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>).</p> <p>Issue #1036 found that implementing that guard produced a second anti-pattern: every adopting use case now runs two separate <code>BTBridge.execute_with_setup()</code> calls per inbox delivery \u2014 one for the use case's main operation (often under the message's own actor identity, e.g. the invitee or accepting actor), and a second, conditionally dispatched call for the guarded commit (under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>). The condition that decides whether the second call happens at all is plain Python control flow (<code>if receiving_actor_id != case_actor_id: return</code>), not a node inside either tree.</p> <p>An audit (issue #1036, broadened during planning to also resolve a follow-on Concern, issue #1047, which independently named the same anti-pattern in <code>status.py</code> and asked for it to be codified as a spec-level invariant) found the underlying violation in 9 use cases across 6 modules, but not all in the same precise shape. There are three distinct ways the \"execute() does nothing but build one tree, run it once, handle the result\" intent was violated:</p> <p>(1) Genuine actor-identity switching \u2014 a real second <code>execute_with_setup()</code> call under a different actor than the main operation's. This is the literal anti-pattern #1036 and #1047 describe:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/embargo.py</code>:   <code>RemoveEmbargoEventFromCaseReceivedUseCase</code>,   <code>InviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase</code>,   <code>AcceptInviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 main tree runs under   <code>request.actor_id</code> / <code>invitee_id</code> / <code>accepting_actor_id</code>; a second,   separately constructed <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>   runs under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>. Notably, the main tree (built by   <code>vultron/core/behaviors/embargo/announce_teardown_tree.py</code>'s factory   functions) already composes the identical guarded-commit branch as its   own last child \u2014 but because the main tree executes under the   invitee's/accepting actor's identity, <code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code> inside it   is a guaranteed no-op (that actor is essentially never the CaseActor).   The second, separately-dispatched call is the one that actually fires,   on the rare second attempt under the correct identity. The fix is not   \"add a guarded-commit branch\" (it already exists) \u2014 it is \"stop calling   the tree under the wrong actor a second time, and run the one tree that   already has the branch under <code>receiving_actor_id</code> instead.\"</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/report.py</code>:   <code>ValidateReportReceivedUseCase</code> (main operation is a separate   <code>ValidateCaseUseCase</code> call under <code>actor_id</code>, not even a tree of its own),   <code>AckReportReceivedUseCase</code> (main tree under <code>request.actor_id</code>) \u2014 both   followed by a second, separately-gated guarded-commit call under   <code>receiving_actor_id</code>/<code>case_actor_id</code>.</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/status.py</code>:   <code>AddParticipantStatusToParticipantReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 main tree   (<code>add_participant_status_tree</code>) under <code>request.actor_id</code>, then a second   guarded-commit call under <code>case_actor_id</code> via <code>_commit_log_cascade_bt()</code>.   This is the exact site #1047 cited as its primary evidence.</li> </ul> <p>(2) Single BT call, but non-BT procedural code precedes it \u2014 only one <code>execute_with_setup()</code> call exists (the commit), but <code>execute()</code> still does domain-significant work outside any tree before reaching it, so it is not \"build one tree, run it, handle the result\" either:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/note.py</code>: <code>AddNoteToCaseReceivedUseCase</code>   \u2014 appends to <code>case.notes</code>, calls <code>dl.save()</code>, and broadcasts to peers, all   in plain Python, before the single guarded-commit <code>execute_with_setup()</code>   call.</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/actor/case_manager_role.py</code>:   <code>OfferCaseManagerRoleReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 idempotent-creates the activity   and calls a trigger-activity port directly in Python, before the single   guarded-commit call. This is a pre-existing BT-06-001 gap (the main   operation was never expressed as a BT at all), not actor-switching.</li> </ul> <p>(3) Single BT call under the correct actor, but assembled ad hoc \u2014 no actor-switching and no procedural code outside the tree, but the tree itself is built inline in <code>execute()</code> rather than via a <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> factory function:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/case/lifecycle.py</code>:   <code>CloseCaseReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 constructs a one-off   <code>py_trees.composites.Sequence</code> directly inside <code>execute()</code>, combining   <code>StoreActivityNode</code> and the guarded-commit subtree, and runs it once   under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>. This already satisfies the actor-identity   requirement; the fix here is purely \"move this tree into a named factory   function in <code>behaviors/case/</code>,\" not an actor-switching repair.</li> </ul> <p>All nine sites import <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code> directly into <code>vultron/core/use_cases/</code>, which is what the structural test (below) detects \u2014 but the underlying defect, and the fix required, differs by category. This is the same class of problem the \"Post-BT Procedural Cascade Anti-Pattern\" (<code>notes/bt-integration.md</code>) already names for the validate\u2192prioritize cascade: a cascade that is a child of the triggering operation in the canonical model must be expressed as a BT subtree, not as a procedural call (or a second, conditionally-dispatched tree execution, or any other domain-significant code) sitting outside the tree in <code>execute()</code>. The fact that the in-tree guard (<code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code>) is itself correctly role-gated does not fix category (1): the decision of whether to even ask the question is still made in Python, once per inbox delivery, instead of being one branch of one BT run.</p> <p>A related architectural question raised during planning \u2014 whether the inbox dispatch pipeline itself needs to be restructured so a use case never has to ask \"which actor am I running as\" \u2014 turned out not to apply. The dispatcher (<code>vultron/core/dispatcher.py</code>) has no CaseActor awareness and needs none \u2014 it is a pure routing-table lookup keyed on <code>semantic_type</code>. The gap is entirely at the use-case/BT boundary, not the dispatch layer; no change to ADR-0020's proposed <code>process_payload</code> seam is required by this decision.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0022-single-bt-execution-for-received-side-case-actor-routing/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The BT is the domain documentation (<code>specs/behavior-tree-integration.yaml</code> BT-06-001); a cascade that is invisible outside the tree structure is   invisible to analysis and audit, regardless of whether the gating logic   is \"correct\" in isolation.</li> <li>CLP-09-001 already requires the commit to be reached only through a   role-gated composition \u2014 a Selector/Sequence/Success idiom evaluated   inside the tree. A concrete capability may embody one shape or combine shapes (e.g., a Participant Discovery capability composes Retriever + Evaluator).</p>"},{"location":"adr/0024-coordination-agent-taxonomy/#three-level-taxonomy","title":"Three-level taxonomy","text":"<p>The taxonomy operates at three levels of specificity:</p> Level Term Definition 1 Capability shape One of the five abstract interface contracts (Sentinel, Evaluator, Retriever, Composer, Actuator); characterises the interaction pattern without prescribing the implementation 2 Capability A specific named call-out point with its own blackboard contract (e.g., <code>EvaluateReportCredibility</code>); implements a capability shape for a particular domain context 3 Capability implementation The factory backend fulfilling a capability at runtime; may be a Python function, a human workflow, a rules engine, or an LLM agent <p>\"Coordination Agent\" is retired. The term implied a specific kind of implementor (an autonomous AI entity) when the shapes are actually abstract interface contracts. A capability implementation may be anything that honours the blackboard contract. The implementation choice is made at deployment time, not at design time.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0024-coordination-agent-taxonomy/#amendment-2026-07-07-fifth-canonical-shape-actuator","title":"Amendment (2026-07-07): Fifth canonical shape \u2014 Actuator","text":"<p>During the FUZZ-08a-ter audit (PR #1195, issue #1239), 11 nodes classified as <code>Composer</code> were found not to generate content artifacts in the ADR-0024 sense. They are side-effect executors \u2014 integration hooks that fire when a protocol state transition occurs and invoke external systems (notification APIs, timer services, case management writes, queue mutations). The Composer lifecycle (reads context \u2192 dispatches \u2192 writes artifact to blackboard) does not map to these nodes: there is no content artifact placed on the blackboard. Expanding the Composer definition to cover side-effect invocation was considered and rejected \u2014 it would obscure the seam and complicate the abstraction layer design (ADR-0025 / issue #1151), which needs an invocation interface for Actuators, not a content-generation interface.</p> <p>A fifth capability shape is added:</p> Shape Role Actuator Receives a trigger and context; invokes an external system to cause a side effect (notification dispatch, state write, queue mutation, API call); returns SUCCESS when the side effect is confirmed, FAILURE otherwise. A Sentinel monitors a condition over time and fires a trigger endpoint when that condition is met.</p> <p>A capability that queries an external system synchronously and returns only a binary (yes/no) result is still a Retriever capability: a boolean is the simplest possible structured fact. The defining characteristic is the synchronous on-demand query pattern, not the richness of the returned data.</p> <p>Nodes such as <code>MitigationDeployed</code>, <code>MitigationAvailable</code>, and <code>HaveExploit</code> fit the Retriever shape: they receive a query (implicitly, \"is X the case?\"), call an external system to retrieve the current status, and return SUCCESS/FAILURE based on that status. They do not monitor continuously or fire a trigger \u2014 they answer a point-in-time question when the BT reaches them.</p> <p>A Sentinel, by contrast, runs continuously (or is invoked by an external event) and calls a trigger endpoint when a condition becomes true. After FUZZ-01 through FUZZ-07 (#860\u2013#866), each call-out point has a probabilistic fuzzer node as its stand-in. The fuzzer is not a permanent implementation: it is an adapter that will be replaced over time by real data lookups, policy evaluations, or capability implementations.</p> <p>Before those replacements can happen, the call-out points must be expressed as proper injection seams: the BT tree must be built so that the fuzzer is the default backend, not the only option. Without an abstraction layer, swapping any call-out point requires finding and editing the concrete node class instead of injecting a different factory \u2014 and with roughly 93 call-out point nodes across all domains, the maintenance burden is unacceptable.</p> <p>The design question is: What mechanism makes each call-out point backend swappable while remaining consistent with the existing py_trees Behaviour pattern, factory-function conventions, and blackboard contract model?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0025-call-out-point-abstraction-layer/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Must be consistent with the existing BT factory-function pattern   (tree composition functions, not ad-hoc node instantiation)</li> <li>Must allow individual call-out points to be swapped without changing the   calling tree structure (incremental replacement)</li> <li>Must maintain the same blackboard contract whether the backend is a fuzzer   or a real implementation \u2014 downstream nodes must be unaffected by the swap</li> <li>Must keep simulation artifacts (<code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/</code>) out of   <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> (BT-16-001)</li> <li>Must be compatible with the five capability shapes from ADR-0024 (Sentinel,   Evaluator, Retriever, Composer, Actuator), each of which has different   input/output semantics</li> <li>Must support partial replacement: a scenario can use real implementations   for some call-out points and fuzzer backends for others in the same run</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0025-call-out-point-abstraction-layer/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>No abstraction \u2014 leave fuzzer nodes as concrete hardcoded classes; This rule is not specific to participant roles. ASK-01-004 states it for every ask: the ask is authoritative and the reply is only a yes. Whatever action a reply authorizes MUST be read from the stored ask, never from the reply's content \u2014 otherwise the answerer can alter what it grants itself, in any exchange, not just this one. ADR-0080 also adds the time dimension: an ask carries a deadline, and for ask kinds whose expiry is void, a reply arriving after it does not authorize the action (ASK-03-006). Trusting when a reply arrives is the same class of mistake as trusting what it claims.</p> <p>The routing tree and stored-ask record described below are the reference implementations the ADR-0080 primitive generalizes; see <code>notes/protocol-asks.md</code>.</p> <p>When the CaseActor processes <code>Accept(Offer(CaseParticipant))</code> from the Case Owner, the roles assigned to the new participant MUST be taken from the stored outgoing <code>Offer(CaseParticipant)</code> that the CaseActor sent, not from the embedded <code>CaseParticipant</code> object inside the received <code>Accept</code>.</p> <p>Why this is a security boundary, not just an implementation detail:</p> <ul> <li>The accepting actor (Case Owner) may modify the embedded <code>CaseParticipant</code>   in the <code>Accept</code> payload, or may send only a bare ID reference.</li> <li>Reading roles from the received <code>Accept</code> allows the accepting actor to   unilaterally escalate or modify the roles the invitee would receive.</li> <li>The stored <code>Offer</code> is the CaseActor's own record of what was proposed;   it is the authoritative source of truth for the intended participant roles.</li> </ul> <p>Failure pattern that violates this rule:</p> <ul> <li>Reading the <code>CaseParticipant</code> role list from <code>event.object_.roles</code>   (the object embedded in the received <code>Accept</code>) instead of from the   stored <code>Offer</code> activity.</li> <li>Reading roles from the BT blackboard across ticks: the blackboard is   cleared between BT executions, so a role written in the offer-received   tick is gone by the accept-received tick.</li> </ul> <p>Implementation: the CaseActor stores the outgoing <code>Offer(CaseParticipant)</code> in its DataLayer at offer-emit time. At accept-received time, it reads the stored offer to recover the intended roles, then creates the participant record. These silent failures propagate far from their source \u2014 the error surfaces at the point of use rather than the point of origin, making debugging difficult and creating a class of bug where program state is quietly corrupted or silently skipped.</p> <p>The root cause is structural: loose wire-layer types (where <code>Optional</code> fields are correct \u2014 AS2 permits many fields to be absent) leak directly into core logic without being promoted to tighter representations. Core functions then defensively guard every field they actually require.</p> <p>A secondary symptom is collection-typed fields and parameters that default to <code>None</code> instead of an empty collection, forcing every call-site to write <code>x or []</code> / <code>x or {}</code> boilerplate before iteration.</p> <p>The DataLayer already established the right precedent: <code>dl.read()</code> raises <code>VultronNotFoundError</code> rather than returning <code>None</code>. Changes","text":""},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p><code>VulnerabilityCase</code> is the canonical \"fat class\" named in ADR-0032: one type represents a case at every lifecycle stage. Core functions that require a case to have reached a particular stage (e.g. \"there is an active embargo\") cannot express that requirement in their type signatures, so they fall back on runtime guards (<code>if case.active_embargo is None: ...</code>, <code>if case.current_status.em_state == EM.ACTIVE: ...</code>).</p> <p>The Idea (#1362) proposed distinct types per lifecycle stage \u2014 illustratively <code>IncomingReport</code>, <code>TriagedCase</code>, <code>ActiveCase</code> \u2014 so a core function accepting a stage-specific type would reject earlier-stage data at the type level, with no <code>if x is None</code> needed. The Idea explicitly deferred deriving the actual stages from the protocol until a design was reviewed.</p> <p>Two protocol facts, verified against the code, shape the answer and make the naive \"one type per RM state\" framing unworkable:</p> <ol> <li>RM state is per-participant, not case-universal. Each <code>CaseParticipant</code>    runs its own RM state machine (<code>ParticipantStatus.rm_state</code>). There is no    such thing as \"the case is in RM.VALID\" \u2014 valid according to whom? A case    type named <code>ValidCase</code>/<code>TriagedCase</code> would be ill-defined.</li> <li>Only a few facts are genuinely case-universal. Case existence,    structural minimums (\u22651 report, reporter + receiver participants), the    embargo state (<code>EM</code>, one per case), and public state (<code>pxa</code>) are the only    monotonic facts that hold case-wide.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Make illegal shapes unrepresentable in core logic (ADR-0032 continuation).</li> <li>Do not introduce a type whose fields are identical to its parent's \u2014 that is   ceremony without a type-checker payoff and invites combinatorial proliferation   (2\u00b3 for the independent P/X/A dimensions alone).</li> <li>The design must survive DataLayer round-trip: rehydration always yields a   valid object, so the design must specify how a rehydrated record acquires its   staged type.</li> <li>Reuse the existing precedents: the role-specific <code>CaseParticipant</code> subclasses,   the <code>RM_ACTIVE</code> / <code>EM_NEGOTIATING</code> state-group tuples, and the   <code>is_rm_at_least()</code> predicate family.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>One type per RM/EM/CS state \u2014 rejected: RM is per-participant, so most    such types are ill-defined at the case level.</li> <li>Staged types on every state-bearing class, keyed on any monotonic    milestone \u2014 rejected: proliferates types that add no fields.</li> <li>Field-set-anchored staged types (chosen): a milestone earns a type only    when it changes the guaranteed (non-None) field set; everything else is    modeled as predicates + preconditions.</li> </ol> <p>For the mechanism of the chosen option, two sub-options were weighed and are recorded under \"Pros and Cons\": Pydantic subclasses narrowing fields (recommended) vs. a discriminated union of sibling types.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: field-set-anchored staged types.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#governing-principle","title":"Governing principle","text":"<p>A lifecycle milestone earns a distinct staged type only when it changes the set of guaranteed (required, non-None) fields. Each Actor is an isolated process: it owns a DataLayer of core domain objects, and (per the Actor Knowledge Model) its knowledge of the world is bounded strictly by what it has received. No actor can reach into another actor's DataLayer. Wire (AS2) exists solely as the transport by which one actor's core state informs another's \u2014 an AS2 Activity is an envelope carrying a core domain fact across the process boundary, not a domain object in its own right.</p> <p>ADR-0017 established that wire is a projection of core, and ARCH-09-001 requires core models to be as rich as or richer than their wire counterparts. The 29 AS2 protocol Activities (<code>Offer</code>, <code>Invite</code>, <code>Accept</code>, <code>Reject</code>, \u2026) break this: they were built wire-first and were never given a core counterpart. For these types the projection is inverted \u2014 wire is the only representation, and is therefore richer than core.</p> <p>The concrete consequence: when an actor must remember what a message told it (the case id an <code>Invite</code> carried, the recommender an <code>Offer</code> named, the report embedded in a submit <code>Offer</code>, the pending embargo proposal for a case), there is no core object to hold that fact, so core reaches back through the DataLayer and re-reads the stored wire envelope \u2014 <code>dl.read(activity_id)</code> inside <code>vultron/core/</code>. Concern #1506 audited these sites. ADR-0034 recognised activity read-back as a boundary violation but explicitly scoped it out and deferred it to a separate concern; this ADR is that concern's decision.</p> <p>The <code>dl.read(activity_id)</code> call in core is a symptom. The root cause is a missing layer of core domain representation for protocol facts. A second, subtler question surfaced during analysis: emitting a reply (e.g. an <code>Accept</code>) requires the full inline verbatim original activity in the reply's <code>object_</code> (the Actor Knowledge Model forbids bare URIs), and activity ids are non-regenerable random <code>urn:uuid:</code> values \u2014 so the original envelope cannot be losslessly reconstructed from core state. Does that legitimise reading a stored activity back?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0035-core-activity-representation-and-envelope-reconstitution/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Restore \"wire is a projection of core\" (ADR-0017) and ARCH-09-001: every   domain fact an actor remembers MUST have a home in core.</li> <li>Honour ARCH-03-001 (AS2\u2194domain mapping happens in exactly one place, the   semantic extractor) \u2014 core MUST NOT re-interpret an activity a second time.</li> <li>Honour ARCH-01-002 / DL-05: wire vocabulary types MUST NOT enter core through   the persistence port.</li> <li>Do not regress into cloning each AS2 Activity into a 1:1 core Activity class \u2014   the generic-event-mirroring-AS2 anti-pattern <code>notes/domain-model-separation.md</code>   warns against.</li> <li>Satisfy the Actor Knowledge Model's requirement that replies embed the full   inline original activity, given that activity ids are not regenerable.</li> <li>Keep the migration measurable and regression-proof via the DL-05-004 ratchet.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0035-core-activity-representation-and-envelope-reconstitution/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>A. The extractor   records the domain fact each inbound message carries as core state (a   transition on an existing core entity or a purpose-built core record) at   interpretation time. Core reads that core state; correlation between messages   (Accept\u2192Invite) flows through a core-entity relationship. Correlation \u2014 which prior message this one answers Core-entity relationship MUST resolve through a domain relationship, not a wire re-read (DL-06-003). That stream travels over a transport with no ordering guarantee, and Vultron may not be the only protocol implementation on the wire, so a replica can receive an entry before its hash-chain predecessor arrives.</p> <p>The original receive path (<code>CheckHashOrRejectOnMismatchNode</code>) treated any entry whose <code>prev_log_hash</code> did not match the local tail as a divergence: it dropped the entry and sent a <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> so the CaseActor would replay the missing prefix. At case closure this stalled a late-joining replica (Vendor2 in the FVV/FVCV demos) indefinitely and <code>wait_for_contiguous_ledger_coverage</code> timed out (issue #1556). How should a replica handle an entry that is valid but arrives before its predecessor?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Convergence must not depend on <code>Announce</code> delivery order (SYNC-10-004 requires   a contiguous prefix; the transport does not provide ordering).</li> <li>The fix must interoperate with unknown implementations \u2014 we cannot assume the   sender retries, or that any recovery message is delivered in order either.</li> <li>Must preserve the effects-before-persist invariant (SYNC-12-001) and the   DataLayer-presence-means-committed invariant (SYNC-13-001).</li> <li>Bounded memory under a broken or hostile peer that streams far-future entries.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>A. Repair the <code>Reject \u2192 replay</code> loop only \u2014 keep dropping out-of-order   entries; make the CaseActor reliably process the participant's Reject and   replay the missing prefix promptly.</li> <li>B. Receiver-side buffering \u2014 hold out-of-order entries locally and apply   them in hash-chain order once their predecessor arrives.</li> <li>C. Both \u2014 buffering plus a hardened replay loop.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: B, receiver-side buffering (which subsumes most of C).</p> <p>Option A alone is insufficient: the replay path re-announces each missing entry as a separate <code>Announce</code>, which travels the same unordered transport and can reorder again \u2014 hitting the very same drop. Repairing replay narrows the race but cannot close it under adversarial reordering. Buffering, by contrast, makes convergence order-independent: any valid entry is retained until the entry that closes its gap arrives, then drained in order.</p> <p>Buffering also makes the existing <code>Reject \u2192 replay</code> recovery order-robust for free, because replayed entries flow through the same (now buffering) receive path. We therefore did not redesign the replay loop; we keep sending the <code>Reject</code> at buffer time purely as the backstop for entries that are genuinely lost (never delivered) rather than merely reordered. A companion correctness fix makes <code>SyncActivityAdapter.send_reject_log_entry</code> enqueue against the explicit receiving <code>actor_id</code> (like the announce path) instead of the DataLayer's own scope, so the Reject is delivered correctly even from a shared or differently-scoped DataLayer.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good: a late-joining replica converges to a contiguous prefix within a few   seconds of the tail arriving, regardless of <code>Announce</code> order (SYNC-10-004).</li> <li>Good: no new dependence on sender retry behavior \u2014 robust against other   implementations and lossy/reordering transports.</li> <li>Good: the buffer is a non-ledger holding area (SYNC-13-003), so the   \"DataLayer presence \u21d2 committed + effects applied\" invariant is preserved.</li> <li>Neutral: buffered state is in-memory and lost on restart; no durability is   required because the committed prefix survives the restart intact, and any   dropped forward-gap entries re-enter via the ordinary diverge/reject/replay   path (SYNC-14-002, SYNC-08-005) when the next <code>Announce</code> does not match the   committed tail.</li> <li>Bad: adds a per-actor in-memory structure and a drain step on the receive   path; bounded by a size cap with farthest-ahead eviction (recoverable via the   Reject backstop).</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#validation","title":"Validation","text":"<ul> <li><code>LedgerGapBuffer</code> unit tests (<code>test/core/models/test_ledger_gap_buffer.py</code>):   O(1) drain-next, multi-hop cascade, per-case isolation, duplicate/fork   handling, size-bound eviction, per-actor registry.</li> <li>Out-of-order regression tests through <code>AnnounceLedgerEntryReceivedUseCase</code>   (<code>test/core/use_cases/received/test_sync.py</code>): fully-reversed delivery,   single-gap click-into-place, multi-gap cascade, shuffled-replay convergence \u2014   each asserting no entry is permanently dropped.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#pros-and-cons-of-the-options","title":"Pros and Cons of the Options","text":""},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#a-repair-the-reject-replay-loop-only","title":"A. Repair the <code>Reject \u2192 replay</code> loop only","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because it reuses the existing recovery mechanism with no new state.</li> <li>Bad, because replay re-announces entries individually over the same unordered   transport, so the reorder-and-drop race reappears \u2014 it cannot guarantee   convergence under adversarial ordering.</li> <li>Bad, because correctness depends on the CaseActor reliably processing every   Reject during a rapid closure fan-out, which is exactly what failed.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#b-receiver-side-buffering","title":"B. Only recipients on a different host/port fall through to HTTP POST (<code>DemoHttpDeliveryAdapter</code>).</p> <p>This in-process shortcut makes the co-located case behave differently from the remote case. Vultron's protocol model treats every actor as an independent, autonomous federated peer whose only knowledge of the world comes from Activities it has received over its inbox (the Actor Knowledge Model, AKM-01). The ASGI shortcut violates the spirit of that model in practice: demos and tests that run actors co-located in one process exercise a delivery path that would not exist if those actors were deployed as separate containers. The result is false confidence \u2014 inter-actor delivery bugs (addressing, serialization, inbox routing) can be masked in-process and only surface once actors are genuinely separated.</p> <p>The shortcut also carries accidental complexity that exists solely to support in-process delivery: a <code>contextvars</code> reentrancy guard, scheme+netloc locality classification, and mount-prefix stripping (root cause of several delivery bugs: #531, #534, #557, and #558).</p> <p>Should Vultron keep the co-located ASGI fast path, or deliver everything uniformly over HTTP as if every recipient were remote?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0042-http-only-inter-actor-delivery/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Fidelity to the autonomous-actor model. \"Something that works for   remote must work for local too.\" Actors are independent peers; delivery   should not depend on co-location.</li> <li>Bug visibility. The reentrancy guard, locality check, and mount-prefix   stripping exist only because of the in-process shortcut.</li> <li>Agent/developer confusion. Its transition table, however, treats <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> as a pre-consent state: the only way out is <code>INVITE</code>, so consent can only ever be reached via <code>NO_EMBARGO \u2192 INVITED \u2192 SIGNATORY</code>.</p> <p>These two readings contradict each other, and the transition table's reading is wrong. Consent does not always arrive through an invitation:</p> <ol> <li> <p>Self-determined embargo. A Finder who creates a case for their own    finding and sets its default embargo is not invited by anyone. There is no    counterparty to issue an <code>Invite</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Embargo created with the case. Under ADR-0041, the CaseActor initializes    the default embargo during case initialization, in the same BT sequence that    adds the vendor (CASE_OWNER) and reporter participants. From the moment those    participants exist, an embargo is already in scope for them \u2014 so there is no    instant at which <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> is a truthful description of their position.</p> </li> <li> <p>Implicit consent (CM-14-005). The reporter's consent is expressed by    submitting the report. The spec requires they be seeded <code>SIGNATORY</code>; no    invitation is ever sent.</p> </li> </ol> <p>Forcing these paths through <code>INVITED</code> requires fabricating an invitation event that never occurred, and writing it into the canonical case ledger as though it had.</p> <p>The contradiction is already causing a silent MUST-level failure in production code. <code>_SignEmbargoConsentLeafNode</code> (<code>vultron/core/behaviors/case/accept_invite_tree.py:493</code>) calls:</p> <pre><code>participant.embargo_consent_state = apply_pec_trigger(\n    PEC.NO_EMBARGO, PEC_Trigger.ACCEPT\n)\n</code></pre> <p><code>apply_pec_trigger</code> rejects this transition, logs a warning, and returns <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> unchanged \u2014 and the node then logs \"signed embargo consent for invitee\" and returns <code>SUCCESS</code>. A participant who accepts an invitation to an embargoed case is recorded as having never consented, violating CM-10-001. The author of that node clearly expected <code>NO_EMBARGO \u2192 SIGNATORY</code> to be legal; the FSM silently disagreed.</p> <p>A second, related defect motivates the same fix. A sweep of <code>embargo_consent_state =</code> finds ten consent-write sites, none of which persists the resulting <code>ParticipantStatus</code>. Three assign the scalar field with no FSM involvement at all (<code>case_proposal_received_tree.py:873</code>, <code>nodes/embargo.py:433</code>, <code>nodes/participant/participant_add.py:389</code>):</p> <pre><code>participant.embargo_consent_state = PEC.SIGNATORY\n</code></pre> <p>This is a plain Pydantic field write. It does not call <code>_sync_latest_status_metadata()</code>, so the participant's existing <code>ParticipantStatus</code> retains <code>consent.state = NO_EMBARGO</code>. The resulting ledger snapshot is internally contradictory \u2014 verified directly:</p> <pre><code>participant.embargo_consent_state = SIGNATORY\nsnapshot: {\"embargoAdherence\": true, \"emConsentState\": \"NO_EMBARGO\"}\n</code></pre> <p>The remaining seven fail more subtly: they route the trigger through <code>apply_pec_trigger()</code> \u2014 so the machine is used correctly \u2014 but the write it feeds is still a scalar assignment, so the snapshot is stale in exactly the same way (<code>accept_invite_tree.py:494</code>, <code>embargo/nodes/proposal.py:84</code>, <code>use_cases/_helpers.py:488</code>, and <code>services/embargo_lifecycle.py:690, 841, 894, 935, 968</code>). Routing through <code>apply_pec_trigger</code> is necessary but not sufficient. Five of the seven are in <code>EmbargoLifecycle</code>, the intended long-term owner of all PEC transitions (#538), which makes them the highest-value conversions rather than the safest to skip.</p> <p>The correct machinery to prevent this already exists and is simply unused: <code>ParticipantStatus.consent</code> is a <code>PecDimension</code> (ADR-0036, SDO-01-001), and <code>PecDimension.transition()</code> performs fail-closed FSM validation, raising <code>VultronInvalidStateTransitionError</code> on an illegal trigger.</p> <p>The question is: is <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> an absence-of-embargo state or a not-yet-consented state, and what follows for the transition table and for case-initialization ledger entries?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0048-pec-no-embargo-is-absence-not-pre-consent/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The PEC docstring's own definition of <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> should be authoritative</li> <li>The ledger MUST NOT record protocol events that did not occur (ADR-0019)</li> <li>Single-actor and self-determined-embargo cases must be representable without   fiction</li> <li>Consent writes should be fail-closed, validated by the dimension object</li> <li>Avoid <code>log_index</code> churn: PR #1746 was reverted for shifting ledger indices and   breaking <code>fvcv-extension</code> VFD replication timing</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0048-pec-no-embargo-is-absence-not-pre-consent/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li> <p><code>NO_EMBARGO</code> is absence of embargo (chosen): add    <code>ACCEPT: NO_EMBARGO \u2192 SIGNATORY</code> and <code>DECLINE: NO_EMBARGO \u2192 DECLINED</code>. But the system underneath is asynchronous \u2014 a trigger endpoint returns HTTP 202 and the protocol effect is committed later by a <code>BackgroundTasks</code> job on a different container. Writing \"A and then B\" when the truth is \"B is only possible because A completed\" makes every step boundary a race.</p> <p>This is not a theoretical concern. Of the nineteen sub-issues of Epic #2136 (\"Demo CI: restore green main\"), seven were the same defect in a different scenario: a step proceeded before the event that would enable it had propagated. Two more were partially this. Each was fixed locally \u2014 a wait inserted here, a different observable polled there \u2014 and the shared cause was never addressed, so the next scenario rediscovered it. Bug #2178's own triage comment states the diagnosis plainly: \"the demo treated async causal steps as sequential (x then y) rather than causally linked (x therefore y).\"</p> <p>Three symptoms show the problem is structural rather than a run of bad luck:</p> <ol> <li> <p>The specs duplicated the workaround instead of stating the rule. Seven    scenario-specific requirements (DEMOMA-06-006, -11-009, -12-004, -19-005,    -19-009, -21-003, -21-004) each say \"poll here before proceeding\" for one    scenario. DEMOMA-11-009 states the general rule correctly but is scoped to    FVCV-handoff alone.</p> </li> <li> <p>The gates did not gate. Both <code>demo_step</code> and <code>demo_check</code> record the    failure and continue \u2014 \"no re-raise\", by their own docstrings and by    DEMOCI-01-003. So a precondition written with <code>demo_check</code> is advisory: it    reads like a gate in review and does nothing at runtime, and the dependent step    proceeds on state that was never established. The concrete instance is the    <code>RM.VALID</code>-before-<code>engage-case</code> gate added by the #2134 fix on the    <code>fix/demo-ci</code> branch, whose regression test passes only because it patches    <code>demo_check</code> out with <code>contextlib.nullcontext</code>. That test idiom is not    isolated: seven demo test modules on <code>main</code> patch these context managers out    the same way, so no test in the suite exercises their real control flow.</p> </li> <li> <p>Which observable proves the cause landed was guesswork. The gate before    <code>validate-report</code> in <code>run_invite_path_rm_triage</code> was re-picked three times in    one week: a ledger <code>submit_report</code> entry, then a <code>VultronOfferRecord</code> object,    then a ledger <code>add_report_to_case</code> entry.</p> </li> </ol> <p>The question this ADR answers: what should the demo harness be required to observe before advancing, and where should that requirement live?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0058-causal-gating-in-demo-scenarios/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The same defect class must not be able to recur in the next scenario written.</li> <li>The prototype's observability is limited: an actor having processed a   delivery leaves no completion record, so not every precondition is directly   observable.</li> <li>Demo CI must keep reporting every failure in a run (DEMOCI-01-003), so a fix   cannot simply convert gates into hard aborts.</li> <li>Nine scenario modules totalling roughly 9,700 lines already exist; a solution   requiring all of them to be rewritten in a new form is unlikely to be finished.</li> <li>ADR-0037 and ADR-0059 (buffer pre-genesis ledger entries) already moved one   class of ordering problem into actor-side buffering. A harness rule must not   contradict that.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0058-causal-gating-in-demo-scenarios/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Causal gates in shared helpers, plus domain narratives as a conformance   oracle \u2014 state the rule once, express preconditions with a gating primitive   that actually stops dependent work, and check the intended causal chain against   the observed one.</li> <li>Keep per-scenario polling with tuned timeouts \u2014 the status quo: continue   adding scenario-specific wait requirements and raising timeouts as CI reveals   races.</li> <li>Push all ordering into the actors \u2014 extend the ADR-0037/0055 buffering   approach until the harness never needs to sequence around delivery at all.</li> <li>Declarative scenario dependency graph with static validation \u2014 replace   imperative phase functions with declared causal edges validated before a run.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0058-causal-gating-in-demo-scenarios/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: causal gates in shared helpers, plus domain narratives as a conformance oracle.</p> <p>The rule is stated once, at the conceptual layer that already governs demo scripts (<code>EDF-06</code>), and generalized across scenarios in <code>DEMOMA-22</code>. Concretely:</p> <ul> <li>A step that depends on an asynchronous effect is gated on positive evidence   that the effect was committed by the actor that produces it, read from   that actor's own container. Elapsed time, step position, and an HTTP 202   return are not evidence.</li> <li>Gating on an observable that resolves synchronously during the triggering   request is prohibited \u2014 that observable proves the cause started, not that it   finished. This is the #2134 defect.</li> <li>A causally derived object (one created by a received-side use case forwarding a   new activity) is discovered by scanning the recipient's state for semantic   properties \u2014 type, target, object \u2014 never by polling for the sender's original   identifier. This is the #2178 defect.</li> <li>Preconditions are expressed with a new <code>demo_gate</code> context manager that   accumulates the failure exactly as <code>demo_check</code> does but additionally stops the   steps that depend on it. <code>demo_check</code> stays advisory. This resolves the tension   with DEMOCI-01-003 by separating reporting from control flow rather than   choosing between them.</li> <li>Waits that are irreducibly temporal \u2014 liveness probes, embargo deadlines,   transport backoff \u2014 are identified as temporal and are not counted as causal   gates.</li> </ul> <p>Each scenario additionally gets a narrative page under <code>docs/topics/scenarios/</code> describing the case's progress in CVD domain terms with each step's antecedent named, carrying a machine-readable list of causal edges. The invariant harness asserts every declared edge appears in the observed case ledger with the antecedent's <code>log_index</code> preceding the consequent's. Because <code>log_index</code> order is causal order (ADR-0079, CLP-14-001) and the harness already reads per-scenario ledger dumps, this needs no new instrumentation.</p> <p>The narrative is the part of this decision that does work the gates cannot. A gate enforces that the harness waited for the right thing. The narrative states, independently of the implementation, what the protocol is supposed to cause \u2014 so it can disagree with the code. That is what makes it an oracle rather than a restatement.</p> <p>Resolved: nested-block scoping model (PR #2348). The <code>demo_gate</code> context manager is implemented in <code>vultron/demo/utils.py</code> and validated by 14 unit tests in <code>TestDemoGate</code>. The scoping question the ADR left open \u2014 \"whether by phase function, by nested block, or by an explicit sentinel\" \u2014 is answered: nested block. Python's native exception unwinding exits the <code>with</code> body on failure; dependent steps follow the precondition assertion inside the same block. No sentinel variable, no return value, no modified calling convention.</p> <p>The causal-edge schema for scenario narratives (<code>docs/topics/scenarios/</code>) was finalised in PR #2204. Adjudicating each dimension on its own cannot see a claim that is impossible only in combination. A snapshot can pass every rule above and still describe a state no sequence of events could produce \u2014 a fix reported ready or deployed by a participant whose <code>rm</code> has not reached acceptance, or a fix deployed without being ready.</p> <p>A final pass therefore evaluates the cross-machine entailments \u2014 RM\u2194VF and RM\u2194D (CSB-18-001) and VF\u2194D (CSB-17-001) \u2014 and refuses the dimension whose asserted value moved, carrying the current value forward like any other refusal (RSH-05-020). Which side gets refused is load-bearing: VF\u2194D constrains a pair, and refusing the incumbent side carries its value straight back, which would leave the impossible combination recorded while reporting a refusal that changed nothing. A dimension the sender omitted is never reported as refused.</p> <p>The pass runs on the effective post-adjudication state so a refused or carried-forward <code>vf</code> cannot license the <code>d</code> the sender paired it with. For <code>rm</code> this is not a tightening \u2014 <code>rm</code> is refused only when the asserted value is not a forward move, so the carried value always ranks at or above the asserted one on the RM progress scale.</p> <p>Emit and receive share one evaluator, <code>composite_state_violations()</code> in <code>vultron/core/states/composite_state_invariants.py</code>. Before this amendment the receive path composed only VF\u2194D by hand while the emit path composed all three, so an assertion the actor would have refused to emit was accepted, hash-chained and replicated when it arrived from a peer instead.</p> <p>The guarantee is conditional: if the participant's current state satisfies the entailments, so does the recorded state. An already-impossible incumbent state cannot be repaired by refusing a dimension, because every carry-forward writes the offending value back; that case is logged instead. It is reachable via the replica-apply path, which detects the violation, emits <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code>, and refuses the entry (RSH-05-021).</p> <p>This does not narrow the monotone-forward rule above: multi-step <code>vf</code>, <code>d</code> and <code>pxa</code> advances remain accepted (CSB-16-001), because a peer may have advanced several steps between status messages. Nor does it treat an absent dimension as an initial state \u2014 a non-VENDOR participant has no vendor path (ADR-0075), so no entailment applies through it, and a first observation of a dimension is accepted when nothing contradicts it.</p> <p>Under the ADR-0075 VFD split the <code>vfd</code> rule above now reads as two independent dimensions, <code>vf</code> (<code>v\u2192V</code>, <code>f\u2192F</code>) and <code>d</code> (<code>d\u2192D</code>).</p> <p>The refusal is made visible through the canonical ledger rather than a new wire message: the committed entry snapshots the accepted portion, so it differs from what the sender asserted and every participant sees the receiver's actual view. No new message type is introduced (an outbound refusal is deferred; see ISSUE-2255 for the separate problem that the HTTP response is <code>202 Accepted</code> regardless of outcome).</p> <p>A status update whose accepted portion is indistinguishable from the participant's current state is refused in full \u2014 nothing appended, no ledger entry committed. Such an assertion carries no acceptable information, and recording it would grow both the status history and the hash chain with no state change.</p> <p>On the replica side, <code>ApplyParticipantStatusFromLedgerNode</code> enforces two invariants. The core types nest their dimensions (<code>rm: RmDimension</code>, <code>vfd: VfdDimension</code> \u2014 SDO-03-002, ADR-0036); the wire projections carry them flat (<code>rm_state</code>, <code>vfd_state</code>). Reading a nested dimension off a wire-shaped object yields <code>None</code>, and every core reader substituted an initial state for that <code>None</code> \u2014 silently resetting a participant's RM ladder (#2232, with #2264 as the symptom).</p> <p><code>Record.from_obj()</code> was supposed to keep wire objects out of the store, but its guard was <code>type_.startswith(\"as_\")</code> and wire vocabulary <code>type_</code> values are bare (<code>\"CaseParticipant\"</code>). Fifteen wire classes therefore shadowed a <code>CORE_VOCABULARY</code> entry and were written into core-typed rows unchallenged.</p> <p>So the question is not only how to normalise, but where: a wire-shaped object can enter the system at an HTTP ingress boundary, and it can reach the persistence boundary from several call paths. Enforcing in the wrong place either misses paths or breaks legitimate inbound traffic.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0062-normalise-wire-to-core-at-both-ingress-and-persistence/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>No wire-shaped row may exist in the DataLayer \u2014 that is the invariant #2232   asks for, and rows outlive whichever code wrote them.</li> <li>A wire-shaped object arriving over HTTP is legitimate inbound data, not   corruption. Treating it as an error is a denial of service against the   protocol.</li> <li>A shape mismatch discovered while reading a stored row is corruption and   must fail loudly (ARCH-15-001, ARCH-15-002) \u2014 the silent degrade is the whole   defect.</li> <li>The received-side behavior tree must not abort because one embedded   participant is malformed; the HTTP inbox re-queues on exception, so an   escaping raise becomes an undrainable poison message.</li> <li>Enforcement must be verifiable by a test, not by reviewer vigilance: 15 types   shadow a core type and the count will change.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0062-normalise-wire-to-core-at-both-ingress-and-persistence/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Normalise at wire\u2192core ingress only</li> <li>Normalise at the persistence boundary only</li> <li>Normalise at ingress, and enforce again at the persistence boundary</li> <li>Unify the two shapes into one class</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0062-normalise-wire-to-core-at-both-ingress-and-persistence/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: \"Normalise at ingress, and enforce again at the persistence boundary\", because the two placements answer different questions and neither subsumes the other. Ingress projection is what makes the behaviour correct \u2014 inbound data is converted where it arrives, so no core reader ever sees a wire shape and no reader has to degrade. Persistence-boundary normalisation is what makes the invariant hold \u2014 it is the single choke point every write passes through, so it can guarantee the stored row is canonical no matter which ingress path missed.</p> <p>Concretely:</p> <ul> <li>Ingress (primary). <code>_project_to_core_participant()</code> in   <code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/case/_helpers.py</code> projects each embedded   participant of a received case snapshot via <code>to_core()</code> before anything reads   it. An unprojectable participant is logged at ERROR and skipped, not   raised: losing one malformed participant is strictly better than losing the   case.</li> <li>Persistence (backstop). <code>_normalize_to_core()</code> in   <code>vultron/adapters/driven/db_record.py</code> projects the object and its direct   children for every <code>type_</code> in <code>_NORMALIZE_WIRE_TO_CORE</code>. Children matter   because a <code>VulnerabilityCase</code> row stores <code>case_participants</code> inline; one level   suffices because <code>to_core()</code> recurses.</li> <li>Readers stay strict. <code>participant_status_rm_state()</code> and   <code>participant_status_vfd_state()</code> raise <code>VultronValidationError</code> on a non-core   shape. Absence (an empty status list) remains a legitimate <code>None</code>.</li> </ul> <p>Rejected for now: unifying the two shapes. It is the right end state \u2014 one class per concept, wire as a pure projection (ADR-0017) \u2014 but it is a breaking change across the AS2 vocabulary and the persisted-row format, and #2232 is a live data corruption bug. ARCH-12-003 forbids exactly this \u2014 <code>alias_generator=to_camel</code> is a wire-specific concern and core-branch types MUST NOT carry it. The violation has been tracked as a known deviation (#1991) behind an <code>xfail(strict=False)</code> ratchet in <code>test/architecture/test_hierarchy_invariants.py</code> for long enough that downstream code came to depend on it.</p> <p><code>ParticipantStatus</code> compounds the problem with a <code>_migrate_flat_fields</code> <code>model_validator(mode=\"before\")</code> that accepts flat wire spellings (<code>rm_state</code>/<code>rmState</code>, <code>vfd_state</code>/<code>vfdState</code>, <code>em_consent_state</code>/<code>emConsentState</code>) and rewrites them into the ADR-0036 dimension objects. SDO-03-003 says the old flat enum fields MUST NOT be retained as aliases or shim properties after the dimension migration \u2014 so this shim violates a MUST-level requirement independently of ARCH-12-003.</p> <p>The reason the alias generator is load-bearing rather than merely wrong is that core code needs camelCase JSON for one specific purpose: building <code>CaseLedgerEntry.payloadSnapshot</code> values. The case ledger's purpose is to wrap \"things that were received or sent to/from the case manager in the course of managing the case\", and those are by definition wire-shaped. CLP-07-001 requires the snapshot to be the verbatim AS2 activity or a deterministic canonical normalization of it, and CLP-01-003/CLP-01-004 make the ledger the replication substrate that receivers project into their own replica. A payload snapshot must therefore be valid wire JSON that a receiver can reconstitute \u2014 camelCase is correct there.</p> <p>So core reached for the nearest thing that produced camelCase: it set <code>alias_generator</code> on the core class and called <code>model_dump(by_alias=True)</code>. That is a wire concern implemented by mutating the domain model, and it does not even work correctly: <code>build_add_participant_status_snapshot</code> in <code>vultron/core/behaviors/case/ledger_snapshots.py</code> has to hand-patch <code>consent</code> \u2192 <code>emConsentState</code> after the dump, because a core <code>model_dump</code> cannot produce the wire's flat <code>emConsentState</code> field from the nested <code>PecDimension</code>. That hand-patch is a partial, drifting reimplementation of <code>as_ParticipantStatus.from_core()</code>.</p> <p>Three additional consumers depend on the same core-side aliasing: <code>_inline_snapshot_reference_value</code> in <code>vultron/core/use_cases/_helpers.py</code> (CLP-07-006 inline nesting of <code>dl.read()</code> results, which are core objects per DL-05-001); <code>GET /actors/{id}</code> in <code>vultron/adapters/driving/fastapi/routers/actors/_routes.py</code>, which dumps a core actor class with <code>by_alias=True</code> straight into an <code>AS2JSONResponse</code>; and <code>vultron/demo/utils.py</code>, which dumps core objects the same way for demo output.</p> <p>A fifth consumer depends on the shim rather than the alias generator: <code>FilterParticipantStatusDimensionsNode._to_core_status</code> (added by ADR-0061) normalises a wire status by dumping it <code>by_alias=True</code> and revalidating through core <code>ParticipantStatus</code>, and its docstring names the dependency outright \u2014 \"the core model's <code>_migrate_flat_fields</code> validator accepts that shape, so a dump-and-revalidate normalises both\". The shim and that idiom have to retire together.</p> <p>The hand-patching is likewise not confined to one site: <code>_build_patch</code> in the same module writes <code>patch[\"caseStatus\"] = {\"emState\": ..., \"pxaState\": ...}</code>, and <code>accept_invite.py</code>'s <code>_build_snapshot</code> hand-builds a wire-spelled fallback dict. The same value the constructor rejects is silently accepted through two other doors:</p> <pre><code>case = VulnerabilityCase(case_participants=[wire_obj])  # ValidationError\ncase.case_participants = [wire_obj]                     # accepted\ncase.case_participants.append(wire_obj)                 # accepted\n</code></pre> <p>This matters because the core and wire branches (ADR-0017) carry structurally incompatible shapes for the same concepts. A wire-shaped object in a core-typed field does not raise when read \u2014 it reads as absent, and readers substitute an initial state, silently resetting a participant's RM ladder. That is the failure mode of #2232 / #2264, and it is the same class of defect as #2233, which had seven Demo Integration scenarios red on <code>main</code> at the time of writing.</p> <p>ADR-0062 already closed the two boundaries where wire data crosses into persistence: normalisation at ingress and again at the persistence boundary. What remains unenforced is the in-memory invariant \u2014 nothing stops code already inside the core from planting a wrong-shaped object in a typed field.</p> <p>The obvious remedy is <code>validate_assignment=True</code> on <code>VultronBase</code>. Twenty three core validators do this (plus twelve in the wire branch). Guarded ones terminate at depth 2; unguarded ones \u2014 <code>FinderParticipant._set_role</code>, <code>ReporterParticipant._set_accepted_status</code>, <code>as_EmbargoEvent.set_name</code> and others \u2014 recurse until the stack is gone. The protocol has no bounded commitment window, so a coordinator waiting on one non-responsive invitee cannot tell whether the invite is still live, and coordination stalls without anyone having decided anything.</p> <p>A deadline mechanism is in fact already specified. CM-18-002 defines the pocket veto: <code>INVITED \u2192 DECLINED</code> MAY be driven by timer expiry on \"a configurable policy window (default: 7 days).\" That window is receiver-local and implicit \u2014 nothing about it appears on the wire, so the two parties have no shared instant at which the invite lapses. It is also entirely unimplemented: <code>PEC_Trigger.DECLINE</code> was fired from exactly two sites (<code>vultron/core/behaviors/embargo/announce_teardown_tree.py</code>, <code>vultron/core/services/embargo_lifecycle.py</code>), both explicit-<code>Reject</code> paths. An invitee who never responds is by   definition the party least likely to send a notification.</li> <li>No new AS2 noun or verb should be required. Epic #2088 is vocabulary   extension, not vocabulary invention.</li> <li>The existing pocket veto must be reconciled, not duplicated. Two parallel   notions of \"the invite timed out\" would drift.</li> <li>A deadline is coercive if unbounded downward: an artificially short window   weaponises the mechanism to exclude a participant who had no realistic   chance to answer.</li> <li>Being liberal in what is accepted serves CVD outcomes.
