But two gaps break this model at the edges:</p> <ol> <li> <p>Vendor awareness has no self-report path (CONCERN-2087). The <code>v\u2192V</code>    (vendor unaware \u2192 aware) transition and the <code>CV</code> message exist in the design,    but nothing lets any actor record that a vendor has been made aware. The    design intent \u2014 captured in a 2026-08-07 review \u2014 is that whoever notifies a    vendor, or invites one to a case, MAY assert that the vendor is aware, so a    vendor can be marked informed even if it never joins the case.</p> </li> <li> <p>There is no stated line between what a participant may assert about    itself and what requires the Case Owner's authority (part of CONCERN-1752,    CONCERN-3020). Role and roster changes clearly need owner approval    (ADR-0026); individual state transitions clearly do not. But the boundary was    never written down, so each new assertion path re-litigates it.</p> </li> </ol> <p>The question: what may a participant assert on its own authority, and which transitions may a Case Manager or Case Owner assert on another participant's behalf?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0084-participant-assertion-authority/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Participant status is the mechanism by which participants report their own   state; self-declaration is the default, not the exception.</li> <li>Some transitions are externally evidenced \u2014 the act of notifying a vendor is   itself proof the vendor was made aware \u2014 and must be recordable even when the   role-holder never actively participates.</li> <li>Some transitions are not externally knowable (<code>f\u2192F</code>, fix readiness) and must   never be assertable by anyone but the role-holder, or the Case Actor could   fabricate protocol-visible fix state.</li> <li>Vendor and Deployer are distinct roles held by distinct actors; a Vendor is   never implicitly a Deployer. The <code>v\u2192V</code> and <code>d\u2192D</code> transitions belong to   different role-holders.</li> <li>Role and roster changes are already owner-authorized (ADR-0026, CM-02-001);   this decision must not weaken that.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0084-participant-assertion-authority/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>Strictly self-reported, no exceptions. Every dimension of    <code>ParticipantStatus</code> is only ever the reporting participant's own claim.</li> <li>Case Manager / Case Owner may assert any dimension on any participant's    behalf. The Case Actor becomes a general proxy for participant state.</li> <li>Self-declaratory by default, with narrow externally-evidenced on-behalf    exceptions. Participants self-report; a Case Manager/Owner MAY assert only    those transitions that are externally evidenced, on behalf of the specific    role-holder.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0084-participant-assertion-authority/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: Option 3 \u2014 self-declaratory by default, with narrow externally-evidenced on-behalf exceptions, because it preserves the meaning of participant status as self-declaration while closing the vendor-awareness gap without letting the Case Actor fabricate state it cannot observe.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0084-participant-assertion-authority/#the-rules","title":"The rules","text":"<ul> <li>Default: participant status is self-declaratory. A participant asserts its   own RM and VFD state; no approval is required. This is why they are   participant status items.</li> <li><code>v\u2192V</code> (vendor aware) MAY be asserted on behalf of the Vendor-role holder   by a Case Manager or Case Owner, because the notification event is itself   observable evidence. Any acknowledgement from the vendor of any message sent to   it \u2014 even a <code>Read(Invite(Case))</code> \u2014 is sufficient evidence to set <code>v\u2192V</code>. The   vendor SHOULD also assert it once it joins.</li> <li><code>d\u2192D</code> (fix deployed) MAY be asserted on behalf of the Deployer-role holder   by a Case Manager or Case Owner under the same externally-evidenced pattern,   but only in exceptional circumstances (a MAY, expected to be rare). A census of the <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> tree (#3101) found that lookup open-coded at ~78 call sites, each having independently re-invented the \"case evaporated underneath me\" branch. The dispositions had drifted apart along two axes that no design ever reconciled:</p> <ul> <li>Verdict on absence. Some sites returned <code>FAILURE</code>, some <code>SUCCESS</code>, some   fell through with an empty result \u2014 with no principle distinguishing them.</li> <li>Loudness. Among the <code>FAILURE</code> sites, the log level ranged over silent,   <code>debug</code>, <code>warning</code>, and <code>error</code>, and the <code>feedback_message</code> text was   bespoke at every site (or absent).</li> </ul> <p>This drift was not merely cosmetic. The bug was possible only because \"what to do when a case disappears\" lived at the call site instead of in one shared place.</p> <p>The question this ADR settles: when a BT node cannot resolve the case it was told to coordinate, what is the correct disposition \u2014 and where does that decision live?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0087-case-resolution-disposition-policy/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>One canonical decision about case-absence, not a per-site accident (#3101).</li> <li>DRY: a single implementation activated from everywhere that needs it, with   no parallel implementations of the same idea.</li> <li>Error handling should clean up when an error occurs; teardown hygiene must   not depend on which node happened to short-circuit a Sequence.</li> <li>The default must be safe: continuing to coordinate a case that does not   exist is almost never legitimate.</li> <li>Genuine exceptions (partial replicas, cases mid-construction) must remain   expressible without reopening the default.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0087-case-resolution-disposition-policy/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>A. One helper, one disposition \u2014 force every site to hard-fail through a   single function.</li> <li>C. Role-indexed disposition helpers \u2014 a small closed set of   dispositions, each with one shared entry point, chosen by the node's role.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0087-case-resolution-disposition-policy/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: C, role-indexed disposition helpers. Each disposition gets exactly one shared implementation, and a node selects its disposition by which helper it calls \u2014 never by re-deciding the branch inline. The authority commits a <code>CaseLedgerEntry</code> and broadcasts; the participant asserts and waits for the broadcast.</p> <p>The distinction is correct and load-bearing. The problem is twofold.</p> <p>First, the question is answered in many places, in different ways. There is no single shared way to determine authority, so the check is re-derived per site and the discipline is held together only by convention. Specs CLP-09-002 and CLP-09-003 mandate commit-authorization ratchets \u2014 an enumeration that fails when a site commits unguarded, and a coverage test that every use case reaches a commit \u2014 but those enforcement tests are not yet implemented; only CLP-09-001's per-node role check has unit tests today. A ratchet, specified or in place, only fires when a site forgets to check \u2014 the signature of a convention, not a structural guarantee (<code>notes/case-ledger-authority.md</code>, \"Authorization Was a Convention, Not a Gate\").</p> <p>Second \u2014 and this is the deeper error \u2014 some of those ways determine authority from the wrong thing. Nobody adopts a \"Case Actor\" identity. The identity is defined entirely by \"the entity enacting <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> must do these things.\" Treating the name or URL as a protocol signal elevates a demo convention to protocol truth.</p> <p>This ADR settles one decision: authority, recognition, and routing key off the <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> role, and nothing else. Two of its decisions were being made on the wrong question, and the second of them failed silently.</p> <p>The field guards asked about the key, not the value. Both required-field guards were spelled <code>if body.get(field) is None</code>, which answers \"was the key absent?\" The requirements they enforce are about the value: CLP-15-006 refuses an inbound activity that \"carries no <code>published</code>\", and MV-01-001 requires a recognisable <code>type</code>. A sender who transmits <code>\"\"</code> has supplied the key and nothing else, so the guard passed and the value went on to <code>model_validate</code>, which reported it as a schema fault. The consequences differed by field:</p> <ul> <li><code>published: \"\"</code> still produced a 422, but with a Pydantic isoformat dump in   place of the CLP-15-006 explanation the sender needed.</li> <li><code>type: \"\"</code> produced <code>UnknownTypeError</code> and therefore a 422, while an   omitted <code>type</code> produces <code>MissingTypeError</code> and a 400 \u2014 two spellings of   the same omission drawing two different status codes.</li> </ul> <p>A nested object that failed validation was silently downgraded. <code>_expand_inline_value</code> types nested dicts so pattern matching can see structures like <code>Accept(Invite(...))</code>. It wrapped that validation in <code>except Exception: return expanded</code>, handing the parent the raw dict instead. The parent then accepted the dict as a bare <code>as_Link</code>, so the activity parsed successfully, extracted as <code>UNKNOWN</code>, lost the case id, and drew a 202 for a message the receiver never understood. No log line, no error.</p> <p>Instrumenting that fallback and running the whole suite showed it fired 52 times, and every single occurrence was one cause: <code>find_in_vocabulary</code> falls back to <code>CORE_TYPE_MAP</code> (ARCH-12-003), and <code>OrderedCollection</code> is registered only there. Absent, <code>null</code>, and blank (including whitespace-only) all raise the same \"missing field\" error. Blankness is decided by <code>not value.strip()</code>, matching the project's canonical predicate in <code>core.models.base._non_empty</code>. The Vultron Protocol defines four levels, each building on the previous:</p> L1 \u2014 Syntax Well-formed messages that conform to the wire format.   This level is covered by the wire format specifications. L2 \u2014 Semantic Correct state transitions in response to received messages and local events.   This level is covered by the Vultron Protocol spec (VP) and the   Transition Functions. L3 \u2014 Behavioral <p>Correct observable outputs \u2014 the right messages emitted and the right states reached   in response to a given (input state + received message/event) combination.   This level is covered by the protocol behavioral specifications:</p> <ul> <li>RMB \u2014 Report Management Behavioral Requirements</li> <li>EMB \u2014 Embargo Management Behavioral Requirements</li> <li>CSB \u2014 CVD Case State Behavioral Requirements</li> </ul> L4 \u2014 Process Correct internal decision structure \u2014 for example, precondition checks before state writes   before protocol effects, audit-log ordering, and idempotency guarantees. During development and simulation, each call-out point is filled by a fuzzer node: a stub that returns a random SUCCESS or FAILURE based on a probability. In production, you replace a fuzzer node with a real capability backend that applies actual business logic.</p> <p>The three-step process is:</p> <ol> <li>Identify the call-out point you want to implement (find the fuzzer node, read its blackboard contract).</li> <li>Implement a backend factory that satisfies the <code>CallOutBackendFactory</code> Protocol.</li> <li>Wire the backend by passing it through the domain bundle to the tree builder.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#step-1-identify-the-call-out-point","title":"Step 1 \u2014 Identify the call-out point","text":""},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#find-the-fuzzer-node","title":"Find the fuzzer node","text":"<p>Every call-out point in the reference implementation has a corresponding fuzzer node in <code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/</code>. Any callable that matches this signature is valid \u2014 a plain function, a lambda, or a class with <code>__call__</code>. No registration, inheritance, or decorator is required.</p>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#implementing-as-a-py_treesbehaviourbehaviour-subclass","title":"Implementing as a <code>py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour</code> subclass","text":"<p>Subclass <code>py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour</code> and implement both <code>setup()</code> and <code>update()</code>. The <code>setup()</code> method runs once when the tree is first started \u2014 it registers the blackboard keys your node will write. The <code>update()</code> method runs on every BT tick.</p> <p>Blackboard access requires <code>setup()</code></p> <p>py_trees does not create <code>self.blackboard</code> automatically. You must call <code>self.attach_blackboard_client()</code> in <code>setup()</code> and register each key before <code>update()</code> can use them. Skipping this raises <code>AttributeError</code> on the first tick.</p> <pre><code>import py_trees\nfrom py_trees.common import Access, Status\n\n\nclass MyCredibilityEvaluator(py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour):\n    \"\"\"Real credibility evaluator backed by a reputation scoring service.\n\n    Blackboard contract (BT-18-001):\n      Input keys:  (none \u2014 queries reputation service using DataLayer context)\n      Output keys: report_credibility_verdict: str  (SUCCESS only)\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self, name: str) -&gt; None:\n        super().__init__(name=name)\n\n    def setup(self, **kwargs) -&gt; None:\n        # Register every blackboard key this node writes before update() runs.\n        self.blackboard = self.attach_blackboard_client(name=self.name)\n        self.blackboard.register_key(\n            \"report_credibility_verdict\", access=Access.WRITE\n        )\n\n    def update(self) -&gt; Status:\n        verdict = my_reputation_service.evaluate(...)\n        if verdict.credible:\n            self.blackboard.report_credibility_verdict = verdict.summary\n            return Status.SUCCESS\n        return Status.FAILURE\n\n\n# This function is the CallOutBackendFactory.\ndef my_credibility_factory(name: str) -&gt; py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour:\n    return MyCredibilityEvaluator(name)\n</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#implementing-as-a-factory-function-no-blackboard-writes","title":"Implementing as a factory function (no blackboard writes)","text":"<p>When your backend has no blackboard output keys \u2014 for example, a binary yes/no condition check that only needs to return SUCCESS or FAILURE \u2014 a plain module-level function and a minimal class are sufficient:</p> <pre><code>import py_trees\nfrom py_trees.common import Status\n\n\nclass _CredibilityCheck(py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour):\n    \"\"\"Backend that consults a reputation service. The reference implementation has nowhere to suspend a tick (ADR-0080), so this is enforced, not advisory. The domain bundle wraps every backend it hands out in a <code>SynchronousCallOut</code> guard: a <code>RUNNING</code> return raises <code>CallOutContractError</code> immediately, naming the offending node, instead of silently stalling the tree.</p>"},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#step-3-wire-the-backend-via-the-domain-bundle","title":"Step 3 \u2014 Wire the backend via the domain bundle","text":""},{"location":"howto/wire_capability/#domain-bundles","title":"Domain bundles","text":"<p>Call-out factories are grouped into domain bundles \u2014 one frozen <code>@dataclass</code> per domain area. The bundle lives in <code>vultron/core/behaviors/call_out/bundles/</code>.</p> <p>To wire in your backend, instantiate the appropriate bundle with your factory in the relevant field. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Activities are the core of the ActivityPub protocol. They are used to represent actions that are performed by actors. The ActivityStreams vocabulary defines a number of activities, extended with specific activities used in the Vultron AS vocabulary. The ActivityStreams vocabulary is sufficient for Vultron's needs, so extensions are limited to specifying the types of activities, actors, and objects that are used in the Vultron protocol.</p> <p>A full mapping of Vultron to ActivityStreams is available in the Vultron ActivityStreams Ontology.</p> <p>Design Goals</p> <p>The goal of each activity definition is to</p> <ul> <li>Avoid creating new activity types when an existing activity type can be used.</li> <li>Avoid creating defined activity types with the same objects and targets to avoid confusion. Each activity type / object / target combination should have a single meaning within the protocol.</li> </ul> <p>The Vultron AS activities are organized by user flow. These include:</p> <ul> <li><code>as:Read</code></li> <li><code>as:View</code></li> <li><code>as:Listen</code></li> </ul> <p>Since most CVD cases are text-centric, <code>as:Read</code> is the most commonly used activity. <code>as:View</code> and <code>as:Listen</code> activities may be used in some cases, such as when a case participant views a video or listens to an audio recording.</p> <p><code>RmReadReport</code> is defined as a subclass of <code>as:Read</code> to indicate that a report has been read. This allows the receiver of a report to acknowledge receipt without indicating anything more than that the report has been read. That leaves <code>RmValidateReport</code> and <code>RmInvalidateReport</code> to indicate a more specific action (accept, reject) on the part of the receiver.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\n    subgraph RM:Received\n        a{Accept?}\n        subgraph as:Read\n            RmReadReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Start\n        subgraph as:Offer\n            RmSubmitReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Accepted\n        subgraph as:Accept\n            RmValidateReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Invalid\n        subgraph as:Reject\n            RmInvalidateReport\n        end\n    end\n    a --&gt;|y| RmValidateReport\n    a --&gt;|undecided| RmReadReport\n    a --&gt;|n| RmInvalidateReport\n    RmSubmitReport --&gt; a</code></pre> <p>More Acknowledgements in the Ontology</p> <p>The Vultron AS ontology defines a number of ActivityStreams activities that can serve as the various acknowledgements that are used in the Vultron protocol. These include messages that are specifically <code>as:inReplyTo</code> a message defined as one of the core protocol message types.</p> <p>For example, it is not necessary to send a separate <code>RmReadReport</code> message if the <code>RmValidateReport</code> message is sent as a reply to the <code>RmSubmitReport</code> message. The <code>RmValidateReport</code> message logically indicates that the report has been read in order to have been validated.</p> <p>Like, Dislike and Flag</p> <p>The ActivityStreams vocabulary also includes actions that indicate an opinion  about a message or object, such as <code>as:Like</code>, <code>as:Dislike</code>, and <code>as:Flag</code>. While these may be relevant to implementations of the Vultron protocol, no specific use cases for them are defined at this time.</p>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/acknowledge/#acknowledgement-for-ledger-replicated-state","title":"Acknowledgement for ledger-replicated state","text":"<p>The <code>RK</code> pattern above applies to report submission, which is not ledger-replicated. part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Inviting an actor to a case is a way to add them as a participant in the case. The invitation is sent to the actor as an <code>as:Invite</code> activity. Depending on the actor's response, they may become a participant in the case.</p> <p> </p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Invite Actor to Case\n---\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor O as Case Owner\n    participant CA as CASE_MANAGER\n    actor A as Actor\n    activate O\n    O -&gt;&gt; CA: [trigger invite]\n    activate CA\n    CA -&gt;&gt;+ A: Invite(actor=CASE_MANAGER, object=Actor, target=Case, attributedTo=CaseOwner)\n    note over A: Consider invitation\n    alt Accept Invitation\n        A --&gt;&gt; CA: Accept(object=Invite)\n        CA -&gt;&gt; CA: Create(object=CaseParticipant(actor=Actor), target=Case)\n        note over CA: Actor becomes participant in case\n    else Reject Invitation\n        A --&gt;&gt; CA: Reject(object=Invite)\n        note over CA: Actor is not participant in case\n    end\n    deactivate A\n    deactivate CA\n    deactivate O</code></pre> <p>CASE_MANAGER routing (PCR-08-007, PCR-08-008)</p> <p>The <code>Invite</code> activity is sent by the CASE_MANAGER, not the Case Owner. The Case Owner triggers the invite, but the CASE_MANAGER MUST be the ActivityStreams <code>actor</code> on the outbound <code>Invite</code>. The <code>attributedTo</code> field on the activity MAY carry the Case Owner's ID to record who initiated it.</p> <p>The invitee MUST address their <code>Accept</code> or <code>Reject</code> reply to the CASE_MANAGER, not directly back to the Case Owner. The CASE_MANAGER is the authoritative recipient of all case-management handshake messages after case creation.</p> <p>Invite vs Add?</p> <p>When a case is first created, the Case Owner and any known participants (e.g., the Reporter) should be automatically added to the case. It's not even necessary for these to be emitted as separate <code>as:Add</code> activities. The <code>as:Create</code> activity for the case can include the Case Owner and any known participants as <code>CaseParticipant</code> objects. See Initializing a Case for more.</p> <p>However, over the lifespan of a case, there may be other actors that were not already involved at the time the case was created, but who should be invited to participate in the case. This is where the <code>as:Invite</code> activity comes in.</p> <p>Avoid bogging down in details</p> <p>Adding a participant to a case involves creating the participant object and a participant status object. As discussed elsewhere, emitting separate <code>as:Create</code> and <code>as:Add</code> events for each of these events is likely overkill.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\n\na[create participant] --&gt; b[create participant status]\nb --&gt; c[add participant status to participant]\nc --&gt; d[add participant to case]</code></pre> <p>Instead, a single <code>as:Create</code> event for the participant, already containing a status object, could be emitted, with the <code>target</code> of the <code>as:Create</code> event as the case object.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\na[create particpant with status] --&gt;|target| b[case]</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/invite_actor/#invite-to-case","title":"Invite to Case","text":"<p>A vendor invites a coordinator to a case.</p> page is not normative</p> <p>This page is not considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>These activities implement the CASE_MANAGER's canonical log replication pipeline. After each new log entry is committed to the case ledger, the CASE_MANAGER fans out <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> to every participant. Participants buffer out-of-order entries and drain them once their hash-chain predecessor arrives (ADR-0037). When a new participant joins for the first time, the CASE_MANAGER seeds their replica with <code>Announce(VulnerabilityCase)</code> (ADR-0059).</p> <p>See also:</p> <ul> <li>Case Ledger Synchronization \u2014 why the   ledger is ordered this way and what the buffering guarantees</li> <li>ADR-0037 \u2014 Buffer Out-of-Order Ledger   Entries</li> <li>ADR-0059 \u2014 Buffer Pre-Genesis Ledger   Entries</li> <li>ADR-0077 \u2014 Ledger Replication Companion   Spec</li> <li>Spec: <code>specs/sync-ledger-replication.yaml</code> (SYNC-09, SYNC-10, SYNC-14, SYNC-15)</li> </ul>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/ledger_replication/#announcecaseledgerentry-log-replication","title":"Announce(CaseLedgerEntry) \u2014 Log Replication","text":"<p>The CASE_MANAGER is the single-writer authority for the canonical case ledger. After committing each <code>CaseLedgerEntry</code>, it broadcasts the entry to all case participants via <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code>.</p> <p>Each entry includes a content hash and the hash of its predecessor, forming a Merkle chain. Participants verify the chain on receipt and buffer any entry that arrives before its predecessor.</p> <pre><code>sequenceDiagram\n    participant CA as Case Actor\n    participant P1 as Participant 1\n    participant P2 as Participant 2\n    CA -&gt;&gt; P1: Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)\n    CA -&gt;&gt; P2: Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)\n    note over P1,P2: Verify hash chain; apply or buffer</code></pre> <p>Pattern: <code>AnnounceLogEntryPattern</code> in <code>vultron/wire/as2/extractor/_instances.py</code></p> <p>Factory: <code>announce_log_entry_activity</code> in <code>vultron/wire/as2/factories/sync.py</code></p> <pre><code>from vultron.wire.as2.factories.sync import announce_log_entry_activity\n\nactivity = announce_log_entry_activity(\n    entry,        # as_CaseLedgerEntry\n    actor=case_actor_id,\n    to=[participant_actor_id],\n)\n</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/ledger_replication/#rejectcaseledgerentry-hash-chain-mismatch","title":"Reject(CaseLedgerEntry) \u2014 Hash-Chain Mismatch","text":"<p>When a participant receives an <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> whose <code>prev_log_hash</code> does not match its local tail hash (and the entry cannot be resolved as a forward-gap via buffering), it sends <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> back to the CASE_MANAGER. The <code>context</code> field carries the participant's last accepted entry hash so the CASE_MANAGER can replay the missing prefix.</p> <p>Buffering takes priority (ADR-0037)</p> <p>A <code>Reject</code> is only sent for entries that are genuinely missing from the chain \u2014 not for entries that are merely out of order. Out-of-order entries are held in the <code>LedgerGapBuffer</code> and applied when their predecessor arrives, avoiding a spurious reject-replay cycle.</p> <p>Pattern: <code>RejectLogEntryPattern</code> in <code>vultron/wire/as2/extractor/_instances.py</code></p> <p>Factory: <code>reject_log_entry_activity</code> in <code>vultron/wire/as2/factories/sync.py</code></p> <pre><code>from vultron.wire.as2.factories.sync import reject_log_entry_activity\n\nactivity = reject_log_entry_activity(\n    entry,                  # as_CaseLedgerEntry (the rejected entry)\n    context=last_good_hash, # last accepted entry hash\n    actor=participant_id,\n    to=[case_actor_id],\n)\n</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/ledger_replication/#announcevulnerabilitycase-case-seeding","title":"Announce(VulnerabilityCase) \u2014 Case Seeding","text":"<p>When a participant's replica is being initialized for the first time (e.g., after they accept an <code>Invite</code> or after a <code>Create(CaseProposal)</code> is accepted), the CASE_MANAGER sends <code>Announce(VulnerabilityCase)</code> to seed the replica. The Case Owner triggers the invite action, but the CASE_MANAGER MUST be the ActivityStreams <code>actor</code> on the outbound <code>Invite</code> activity. The invited actor MUST send their <code>Accept</code> or <code>Reject</code> reply to the CASE_MANAGER, not directly to the Case Owner. See Inviting an Actor to a Case for the full sequence diagram.</p> <p>Create or Add?</p> <p>There appears to be some logical interchangeability of <code>as:Create</code>  with <code>as:Add</code> since both include a <code>target</code> property that can be used to specify the object to which the new object is being added. We chose to  represent them separately here to acknowledge the difference between creating a new object and adding an existing object to another object, but in an actual implementation it may be acceptable to use either activity for both cases. It seems likely that the general idea should be to use <code>as:Create</code> when creating a new object to  add to another object (as the <code>target</code> of the activity), and <code>as:Add</code> when adding an existing object to another object. </p> <p>Vultron intends to be consistent with however ActivityPub handles this. If the approach described here is inconsistent with ActivityPub, please report it as an issue or  pull An <code>Offer</code> can include a <code>Report</code> object that the sender created immediately before sending. While a <code>Create(Report)</code> technically precedes an <code>Offer(Report)</code>, in practice the receiver usually only observes the <code>Offer</code> because the report was created entirely on the sender's side.</p> <p>In other cases the <code>Report</code> may have been created earlier or by a different actor (for example, a platform or intermediary). When that happens the <code>Create(Report)</code> and <code>Offer(Report)</code> are distinct activities. We show both patterns here to cover both workflows.</p> <p>When would <code>Create(Report)</code> be separate from <code>Offer(Report)</code>?</p> <p>A Reporter files a report with a bug-bounty platform that implements Vultron. The <code>Create(Report)</code> activity happens between the Reporter and the platform. Later, the platform submits the <code>Report</code> to a vendor by sending an <code>Offer(Report)</code>. The vendor receives the <code>Offer</code> (which contains the <code>Report</code> object) and may not be aware of the earlier <code>Create(Report)</code> activity.</p>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/report_vulnerability/#submit-report","title":"Submit Report","text":"<p>The finder submits a vulnerability report to the vendor.</p> <pre><code>{\n  \"id\": \"urn:uuid:aecee3d6-9522-4125-bf17-b47c55e73802\",\n  \"type\": \"Offer\",\n  \"name\": \"https://vultron.example/users/finndervul Offer FDR-8675309\",\n  \"to\": [\n    \"https://vultron.example/organizations/vendorco\"\n  ],\n  \"@context\": \"https://www.w3.org/ns/activitystreams\",\n  \"actor\": \"https://vultron.example/users/finndervul\",\n  \"object\": {\n    \"id\": \"https://demo.vultron.local/VulnerabilityReport/3b0d1b1e-a06c-4662-8744-666365fc8a3e\",\n    \"type\": \"VulnerabilityReport\",\n    \"name\": \"FDR-8675309\",\n    \"published\": \"2026-09-17T14:25:47+00:00\",\n    \"updated\": \"2026-09-17T14:25:47+00:00\",\n    \"content\": \"I found a vulnerability!\",\n    \"attributedTo\": [\n      \"https://vultron.example/users/finndervul\"\n    ],\n    \"@context\": \"https://certcc.github.io/Vultron/ns/context.jsonld\"\n  }\n}\n</code></pre> <p>Report submission might be followed by either a <code>Read</code> or <code>Accept</code> activity.</p> <p>The <code>Read</code> activity is optional and should be used when the vendor wants to acknowledge that they have received the report without accepting or rejecting it.</p>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/report_vulnerability/#read-report","title":"Read Report","text":"<p>The vendor reads the vulnerability report, acknowledging that they have received it.</p> <pre><code>{\n  \"id\": \"urn:uuid:83e68e7c-ed51-43b2-ae3d-44fc8476d171\",\n  \"type\": \"Read\",\n  \"name\": \"https://vultron.example/organizations/vendorco Read FDR-8675309\",\n  \"content\": \"We've read the report. Case","text":"<p>This page is not normative</p> <p>This page is not considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>During the course of coordinating a case, an existing case participant might recognize that another actor should be invited to participate in the case. The following mechanisms provide a way for a case participant to suggest that another actor be invited to participate in the case.</p> <p> </p> <p>Why Suggest instead of just Invite?</p> <p>The process described here makes an assumption that there is a case owner who is responsible for coordinating the  case. Participants having the case owner role can in principle just directly invite other actors to participate in  the case, and they might not need the suggestion mechanism described here. However, this mechanism is included to account for the possibilities that:</p> <ul> <li>there could be multiple case owners, and they might not all agree on who should be invited to participate in the    case.</li> <li>a non-case-owner participant might want to suggest that another actor be invited to participate in the case</li> </ul> <p>Of these, the latter is the more likely scenario, but the mechanism described here can be used in either case.    </p> <p>Reasons to Invite other Actors</p> <p>There are many reasons why a case participant might want to suggest another actor to participate in a case. The following are some examples:</p> <ul> <li>A finder, having reported to one vendor, might further discover that the vulnerability is actually in a    third-party library, and suggest inviting the library vendor to participate in the case.</li> <li>A vendor might be a participant in (but not the owner of) a case, and wants to suggest that the case owner   invite a sector-specific coordinator to participate in the case to address critical infrastructure concerns.</li> <li>A reporter participant might suggest a technical expert (for example, a member of a protocol working group) to    include in the case.</li> <li>A coordinator might suggest to the case owner that a large deployer be invited to participat in a case to    address concerns about the impact of deploying a fix for a vulnerability on infrastructure and operations.</li> </ul> <p>Below is a sequence diagram showing the process of suggesting an actor for a case. We used a sequence diagram instead of a flow chart since the process is relatively simple and the sequence diagram is easier to read.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Suggesting an Actor for a Case (ADR-0026 CaseActor-routed)\n---\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor A as Recommender\n    participant CA as CaseActor\n    actor B as Case Owner\n    actor D as Invitee\n    Note over A: Recognize that Actor should be invited\n    A -&gt;&gt; CA: Offer(object=Actor, target=Case)\n    activate CA\n    Note over CA: Record in ledger, assign default roles\n    CA -&gt;&gt; B: Offer(object=CaseParticipant{actor,roles}, target=Case, origin=Offer.id)\n    activate B\n    alt Accept Suggestion\n        B -&gt;&gt; CA: Accept(object=Offer(CaseParticipant))\n        CA -&gt;&gt; A: AcceptActorRecommendation\n        CA -&gt;&gt;+ D: Invite(CaseStub + embargo + roles)\n        note over D: Respond to invitation (not shown)\n        deactivate D\n    else Reject Suggestion\n        B -&gt;&gt; CA: Reject(object=Offer(CaseParticipant))\n        CA -&gt;&gt; A: RejectActorRecommendation\n    end\n    deactivate B\n    deactivate CA</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/suggest_actor/#recommend-actor","title":"Recommend Actor","text":"<p>A participant recommends another actor to the CaseActor by sending an <code>Offer</code> activity with the <code>object</code> property set to the actor being recommended and the <code>target</code> set to the case. Not a distinct protocol role per ADR-0078; an actor who discovers and reports holds the Reporter role. Discoverer identity is recorded in Report content or case Note entries. Researcher, discoverer Reporter The person or organization that submits a vulnerability report to affected parties (often the same as Finder) Submitter, notifier Vendor The organization that maintains or supplies the affected product or service Developer, supplier, maintainer Deployer An organization that deploys the Vendor's product and is responsible for applying patches in their own environment (distinct from Vendor) Operator, customer Coordinator A neutral third party (often a national CERT) that facilitates communication and negotiates embargo terms between other parties Mediator, facilitator Participant Any Actor engaged in a Case, holding one or more CVD Roles Stakeholder, party Actor Any URI-identified federated peer (person or organization) in the protocol Agent, endpoint Case Owner The Actor who creates and administers a Case (typically the party seeking vulnerability coordination) Case creator Case Actor The concrete actor the prototype/demo implements to hold <code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code> \u2014 an automated software actor spawned to enact the role and automate its duties (emitting activities, maintaining the canonical ledger). It is a specific identity/label (<code>case-actor</code>, <code>.../actors/case-actor</code>) with no protocol meaning. It is not a synonym for the authority and not an identity to match on: authority, recognition, and routing derive from the <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> role, never from this actor's name or URL, and code MUST NOT compare <code>actor_id</code> against a computed <code>case_actor_id</code> to decide authority (ADR-0088, refining ADR-0041). Name the authority Case Manager (the role holder); use Case Actor only for the prototype actor that happens to hold it. Case service actor, case coordinator, \"the CaseActor authority\" Case Manager The <code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code> role \u2014 the single-writer authority for a case. Whichever Participant holds it is authoritative for the canonical case ledger and case-scoped routing; authority is determined by the role and nothing else (ADR-0088). Often assigned via Offer \u2192 Accept handoff during case creation, and may co-manage embargo negotiations. Protocol-normative prose names the authority the CASE_MANAGER (the role holder), never the CaseActor (the prototype identity). Admin role, management role Case Actor Service The provisioning endpoint (configured as <code>case_actor_service_url</code>) that receives <code>CaseProposal</code>s and spawns the <code>case-actor</code> identities that enact <code>CASE_MANAGER</code>. A hosting/provisioning concern \u2014 distinct from the authority (the role) and from any one Case Actor identity it spawns. Hosting location and URL shape carry no authority signal (ADR-0088). Case actor URL, provisioning service CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) An organization authorized to directly assign CVE IDs; modeled as <code>CVDRole.CVE_NUMBERING_AUTHORITY</code>. The 2^6 combinations give a 64-state lattice, of which only 32 are reachable: <code>vF*</code> (fix ready, vendor unaware) and <code>*fD*</code> (fix deployed, fix not ready) are structurally impossible, per SM-09-002 and CSB-17-001.</p>"},{"location":"reference/glossary/#state-machines-and-status","title":"State Machines and Status","text":"Term Definition Aliases to avoid Report Management (RM) Per-participant state machine tracking a Report's lifecycle: Start \u2192 Received \u2192 {Invalid | Valid} \u2192 {Accepted | Deferred} \u2192 Closed; used to track embargo history Embargo record Embargo Consent A Participant's individual agreement to or rejection of an Embargo (a personal commitment, distinct from the Embargo itself); tracked as a per-participant 5-state machine over NO_EMBARGO, INVITED, SIGNATORY, LAPSED, and DECLINED. NO_EMBARGO means no embargo is in scope for this participant \u2014 not \"has not consented yet\" \u2014 so ACCEPT and DECLINE are valid directly from it, without an intervening invitation (ADR-0048, CM-18-003) Embargo acceptance, embargo stance Active Embargo The currently in-force Embargo for a Case; there is at most one Current embargo, ongoing embargo Proposed Embargo An Embargo that has been offered but not yet accepted by all parties Embargo offer, pending embargo Pocket Veto A timer-based transition in the Embargo Consent state machine where a Participant in INVITED or LAPSED state automatically transitions to DECLINED if they do not respond within a configurable timeout window (inaction = rejection). The window is the implicit form of the RSVP Deadline: when an invitation carries an explicit <code>Invite.end_time</code> that value supersedes it (CM-27-002); the policy default (7 days, EP-07-001) applies only when it is absent. The two are one mechanism, not two (ADR-0065) Embargo invitation timeout, implicit rejection RSVP Deadline The activity-level <code>end_time</code> on an <code>Invite(EmbargoEvent)</code>, giving the invitee an explicit respond-by instant after which the invitation is no longer open. Distinct from the nested <code>Invite.object_.end_time</code>, which is when the Embargo itself ends \u2014 the same invitation carries both, one nesting level apart. Enforced lazily by the CASE_MANAGER (CM-27-003); a late Accept is never refused outright (EMB-17). Introduced by ADR-0065 Invite expiry, respond-by deadline, invite end_time EmbargoPolicy An actor-level declaration of embargo preferences (preferred, minimum, and maximum duration); allows coordinators to evaluate compatibility before proposing an embargo. Embargo preferences, embargo terms Embargo Adherence A derived indicator on a Participant's status recording whether that Participant is currently bound by the active Embargo; <code>True</code> only when their Embargo Consent state is <code>SIGNATORY</code>. Computed from consent state rather than stored independently, preventing the two from drifting out of sync. Embargo acceptance, embargo compliance"},{"location":"reference/glossary/#messaging-and-protocol","title":"Messaging and Protocol","text":"Term Definition Aliases to avoid Semantic Type (or MessageSemantics) The classification of an Activity's meaning (e.g., <code>CreateReport</code>, <code>AcceptEmbargoOnCase</code>, <code>ProposeEmbargo</code>); determines how it is processed Activity type, message type Message Type One of 29 formal protocol message categories: RM messages (RS, RI, RV, RD, RA, RC, RK, RE), EM messages (EP, ER, EA, EV, EJ, EC, ET, EK, EE), CS messages (CV, CF, CD, CP, CX, CA, CK, CE), or General (GI, GK, GE) Protocol message category State-Change Notification The core protocol principle: every participant state transition SHOULD generate a message to inform other participants; implements \"Avoid Surprise\" Status announcement, state broadcast Inbox The protocol endpoint where an Actor receives incoming Activities from other parties Receiver, endpoint Outbox The protocol channel through which an Actor broadcasts Activities to other known parties Sender, distribution Precondition The required state(s) that must be true before a message can be sent or a state transition is valid (e.g., Participant must be in RM Accepted to send RS) State requirement, prerequisite CaseProposal An AS2 negotiation object sent by any actor (typically a Vendor or Coordinator) to a case actor service to request the creation and management of a new Case; the CASE_MANAGER, not the requesting actor, is the authoritative case creator. The CaseProposal is the mechanism by which an actor delegates case initialization to a case actor service (ADR-0023, ADR-0041). \"Participant\" for case-specific engagement; \"Process\" for formal protocol math.</p> </li> <li> <p>\"Reachable\" vs. \"Valid\":</p> </li> <li>Reachable = logically possible given protocol constraints (state might not occur in practice but conforms to rules).</li> <li>Valid = permissible per protocol rules (state satisfies all constraints).</li> <li>Unreachable = impossible due to hard constraints (violates protocol rules).</li> <li> <p>Recommendation: Use \"Reachable State\" for logical possibility; \"Valid Transition\" for rule compliance.</p> </li> <li> <p>\"CS Event\" vs. \"Message Type\":</p> </li> <li>A CS Event (V, F, D, P, X, A) is a formal state transition in the Case State lattice.</li> <li>A Message Type (CV, CF, CD, CP, CX, CA) is the protocol message announcing that event.</li> <li>Not all CS Events are announced (e.g., a Vendor may internally transition Vfd\u2192VFd without sending CF).</li> <li> <p>Recommendation: Use \"CS Event\" for state transitions; \"Message Type\" for protocol announcements.</p> </li> <li> <p>\"Activity\" direction \u2014 The term Activity is used for both Inbound and Outbound. Both follow the same ActivityStreams 2.0 format, but the context (inbox vs. outbox, received vs. constructed) determines meaning.</p> </li> <li> <p>Recommendation: Always qualify as \"inbound Activity\" or \"outbound Activity\" when direction matters.</p> </li> <li> <p>\"Factory\" scope \u2014 The term Factory can mean:</p> </li> <li>The set of Factory Functions in the <code>vultron/wire/as2/factories/</code> package (the public API)</li> <li>A single Factory Function (e.g., <code>create_report()</code>)</li> <li> <p>Never use \"factory\" to mean \"the place where activities are made\" \u2014 always say Factory Function or factories package.</p> </li> <li> <p>\"Port\" (hexagonal vs. TCP) \u2014 In this domain, Port always means a hexagonal architecture interface contract, never a TCP port. No TCP concepts are in scope.</p> </li> <li> <p>\"Deprecated\" methods \u2014 <code>get()</code> and <code>by_type()</code> on DataLayer are called \"deprecated\" but still exist in the codebase. This means they are marked for removal and are being gradually replaced by Narrow Ports (CasePersistence, CaseOutboxPersistence) and Rehydration. \"Deprecated\" \u2260 \"removed yet.\"</p> </li> <li> <p>\"Narrow\" vs. \"broad\" ports \u2014 A Narrow Port is small, typed, domain-specific (e.g., <code>CasePersistence</code> with <code>read_by_id()</code>, <code>list_by_status()</code>). A broad port is generic and untyped (e.g., <code>DataLayer</code> with <code>get(table, id)</code>, <code>by_type(type)</code>). The goal is to replace broad ports with Narrow Ports to improve type safety and reduce coupling.</p> </li> <li> <p>\"Report\" vs. \"Case\":</p> <ul> <li>A Report is a one-time vulnerability notification from a Reporter.</li> <li>A Case is the ongoing coordination container with state machines (RM, EM, CS) and participants.</li> <li>Multiple Reports may consolidate into one Case; one Report may split into multiple Cases.</li> <li>Recommendation: \"Report\" = inbound notification; \"Case\" = coordination entity with state machines.</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"Embargo\" vs. \"Embargo Consent\":</p> <ul> <li>An Embargo is a shared agreement (one per Case) that all parties will not disclose until a certain date.</li> <li>Embargo Consent is each Participant's individual acceptance or rejection of that embargo.</li> <li>Recommendation: If discussing terms/dates, say \"Embargo\"; if discussing one party's stance, say \"Embargo Consent\".</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"Case Owner\" vs. \"Case Manager\" (role) vs. \"Case Actor\" (prototype identity) vs. \"case actor service\":</p> <ul> <li>A Case Owner is a human Participant (e.g., Reporter) with a CVDRole.CASE_OWNER value; the decision-maker and administrator of the Case.</li> <li>Case Manager (<code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code>) is the role that carries single-writer authority over the canonical case ledger. It is the only protocol-salient signal of authority: an actor is the authority for a case iff it holds this role in the case roster.</li> <li>A Case Actor is the concrete actor the prototype/demo implements to hold <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> \u2014 a specific identity labelled <code>case-actor</code>. It is not a synonym for the authority and not an identity to match on: its name and URL are cosmetic and carry no protocol meaning (ADR-0088).</li> <li>A case actor service is the provisioning endpoint (<code>case_actor_service_url</code>) that spawns <code>case-actor</code> identities \u2014 a hosting concern, not the authority.</li> <li>Recommendation: In protocol-normative prose, name the authority \"the CASE_MANAGER\" (the role holder), never \"the CaseActor\". Reserve \"CaseActor\" for the prototype/demo actor that enacts the role, and \"case actor service\" for the provisioning endpoint. Never determine authority, recognition, or routing from the <code>case-actor</code> name or URL shape, and never compare <code>actor_id</code> against a computed <code>case_actor_id</code> to decide authority \u2014 gate on the role (CM-24-004, CM-02-011).</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"Participant Case Replica\" vs. \"Case State\":</p> <ul> <li>A Participant Case Replica is a local copy of case state on a participant's node; must be seeded via Trust Bootstrap and maintain Eventual Consistency with the CASE_MANAGER's authoritative state.</li> <li>Case State (CS) is the formal six-dimensional state model (VfDpxa lattice) tracking vulnerability awareness and readiness.</li> <li>Recommendation: Use \"Participant Case Replica\" for participant-local state copies; \"Case State\" for the formal model.</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"CVDRole\" vs. \"CVDRolesFlag\":</p> <ul> <li>CVDRole is a StrEnum (string enum) representing individual, atomic roles; participants hold zero or more roles as <code>list[CVDRole]</code>; this is the preferred representation for all new code.</li> <li>CVDRolesFlag is a legacy Flag enum (bitmask) used only by the <code>vultron.bt</code> simulator layer; it existed before the migration to list-based roles and is retained for backward compatibility only.</li> <li>Recommendation: Always use <code>list[CVDRole]</code> in new code; never use CVDRolesFlag outside the <code>vultron.bt</code> simulator. When discussing roles, say \"CVDRole\" or \"role list,\" never \"CVDRoles\" (plural, deprecated name).</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"Call-Out Point\" vs. \"Fuzzer Node\":</p> <ul> <li>A Call-Out Point is the abstract concept \u2014 a BT location requiring external input.</li> <li>A Fuzzer Node is the concrete simulator-layer stub that occupies that location until a real capability is wired in.</li> <li>Recommendation: Use \"Call-Out Point\" when discussing design or integration seams; use \"Fuzzer Node\" only when discussing the simulator implementation.</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"Composer\" vs. \"Actuator\" (capability shape classification):</p> <ul> <li>A Composer reads context, runs a generation process, and writes a content artifact to the blackboard (e.g., advisory draft text).</li> <li>An Actuator receives a trigger, calls an external system, and confirms the side effect; no artifact is placed on the blackboard.</li> <li>Misclassification risk: nodes that \"do something\" to an external system look like Composers if you only notice they dispatch outbound calls. The discriminator is whether a content artifact lands on the blackboard. If not, it is an Actuator capability shape.</li> <li>Recommendation: Before classifying a node as Composer, verify it writes a content artifact to the blackboard. If the only output is a SUCCESS/FAILURE confirming an external side effect, it is an Actuator capability shape.</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"Coordination Agent\" vs. \"Capability shape\":</p> <ul> <li>A Capability shape is the current term for the abstract interface contract at a call-out point (Sentinel, Evaluator, Retriever, Composer, Actuator).</li> <li>Coordination Agent was the previous term. It is deprecated because \"agent\" has acquired connotations of LLM-based autonomous systems, which was not the original intent.</li> <li>Recommendation: Use \"capability shape\" in all new text. When reading older code or docs, treat \"Coordination Agent\" as a synonym for \"capability shape.\"</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>\"Dimension Object\" vs. \"status field\":</p> <ul> <li>A Dimension Object (per ADR-0036) is an immutable <code>BaseModel</code> containing the state of one machine; it is a first-class structured type, not a flat field.</li> <li>\"Status field\" is informal language that may mean a flat scalar (<code>rmState: \"ACCEPTED\"</code>) or a Dimension Object (<code>rm: {\"state\": \"ACCEPTED\"}</code>); both appear in real ledger snapshots.</li> <li>Recommendation: Say \"Dimension Object\" when referring to the structured sub-model; say \"flat legacy field\" when referring to the pre-ADR-0036 serialization. Several of the modules it names no longer exist, and the semantics-to-pattern mapping shown below as a <code>dict</code> is now the ordered <code>SEMANTIC_REGISTRY</code> list in <code>vultron/semantic_registry/</code>. Read it for the design reasoning, not for current file locations or symbol names.</p> <p>Vultron is designed with the ActivityPub protocol in mind. Most activity in Vultron involves actors exchanging activity messages containing objects.</p> <p>Submitting a Vulnerability Report</p> <p>For example, an actor might create a <code>VulnerabilityReport</code> object and then offer it to another actor, who can then accept, tentatively reject, or  reject the offer.</p> <p>Actors in ActivityPub can be of various types, such as <code>Person</code>, <code>Organization</code>, <code>Group</code>, <code>Application</code>, <code>Service</code>, etc. Each actor has an inbox and an outbox. The inbox is where the actor receives activities, and the outbox is where the actor sends activities.</p> <p>Actor Inboxes and Outboxes</p> <p>For example, if Alice is a <code>Person</code> actor, she has an inbox at <code>https://example.com/users/alice/inbox</code> and an outbox at <code>https://example.com/users/alice/outbox</code>. If Bob is another <code>Person</code> actor, he has his own inbox and outbox.</p> <p>When Alice wants to send an activity to Bob, she creates the activity with the <code>to</code> field set to Bob's actor ID (e.g., <code>https://example.com/users/bob</code>) and places it in her outbox. The ActivityPub server then delivers the activity to Bob's inbox. Bob can then process the activity and respond by sending an activity to his outbox, with the <code>to</code> field set to Alice's actor ID. He can also set the <code>inReplyTo</code> field to reference the original activity from Alice to indicate that it is a response. The ActivityPub server handles the delivery of the activity to Alice's inbox,  and the cycle continues.</p> <p>Scope of Vultron's ActivityPub Implementation</p> <p>However, the Vultron prototype does not implement a full ActivityPub server. Instead, it initially focuses on the core functionality of actors sending activities directly to each other's inboxes. This simplifies the implementation while still demonstrating the core concepts of ActivityPub interactions.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#inbox-handler-architecture","title":"Inbox Handler Architecture","text":"<p>The initial architecture is as follows: An actor has an inbox implemented as a FastAPI endpoint that accepts POST requests containing activity messages. When a message is received, the inbox handler processes the activity and routes it to an appropriate handler based on the activity's semantics.</p> <p>Activity Handling</p> <p>For example, if the activity is an <code>Offer</code> of a <code>VulnerabilityReport</code>, it would be routed to a <code>submit_report</code> handler function, which contains the logic for processing a vulnerability report submission.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#out-of-scope","title":"Out of scope","text":"<p>Authentication, authorization, and server-to-server federation are deferred to future implementation.</p> <p>This design also does not describe what happens inside each handler function; that is left to the specific handler implementations to come later. The focus of this design is on the inbox handler and dispatching logic that routes activities to the appropriate handler functions.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#inbox-handler-process","title":"Inbox Handler Process","text":"<p>The inbox handler process consists of the following steps:</p> <ol> <li>Receive Activity: The inbox endpoint receives a POST request containing an activity message in JSON format.</li> <li>Validate Activity: The inbox endpoint validates the activity message structure to ensure it conforms to the ActivityPub specification.</li> <li>Log Activity: The inbox endpoint logs the received activity message for debugging and auditing purposes.</li> <li>Queue Activity: (only if Validate Activity succeeds) The inbox endpoint places the activity message into an asynchronous processing call to the inbox handler function, allowing the endpoint to respond immediately while the activity is processed in the background.</li> <li>Acknowledge Receipt: The inbox endpoint responds to the POST request with a 200 OK status to acknowledge receipt of the activity message. If the validation failed, it can respond with an appropriate error status (e.g., 400 Bad Request) and log the error.</li> <li>Extract Routing Information: The inbox handler extracts key fields from the activity message (e.g., <code>type</code>, <code>object</code>, <code>to</code>, <code>inReplyTo</code>) to determine routing.    It creates a <code>DispatchEvent</code> header object containing the routing information and attaches the original activity message as the payload.</li> <li>Dispatch Activity: The inbox handler invokes a dispatch function that routes the <code>DispatchEvent</code> object to the appropriate handler function based on the activity's semantic type.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#activity-patterns-and-semantics","title":"Activity Patterns and Semantics","text":"<p>Routing semantics are identified by <code>ActivityPattern</code> objects, which define patterns for matching activity messages to specific enumerated semantic meanings. This decouples the raw activity message structure from the higher-level semantics of the Vultron protocol, allowing raw messages to be translated into meaningful semantics that drive application logic.</p> <p>Defining Activity Patterns</p> <p>An activity pattern for submitting a vulnerability report might be defined as an <code>Offer</code> activity with an object of type <code>VulnerabilityReport</code>.  Responses to that offer follow their own patterns:</p> <pre><code>ReportSubmission = ActivityPattern(\n    activity_=TAtype.OFFER,\n    object_=VOtype.VULNERABILITY_REPORT,\n)\nAckReport = ActivityPattern(activity_=TAtype.READ, object_=ReportSubmission)\nValidateReport = ActivityPattern(\n    activity_=TAtype.ACCEPT, object_=ReportSubmission\n)\nInvalidateReport = ActivityPattern(\n    activity_=TAtype.TENTATIVE_REJECT, object_=ReportSubmission\n)\nCloseReport = ActivityPattern(\n    activity_=TAtype.REJECT, object_=ReportSubmission\n)\n</code></pre> <p>The various <code>*type</code>s are string enumerations defined elsewhere.</p> <p>Mapping Activity Patterns to Semantics</p> <p>The mapping from raw activity message patterns to higher-level semantics is defined as follows:</p> <pre><code>SEMANTICS_ACTIVITY_PATTERNS: dict[MessageSemantics, ActivityPattern] = {\n    MessageSemantics.SUBMIT_REPORT: ap.ReportSubmission,\n    MessageSemantics.ACK_REPORT: ap.AckReport,\n    MessageSemantics.VALIDATE_REPORT: ap.ValidateReport,\n    MessageSemantics.INVALIDATE_REPORT: ap.InvalidateReport,\n    MessageSemantics.CLOSE_REPORT: ap.CloseReport,\n    # ...etc.\n}\n</code></pre> <p>Activity semantics are determined by the <code>type</code> field of the activity message, along with fields such as <code>object</code>, <code>to</code>, and <code>inReplyTo</code>. The dispatch function uses this information to determine which handler function should process the activity.</p> <p>DispatchEvent Object</p> <p>A <code>DispatchEvent</code> object encapsulates the routing information needed by the dispatch function. The handler function is then invoked with the <code>DispatchEvent</code> object as an argument.</p> <p>Example</p> <p>The following is an example of the <code>ActivityDispatcher</code> Protocol that defines   the interface for dispatching activities:</p> <pre><code>class ActivityDispatcher(Protocol):\n    \"\"\"\n    Protocol for dispatching activities to their corresponding handlers based on message semantics.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def dispatch(self, dispatchable: DispatchEvent) -&gt; None:\n        \"\"\"Dispatches an activity to the appropriate handler based on its semantic type.\"\"\"\n        ...\n</code></pre> <p>On the Modularity of Dispatchers</p> <p>The dispatch function is designed as a Python <code>Protocol</code> to allow for different dispatcher implementations. This provides flexibility in connecting the inbox  handler to specific handler functions for each semantic type. A simple  implementation might use a dictionary mapping from semantic types to handler  functions, while a more complex implementation could involve message queues  or other routing mechanisms.</p> <p>This modularity allows dispatching logic to be extended easily by defining new  <code>ActivityPattern</code>s with corresponding <code>MessageSemantics</code>, then adding new  handler functions to the dispatch mapping. Decoupling routing logic from  handling logic maintains clean separation of concerns and facilitates  future protocol extensions.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#direct-dispatch-implementation","title":"Direct Dispatch Implementation","text":"<p>The first dispatch function implementation uses a simple direct dispatch approach with a dictionary mapping from <code>MessageSemantics</code> to handler functions. The dispatch function looks up the <code>semantic_type</code> from the <code>DispatchEvent</code> object in the mapping and invokes the corresponding handler function with the <code>DispatchEvent</code> as an argument.</p> <p>This direct dispatch implementation is straightforward and allows activities to be handled quickly based on their semantics.</p> <p>Into the Unknown?</p> <p>What happens if an activity is received that does not match any known <code>ActivityPattern</code>? This distinction is most prominent in the connections from the Received and Deferred RM states in the two figures above. These differences are the result of the relative timing of the two different decisions they support within a CVD case.</p> <p>The decision to Coordinate (i.e., whether the Coordinator should move from RM Valid to RM Accept  (\\(q^{rm} \\in V \\xrightarrow{a} A\\)) occurs early in the Coordinator's RM process. The SSVC Supplier Engagement decision point is an attempt to capture this information. This early in the process, allowances must be made for Vendors who may not have completed their own validation or  prioritization processes.  Hence, the mapping allows Vendors in any valid yet unclosed state (\\(q^{rm} \\in \\{R,V,A,D\\}\\)) to be categorized as  Active for this decision point.</p> <p>On the other hand, the decision to Publish\u2014a choice that falls entirely within the Coordinator's RM Accepted  state\u2014occurs later, at which time, more is known about each Vendor's level of involvement in the case to that point. They might already have a Fix-Ready (\\(q^{cs} \\in VF \\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\)), or they might be working toward it (i.e., SSVC Cooperative). However, if the Coordinator has reached the point where they are making a publication decision, and the Vendor has  yet to actively engage in the case for whatever reason\u2014as indicated by their failure to reach the RM Accepted state or demonstrate progress toward it by at least getting to RM Valid  (\\(q^{rm} \\in \\{A,V\\}\\))\u2014then they can be categorized as Uncooperative/Unresponsive.</p> <p>SSVC Decision Points and Anticipated Transitions</p> <p>Other SSVC decision points may be informative about which transitions to expect in a case. For the first (or only) release in a given month, the patch number     starts at <code>0</code> and is normally omitted, so <code>2024.4.0</code> and <code>2024.4</code>     denote the same version.</p> </li> </ul> <p>Version increments work as follows:</p> <ul> <li> <p>Significant releases use the current year and month, with the patch     number starting at <code>0</code> (normally omitted).     Example: the first significant release in April 2024 is <code>2024.4</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Patch releases increment the patch number from the most recent     non-patch release, even if the patch is published in a later month or year.     Example: the third small update to <code>2024.4</code> is <code>2024.4.3</code>, even if it     is released in May 2024 or later.</p> </li> </ul> <p>No backward compatibility commitments are made or implied at this stage. The abstract Vultron protocol: the state machines (RM, EM, PEC, VFD, PXA), the valid transitions between states, the process logic that drives those transitions, and the behavioral conformance rules that define correct observable behavior.</p> <p>What is in scope.</p> <ul> <li>The five state machines and their transition tables</li> <li>The behavioral conformance specifications (RMB, EMB, CSB) that state correct outputs for given inputs</li> <li>The ordering and cascade rules between dimensions (for example, when an EM transition must trigger a PEC bulk update)</li> <li>The process model: how N independent participants coordinate through message passing</li> </ul> <p>What is out of scope.</p> <ul> <li>The Python module <code>vultron/core/</code> \u2014 that is the reference implementation of this concept, not the concept itself</li> <li>The behavior trees \u2014 those are one valid mechanism for executing vultron-core, not a required part of it</li> <li>The message format \u2014 that is vultron-wire</li> <li>The delivery mechanism \u2014 that is vultron-transport</li> </ul> <p>Relationship to other concepts.</p> <ul> <li>vultron-wire carries the semantic meaning that vultron-core defines.</li> <li>vultron-transport moves vultron-wire messages between participants.</li> <li>The behavioral conformance specifications (RMB, EMB, CSB) are part of the vultron-core capability set. They are not a separate layer.</li> <li>An implementation of vultron-core is a \"coordination engine\" for CVD. That label describes what the implementation does, not a separate concept.</li> </ul> <p>Implementation note (reference only)</p> <p>In the Python reference implementation, vultron-core maps to the <code>vultron/core/</code> module: the hexagonal inner circle that has no imports from the wire or adapter layers. The taxonomy of optional, pluggable capability patterns. Each capability shape defines a contract for a specific category of automation that can connect to the behavior engine at a call-out point.</p> <p>Previous name. This concept was previously named \"agent shapes\" or \"coordination agent taxonomy.\" That name was accurate when written. It is now replaced because \"agent\" has acquired strong connotations of LLM-based autonomous systems, which was not the original intent. \"Capability shape\" describes what the concept actually covers: the pattern that a capability takes.</p> <p>The five capability shapes.</p> Shape What it does Connection type Sentinel Independently monitors an external condition; when the condition fires, calls a Vultron trigger endpoint. Not called by the behavior engine. Call-in surface (no call-out point node) Evaluator Receives a situation and a set of options. Returns a structured recommendation. Gates downstream execution. Call-out point Retriever Receives a query. Returns structured facts from an external source. Call-out point Composer Receives context. Generates and records a new content artifact. Call-out point Actuator Receives a trigger. Invokes an external system for a side effect. Confirms success or failure. Produces no content artifact. Call-out point <p>A capability shape defines the contract. A concrete implementation that satisfies the contract is a Vultron-compatible capability of that shape.</p> <p>What is in scope.</p> <ul> <li>The five shapes and their contracts (what each shape accepts and returns)</li> <li>The classification rule for each shape</li> </ul> <p>What is out of scope.</p> <ul> <li>The specific technology used to fulfill a shape (a shape may be fulfilled by a human, an automated script, an LLM, or any other mechanism)</li> <li>The Fuzzer Node \u2014 that is a simulator-layer stub that occupies a call-out point until a real capability is wired in; it is not a capability shape itself</li> </ul> <p>Relationship to other concepts.</p> <ul> <li>Capability shapes are orthogonal to capability sets. An Observer implementation may have zero capability shapes implemented. A Sentinel capability does not require anything beyond what the host behavior engine provides.</li> <li>Capability shapes are the taxonomy for the optional capabilities in Vultron capability sets.</li> <li>In the reference implementation, a capability shape maps to a Port (abstract interface). A concrete capability implementation maps to an Adapter. This mapping is specific to the hexagonal architecture of the Python codebase and is not required of other implementations.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-taxonomy/#participation-concepts","title":"Participation Concepts","text":""},{"location":"reference/vultron-taxonomy/#vultron-roles","title":"Vultron roles","text":"<p>Definition. Case-level participation assignments. A role describes what an actor is doing in a specific case.</p> <p>Roles are not properties of systems. They are assignments within a case.</p> <p>Two categories of roles.</p> <p>Process roles define what an actor does within a case and which protocol transitions it is authorized to drive.</p> Role Drive authority Reporter Initiates cases; drives RS (report submission) Vendor Drives its own VFD fix-ready transition (CF) Deployer Drives its own VFD fix-deployed transition (CD) Coordinator Drives case participant management; coordinates multi-party disclosure CNA May directly assign CVE IDs Observer No VFD drive obligations; may report PXA observations <p>Protocol authority roles define what an actor controls in the protocol machinery.</p> Role Protocol authority Case Owner Authoritative decision-maker for a case Case Manager AS actor performing case replica synchronization on behalf of the Case Owner <p>Role assignment.</p> <p>Roles are assigned, not self-declared.</p> <ol> <li>A case starts with a Case Owner (the actor who initiated the case).</li> <li>The Case Owner may delegate the Case Manager role to another actor.</li> <li>The Case Manager designates other actors into process roles.</li> </ol> <p>Self-assignment is not permitted. This rule prevents an actor from declaring a role (for example, Coordinator) on a case it is not ready to coordinate.</p> <p>Capabilities and roles.</p> <p>The relationship between capabilities and roles is bidirectional.</p> <ul> <li>Capabilities are a prerequisite for a role. Having the right capabilities means an actor can perform the role. It does not mean the actor automatically holds the role.</li> <li>Holding a role in a case means other participants expect the actor to have the capabilities that role requires.</li> </ul> <p>What is in scope.</p> <ul> <li>The two categories of roles and their definitions</li> <li>The assignment chain (Case Owner \u2192 Case Manager \u2192 others)</li> <li>The bidirectional relationship between capabilities and roles</li> </ul> <p>Relationship to other concepts.</p> <ul> <li>A role claim creates capability expectations. This design allows us to separate the core domain logic from the infrastructure and external interfaces, making the system more modular, testable, and adaptable to different use cases and environments.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Hexagonal Architecture Overview\n---\nflowchart LR\n\nadapters1[Driving Adapters]\nadapters2[Driven Adapters]\nports1[Driving Ports]\nports2[Driven Ports]\ncore{{Core Domain Logic}}\nadapters1 --o ports1\nports1 --o core\ncore --o ports2\nports2 --o adapters2</code></pre> <p>In this architecture:</p> <ul> <li>The Driving Adapters implement the driving ports using specific   technologies (e.g., FastAPI endpoints, CLI commands, etc.) and translate   external inputs into calls to the core domain logic.</li> <li>The Driving Ports define the interfaces through which external actors   (e.g., finders, vendors, coordinators) can interact with the core domain logic. These are the entry points for commands and queries that drive the system's behavior.</li> <li>The Core Domain Logic contains the business rules, policies, and behavior trees that govern how the system operates. It is completely agnostic to how it is accessed or what technologies are used to implement the interfaces.</li> <li>The Driven Ports define the interfaces through which the core domain   logic can interact with external systems (e.g., databases, message queues,   external APIs). These are the exit points for the core to perform actions   that have side effects or require external resources.</li> <li>The Driven Adapters implement the driven ports using specific technologies   (e.g., MongoDB for database access, Celery for task queues, etc.)   and   translate calls from the core domain logic into interactions with external   systems.</li> </ul> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Hexagonal Architecture Details\n---\nflowchart LR\n\nsubgraph driving_adapters [Driving Adapters]\n    direction LR\n    api[API Endpoints]\n    cli[CLI Commands]\n    mcp[MCP Tools]\nend\nsubgraph driving_ports [Driving Ports]\n    direction LR\n    use_cases[Use Cases]\n    commands[Commands]\nend\nsubgraph core [Core Domain Logic]\n    direction LR\n    domain_models[Domain Models]\n    services[Domain Services]\n    behavior_trees[Behavior Trees]\nend\nsubgraph driven_ports [Driven Ports]\n    direction LR\n    database[Database Access]\n    message_queue[Message Queue]\n    external_apis[External APIs]\nend\nsubgraph driven_adapters [Driven Adapters]\n    direction LR\n    mongo[MongoDB Adapter]\n    celery[Celery Adapter]\n    vince[VINCE Adapter]\nend\n\ndriving_adapters --&gt; driving_ports\ndriving_ports --&gt; core\ncore --&gt; driven_ports\ndriven_ports --&gt; driven_adapters</code></pre>"},{"location":"reference/code/api/actor_inbox_handler/","title":"Actor Inbox Handler","text":"<p>The Actor Inbox Handler is the hub that processes incoming activities. The blank test comes from <code>vocab.base.utils.is_blank</code>, the wire layer's single definition of blank, shared with <code>parser.parse_activity</code>'s required-field guards (CS-22-001).</p> <p>A blank string is absence, not a malformed value: it carries no time, and the alternative \u2014 raising \u2014 is not available to a nested object. <code>parser._expand_inline_value</code> refuses an inline object that fails its own class's validation, so treating a cosmetic blank as a fault would reject the whole message over a field the nested object is allowed to omit outright.</p> <p>Absence here means <code>None</code>, not the field default.  <code>published</code> and <code>updated</code> carry <code>default_factory=now_utc</code>, so omitting the key yields the receiver's clock while a blank yields <code>None</code> \u2014 blank is therefore equivalent to an explicit <code>null</code>, not to omission.  That is the more honest of the two: <code>None</code> records that the sender supplied no time, where the default would fabricate one and present it as the sender's claim.  <code>start_time</code> and <code>end_time</code> default to <code>None</code> already, so for them the two spellings do coincide.</p> <p>A non-blank string that is not a timestamp stays an error: blank means \"not provided\", and reporting corrupt data as missing data would tell the sender to supply a field they already sent (ISSUE-3217).</p>"},{"location":"reference/code/as_vocab/as_objects/#vultron.wire.as2.vocab.base.objects.actors","title":"<code>vultron.wire.as2.vocab.base.objects.actors</code>","text":"<p>This module provides actor classes</p>"},{"location":"reference/code/as_vocab/as_objects/#vultron.wire.as2.vocab.base.objects.actors.as_Actor","title":"<code>as_Actor</code>","text":"<p>               Bases: <code>as_Object</code></p> <p>Base class for all ActivityPub actors. and runs it until either it closes or 1000 ticks have passed. This demo is basically simulating a CVD agent coordinating a CVD case with itself. The agent's role is set to <code>FINDER_REPORTER_VENDOR_DEPLOYER_COORDINATOR</code>, which means it will perform all the roles in the CVD case. Messages emitted in one tick might be received later in the same tick, or in a future tick.</p> <p>Tip</p> <p>This demo leverages the ability to use leaf nodes as stochastic process fuzzers.  Using this feature, we can simulate the behavior of a CVD agent without having to  implement any actual communication mechanisms or simulate any complex real-world processes.</p> <p>One interesting effect of this design is that the places where the demo uses a fuzzer node are often  indicative of places where an actual bot would either need to call out to either a data source or  a human to decide what to do next. This is a good example of how the Vultron behavior tree  can be used to model complex reactive processes in a way that is still easy to understand and reason about.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>There is no underlying communication mechanism in this demo, so messages are not actually  sent anywhere. Instead, they are just added to the blackboard's incoming message queue.  They also have no content, and are only represented as message types.</p> <p>Warning</p> <p>This demo is not intended to be a fully realistic simulation of a CVD case. It is only intended  to demonstrate the behavior of the Vultron behavior tree.</p>"},{"location":"reference/code/demo/","title":"Demo Package","text":"<p>The <code>vultron.demo</code> package contains Finder submits a vulnerability report to C1's inbox.   3. C1 validates and engages the case; invites C2 with CVDRole.COORDINATOR.   4. The inbox route resolves the actor from the store its URI names, so the CaseActor has to be a hosted actor before the proposal is delivered or the round-trip never starts.</p> <p>In the exchange demos one container plays both the participant node and the CaseActor service, so that container is the one that must host it. A derived-but-unregistered identity cannot be provisioned in time by a third party, because the sender computes it from data the receiver has not seen.
