Brand and Zafiropulo defined a protocol as follows.</p> <p>Protocol Formally Defined</p> <p>A protocol with \\(N\\) processes is a quadruple:</p> \\[ protocol =      \\Big \\langle          { \\langle S_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1},          { \\langle o_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1},         { \\langle M_{i,j} \\rangle}^N_{i,j=1},         { succ }     \\Big \\rangle\\] <p>Where</p> <ul> <li> <p>\\(N\\) is a positive integer representing the number of processes.</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(\\langle S_i \\rangle_{i=1}^N\\) are \\(N\\) disjoint finite sets (\\(S_i\\) represents the set of states of process \\(i\\)).</p> </li> <li> <p>Each \\(o_i\\) is an element of \\(S_i\\) representing the initial state of process \\(i\\).</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(\\langle M_{ij} \\rangle_{i,j=1}^N\\) are \\(N^2\\) disjoint finite sets with \\(M_{ii}\\) empty for all \\(i\\). \\(M_{ij}\\) represents the messages that can be sent from process \\(i\\) to process \\(j\\),</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(succ\\) is a partial function mapping for each \\(i\\) and \\(j\\), $\\(S_i \\times M_{ij} \\rightarrow S_i \\textrm{ and } S_i \\times M_{ji} \\rightarrow S_i\\)$ \\(succ(s,x)\\) is the state entered after a process transmits or receives message \\(x\\) in state \\(s\\). It is a transmission if \\(x\\) is from \\(M_{ij}\\) and a reception if \\(x\\) is from \\(M_{ji}\\).</p> </li> </ul> <p>Global State Formally Defined</p> <p>The global state of a protocol given by the above is a pair \\(\\langle S, C \\rangle\\), where</p> <ul> <li> <p>\\(S\\) is an \\(N\\)-tuple of states \\(\\langle s_1,\\dots,s_N \\rangle\\) with each \\(s_i\\) representing the current state of process \\(i\\).</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(C\\) is an \\(N^2\\)-tuple \\(\\langle c_{1,1},\\dots, c_{1,N}, c_{2,1}, \\dots \\dots, c_{N,N} \\rangle\\), where each \\(c_{i,j}\\) is a sequence of messages from \\(M_{i,j}\\). The message sequence \\(c_{i,j}\\) represents the contents of the channel from process \\(i\\) to \\(j\\). (Note that \\(c_{i,j}\\) is empty when \\(i = j\\) since processes are presumed to not communicate with themselves.)</p> </li> </ul> <p>Each of these is detailed below or in subsequent pages:</p> <ul> <li>\\(N\\) below</li> <li>\\({ \\langle S_i \\rangle}^N_{i=1}\\), and \\({ \\langle o_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1}\\) in States,</li> <li>\\({ \\langle M_{i,j} \\rangle }^N_{i,j=1}\\) in Message Types,</li> <li>\\({ succ }\\) in Transition Functions</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/formal_protocol/#number-of-processes","title":"Number of Processes","text":"<p>The processes in an MPCVD case represent the different Participants in their roles (Reporter, Vendor, Coordinator, Deployer, and Observer). The importance of clearly communicating expectations across all parties involved in a CVD process cannot be overemphasized. If we expect cooperation between all parties and stakeholders, we should do our best to match their expectations of being \"in the loop\" and minimize their surprise. Publicly disclosing a vulnerability without coordinating first can result in panic and an aversion to future cooperation from Vendors and Finders alike. CVD promotes continued cooperation and increases the likelihood that future vulnerabilities will also be addressed and remedied.</p> <p>That principle condenses into the following protocol recommendation:</p> <p>Participants whose state changes in the RM, EM, or CVD State Models SHOULD send a message to other Participants for each transition.</p> <p>If you are looking for a one-sentence summary of the entire Vultron Protocol, that was it.</p> <p>State Transitions</p> <ul> <li>RM state transitions \\(\\Sigma^{rm} = \\{ r,v,a,i,d,c\\}\\)</li> <li>EM state transitions \\(\\Sigma^{em} = \\{ p,a,r,t\\}\\)</li> <li>CVD state transitions \\(\\Sigma^{cs} = \\{\\mathbf{V},\\mathbf{F},\\mathbf{D},\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{X},\\mathbf{A}\\}\\)</li> </ul> <p>As a reminder, those transitions are shown at right.</p> <p>The specific circumstances when each message should be emitted are addressed in Transitions; but first, the message types this recommendation implies are introduced here. Ignoring transient states while Participants converge on a consistent view of the global state of a case drastically reduces the state space for an MPCVD case. Why? There are two reasons:</p> <ol> <li> <p>Because they represent facts about the outside world, the eight     \\(\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot pxa \\rightarrow \\cdot\\cdot\\cdot PXA\\) CS substates are global to the case, not     to individual Participants. This means all Participants should     rapidly converge to the same substate.</p> </li> <li> <p>Similarly, the five EM states are also global to the case and should converge rapidly.</p> </li> </ol> <p>Given these two observations, those Participant-agnostic terms can be pulled out of the state calculations for individual Participants,</p> <p>MPCVD State Space With Participant-Agnostic Terms Factored Separately</p> \\[|S_{total}| = \\prod_{i=1}^{N} |S_i| = |S_{global}| \\times \\prod_{i=1}^{N} |S_{Participant}|\\] <p>where </p> \\[ |S_{global}| = 8 \\times 5 = 40 \\] <p>which leaves</p> <p>Participant-Specific State Spaces</p> \\[|S_{Participant}| =     \\begin{cases}         Reporter = 1 + 2 = 3 \\\\         Vendor =  2 + 3 + (2 \\cdot 2) + 3 + (2 \\cdot 2 ) = 16 \\\\         Vendor/Deployer =  2 + 3 + (2 \\cdot 3) + 3 + (2 \\cdot 3) = 20 \\\\         Coordinator = 2 + 5  = 7 \\\\         Deployer = 2 + 3 = 5\\\\         Others = 2 + 5  = 7 \\\\     \\end{cases}\\] <p>So the state space looks like</p> <p>MPCVD State Space Size Formula</p> \\[\\begin{split}     |S_{total}| = 40 &amp; \\times         3^{N_{Reporter}} \\times         16^{N_{Vendor}} \\times         20^{N_{\\frac{Vendor}{Deployer}}} \\\\         &amp; \\times         7^{N_{Coordinator}} \\times          5^{N_{Deployer}} \\times          7^{N_{Other}} \\\\     \\end{split}\\] <p>With these values in mind:</p> <ul> <li> <p>A two-party (Finder-Vendor) case might have a lower bound state space of \\(40 \\times 3 \\times 16 = 1,920\\) states.</p> </li> <li> <p>A case like Meltdown/Spectre (with six Vendors and no Coordinators) might have \\(40 \\times 3 \\times 16^{6} \\approx 10^{9}\\) states.</p> </li> <li> <p>A large, but not atypical, 200-Vendor case handled by the CERT/CC might have     \\(40 \\times 3 \\times 16^{200} \\times 7 \\approx 10^{244}\\) possible configurations.</p> </li> <li> <p>In the case of the log4j vulnerability CVE-2021-44228 in December     2021, the CERT/CC notified around 1,600 Vendors after the vulnerability had been made public. Had this been an     embargoed disclosure, the case would have a total state space around \\(10^{2000}\\).</p> </li> </ul> <p>That said, while these are dramatic numbers, the reader is reminded that the whole point of the Vultron Protocol is to coordinate the process so that it is not just hundreds or thousands of Participants behaving randomly.</p>"},{"location":"reference/formal_protocol/states/#starting-states","title":"Starting States","text":"<p>Each Participant begins a case in the state where the report management process is in the start state, there is no embargo in place, and the case has not made any progress.</p> <p>Participant Start State Formally Defined</p> \\[o_i = (o_i^{rm},~o_i^{em},~o_i^{cs}) = (S,N,vfdpxa)\\] <p>Following the discussion above, the starting states for Vendors, Deployers, and other Participants are shown below.</p> <p>Participant Start States</p> Participant Role Start State (\\(o_i\\)) Vendor \\((S,N,vfdpxa)\\) Deployer \\((S,N,dpxa)\\) Other \\((S,N,pxa)\\) Finder/Reporter \\((A,N,pxa)\\) <p>For a case to really begin, the Finder must at least reach the \\(A\\) state. The Status column states the kind of relationship:</p> Status Meaning <code>direct</code> One shorthand maps to exactly one wire activity. <code>collapse</code> Several shorthands share one wire activity. Multiple shorthands appear in a single row; the Discriminator column names the payload field (or context) that distinguishes them. <code>expansion</code> One shorthand is realized by several wire activities. The same shorthand appears in more than one row. <code>evolved</code> The shorthand's purpose is served by a mechanism partitioned on a different axis (fault reporting or cumulative acknowledgement), not by a dedicated wire activity. <code>\u2014</code> The wire activity has no formal shorthand counterpart. <p>Reading the many-to-many relationship from a table:</p> <ul> <li>Multiple shorthands in one row is a collapse \u2014 for example <code>CP CX CA</code>   ride a single <code>Add(CaseStatus)</code>, discriminated by <code>pxa_state</code>.</li> <li>One shorthand across multiple rows is an expansion \u2014 for example <code>EP</code>   spans four embargo wire activities.</li> </ul> <p>The <code>evolved</code> shorthands (<code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code>, <code>CE</code>, <code>GE</code>, <code>EK</code>, <code>CK</code>, <code>GK</code>) have no dedicated wire activity. Faults are conveyed by <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code>, <code>as:Reject</code>, or <code>Create(Note)</code>, partitioned by failure mode. Acknowledgement of ledger-replicated state is cumulative and implicit through hash-chain continuity; <code>RK</code> survives as a real wire activity because report submission is not ledger-replicated. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>The Vultron Protocol does not make its appearance in uncharted territory, where no existing CVD systems or processes exist. Rather, it is offered as an improvement to interactions among humans, systems, and business processes that already perform MPCVD around the world every day. Thus, for adoption to occur, it will be necessary to map existing systems and processes into the semantics (and eventually, the syntax) of whatever protocol emerges as a descendant of this proposal.</p> <p>Combined with the abstract case class model, an ontology (e.g., using OWL) can accelerate the semantic interoperability between independent Participant processes and tools that this effort set out to improve.</p> <p>A few OWL ontology files describe the Vultron protocol. The core MUST NOT receive a bare <code>BaseObject</code> or generic <code>BaseModel</code> when a more specific type is determinable from the wire payload.Promoting at the boundary (\"validate at edge\") ensures that core handlers receive fully typed objects and never need to downcast or call <code>isinstance()</code> to recover type information that was present on the wire. Two ways a cancelled run otherwise registers as a failure: (1) a guard that files on cancellation directly (e.g. <code>&amp;#124;&amp;#124; contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled')</code>), and (2) a cancelled upstream job that leaves a downstream job to hard-fail on a missing artifact (#3249), laundering the cancellation into a <code>failure</code> result in the <code>needs.*.result</code> aggregate. Implements: BT-16-003 \u2014 Call-out points are the named integration seam that BT-16-003 requires to be documented; the blackboard contract is the required documentation format for data-producing nodes. <code>BT-18-002</code> MUST A call-out point backend \u2014 fuzzer or real implementation \u2014 MUST write to all declared output keys when it returns SUCCESS. A backend MUST NOT return SUCCESS without writing the declared outputs.Downstream BT nodes rely on declared output keys being present after a call-out point succeeds. A fuzzer that returns SUCCESS without writing synthetic output to those keys produces a contract violation: a downstream node reads a missing key and fails, but the failure is attributed to the downstream node rather than the backend. Both fuzzer and real backends must be contract-conformant to make backend swaps transparent. <code>BT-18-003</code> MUST The fuzzer backend for a data-producing call-out point (Evaluator, Retriever, or Composer shape) MUST write synthetic but type-conformant data to the declared output keys. Maintaining the same output contract ensures that demo scenarios exercise the same downstream code paths as production runs. <code>BT-18-004</code> MUST A call-out point node MUST be constructed via a backend factory callable.Factory-based injection is the established BT construction pattern in this codebase. Requiring the factory as a parameter (rather than hardcoding the fuzzer import) is what makes each call-out point an actual injection seam rather than a tightly-coupled stub. Without this, replacing any backend requires editing the tree-building function, defeating the abstraction layer's purpose. Implements: BT-04-001 \u2014 Factory-based injection for call-out points is an application of the existing factory pattern required for all BT construction. <code>BT-18-008</code> MUST Tree-building functions that contain call-out points MUST accept the backend factory as a parameter (or as an entry in a factory mapping).Accepting the factory as a parameter makes each call-out point an actual injection seam rather than a tightly-coupled stub; replacing a backend then requires no changes to the tree-building function. <code>BT-18-009</code> MUST The fuzzer factory MUST be the default value for the backend factory parameter of tree-building functions.A fuzzer default ensures demo scenarios work without explicit backend configuration until a real implementation is available, while still allowing injection of alternative backends at call sites that opt in. <code>BT-18-005</code> MUST The call-out point shape of a fuzzer node MUST be determined solely by the ADR-0024 seam-structure decision tree (how external input enters and output exits the call-out point). Automation potential MUST NOT be used as a criterion for assigning shape = ProtocolInternal. A node whose automation potential is High but whose inputs arrive from an external source or whose outputs affect an external system is a Retriever, Sentinel, Evaluator, Composer, or Actuator \u2014 not ProtocolInternal \u2014 regardless of how automated the implementation may be.Automation potential and call-out point shape are orthogonal dimensions. Automation potential describes whether the call-out point logic can be executed without human involvement; shape describes the structural pattern of the seam (what flows in, what flows out, and in what direction). A Retriever backed by a REST API is still a Retriever; the automation just means the Retriever implementation does not require human action. Conflating the two dimensions caused the FUZZ-08a misclassification tracked in issue #1188, where ~38 nodes with High automation potential were incorrectly assigned ProtocolInternal shape, causing downstream work (FUZZ-08a-bis, FUZZ-08d through FUZZ-08g) to build wrong seams. The five canonical shapes are: Sentinel, Evaluator, Retriever, Composer, and Actuator (added in issue #1239). Nodes that invoke external systems to cause side effects without producing a content artifact MUST be classified as Actuator, not Composer. Implements: BT-16-005 \u2014 BT-16-005 defines automation potential categories; BT-18-005 clarifies that those categories govern the automation-potential field only and have no bearing on call-out point shape assignment. <code>BT-18-006</code> MUST A node that queries an external system synchronously and returns only a binary (SUCCESS/FAILURE) result MUST be classified as a Retriever, not a Sentinel. The defining criterion for Retriever shape is the synchronous on-demand query pattern, not the richness of the returned data; a boolean is the simplest possible structured fact a Retriever may return. A Sentinel, by contrast, monitors a condition continuously or is triggered by an external event and calls a trigger endpoint when the condition becomes true \u2014 the flow direction is Sentinel \u2192 trigger endpoint \u2192 protocol, not protocol \u2192 query \u2192 external system.The Sentinel vs. Retriever ambiguity surfaced with nodes such as MitigationDeployed, MitigationAvailable, and HaveExploit (issue #1240). These nodes appear sentinel-like because they return only SUCCESS/FAILURE, but they are invoked synchronously by the BT (on-demand) and query an external system to determine the current status. That is the Retriever pattern. A true Sentinel is not invoked by the BT; it runs independently and calls a trigger endpoint when a condition fires. Clarifying this distinction prevents future misclassification of on-demand binary-query nodes as Sentinels. Rejecting atomically does not license reporting a single reason: no partial progress was accepted, so a caller told one reason at a time gains nothing from the round trip.Atomicity governs what is written; diagnostic completeness governs what is reported. The two are independent, and conflating them produced a fix-one-resubmit loop on the add-participant-status trigger path (ISSUE-2112). <code>EH-07-002</code> MUST When a validation boundary reports multiple violations, each violation MUST be classified as root or derived. A rule reading a single dimension is always root. A rule reading more than one dimension is derived when any dimension it reads already carries a single-dimension violation, and root otherwise. Dimension overlap is a proxy for the real test, which is remediation: a violation is derived when the remediation the caller is expected to apply to the overlapping single-dimension violation also clears it. The proxy holds only while that premise does. For a transition fault the expected remediation is asserting a legal value, which clears the entailment that read the illegal one. For a role gate the expected remediation is withdrawing the assertion, not acquiring the role \u2014 a participant does not hold a dimension it has no role for at all (a non-DEPLOYER's <code>d</code> is absent, not initial; ADR-0075) and an actor cannot grant itself a role. Any rule family added later whose expected remediation is neither of those MUST be checked against the remediation test before relying on the overlap proxy.One bad dimension frequently entails further violations, so unranked thoroughness degrades into a wall of errors that one fix clears most of. The classification test is dimension overlap rather than a rule-to-rule dependency graph, so a newly added rule is classified correctly by construction and the labelling cannot go stale. The root multi-dimension case is the informative one: every dimension moved legally on its own and the combination is impossible. The remediation premise is stated normatively above because it is load-bearing and was previously left implicit: three separate reviewers read the overlap rule as a pure graph property, concluded a role gate mislabels its entailments, and built a repro that put a participant on a dimension it had no role for \u2014 a state ADR-0075 makes unreachable. The finding dissolved each time, but only after re-deriving the domain premise the requirement never stated. Puppeteering an actor means calling a trigger endpoint that invokes the actor's own use case, which in turn emits the correct protocol message and awaits any required round-trip confirmation (e.g., a CaseActor ledger entry).Direct DataLayer writes bypass the protocol entirely: no ActivityStreams message is emitted, no CaseActor ledger round-trip occurs, and the actor's local state is never established through the protocol. This produces demos that appear to work but do not exercise the real protocol path. For example, a demo that stamps RM.CLOSED directly via <code>add_participant_status</code> gives the appearance that the participant left the case, but no <code>Leave(VulnerabilityCase)</code> message was ever sent or confirmed by the CaseActor. An actor participates in many cases; the CASE_MANAGER is whichever participant the case owner delegated <code>CVDRole.CASE_MANAGER</code> to. That is the role, not an entity, which is why the role is the marker and a <code>Service</code> record is redundant with it. Resending <code>Accept</code> on retry would cause the vendor to see a duplicate acceptance and potentially re-enter the initialization flow. Re-sending the frozen original (VM-08-003) reads as the first acceptance arriving late; a new <code>Accept</code> is indistinguishable from a second, independent decision, which CP-05-005's irrevocability rule precludes. Refines: ASK-08-001 <code>CP-05-007</code> MUST A vendor that has sent <code>Create(as_CaseProposal)</code> and received neither <code>Accept(as_CaseProposal)</code> nor <code>Reject(as_CaseProposal)</code> by the proposal's deadline MUST treat the proposal as expired and MUST NOT continue waiting indefinitely.CONCERN-2367 found that a silently lost <code>Accept</code> stalls the handshake permanently, because no party holds a timeout. The proposal is an ask (ASK-01-001), so it carries a deadline (ASK-03-004) and sits in the vendor's outstanding-ask register (ASK-04-001), which is actor-scoped and therefore works before a case exists. Re-proposal is a later decision, not an automatic retry (ASK-05-004) \u2014 and it is also what lets the case-actor recover (CP-05-006). The formal set partitions both concerns by which state machine the message belonged to; the implementation partitions faults by failure mode and acknowledges replicated state cumulatively. These are orthogonal axes, so the shorthands have no one-to-one wire counterparts even though the behaviours they describe are implemented.</p> ID Priority Requirement Related <code>MSM-05-001</code> MUST Fault reporting MUST be partitioned by failure mode rather than by state machine, using exactly three mechanisms: <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code> when a message was received but not understood; <code>as:Reject</code> when a message was received and understood but declined; and <code>Create(Note)</code> or <code>Add(Note)[target=VulnerabilityCase]</code> when the condition requires narrative explanation.Failure mode is actionable to a receiver in a way that originating state machine is not. Not-understood calls for a format or version fix, declined calls for a protocol-level decision, and needs-explanation calls for a human. The formal RE, EE, CE and GE partition carries no such signal, which is why it was not reproduced. <code>MSM-05-002</code> MUST Acknowledgement of replicated case-ledger state MUST be cumulative and implicit via hash-chain continuity. A receiver whose <code>prev_log_hash</code> matches its local tail MUST NOT emit an acknowledgement, and MUST emit <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> on a mismatch, whereupon the CASE_MANAGER replays all entries after the last accepted hash.A matching <code>prev_log_hash</code> already proves receipt of every prior entry, so per-message positive acknowledgement would be redundant. PEC is a participant-local state machine tracking each actor's relationship to the shared case embargo; its transitions are not independent protocol messages and have no formal shorthands in the 28-shorthand set. PEC state answers the question: \"has this participant explicitly accepted or rejected the current active embargo?\" Unlike RM state (self-reported by the participant) and VF/D state (self-reported by vendor/deployer), PEC state is set by the CASE_MANAGER (CM-28-003) based on observed participant behavior \u2014 incoming Accept/Reject wire activities, timer-enforced lapses, and cascades from shared EM state changes. The five states are NO_EMBARGO (no embargo in scope), INVITED (awaiting response), SIGNATORY (accepted current terms), LAPSED (terms changed since last acceptance), and DECLINED (explicitly refused or timed out without responding). Normative authority: specs/case-management.yaml CM-18. Decision: ADR-0048.</p> ID Priority Requirement Related <code>MSM-07-001</code> MUST The Participant Embargo Consent (PEC) state machine MUST NOT be assigned any formal shorthand in the 28-shorthand protocol message set; all PEC transitions are either side-effects of EM wire activities (MSM-07-002 through MSM-07-005) or timer-based internal events (MSM-07-006) with no dedicated wire message or dispatch value of their own.PEC is participant-local state tracking each actor's relationship to the shared EM state, not a parallel message-driven machine. Extending the formal set with PEC-specific shorthands would imply dedicated wire messages where none exist and none are needed \u2014 the EM messages already carry the PEC signal as a side-effect. Documenting PEC as a side-effect is the faithful description of the design. Derives from: CM-18-003 <code>MSM-07-002</code> MUST The wire activity INVITE_TO_EMBARGO_ON_CASE (EP wire form: Invite(Event)[context=VulnerabilityCase]) MUST apply the PEC INVITE trigger to the invited participant, advancing their consent state from NO_EMBARGO, DECLINED, or LAPSED to INVITED.An embargo proposal is an invitation to consent; the EP wire activity conveys the invitation and the PEC machine records each participant's position. Participants already in SIGNATORY are unaffected by EP; INVITE is a no-op from SIGNATORY (CM-18-004). The PEC trigger is applied via EmbargoLifecycle.record_participant_consent() inside the InviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase received-side handler. An unacceptable value in one dimension MUST NOT cause the values reported in the other dimensions to be discarded. *RM, VFD, EM, PXA and PEC are independent state machines. A value that is unacceptable in one dimension carries no information about the others, so discarding the whole snapshot destroys state the receiver has no grounds to refuse. Liberal accept (ISSUE-2229): accept everything acceptable. * <code>RSH-05-002</code> MUST When a dimension is refused, the receiver MUST record the participant's current value for that dimension alongside the accepted values from the other dimensions, as a single <code>ParticipantStatus</code>. *The recorded status must remain a coherent snapshot of the receiver's view of the participant. Omitting the refused dimension would leave it undefined; recording the asserted value would adopt a claim the receiver just refused. * <code>RSH-05-003</code> MUST A refused dimension MUST NOT prevent the StatusAdoptionGate emit (RSH-01-003) from running. Appending it would grow the participant's status history and the hash chain without recording any state change. * <code>RSH-05-006</code> MUST <code>RM.CLOSED</code> MUST be treated as terminal for the <code>rm</code> dimension only. The local value MUST be carried forward for that dimension; all other dimensions are applied as the entry describes them. *Monotonic visibility (see notes/sync-ledger-replication.md). The Case Actor is authoritative for which transition happened, but a replayed, reordered, or divergent entry would otherwise un-see progress the replica has already observed. Lateral moves at the same rank (<code>VALID</code> &lt;-&gt; <code>INVALID</code>) are re-adjudication, not regression, and are applied unchanged. * <code>RSH-05-008</code> SHOULD The <code>em</code> dimension SHOULD NOT be adjudicated at StatusAdoptionGate; embargo state belongs to EmbargoTeardownAuthorizationGate (<code>add_case_status_tree</code>). *EM is per-case rather than per-participant and its authorization gate is the EmbargoTeardownAuthorizationGate (RSH-02-001). Publishing a field patch instead makes shape preservation structural rather than a property the guard has to remember to maintain. * <code>RSH-05-010</code> MUST A producer of <code>ledger_payload_object_override</code> MUST write <code>None</code> to the key unconditionally at the start of every tick \u2014 before any early return \u2014 so that a stale value from a previous execution cannot bleed into the current one. *The py_trees blackboard is process-global. <code>BTBridge.execute_with_setup</code> does not reset application-level keys between runs, so a producer that only writes on its active path leaves the key at its previous value on every no-op tick. <code>CommitCaseLedgerEntryNode</code> would then apply that stale patch to a different payload snapshot. The required shape is <code>{\"object_id\": &lt;id&gt;, \"producer_type\": &lt;str&gt;, \"fields\": {&lt;wire alias&gt;: &lt;value&gt;}}</code>. *Multiple producers are anticipated (ISSUE-2256 adds EM adjudication in <code>EmbargoTeardownAuthorizationGate</code> as a second producer). Any other asserted PXA value MUST be refused and the current PXA value carried forward (RSH-05-016). *PXA state is monotone: bits only advance from unaware to aware (p\u2192P, x\u2192X, a\u2192A) and never reverse. The received-side filter uses the weaker <code>is_monotonic_pxa_forward()</code> check \u2014 not the strict single-step adjacency <code>is_valid_pxa_transition()</code> that applies to local write nodes (CSB-16-002) \u2014 because a remote peer may have observed multiple PXA events between messages and report a combined advance that skips intermediate steps. Applying the strict check would refuse a valid multi-step advance from a peer that simply missed delivering earlier messages. * <code>RSH-05-020</code> MUST After adjudicating each dimension of a received <code>Add(ParticipantStatus, CaseParticipant)</code> independently, the receiver MUST evaluate the cross-machine entailments (RM\u2194VF and RM\u2194D per CSB-18-001, VF\u2194D per CSB-17-001) against the effective \u2014 post-adjudication \u2014 state. For each violated entailment the receiver MUST refuse the dimension whose asserted value the sender moved, carrying the participant's current value for it forward (RSH-05-002), and MUST NOT report as refused a dimension the sender omitted or restated unchanged. The receiver MUST evaluate the same entailment set the emit path evaluates. Per-dimension adjudication cannot see a claim that is impossible only in combination: a fix that is ready or deployed entails a report the participant has already accepted, and a deployed fix entails a ready one. Before this requirement the receive path composed only VF\u2194D, so an assertion the actor would have refused to emit was accepted, recorded, hash-chained and replicated to every participant when it arrived from a peer instead (ISSUE-2906). Refusing the dimension that moved* is what makes the refusal effective rather than cosmetic. VF\u2194D constrains a pair, so either side can be the offending claim; refusing the incumbent side carries its value straight back, which leaves the impossible combination recorded while reporting a refusal that changed nothing. Requiring one shared evaluator rather than two equivalent ones is what keeps the emit and receive paths from silently diverging again. Silence is the specific problem: the contradiction is only discoverable by reading devlogs. Using <code>Create(ProcessingFault)</code> rather than <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> avoids triggering a CASE_MANAGER replay loop \u2014 the committed entry cannot be uncommitted, so replaying it would produce the same refusal indefinitely. <code>ProcessingFault</code> is the right signal for semantic invalidity (ASK-07-001). persistence layer. The CS participant-specific axes (RM, VFD) are owned by each participant's <code>CaseParticipant</code> record and are intentionally excluded from this restriction. This path is distinct from VP-17-001 and is not a bypass of the CASE_MANAGER write constraint. Participants exchange asynchronous messages and track the case across four dimensions of shared state, realized as five state machines. Any number of organizations may take part in a single case.</p> <p>Coordination is scoped to the case rather than to a system: the case-management role is held per case, and different cases may be managed by different actors. No single service holds every case. Within a case, one participant holds write authority over the case's shared state, so that concurrent claims resolve to one answer.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#1-introduction-i","title":"1. Introduction [I]","text":""},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#11-background-and-motivation","title":"1.1 Background and Motivation","text":"<p>A vulnerability divides the world into two sets: those who know about it, and those who do not. From the moment of discovery, every party in the knowing set repeatedly answers two questions. What should it do next, and who else needs to know what, and when? Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) continues until the answers are \"nothing\" and \"nobody\".</p> <p>Multi-Party CVD (MPCVD) is CVD involving three or more independent organizations with different interests and roles. The shapes vary. A reporter may go to one vendor, which discovers that other vendors ship the same component. A reporter may go to a coordinator, which finds and notifies the affected vendors. A reporter may go to a vendor and a coordinator at once. What the cases have in common is that the set of participants grows after coordination has begun, each vendor works to its own timeline, and the parties must agree when disclosure happens.</p> <p>Each of those organizations usually already runs its own vulnerability tracking system. The coordination problem is therefore not only one of people talking to each other; it is one of separate systems needing to stay consistent about a shared case. That is the problem Vultron addresses.</p> <p>Email carries the content of a CVD case but records none of its state. No participant can see which vendors have read the report, which have agreed to an embargo, or in what order events occurred. Adding a party mid-case means re-sending the history by hand, and nothing detects the gap if that fails. Vultron gives each of these an explicit, machine-checkable representation: report status per participant (\u00a76), embargo agreement per participant (\u00a79), and an ordered case ledger that every participant replicates (\u00a75.4).</p> <p>Embargo timing is worth noting early. In practice the first two parties to a case establish the initial embargo, and it carries forward as further participants join and agree to it. Establishing terms early is generally easier than negotiating them once many parties are already involved.</p> <p>The protocol tracks coordination state across four dimensions: the report lifecycle (RM), the embargo (EM), what is known about the vulnerability (CS), and each participant's agreement to the embargo (PEC). Because CS is a compound of two independent axes, an implementation runs five state machines (\u00a73.3). Messages are ActivityStreams 2.0 Activities delivered over HTTP. Delivery is asynchronous: no exchange requires both parties to be available at the same moment.</p> <p>Who this specification is for</p> <p>This specification is written for implementers building software that takes part in Vultron cases, and for reviewers assessing whether an implementation conforms.</p> <p>It assumes familiarity with coordinated vulnerability disclosure as a practice \u2014 reporters, vendors, coordinators, embargoes, CVE IDs. It does not assume prior knowledge of Vultron. Where it relies on an external specification, it says so and cites it (\u00a71.3).</p> <p>See also</p> <ul> <li>CVD as a Coordination Problem</li> <li>What Does Success Mean in CVD?</li> <li>The Need for Interoperability</li> <li>CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#12-design-goals","title":"1.2 Design Goals","text":"<p>Actor-local state. Each participant keeps its own replica of the case, assembled from the messages it has received. A participant is the authority on its own report and fix status. What the case as a whole asserts \u2014 its embargo state and what is publicly known \u2014 has a single writer, the participant holding the Case Manager role, so that concurrent claims resolve to one answer (\u00a75.4.1).</p> <p>Coordination is scoped to a case, not to a system. The Case Manager role is held per case, and different cases may be managed by different actors. The protocol does not require every case to pass through one shared service. It does require, within a case, that shared state have one writer.</p> <p>Informative: how centralized is this?</p> <p>Two readings should both be avoided.</p> <p>Vultron does not require a single central authority holding all cases. Any actor able to satisfy the Case Manager role can manage a case, and the role is transferable (\u00a711.3).</p> <p>Equally, Vultron as it stands is not a fully decentralized design. Within a case there is one writer, and its availability bounds how fast the case can progress. The current reference implementation goes further and runs a dedicated service actor per case.</p> <p>The protocol leaves more distributed realizations open \u2014 a shared ledger among peers, for instance \u2014 and this version does not specify one (\u00a75.4.2).</p> <p>Asynchronous, message-driven coordination. Participants announce their own transitions rather than being polled, and no exchange requires two parties to be online at once. A participant that is temporarily unreachable does not block the others from making progress.</p> <p>Extensible role model. Roles are not exclusive: a participant may hold Reporter, Vendor and Coordinator at the same time (\u00a73.5). Roles that confer protocol authority are kept separate from roles that describe what an actor does in the world, so the two can vary independently.</p> <p>Interoperable wire format. ActivityStreams 2.0 is the normative wire vocabulary. Reusing an established open standard means the message format is already specified and already understood, and it leaves ActivityPub-based delivery available as a path to potentially compatible tooling. Vultron has not yet been integrated with the wider ActivityPub ecosystem.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#13-relationship-to-existing-standards","title":"1.3 Relationship to Existing Standards","text":"<p>ActivityStreams 2.0 and ActivityPub. Vultron uses the ActivityStreams 2.0 vocabulary as its wire format, and ActivityPub HTTP delivery is the anticipated transport.</p> <p>This version requires the vocabulary but not full ActivityPub server behavior: inbox and outbox HTTP delivery, WebFinger discovery and HTTP Signatures are not conformance requirements here. This specification writes state names in full, in prose form: Received, Active, Signatory, Fix Ready. Where the name of a specific enumerated value matters \u2014 for example when citing an implementation's enumeration \u2014 the value is written in code font with its machine as a prefix, as in <code>RM.RECEIVED</code> or <code>PEC.SIGNATORY</code>. Vulnerabilities are the subject of every Vultron case. Report A document describing a specific vulnerability, submitted to initiate coordination. It determines what a participant is obliged to do and which transitions it is authorized to cause. Roles are granted through the case's authority chain (\u00a711.1), not claimed. A participant may hold several at once.</p> <p>Roles fall into two categories, which \u00a712.3 develops further.</p> <p>Process roles describe what an actor does in a case:</p> Role Definition Reporter A participant that submitted the report. The protocol is concerned with who reported the vulnerability, not who discovered it; a discoverer who reports holds the Reporter role. Vendor A participant that produces a product containing the vulnerability and is responsible for developing a fix. Coordinator A participant that facilitates multi-party coordination without being responsible for developing a fix itself. Deployer A participant that deploys a vendor's fix to systems it operates. Distinct from Vendor: producing a fix and applying it are separate acts. CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) A participant authorized to assign CVE IDs directly, rather than delegating assignment to an external service. Orthogonal to the other process roles and commonly held alongside Coordinator or Vendor. Observer A participant with no obligation to drive vendor/fix/deploy transitions. An Observer still tracks case state, is subject to embargo consent, and may report observations about the world. <p>Protocol authority roles describe what an actor controls in the protocol itself:</p> Role Definition Case Owner The party whose disclosure decision the case exists to serve. It decides who is admitted, which roles they hold, and whether embargo terms are accepted or torn down. Case ownership is never delegated, though it may be transferred (\u00a711.3). Case Manager The participant that writes the canonical case ledger and relays case-scoped messages, acting on the Case Owner's behalf. It is the case's single-writer authority (\u00a75.4.1). The Case Owner may delegate this role. <p>Observer names two different things</p> <p>Observer is used in this specification for the process role defined above, and also as the name of the minimum conformance capability set that every participant must provide (\u00a712.2). The reuse is deliberate \u2014 the capability set is named after the least-privileged role \u2014 but the two are not the same kind of thing. A role is a position in a case; a capability set is a property of software (\u00a712.3.3).</p> <p>Informative: the CASE_MANAGER role and the actor that holds it</p> <p>Authority over a case follows the Case Manager role. It does not follow any actor's name, URI, or hosting location. The reporter's first message goes to a vendor directly, because no case exists and so no CASE_MANAGER exists to route through. Every later message routes through the CASE_MANAGER (\u00a75.4.2). The transition between those two regimes is the bootstrap, and it is where a case's trust is established.</p> <p>The case-creation message is the trust root. When the receiving party creates the case, it sends the reporter a case-creation message signed by the creating actor. That message introduces the actor holding the <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> role. Every participant's trust in the ledger derives from it: a participant accepts entries from the CASE_MANAGER because it accepts the message that established which actor holds the role.</p> <p>A late joiner inherits that trust transitively. An actor invited after the case is under way never sees the original creation message. It receives the case snapshot and the prior ledger entries from the CASE_MANAGER (\u00a710.1), and it trusts them because it trusts the invitation that named the CASE_MANAGER. The hash-chaining of the ledger lets the joiner verify it received an unbroken history \u2014 a check against tampering and omission, not a second source of trust.</p> <p>Messages that arrive before their case. A case-scoped message may reach a participant before the case it refers to has. A participant MUST NOT apply such a message to a case it has not yet received. It holds the message until the case arrives, and discards it if the case never does. Applying it early would create case state from a message whose context was never established.</p> <p>The threat model, identity verification, and the limits of this trust chain are covered at \u00a714.1.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#46-error-and-acknowledgement-messages","title":"4.6 Error and Acknowledgement Messages","text":"<p>The formal protocol defines an acknowledgement and an error message for each of the three state machines: <code>RK</code>, <code>EK</code>, <code>CK</code> and <code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code>, <code>CE</code>. Their status here is not uniform, and an implementation MUST NOT assume symmetry across the three.</p> <p>Of the six, only <code>RK</code> exists on the wire. <code>EK</code>, <code>CK</code>, <code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code> and <code>CE</code> have no wire representation. An implementation MUST NOT expect to receive any of the five, and MUST NOT wait on one.</p> <p>The two absences have different reasons.</p> <p><code>EK</code> and <code>CK</code> are redundant. Embargo and case state changes are replicated through the case ledger, and a participant establishes that it received them by holding an unbroken hash chain. A per-message acknowledgement would restate what the chain already shows. <code>RK</code> survives because report submission happens before the case exists, so there is no ledger to carry it.</p> <p><code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code> and <code>CE</code> are deliberately unmodeled, not merely unimplemented. The protocol does not model inbound error messages typed by the state machine that produced them, because that grouping tells a receiver nothing it can act on: knowing which machine was confused does not indicate what to do about it. Errors are grouped by failure mode instead, which is actionable:</p> Failure mode When it applies What the sender can do Not understood The message could not be parsed, or its meaning is unrecognized Re-send, or send a simpler equivalent Understood but declined The message was well-formed and meaningful, but the receiver will not act on it given the case's state Reconsider; the state, not the message, is the obstacle Needs explanation The condition cannot be expressed as a structured message and requires prose Read the explanation; there is no automatic recovery <p>\u00a75.3 gives the wire form of each failure mode.</p> <p>What is still missing. A message that cannot be processed is currently set aside for administrative attention, and its sender is not told. The three failure modes give a receiver a way to report a problem where it is implemented, but this version does not require it to.</p> <p>Open question: negative-acknowledgement semantics are unspecified</p> <p>Error message types (<code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code>, <code>CE</code>) are deliberately unmodeled (ADR-0049). Unprocessable inbound messages are dead-lettered with no sender notification. The three-way fault partition (\u00a74.6, ADR-0083) provides structured error signaling where it is implemented, but whether the protocol needs a normative negative-acknowledgement facet \u2014 and if so, what the expected sender behavior (retry, suppress, escalate) should be \u2014 remains open.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#47-knowledge-model-and-actor-isolation","title":"4.7 Knowledge Model and Actor Isolation","text":"<p>Each participant knows only what it has been told. Three are defined: Observer, which every participant must provide, and Authority and Hosting, which add the obligations of deciding for a case and of running one.</p> <p>Most of what a capability set requires is expressed as maintaining a state machine, so that phrase needs pinning down first.</p> <p>What 'implement a state machine' means</p> <p>Implementing a state machine has two components:</p> <ol> <li>Track: maintain a local value for the machine, and update it as    incoming messages report transitions.</li> <li>Drive: cause a transition that the participant's roles authorize, and    announce it so the other participants learn of it.</li> </ol> <p>The two are separate obligations. A test supplies a sequence of messages and an input state, and checks the messages the implementation emits and the state it reaches. It does not inspect internal structure.</p> <p>Each test case is therefore a message-sequence scenario paired with the state outcome it expects.</p> <p>Some capabilities that define a role are not protocol-observable at all. Developing a fix, deploying a fix and publishing an advisory happen outside the protocol. Conformance verifies the protocol messages that this work produces, not the work itself.</p> <p>Conformance testing is organized in four layers, which describe what a test verifies. Layers are orthogonal to the capability sets of \u00a712.2, which describe what an implementation provides (see the warning in \u00a712.1):</p> Layer Verifies L1 \u2014 Syntax Messages are well-formed against the wire format (\u00a75) L2 \u2014 Semantics Each message drives the correct state transition (\u00a74, \u00a76\u2013\u00a711) L3 \u2014 Behavior Correct observable outputs: right messages emitted and states reached, given input state plus received message L4 \u2014 Process Correct internal decision structure (e.g. precondition before state write before side-effect) <p>L4 is only enforceable against a reference implementation and is therefore outside the scope of independent conformance claims. The protocol uses actor URIs as process identifiers. An actor URI is the identity anchor for all messages sent by that actor, and for the canonical case ledger if the actor holds the CASE_MANAGER role. Implementations MUST treat actor URI equality as identity equality: two messages with the same <code>actor</code> URI are from the same actor.</p> <p>Verification. The protocol does not currently mandate a specific identity verification mechanism. The reference implementation anticipates HTTP Signatures (as used in ActivityPub) as the authentication layer for inbound messages. A future version of this specification is expected to normatively require HTTP Signatures at the transport layer.</p> <p>Case bootstrap as the trust establishment mechanism. The <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code> message signed by the originating actor is the trust root for a case. Late joiners receive a case snapshot and prior ledger entries from the CASE_MANAGER. A late joiner trusts the CASE_MANAGER's delivery because it trusts the <code>Create</code> message that introduced the CASE_MANAGER. This chain is the minimal trust model; cryptographic ledger integrity (hash-chaining) provides tamper detection.</p> <p>See also</p> <ul> <li>\u00a74.5 (trust and bootstrap semantics)</li> <li>\u00a75.4 (addressing and channels)</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/#142-embargo-integrity","title":"14.2 Embargo Integrity","text":"<p>Protocol adherence. An active embargo is an agreement, not a technical enforcement. The protocol provides the signaling infrastructure \u2014 PEC state tracks which participants have consented, \u00a79.5 ensures all participants receive meta-protocol messages \u2014 but it cannot prevent a participant from disclosing outside the protocol.</p> <p>Defection. If a participant discloses publicly while an embargo is <code>ACTIVE</code>, the <code>CP</code> (public awareness) message will trigger the embargo teardown cascade (\u00a710.3). The teardown is a state machine consequence, not a penalty mechanism. The protocol has no built-in penalty for defection; enforcement is an out-of-band organizational matter.</p> <p>Confidentiality gate. Sensitive case content is gated on embargo consent (\u00a79.7). A participant that has not achieved <code>PEC.SIGNATORY</code> does not receive full case details. Every one also appears inline at the point in the specification where it first matters, so a reader meeting the gap in context sees it there rather than only here.</p> <p>Open question: CS ordering constraints are unspecified</p> <p>CS ordering constraints \u2014 including the <code>pX\u2192PX</code> invariant (exploit-public implies public-aware) and the rule that <code>CP</code> must precede <code>ET</code> where public disclosure triggers embargo teardown \u2014 exist in three non-normative places: a code docstring, a measurement-oriented reference document (Possible Histories), and a design note. No spec group covers them normatively.</p> <p>A conformance claim cannot meaningfully cover CS ordering until this gap is closed. Treat the material cited here as informative until a normative spec is issued.</p> <p>Open question: who may assert that a vendor became aware</p> <p>The first VFD transition \u2014 <code>v\u2192V</code>, vendor becomes aware \u2014 has no trigger-side specification and no implementation. Design intent is a third-party assertion (\"I notified this Vendor\"), not a self-report.</p> <p>Open questions: who may assert it, whether the subject Vendor may dispute it, and whether transport-level delivery success (HTTP 200) suffices to constitute the assertion.</p> <p>Do not infer a rule from this document's silence.</p> <p>Open question: negative-acknowledgement semantics are unspecified</p> <p>Error message types (<code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code>, <code>CE</code>) are deliberately unmodeled (ADR-0049). Unprocessable inbound messages are dead-lettered with no sender notification. The three-way fault partition (\u00a74.6, ADR-0083) provides structured error signaling where it is implemented, but whether the protocol needs a normative negative-acknowledgement facet \u2014 and if so, what the expected sender behavior (retry, suppress, escalate) should be \u2014 remains open.</p> <p>Open question: two machines have a state called \\\"no embargo\\\"</p> <p>Embargo Management has a None state meaning no embargo is in effect for the case. Embargo consent has a No Embargo state meaning no embargo is in scope for one participant. The reference implementation spells both <code>NO_EMBARGO</code> \u2014 in the embargo enumeration as an alias for <code>NONE</code>, and in the consent enumeration as a state in its own right.</p> <p>The two are genuinely different states in different machines, and they can legitimately disagree. But sharing a name invites the reading that the consent state is a projection of the case's embargo state, which is exactly the conflation these two machines exist to prevent.</p> <p>Open: whether the consent state should be renamed to something that states its meaning more plainly, whether the embargo alias should be dropped, and whether either can be changed without altering the values that appear in the case ledger. Until that is settled, this specification names the machine wherever the distinction matters.</p> <p>Open question: acquiring a role after joining a case</p> <p>This specification says how the Case Owner assigns a role and how a role is offered and accepted. It does not say how a participant already in a case asks for an additional one.</p> <p>A participant admitted as a Vendor that later also needs the Coordinator role has no protocol path to request it. In practice the request is made out of band, or as a <code>Add(Note)</code> on the case, and the Case Owner then issues a role offer. Neither is a specified mechanism.</p> <p>Open: whether the protocol should define a role-request activity, whether a participant may decline a role it was assigned, and how a role that is removed rather than added is represented in the case history.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_abstract/","title":"abstract","text":""},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_abstract/#abstract","title":"Abstract","text":"<p>The Vultron Protocol coordinates vulnerability disclosure among multiple organizations. Participants exchange asynchronous messages and track the case across four dimensions of shared state, realized as five state machines. Any number of organizations may take part in a single case.</p> <p>Coordination is scoped to the case rather than to a system: the case-management role is held per case, and different cases may be managed by different actors. No single service holds every case. Case State (CS) Dimensions [N]","text":"<p>Case State records what is known about the vulnerability. It answers two different questions, and it is a compound of two machines because those questions have different owners.</p> <p>The first is what each vendor has done about the vulnerability: is it aware, does it have a fix, has the fix been deployed? The participants are refusing the proposed change, not the embargo. The previously agreed terms remain in force. An implementation that returns to None here silently drops an embargo that everyone still expects to hold.</p> <p>Reaching Exited. Exited means the embargo has been torn down at the case level. A participant does not put the case into Exited by deciding to stop observing the embargo. What a participant may do is report that it intends to exit, propose a shorter embargo, or propose an earlier end date; the CASE_MANAGER then terminates the embargo and records the termination (\u00a710.2). Terminating an embargo requires Case Owner authorization by default, on the same terms as any other change to canonical case state (\u00a710.3).</p> <p>Embargo duration selection. Other policies are also admissible: an implementation MAY defer the choice to the Case Owner, or apply its own organizational policy. This specification does not mandate shortest-wins.</p> <p>Tacit acceptance. A receiver MAY publish a default embargo policy. Introduction [I]","text":""},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_introduction/#11-background-and-motivation","title":"1.1 Background and Motivation","text":"<p>A vulnerability divides the world into two sets: those who know about it, and those who do not. From the moment of discovery, every party in the knowing set repeatedly answers two questions. What should it do next, and who else needs to know what, and when? Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) continues until the answers are \"nothing\" and \"nobody\".</p> <p>Multi-Party CVD (MPCVD) is CVD involving three or more independent organizations with different interests and roles. The shapes vary. A reporter may go to one vendor, which discovers that other vendors ship the same component. A reporter may go to a coordinator, which finds and notifies the affected vendors. A reporter may go to a vendor and a coordinator at once. What the cases have in common is that the set of participants grows after coordination has begun, each vendor works to its own timeline, and the parties must agree when disclosure happens.</p> <p>Each of those organizations usually already runs its own vulnerability tracking system. The coordination problem is therefore not only one of people talking to each other; it is one of separate systems needing to stay consistent about a shared case. That is the problem Vultron addresses.</p> <p>Email carries the content of a CVD case but records none of its state. No participant can see which vendors have read the report, which have agreed to an embargo, or in what order events occurred. Adding a party mid-case means re-sending the history by hand, and nothing detects the gap if that fails. Vultron gives each of these an explicit, machine-checkable representation: report status per participant (\u00a76), embargo agreement per participant (\u00a79), and an ordered case ledger that every participant replicates (\u00a75.4).</p> <p>Embargo timing is worth noting early. In practice the first two parties to a case establish the initial embargo, and it carries forward as further participants join and agree to it. Establishing terms early is generally easier than negotiating them once many parties are already involved.</p> <p>The protocol tracks coordination state across four dimensions: the report lifecycle (RM), the embargo (EM), what is known about the vulnerability (CS), and each participant's agreement to the embargo (PEC). Because CS is a compound of two independent axes, an implementation runs five state machines (\u00a73.3). Messages are ActivityStreams 2.0 Activities delivered over HTTP. Delivery is asynchronous: no exchange requires both parties to be available at the same moment.</p> <p>Who this specification is for</p> <p>This specification is written for implementers building software that takes part in Vultron cases, and for reviewers assessing whether an implementation conforms.</p> <p>It assumes familiarity with coordinated vulnerability disclosure as a practice \u2014 reporters, vendors, coordinators, embargoes, CVE IDs. It does not assume prior knowledge of Vultron. Where it relies on an external specification, it says so and cites it (\u00a71.3).</p> <p>See also</p> <ul> <li>CVD as a Coordination Problem</li> <li>What Does Success Mean in CVD?</li> <li>The Need for Interoperability</li> <li>CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_introduction/#12-design-goals","title":"1.2 Design Goals","text":"<p>Actor-local state. Each participant keeps its own replica of the case, assembled from the messages it has received. A participant is the authority on its own report and fix status. What the case as a whole asserts \u2014 its embargo state and what is publicly known \u2014 has a single writer, the participant holding the Case Manager role, so that concurrent claims resolve to one answer (\u00a75.4.1).</p> <p>Coordination is scoped to a case, not to a system. The Case Manager role is held per case, and different cases may be managed by different actors. The protocol does not require every case to pass through one shared service. It does require, within a case, that shared state have one writer.</p> <p>Informative: how centralized is this?</p> <p>Two readings should both be avoided.</p> <p>Vultron does not require a single central authority holding all cases. Any actor able to satisfy the Case Manager role can manage a case, and the role is transferable (\u00a711.3).</p> <p>Equally, Vultron as it stands is not a fully decentralized design. Within a case there is one writer, and its availability bounds how fast the case can progress. The current reference implementation goes further and runs a dedicated service actor per case.</p> <p>The protocol leaves more distributed realizations open \u2014 a shared ledger among peers, for instance \u2014 and this version does not specify one (\u00a75.4.2).</p> <p>Asynchronous, message-driven coordination. Participants announce their own transitions rather than being polled, and no exchange requires two parties to be online at once. A participant that is temporarily unreachable does not block the others from making progress.</p> <p>Extensible role model. Roles are not exclusive: a participant may hold Reporter, Vendor and Coordinator at the same time (\u00a73.5). Roles that confer protocol authority are kept separate from roles that describe what an actor does in the world, so the two can vary independently.</p> <p>Interoperable wire format. ActivityStreams 2.0 is the normative wire vocabulary. Reusing an established open standard means the message format is already specified and already understood, and it leaves ActivityPub-based delivery available as a path to potentially compatible tooling. Vultron has not yet been integrated with the wider ActivityPub ecosystem.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_introduction/#13-relationship-to-existing-standards","title":"1.3 Relationship to Existing Standards","text":"<p>ActivityStreams 2.0 and ActivityPub. Both timer paths end in Declined.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_pec-state-machine/#93-what-no-embargo-means","title":"9.3 What No Embargo Means","text":"<p>No Embargo means there is no embargo in scope for this participant. It does not mean \"has not yet agreed\".</p> <p>That reading matters because consent does not always arrive through an invitation. A finder who opens a case for its own finding and sets its default embargo was invited by nobody. A reporter's consent is expressed by submitting the report. In both cases the participant is a signatory without any invitation having been sent, and the case history MUST NOT record an invitation that did not happen.</p> <p>Two consequences follow:</p> <ul> <li>Accept and decline are valid directly from No Embargo. No invitation is   required.</li> <li>The transition from Signatory to Invited MUST be rejected. Consent already   given cannot be withdrawn by re-inviting the participant; if the terms change,   the revise trigger lapses the consent instead.</li> </ul> <p>No Embargo is also the state every participant returns to when an embargo ends, which is independent evidence for the absence reading: reset fires when the embargo goes away, not when an answer is pending.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_pec-state-machine/#94-deadlines-and-the-pocket-veto","title":"9.4 Deadlines and the Pocket Veto","text":"<p>An embargo invitation does not stay open indefinitely. A participant that neither accepts nor declines before the deadline is recorded as having declined \u2014 the pocket veto. Silence is treated as refusal rather than assent, because proceeding on an unanswered invitation would mean asserting agreement the participant never gave.</p> <p>The deadline may be explicit or defaulted:</p> <ul> <li>An embargo invitation MAY carry its own <code>endTime</code>, giving an explicit   respond-by instant. Where present, it is authoritative.</li> <li>Where absent, a configurable policy window applies. The default window is   7 days.</li> </ul> <p>The pocket veto is the implicit form of this one mechanism, not a second mechanism alongside it.</p> <p>One invitation carries two different end times</p> <p>The invitation's <code>endTime</code> is the respond-by deadline for the invitee. The embargo event nested inside the invitation has its own <code>endTime</code>, which is when the embargo would expire. They sit one nesting level apart and mean different things.</p> <p>An implementation that reads the embargo's expiry as the RSVP deadline will hold invitations open for the entire embargo period. One that reads the RSVP deadline as the embargo expiry will tear down embargoes days after they were agreed.</p> <p>Enforcing the deadline. The CASE_MANAGER enforces it. It does so lazily: when it next handles the case, it compares the deadline against the current time. No scheduler or timer service is required.</p> <p>A minimum window applies. The CASE_MANAGER MUST enforce a minimum respond-by window, by default 72 hours. Where an invitation carries a shorter deadline, the CASE_MANAGER MUST extend the deadline to the minimum. It MUST NOT reject the invitation for this reason: a too-short deadline is the proposer's error, and refusing the invitation would penalize the invitee for it.</p> <p>A late acceptance is not refused. The CASE_MANAGER MUST NOT refuse a late accept on deadline grounds. Three cases apply. If the terms it accepts are still current, the CASE_MANAGER records the consent. If the terms are stale, the CASE_MANAGER sends a fresh invitation carrying the current terms. If no embargo remains, the CASE_MANAGER records the accept as a no-op; the participant keeps its place in the case either way.</p> <p>A lapse and a refusal reach the same state. Both record Declined. The case history distinguishes them \u2014 it holds the decline that was sent, or the absence of any answer \u2014 but the consent machine does not, because nothing in the protocol treats the two differently. Both can be invited again.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_pec-state-machine/#95-embargo-traffic-reaches-non-signatories","title":"9.5 Embargo Traffic Reaches Non-Signatories","text":"<p>Embargo consent gates case content. No participant reads another's state directly. Each learns about the others from the messages it receives.</p> <p>A participant's own view is therefore always a replica: its local copy of what it believes the case state to be, assembled from the messages that have reached it. The protocol uses actor URIs as process identifiers. An actor URI is the identity anchor for all messages sent by that actor, and for the canonical case ledger if the actor holds the CASE_MANAGER role. Implementations MUST treat actor URI equality as identity equality: two messages with the same <code>actor</code> URI are from the same actor.</p> <p>Verification. The protocol does not currently mandate a specific identity verification mechanism. The reference implementation anticipates HTTP Signatures (as used in ActivityPub) as the authentication layer for inbound messages. A future version of this specification is expected to normatively require HTTP Signatures at the transport layer.</p> <p>Case bootstrap as the trust establishment mechanism. The <code>Create(VulnerabilityCase)</code> message signed by the originating actor is the trust root for a case. Late joiners receive a case snapshot and prior ledger entries from the CASE_MANAGER. A late joiner trusts the CASE_MANAGER's delivery because it trusts the <code>Create</code> message that introduced the CASE_MANAGER. This chain is the minimal trust model; cryptographic ledger integrity (hash-chaining) provides tamper detection.</p> <p>See also</p> <ul> <li>\u00a74.5 (trust and bootstrap semantics)</li> <li>\u00a75.4 (addressing and channels)</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_security/#142-embargo-integrity","title":"14.2 Embargo Integrity","text":"<p>Protocol adherence. An active embargo is an agreement, not a technical enforcement. The protocol provides the signaling infrastructure \u2014 PEC state tracks which participants have consented, \u00a79.5 ensures all participants receive meta-protocol messages \u2014 but it cannot prevent a participant from disclosing outside the protocol.</p> <p>Defection. If a participant discloses publicly while an embargo is <code>ACTIVE</code>, the <code>CP</code> (public awareness) message will trigger the embargo teardown cascade (\u00a710.3). The teardown is a state machine consequence, not a penalty mechanism. The protocol has no built-in penalty for defection; enforcement is an out-of-band organizational matter.</p> <p>Confidentiality gate. Sensitive case content is gated on embargo consent (\u00a79.7). A participant that has not achieved <code>PEC.SIGNATORY</code> does not receive full case details. Duplicate delivery does not change state.</p> <p>Ledger idempotency. The canonical case ledger is append-only and hash-chained. Content-level encryption \u2014 protecting case details from the CASE_MANAGER itself, or supporting future multi-party computation \u2014 is not specified by this version. Implementations SHOULD treat any unencrypted case content as accessible to whoever operates the CASE_MANAGER.</p> <p>Scope. This section covers security requirements for the protocol as specified. The transition between those two regimes is the bootstrap, and it is where a case's trust is established.</p> <p>The case-creation message is the trust root. When the receiving party creates the case, it sends the reporter a case-creation message signed by the creating actor. That message introduces the actor holding the <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> role. Every participant's trust in the ledger derives from it: a participant accepts entries from the CASE_MANAGER because it accepts the message that established which actor holds the role.</p> <p>A late joiner inherits that trust transitively. An actor invited after the case is under way never sees the original creation message. It receives the case snapshot and the prior ledger entries from the CASE_MANAGER (\u00a710.1), and it trusts them because it trusts the invitation that named the CASE_MANAGER. The hash-chaining of the ledger lets the joiner verify it received an unbroken history \u2014 a check against tampering and omission, not a second source of trust.</p> <p>Messages that arrive before their case. A case-scoped message may reach a participant before the case it refers to has. A participant MUST NOT apply such a message to a case it has not yet received. It holds the message until the case arrives, and discards it if the case never does. A per-message acknowledgement would restate what the chain already shows. <code>RK</code> survives because report submission happens before the case exists, so there is no ledger to carry it.</p> <p><code>RE</code>, <code>EE</code> and <code>CE</code> are deliberately unmodeled, not merely unimplemented. Vulnerabilities are the subject of every Vultron case. Report A document describing a specific vulnerability, submitted to initiate coordination. Case The coordination context around a specific vulnerability: the participants, the shared state, the messages exchanged, and any embargo agreement. The case is the unit of Vultron protocol activity. Actor An identity in the protocol, named by a URI. An actor may be an organization, a person, or a service. Actors exist independently of any case. Participant An actor that has joined a specific case. The case holds a <code>CaseParticipant</code> record for each participant, associating that actor with the roles it holds and the state it owns. An actor is a participant in a case; the same actor may participate in many. <p>Source of the vulnerability definition</p> <p>The definition of vulnerability above is taken unchanged from the CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure. It is also consistent with ISO/IEC 29147:2018 \u00a75.4, which defines the term in the same policy-violation terms (ISO crosswalks).</p> <p>Note what the definition does not require: it says nothing about whether the vulnerability is known, reported, fixed or public. It determines what a participant is obliged to do and which transitions it is authorized to cause. Roles are granted through the case's authority chain (\u00a711.1), not claimed. A participant may hold several at once.</p> <p>Roles fall into two categories, which \u00a712.3 develops further.</p> <p>Process roles describe what an actor does in a case:</p> Role Definition Reporter A participant that submitted the report. The protocol is concerned with who reported the vulnerability, not who discovered it; a discoverer who reports holds the Reporter role. Vendor A participant that produces a product containing the vulnerability and is responsible for developing a fix. Coordinator A participant that facilitates multi-party coordination without being responsible for developing a fix itself. Deployer A participant that deploys a vendor's fix to systems it operates. Distinct from Vendor: producing a fix and applying it are separate acts. CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) A participant authorized to assign CVE IDs directly, rather than delegating assignment to an external service. Orthogonal to the other process roles and commonly held alongside Coordinator or Vendor. Observer A participant with no obligation to drive vendor/fix/deploy transitions. An Observer still tracks case state, is subject to embargo consent, and may report observations about the world. <p>Protocol authority roles describe what an actor controls in the protocol itself:</p> Role Definition Case Owner The party whose disclosure decision the case exists to serve. It decides who is admitted, which roles they hold, and whether embargo terms are accepted or torn down. Case ownership is never delegated, though it may be transferred (\u00a711.3). Case Manager The participant that writes the canonical case ledger and relays case-scoped messages, acting on the Case Owner's behalf. It is the case's single-writer authority (\u00a75.4.1). The Case Owner may delegate this role. <p>Observer names two different things</p> <p>Observer is used in this specification for the process role defined above, and also as the name of the minimum conformance capability set that every participant must provide (\u00a712.2). The reuse is deliberate \u2014 the capability set is named after the least-privileged role \u2014 but the two are not the same kind of thing. A role is a position in a case; a capability set is a property of software (\u00a712.3.3).</p> <p>Informative: the CASE_MANAGER role and the actor that holds it</p> <p>Authority over a case follows the Case Manager role. It does not follow any actor's name, URI, or hosting location. Normative text in this specification therefore names the authority the CASE_MANAGER, meaning whichever participant currently holds the role.</p> <p>The reference implementation happens to satisfy the role with an automated software actor it labels a case actor, provisioned by a case actor service. Those are implementation labels with no protocol meaning. An implementation MUST NOT infer authority from them.</p> <p>Informative: Finder is not a protocol role</p> <p>Earlier CVD models distinguish the finder of a vulnerability from its reporter. Vultron does not: nothing in the protocol depends on who discovered the vulnerability, so an actor that discovers and reports holds the Reporter role. The discoverer's identity may be recorded in the report content or in a case note.</p>"},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_terminology/#23-protocol-objects-and-messages","title":"2.3 Protocol Objects and Messages","text":"<p>These terms name the things a case is made of and the messages that move between participants.</p> Term Definition Activity The wire form of a Vultron message: an ActivityStreams 2.0 Activity. The last two are the pair most often conflated.</p> Term Definition State The current value of one state machine. Always qualified in this specification \u2014 RM state, embargo state, case state \u2014 because the unqualified word is ambiguous. Transition A change from one state to another. Track To maintain a local value for a state machine and update it as incoming messages report transitions. Every participant tracks all five machines (\u00a712.2). Drive To cause a transition that the participant's roles authorize, and announce it so the other participants learn of it. Which transitions a participant may drive depends on its roles (\u00a712.4). Embargo A time-bounded agreement among the participants of a case not to disclose the vulnerability publicly before an agreed point. Tracked for the case by the embargo state machine (\u00a77) and per participant by embargo consent (\u00a79). Teardown Ending an active embargo. The CASE_MANAGER performs the teardown and records it; a participant may report that it intends to exit, or propose an earlier end, but does not end the case's embargo itself (\u00a710.2). Publication is something a participant does, and the embargo constrains when a participant may do it. Public awareness may arise with no participant publishing anything: an attacker may discover the vulnerability independently, a commit may reveal it, or a non-participant may write about it. <p>Publication and public awareness are not the same thing</p> <p>Vultron governs publication \u2014 what a participant may deliberately disclose, and when. A test supplies a sequence of messages and an input state, and checks the messages the implementation emits and the state it reaches. It does not inspect internal structure.</p> <p>Each test case is therefore a message-sequence scenario paired with the state outcome it expects.</p> <p>Some capabilities that define a role are not protocol-observable at all. Developing a fix, deploying a fix and publishing an advisory happen outside the protocol. Conformance verifies the protocol messages that this work produces, not the work itself.</p> <p>Conformance testing is organized in four layers, which describe what a test verifies. Layers are orthogonal to the capability sets of \u00a712.2, which describe what an implementation provides (see the warning in \u00a712.1):</p> Layer Verifies L1 \u2014 Syntax Messages are well-formed against the wire format (\u00a75) L2 \u2014 Semantics Each message drives the correct state transition (\u00a74, \u00a76\u2013\u00a711) L3 \u2014 Behavior Correct observable outputs: right messages emitted and states reached, given input state plus received message L4 \u2014 Process Correct internal decision structure (e.g. precondition before state write before side-effect) <p>L4 is only enforceable against a reference implementation and is therefore outside the scope of independent conformance claims.
