Conformance [N]","text":""},{"location":"reference/vultron-spec/_conformance/_intro/#121-conformance-model-overview","title":"12.1 Conformance Model Overview","text":"<p>Conformance is two-dimensional: capability sets (what protocol machinery an implementation provides) and a role profile (which roles it claims). A conformance claim names capability sets and roles directly:</p> <p><code>CapabilitySet [+ CapabilitySet ...] / Role [+ Role ...]</code></p> <p>Examples: <code>Observer / Reporter</code>, <code>Observer / Vendor</code>, <code>Observer / Vendor + Deployer</code>, <code>Observer + Authority + Hosting / Coordinator + Case Owner</code>.</p> <p>The Observer capability set is required for all participation. Role obligations are additive and orthogonal: no role subsumes another.</p> <p>Capability set names and role names come from \u00a712.2 and \u00a712.3 respectively.</p> <p>Roles and capability expectations. The relationship between roles and capabilities is bidirectional. An implementation must have the capability prerequisites for a role before it can be assigned that role (\u00a712.3.1). Conversely, holding a role in a case creates an expectation that the implementation has those capabilities \u2014 other participants act on that assumption. It is for implementers who want to understand why the protocol behaves as it does, in any programming language.</p> <p>Read this page to learn three things:</p> <ul> <li>Each actor works like a worker that reads messages from a queue.</li> <li>One message can cause a chain of further messages. This is a cascade.</li> <li>Some steps stop because the actor must ask another actor for permission. The actor asks, and then it stops. It does not wait.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#an-actor-is-a-worker-with-two-queues","title":"An actor is a worker with two queues","text":"<p>Each actor in Vultron has an inbox and an outbox.</p> <ul> <li>The inbox holds messages that other actors sent to this actor.</li> <li>The outbox holds messages that this actor sends to other actors.</li> </ul> <p>The actor takes one message from its inbox. It processes that message. If the result is that other actors must be told something, the actor puts new messages in its outbox. Delivery then moves each outbox message to the inbox of the actor it is addressed to.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Two actors exchanging messages\n---\nflowchart LR\n    subgraph A[\"Actor A\"]\n        a_in([inbox]) --&gt; a_proc[process] --&gt; a_out([outbox])\n    end\n    subgraph B[\"Actor B\"]\n        b_in([inbox]) --&gt; b_proc[process] --&gt; b_out([outbox])\n    end\n    a_out --&gt;|delivery| b_in</code></pre> <p>This model has one important consequence. An actor never reaches into another actor's state. It can only send a message. The other actor decides what that message means and what to do about it. Every rule in the protocol follows from this limit.</p> <p>The queue model is a way to think, not a required design</p> <p>Vultron does not require message-broker software. The reference implementation is a single process and uses ordinary HTTP requests for delivery. The queue model is useful because it shows the intended flow of information, and because it keeps a distributed implementation possible later.</p>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#primary-events-and-cascades","title":"Primary events and cascades","text":"<p>Two kinds of things happen in Vultron, and the difference matters.</p> <p>A primary event comes from outside the protocol. Something in the world changed, and a person, a service, or another organisation must tell Vultron. Examples:</p> <ul> <li>A finder submits a vulnerability report.</li> <li>A vendor decides the report is valid.</li> <li>A participant proposes an embargo period.</li> </ul> <p>A cascade is everything that follows automatically from a primary event. The actor that received the primary event updates its own state and sends the messages the protocol requires. Each actor that receives one of those messages runs its own cascade. Together these form a chain.</p> <p>For example, one primary event \u2014 a finder submits a report \u2014 causes this chain:</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Cascade from a single primary event\n---\nflowchart TD\n    A[finder submits report] --&gt; B[vendor records the report]\n    B --&gt; C[vendor opens a case]\n    C --&gt; D[vendor adds the finder as a participant]\n    D --&gt; E[vendor tells the finder the case exists]</code></pre> <p>Nobody instructs the vendor to open a case. The vendor does it because it received a report. This is the central design rule: supply the primary event only, and let the protocol produce the consequences.</p>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#why-this-rule-is-useful","title":"Why this rule is useful","text":"<p>The rule gives you a test for correctness. If you must send a second message by hand to make the process continue, then one of two things is true:</p> <ul> <li>That step is genuinely a new primary event, because new information from outside was needed.</li> <li>Or the implementation has a gap, because the step should have happened automatically.</li> </ul> <p>The test tells you which kind of problem you have. It is the reason Vultron test scenarios inject only primary events and then check the resulting state.</p>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#causal-order-not-time-order","title":"Causal order, not time order","text":"<p>It is natural to describe a process as a list of steps in time: A, then B, then C. The protocol is not built on time. It is built on cause: A, and therefore B, and therefore C.</p> <p>The difference is not a matter of style. Delivery and processing take time, and they can fail. So \"B happened five seconds after A\" tells you almost nothing, while \"B happened because A happened\" tells you the process is correct.</p> <p>A single step between two actors is really a chain of smaller events:</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Steps in a single message delivery\n---\nflowchart LR\n    addr[\"A addresses\"] --&gt; send[\"A sends\"] --&gt; arr[\"arrives at B\"] --&gt; proc[\"B processes\"] --&gt; rec[\"B records\"] --&gt; rep[\"B replies\"]</code></pre> <p>Only the last links prove anything. That a message was sent proves only that the sender tried. That it arrived proves only that the network worked. That the receiver recorded it proves the receiver accepted it and acted.</p> <p>If you write tests or monitoring for a Vultron implementation, check the recorded state of the actor that owns the effect, and read it from that actor. Do not accept elapsed time as evidence, and do not accept an acknowledgement of receipt as evidence that processing succeeded.</p>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#when-an-actor-must-ask-permission","title":"When an actor must ask permission","text":"<p>Some steps in a cascade cannot be automatic, because the actor is not allowed to decide alone. A participant may report that a vulnerability is now public. Whether that report becomes the shared, agreed state of the case is not the reporting participant's decision. The case owner decides.</p> <p>Here Vultron does something that surprises people. The actor asks, and then it stops.</p> <ol> <li>The actor needs permission.</li> <li>The actor sends the case owner a request that carries a deadline.</li> <li>The actor finishes. Its work succeeded, because asking was the work.</li> <li>Later, the case owner replies: agreed, or refused.</li> <li>That reply is a new message. It arrives in an inbox, and it starts new work.</li> </ol> <p>Step 3 is the part worth understanding. Success means \"I asked\", not \"I was told yes.\" Nothing is left waiting or held open. The work is divided at the question rather than paused there. Asking is one complete piece of work; acting on the answer is another piece of work, and the answer's arrival is what starts it.</p> <p>This is why the request carries a deadline. The deadline is part of the message, so the case owner can see how long they have, and the asking actor knows when the question has gone stale.</p>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#what-happens-while-the-actor-waits","title":"What happens while the actor waits","text":"<p>Nothing is held open, so the case must be in a sensible state during the wait. It usually already is. In the example above, the participant's report is recorded as what that participant claims. Only its promotion to what the case agrees waits for permission. Those are two different facts, and recording the first while the second is undecided is honest and useful.</p> <p>This gives a rule for implementers: you may only ask about an action whose not-yet-done state can be described. If \"not yet decided\" cannot be represented, the actor must refuse instead of asking, because there is nowhere for the case to rest.</p>"},{"location":"topics/protocol_flow/#asking-twice-and-not-asking-twice","title":"Asking twice, and not asking twice","text":"<p>Because an actor stops after asking, it may reach the same point again later \u2014 for instance, when the same participant reports the same thing again. So an actor that reaches a step needing permission first works out where the conversation stands:</p> What the actor finds What it does A reply agreeing Do the action. A reply refusing Do not do the action. Record the refusal. A request already sent, deadline not passed Nothing. Do not ask twice. A request already sent, deadline passed Ask again, with a new deadline. No request yet Record the not-yet state, ask, and stop. <p>These situations do not overlap, so returning to this step is always safe. Whether to admit a new participant to a case is one \u2014 the answer is as useful next week as it is today.</p> <p>Other questions are not. Permission to change the agreed state of a case is granted against the case as it was when the question was asked. If the reply arrives after the deadline, the case may have moved on: an embargo may have been agreed, or another participant may have published. Acting on that permission would apply an old decision to a new situation.</p> <p>So each kind of request declares which it is. For requests of the second kind, a late reply does not grant permission, and the asking actor must ask again if it still wants to act. It is the list a person, an interface, or an automated service works from. Without it, a case owner has no way to discover that a decision is waiting for them, so permission could only ever be granted by accident. This list is what makes the case owner's role something they can actually perform.</p> <p>Both lists are working notes. They say what is outstanding. They never say what was permitted \u2014 for that, an actor reads the recorded history of the case, which is the shared, verifiable record. No message arrives when time runs out. So something must look.</p> <p>Vultron uses two mechanisms, and neither is a timer inside the protocol.</p> <p>Looking when you pass by. The next time an actor reaches the step that asked the question, it notices the deadline has passed. This is often enough. When a message is lost, the sender usually sends it again, and that repeat is what causes both actors to look. In that case the other party's retry is the clock.</p> <p>An external watcher. For prompt handling, an implementation can run a service that watches for passed deadlines and notifies the actor. This is deliberately outside the protocol: watching the clock is not a protocol behaviour, and keeping it outside means an implementation can choose how attentive to be. It also means deadline behaviour can be tested by asking for a check directly, rather than by waiting.</p> <p>Noticing an expired request never sends it again by itself. Expiry is information. The message may be malformed, or it may refer to something the actor does not know about, or the sender may not be permitted to send it.</p> <p>Silence is a poor answer. A sender waiting for a reply would wait for its whole deadline over a failure that took a fraction of a second.</p> <p>So an actor that cannot process a message from a known, authenticated sender tells that sender so. Two reasons: those details are useless to the sender, and explaining exactly why a message was refused helps an attacker probe the receiver.</p> <p>An actor does not answer a message it cannot authenticate. It answers three questions: what the hexagonal boundary means, how an incoming message flows from Hyper Text Transfer Protocol (HTTP) delivery to behavior-tree execution, and what the reference implementation supplies versus what an adopter must build.</p> <p>Reference implementation, not the protocol</p> <p>Vultron is a reference implementation of the CVD coordination protocol. The structure described here \u2014 hexagonal layering, an ActivityStreams Vocabulary 2.0 (AS2) inbox pipeline, behavior-tree orchestration \u2014 is one valid way to realize the protocol. The domain logic sits in an inner circle that knows nothing about how messages arrive, how they are formatted, or where state is stored. Everything external reaches the domain only through ports \u2014 typed interface contracts \u2014 and each port is fulfilled by an adapter at the edge.</p> <p>The codebase splits into three concentric responsibilities.</p> Layer Python package Owns Must not import Core <code>vultron/core/</code> Domain models, state machines, use cases, ports, behavior trees <code>vultron/wire/</code>, <code>vultron/adapters/</code>, web frameworks Wire <code>vultron/wire/as2/</code> AS2 vocabulary, structural parser, semantic extractor, activity factories Core domain logic, web frameworks Adapters <code>vultron/adapters/</code> HTTP inbox, CLI, persistence, outbound delivery, connectors Core domain rules <p>The wire format is a separate concern from the domain, not a subset of it. AS2 was chosen because it maps cleanly to Vultron semantics (ADR-0005), but that alignment does not make it a domain dependency. Domain objects and their wire counterparts share a common base but form two structurally distinct branches: a strict core branch and a lenient wire branch (ADR-0017). The core branch is authoritative and represents every field the wire can carry; the wire branch tolerates the loose, optional shapes that arrive over the network.</p> <p>We keep this boundary for two reasons. Wire formats change, and the domain logic should not have to change with them. Parsing and shape validation are edge concerns, so pushing them out of the core keeps the state-machine logic small and testable. The rule that core carries no wire or framework imports (ARCH-01-001) is enforced by ratchet tests under <code>test/architecture/</code>, so a violation fails continuous integration rather than merely drawing a review comment.</p> <p>vultron-core the concept versus <code>vultron/core/</code> the package</p> <p>vultron-core names the abstract protocol. <code>vultron/core/</code> names the Python package that implements it here. The package is the reference realization of the concept, not the concept itself.</p>"},{"location":"topics/reference_architecture/#from-http-delivery-to-behavior-tree-the-inbox-pipeline","title":"From HTTP delivery to behavior tree: the inbox pipeline","text":"<p>An incoming message crosses every layer of the hexagon in one pass. It arrives as AS2 JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) at an HTTP endpoint and leaves as a committed state change with any resulting messages queued for delivery. The stages below each do one job and hand off to the next.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Inbound message pipeline\n---\nflowchart TD\n    http[\"HTTP POST /inbox&lt;br/&gt;(AS2 JSON)\"]\n    parse[\"AS2 parser&lt;br/&gt;structural validity\"]\n    rehydrate[\"rehydrate&lt;br/&gt;resolve referenced objects\"]\n    extract[\"semantic extractor&lt;br/&gt;AS2 pattern \u2192 MessageSemantics\"]\n    dispatch[\"behavior dispatcher&lt;br/&gt;semantics \u2192 use case\"]\n    bt[\"use case runs a behavior tree&lt;br/&gt;guards \u2192 commit \u2192 effects\"]\n    persist[\"persist via DataLayer&lt;br/&gt;and queue outbound messages\"]\n\n    http --&gt; parse\n    parse --&gt; rehydrate\n    rehydrate --&gt; extract\n    extract --&gt; dispatch\n    dispatch --&gt; bt\n    bt --&gt; persist</code></pre> <p>A driving adapter receives the request. The AS2 parser checks structural validity, <code>rehydrate()</code> resolves referenced objects into full inline objects, and the semantic extractor (<code>vultron/wire/as2/extractor/</code>) matches the activity against an ordered pattern registry to produce a domain-level <code>MessageSemantics</code> value. The semantic extractor is the single place where AS2 structure becomes domain intent (ARCH-03-001), so the rest of the core never inspects wire shapes.</p> <p>The core layer decides what to do. The behavior dispatcher (<code>vultron/core/dispatcher.py</code>) maps the extracted semantics to a use case through a table lookup, and the use case runs the appropriate behavior tree. Routing all inbound case activity through the Case Actor is what lets a single behavior-tree execution produce a canonically ordered ledger entry (ADR-0021, ADR-0022). The reference implementation retired an earlier in-process shortcut so that co-located actors talk to each other exactly as remote actors would (ADR-0042). This keeps the transport uniform: the same JSON payload is deliverable whether the recipient is in the same process or across the internet.</p> <p>Delivery is treated as unreliable and bounded. The outbox retries with backoff, classifies <code>4xx</code> responses as terminal, and moves an activity to a dead-letter store once its per-activity attempt budget is exhausted rather than retrying forever (ADR-0066). A behavior tree is a hierarchy of nodes ticked from the root; each node returns Success, Failure, or Running, and the control-flow nodes above them compose those results into higher-level behavior. Vultron uses this structure because CVD activities compose the same way: validate a report, propose an embargo, publish an advisory \u2014 each is a small tree that slots into a larger one (ADR-0002).</p> <p>On the received side, a tree runs guards first, commits the ledger entry, then fires effects, in that order (CLP-10-006). A read or write of Report Management (RM), Embargo Management (EM), or Case State (CS) goes through a dedicated state node rather than touching state inline, which keeps every transition auditable.</p> <p>This page stays at the summary level by design. These are call-out points \u2014 locations where automated execution pauses and waits for an answer from an external service.</p> <p>During development and simulation, a call-out point is filled by a Fuzzer Node that returns a probabilistic success or failure. In production, an adopter replaces that stub with a real service that satisfies one of five capability shapes \u2014 Sentinel, Evaluator, Retriever, Composer, or Actuator (ADR-0024). In the hexagonal layout, a capability shape is a port and a concrete capability is the adapter that fulfills it.</p> <p>Not every external question is a call-out point. The reference implementation provides the protocol machinery: the five state machines, the wire vocabulary and its semantic mapping, the inbox and outbox pipelines, the behavior trees that orchestrate transitions, and the persistence and delivery adapters that make a local actor run. What an adopter supplies are the capabilities behind the call-out points \u2014 the judgment and the connections to outside systems that the protocol deliberately leaves open.</p> <p>This division tracks the protocol's conformance levels. Correct message syntax and correct state transitions (levels L1 and L2) come from using a conformant serializer and implementing the state machines. Correct observable behavior (L3) is stated by the behavioral conformance specifications. Correct internal decision structure \u2014 precondition checks before state writes before effects, audit-log ordering, idempotency \u2014 is level L4, which is only demonstrable through a reference implementation, and the <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> behavior-tree layer is that demonstration. As we wrote in The CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure:</p> <p>Excerpt from The CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure</p> <p>Perhaps the simplest description of the CVD process is that it starts with at least one individual becoming aware of a vulnerability in a product. In the Voltron animated series, a team of protectors joins forces to defend the universe from their adversaries. Their defensive mission requires a combination of independent defenders coordinating their efforts to achieve their goals. Like Voltron, our Vultron Protocol comprises a combination of humans and the technical processes and mechanisms that empower them. The goal of this documentation is to lay the foundation for the semantic interoperability of CVD processes across Participants. Syntactic interoperability, in the form of message formats and the like, is the focus of our ongoing effort.</p> <p>Addressing semantic interoperability first is a deliberate choice. If we were to go in the reverse order, we might wind up with systems that exchange data quickly and accurately yet still fail to accomplish the mutually beneficial outcomes that MPCVD sets out to achieve. Carney et al. illustrate the importance of semantic interoperability in their 2005 report Some Current Approaches to Interoperability:</p> <p>Carney et al. on semantic interoperability</p> <p>There is a limited number of ways that agreements on meaning can be achieved. In the context of design-time interoperability, semantic agreements are reached in the same manner as interface agreements between the constituent systems... However, in the context of run-time interoperability, the situation is more complex, since there is need for some manner of universal agreement, so that a new system can join, ad-hoc, some other group of systems. The new system must be able to usefully share data and meaning with those other systems, and those other systems must be able to share data and meaning from an unfamiliar newcomer.</p> <p>In this excerpt, replace the word \"system\" with the concept of a \"CVD Case Participant,\" and the need for semantic interoperability as a means of achieving coordination in MPCVD becomes clear:</p> <p>Paraphrasing Carney et al. in the context of CVD</p> <p>[...] However, in the context of run-time interoperability, the situation is more complex, since there is need for some manner of universal agreement, so that a new CVD Participant can join, ad-hoc, some other group of CVD Participants [in a CVD Case]. The new CVD Case Participant must be able to usefully share data and meaning with those other CVD Case Participants, and those other Participants must be able to share data and meaning from an unfamiliar newcomer.</p> <p>Elsewhere in the same report, Carney et al. write,</p> <p>Carney et al. on the necessity of trust in interoperability</p> <p>In the hoped-for context of unbounded systems of systems, trust in the actions and capabilities provided by interoperating parties is essential. Each party to an interaction must have, develop, or perceive a sense of whether the actions of interoperating parties can be trusted. This sense of trust is not Boolean (e.g., parties can be trusted to varying degrees), is context dependent (Party A can be trusted in a particular context but not in another), and is time sensitive (Party A can be trusted for a certain period). Further, the absence of trust-----distrust-----is less dangerous than misplaced trust: it is better to know that you cannot trust a particular party than to misplace trust in a party</p> <p>The protocol we propose is intended to promote trust between MPCVD Participants both within an individual case as well as over time and across cases.</p>"},{"location":"topics/background/interoperability/#objectives","title":"Objectives","text":"<p>The objectives of this documentation are as follows:</p> <ol> <li> <p>Provide a set of common primitives to serve as an ontological     foundation for CVD process definitions across     organizations.</p> </li> <li> <p>Construct abstract workflows that support the inter-organizational     coordination and synchronization required for the     CVD process to     be successful.</p> </li> <li> <p>From those primitives and workflows, identify a set of message types     needed for the CVD process to function.</p> </li> <li> <p>Provide high-level requirements for the semantic content of those     message types.</p> </li> <li> <p>Explore options for the syntactic representation of those message     types.</p> </li> </ol>"},{"location":"topics/background/what-is-vultron/","title":"What Is Vultron?","text":"<p>Is this page for me?</p> <p>This page is written for two readers:</p> <ul> <li>A CVD practitioner (security researcher, coordinator, CERT/CSIRT   analyst) who wants to know whether Vultron solves a problem they   actually have.</li> <li>A systems architect who wants to understand what \"Vultron   conformance\" would mean for their organization's tools and processes.</li> </ul> <p>If you are already sold and want to implement, jump to How-to Guides.</p> <p>CVD is a multi-party coordination problem. See the Behaviors Reference for auto-generated documentation from the current implementation.</p> <p>With the formal definition of the Vultron Protocol behind us, we now turn our attention to reflect on one of many possible paths toward implementation. We find that Behavior Trees have a number of desirable properties when it comes to automating the kinds of complex behaviors our protocol demands.</p> <p>For more about Behavior Trees</p> <p>For more about Behavior Trees, see </p> <ul> <li>Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction</li> <li>A behavior language for story-based believable agents</li> <li>GDC 2005 Proceeding: Handling Complexity in the Halo 2 AI</li> <li>Increasing Modularity of UAV Control Systems using Computer Game Behavior Trees</li> <li>An integrated system for autonomous robotics manipulation</li> </ul> <p>Behavior Trees are a way of designing and programming hierarchical behaviors. They originated in the computer gaming industry to develop realistic AIs to control NPCs in games. More recently, Behavior Trees have been used in robotics to create adaptive behaviors using autonomous AI agents. Behavior Trees offer a high potential for automating complex tasks. Agent processes can be modeled as sets of behaviors (pre-conditions, actions, and post-conditions) and the logic that joins them. Behavior Trees offer a way to organize and describe agent behaviors in a straightforward, understandable way.</p> <p>In this section, we use Behavior Trees as a method for describing MPCVD Participant activities and their interactions with the formal protocol. These behaviors map approximately to the activities described in the CVD Guide (e.g., validate report, prioritize report, create fix, publish report, publish fix, deploy fix).</p> <p>If Behavior Trees were merely a notational convention, they would already have been useful enough to include here to structure the high-level business logic of the Vultron Protocol. But they also offer a way to prototype software agents that reflect the activities of CVD Participants. Because Behavior Trees are inherently hierarchical, they are composable. Both conditions and actions can be composed into small task-oriented behaviors, which can, in turn, be composed to represent more complex agent behaviors. As a result, independent agents using Behavior Trees can be composed into multi-agent behaviors that achieve goals.</p>"},{"location":"topics/behavior_logic/#a-brief-introduction-to-behavior-tree-notation","title":"A Brief Introduction to Behavior Tree Notation","text":"<p>Behavior Trees consist of a hierarchy of nodes represented as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). A Behavior Tree execution always begins at the root node, and execution is passed along the tree by ticking each child node according to the logic built into the tree. When ticked, each node does its job and returns one of three statuses: Success, Failure, or Running. A full introduction to Behavior Trees can be found in Colledanchise and \u00d6gren's book Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction.</p> <p>Behavior Tree Node Types</p> Node Type Shape or Symbol Description Root any control flow type has no parent nodes, has one or more child nodes, and can be of any of the control-flow types. Condition rounded oval does not change the state of the world, has no child nodes, and returns only Success or Failure. Task rectangle has no child nodes; performs a task, which might change the state of the world; and returns Success, Failure, or Running. Sequence \u2192 ticks each child node, returning the last Success or the first Failure, or Running if a child returns Running. Fallback ? ticks each child node, returning the first Success or the last Failure, or Running if a child returns Running. Loop \u21ba repeatedly ticks child nodes until an exit condition is met. Parallel \u21c9 ticks all child nodes simultaneously, and returns Success when \\(m\\) of \\(n\\) children have returned Success. <p>A basic Behavior Tree is shown below. When a tree is presented in the vertical orientation, each node's children should be read left to right. In the example below, we see two motifs that come up through the remainder of this section. On the left side is a Fallback node (\\(\\boxed{?}\\)), which short-circuits to Success when the \\(postcondition\\) is already met. Otherwise, some activity will occur in \\(task_a\\) and, assuming that it succeeds, the \\(postcondition\\) is set. As a result, the fallback node ensures that Success means that the \\(postcondition\\) is met.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: A Basic Behavior Tree\n---\nflowchart TD\n    root[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    l[?]\n    root --&gt; l\n    r[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    root --&gt; r\n    l0([postcondition])\n    l --&gt; l0\n    l1[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    l --&gt; l1\n    l10[task_a]\n    l1 --&gt; l10\n    l11[set postcondition]\n    l1 --&gt; l11\n    r0([precondition])\n    r --&gt; r0\n    r1[task_b]\n    r --&gt; r1\n    r2[?]\n    r --&gt; r2\n    r20[task_c]\n    r2 --&gt; r20\n    r21[task_d]\n    r2 --&gt; r21</code></pre> <p>On the right side is a sequence (\\(\\boxed{\\rightarrow}\\)) that hinges on a \\(precondition\\) being met prior to some set of actions being taken. Assuming the \\(precondition\\) is met, \\(task_b\\) fires and, assuming it succeeds execution, proceeds to another fallback node. This fallback node represents a set of tasks in which one only needs to succeed for the fallback to return Success. If \\(task_c\\) succeeds, then \\(task_d\\) does not run.</p> <p>Behavior Trees can sometimes be wider than they are tall, so we sometimes display them in a horizontal orientation to save space. The semantics remain the same, but each node's children should be read top-to-bottom rather than left-to-right. The same tree as above is shown below in horizontal form.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: A Basic Behavior Tree (horizontal)\n---\nflowchart LR\n    root[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    l[?]\n    root --&gt; l\n    r[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    root --&gt; r\n    l0([postcondition])\n    l --&gt; l0\n    l1[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    l --&gt; l1\n    l10[task_a]\n    l1 --&gt; l10\n    l11[set postcondition]\n    l1 --&gt; l11\n    r0([precondition])\n    r --&gt; r0\n    r1[task_b]\n    r --&gt; r1\n    r2[?]\n    r --&gt; r2\n    r20[task_c]\n    r2 --&gt; r20\n    r21[task_d]\n    r2 --&gt; r21</code></pre> <p>Behavior Trees are composable\u2014that is, a task node in one tree can be replaced with a more refined Behavior Tree in another. We leverage this feature throughout the remainder of this chapter to describe an agent model for an MPCVD Participant as a set of nested Behavior Trees that reflect the protocol described in the previous chapters.</p>"},{"location":"topics/behavior_logic/acquire_exploit_bt/","title":"Acquire Exploit Behavior","text":"<p>Some Vendors or other CVD Participants might require a proof-of-concept exploit to accompany an incoming report for it to pass their validation checks. It bears some structural similarity to the Report Validation Behavior Tree just described: An initial post-condition check (A) falls back to the main process (B) leading toward \\(accept\\), which, in turn, falls back to the deferral process (C).</p> <p>In more detail, (A) if the report is already in either the Accepted or Deferred states and no new information is available to prompt a change, the behavior ends.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Report Prioritization Behavior Tree\n---\nflowchart LR\n    fb[\"?\"]\n    seq1[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    fb --&gt;|A| seq1\n    rm_d_or_a([\"RM in D or A?\"])\n    seq1 --&gt; rm_d_or_a\n    seq1fb[\"?\"]\n    seq1 --&gt; seq1fb\n    enough_info([\"enough info?\"])\n    seq1fb --&gt; enough_info\n    gather_seq[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    seq1fb --&gt; gather_seq\n    gather_info[\"gather info\"]\n    gather_seq --&gt; gather_info\n    no_info[\"no new info\"]\n    gather_seq --&gt; no_info\n    seq2[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    fb --&gt;|B| seq2\n    rm_v_d_a([\"RM in V, D, or A?\"])\n    seq2 --&gt; rm_v_d_a\n    eval_priority[\"evaluate priority\"]\n    seq2 --&gt; eval_priority\n    priority_not_defer([\"priority is not defer?\"])\n    seq2 --&gt; priority_not_defer\n    accept_fb[\"?\"]\n    seq2 --&gt; accept_fb\n    rm_a([\"RM in A?\"])\n    accept_fb --&gt; rm_a\n    accept_seq[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    accept_fb --&gt; accept_seq\n    accept[\"accept\"]\n    accept_seq --&gt; accept\n    accept_to_a[\"RM &amp;rarr; A&lt;br/&gt;(emit RA)\"]\n    accept_seq --&gt; accept_to_a\n    defer_fb[\"?\"]\n    fb --&gt;|C| defer_fb\n    rm_d([\"RM in D?\"])\n    defer_fb --&gt; rm_d\n    defer_seq[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    defer_fb --&gt; defer_seq\n    defer[\"defer\"]\n    defer_seq --&gt; defer\n    defer_to_d[\"RM &amp;rarr; D&lt;br/&gt;(emit RD)\"]\n    defer_seq --&gt; defer_to_d</code></pre> <p>Failing that, we enter the main prioritization sequence (B). The preconditions of the main sequence are that either the report has not yet been prioritized out of the Valid state (\\(q^{rm} \\in V\\)) or new information has been made available to a report in either \\(q^{rm} \\in \\{ D, A \\}\\) to trigger a reevaluation.</p> <p>Assuming the preconditions are met, the report priority is evaluated. For example, a Participant using SSVC could insert that process here. The evaluation task is expected to always set the report priority. The subsequent check returns Failure on a defer priority or Success on any non-deferral priority. On Success, an accept task is included as a placeholder for any intake process that a Participant might have for Accepted reports. Assuming that it succeeds, the report is explicitly moved to the Accepted (\\(q^{rm} \\xrightarrow{a} A\\)) state, and an \\(RA\\) message is emitted.</p> <p>(C) Should any item in the main sequence fail, the case is deferred, its state set to \\(q^{rm} \\xrightarrow{d} D\\), and an \\(RD\\) message is emitted accordingly. If the current information available in the report is sufficient, no further action is necessary and the entire behavior returns Success. However, a previous validation pass might have left some indicator that more information was needed. In that case, execution proceeds to the sequence in which the gather info task runs. If nothing new is found, the entire branch returns Success, and the report remains Invalid. If new information is found, though, the branch fails, driving execution over to the main validation sequence.</p> <p>(C) The main validation sequence follows when none of the above conditions have been met. In other words, the validation sequence is triggered when the report is in Received and its validity has never been evaluated or when the report was originally determined to be Invalid but new information is available to prompt reconsideration. The validation process shown here is comprised of two main steps: a credibility check followed by a validity check as outlined in our introduction of the Received (R) state.</p> <p>As a reminder, a report might be in one of three categories: (a) neither credible nor valid, (b) credible but invalid, or (c) both credible and valid. Vultron handles all of that automatically using behavior trees (BTs) \u2014 a kind of state machine that runs as protocol activities arrive.</p> <p>But some steps require judgment that Vultron cannot make by itself:</p> <ul> <li>Is this vulnerability report credible?</li> <li>Should we accept this embargo proposal?</li> <li>Has a CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) ID already been assigned?</li> <li>Is it time to publish the advisory?</li> </ul> <p>These are call-out points \u2014 places where the BT pauses and waits for an answer from an external service before it can continue.</p> <p>A call-out point is answerable now; asking another actor is not</p> <p>A call-out point waits for a service you run, so it can be answered while the BT is still running. That is what makes pausing viable.</p> <p>Some questions cannot be answered that way, because they need a decision from another actor in the case \u2014 for example, whether the case owner permits a change to the case's agreed state. No service can answer that on the owner's behalf, and the answer may take days. There the actor does not pause: it sends a request and finishes, and the reply starts new work when it arrives. See Protocol Event Flow.</p> <p>During development and simulation, call-out points are filled by fuzzer nodes \u2014 stubs that return a random success or failure based on a probability. In production, you replace a fuzzer node with a real service: a capability implementation.</p>"},{"location":"topics/capability_model/#the-two-integration-surfaces","title":"The two integration surfaces","text":"<p>There are two ways an external service interacts with Vultron:</p> <p>Call-out \u2014 Vultron calls you. The BT reaches a call-out point, packages up a question as a structured payload, sends it to your service, and waits for a structured answer. Your service decides and responds.</p> <p>Call-in \u2014 You call Vultron. Your service monitors something externally \u2014 a timer, a threat feed, a deployment system \u2014 and, when a condition is met, sends a trigger to Vultron. Vultron acts on it.</p> <p>Most services use the call-out surface. One shape \u2014 the Sentinel \u2014 works exclusively on the call-in side (see The five shapes below).</p>"},{"location":"topics/capability_model/#three-level-taxonomy","title":"Three-level taxonomy","text":"<p>Every integration point in Vultron fits into a three-level hierarchy:</p> <p>Shape \u2192 Capability \u2192 Capability implementation</p> Level What it is Example Shape The abstract type of interaction \u2014 what the service receives, what it returns, and how the BT uses the result Evaluator Capability A specific named integration point with its own input/output contract <code>EvaluateCveEligibility</code> Capability implementation The concrete service you build that fulfills a capability at runtime A microservice that applies CNA Operational Rules and returns pass/fail <p>Think of the shape as a job description, the capability as the open role, and your implementation as the service hired into that role.</p> <p>Some capabilities are sub-steps of a larger workflow capability. Each one keeps its own copy of the case. This page explains how those copies stay in agreement, and it answers two questions:</p> <ul> <li>Who decides the order in which things happened?</li> <li>What happens when messages arrive in the wrong order?</li> </ul> <p>Vultron answers the first question with a single writer. It answers the second by holding an early message until the message it depends on arrives.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#one-writer-many-copies","title":"One writer, many copies","text":"<p>Every participant in a case keeps a local copy of the case, called a replica. No participant can read or write another participant's replica. Knowledge travels only in messages \u2014 see the Actor Knowledge Model.</p> <p>One peer is different. Whichever participant holds the <code>CASE_MANAGER</code> role is the case's single-writer authority \u2014 the CASE_MANAGER. It keeps the case ledger: the append-only history that is authoritative for the case, and it is the only peer that appends to that history (CLP-01-003). In the prototype this authority is enacted by a dedicated service actor (the Case Actor), but the authority derives from the role, never from that actor's name or URL (ADR-0088).</p> <p>The flow of a change is always the same:</p> <ol> <li>A participant sends the CASE_MANAGER an assertion \u2014 I accept the embargo,    my report is now validated, here is a note.</li> <li>The CASE_MANAGER judges the assertion and appends one entry recording the    outcome. An entry's <code>disposition</code> says whether the assertion was    <code>recorded</code> (accepted) or <code>rejected</code>, so a refusal leaves a trace rather    than a silence.</li> <li>The CASE_MANAGER sends the new entry to every participant as    <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code>.</li> <li>Each participant records the entry, and applies its effects to its own    replica if the entry was <code>recorded</code>.</li> </ol> <p>Because there is exactly one writer, no participant ever has to reconcile two competing versions of the case history. There is only one version. A participant's replica is a projection of that history, not an independent record.</p> <p>The same rule applies in reverse: a participant accepts a case update only from the CASE_MANAGER for that case, and rejects an update from any other sender (PCR-03-001). Nobody else can write to a replica, and the replica's owner does not edit it directly either \u2014 even when that owner is the organization that opened the case.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#two-views-of-the-ledger","title":"Two views of the ledger","text":"<p>The ledger can be read two ways, and most of this page is about the second one.</p> <ul> <li>The audit log is every entry the CASE_MANAGER appended, in the order it   appended them \u2014 rejections included.</li> <li>The recorded projection is the subset whose <code>disposition</code> is <code>recorded</code>.   That projection is the authoritative history of the case   (CLP-04-001).</li> </ul> <p>Case state is reconstructed from the recorded projection alone; a replica ignores rejected entries when working out what is true of the case (CLP-04-002). The hash chain is computed over that projection too (CLP-04-003), so a rejection does not advance the chain: the next recorded entry names the previous recorded entry as its predecessor, not a rejection appended in between.</p> <p>A rejection is therefore evidence \u2014 the CASE_MANAGER saw this assertion and refused it \u2014 rather than a fact about the case. Where the rest of this page says \"the chain\" or \"the history\", it means the recorded projection.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-a-ledger-entry-carries","title":"What a ledger entry carries","text":"<p>Each entry is a small, immutable record. These are the fields that carry the ordering and integrity guarantees this page is about.</p> Field Meaning <code>case_id</code> The case this entry belongs to <code>log_index</code> Position in the case history; starts at 0 and counts up <code>published</code> When the CASE_MANAGER stamped the entry, by its own clock <code>prevLogHash</code> Hash of the previous <code>recorded</code> entry <code>entryHash</code> Hash of this entry's own content <code>payloadSnapshot</code> A copy of the assertion the entry records <p><code>prevLogHash</code> and <code>entryHash</code> link the entries into a chain, like the teeth of a zipper. Each entry names its predecessor in the recorded projection, so a receiver can tell whether an entry belongs at the end of the history it already holds. The first entry in a case names the genesis hash, a value derived from the case object itself, so the chain is anchored to the case it describes.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#log-index-is-the-causal-order","title":"Log index is the causal order","text":"<p>The <code>log_index</code> sequence is the causal order of the case. If the CASE_MANAGER observed event A before event B, then A has the lower <code>log_index</code> (CLP-14-001, ADR-0079). Anything that needs to know what happened first compares log indexes. It does not compare clocks.</p> <p>This matters because clocks disagree. Two organizations on different continents, running different software, will not agree on the millisecond at which an event occurred. Sorting a shared history by wall-clock time would make the order depend on whose clock was fast. Sorting by <code>log_index</code> does not.</p> <p>Timestamps are still recorded, and they are still useful \u2014 as corroborating evidence, and for spotting a participant whose clock is wrong. They are not the order.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-the-ledger-claims-and-what-it-does-not","title":"What the ledger claims, and what it does not","text":"<p>The ledger is authoritative from the CASE_MANAGER's point of view. It is a postmark, not a forensic reconstruction. It records the sequence in which the CASE_MANAGER observed and processed events, and it makes no claim about when those events happened inside another organization (CLP-15-005).</p> <ul> <li>For events the CASE_MANAGER generates itself, causal order is known by   construction: the entries are written one after another on a single path.</li> <li>For events reported by participants, the CASE_MANAGER's own receive-and-commit   order is the order. The CASE_MANAGER cannot verify a causal claim about   something it did not see.</li> </ul> <p>The CASE_MANAGER never reorders entries to match timestamps supplied by someone else. Doing so would let external data override the one thing the CASE_MANAGER knows first-hand.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#rules-the-case_manager-follows","title":"Rules the CASE_MANAGER follows","text":"Rule Requirement Order is never reversed: an event observed earlier never gets a higher <code>log_index</code> CLP-14-001 Every entry carries a timestamp; none may be empty CLP-14-002 Timestamps on consecutive recorded entries never move backwards as <code>log_index</code> increases CLP-14-003 Every entry in a ledger belongs to the same case CLP-14-004 No two entries in a case share a <code>log_index</code> CLP-14-005 No entry predates the case it belongs to CLP-14-006 <p>Whether the index run may contain holes is not settled. A replica must hold a contiguous run from the genesis entry through the position it has acknowledged before it may take new protocol-significant actions on the case (SYNC-10-004), and in practice a receiver treats a hole as a missing entry. But <code>log_index</code> is consumed by every appended entry, rejections included, and rejections are not part of the recorded projection \u2014 so a hole in that projection is not by itself proof of loss. ADR-0079 states the rule both ways in different sections; the contradiction is tracked in #2752 and is not resolved here.</p> <p>The CASE_MANAGER should also refuse an assertion whose own timestamp is far in the future or far in the past compared to its clock \u2014 by default, more than five minutes ahead or more than seven days old (CLP-14-007, CLP-14-008). A deployment that knows its own clock conditions may tune both thresholds (CLP-14-009). These are sanity checks, not proof of honesty; a participant with a badly wrong clock can still produce a well-formed but misleading assertion.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#two-timestamps-two-different-rules","title":"Two timestamps, two different rules","text":"<p>An entry carries two timestamps, and the rules above do not all apply to the same one:</p> Timestamp Written by Rules it answers to <code>published</code> on the entry the CASE_MANAGER, at commit time CLP-14-002, CLP-14-003, CLP-14-006 read across the whole ledger <code>published</code> inside <code>payloadSnapshot</code> the asserting participant CLP-14-006 at the commit boundary, CLP-14-007, CLP-14-008, CLP-15-003, CLP-15-006 <p>The distinction matters most for the \"never move backwards\" rule. Across the CASE_MANAGER's own commit timestamps it holds because one writer stamps every entry from one clock. Applied to participants' timestamps it would be wrong: two participants' clocks are not synchronized, so an assertion recorded later by one of them can legitimately claim an earlier time than an assertion recorded earlier by the other. The CASE_MANAGER therefore compares a participant's claimed timestamp only against that same participant's previous assertion, and allows a small tolerance when comparing it against the case's creation time.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-participants-must-do","title":"What participants must do","text":"<p>The CASE_MANAGER can only record the order it sees. That places an obligation on each participant: send events in the order they happened.</p> <ul> <li>If A caused B, send A first   (CLP-15-001).</li> <li>Do not collect several related events and send them in an arbitrary order   (CLP-15-002).</li> <li>Give B a timestamp no earlier than A's   (CLP-15-003).</li> <li>Timestamp an event with when it happened, not when the batch went out or a   retry was attempted   (CLP-15-004).</li> </ul> <p>A participant that breaks these rules produces a malformed assertion. That is a fault on the sending side, not a CASE_MANAGER failure.</p> <p>The CASE_MANAGER cannot police these at the moment an assertion arrives, and it must not try: it may not reconstruct an order it did not observe (CLP-15-005). It sees the order messages arrived in, which is not the order they were sent in \u2014 the transport makes no such promise.</p> <p>So when an assertion's claimed time falls behind the same participant's previous assertion, the CASE_MANAGER records it and says so, rather than refusing it. A small regression is reported quietly; one beyond the configured tolerance is reported as a warning. Refusing would throw the message away \u2014 the ledger commit happens before any of the receiving work, so a refusal loses the whole thing \u2014 and the CASE_MANAGER cannot tell a participant that really did misorder its events from two messages that simply arrived out of order.</p> <p>The two ordering rules are visible only across a whole case, by comparing the causal links a scenario declares against the order the ledger recorded; the conformance suite checks them there.</p> <p>One thing the CASE_MANAGER does refuse outright: an activity that arrives with no <code>published</code> time at all. Because the field is optional in ActivityStreams, a receiver that filled in the blank with its own clock could no longer tell what the sender claimed from what it invented \u2014 and every check above would then be comparing the CASE_MANAGER's clock against itself. A message without a claimed time is therefore rejected at the door (CLP-15-006).</p> <p>A field that is present but empty carries no claimed time either. A blank <code>published</code> \u2014 an empty string, or one holding only whitespace \u2014 is refused the same way as an omitted one, and reports the same reason (MV-03-002).</p> <p>A value that is present and not blank but unreadable as a timestamp is a different fault. The CASE_MANAGER reports it as malformed data, not as a missing field, so a sender is never told to supply something it already sent.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#when-entries-arrive-out-of-order","title":"When entries arrive out of order","text":"<p>Ledger entries travel over ordinary message transport, which gives no ordering guarantee. Vultron may also not be the only implementation on the wire. So a replica can receive entry 7 before entry 6.</p> <p>The naive response is to reject entry 7, on the grounds that it does not extend the chain, and wait for the CASE_MANAGER to send it again. That does not work. The replay travels the same unordered transport and can arrive out of order again, so under repeated reordering an entry can be lost indefinitely. In an earlier version of this implementation, that is what stalled a late-joining vendor at case closure.</p> <p>Instead, a replica keeps an early entry (ADR-0037, SYNC-14-001). It puts the entry in a holding area and waits for the predecessor. Convergence then no longer depends on delivery order at all.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-gets-held-and-what-does-not","title":"What gets held, and what does not","text":"<p>A replica holds an entry when the entry does not extend its chain but belongs later in the history \u2014 its <code>log_index</code> is more than one past the end of what the replica holds. That is a forward gap: the predecessor has not arrived yet.</p> <p>Two kinds of entry are not held:</p> <ul> <li>An entry at or behind the end of the chain. That is a duplicate or a stale   replay, not a gap.</li> <li>An entry exactly one past the end of the chain whose <code>prevLogHash</code> does not   match the hash of the replica's last recorded entry. Nothing is missing in   front of it, so it is not a gap \u2014 it is a fork, a claim about a history the   replica does not share.</li> </ul> <p>Both go to the ordinary duplicate and divergence handling instead.</p> <p>Even when it does hold an entry, the replica still sends <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> naming the last entry it accepted (SYNC-14-002). Holding solves reordering; it cannot solve loss. If the missing entry was never delivered at all, the reject is what prompts the CASE_MANAGER to send it again.</p> <p>The CASE_MANAGER does not replay on demand without limit. If a peer keeps rejecting from the same position, the CASE_MANAGER waits out a short cooldown before replaying to it again (SYNC-15-003). Without that bound, a peer that cannot anchor its chain rejects every entry it is sent, each reject triggers another full replay, and the two feed each other into a storm. A reject from a position that has advanced always triggers a replay, so a peer making progress is never held back.</p> <p>The holding area should also be bounded, so that a hostile or broken peer streaming far-future entries cannot exhaust memory. When it is full, the replica discards the entry farthest ahead of the gap and logs a warning (SYNC-14-006). Discarding is safe because the reject for that gap has already been sent \u2014 but the eviction itself sends nothing, so recovery waits on the replay that reject triggers, or on the next entry that fails to match the tail. The cooldown above may delay either.</p> <p>The holding area is deliberately not the ledger (SYNC-14-005). Across Vultron, the presence of an entry in an actor's own store means this entry is committed and its effects are applied (SYNC-13-001). A held entry is neither, so storing it would break that meaning.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#entries-that-arrive-before-the-case","title":"Entries that arrive before the case","text":"<p>The same holding area covers a related race: an entry can arrive before the participant has the case object at all. Without the case, the replica cannot compute the genesis hash and so cannot anchor the chain.</p> <p>A replica holds these entries too (SYNC-15-004), with no gap comparison \u2014 there is no chain yet to compare against, so every entry for the unknown case is held, including entry 0. When the case is later delivered, the replica drains the holding area for that case (SYNC-15-005). Seeding the case is enough, because the genesis hash is derived from the case object; the genesis ledger entry does not have to be re-sent (ADR-0059).</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#draining-the-held-entries","title":"Draining the held entries","text":"<p>Each held entry is filed under the hash of the predecessor it is waiting for. So after the replica commits a new last entry, finding the successor is a single lookup: the held entry whose <code>prevLogHash</code> equals the hash of the entry just committed.</p> <p>The drain then repeats. Commit the successor, look up its successor, and continue until no held entry extends the chain (SYNC-14-003). A run of ten entries that arrived in reverse order clicks into place in one cascade, in <code>log_index</code> order.</p> <p>Three properties make the drain safe:</p> <ul> <li>Same path. A drained entry goes through the same processing as an entry   that arrived in order \u2014 no separate code path with its own behavior   (SYNC-14-008). In this   implementation that means the drain re-runs the announce receive behavior   tree on each held entry, in <code>log_index</code> order.</li> <li>Effects before storage. The entry's consequences \u2014 an embargo ending, a   participant joining, a status changing \u2014 are applied first, and the entry is   stored only if they all succeed   (SYNC-12-001,   SYNC-14-004).</li> <li>Applied once. An entry already in the local ledger is skipped entirely,   so a replay or a duplicate cannot apply the same effects twice   (SYNC-12-003,   SYNC-14-007).</li> </ul> <p>Because held entries are replayed through the ordinary path, the reject-and-replay recovery becomes order-tolerant as well, at no extra cost.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#why-state-checks-wait-for-the-drain","title":"Why state checks wait for the drain","text":"<p>Holding an entry has a consequence that is easy to get wrong. Case State (CS) has ordering rules of its own: an ephemeral state cannot be a resting place, so it has exactly one permitted successor and must be followed by it; the recorded history must remain a valid sequence throughout; and a move to public awareness must be recorded before the embargo termination that it triggers.</p> <p>If a replica checked those rules at the moment an entry arrived, an out-of-order entry would look like a violation. An entry naming a state that is only reachable from its predecessor would appear to arrive from nowhere.</p> <p>That is why the checks run at drain time instead (CSB-19-001). A held entry is parked before any case-state effect is applied, so the state machine is never touched at arrival time. When the gap closes, the entries replay in <code>log_index</code> order \u2014 which is causal order \u2014 and the guards see them in the sequence they were meant to be seen in.</p> <p>An entry waiting in the holding area therefore raises no state violation at all (CSB-19-002). An entry naming an ephemeral state is perfectly well-formed on its own; it would only be a real violation if the entry that resolves it never arrived. Flagging it on arrival would be a false alarm, and rejecting it would prevent the replica from ever converging.</p> <p>The public-awareness-before-embargo-termination ordering survives reordering for free (CSB-19-003). The CASE_MANAGER commits the public-awareness entry first, so it holds the lower <code>log_index</code>. The drain works in <code>log_index</code> order, so it can never present the termination entry first. No receiver-side re-check of the timing is needed; the order in the ledger is sufficient.</p>"},{"location":"topics/case_lifecycle/case_ledger_sync/#what-a-replica-guarantees","title":"What a replica guarantees","text":"<p>Taken together, the ledger rules and the holding area give each participant these properties:</p> Property Meaning Append-only A committed entry is immutable and identified by its content hash Deterministic projection The same run of entries produces the same state in every conforming implementation Idempotent replay Re-processing entries already seen changes nothing Monotonic progress A replica never regresses the position it has acknowledged Reject on divergence An entry that does not extend the chain is not silently accepted Order-independent convergence Delivery order does not affect the final state <p>The result is eventual consistency with a strong bound: given the same entries, every replica reaches the same state as the CASE_MANAGER, no matter what order those entries arrived in.</p> <p>The holding area itself is in memory only, and is lost on restart. considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Our Observational analysis supports the conclusion that vulnerability disclosure as currently practiced demonstrates skill. In both data sets examined, our estimated \\(\\alpha_d\\) is positive for most \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\). However, there is uncertainty in our estimates due to the application of the principle of indifference to unobserved data. This principle assumes a uniform distribution across event transitions in the absence of CVD, which is an assumption we cannot readily test. The spread of the estimates in Observing Skill represents the variance in our samples, not this assumption-based uncertainty. Our interpretation of \\(\\alpha_d\\) values near zero is therefore that they reflect an absence of evidence rather than evidence that skill is absent. While we cannot rule definitively on luck or low skill, values of \\(\\alpha_d &gt; 0.9\\) should reliably indicate skillful defenders.</p> <p>If, as seems plausible from the evidence, it turns out that further observations of \\(h\\) are significantly skewed toward the higher end of the poset \\((\\mathcal{H},\\leq_{\\mathbb{D}})\\), then it may be useful to empirically calibrate our metrics rather than using the a priori frequencies in Reasoning over Histories as our baseline. We can at least state that we would prefer that most cases reach fix ready before attacks (\\(\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{A}\\)).</p> <p>Per the Event Frequency table in Reasoning Over Possible Histories, (reproduced below for convenience), even in a world without skill we would expect \\(\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{A}\\) to hold in 37.5% of cases.</p> <p>Expected Frequency of \\({row} \\prec {col}\\) when events are chosen uniformly from possible transitions in each state</p> \\(\\mathbf{V}\\) \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) \\(\\mathbf{P}\\) \\(\\mathbf{X}\\) \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) \\(\\mathbf{V}\\) 0 1 1 0.333 0.667 0.750 \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) 0 0 1 0.111 0.333 0.375 \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) 0 0 0 0.037 0.167 0.187 \\(\\mathbf{P}\\) 0.667 0.889 0.963 0 0.500 0.667 \\(\\mathbf{X}\\) 0.333 0.667 0.833 0.500 0 0.500 \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) 0.250 0.625 0.812 0.333 0.500 0 <p>This means that \\(\\alpha_{\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{A}} &lt; 0\\) for anything less than a 0.375 success rate.</p> <p>Benchmarking CVD</p> <p>In fact, we propose to generalize this for any \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\), such that \\(\\alpha_d\\) should be greater than some benchmark constant \\(c_d\\):</p> \\[\\alpha_d \\geq c_d \\geq 0\\] <p>where \\(c_d\\) is a based on observations of \\(\\alpha_d\\) collected across some collection of CVD cases.</p> <p>We propose as a starting point a na\u00efve benchmark of \\(c_d = 0\\). This is a low bar, as it only requires that CVD actually do better than possible events which are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) within each case. For example, given a history in which \\((\\mathbf{V}, \\mathbf{F}, \\mathbf{P})\\) have already happened (i.e., state \\(q \\in VFdPxa\\)), \\(\\mathbf{D}\\), \\(\\mathbf{X}\\), or \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) are equally likely to occur next.</p> <p>The i.i.d. assumption may not be warranted.</p> <p>We anticipate that event ordering probabilities might be conditional on history: for example, exploit publication may be more likely when the vulnerability is public (\\(p(\\mathbf{X}|q \\in \\mathcal{Q}_P) &gt; p(\\mathbf{X}|q \\in \\mathcal{Q}_p)\\)) or attacks may be more likely when an exploit is public (\\(p(\\mathbf{A}|q \\in \\mathcal{Q}_{X}) &gt; p(\\mathbf{A}|q \\in \\mathcal{Q}_{x})\\)). If the i.i.d. assumption fails to hold for transition events \\(\\sigma \\in \\Sigma\\), observed frequencies of \\(h \\in \\mathcal{H}\\) could differ significantly from the rates predicted by the uniform probability assumption behind the Event Frequency table above.</p> <p>Supporting Observations</p> <p>Some example suggestive observations are:</p> <ul> <li> <p>There is reason to suspect that only a fraction of vulnerabilities ever reach the exploit public event \\(\\mathbf{X}\\), and fewer still reach the attack event \\(\\mathbf{A}\\). Recent work by the Cyentia Institute found that \"5% of all CVEs are both observed within organizations AND known to be exploited\", which suggests that \\(f_{\\mathbf{D} \\prec \\mathbf{A}} \\approx 0.95\\).</p> </li> <li> <p>Likewise, \\(\\mathbf{D} \\prec \\mathbf{X}\\) holds in 28 of 70 (0.4) \\(h\\). However, we could choose a slightly different goal than differentiating skill and \"blind luck\" as represented by the i.i.d. assumption. One could aim to measure \"more skillful than the average for some set of teams\" rather than more skillful than blind luck.</p> <p>If this were the \"reasonable\" baseline expectation, the primary limitation is available observations. The need for MPCVD arises due to the inherent nature of the software supply chain CERT Guide to CVD. A vulnerability that affects a low-level component (such as a library or operating system API) can require fixes from both the originating vendor and any vendor whose products incorporate the affected component. Known only to its finder, the vulnerability can be described by that singular state.</p> <p>As it becomes clear that the vulnerability affects multiple vendors' products, both finder/reporters and coordinators might begin to track the state of each individual vendor as a separate instance of the model. For example, if 3 vendors are known to be affected, but only 1 has been notified, the case might be considered to be in a superposition of states \\(\\{Vfdpxa,vfdpxa,vfdpxa\\}\\).</p> <p>Each vendor, in turn, might then ascertain whether they are able to produce fixes for all their available products at once, or if those fixes will be staggered over time. In either case, the vendor might track the case as a superposition of states for each affected product dependent on its fix readiness status. For example, a vendor might have four products affected, with two in the fix-ready state and two fixes still in progress. Should they opt for transparency into their internal process, they might communicate their status as the superposition of \\(\\{VFdpxa,VFdpxa,Vfdpxa,Vfdpxa\\}\\). Alternatively, they might choose to only share the lowest state across their products, which in this example would be \\(\\{Vfdpxa\\}\\).</p> <p>The above example implies a need to expand our notation.</p> <p>MPCVD Cases have Participant-Specific States</p> <p>In the MPCVD case, we need to think of each state \\(q \\in \\mathcal{Q}\\) as a set of states \\(q_M\\):</p> \\[ q_M \\stackrel{\\mathsf{def}}{=}\\{ q_1,q_2,\\dots,q_n \\} \\] <p>where \\(q_i\\) represents the state \\(q\\) for the \\(i\\)th affected vendor and/or product. For example, \\(\\{ {Vfdpxa}_1, {vfdpxa}_2 \\}\\) would represent the state in which vendor 1 has been notified but vendor 2 has not. Very often, vendor notification occurs as new products and vendors are identified as affected in the course of analyzing a vulnerability report. So the individual events \\(\\mathbf{V}_i\\) in \\(\\mathbf{V}_M\\) (representing the status of all the vendor notifications) might be spread out over a period of time.</p> <p>Some transitions are more readily synchronized than others. For example, if an MPCVD case is already underway, and information about the vulnerability appears in a public media report, we can say that \\(\\mathbf{P}_M\\) occurred simultaneously for all coordinating vendors.</p> <p>Regardless, in the maximal case, each vendor-product pair is effectively behaving independently of all the others. Therefore:</p> <p>Dimensionality of an MPCVD Case</p> <p>The maximum dimensionality of the MPCVD model for a case is</p> \\[ D_{max} = 5 * N_{vprod} \\] <p>where \\(N_{vprod}\\) represents the number of vendor-product pairs.</p> <p>This is undesirable, as it would result in a wide distribution of realized histories that more closely resemble the randomness assumptions outlined above than a skillful, coordinated effort. Further discussion of measuring MPCVD skill can be found below.</p> <p>Reducing Dimensionality of MPCVD Cases is a good thing</p> <p>For now, we posit that the goal of a good MPCVD process is to reduce the dimensionality of a given MPCVD case as much as is possible (i.e., to the 5 dimensions of a single vendor CVD case we have presented above). Experience shows that a full dimension reduction is unlikely in most cases, but that does not detract from the value of having the goal.</p> <p>Reducing Complexity within a Vendor Organization</p> <p>Vendors may be able to reduce their internal tracking dimensionality---which may be driven by things like component reuse across products or product lines---through in-house coordination of fix development processes. Within an individual vendor organization, PSIRTs are a common organizational structure to address this internal coordination process.</p> <ul> <li>The FIRST PSIRT Services Framework provides guidance regarding vendors' internal processes for coordinating vulnerability response.</li> <li>Additional guidance can be found in ISO/IEC 30111:2019.</li> </ul> <p>Regardless, the cross-vendor dimension is largely the result of component reuse across vendors, for example through the inclusion of third party libraries or OEM SDKs. Visibility of cross-vendor component reuse remains an unsolved problem, although efforts such as the Software Bill of Materials are promising in this regard. Thus, dimensionality reduction can be achieved through both improved transparency of the software supply chain and the process of coordination toward synchronized state transitions, especially for \\(\\mathbf{P}\\), if not for \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) and \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) as well.</p> <p>As a result of the dimensionality problem, coordinators and other parties to an MPCVD case need to decide how to apply disclosure policy rules in cases where different products or vendors occupy different case states with potentially contradictory recommended actions. For example, when four out of five vendors involved in a case have reached \\(VFdpxa\\) and are ready to publish, but the fifth is still in \\(Vfdpxa\\). Essentially this can be expected to take the form of a weighting function that acts on a vector of case states, and outputs a set of recommended actions derived from those states.</p> <p>One possible function would be to apply a simple voting heuristic such as waiting for a simple majority of vendors to reach a state before taking action as that state recommends. In our 4/5 \\(VFdpxa\\) example, the coordinating parties would behave as if the case were in that state for all.</p> <p>Another function could be to weight vendors and products by some other factor, such as size of the installed user base, or even based on a risk analysis of societal costs associated with potential actions. Here we acknowledge that our example is under-specified: does the fifth vendor (the one in \\(Vfdpxa\\)) represent a sizable fraction of the total user base? Or does it concentrate the highest risk use cases for the software? Challenges in efficiently assessing consistent answers to these questions are easy to imagine. The status quo for MPCVD appears consistent with defaulting to simple majority in the absence of additional information, with consideration given to the distribution of both users and risk on a case-by-case basis. At present, there is no clear consensus on such policies, although we hope that future work can use the model presented here to formalize the necessary analysis.</p> <p>Integrating FIRST MPCVD Guidance</p> <p>FIRST has published Guidelines and Practices for Multi-Party Vulnerability Coordination and Disclosure. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Does CVD as observed in the wild demonstrate skillful behavior?</p> <p>In order to answer this question, we need a way to measure skillful behavior in CVD. This section defines a method for measuring skill in CVD.</p> <p>The measurement method makes use of all the modeling tools and baselines established thus far: a comprehensive set of possible histories \\(\\mathcal{H}\\), a partial order over them in terms of the presence of desired event precedence \\((\\mathcal{H},\\leq_{\\mathbb{D}})\\), and the a priori expected frequency of each desiderata \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\).</p> <p>If we expected to be able to observe all events in all CVD cases, we could be assured of having complete histories and could be done here. But the real world is messy. Not all events \\(\\mathbf{e} \\in \\mathcal{E}\\) are always observable. We need to develop a way to make sense of what we can observe, regardless of whether we are ever able to capture complete histories. Continuing towards our goal of measuring efficacy, we return to considering the balance between skill and luck in determining our observed outcomes.</p>"},{"location":"topics/measuring_cvd/discriminating_skill_and_luck/#a-measure-of-skill-in-cvd","title":"A Measure of Skill in CVD","text":"<p>We have established a set of desiderata \\(\\mathbb{D}\\) that we would like to see in a CVD case. Now, we want to measure the degree to which a CVD practice is skillful in achieving those desiderata. In a world of pure skill, one would expect that a player could achieve all 12 desiderata \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\) consistently. That is, a maximally skillful player could consistently achieve the specific ordering \\(h=(\\mathbf{V},\\mathbf{F},\\mathbf{D},\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{X},\\mathbf{A})\\) with probability \\(p_{skill} = 1\\).</p> <p>Factors that could affect the observed frequency of a desideratum</p> <p>There are many reasons why we might expect our observations to differ from the expected frequencies we established  in Reasoning Over Possible Histories. Adversaries might be rare, or conversely very well equipped. Vendors might be very good at releasing fixes faster  than adversaries can discover vulnerabilities and develop exploits for them. System owners might be diligent at applying patches. (We did say might, didn't we?) Regardless, for now we will lump all of those possible explanations into a single attribute called \"skill.\"</p> <p>Thus, we construct the following model: for each of our preferred orderings \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\), we model their occurrence due to luck using the binomial distribution with parameter \\(p_{luck} = f_d\\) taken from the event frequency table in Reasoning Over Possible Histories, reproduced below for convenience:</p> <p>Expected Frequency of \\({row} \\prec {col}\\) when events are chosen uniformly from possible transitions in each state</p> \\(\\mathbf{V}\\) \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) \\(\\mathbf{P}\\) \\(\\mathbf{X}\\) \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) \\(\\mathbf{V}\\) 0 1 1 0.333 0.667 0.750 \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) 0 0 1 0.111 0.333 0.375 \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) 0 0 0 0.037 0.167 0.187 \\(\\mathbf{P}\\) 0.667 0.889 0.963 0 0.500 0.667 \\(\\mathbf{X}\\) 0.333 0.667 0.833 0.500 0 0.500 \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) 0.250 0.625 0.812 0.333 0.500 0 <p>Recall that the mean of a binomial distribution is the probability of success \\(p\\), and that the mean of a weighted mixture of two binomial distributions is the weighted mixture of the individual means. Therefore our model adds a parameter \\(\\alpha_d\\) to represent the weighting between our success rates arising from skill \\(p_{skill}\\) and luck \\(p_{luck}\\). Because there are 12 desiderata \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\), each \\(d\\) will have its own observations and corresponding value for \\(\\alpha_d\\) for each history \\(h_a\\).</p> <p>Modeling Skill and Luck in Observations</p> <p>We model the observed frequency of desiderata \\(d\\) as a weighted mixture of the success rates due to skill and luck:</p> \\[ f_d^{obs} = \\alpha_d \\cdot p_{skill} + (1 - \\alpha_d) \\cdot p_{luck} \\] <p>Where \\(f_d^{obs}\\) is the observed frequency of successes for desiderata \\(d\\). Because \\(p_{skill} = 1\\), one of those binomial distributions is degenerate. Substituting \\(p_{skill} = 1\\), \\(p_{luck} = f_d\\) and solving the previous equation for \\(\\alpha\\), we get</p> <p>Skill Coefficient</p> <p>The value of \\(\\alpha_d\\) therefore gives us a measure of the observed skill normalized against the background success rate provided by luck \\(f_d\\).</p> \\[ \\alpha_d \\stackrel{\\mathsf{def}}{=}\\frac{f_d^{obs} - f_d} {1 - f_d} \\] <p>Skill Coefficient Set</p> <p>We denote the set of \\(\\alpha_d\\) values for a given history as \\(\\alpha_\\mathbb{D}\\). When we refer to the \\(\\alpha_d\\) coefficient for a specific \\(d\\) we will use the specific ordering as the subscript, for example: \\(\\alpha_{\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{P}}\\).</p> \\[ \\alpha_\\mathbb{D} \\stackrel{\\mathsf{def}}{=}\\{ \\alpha_d : d \\in \\mathbb{D} \\} \\] <p>The concept embodied by \\(f_d\\) is founded on the idea that if attackers and defenders are in a state of equilibrium, the frequency of observed outcomes (i.e., how often each desiderata \\(d\\) and history \\(h\\) actually occurs) will appear consistent with those predicted by chance. So another way of interpreting \\(\\alpha_d\\) is as a measure of the degree to which a set of observed histories is out of equilibrium.</p> <p>Interpreting \\(\\alpha_d\\) Behavior</p> <p>The following are a few comments on how \\(\\alpha_d\\) behaves. Note that \\(\\alpha_d &lt; 0\\) when \\(0 \\leq f_d^{obs} &lt; f_d\\) and \\(0 \\leq \\alpha_d \\leq 1\\) when \\(f_d \\leq f_d^{obs} \\leq 1\\). The implication is that a negative value for \\(\\alpha_d\\) indicates that our observed outcomes are actually worse than those predicted by pure luck. In other words, we can only infer positive skill when the observations are higher (\\(f_d^{obs} &gt; f_d\\)). That makes intuitive sense: if you are likely to win purely by chance, then you have to attribute most of your wins to luck rather than skill. From the event frequency table above, the largest value for any \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\) is \\(f_{\\mathbf{V} \\prec \\mathbf{A}}=0.75\\), implying that even if a vendor knows about 7 out of 10 vulnerabilities before attacks occur (\\(f_{\\mathbf{V} \\prec \\mathbf{A}}^{obs} = 0.7\\)), they are still not doing better than random.</p> <p>On the other hand, when \\(f_d\\) is small it is easier to infer skill should we observe anything better than \\(f_d\\).
